title: Dred Scott v. Sandford
subtitle: The Supreme Court denies Black citizenship and opens the territories to slavery, 1857
summary: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, and his wife, Harriet, sued for their freedom in 1846 because their enslaver had held them for years at army posts in free territory. After an eleven-year legal struggle, the Supreme Court ruled against them on March 6, 1857. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney declared that people of African descent could not be citizens of the United States, and that Congress had no power to ban slavery from the federal territories, which meant the Missouri Compromise had been unconstitutional. Meant to settle the slavery question, the decision inflamed it and moved the nation closer to civil war. The National Archives notes that many legal scholars consider it the worst decision the Court has ever issued. The Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments overturned it.
thumbAlt: The Supreme Court’s judgment in Dred Scott v. Sandford
aliases: Scott v. Sandford Dred Scott decision Roger Taney Harriet Scott
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Constitution and law Civil rights and citizenship African American history
text: 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857) 7–2 Chief Justice Roger B. Taney Washington, D.C. Suit filed 1846, St. Louis Circuit Court, by Dred and Harriet Scott Basis Years of residence with their enslaver, army surgeon John Emerson, at Fort Snelling in free territory and at Rock Island, Illinois Decided March 6, 1857, two days after James Buchanan’s inauguration Holding Black Americans could not be U.S. citizens; Congress could not bar slavery from the territories Overturned by The Thirteenth (1865) and Fourteenth (1868) Amendments Dred Scott had been held by John Emerson, a U.S. Army surgeon. In the 1830s Emerson took him from Missouri to the army post at Rock Island in the free state of Illinois. From about 1836 to 1838 he held Scott at Fort Snelling, on the west bank of the Mississippi north of 36°30′, where the Missouri Compromise had banned slavery. Harriet was also held there. In 1846 the Scotts sued for their freedom in the St. Louis Circuit Court. They argued that residence in free territory had made them free, and as the National Archives notes, courts had ruled that way in the past. What began as a private lawsuit became an eleven-year struggle. Scott lost in the Missouri courts and then filed a new suit in federal court, which eventually reached the Supreme Court. Along the way slavery became the most explosive issue in American politics. The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which critics exposed as a measure to overturn the Missouri Compromise and open western lands to slavery, had inflamed the question, and by the time the justices heard the case it carried enormous political stakes. Before his inauguration, President-elect James Buchanan learned from members of the Court how they were likely to rule. In his inaugural address on March 4, 1857, he said that the Court was about to decide the question and urged “all good citizens” to accept its ruling. Could a Black man descended from enslaved Africans be a citizen of the United States entitled to sue in federal court? And did Scott’s residence in a free state and a free territory make him free? That raised the further question of whether Congress had the power to prohibit slavery in the territories. By 7 to 2, the Court ruled against Scott. People of African descent, whether enslaved or free, were not and could not be citizens of the United States, so Scott could not sue in federal court. The Missouri Compromise’s ban on slavery north of 36°30′ was unconstitutional, so Scott had not become free by living at Fort Snelling. Chief Justice Taney read the majority opinion on March 6, 1857. He held that people of African descent “are not included, and were not intended to be included, under the word ‘citizens’ in the Constitution.” At the founding, he wrote, they “had for more than a century before been regarded as beings of an inferior order … and so far inferior, that they had no rights which the white man was bound to respect.” The words of the Declaration of Independence, he argued, could not have included “the enslaved African race,” or its signers would have been “utterly and flagrantly inconsistent with the principles they asserted.” Taney then went further. Treating enslaved people as property protected by the Constitution, he concluded that the act of Congress prohibiting slavery “north of the line therein mentioned, is not warranted by the Constitution, and is therefore void.” Neither Scott nor his family had been made free by being taken there. Justices John McLean and Benjamin Curtis dissented. The decision was meant to end the dispute over slavery in the territories. Instead, as the American Yawp puts it, it “seemed to settle the sectional crisis by making slavery fully national, but in reality it just exacerbated sectional tensions further.” Southerners cited it to claim the right to take enslaved people into every territory, while Republicans recognized no such right. Abraham Lincoln answered with his “House Divided” speech in June 1858: “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” In his debates with Lincoln, Stephen Douglas argued that local communities could still keep slavery out by refusing to pass laws to protect it. The National Archives concludes that the ruling “moved the nation a step closer to the Civil War.” For Black Americans, the National Archives notes, the ruling meant that they could expect no protection from the federal government or the courts. The Civil War and Reconstruction undid the decision. The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery, and the Fourteenth (1868) declared that all persons born or naturalized in the United States are citizens. Dred Scott became a byword for judicial error. In 1896 Justice John Marshall Harlan warned in his Plessy v. Ferguson dissent that that decision would “prove to be quite as pernicious as the decision made by this tribunal in the Dred Scott Case.” The sources differ slightly on the scope of Taney’s ruling. The National Archives summarizes it as denying citizenship to enslaved people, while the opinion itself and the American Yawp make clear that it covered all Black Americans, whether enslaved or free. Dred Scott v. Sandford tried to settle the slavery question in the South’s favor by judicial decree. It denied Black Americans any claim to citizenship and declared the federal territories open to slavery. Its failure helped bring on the Civil War and the constitutional amendments that reversed it. They are not included, and were not intended to be included, under the word ‘citizens’ in the Constitution. Chief Justice Roger B. title: Korematsu v. United States
subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds the wartime exclusion of Japanese Americans
summary: Fred Korematsu, a 23-year-old American citizen of Japanese ancestry, refused to leave his home in the San Francisco Bay Area when the Army ordered all Japanese Americans removed under Executive Order 9066. In Korematsu v. United States, the Supreme Court upheld his conviction 6–3, accepting the government’s claim of military necessity. Three justices dissented, one of them condemning the decision as racism. Decades later, evidence that the government had suppressed proof undermining its case led a federal court to overturn Korematsu’s conviction.
thumbAlt: Fred Korematsu
themeText: Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship Constitution and law War and the military
text: 323 U.S. 214 (1944) 6–3 Justice Hugo Black Washington, D.C. Decided December 18, 1944 Vote 6–3 Majority Justice Hugo Black Dissents Justices Owen Roberts, Frank Murphy, and Robert Jackson Conviction vacated November 10, 1983, by federal judge Marilyn Hall Patel After Executive Order 9066, General John L. DeWitt ordered all people of Japanese ancestry out of designated West Coast areas. Korematsu’s parents abandoned their home and flower nursery to report, but he stayed. He changed his name, claimed to be of Spanish and Hawaiian descent, and even had plastic surgery on his eyes to alter his appearance. On May 30, 1942, he was arrested. With the help of the American Civil Liberties Union, he made his case a test of the order’s constitutionality. He was convicted in federal court in San Francisco, given probation, and sent to an assembly center in San Bruno; the appeals court affirmed. Did the president and Congress exceed their war powers by excluding Americans of Japanese descent from the West Coast and restricting their rights? The Court upheld the exclusion order and Korematsu’s conviction by a vote of 6–3. Writing for the majority, Justice Hugo Black held that the order did not reflect racial prejudice but responded to the military imperative of protecting the West Coast from invasion, and that wartime decisions of the military, validated by Congress, deserved great deference. The Court relied heavily on its 1943 decision in Hirabayashi v. United States, which had upheld a curfew. Justice Felix Frankfurter concurred. Three justices dissented. Justice Owen Roberts wrote that Korematsu was being punished for refusing to submit to imprisonment “based on ancestry, and solely because of his ancestry.” Justice Frank Murphy noted that people of German and Italian ancestry had been given individual investigations and hearings, and wrote that “racial discrimination in any form and in any degree has no justifiable part whatever in our democratic way of life.” Justice Robert Jackson warned that by upholding the order, the Court had “validated the principle of racial discrimination,” and he likened the principle of military necessity to “a loaded weapon.” In the early 1980s, newly discovered documents showed that government lawyers had suppressed or destroyed evidence contradicting the claim of military necessity. Korematsu and others filed petitions for a writ of coram nobis, and on November 10, 1983, Judge Marilyn Hall Patel overturned his conviction in the same San Francisco courthouse where he had been convicted. The federal Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians concluded in its report Personal Justice Denied that Korematsu “lies overruled in the court of history.” The 1983 ruling cleared Korematsu’s own conviction in a lower court; it did not by itself reverse the Supreme Court’s 1944 decision. Korematsu shows how courts can fail to protect constitutional rights in wartime, and Fred Korematsu’s long fight to clear his name became a symbol of resistance to injustice. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rRiHumq_wdI When the Supreme Court Justified Japanese Internment Camps | Korematsu v. title: Loving v. Virginia
subtitle: The Supreme Court strikes down bans on interracial marriage, 1967
summary: Mildred Jeter, a woman of African American and Native descent, and Richard Loving, a white man, married in Washington, D.C., in 1958 and went home to Caroline County, Virginia. There they were arrested and convicted under the state’s ban on interracial marriage and ordered to leave Virginia for twenty-five years. In Loving v. Virginia (1967) a unanimous Supreme Court struck down the law, holding that it violated both the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. “Under our Constitution, the freedom to marry, or not marry, a person of another race resides with the individual and cannot be infringed by the State,” Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote. The decision ended such bans in Virginia and the fifteen other states that still had them.
thumbAlt: Mildred and Richard Loving
aliases: Richard Loving Mildred Loving Racial Integrity Act antimiscegenation laws interracial marriage
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship Constitution and law African American history
text: 388 U.S. 1 (1967) 9–0 Chief Justice Earl Warren Washington, D.C.; Caroline County, Virginia Parties Richard and Mildred Loving against the Commonwealth of Virginia Lawyers Bernard S. Cohen and Philip J. Hirschkop, for the ACLU Argued April 10, 1967 Laws struck down Virginia’s ban on interracial marriage, part of a scheme dating from the Racial Integrity Act of 1924, and similar laws in 15 other states Clauses Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment Virginia had regulated interracial marriage since 1691. In 1849 it declared marriages between whites and African Americans “absolutely void,” and in 1878 it made both partners liable to two to five years in the penitentiary. The laws existed because such marriages kept happening. In 1924, amid a eugenics movement that taught that races should not mix, the General Assembly passed the Act to Preserve Racial Integrity. It defined a white person as someone with “no trace whatsoever of any blood other than Caucasian,” with an exception for those who counted Pocahontas among their ancestors, and it barred white people from marrying anyone but white people. The Supreme Court had refused to hear earlier challenges. In 1883, in Pace v. Alabama, it held that a law that punished both races equally did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Richard Loving, born in 1933, was a white construction worker from Central Point in Caroline County. Mildred Jeter, born in 1939 in the same community, was of African American and Native ancestry, and later in life identified herself as Indian. They married in Washington, D.C., on June 2, 1958, and moved in with her parents. In July the county prosecutor obtained warrants. A few days later, in the early morning, the sheriff and two deputies broke into the couple’s bedroom. “They asked Richard who was that woman he was sleeping with,” Mildred Loving recalled. “I said, ‘I’m his wife,’ and the sheriff said, ‘Not here you’re not.’” They were indicted in October 1958. On January 6, 1959, Judge Leon M. Bazile sentenced each of them to a year in jail, suspended on condition that they leave Virginia and not return together for twenty-five years. The Supreme Court’s opinion says they pleaded guilty; Encyclopedia Virginia adds that they first pleaded not guilty and changed their pleas at the end of the arguments. The Lovings moved to Washington. Mildred came back alone to Central Point to give birth to their children. In 1963 she wrote to Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, who referred her to the American Civil Liberties Union. “I wasn’t in anything concerning civil rights,” she said later. “We were trying to get back to Virginia. That was our goal, to get back home.” Does a state law that forbids and punishes marriages between people solely because of their race violate the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment? The ACLU lawyers Bernard Cohen and Philip Hirschkop asked Judge Bazile to set aside the conviction in November 1963. He refused on January 22, 1965, in an opinion declaring that “Almighty God created the races white, black, yellow, malay and red, and he placed them on separate continents… The fact that he separated the races shows that he did not intend for the races to mix.” Hirschkop later said the judge “couldn’t have done us a bigger favor.” On March 7, 1966, the Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia upheld the law, though it found the order to leave the state unreasonable. The U.S. Supreme Court heard argument on April 10, 1967. Virginia argued that the law protected the state from the “sociological [and] psychological evils” of interracial marriage. Hirschkop called the statutes “slavery laws, pure and simple.” Cohen told the Court what Richard Loving had told him: “Mr. Cohen, tell the Court I love my wife and it is just unfair that I can’t live with her in Virginia.” On June 12, 1967, the Court ruled unanimously for the Lovings. Chief Justice Warren wrote that the statutes “cannot stand consistently with the Fourteenth Amendment.” The Court reversed the convictions on two separate grounds: equal protection and due process. Equal protection. Virginia argued that its law was not discriminatory because it punished the white and the Black partner equally. The Court rejected this “equal application” theory. Racial classifications, especially in criminal laws, demanded “the most rigid scrutiny.” The Court found “patently no legitimate overriding purpose independent of invidious racial discrimination.” The fact that Virginia banned only marriages involving white people showed that the law was designed “to maintain White Supremacy.” The Court also noted that the Virginia court’s earlier defense of the law, in Naim v. Naim (1955), spoke of preventing “a mongrel breed of citizens,” which Warren called “obviously an endorsement of the doctrine of White Supremacy.” Due process. The Court also held that marriage “is one of the ‘basic civil rights of man,’ fundamental to our very existence and survival.” To deny it “on so unsupportable a basis as the racial classifications embodied in these statutes” was “surely to deprive all the State’s citizens of liberty without due process of law.” The National Constitution Center describes the decision as an expansion of the Court’s reading of the Equal Protection Clause. The ruling ended laws against interracial marriage in Virginia and the fifteen other states that still had them; Maryland had repealed its law while the case was pending. In August 1967 the Associated Press reported the first known interracial wedding in Virginia since the decision, in Norfolk. On the day of the ruling Mildred Loving told reporters, “I feel free now.” The couple, who had avoided publicity throughout, built a house in Central Point. Richard Loving was killed by a drunk driver in 1975. Mildred Loving died in 2008. Encyclopedia Virginia writes that the case laid the legal basis for a cultural redefinition of marriage, and that over time marriages between white and Black Americans became both more common and more accepted. The National Constitution Center notes that the holding expanded the Court’s reading of the Equal Protection Clause, and its description of marriage as a fundamental freedom protected by due process became an important precedent. Loving v. Virginia swept away the last legal bans on interracial marriage, which had deep roots in slavery, and showed how two people who simply wanted to live at home together could change constitutional law. Under our Constitution, the freedom to marry, or not marry, a person of another race resides with the individual, and cannot be infringed by the State. title: Marbury v. Madison
subtitle: The case in which the Supreme Court first struck down an act of Congress
summary: In Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall turned a small dispute over an undelivered commission into the foundation of American judicial power. The Court ruled that William Marbury had a right to his appointment as a justice of the peace, but that it could not order the commission delivered, because the part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that gave it that power conflicted with the Constitution. It was the first time the Supreme Court declared an act of Congress unconstitutional. In doing so it asserted the power of judicial review, the authority to decide whether laws conform to the Constitution, which the Constitution itself nowhere spells out.

text: 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803) 4–0 Chief Justice John Marshall Washington, D.C. Parties William Marbury, appointed a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia, against James Madison, Secretary of State Justices Marshall, Paterson, Chase, and Washington in the majority; Cushing and Moore took no part Law struck down Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, insofar as it let the Court issue writs of mandamus in its original jurisdiction Next federal law struck down Not until Dred Scott v. Sandford in 1857 Famous line “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” The case grew out of the bitter transfer of power after the election of 1800, when Thomas Jefferson’s Republicans defeated John Adams and the Federalists. Just before Jefferson’s inauguration, the lame-duck Federalist Congress passed the Judiciary Act of 1801, which created new courts and judgeships, and Adams filled them with Federalists, the so-called midnight appointees. One was William Marbury, a wealthy Washington land speculator named a justice of the peace in the last hours of the Adams administration. His commission was signed and sealed but not delivered before Adams left office. Jefferson’s Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to deliver it. Radical Republicans pressed Jefferson to make war on the Federalist judiciary. In 1802 the Republican Congress repealed the Judiciary Act of 1801, abolishing the new judgeships, and the House later impeached Justice Samuel Chase, a fierce anti-Jeffersonian, though the Senate did not convict him. Marbury asked the Supreme Court for a writ of mandamus, a court order compelling Madison to hand over the commission, and the Court ordered Madison to show cause why it should not issue. The case put the Court, led by Chief Justice John Marshall, a Federalist and a recent Adams appointee, in a delicate position. Marshall framed three questions: Does Marbury have a right to the commission he demands? If he has a right, and that right has been violated, do the laws of his country afford him a remedy? If they do, is it a mandamus issuing from the Supreme Court? The third question raised a deeper one: “whether an act, repugnant to the constitution, can become the law of the land.” The Court held unanimously that Marbury had a right to his commission. In Marshall’s words, a commission “is complete, when the seal of the United States has been affixed to it by the secretary of state,” so withholding it violated “a vested legal right.” The laws gave him a remedy, because the government of the United States “has been emphatically termed a government of laws, and not of men,” and it would not deserve that name “if the laws furnish no remedy for the violation of a vested legal right.” Marshall drew a line between the president’s political powers, which no court could control, and specific duties assigned to an officer by law, on which individual rights depended. But the Court could not issue the writ. Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 authorized it to issue writs of mandamus “to any courts appointed, or persons holding office, under the authority of the United States.” Article III, however, gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction only in cases “affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a state shall be a party,” and appellate jurisdiction in all others. Ordering an officer to deliver a paper, Marshall reasoned, amounted to an original action, not an appeal. Congress could not add to the Court’s original jurisdiction by ordinary law, so that part of the act was “not warranted by the constitution,” and Marbury’s petition failed. The Miller Center summarizes the holding more broadly, as a ruling that the Constitution did not give the Supreme Court the power to issue such writs. Marshall then explained why the Court could refuse to apply an unconstitutional law. The people had an “original right” to establish the principles of their government, and having done so in a written constitution, they meant those principles to be “fundamental” and “permanent.” “The powers of the legislature are defined and limited; and that those limits may not be mistaken or forgotten, the constitution is written,” he wrote. Either the Constitution is “a superior, paramount law, unchangeable by ordinary means,” or it is no different from an ordinary act, “alterable when the legislature shall please to alter it.” If the latter, then “written constitutions are absurd attempts on the part of the people to limit a power in its own nature illimitable.” It followed that “an act of the legislature repugnant to the constitution is void,” and that courts could not be bound to enforce it: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. Those who apply the rule to particular cases must, of necessity, expound and interpret that rule.” He added that the Constitution requires judges to take an oath to support it: “Why otherwise does it direct the judges to take an oath to support it?” The National Archives notes that nothing in the Constitution gave the Court this specific power, and that Marshall believed the Court should have a role equal to the other two branches. Politically, Marshall avoided a confrontation the Court could not win. Jefferson’s administration got the result it wanted, since Marbury never received his commission, so there was no order to defy. Yet the Court claimed a far larger power for itself. The Republican Congress, the Miller Center notes, preferred to repeal the Judiciary Act of 1801 rather than challenge Marshall head on, and Jefferson, who admired Marshall’s intelligence, sided with moderates who did not see an independent judiciary as a threat to republican liberty. The Court did not strike down another act of Congress until Dred Scott in 1857. Over time Marbury became the cornerstone of judicial review. The National Archives writes that the decision completed the “triangular structure of checks and balances,” and that the Court’s power “to invalidate federal and state laws that are contrary to the Constitution has never been seriously challenged.” The sources describe Marshall’s achievement in slightly different words: the National Archives says the case “established” the principle of judicial review, while the National Constitution Center’s summary says the decision “confirmed” it, a difference that reflects a long debate over whether judicial review was already accepted before 1803 or was Marshall’s creation. Marbury v. Madison made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch with the power to measure laws against the Constitution. Later landmark decisions on federal power and individual rights rest on the authority it asserted. It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. title: McCulloch v. Maryland
subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds broad federal power and bars states from taxing the national bank
summary: When Maryland taxed the Baltimore branch of the Second Bank of the United States, the bank’s cashier, James W. McCulloch, refused to pay. On March 6, 1819, the Supreme Court, speaking through Chief Justice John Marshall, ruled that Congress had the implied power to charter a bank under the Constitution’s “necessary and proper” clause. It also ruled that states could not tax the federal government, because “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” The decision became a cornerstone of national power and of American federalism.
thumbAlt: Page from the Supreme Court’s decision in McCulloch v. Maryland
aliases: McCulloch Necessary and proper clause Elastic clause Implied powers Second Bank of the United States The power to tax involves the power to destroy
themeText: Constitution and law Economy and finance
text: 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819) Unanimous (6–0) Chief Justice John Marshall Washington, D.C. Parties James W. McCulloch, cashier of the Baltimore branch of the Second Bank of the United States, v. the State of Maryland Argued February 22 to March 3, 1819 Decided March 6, 1819, unanimously Clause at issue The necessary and proper clause (Article I, Section 8), the “elastic clause” Famous lines “The power to tax involves the power to destroy”; “we must never forget that it is a constitution we are expounding” Whether Congress could create a national bank had divided the founders. In 1791 Alexander Hamilton’s plan for a Bank of the United States won congressional approval over strong opposition: Jefferson and other Republicans argued that “the Constitution did not authorize Congress to create a bank,” while Hamilton argued it was both constitutional and important for the country’s prosperity. The Constitution Center’s commentary adds that Madison and Jefferson feared a bank would serve Northern merchants and create “a financial aristocracy.” The First Bank’s twenty-year charter expired in 1811. In 1816 Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States to help control the unregulated currency issued by state banks. Many states doubted its constitutionality, and in 1818 Maryland passed a law taxing all banks not chartered by the state, which in practice meant the national bank’s Baltimore branch. Its cashier refused to pay, and Maryland sued him. Does the Constitution give Congress the power to create a bank? If so, may a state tax that bank? Beneath both, the National Archives notes, lay a larger question: “Does the Federal Government hold sovereign power over states?” The Court held that Congress had the power to incorporate the bank, and that Maryland could not tax an instrument the national government used to carry out its constitutional powers. Maryland’s tax was unconstitutional. Implied powers. Marshall admitted that among the enumerated powers “we do not find that of establishing a bank or creating a corporation.” But unlike the Articles of Confederation, the Constitution contains no phrase excluding “incidental or implied powers.” A constitution that tried to list every means of government “would partake of the prolixity of a legal code, and could scarcely be embraced by the human mind.” Hence his most quoted line: “we must never forget that it is a constitution we are expounding.” It was “intended to endure for ages to come, and consequently, to be adapted to the various crises of human affairs.” Necessary and proper. The clause lets Congress choose its means: “Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the constitution, are constitutional.” Supremacy. The government of the Union, “though limited in its powers, is supreme within its sphere of action.” So a state could not tax it: “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” If states could tax one federal instrument, Marshall warned, “they may tax the mail; they may tax the mint,” and the people “did not design to make their government dependent on the states.” The decision secured the Second Bank, but not for long. Andrew Jackson, who blamed the bank for the Panic of 1819, vetoed its recharter in 1832, calling it unconstitutional and “dangerous to the liberties of the people.” In that veto he rejected the idea that the Court had settled the matter: “The Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution,” and “the opinion of the judges has no more authority over Congress than the opinion of Congress has over the judges.” McCulloch is regarded as one of the most important decisions in American constitutional history. Its broad reading of implied powers gave Congress wide latitude to choose how to exercise its powers and confirmed that states could not interfere with legitimate federal operations. The balance between national authority and states’ rights that it addressed, which Marshall himself predicted “will probably continue to arise, so long as our system shall exist,” has remained contested ever since. McCulloch v. Maryland established that the federal government has powers implied by, but not listed in, the Constitution, and that federal law prevails over conflicting state action. Those principles lie at the heart of American federalism. The lawyers The case was argued for nine days, from February 22 to March 3, 1819, by some of the most famous lawyers of the age. Daniel Webster, the attorney general and William Pinkney argued for the bank; Joseph Hopkinson, Walter Jones and Maryland’s attorney general, Luther Martin, for the state. We must never forget that it is a constitution we are expounding. John Marshall McCulloch v. Maryland, 1819 The power to tax involves the power to destroy. John Marshall McCulloch v. title: Miranda v. Arizona
subtitle: The ruling that requires police to warn suspects of their rights
summary: In Miranda v. Arizona (1966) the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that the Fifth Amendment’s privilege against self-incrimination applies when police question a suspect in custody. Writing for the Court, Chief Justice Earl Warren held that before questioning, a person must be warned “that he has a right to remain silent, that any statement he does make may be used as evidence against him, and that he has a right to the presence of an attorney, either retained or appointed.” Statements taken without these safeguards could not be used in court. The “Miranda warnings” became a routine part of American policing, and in 2000 the Court declined to overrule the decision.
thumbAlt: Document from Miranda v. Arizona signed by Chief Justice Earl Warren
aliases: Miranda warnings Miranda rights right to remain silent custodial interrogation Dickerson v. United States Escobedo v. Illinois
themeText: Constitution and law Civil rights and citizenship
text: 384 U.S. 436 (1966) 5–4 Chief Justice Earl Warren Washington, D.C.; Phoenix, Arizona Argued February 28 to March 2, 1966 Decided June 13, 1966 Cases decided together Miranda v. Arizona, Vignera v. New York, Westover v. United States, California v. Stewart Dissenters Justices Tom Clark, John Marshall Harlan, Potter Stewart, and Byron White Rule Warnings required before custodial interrogation Reaffirmed Dickerson v. United States, June 26, 2000 For decades the Court had judged confessions by asking whether they were voluntary, looking at the “totality of circumstances” in each case. In Escobedo v. Illinois (1964) it had reversed a conviction where police questioned a man at a station without effectively advising him of his right to remain silent or to consult his lawyer, and Miranda was meant to give “concrete constitutional guidelines for law enforcement agencies and courts to follow.” The case was part of what the National Constitution Center calls the Warren Court’s “revolution in criminal procedure,” along with Gideon v. Wainwright and Mapp v. Ohio. The Court decided four cases together. In each, a suspect was questioned in a room “cut off from the outside world” and was not given “a full and effective warning of his rights at the outset.” On March 13, 1963, Ernesto Miranda was arrested at his home and taken to a Phoenix police station, where the complaining witness identified him. Two officers took him to “Interrogation Room No. 2” of the detective bureau. They admitted at trial that they had not told him he had a right to have a lawyer present. Two hours later they came out with a written confession. A typed paragraph at the top said it was made “with full knowledge of my legal rights.” Miranda was convicted of kidnapping and rape and sentenced to 20 to 30 years on each count. The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed, stressing that he had not specifically asked for a lawyer. Does the Fifth Amendment’s privilege against self-incrimination apply when police question a suspect in custody, and if so, what must police do to protect it? The Court held that the prosecution “may not use statements, whether exculpatory or inculpatory, stemming from custodial interrogation of the defendant unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards effective to secure the privilege against self-incrimination.” By custodial interrogation it meant “questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of his freedom of action in any significant way.” Before questioning, the person must be told of the right to remain silent, that any statement may be used as evidence, and of the right to a lawyer, “either retained or appointed.” A suspect may waive these rights, but only “voluntarily, knowingly and intelligently,” and a “heavy burden” rests on the government to prove it. If the suspect “indicates in any manner and at any stage” that he wants a lawyer, “there can be no questioning.” The convictions of Miranda, Vignera, and Westover were reversed. In the fourth case the Court affirmed the California Supreme Court, which had already overturned Stewart’s conviction. The interrogation room. Warren drew on police training manuals to show that modern questioning was “psychologically rather than physically oriented.” The manuals advised keeping the suspect “off balance” and even conceding the right to silence as a tactic to win his trust. Even without violence, he wrote, “the very fact of custodial interrogation exacts a heavy toll on individual liberty and trades on the weakness of individuals.” The records in the four cases showed no “overt physical coercion,” but none of the suspects had been given safeguards to make sure their statements “were truly the product of free choice.” A simple, uniform rule. The privilege was “so fundamental” and a warning “so simple” that the Court would not ask in each case whether the defendant already knew his rights. Warren noted that the FBI already warned suspects that they could say nothing and could have a lawyer, and he cited its “exemplary record of effective law enforcement.” He wrote that the decision was “not intended to hamper the traditional function of police officers,” and that general questioning at a crime scene was not affected. The dissents. Justice Clark dissented in three of the cases and concurred in the result in the fourth. He wrote that the majority went “too far on too little” and would have kept a case-by-case test of voluntariness. Justice Harlan, joined by Stewart and White, called the decision “poor constitutional law” with “harmful consequences for the country at large.” Justice White, joined by Harlan and Stewart, found “no significant support” for the rule in the history of the privilege. He warned that in some cases it would “return a killer, a rapist or other criminal to the streets.” Warnings modeled on the decision became standard in police stations across the country. Their wording is so familiar that the Court later called the warnings “part of our national culture.” Critics kept arguing that the rule let guilty people go free. Soon after the decision, Congress passed a law, 18 U.S.C. § 3501, that made the admissibility of a confession in federal court depend only on whether it was voluntary. The conflict came to a head in Dickerson v. United States. A federal appeals court held that Miranda was not a constitutional rule and that the statute controlled. On June 26, 2000, the Supreme Court reversed by 7 to 2. Chief Justice William Rehnquist wrote that “Miranda, being a constitutional decision of this Court, may not be in effect overruled by an Act of Congress, and we decline to overrule Miranda ourselves.” He added that Miranda “has become embedded in routine police practice to the point where the warnings have become part of our national culture,” and that later cases had “reduced Miranda’s impact on legitimate law enforcement while reaffirming the decision’s core ruling.” Justice Antonin Scalia, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented. Miranda v. Arizona turned the privilege against self-incrimination into a concrete routine that applies at the moment a person is most exposed to the power of the state. It remains one of the best known decisions of the Warren Court and a lasting point of debate about how to balance individual rights against effective law enforcement. Prior to any questioning, the person must be warned that he has a right to remain silent, that any statement he does make may be used as evidence against him, and that he has a right to the presence of an attorney, either retained or appointed. Chief Justice Earl Warren opinion of the Court, June 13, 1966 Even without employing brutality, the ‘third degree’ or the specific stratagems described above, the very fact of custodial interrogation exacts a heavy toll on individual liberty and trades on the weakness of individuals. Chief Justice Earl Warren opinion of the Court I believe the decision of the Court represents poor constitutional law and entails harmful consequences for the country at large. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissent, joined by Justices Stewart and White Miranda has become embedded in routine police practice to the point where the warnings have become part of our national culture. title: Plessy v. Ferguson
subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds “separate but equal,” 1896
summary: In 1892 Homer Plessy, a New Orleans man who was seven-eighths white, deliberately sat in a whites-only railroad car to challenge Louisiana’s law requiring segregated trains. On May 18, 1896, the Supreme Court upheld the law by 7 to 1, ruling that “equal but separate” accommodations did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented alone, declaring that “our constitution is color-blind.” The decision gave constitutional approval to the Jim Crow system of segregation for more than half a century, until Brown v. Board of Education rejected it in 1954.
thumbAlt: The Supreme Court’s judgment in Plessy v. Ferguson
aliases: separate but equal Separate Car Act Homer Plessy Harlan dissent color-blind Constitution
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship Constitution and law African American history
text: 163 U.S. 537 (1896) 7–1 Justice Henry Billings Brown Washington, D.C. Law challenged Louisiana’s 1890 Separate Car Act: separate or partitioned coaches; $25 fine or 20 days in jail for violators Test case Organized by the New Orleans Citizens’ Committee; Plessy arrested June 7, 1892 Lawyer Albion W. Tourgée Decided May 18, 1896, by 7 to 1; Justice Henry Brown for the majority Dissent Justice John Marshall Harlan of Kentucky, alone Overruled in effect Brown v. Board of Education (1954), for public schools During Reconstruction, three constitutional amendments and a series of federal laws affirmed Black Americans’ rights. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 made it a crime to deny anyone “the full and equal enjoyment” of inns, public conveyances, and theaters. In 1883 the Supreme Court struck down that act, ruling that the Fourteenth Amendment did not give Congress power to stop discrimination by private individuals and leaving Black citizens to seek relief from the states. At the same time, Southern states were writing inequality into law. Separate schools came first, and segregation soon spread to most public facilities. From the early 1890s these states also used literacy tests and “grandfather clauses” to take the vote from Black men. Railroads were a key battleground. Beginning with an 1887 Florida law, states required separate cars for each race. When a bill was proposed in Louisiana in 1890, the Black community of New Orleans protested, but the law passed despite the presence of sixteen Black legislators. It required separate or partitioned coaches and punished passengers who sat in the wrong section with a $25 fine or twenty days in jail. Black nurses caring for white children, however, could ride in white compartments. The railroads themselves disliked the law because of the cost of adding cars. In 1891 young Black men in New Orleans formed the “Citizens’ Committee to Test the Constitutionality of the Separate Car Law” and hired Albion W. Tourgée, a Radical Republican writer and politician, as their lawyer. After the Louisiana Supreme Court ruled in May 1892 that the law could not be applied to interstate travel, the committee arranged a test case on a trip within the state. With the cooperation of the East Louisiana Railroad, on June 7, 1892, Homer Plessy took a seat in a white compartment, was challenged by the conductor, and was arrested. Judge John H. Ferguson of the Orleans Parish criminal court ruled against him, and the Louisiana Supreme Court upheld the law but allowed an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. (The American Yawp describes Plessy’s challenge as aimed at the segregation of streetcars. The National Archives’ account describes railroad coaches.) Does a state law requiring separate railway accommodations for white and Black passengers violate the Thirteenth Amendment’s ban on slavery or the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of the equal protection of the laws? By a vote of 7 to 1, the Court upheld the Louisiana law. As long as the separate accommodations were equal, segregation did not violate the Constitution. Justice Henry Brown of Michigan wrote for the majority. He argued that “social prejudice” could not be overcome by legislation and that, if the civil and political rights of both races were equal, neither could be inferior to the other civilly or politically. He rejected the argument that segregation was a mark of inferiority: “We consider the underlying fallacy of the plaintiff’s argument to consist in the assumption that the enforced separation of the two races stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority. If this be so, it is not by reason of anything found in the act, but solely because the colored race chooses to put that construction upon it.” “If one race be inferior to the other socially,” he concluded, “the Constitution of the United States cannot put them upon the same plane.” Justice John Marshall Harlan of Kentucky dissented alone. “In the eye of the law, there is in this country no superior, dominant, ruling class of citizens. There is no caste here. Our constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.” He warned that the law put “the brand of servitude and degradation upon a large class of our fellow citizens,” that “the thin disguise of ‘equal’ accommodations for passengers in railroad coaches will not mislead any one,” and that the decision would “prove to be quite as pernicious as the decision made by this tribunal in the Dred Scott Case.” Plessy gave constitutional approval to the Jim Crow system. Segregation, already spreading, now extended to schools, transportation, and most public and semi-public places across the South, and for more than fifty years the great majority of African Americans lived under what the National Archives calls “second-class citizenship.” Just one year before the decision, Booker T. Washington had told white Southerners in his Atlanta speech that “in all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers.” The NAACP spent decades attacking “separate but equal.” In 1930 it commissioned the Margold Report, which became the basis for its legal campaign against the doctrine. On May 17, 1954, in Brown v. Board of Education, a unanimous Court under Chief Justice Earl Warren held that segregated public schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment. “We cannot turn the clock back to 1868, when the Amendment was adopted, or even to 1896, when Plessy v. Ferguson was written,” the Court said, and “any language in Plessy v. Ferguson contrary to this finding is rejected.” After Brown and the civil rights laws of the 1950s and 1960s, many states rewrote their constitutions to conform with the spirit of the Fourteenth Amendment. “For Homer Plessy,” the National Archives notes, “the remedies came too late.” Plessy v. Ferguson made segregation constitutional law, shaping American life until the civil rights movement and Brown dismantled it. Our constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissent, Plessy v. Ferguson, 1896 If one race be inferior to the other socially, the Constitution of the United States cannot put them upon the same plane. title: Roe v. Wade
subtitle: The Supreme Court recognizes a constitutional right to abortion, 1973
summary: In Roe v. Wade (1973) the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that a Texas law banning abortion except to save the mother’s life violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Writing for the Court, Justice Harry Blackmun held that the constitutional right of privacy “is broad enough to encompass a woman’s decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy,” but that the right was “not unqualified” and had to be weighed against the state’s interests in health and in “potential life.” The Court set out a framework based on the trimesters of pregnancy. Roe became one of the most debated decisions in American history. The Court modified it in 1992 and overruled it in 2022, returning the question to the states.

text: 410 U.S. 113 (1973) 7–2 Justice Harry Blackmun Washington, D.C.; Dallas County, Texas Parties “Jane Roe,” a pregnant single woman in Dallas County, against Henry Wade, the county district attorney Argued December 1971; reargued October 1972 Majority Blackmun, joined by Burger, Douglas, Brennan, Stewart, Marshall, and Powell Dissent Justices Byron White and William Rehnquist Companion case Doe v. Bolton, on Georgia’s abortion law Overruled Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, June 24, 2022 Texas first made abortion a crime in 1854. Its law, which had remained substantially unchanged since 1857, allowed an abortion only “by medical advice for the purpose of saving the life of the mother,” and similar laws existed in a majority of states. By the early 1970s some states, such as Georgia, had adopted more modern laws, which the Court described as reflecting “recent attitudinal change” and “new thinking about an old issue.” The Court’s decision built on earlier rulings that recognized a constitutional “right to privacy,” among them a 1965 case striking down a Connecticut law that banned married couples from using birth control. In March 1970 a single woman living in Dallas County, using the pseudonym Jane Roe, sued the county district attorney, Henry Wade. She said she was unmarried and pregnant, could not get a legal abortion in Texas because her life was not in danger, and could not afford to travel to another state. A doctor facing prosecution under the law, and a married couple, joined the challenge. A three-judge federal court ruled the Texas law unconstitutional, and Texas appealed. The Court held that her case was not moot even though her 1970 pregnancy had ended. Does the Constitution protect a woman’s decision to end a pregnancy, and if so, how far may a state restrict or forbid abortion? The Court held that a law like Texas’s, which allowed abortion only to save the mother’s life “without regard to pregnancy stage and without recognition of the other interests involved,” violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. It then set out a framework. Before about the end of the first trimester, the decision had to be left to “the medical judgment of the pregnant woman’s attending physician.” After the first trimester, the state could regulate abortion “in ways that are reasonably related to maternal health.” After viability, the state could “regulate, and even proscribe, abortion except where it is necessary… for the preservation of the life or health of the mother.” The vote was 7 to 2. Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Douglas and Stewart wrote concurrences, and Justices Byron White and William Rehnquist dissented. The right of privacy. Blackmun acknowledged that the Constitution does not mention a right of privacy, but he wrote that the Court had found its roots in the First, Fourth, Fifth, Ninth, and Fourteenth Amendments, and that it covered matters of marriage, procreation, contraception, family, and child rearing. That right, “whether it be founded in the Fourteenth Amendment’s concept of personal liberty… or… in the Ninth Amendment,” was “broad enough to encompass a woman’s decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy.” He pointed to the medical, psychological, and social harms that denying the choice could impose. State interests. The Court rejected the idea that the right was absolute. The state had legitimate interests “in safeguarding health, in maintaining medical standards, and in protecting potential life,” and those interests grew stronger as pregnancy advanced, becoming “compelling” at different points. The Court concluded that “the right of personal privacy includes the abortion decision, but that this right is not unqualified and must be considered against important state interests in regulation.” The dissents. Justice Rehnquist argued that an abortion performed by a doctor was not “private” in the ordinary meaning of the word. He noted that at least 36 state and territorial laws restricted abortion when the Fourteenth Amendment was adopted in 1868, and he concluded that its framers had not meant to take that power from the states. Justice White also dissented. The ruling made the abortion decision a matter of federal constitutional rights, and laws like the Texas statute could no longer stand. The American Yawp writes that Roe and another 1973 ruling “established the battle lines for the ‘sex wars’ of the 1970s,” and abortion became one of the most divisive issues in American politics. In Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) the Court reaffirmed what it called Roe’s “essential holding,” the right to choose abortion before viability. But it rejected the trimester framework and replaced it with an “undue burden” test, under which a law was invalid if it placed “substantial obstacles in the path of a woman seeking an abortion before the fetus attains viability.” On June 24, 2022, in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, a case about a Mississippi law banning most abortions after fifteen weeks, the Court overruled Roe and Casey. Writing for a majority of five, Justice Samuel Alito held that “the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion” and that the right was not “deeply rooted in this Nation’s history and tradition.” He called Roe “egregiously wrong from the start” and returned the authority to regulate abortion “to the people and their elected representatives.” Chief Justice John Roberts concurred in the judgment, and Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan dissented. Roe v. Wade made the right to abortion a question of constitutional law for half a century and shaped American politics, elections, and Supreme Court nominations. Its overruling in 2022 returned the issue to the states and remains fiercely debated. This right of privacy… is broad enough to encompass a woman’s decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy. Justice Harry Blackmun opinion of the Court, January 22, 1973 We, therefore, conclude that the right of personal privacy includes the abortion decision, but that this right is not unqualified and must be considered against important state interests in regulation. title: Schenck v. United States
subtitle: Free speech in wartime and the “clear and present danger” test, 1919
summary: During World War I, socialists Charles Schenck and Elizabeth Baer mailed leaflets urging men to resist the draft, which they called involuntary servitude. Convicted under the Espionage Act, they argued that the law violated the First Amendment. In 1919 a unanimous Supreme Court upheld their convictions. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes introduced the “clear and present danger” test and compared their leaflets to falsely shouting “fire” in a crowded theater.
thumbAlt: The antidraft leaflet distributed by Charles Schenck
themeText: Constitution and law War and the military Civil rights and citizenship
text: 249 U.S. 47 (1919) 9–0 Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. Washington, D.C. Law Espionage Act of 1917 Defendants Charles Schenck and Elizabeth Baer, Socialist Party officials Test announced “Clear and present danger” Later fate Narrowed in later decisions, especially Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) When the United States entered World War I in 1917, the Wilson administration sponsored the Espionage and Sedition Acts, which outlawed criticism of the government, the armed forces, and the war effort. The government imprisoned or fined violators and even censored or banned mainstream publications. Schenck and Baer, of the Socialist Party in Philadelphia, distributed leaflets declaring that the draft violated the Thirteenth Amendment’s ban on involuntary servitude and urging the public to oppose it, though by peaceful means. Did Schenck’s conviction under the Espionage Act for distributing leaflets opposing the draft violate his First Amendment right to freedom of speech? No. The Court unanimously held that the Espionage Act, as applied, did not violate the First Amendment and was an appropriate exercise of Congress’s wartime authority. Justice Holmes reasoned that the character of every act depends on the circumstances, and that courts owe greater deference to the government in wartime. Articulating the “clear and present danger” test for the first time, he concluded that the First Amendment does not protect speech that creates a clear and present danger of bringing about substantive evils that Congress has the power to prevent. The widespread distribution of the leaflets, he reasoned, was sufficiently likely to obstruct recruitment. Free speech, he wrote, would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theater and causing a panic. Schenck upheld the government’s wartime prosecutions of dissenters, including socialists and pacifists. Within months, in Abrams v. United States (1919), Holmes himself dissented from another conviction, beginning to reinterpret the test as more protective of speech. The “clear and present danger” test shaped free-speech law for half a century. In Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), the Court adopted a more protective standard: speech can be punished only if it is “directed at inciting or producing imminent lawless action” and is likely to produce it. Holmes’s “shouting fire in a crowded theater” line is still widely quoted, often as if it stated current law, though the decision that coined it has been superseded. Schenck was the Supreme Court’s first major ruling on the limits of free speech, and the debate it started over speech in times of crisis continues today. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xkGs-Dpaf6w Schenck v. the United States, EXPLAINED [AP Gov Required Supreme Court Cases] Heimler's History 3:32 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gbtrI7rgrjs When Can Speech Be Banned? | Schenck v. title: United States v. Nixon
subtitle: The Supreme Court orders a president to surrender the Watergate tapes, 1974
summary: In United States v. Nixon, decided July 24, 1974, the Supreme Court unanimously rejected President Richard Nixon’s claim that “executive privilege” allowed him to withhold White House tape recordings subpoenaed for the trial of his aides in the Watergate cover-up. The Court recognized that presidents have a real but limited privilege to keep their conversations confidential. It held that a “generalized” claim of confidentiality must yield to the needs of a criminal trial. Among the tapes Nixon was forced to release was the June 23, 1972, “smoking gun,” which proved he had obstructed the FBI’s investigation. Within sixteen days he resigned.
thumbAlt: The edited transcripts of the White House tapes released by Nixon
aliases: executive privilege Watergate tapes smoking gun tape Leon Jaworski unindicted coconspirator
themeText: The presidency Constitution and law
text: 418 U.S. 683 (1974) 8–0 Chief Justice Warren Burger Washington, D.C. Argued July 8, 1974; decided July 24, 1974 Vote 8–0; Justice William Rehnquist took no part Subpoena Issued April 18, 1974, for tapes and documents of precisely identified conversations The underlying case United States v. Mitchell et al., the trial of seven Nixon aides indicted March 1, 1974 Result Nixon released the tapes and resigned August 9, 1974 By 1974 the Watergate scandal had moved from the break-in at the Democratic National Committee to the White House itself. In July 1973 a former aide, Alexander Butterfield, had revealed that Nixon secretly recorded his Oval Office conversations. Nixon refused to turn the tapes over, arguing that the confidentiality of presidential conversations was at stake. In October 1973 he fired the first special prosecutor, Archibald Cox, in the “Saturday Night Massacre,” and public outrage forced him to release some tapes. On March 1, 1974, a federal grand jury indicted seven men, among them former Attorney General John Mitchell and the former White House aides H. R. Haldeman and John Ehrlichman, for conspiracy to defraud the United States and to obstruct justice. The grand jury also named the president as an “unindicted coconspirator.” On April 18 the new special prosecutor, Leon Jaworski, obtained a subpoena ordering Nixon to produce tapes and documents of precisely identified meetings, for use at the trial set for September. The White House instead released more than 1,250 pages of edited transcripts. Nixon’s lawyers moved to quash the subpoena. They claimed an absolute executive privilege and argued that a dispute inside the executive branch was not something a court could decide. When the district court ordered the materials turned over, both sides asked the Supreme Court to hear the case at once, and the justices agreed to hear it before the court of appeals ruled. Does the president have an absolute privilege, rooted in the separation of powers, to withhold confidential communications from a judicial subpoena in a criminal case? And is the courts’ power to decide that question limited by the fact that the special prosecutor worked inside the executive branch? The Court ruled 8 to 0 against the president. Justice William Rehnquist took no part, and Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the opinion. The Court first held that the dispute was a real case the courts could hear, because the Attorney General had given the special prosecutor independent authority by regulation. It then held that the subpoena met the legal requirements and that the tapes probably contained evidence relevant to the charges. On the central question, it held that “neither the doctrine of separation of powers nor the generalized need for confidentiality of high-level communications, without more, can sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances.” The president’s “generalized assertion of privilege must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.” The district court was to review the tapes privately in chambers before passing them to the prosecution. Burger began with Marbury v. Madison. Each branch must interpret the Constitution in its own work, he wrote, but “it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is,” including on a president’s claim of privilege. The judicial power could no more be shared with the executive than the president could share his veto with the courts. The Court did not deny that a privilege existed. A president and his advisers “must be free to explore alternatives in the process of shaping policies and making decisions,” and the privilege was “fundamental to the operation of Government and inextricably rooted in the separation of powers.” But it was presumptive, not absolute. It had to be weighed against “our historic commitment to the rule of law” and the principle that “the public… has a right to every man’s evidence.” The Court noted that Nixon claimed no military, diplomatic, or sensitive national security secrets. He relied only on a general interest in confidentiality, and that interest would not be badly harmed by a private review by a judge. An absolute privilege, by contrast, “would plainly conflict with the function of the courts under Art. III.” Nixon complied. The New York Times, quoted by the Miller Center, wrote that the decision “adds to the feeling that the last act of Richard Nixon’s drama is at hand.” Three days after the ruling, on July 27, the House Judiciary Committee approved the first of three articles of impeachment, for obstruction of justice. The released tapes included Nixon’s June 23, 1972, conversation with H. R. Haldeman, in which he agreed to have the CIA tell the FBI to stop its investigation of the break-in, falsely claiming it would expose CIA secrets. After the transcript was published, Republican leaders in Congress told Nixon they could not protect him from impeachment or conviction. Senator Barry Goldwater said there were at most eighteen senators who might vote to acquit. On August 8 Nixon announced his resignation, which took effect at noon the next day. Mitchell, Haldeman, and Ehrlichman were later convicted and sent to prison. The case remains the leading decision on executive privilege. It confirmed that presidents have a constitutionally based privilege of confidentiality, but that in a criminal case a general claim of confidentiality must give way to specific need. It left open how the balance would come out for military, diplomatic, or national security secrets. It also reaffirmed, in the words of Marbury, that the courts decide what the law is, even against a sitting president. United States v. Nixon showed that the president is not above the law. A unanimous Court ordered him to produce the evidence that ended his presidency. Neither the doctrine of separation of powers, nor the need for confidentiality of high-level communications, without more, can sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances. Chief Justice Warren Burger opinion of the Court, July 24, 1974 The very integrity of the judicial system and public confidence in the system depend on full disclosure of all the facts, within the framework of the rules of evidence. title: Worcester v. Georgia
subtitle: The Supreme Court recognizes Cherokee sovereignty, and the president refuses to enforce it
summary: Samuel Worcester, a missionary living in the Cherokee Nation, was imprisoned by Georgia for refusing to obtain a state license. In 1832 the Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokee Nation was “a distinct community occupying its own territory in which the laws of Georgia can have no force,” and that only the federal government could deal with it. The decision affirmed tribal sovereignty in principle, but Georgia ignored it and President Jackson declined to enforce it, and the Cherokee were forcibly removed six years later.
thumbAlt: First issue of the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper, printed in English and Cherokee
themeText: Indigenous history Constitution and law
text: 31 U.S. (6 Pet.) 515 (1832) 5–1 Chief Justice John Marshall Washington, D.C. Parties Samuel A. Worcester, a missionary, v. the State of Georgia Holding Georgia’s law regulating whites in Cherokee territory violated the Constitution, federal treaties, and federal law Related case Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), in which the Court called tribes “domestic dependent nations” Georgia was determined to take Cherokee land. After the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and the discovery of gold, the state passed laws asserting authority over Cherokee territory, including an 1830 act requiring all white people living there to obtain a state license and swear an oath to Georgia’s laws, a measure aimed at missionaries who supported Cherokee resistance. In 1831 the Cherokee had brought their own suit, Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, but the Court ruled it lacked jurisdiction because a tribe was not a foreign state. Does the state of Georgia have authority to regulate relations between its citizens and members of the Cherokee Nation within Cherokee territory? No. The Court held that the Georgia act under which Worcester was prosecuted violated the Constitution, treaties, and laws of the United States, and was therefore void. Worcester’s conviction was reversed. Justice Henry Baldwin dissented on procedural grounds. Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that U.S. treaties and laws treated Indian territory as completely separate from the states and placed all relations with Native nations in the hands of the federal government. “The Cherokee nation, then, is a distinct community occupying its own territory in which the laws of Georgia can have no force,” he wrote. “The whole intercourse between the United States and this nation, is, by our constitution and laws, vested in the government of the United States.” Georgia’s law interfered with that federal authority. Georgia refused to comply. President Jackson did nothing to enforce the decision; he is reported to have said, “John Marshall has made his decision; let him enforce it now if he can.” Whether or not he used those words, they captured his policy. Without federal protection, the Cherokee were pressured into the Treaty of New Echota and forced west on the Trail of Tears in 1838. Worcester became one of the foundations of federal Indian law. Its principle, that tribes are sovereign nations whose relations are governed by the federal government, not the states, has been cited by courts and tribal governments ever since, including in modern disputes over tribal jurisdiction. At the same time, its failure in 1832 is a lasting lesson in the limits of judicial power when the executive will not act. Worcester v. Georgia recognized Native nations as distinct political communities beyond the reach of state law, a principle that the federal government abandoned in practice in the 1830s but that remains central to tribal sovereignty today. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TwBRrsHAodY When The Supreme Court Tried to Prevent Indian Removal | Worcester v. title: The Articles of Confederation
subtitle: The first constitution of the United States, 1781–1789
summary: The Articles of Confederation were the first constitution of the United States. Drafted mainly by John Dickinson and adopted by the Continental Congress on November 15, 1777, they created “a firm league of friendship” among thirteen states that each kept their “sovereignty, freedom and independence.” They took effect only on March 1, 1781, when Maryland ratified. Congress had one house, and each state one vote. It could make war and treaties but could not tax, regulate commerce, or establish federal courts, weaknesses that, after the war, led James Madison, George Washington, and others to fear the union would collapse and to replace the Articles with the Constitution in 1787.
thumbAlt: First page of the Articles of Confederation
aliases: Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union Confederation Congress league of friendship Dickinson Draft
themeText: Constitution and law Political thought
text: John Dickinson (principal drafter) Second Continental Congress Read the full text at the National Archives Drafted by A committee of one member from each colony, appointed June 11, 1776; John Dickinson of Delaware principal writer Adopted November 15, 1777 In force March 1, 1781 – 1789 Representation One vote per state, regardless of population Major decisions Needed the assent of nine states Amendments Required the approval of every state legislature After Richard Henry Lee proposed independence in June 1776, the Second Continental Congress appointed three committees on June 11. One, with a member from each colony, was to decide what form a union should take; John Dickinson of Delaware was its principal writer. His draft named the confederation “the United States of America.” Americans had just rebelled against a distant government that taxed them without consent, and the plan reflected that suspicion of central power. After long debate, Congress adopted the Articles on November 15, 1777. Ratification required all thirteen states, and quarrels over representation, voting, and the western lands some states claimed held it up for more than three years, until Maryland ratified on March 1, 1781. The American Yawp says Congress “ratified” the Articles in 1781; more precisely, Congress had adopted them in 1777, and 1781 was when the last state approved. A league of states. “The said States hereby severally enter into a firm league of friendship with each other, for their common defense, the security of their liberties, and their mutual and general welfare.” State sovereignty. Each state kept “its sovereignty, freedom and independence, and every Power, Jurisdiction and right, which is not by this confederation expressly delegated to the United States.” One state, one vote. “In determining questions in the United States in Congress assembled, each State shall have one vote.” Supermajorities. War, treaties, coining or borrowing money, and other major acts required the assent of nine states. No power to tax. Congress could request money from the states but had no power to levy or collect taxes, regulate foreign or interstate commerce, or create a federal judiciary. Hard to change. No alteration could be made unless agreed to by Congress “and be afterwards confirmed by the legislatures of every State.” Cooperation among states. States had to give “full faith and credit” to each other’s court records and hand over fugitives from justice. The Articles carried the United States through the end of the Revolution and produced the Northwest Ordinance, but their weaknesses convinced many leaders that the union needed a stronger government. Their failures shaped nearly every major feature of the Constitution that replaced them, from the power to tax to the method of amendment. A government without money The National Archives describes a Congress that “could not tax and was generally impotent in setting commercial policy,” with a depleted treasury and paper money flooding the country and causing extraordinary inflation. Because the national government could not tax, the burden of repaying war debts fell on the states. The Yawp notes that this helped push Massachusetts to side with its bondholders against debt-ridden farmers. Crisis and replacement Disputes among the states over territory, war pensions, taxes, and trade threatened to tear the country apart. When farmers rose in Shays’ Rebellion in 1786–87, the Confederation government could not help put it down; Massachusetts relied on a militia paid for by private Boston businessmen. In May 1787 the Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia, officially to revise the Articles. By mid-June the delegates had decided to redesign the government entirely, and the new Constitution took effect in 1789. The said States hereby severally enter into a firm league of friendship with each other, for their common defense, the security of their liberties, and their mutual and general welfare. title: The Bill of Rights
subtitle: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
summary: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified on December 15, 1791. It protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, and assembly, the right to bear arms, security against unreasonable searches, and the rights of people accused of crimes, and it reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people. It was added to answer Anti-Federalist critics who feared that the new national government would trample individual liberties. James Madison, once its opponent, guided it through the First Congress. At first it limited only the federal government. The author of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) meant that amendment to make the Bill of Rights binding on the states as well, a question the Supreme Court long resisted.
