title: The Overthrow and Annexation of Hawaiʻi
subtitle: How American sugar planters toppled Queen Liliʻuokalani and the United States took the islands in 1898
summary: In the nineteenth century the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi came to be dominated by American missionaries, businessmen, and sugar planters. In 1887 armed businessmen forced King Kalākaua to accept the “Bayonet Constitution,” and on January 17, 1893, with the support of the U.S. minister and Marines from the USS Boston, they overthrew his sister, Queen Liliʻuokalani. A U.S. investigation found the overthrow illegal, and more than half of Native Hawaiians signed a petition against annexation. But during the Spanish-American War, Congress annexed the islands by joint resolution, signed on July 7, 1898. Hawaiʻi became the fiftieth state in 1959.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Liliʻuokalani, the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, around 1891
aliases: annexation of Hawaii Hawaii Hawaiian Kingdom Queen Liliuokalani Liliuokalani Newlands Resolution Bayonet Constitution
themeText: Territorial expansion Indigenous history Foreign policy and diplomacy Economy and finance
text: Honolulu, Kingdom of Hawaiʻi Overthrow January 17, 1893: a “Committee of Safety” of American businessmen, backed by U.S. Marines, deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani Investigation President Cleveland’s Blount Commission found the overthrow illegal Petition 21,269 Native Hawaiians, more than half, signed a petition against annexation in 1897 Annexation Newlands Resolution, signed by President McKinley on July 7, 1898 Statehood August 21, 1959: Hawaiʻi became the fiftieth state The annexation of Hawaiʻi marked the United States’ turn toward overseas empire in the Pacific. It was carried out against the will of most Native Hawaiians, after a coup that a U.S. investigation called illegal, and by a joint resolution that bypassed the treaty process. King Kamehameha united the Hawaiian Islands into one kingdom in 1810. American missionaries arrived in 1820 and, working alongside business interests, acquired large tracts of land and started lucrative sugar plantations; over the century an oligarchy of sugar companies, the “Big Five,” gained enormous power. A reciprocity treaty let Hawaiian sugar enter the U.S. market tax-free, and as planters came to dominate the islands, traditional culture suffered: teaching the Hawaiian language and performing the hula were among the practices prohibited. The planters wanted to protect their profits. They feared that the United States would impose a tariff on Hawaiian sugar and wanted to protect the islands’ free-trade status with the United States, their main customer. Expansionists in Washington, among them Theodore Roosevelt, also valued the islands for an excellent harbor at Pearl Harbor, a fueling station on the way to Asian markets, and a barrier against Japanese expansion. On July 6, 1887, a militia tied to the Hawaiian League, a party of mostly American businessmen led by Lorrin Thurston, forced King Kalākaua to sign a constitution that stripped him of power and many Native Hawaiians of their rights, the “Bayonet Constitution.” When Kalākaua died in 1891, his sister Liliʻuokalani succeeded him and moved to restore royal power and Hawaiian rights with a new constitution. A Committee of Safety led by Sanford Dole struck back. Supported by the American minister, John Stevens, and Marines from the warship USS Boston, it overthrew the queen in a bloodless coup on January 17, 1893, and declared itself the Provisional Government; Stevens, without State Department approval, proclaimed Hawaiʻi a U.S. protectorate. President Benjamin Harrison signed an annexation treaty, but his successor, Grover Cleveland, withdrew it and sent an investigator, James Blount, who concluded that the queen had been overthrown illegally. Dole refused to give up power and in 1894 proclaimed the Republic of Hawaiʻi. An armed Native Hawaiian revolt in January 1895 was crushed, and the queen was imprisoned. When President William McKinley signed a new annexation treaty in 1897, Native Hawaiians organized a mass petition against it; 21,269 people signed, and a delegation carried it to Washington. The treaty failed in the Senate. Then the Spanish-American War made the islands look strategically vital, and annexationists turned to a joint resolution, which needed only a simple majority in each house rather than two-thirds of the Senate. McKinley signed the Newlands Resolution on July 7, 1898. Sanford Dole became the first governor of the Territory of Hawaiʻi. In a last attempt to regain her homeland for its people, Liliʻuokalani sent a protest to the House of Representatives, declaring that her throne had been taken illegally. As a territory, Hawaiʻi had only a non-voting delegate in Congress and appointed governors and judges, an arrangement that let wealthy white planters import cheap labor and keep their markets. Native Hawaiians and other non-white residents pushed for statehood for more than half a century. A 1937 congressional committee found Hawaiʻi qualified, but the attack on Pearl Harbor and suspicion of Japanese Hawaiians stalled the effort. Congress finally paired Hawaiʻi with Alaska; after Alaska’s admission in early 1959, a Hawaiʻi statehood bill passed in March, voters approved it, and on August 21, 1959, President Eisenhower proclaimed Hawaiʻi the fiftieth state. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C2bjjwv4134 The dark history of the overthrow of Hawaii - Sydney Iaukea TED-Ed 5:46 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XOj8xkeRCUU The Story of America's Annexation of Hawaiʻi | PBS Hawaiʻi Presents PBS Hawaiʻi 1:26:40 2026-10-22

title: Apollo 11
subtitle: The first human landing on the Moon, July 1969
summary: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle on the Moon’s Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins orbited overhead in the command module Columbia. An estimated 650 million people watched as Armstrong stepped onto the surface, describing it as “one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.” The mission fulfilled President Kennedy’s 1961 goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth, and it was a triumph for the United States in the space race with the Soviet Union.
location: Launched from Cape Kennedy, Florida; landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon
thumbAlt: Buzz Aldrin standing on the Moon in his spacesuit
aliases: Moon landing Eagle Neil Armstrong Buzz Aldrin space race
themeText: Science and technology The Cold War
text: Launched from Cape Kennedy, Florida; landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon Launch July 16, 1969, Cape Kennedy Crew Neil Armstrong (commander), Michael Collins (command module pilot), Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin (lunar module pilot) Landing July 20, 1969, Sea of Tranquility Audience An estimated 650 million people Splashdown July 24, 1969, Pacific Ocean, 13 miles from USS Hornet The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957, and the United States created NASA in 1958 to compete in space. On May 25, 1961, President John F. Kennedy set the national goal of landing astronauts on the Moon and returning them safely before the decade ended. The space race was a Cold War contest for prestige and technological leadership. Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969. On July 20, Eagle separated from Columbia and, partly piloted by hand by Armstrong, landed in the Sea of Tranquility. Hours later Armstrong stepped onto the surface, followed about 20 minutes later by Aldrin. They ranged up to 300 feet from the lander, set up scientific experiments, and gathered samples of lunar rock and soil. After rejoining Collins, the crew returned to Earth and splashed down in the Pacific on July 24, after a flight of about 195 hours. Americans hailed the landing as a victory in the space race. The Moon landing was a landmark achievement and a lasting symbol of what the nation could accomplish: even as it came amid the turmoil of the Vietnam War, urban riots, and assassinations. Apollo 11 fulfilled a national goal, gave the United States a decisive symbolic victory in the Cold War space race, and gave the world a shared moment of wonder. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=55Jas5HrzcQ Apollo Program: The Complete Story Epic History 54:08 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OCjhCL2iqlQ Apollo 11’s journey to the moon, annotated Vox 5:14 2026-10-22

title: Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
subtitle: The first and only use of nuclear weapons in war, August 1945
summary: On August 6, 1945, an American B-29 bomber dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Japan; three days later a second bomb struck Nagasaki. Some 70,000 people probably died immediately at Hiroshima, and more than 100,000 by the end of 1945; the best estimate at Nagasaki is 40,000 initial deaths. Japan announced its surrender on August 15. The bombings ended World War II and opened the nuclear age, and whether they were necessary remains one of the most debated questions in American history.
thumbAlt: Mushroom clouds over Hiroshima and Nagasaki
aliases: Manhattan Project Hiroshima Nagasaki Little Boy Fat Man Trinity test Enola Gay
themeText: War and the military Science and technology The presidency Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan Hiroshima August 6, 1945, about 8:15 a.m.; uranium bomb “Little Boy,” about 15 kilotons; dropped from the Enola Gay Nagasaki August 9, 1945, 11:02 a.m.; plutonium bomb “Fat Man,” about 21 kilotons; dropped from Bock’s Car Deaths Hiroshima: about 70,000 initially, probably over 100,000 by end of 1945; Nagasaki: about 40,000 initially Authorized by President Harry S. Truman Japan’s surrender Announced August 15; signed September 2, 1945 Early in the war, fearing that Germany might build an atomic bomb, the United States launched the Manhattan Project, a vast secret program to build a weapon from nuclear fission. Scientists at Los Alamos, New Mexico, directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer, designed the bombs, and on July 16, 1945, the first nuclear device was exploded in the Trinity test in New Mexico. By then Germany had surrendered, but the war with Japan continued. After the bloody battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, U.S. officials expected Japanese forces to fight fiercely for their home islands; some estimated that an invasion could cost half a million American casualties and perhaps millions of Japanese civilians. These estimates were later cited to justify the bombings. President Truman approved its use; his order of July 25 authorized additional bombs as soon as they were ready. Historians continue to debate the many motives behind the decision, and many American officials criticized it. Hiroshima. Hiroshima, a city of almost 300,000 civilians and an important military center, was the primary target. At about 8:15 a.m. on August 6, the B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, released “Little Boy,” which exploded 1,900 feet above the city. Within minutes nine of ten people within half a mile of ground zero were dead. Nearly every structure within a mile was destroyed, and roughly half the city’s population was killed or injured. Nagasaki. On August 9, the B-29 Bock’s Car, commanded by Major Charles Sweeney, found its primary target, Kokura, obscured by smoke and haze and turned to its secondary target, Nagasaki, where “Fat Man” exploded at 11:02 a.m. Though more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb, it caused less damage because of the city’s hilly terrain. Survivors began to show symptoms of radiation sickness within days; deaths from it peaked three to four weeks after the attacks. Emperor Hirohito announced Japan’s surrender on August 15, and Japanese delegates formally signed the surrender aboard the battleship USS Missouri on September 2, 1945. Survivors faced long-term health dangers, including increased cancer risk, for the rest of their lives. The bombings began the nuclear age. The Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb in 1949, and the two superpowers raced to build ever more powerful weapons during the Cold War. Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the deadliest war in history and made the prospect of nuclear annihilation a permanent feature of world politics. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0fmFlJv9cLI Hiroshima A-Bomb: Minute-By-Minute Account Of The Event That Ended WW2 Timeline - World History Documentaries 45:32 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4q1fG1vh5I The Atomic Bomb: Crash Course History of Science #33 CrashCourse 12:04 2026-10-22

title: Battle of Bunker Hill
subtitle: The bloody 1775 fight outside Boston, actually waged on Breed’s Hill
summary: On June 17, 1775, two months after Lexington and Concord, British troops attacked a fort that New England militiamen had built overnight on Breed’s Hill in Charlestown, across the harbor from Boston. The Americans threw back two assaults and gave way on the third only when they ran out of powder. The British took the hill, but the American Battlefield Trust counts 282 British dead and another 800 wounded, more than twice the American losses. The battle showed that the rebellion would not be easily put down and, in the Trust’s words, that reconciliation was “no longer possible.”
thumbAlt: John Trumbull’s painting The Death of General Warren at the Battle of Bunker’s Hill, 1786
aliases: Bunker Hill Breed's Hill Whites of their eyes William Prescott Peter Salem Salem Poor Siege of Boston
themeText: War and the military
text: Charlestown, Massachusetts Date June 17, 1775 Place Breed’s Hill, Charlestown peninsula, outside Boston Commanders British: Gen. Thomas Gage, Gen. William Howe. American: Col. William Prescott, Gen. John Stark British losses 282 killed and about 800 wounded Result British tactical victory at heavy cost Name Fought on Breed’s Hill; named after neighboring Bunker Hill After the fighting at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775, British troops pulled back into Boston, and militiamen from Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire and what is now Vermont gathered around the town. By June the British commander, Gen. Thomas Gage, had reinforcements and new subordinates, Generals William Howe, Henry Clinton and John Burgoyne, and he planned to seize the heights north and south of Boston. A leaked plan. Word of the British plan got out, and about 1,000 Massachusetts and Connecticut men, among them several enslaved and free African Americans, moved to defend high ground in Charlestown. A provocation. On the nights of June 15 and 16 they fortified Breed’s Hill, a position that, the Battlefield Trust writes, “all but invites a British response.” John Stark’s New Hampshire men built a rail barricade along the Mystic River to protect the flank. British pressure to act. Gage was under pressure to crush the rebellion, and the sight of works raised in a single night left him little choice. On the hot afternoon of June 17 British regulars crossed the harbor and landed in Charlestown. Led by General Howe, they advanced up Breed’s Hill in formation. Legend has it that Prescott told his men, “don’t fire until you see the whites of their eyes.” At close range the defenders fired a volley that cut the first assault apart, and the British fell back. The second attack met the same fate. On the third, the Americans ran out of powder and shot, and the British broke into the redoubt. After hand-to-hand fighting inside the fort, the Americans retreated off the peninsula. One British officer wrote that the generals “expected rather to punish a mob than fight with troops that would look them in the face,” and Henry Clinton called it “a dear bought victory.” Badly weakened, the British dropped their plan to seize other high ground and eventually evacuated Boston. The Americans who stayed to besiege the town became the core of the Continental Army, and within two weeks George Washington arrived in Cambridge to take command. Bunker Hill became one of the founding stories of the Revolution. It taught the British that an assault on entrenched Americans would be expensive, and it told the colonists that their militia could stand up to regulars. Fifty years later the Marquis de Lafayette laid the cornerstone of the Bunker Hill Monument, a 221-foot granite obelisk on Breed’s Hill that took more than seventeen years to finish. The British won the ground but suffered more than a thousand casualties. The battle ended hopes of a quick end to the rebellion and showed the colonists they could fight a professional army. Why “Bunker Hill”? Prescott’s orders were to fortify Bunker’s Hill, but he chose the lower Breed’s Hill instead, and no one knows why. A British map of the battle then reversed the names of the two hills. Over time Breed’s Hill was forgotten, and the battle kept the name of its steeper neighbor. Black soldiers and the death of Major Pitcairn Around three dozen Black Americans fought on the American side. Stories later credited “a black soldier named Salem” with killing British Maj. John Pitcairn, but the evidence is thin. Writers in 1818 and 1826 told the story in different ways, naming Peter Salem, while thirteen officers, Prescott among them, petitioned the Massachusetts legislature on December 5, 1775, to recognize another soldier, Salem Poor, who had “behaved like an Experienced officer, as Well as an Excellent Soldier.” A British account written four days after the battle places Pitcairn’s death before the final assault. The Battlefield Trust concludes that the two Salems may have merged in memory, and that no one can say who fired the fatal shot. Don’t fire until you see the whites of their eyes. William Prescott (attributed) Breed’s Hill, June 17, 1775; the Battlefield Trust calls it legend A dear bought victory. title: The Battle of Gettysburg
subtitle: The bloodiest battle of the Civil War, July 1–3, 1863
summary: For three days in July 1863, the Union Army of the Potomac under George G. Meade and Robert E. Lee’s Confederate Army of Northern Virginia fought around the Pennsylvania town of Gettysburg. With as many as 51,000 soldiers killed, wounded, captured, or missing, it was the bloodiest battle of the war. Lee’s defeat, capped by the failed assault known as Pickett’s Charge, ended his second invasion of the North and is often called the turning point of the Civil War.
thumbAlt: Lithograph of Pickett’s Charge at the Battle of Gettysburg
themeText: War and the military
text: Gettysburg, Pennsylvania Dates July 1–3, 1863 Armies Union Army of the Potomac (about 90,000) under Meade; Confederate Army of Northern Virginia (about 75,000) under Lee Casualties As many as 51,000 killed, wounded, captured, or missing Result Union victory; Lee retreated to Virginia After defeating the Union army at Chancellorsville in May 1863, Lee led his army north in June on his second invasion of Union territory. He hoped to win a battle north of the Mason-Dixon line that would force a negotiated end to the war, and to feed his army from Pennsylvania’s farms. President Lincoln, frustrated with General Joseph Hooker, replaced him with George G. Meade in late June. Lee, lacking intelligence because his cavalry under J.E.B. Stuart was absent, learned that Meade’s army was close and ordered his scattered forces to concentrate at Gettysburg, where many roads converged. The battle began almost by accident when Confederate troops seeking supplies met Union cavalry west of town. July 1. Union cavalry under John Buford held off Confederate infantry until Union infantry arrived; their commander, John Reynolds, was killed. By afternoon about 30,000 Confederates had overwhelmed some 20,000 Union troops, who fell back through the town to Cemetery Hill. July 2. The Union army held a fishhook-shaped line of hills and ridges south of town. Lee launched heavy attacks under James Longstreet against the Union left, with ferocious fighting at Devil’s Den, Little Round Top, the Wheatfield, the Peach Orchard, and Cemetery Ridge; Union commanders shifted reinforcements quickly along their shorter interior lines to hold. July 3. After fighting at Culp’s Hill, Lee sent about 12,500 men under Longstreet, including George Pickett’s division, across open ground against the Union center on Cemetery Ridge. The assault, remembered as Pickett’s Charge, was shattered. Lee retreated toward Virginia. Meade did not pursue aggressively, and when Lincoln learned that Lee had escaped across the flooded Potomac, he lamented, “We had only to stretch forth our hands & they were ours.” Coming the same week as Grant’s capture of Vicksburg, Gettysburg nevertheless lifted Northern spirits and ended the Confederacy’s hope of winning independence through a decisive victory on Northern soil. Residents and community leaders established the Soldiers’ National Cemetery on the battlefield, and at its dedication in November 1863 Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address. The battlefield is preserved as Gettysburg National Military Park. Gettysburg was the war’s largest battle and the high-water mark of the Confederacy; after it, Lee never again invaded the North. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DUXpCfcJ7Ng Gettysburg: Animated Battle Map American Battlefield Trust 16:51 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7ALyq3seK2g The Battle of Gettysburg: The Civil War in Four Minutes American Battlefield Trust 5:00 2026-10-22

title: The Battle of the Little Bighorn
subtitle: Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors destroy Custer’s command, June 1876
summary: On June 25–26, 1876, warriors of the Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho defeated the U.S. 7th Cavalry along the Little Bighorn River in Montana, killing Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer and every soldier in the five companies under his immediate command. The battle, which Native people call the Battle of the Greasy Grass, was a stunning victory for the nations resisting confinement to reservations, but a short-lived one. Within a year most had surrendered, and the government seized the sacred Black Hills.
thumbAlt: Pictorial account of the Battle of the Little Bighorn by White Swan
aliases: Greasy Grass Custer's Last Stand
themeText: Indigenous history War and the military Territorial expansion
text: Little Bighorn River, south-central Montana Dates June 25–26, 1876 Native forces Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho; a village of about 8,000 people with 1,500–1,800 warriors U.S. forces 7th Cavalry under Custer, with Crow and Arikara scouts Losses Custer’s five companies annihilated; about 80 Lakota and Cheyenne killed, according to the NPS After fierce fighting in 1865–1867, several Lakota leaders signed the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868, which created the Great Sioux Reservation in the western half of present-day South Dakota, including the Black Hills, sacred to the Lakota. Leaders such as Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse rejected the reservation system, and many bands that had not signed the treaty continued to hunt on unceded lands. In 1874 Custer led an expedition into the Black Hills, inside the reservation; geologists found gold, and miners poured in, in direct violation of the treaty. The United States offered to buy the Hills; the Lakota rejected the price. In the winter of 1875, the government declared that bands not on reservations by January 31, 1876, would be considered hostile, and the army launched a campaign with three columns to force them back. The Lakota and Cheyenne had gathered in large numbers along the Little Bighorn after their annual Sun Dance, where Sitting Bull had a vision of soldiers falling into the village. Custer, ordered to approach from the south, believed his regiment had been detected and attacked on June 25 without waiting for the other columns. He split his command. Major Marcus Reno’s battalion charged the south end of the village, was driven back across the river with heavy losses, and dug in on the bluffs, where Captain Frederick Benteen joined him. Custer led five companies north along the ridges east of the river. Overwhelmed by superior numbers and firepower, his entire command was killed. Reno and Benteen’s men were besieged until the village moved away on the evening of June 26. News of Custer’s defeat shocked the nation, which had not believed Plains peoples capable of destroying a modern cavalry force. The army sent more troops; most of the bands declared “hostile” surrendered within a year, and Sitting Bull led his followers into Canada. The National Park Service calls the battle “a momentary victory” for the Lakota and Cheyenne. The government took the Black Hills without compensation, a seizure the Lakota have contested ever since. In popular culture, “Custer’s Last Stand” became a heroic myth; the battlefield, now Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, today commemorates both the soldiers and the Native warriors who fought there. The Little Bighorn was the greatest Native military victory of the Plains wars and a symbol of resistance, but it also hastened the final conquest of the Northern Plains. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UM4eQBpfGIg The Battle at Little Bighorn | History HISTORY 4:09 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sn5SXMKS1xU Where Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse Defeated Colonel Custer Smithsonian Channel 3:58 2026-10-22

title: The Alamo and the Texas Revolution
subtitle: The thirteen-day siege of 1836 and the war that made Texas an independent republic
summary: In February 1836, during the Texas Revolution against Mexico, a small garrison of Texan and American volunteers held the old Alamo mission at San Antonio against the army of Mexican president Antonio López de Santa Anna. After a thirteen-day siege, some 1,800 Mexican troops stormed the walls before dawn on March 6; within ninety minutes every defender, including William Barret Travis, Jim Bowie, and Davy Crockett, was dead. Six weeks later Sam Houston’s army routed Santa Anna at San Jacinto, and Texas won its independence as a republic that protected slavery.
location: San Antonio de Béxar, Mexican Texas
thumbAlt: Robert Jenkins Onderdonk’s painting The Fall of the Alamo, about 1903, showing Davy Crockett swinging his rifle as Mexican soldiers storm the mission
aliases: Alamo Remember the Alamo Texas Revolution San Jacinto Davy Crockett Jim Bowie William Travis Santa Anna
themeText: Territorial expansion War and the military Slavery and emancipation Latino history
text: San Antonio de Béxar, Mexican Texas Siege February 23 – March 6, 1836 Defenders 189 on the official list; research may raise the total to as many as 257 Mexican losses About 600 killed and wounded Travis’s letter “To the people of Texas & all Americans in the world… Victory or Death” San Jacinto April 21, 1836: the battle lasted eighteen minutes; Santa Anna was captured the next day Texas independence Declared March 2, 1836, at Washington-on-the-Brazos The Alamo became one of the most powerful symbols of patriotic sacrifice in American memory, though legend often obscures the real battle. The revolution it belonged to created the Republic of Texas, whose annexation by the United States in 1845 led toward the Mexican-American War and deepened the national crisis over slavery’s expansion. After Mexico won independence from Spain, its government invited settlers into Texas. Under the Colonization Act of 1825 immigrants poured in, most from the southern United States and many bringing enslaved people. Mexico’s federal constitution of 1824 appealed to them, but Mexican officials grew alarmed: Anglo settlers far outnumbered Mexicans east of San Antonio and seemed only nominally loyal. Mexico outlawed slavery in 1829, and the Law of April 6, 1830, tried to stop American immigration and the further introduction of slaves; the colonists largely ignored both. In 1834 Santa Anna took power, repudiated the federal Constitution of 1824, and ruled as a dictator. Fighting broke out at Gonzales in October 1835. In December Texan volunteers, American volunteers, and their Tejano allies captured San Antonio. Disputes over immigration, customs duties, land titles, military authority, and slavery divided the colonists from the Mexican government; The American Yawp calls the debate over slavery “one of the prime forces behind the Texas Revolution.” The rebels at first presented themselves as defenders of the Constitution of 1824 against Santa Anna’s centralism, then declared independence. The Alamo itself was held because, as its commander James Neill argued, it guarded one of the two main roads into Texas from the Mexican interior; Governor Henry Smith refused Sam Houston’s request for permission to abandon and blow it up. Santa Anna’s army reached San Antonio on February 23, 1836, sooner than the defenders expected. Travis answered a demand for surrender with a cannonball. When Bowie fell gravely ill, Travis took full command and wrote his famous appeal “to the people of Texas & all Americans in the world,” vowing “Victory or Death” but above all pleading for help. Only thirty-two men from Gonzales broke through to join them. “If my countrymen do not rally to my relief,” Travis wrote, “I am determined to perish in the defense of this place, and my bones shall reproach my country for her neglect.” Around 5:00 a.m. on Sunday, March 6, about 1,800 Mexican troops attacked from four directions. Cannon fire tore through their ranks, but they reformed and broke over the walls. Travis was among the first to die; defenders fell back to the Long Barracks, where the bloodiest hand-to-hand fighting took place, and Bowie was killed in his sickbed. The chapel fell last. As many as seven defenders survived the fighting, but Santa Anna ordered them executed; whether Crockett was among them is still debated. Women, children, and enslaved people were spared, among them Susanna Dickinson and her infant daughter, and Travis’s slave, Joe. Dickinson carried the news to Sam Houston at Gonzales, setting off a panicked flight of settlers known as the Runaway Scrape. Meanwhile, on March 2 a convention at Washington-on-the-Brazos (including the Tejanos José Antonio Navarro, Lorenzo de Zavala, and José Francisco Ruiz) had declared Texas independent; its constitution guaranteed the protection of slavery. On March 27 about 350 Texan prisoners who had surrendered at Goliad were executed on Santa Anna’s orders. Then, on April 21, Houston’s army of about 900 surprised Santa Anna’s force at San Jacinto. The battle lasted eighteen minutes, though the killing went on for hours; about 630 Mexican soldiers died and 730 were captured, against 9 Texans killed. Santa Anna was captured the next day and ordered his army out of Texas. Mexico never recognized the Republic of Texas, but the United States did, and in 1845 Texas joined the Union as the twenty-eighth state, an annexation Mexico denounced as an act of aggression. The Alamo’s defenders, the Handbook of Texas stresses, were not suicidal, they held their post on orders, begging for reinforcements a divided government never sent, and the battle’s real military value was in giving the independence convention time to meet. Novels, plays, and films have wrapped it in legend, but even stripped of exaggeration it remains, in the Handbook’s words, “an inspiring moment in Texas history,” and “Remember the Alamo!” has echoed through American history ever since. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cdwf4EH1_dE The Alamo: The Birthplace of Texas Geographics 26:19 2026-10-22

title: Battles of Saratoga
subtitle: The 1777 American victory that brought France into the war
summary: In the autumn of 1777 a British army under General John Burgoyne, marching south from Canada to take the Hudson River Valley, was stopped and forced to surrender near Saratoga, New York. American forces under Horatio Gates fought Burgoyne at Freeman’s Farm on September 19 and at Bemis Heights on October 7, then surrounded his army, which surrendered on October 17. The American Yawp calls the victory “a major turning point in the war”: it convinced France that the American cause could succeed, and France signed treaties with the United States in February 1778.
thumbAlt: John Trumbull’s painting of General Burgoyne surrendering to General Gates at Saratoga
aliases: Saratoga Freeman's Farm Bemis Heights Burgoyne's surrender John Burgoyne Horatio Gates Benedict Arnold Conway Cabal
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Saratoga County, New York Dates September 19 and October 7, 1777; surrender October 17 Place Near Saratoga, on the Hudson River, New York British commander Gen. John Burgoyne American commanders Gen. Horatio Gates, with Benedict Arnold and Daniel Morgan Forces About 7,500 British and German troops; Americans grew from about 8,500 to 13,000 Result Burgoyne’s whole army surrendered; France allied with the United States British strategy for 1777 called for a three-pronged attack on New York, with armies converging near Albany. The aim was to control the Hudson River Valley, the route between Canada and New York City. Burgoyne set out south from Canada with about 7,500 men. By August he had taken Fort Ticonderoga, defeated retreating Americans at Hubbardton in Vermont, and reached Fort Edward on the Hudson. The Hudson strategy. Burgoyne’s campaign depended on the river route and on help from other British forces, above all Gen. Henry Clinton coming up from New York City. Losses on the march. A detachment of Burgoyne’s troops was defeated at the Battle of Bennington, and his reduced army marched toward Saratoga in early September. A strong American position. Gates had his men fortify Bemis Heights, bluffs overlooking both the Hudson and the only road south. The dense forest to the east meant the British would have to use that road, under American guns. Freeman’s Farm, September 19. Burgoyne split his army into three columns to probe the American defenses. Daniel Morgan’s riflemen and light infantry met the center column near Freeman’s Farm, and the field changed hands several times. By evening the British, reinforced by German troops, held the ground, but at the cost of almost 600 men, and their advance had stalled. Expecting Clinton’s relief, Burgoyne dug in. Waiting. No relief came. Food ran short and the British went on half rations, while the American army grew to about 13,000. Bemis Heights, October 7. Burgoyne sent a reconnaissance force against the American lines. The Americans drove it back to the Balcarres Redoubt, then captured the weakly held Breymann Redoubt, with Benedict Arnold riding in front to rally the attack. Arnold was badly wounded in the left leg. Surrender, October 17. On October 8 the British tried to retreat north, but heavy rain stopped them near Saratoga. Within two days they were surrounded, and after negotiations Burgoyne’s army surrendered on October 17. Burgoyne’s men became prisoners of war. Burgoyne himself returned to England in the spring of 1778, was severely criticized, and never received another command. Gates became a celebrated figure. He reported his victory directly to Congress rather than to Washington, and some in Congress talked of putting him in Washington’s place; the scheme, known as the Conway Cabal, failed. News of the victory reached France, and on February 6, 1778, France and the United States signed treaties of commerce and alliance. Saratoga turned a rebellion into an international war. The National Park Service says the victory “renewed patriots’ hopes for independence” and secured “essential foreign recognition and support.” French money, troops and ships followed, and the Battlefield Trust notes that French support contributed to the victory at Yorktown in 1781; Spain and the Dutch Republic later aided the Americans as well. Saratoga ended Burgoyne’s attempt to control the Hudson River Valley. It proved the Americans could defeat a professional army in the field and persuaded France to enter the war, which made eventual independence far more likely. Benedict Arnold at Saratoga Arnold argued with Gates on September 19, pressing him to meet the British advance instead of waiting behind the fortifications. After the battle Gates did not credit Arnold in his report to Congress, and Gates, not Arnold, was hailed as the hero of Saratoga. The American Battlefield Trust suggests this resentment, together with his marriage to the Loyalist Peggy Shippen in 1779, may help explain why in 1780 Arnold tried to hand West Point to the British. Remembering the battlefield The battlefield is preserved as Saratoga National Historical Park. John Trumbull’s painting The Surrender of General Burgoyne hangs in the U.S. Capitol. This crucial American victory renewed patriots’ hopes for independence, secured essential foreign recognition and support, and forever changed the face of the world. title: Bonnie and Clyde
subtitle: Depression-era outlaws whose short, violent crime spree became an American legend
summary: Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were young Texans who, from 1932 to 1934, robbed grocery stores, filling stations, and small banks across the Southwest and Midwest and killed a number of people, several of them law officers. A posse led by former Texas Ranger Frank Hamer killed them in a roadside ambush in Louisiana on May 23, 1934. Small-time criminals in life, they became one of America’s most enduring legends, above all through the 1967 film Bonnie and Clyde.
location: Texas, the Southwest, and the Midwest
thumbAlt: Bonnie Parker leaning on Clyde Barrow’s shoulder as they pose in front of a car, about 1933
aliases: Bonnie Parker Clyde Barrow Barrow gang
themeText: Crime and law enforcement Arts and popular culture
text: Texas, the Southwest, and the Midwest Bonnie Parker Born October 1, 1910, in Rowena, Texas Clyde Barrow Born March 24, 1909, near Telico, Texas The ambush May 23, 1934, near Gibsland, Louisiana, the couple were killed in a barrage of 167 bullets Largest haul Only $1,500, according to the Handbook of Texas The film Bonnie and Clyde (1967), starring Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway: ten Academy Award nominations, two wins Bonnie Parker grew up in “Cement City” in West Dallas after her father died in 1914. She was an honor student who liked writing poetry and reading romance novels; at four feet ten inches and eighty-five pounds, the Handbook of Texas notes, she hardly looked like a future legendary criminal. Clyde Barrow’s family moved to Dallas in 1922. He was first arrested in 1926 for stealing a car and committed a string of robberies in and around Dallas over the next four years. Their crimes unfolded during the Great Depression, and they were later compared with the era’s other famous criminals, such as John Dillinger and Al Capone. Parker met Barrow in January 1930, shortly before he was jailed. She smuggled a pistol into his cell, which he used to escape; he was recaptured in Middletown, Ohio, and sentenced to fourteen years at hard labor. To avoid work on a state prison farm, he had another convict chop two toes off his left foot. In February 1932 Barrow was paroled, and he and Parker (joined at times by bank robber Raymond Hamilton, Clyde’s brother Buck, and Buck’s wife Blanche) began a series of violent holdups. The gang robbed stores, filling stations, and small banks in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Missouri, and beyond, and killed lawmen and civilians along the way. In April 1933 police raided their hideout in Joplin, Missouri; two lawmen died, and the gang escaped but left behind film from which many of the famous photographs of the couple came. Buck Barrow was killed and Blanche captured after another shootout in Platte City, Missouri. In January 1934 the couple attacked the Eastham Prison Farm in Texas to free Raymond Hamilton and Henry Methvin, and a guard was killed. The head of the Texas prison system and the governor then hired former Texas Ranger captain Frank Hamer to track them down. On Easter Sunday 1934 two highway patrolmen were gunned down near Grapevine, Texas, and on April 6 a constable was killed in Commerce, Oklahoma. Hamer and his officers, working with an FBI agent, found the gang through Methvin’s father’s farm near Arcadia, Louisiana, and set a roadside trap. On May 23, 1934, at 9:15 a.m., Bonnie and Clyde drove into it and were killed. The bodies were taken to Arcadia and then to Dallas, where they were put on public display. Thousands came to see the bodies and the bullet-riddled car of the “legendary lovers,” and amid public clamor the two were buried in their families’ burial plots. Barrow and Parker were sometimes later portrayed as latter-day Robin Hoods, and their story became the basis of more than half a dozen movies. The most famous, Arthur Penn’s Bonnie and Clyde (1967), starring Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway, caused controversy for its frank and unprecedented depiction of violence; the New York Times critic Bosley Crowther attacked it, while Newsweek’s critic publicly reversed his own negative review. The film earned ten Academy Award nominations, won two, and was later ranked among the greatest American films by the American Film Institute. Historians stress the gap between legend and reality: despite their glamorous image, the Handbook of Texas calls them ruthless killers who showed little remorse, small-time criminals whose largest haul was only $1,500. Bonnie and Clyde show how Americans turned real Depression-era violence into romantic legend, and how popular culture, especially film, can reshape the memory of history. title: The Boston Massacre
subtitle: British soldiers fire into a Boston crowd, killing five, in March 1770
summary: On the evening of March 5, 1770, a crowd confronted a small group of British soldiers outside the Custom House on King Street in Boston. Taunted and pelted with snowballs, ice, and sticks, the soldiers fired, killing five men, among them Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Indigenous ancestry, and wounding six. Patriots called it a massacre of civilians; loyalists called it self-defense against a mob. John Adams defended the soldiers in court and won acquittals for most of them, but the killings became one of the most powerful stories of the coming Revolution.
thumbAlt: Paul Revere’s 1770 engraving “The Bloody Massacre,” showing a line of British soldiers firing on a crowd on King Street
aliases: King Street Crispus Attucks Thomas Preston Bloody Massacre 29th Regiment Rex v. Preston Rex v. Wemms
themeText: War and the military Political thought African American history Crime and law enforcement
text: King Street, Boston, Massachusetts Date March 5, 1770 Killed Crispus Attucks, Samuel Gray, and James Caldwell that night; Samuel Maverick, 17, the next morning; Patrick Carr almost two weeks later Soldiers Captain Thomas Preston and eight men of the 29th Regiment of Foot Defense lawyers John Adams, Josiah Quincy Jr., Robert Auchmuty, and later Sampson Salter Blowers Verdicts Preston acquitted October 30, 1770; six soldiers acquitted and two convicted of manslaughter on December 5 Punishment The two convicted soldiers were branded on the hand instead of being hanged The Boston Massacre was the first time British soldiers shed colonists’ blood in the quarrel that became the American Revolution. Patriots turned it into propaganda and an annual day of remembrance, while the trials that followed showed that even hated soldiers could get a fair hearing in a Massachusetts court, a principle later written into the Sixth Amendment. The quarrel that ended in bloodshed on King Street began with money. Britain emerged from the French and Indian War victorious but deeply in debt, and Parliament decided that the colonies should help pay for the empire that protected them. Beginning with the Sugar Act in 1764 and continuing with the Stamp Act and the Townshend Acts, it laid duties on sugar, paper, lead, glass, and tea, goods that had become part of colonists’ sense of a comfortable, genteel life. Colonists who had long taxed themselves through their own assemblies saw these measures as a threat to their liberty, and Boston became home to some of the loudest opposition and the largest protests. In 1767 Parliament passed the Townshend Acts, and to restore order in rebellious Boston the government sent the army. On October 1, 1768, a British fleet arrived and hundreds of soldiers marched into the town. Rather than calming Boston, the troops inflamed it. Townspeople felt they were living under the occupation of a foreign army; soldiers were insulted and taunted on patrol, and verbal abuse soon became fistfights in the streets. Middling families worried that they might be forced to lodge soldiers in their homes, and men who made their living from the sea had particular grievances: sailors feared being seized for the Royal Navy, and off-duty soldiers competed with dockworkers and ropemakers for scarce jobs. By the winter of 1769–1770 the confrontations had become personal and violent. For months soldiers and maritime workers traded insults and punches along the wharves. In February 1770 an eleven-year-old boy, Christopher Seider, was killed while protesting with a group outside the home of a loyalist, and thousands of Bostonians turned out for his funeral. Tension and distrust between civilians and soldiers grew sharper still. The Custom House on King Street, where the hated duties were collected, had become a symbol of British taxation. Behind the street confrontations stood deeper divisions as well. Wealthy merchants had been the first to suffer from and protest the new taxes, and when the Sons of Liberty organized a boycott of British goods, small shopkeepers, mechanics, and artisans were drawn in too. By 1770, resentment of the army was shared across Boston society, even if different groups resented it for different reasons. On the evening of March 5, 1770, just eleven days after Seider’s death, Private Hugh White of the 29th Regiment of Foot stood sentry outside the Custom House. When a young wigmaker’s apprentice, Edward Garrick, shouted that a British officer had not paid his bill, White reprimanded him, the two argued, and White struck the young man on the side of the head with his musket. Word spread through the streets, and a crowd began to gather around the lone sentry. White called for help. Captain Thomas Preston marched seven soldiers of the 29th to the Custom House with fixed bayonets. Church bells rang, people poured out of their homes, and the crowd may have grown to three or four hundred. Witnesses later placed Crispus Attucks, a tall sailor of African and Indigenous descent, at the head of a group of sailors carrying clubs. People in the crowd shouted insults, threw snowballs, ice, and sticks, and dared the soldiers to fire; the soldiers loaded their muskets in full view. At some point a club or stick struck one of the soldiers and knocked him down. He got up and fired into the crowd, and seconds later the others fired too. Eleven men were hit. Attucks, struck by two musket balls in the chest, died instantly; Samuel Gray and James Caldwell also died that night, seventeen-year-old Samuel Maverick died the next morning, and Patrick Carr died of his wounds nearly two weeks later. When the smoke cleared, Preston ordered his men to cease fire and called out more soldiers to guard the Custom House. The acting governor, Thomas Hutchinson, came to the scene, calmed the crowd, and promised justice. The next day Preston and the eight soldiers were arrested and jailed. To prevent further violence, Hutchinson moved the troops out of the town to Castle William, a fort on an island in Boston Harbor. Both sides began at once to fight over the meaning of the night. Newspapers, depositions, broadsides, letters, and diaries told the story in competing ways, as a “Horrid Massacre” or as an “Unhappy Disturbance.” Paul Revere sold an engraving, copied from a drawing by Henry Pelham, under the provocative title “The Bloody Massacre,” showing a line of soldiers firing in unison on a peaceful crowd; broadsides decorated with black coffins appeared in newspapers. Because Attucks and Caldwell had no family in Boston, their bodies lay in state at Faneuil Hall, and the funerals of the victims became huge public demonstrations. Finding lawyers for the accused was hard. The day after the shooting, a loyalist merchant, James Forrest, approached John Adams on Preston’s behalf, explaining that the captain wished for counsel and could get none; two other lawyers, Robert Auchmuty and Josiah Quincy Jr., said they would serve only if Adams joined them. Adams agreed, risking his reputation, because he believed that every accused person in a free country deserved a lawyer and a fair trial. The trials were delayed for months, partly by court schedules and partly by Hutchinson, who hoped tempers would cool. Preston was tried first, beginning on October 24, 1770. The prosecution, Robert Treat Paine and Samuel Quincy, had no physical evidence and had to rely on eyewitnesses, whose stories contradicted each other; some could not even agree on what Preston had worn. Several witnesses swore that the captain had stood in front of his men when they fired, which a commander giving an order to shoot would hardly do. One of them, a free Black man named Newton Prince, testified that he “heard no orders given to fire.” On October 30 the jury found Preston not guilty. The trial of the eight soldiers began on November 27, with Adams now leading the defense. More than forty witnesses testified. The most striking evidence came from a dead man: the surgeon John Jeffries repeated the dying words of Patrick Carr, who had told him that he had often seen soldiers fire on crowds in his native Ireland but had never seen them bear half so much before they fired. Samuel Quincy argued for the prosecution that the soldiers could have retreated instead of killing; Adams answered that if the soldiers were attacked and their lives endangered, the law allowed them to defend themselves, and that facts, not passions, must decide the case. On December 5, nine months to the day after the shooting, a jury with no Boston residents acquitted six soldiers and found Hugh Montgomery and Matthew Kilroy guilty of manslaughter. Both escaped hanging by claiming “benefit of clergy,” an old rule that spared first offenders, and were branded with an “M” on the hand where the thumb meets the palm. Bostonians did not let the night be forgotten. From the first anniversary on, they marked each March 5 with public orations, poems, and pictures; speakers such as James Lovell and, in 1775, Joseph Warren used the anniversary to rally opposition to Britain. These commemorations kept anger at the army alive until fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in 1775. Long afterward, John Adams wrote that no battle of the war had been more important than “the battle of King Street,” and in 1786 he remarked that the massacre had laid the foundation of American independence. The trials left a legacy of their own. They showed Britain that a colonial court could give unpopular defendants a fair hearing, yet in 1774, after the Boston Tea Party, Parliament passed the Administration of Justice Act, which took certain trials out of the colonists’ own hands and deepened their mistrust of British rule. The right Adams had defended, the accused’s right to counsel and a fair trial, was later written into the Sixth Amendment of the Bill of Rights. Crispus Attucks became the best-remembered victim, although his own life is barely documented. Early reports called him Michael Johnson, perhaps an alias; a 1750 Boston newspaper advertisement sought a runaway enslaved man named “Crispas” from Framingham, but contemporary sources do not identify Attucks as enslaved, and how he gained his freedom is unknown. In the 1850s Black abolitionists in Boston, led by William Cooper Nell, honored him as the first martyr of the Revolution, and activists later persuaded the city to recognize March 5 as Crispus Attucks Day. The site of the shooting, beneath the balcony of the Old State House, is marked today by a circle of granite pavers on the Freedom Trail. I had no hesitation in answering that Council ought to be the very last thing that an accused Person should want in a free Country. John Adams recalling why he agreed to defend Captain Preston He had seen soldiers often fire on the people in Ireland, but had never seen them bear half so much before they fired in his life. John Jeffries, surgeon reporting in court the dying words of his patient Patrick Carr Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passions, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence. John Adams closing argument for the soldiers, December 1770 Judgment of Death against those Soldiers would have been as foul a Stain upon this Country as the Executions of the Quakers or Witches, anciently. As the Evidence was, the Verdict of the Jury was exactly right. title: The Boston Tea Party
subtitle: Colonists destroy East India Company tea in Boston Harbor
summary: On the night of December 16, 1773, a few dozen men disguised as Indians boarded three ships at Griffin’s Wharf in Boston and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the harbor. They were protesting the Tea Act, which made the company’s tea cheaper but kept a tax that colonists refused to pay to a Parliament in which they had no representatives. Britain answered with the Coercive Acts, which closed Boston’s port and put Massachusetts under tighter royal control. Instead of isolating Boston, the punishment drew the colonies together and led to the First Continental Congress.
thumbAlt: Currier print of colonists dumping tea into Boston Harbor
aliases: Destruction of the Tea Tea Act Coercive Acts Intolerable Acts Boston Port Act Sons of Liberty
themeText: Reform and protest Economy and finance Political thought
text: Griffin’s Wharf, Boston, Massachusetts Date December 16, 1773 Tea destroyed 342 chests from the Dartmouth, Eleanor, and Beaver Participants 30 to 60 men dressed as Indians (Massachusetts Historical Society) Law protested Tea Act, May 10, 1773 British response The Coercive Acts of 1774, called the Intolerable Acts by colonists Name Called the “Destruction of the Tea” at the time; “Boston Tea Party” came later After the Stamp Act was repealed, Parliament passed the Townshend Acts of 1767, with duties on goods including tea. Colonial boycotts led it to repeal all of them except the tax on tea, kept to assert Parliament’s right to tax the colonies. The sources date that repeal slightly differently, the American Yawp to March 1770 and the Massachusetts Historical Society to April. Patriots tried to keep up the boycott of tea, but, as the Massachusetts Historical Society puts it, “people loved their tea, and their resolve weakened.” In 1773 the East India Company was deep in debt and, the Yawp writes, “drowning in tea,” with almost fifteen million pounds stored in warehouses. Parliament passed the Tea Act on May 10, 1773, letting the company sell tea directly in the colonies without paying the usual export tax in London; the tax would be collected when the tea landed in colonial ports. The tea would be cheaper, but merchants resented the company’s monopoly, and many colonists saw a trap: by buying it they would pay the duty and accept Parliament’s right to tax them. A Pennsylvania newspaper called Prime Minister Lord North a “great schemer” trying “to out wit us.” Agents were appointed to receive the tea in Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Charleston. The Dartmouth, carrying 114 chests of tea, arrived in Boston Harbor on November 28, 1773. A mass meeting called “the Body” gathered at Old South Meeting House, demanded that the tea be sent back, and set a watch of 25 men on Griffin’s Wharf. By December 2 the tea agents in three other ports had resigned, and the taunt went out: “Will you shrink at Boston?” In Boston the governor, Thomas Hutchinson, the ships’ owners, and the tea agents all refused to send the tea back to England. Two more ships, the Eleanor and the Beaver, arrived. Under the law, if the duty on the Dartmouth’s tea was not paid by December 17, customs officers could seize the ship and land the tea. On December 16 the Body met again at Old South and resolved to prevent the tea from being landed, stored, sold, or consumed. As the meeting ended, the crowd followed 30 to 60 men dressed as Indians down to the wharf. The Boston Gazette reported that “in less than four hours” they “emptied every chest of tea on board the three ships … amounting to 342 chests, into the sea !! without the least damage done to the ships or any other property.” John Adams called it an intrepid “exertion of popular power.” Governor Hutchinson called the destruction of the tea high treason, while New York and Philadelphia celebrated “Boston’s Indians.” Not everyone approved; the town of Marshfield urged loyal subjects to condemn the act. Tea was dumped or seized in Charleston, Philadelphia, and New York, and other “tea parties” followed through 1774; in Edenton, North Carolina, fifty-one women signed a pledge to support the boycotts. When the ship captains could not identify the men responsible, the government decided to punish the whole town. In the spring of 1774 Parliament passed the Coercive Acts. The Boston Port Act closed the harbor until the company was repaid; the Massachusetts Government Act put the colony’s government under royal control and restricted town meetings; the Administration of Justice Act let royal officials accused of crimes be tried in Britain; and a new Quartering Act applied to all colonies. The Crown expected to isolate Massachusetts. Instead, the Yawp writes, the Coercive Acts “fostered the sense of shared identity” built over the previous decade: if Parliament could dissolve one colony’s government, it could do the same to any. Colonists sent food to Boston, Virginia called a day of prayer and fasting, and committees seized power from royal governments across the colonies. Committees of Correspondence called the First Continental Congress, which met on September 5, 1774, and organized a boycott of British trade. By destroying the tea and provoking Britain’s crackdown, Boston’s protesters turned a dispute over a tax into a confrontation over Parliament’s power to govern the colonies at all, and forced the other colonies to decide whether they stood with Massachusetts. Most did. A number of brave & resolute men, determined to do all in their power to save their country from the ruin which their enemies had plotted, in less than four hours, emptied every chest of tea on board the three ships . . . amounting to 342 chests, into the sea ! ! without the least damage done to the ships or any other property. title: The California Gold Rush
subtitle: The 1848 discovery at Sutter’s Mill that sent fortune seekers flooding west
summary: On January 24, 1848, James W. Marshall, building a sawmill for John Sutter on the South Fork of the American River, found gold. Fortune seekers, mostly young men, poured in from the eastern states and from around the world, and San Francisco grew from about five hundred people to almost fifty thousand in five years. Few miners got rich, but within two years California had applied to join the Union as a free state; the rush brought violence against Native Americans and long-established Mexican communities, and drew immigrants from China.
location: Coloma and the Sierra Nevada foothills, California
thumbAlt: Daguerreotype of California gold miners working a long tom sluice, about 1850–1852
aliases: Gold Rush forty-niners Sutter's Mill 1849 James Marshall
themeText: Territorial expansion Economy and finance Immigration Indigenous history Asian American history Latino history
text: Coloma and the Sierra Nevada foothills, California Discovery January 24, 1848, at Sutter’s sawmill in Coloma, by James W. Marshall San Francisco About 500 people in 1848; almost 50,000 by 1853 Who came Mostly young single men, plus some women; by the late 1850s Chinese and Mexican immigrants were a fifth of California’s miners Statehood California asked to join the Union as a free state in 1849 and was admitted in 1850 Today Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park, Coloma The gold rush transformed California within a few years, intensified the national crisis over slavery when the new state sought admission, set a pattern of mining rushes across the West, and brought violence and dispossession to Native peoples. California had belonged to Mexico until the Mexican-American War. It was at least three hard months’ travel from the nearest American settlements, and before 1848 it drew far fewer settlers than the farmland of Oregon. In the Sacramento Valley area, John Sutter hired a contractor, James W. Marshall, to build a sawmill at Coloma. In the historian’s phrase in The American Yawp, if the pull of the West was manifest destiny’s kindling, “the discovery of gold in California was the spark that set the fire ablaze.” Most western migrants wanted land to farm, but the lure of getting rich quick drew a different crowd: young, mostly single men willing to gamble everything on a strike. Marshall found gold on January 24, 1848, and word soon spread. In 1848 and 1849 fortune seekers poured in from the eastern states and abroad; immigrants from China’s Guangdong Province, driven by famine, rebellion, and economic collapse, came as laborers. Gold towns sprang up across the foothills, and merchants, saloon keepers, and boardinghouse owners followed the miners. San Francisco exploded from about five hundred residents in 1848 to almost fifty thousand by 1853. Most prospectors failed: as later rushes also showed, the business of the rush often generated more wealth than the mines. Even Frederick Douglass, listing the ordinary work of free Black Americans in 1852, mentioned men “digging gold in California.” With its population soaring, California asked in 1849 to enter the Union as a free state. That request threatened the balance between slave and free states in the Senate and led to the Compromise of 1850, which admitted California as a free state. In the mining districts, lawlessness and racial conflict were common; whites dominated as landowners and managers while poorer whites and ethnic minorities did the hardest labor, and competition for land and gold brought violence and abuse, especially against Native Americans and long-established Mexican communities. California’s rush became the model for a generation of strikes (Colorado in 1858, Nevada in 1859, Idaho, Montana, and the Black Hills in 1874) that pulled settlers into the interior West and repeatedly overran Native lands and treaty rights. Californians soon demanded a transcontinental railroad to link them to the East. Chinese immigrants, at first welcomed as workers during the gold rush and railroad boom, later became scapegoats, culminating in the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. The discovery site at Coloma is preserved as Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xGc3DiiTmH8 Buried Secrets of the Gold Rush (Full Episode) | National Geographic National Geographic 47:22 2026-10-22

title: The Voyages of Columbus
subtitle: Spanish-sponsored voyages that began sustained contact between Europe and the Americas
summary: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus, a Genoese sailor sailing for Spain in search of a western route to Asia, came ashore on an island in the Bahamas that its Lucayan people called Guanahani. He never reached Asia. His four voyages between 1492 and 1504 began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, and set off the Columbian Exchange and the Spanish conquest. They also brought catastrophe to the Taíno and other peoples of the Caribbean: enslavement, forced labor, and epidemics destroyed much of the population within a few decades. Columbus is still honored by some Americans and condemned by others, and the old language of “discovery” describes only one side of the encounter.
location: The Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Caribbean
thumbAlt: Map of the four voyages of Columbus
aliases: Christopher Columbus Cristoforo Colombo 1492 Guanahani San Salvador La Navidad Taíno Treaty of Tordesillas Columbus Day Indigenous Peoples’ Day
themeText: Colonial encounters Indigenous history Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: The Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Caribbean Sponsors The Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella First voyage Sailed August 3, 1492, with three ships (Niña, Pinta, Santa María) and about ninety men First landfall October 12, 1492, on Guanahani in the Bahamas, which Columbus renamed San Salvador Voyages 1492–1493, 1493–1496, 1498–1500, 1502–1504 People met The Lucayan and other Taíno peoples Columbus’s error He underestimated the size of the globe by about two thirds By 1492 Europe was changing fast. The Crusades had linked Europe to the wealth and learning of Asia, and Asian goods created a hunger for new trade. Strong monarchies were forming. In Spain the marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile joined the two most powerful kingdoms of the Iberian peninsula, and in 1492 the crown completed the centuries-long Reconquista by expelling Muslims and Jews from Spain, just as Columbus sailed. Italian traders controlled the Mediterranean trade with Asia, so Spain and Portugal, at the edge of Europe, paid middlemen higher prices for Asian goods and looked to the Atlantic for a more direct route. Portugal led the way. Under Prince Henry the Navigator, Portuguese sailors perfected the astrolabe and the caravel, a rugged ship that could make long voyages on the open ocean and carry cargo. They built forts along the African coast and, by the end of the fifteenth century, Vasco da Gama had reached India. On the Atlantic islands that Iberian sailors came across, the Azores, Canaries, and Cape Verde, Europeans grew sugar with enslaved labor. The Canary Islands’ Native people, the Guanches, were enslaved or died soon after Europeans arrived, which the American Yawp calls a preview of what followed in the Americas. Europeans had also crossed the Atlantic before. Norse seafarers reached Newfoundland around the year 1000, but their colony failed. Columbus, born in Genoa in 1451, had sailed for Portugal and studied under Portuguese navigators. He was not trying to prove the earth was round, a fact that educated Europeans and Asians already knew. They also knew it was too large for any caravel to cross to Asia without starving. Columbus believed otherwise because he underestimated the size of the globe by two thirds. The World History Encyclopedia says that he based his estimate of about 2,300 miles from the Canaries to Asia on Marco Polo and the map of the Florentine Toscanelli, and that Portugal’s King John II turned him down because the distance seemed too low. The real distance, it notes, is about 12,200 miles. After being refused in several European courts, Columbus won the backing of Isabella and Ferdinand. The Spanish monarchs hoped to reach the riches of Asia without the Italian and Portuguese middlemen. The World History Encyclopedia adds that they told him to claim any land not already under a sovereign for Spain and the Catholic Church, and gave him a contract making him governor of the lands he took. Columbus himself, according to the American Yawp, was “confoundingly wrong about the size of the earth and spectacularly lucky that two large continents lurked in his path.” First voyage (1492–1493). Columbus sailed from Spain on August 3, 1492, with three small ships, the Niña, Pinta, and Santa María, and some ninety men. After about two months at sea they landed on October 12 on an island of the modern Bahamas. The Lucayan people, who belonged to the wider Taíno world, called it Guanahani. Columbus renamed it San Salvador. Which modern island this was is still debated, and Sanama Cay, Rum Cay, Grand Turk, and the Plana Cays have all been proposed. The most popular theory is the island formerly called Watling Island, which was officially renamed San Salvador in 1925. Columbus sailed on to Cuba and Hispaniola. The Taíno fished and grew corn, yams, and cassava, and he wrote to the Spanish crown that they were “very gentle and without knowledge of what is evil.” But he had come for wealth, and he found little. He saw that some Taíno wore small gold ornaments and reported that “with fifty men they can all be subjugated and made to do what is required of them.” He left thirty-nine Spaniards at a fort on Hispaniola and returned to Spain with about a dozen captured Taíno. Second voyage (1493–1496). Columbus came back as governor with seventeen ships and over a thousand men, still believing he had reached the East Indies. When gold proved hard to find, the Spanish turned to forced labor and violence. The World History Encyclopedia says that the settlers established the encomienda, a grant of land and Native laborers, and that they used mastiffs to terrorize Native fighters. The Yawp calls the encomienda an exploitative feudal arrangement in which Native workers were tied to estates. Third and fourth voyages (1498–1504). On the third voyage Columbus reached the mainland of South America. The World History Encyclopedia says that his colonists were by now capturing and selling Native people, and that after charges of tyranny and corruption Columbus and his brother were arrested and sent to Spain, where the monarchs acquitted them. On his last voyage, in 1502, he explored the coast of Central America, but a storm drove his ship onto Jamaica, where he and his men were stranded until they were rescued, largely through their own efforts. He returned to Spain, where he died in Valladolid in May 1506. He had believed throughout that the lands he found were part of Asia. The Spanish seized Taíno labor and land. The Lucayans of the Bahamas, whom Columbus first met, were taken as slaves, and “in less than 30 years, through enslavement, murder, and disease,” National Geographic writes, they were essentially wiped out. On Hispaniola the Taíno, who had at first been friendly, resisted Spanish efforts to kill, enslave, or assimilate them. The priest Bartolomé de Las Casas, who sailed to the New World in 1502, was a witness. He wrote of Spanish cruelty and asked: “Who in future generations will believe this?” Within a few generations Hispaniola was depopulated. The estimates of its population before contact range from fewer than one million to as many as eight million, and Las Casas thought it was three million. Disease did even more than violence. Native peoples had no immunity to smallpox, typhus, influenza, measles and other Old World illnesses, which carried off millions. Alfred Crosby notes that the diseases brought from Europe included smallpox, malaria, yellow fever, measles, cholera, typhoid, and bubonic plague, while the list of infections native to the New World was very short. Columbus’s voyages opened the way to the conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires, with Spanish soldiers aided by smallpox and by the enemies of those empires. Spain and Portugal divided the New World between them in the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494, after the pope intervened, and Spanish conquerors set up the framework of the Atlantic slave trade over a century before the first Africans reached Jamestown. After Las Casas published his account of Spanish abuses, the crown abolished the encomienda in 1542 and replaced it with the repartimiento, which was meant to be milder but kept many of the same abuses. Las Casas’s writings also gave other European powers a humanitarian argument for challenging Spain, and the Spanish called this the “Black Legend.” No one knows how many people lived in the Americas in 1492. Estimates run from 2 million to 100 million. Henry Dobyns put the figure at 18 million and estimated that 95 percent of Native Americans died in the first 130 years after contact. Some scholars estimate that as much as 90 percent of the population perished within a century and a half. Nothing else in history, the Yawp argues, rivals this demographic disaster. The exchange of plants and animals that followed changed diets and landscapes across the world. Potatoes, tomatoes, and chocolate came to Europe, and horses and pigs came to the Americas. Columbus’s reputation has changed. The World History Encyclopedia argues that the familiar story of Columbus as the hero who discovered America, and who proved the world round, owes much to Washington Irving’s popular biography of 1828 and not to Columbus’s own writings. President Benjamin Harrison called for a national celebration in 1892, and Colorado made it a state holiday in 1906. It adds that Italian American groups, who had faced prejudice, did much to establish Columbus Day, and that since the 1970s there have been calls to honor the Indigenous peoples harmed by the voyages instead. The debate continues. National Geographic adds that Indigenous activists in the Caribbean today work to preserve the language, culture, and arts of the peoples who survived. Whatever one thinks of Columbus, 1492 began lasting contact between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. It transformed the peoples, plants, animals, and diseases of both and began a long collision of cultures. They are very gentle and without knowledge of what is evil. Christopher Columbus report to the Spanish crown on the Taíno With fifty men they can all be subjugated and made to do what is required of them. Christopher Columbus report to the Spanish crown Who in future generations will believe this? I myself writing it as a knowledgeable eyewitness can hardly believe it.
