title: The Compromise of 1850
subtitle: Congress tries to settle the slavery question after the Mexican War
summary: The lands taken from Mexico forced Congress to decide whether slavery could spread west. In 1850, after seven months of debate, Congress passed five laws: California entered as a free state; New Mexico and Utah territories would decide on slavery themselves; the slave trade (but not slavery) was abolished in Washington, D.C.; a Texas boundary dispute was settled; and a harsh new Fugitive Slave Act required people in free states to help capture freedom seekers. The compromise postponed disunion but deepened Northern anger over slavery.
thumbAlt: Engraving of the U.S. Senate in session in 1850
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Territorial expansion Constitution and law
text: Washington, D.C. Architects Senator Henry Clay proposed the package; Senator Stephen A. Douglas passed it as separate bills California Admitted as a free state Utah and New Mexico Organized as territories under popular sovereignty Fugitive Slave Act Required officials in all states to arrest suspected fugitives and punished anyone who helped them The Mexican-American War added vast western lands. In 1849, swelled by the gold rush, California asked to join the Union as a free state. Its admission would upset the balance of slave and free states in the Senate that had held since the Missouri Compromise, and Southerners threatened secession. Northerners wanted slavery kept out of the new territories; many Southerners insisted on their right to take enslaved people anywhere; others proposed extending the Missouri line to the Pacific or letting settlers decide. Southerners also complained that Northern states were not returning people who escaped slavery. In January 1850, Senator Henry Clay of Kentucky proposed resolutions to “adjust amicably all existing questions of controversy … arising out of the institution of slavery.” In one of the most famous debates in congressional history, the Senate argued over his package for seven months and then voted it down. Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois broke the package into separate bills, which passed with shifting majorities. Five statutes were enacted in September 1850. The compromise calmed the immediate crisis. But the new Fugitive Slave Act enraged many Northerners: it required federal and local officials everywhere to help capture suspected fugitives and fined and imprisoned anyone who aided them. Abolitionists resisted enforcement, the Underground Railroad became more organized, and many free Black Northerners fled to Canada. The principle of popular sovereignty adopted for Utah and New Mexico would be extended, disastrously, by the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854. The Compromise of 1850 turned out to be the last great sectional bargain before the Civil War. The Compromise of 1850 bought a decade of uneasy peace, but by forcing free states to enforce slavery, it made the institution a personal matter for millions of Northerners. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aHIZONFF4nk The COMPROMISE of 1850 [APUSH Review Unit 5 Topic 4] Period 5: 1844-1877 Heimler's History 7:09 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uvlUqV1vwTc The Compromise of 1850 Explained: US History Review Hip Hughes (HipHughes) 5:01 2026-10-22

title: The Disputed Election of 1876 and the End of Reconstruction
subtitle: The “Compromise of 1877”
summary: The presidential election of 1876 between Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel J. Tilden produced disputed returns in three Southern states and Oregon. Tilden led the popular vote by about 250,000 but was one electoral vote short. Congress created a special Electoral Commission, which awarded all the disputed votes to Hayes. As Democrats threatened to obstruct the count, Hayes’s allies and Southern Democrats negotiated, and Hayes withdrew the federal troops protecting the last Republican governments in the South. The settlement, often called the Compromise of 1877, marked the end of Reconstruction.
location: Washington, D.C.; Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon
thumbAlt: Political cartoon about the disputed election of 1876
aliases: Hayes-Tilden Electoral Commission election of 1876
themeText: Parties and elections Civil rights and citizenship Voting rights African American history
text: Washington, D.C.; Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon Candidates Rutherford B. Hayes (Republican) vs. Samuel J. Tilden (Democrat) Popular vote Tilden ahead by about 250,000 Disputed Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and one Oregon elector Electoral Commission 15 members; Republicans held an 8–7 edge after Justice Joseph Bradley replaced David Davis Result Hayes president; federal troops withdrawn from New Orleans and Columbia By 1876 Republicans were weakened by the depression that followed the Panic of 1873 and by scandals in the Grant administration. Democrats had regained control of most Southern states, often through intimidation and violence against Black and white Republican voters. Only Louisiana, South Carolina, and Florida still had Republican governments, protected by small numbers of federal troops. The election was the longest, closest, and most bitterly contested in the nation’s history to that time. Tilden carried the popular vote and was one electoral vote short of a majority. In Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina, both parties claimed victory; Republican-controlled returning boards, citing intimidation, threw out enough Democratic votes to give Hayes the states. In Oregon, one Hayes elector was ineligible because he held federal office. In January 1877 Congress passed the Electoral Commission Act, creating a commission of five senators, five representatives, and five Supreme Court justices to decide which returns to count. The swing member was to be Justice David Davis, an independent, but he withdrew after being elected to the Senate, and was replaced by Republican Joseph Bradley, giving Republicans an 8–7 majority. The commission awarded every disputed state to Hayes. Furious Democrats delayed the count with filibusters, threatening to leave the country without a president on inauguration day. Southern Democrats and politicians close to Hayes negotiated. Southerners sought the removal of the troops protecting Republican governments in New Orleans and Columbia, a federal subsidy for the Texas & Pacific Railroad, and cabinet posts. Historians at the Miller Center note that negotiations almost certainly took place, but that any formal “deal” beyond what Hayes had already promised is doubtful. Hayes was declared the winner and took office in March 1877. Hayes withdrew the federal troops, and the remaining Republican state governments collapsed. Democrats branded him “Rutherfraud” and “His Fraudulency.” With the withdrawal of federal support, the number of Black officeholders declined significantly. Whether or not there was an explicit bargain, 1877 marked the end of federal efforts to protect Black citizenship in the South. White Democratic “Redeemer” governments consolidated power, and over the next two decades Southern states disenfranchised Black voters and built the system of Jim Crow segregation. The election remained the most disputed in American history until the contest of 2000. The resolution of the 1876 election traded the protection of Black Southerners’ rights for political peace between white North and South, closing Reconstruction and opening the Jim Crow era. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nowsS7pMApI Reconstruction and 1876: Crash Course US History #22 CrashCourse 13:00 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LjA1MzUuHk8 How close was the US to another Civil War in 1876? title: The Constitutional Convention
subtitle: Fifty-five delegates meet in secret to redesign the American government
summary: In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve of the thirteen states met in secret in Philadelphia, officially to revise the Articles of Confederation. Instead, they wrote a new Constitution. They argued bitterly over how to represent large and small states, how much power to give the central government, and how to count enslaved people, and they settled each dispute by compromise. Only 55 of the 74 delegates appointed ever attended. Three of those who stayed to the end refused to sign. The document the others signed on September 17 became the framework of the United States government.
thumbAlt: Howard Chandler Christy’s painting of the signing of the Constitution
aliases: Federal Convention Philadelphia Convention Virginia Plan New Jersey Plan Great Compromise Connecticut Compromise Committee of Style Madison's notes
themeText: Constitution and law Political thought Slavery and emancipation
text: Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall), Philadelphia Delegates 74 appointed, 55 attended; twelve states represented Presiding officer George Washington, elected unanimously on May 25 Absent state Rhode Island refused to send delegates Secrecy Sessions were closed; James Madison’s daily notes are the fullest record Refused to sign George Mason, Edmund Randolph, Elbridge Gerry Adjourned September 17, 1787, at 4 p.m. By 1786 many leaders believed the union was failing. Under the Articles of Confederation, in force since 1781 as a “league of friendship” among thirteen sovereign states, the central government could not tax, could not effectively regulate commerce, and had little power to settle quarrels between the states. Congress faced an empty treasury and a flood of paper money. Many farmers were jailed for debt or lost their farms for unpaid taxes. The burden of paying Revolutionary War debts fell on the states, which owed money to the lenders who held their war bonds. In 1786 farmers in western Massachusetts, led by the veteran Daniel Shays, blocked courts to stop foreclosures. They saw their cause as an extension of the “Spirit of 1776.” The state militia put them down in January 1787. The rebellion frightened wealthy Americans. George Washington wrote to Madison from Mount Vernon: “Wisdom and good examples are necessary at this time to rescue the political machine from the impending storm.” For Madison, the lesson was that “liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as the abuses of power.” A meeting at Annapolis in September 1786 had called for a broader convention. Madison and Alexander Hamilton wrote its report, which called on Congress to summon delegates from all the states to revise the Articles, and Congress issued the call even though many saw the report as a usurpation of its authority. James Madison had spent years studying the history of confederacies and republics and was convinced that the Articles had to be replaced. The research gave him a bold idea. Classical learning said that a republic could survive only in a small, uniform state, but Madison believed that an “extended republic” of diverse people could work. Other leaders wanted a government that could raise revenue, pay debts, and regulate trade. Some delegates came mainly to protect their states’ interests. Some of the era’s major figures were missing. Thomas Jefferson and John Adams were abroad, John Jay was at the Foreign Office in New York, and Patrick Henry, who said he “smelt a rat,” refused to attend. He rightly suspected that Madison wanted a powerful central government that would weaken the state legislatures. Rhode Island, whose leaders saw a conspiracy against the existing government, sent no one. Washington, who was suffering from rheumatism and doubted the convention would accomplish much, agonized for months before agreeing to attend. The delegates averaged 42 years of age. Benjamin Franklin, at 81, was the oldest, and Jonathan Dayton, at 27, the youngest. Opening and secrecy. The convention formally got under way on May 25, 1787, when a quorum of seven states was finally present. Dirt was spread on the street outside the State House to muffle the noise of carriages, and guards kept the curious away. On the motion of Robert Morris, Washington was unanimously elected president of the convention. No reporters or visitors were allowed. Jefferson, writing from Paris, thought it “so abominable a precedent” to tie up the delegates’ tongues. Madison sat in front of the presiding officer and recorded the debates, missing no day and no major speech, and he said later that sitting in the stifling hall almost killed him. The Virginia Plan (May 29). Edmund Randolph opened the debate with a plan the Virginians had drawn up. It proposed a government with a legislature, an executive, and a judiciary, each checking the others, and a national veto over state laws. The Yawp adds that the legislature would have two houses, with states represented according to population or tax base. Randolph admitted that it “meant a strong consolidated union in which the idea of states should be nearly annihilated.” By mid-June, as the National Archives puts it, “rather than amend the existing Articles, the Convention would draft an entirely new frame of government.” The delegates also agreed that the new Constitution should be ratified by conventions of the people, not by the state legislatures, where officeholders had power to lose. The New Jersey Plan and Hamilton (June). On June 13 delegates from the smaller states rallied around William Paterson’s plan, which would only have revised the Articles to give Congress the power to raise revenue and regulate commerce. After three days of debate the convention voted it down. On June 18 Hamilton presented his own plan, with an executive and senators who would serve for life or during good behavior. He called the British government “the best in the world.” It won no following. The great deadlock. By late June the large and small states were arguing over representation in the legislature, and the debate descended into threats and accusations. Franklin urged the delegates to begin each day with prayer, but the convention, Hugh Williamson noted, had no money to pay a preacher. On June 29 the convention voted that the House of Representatives would be based on population. A motion for equal state representation in the Senate ended in a tie, and one member said the convention “was on the verge of dissolution, scarce held together by the strength of an hair.” On July 10 Washington complained that he regretted having had “any agency” in the proceedings. The compromises on representation and slavery. On July 12 Oliver Ellsworth proposed that House seats be based on the free population plus three-fifths of “all other persons.” In the following week the members agreed that direct taxes would follow representation, and then approved equal representation in the Senate. The Yawp credits Roger Sherman with the compromise and notes that the final version gave each state two senators who voted independently. A Committee of Detail wrote a first draft, which the convention took up on August 6. The delegates then fought over commerce. Charles Pinckney warned that if Congress controlled trade, the southern states would be “nothing more than overseers for the Northern States.” On August 21 the dispute became bound up with slavery when Luther Martin proposed a tax on imported slaves. John Rutledge of South Carolina insisted that “Interest alone is the governing principle with nations.” Mason opposed unlimited importation but also wanted federal protection for existing slave property. He later described what happened as “a bargain”: South Carolina and Georgia accepted a simple majority for navigation laws, and in exchange New England delegates supported allowing the slave trade to continue for twenty years. The Constitution says that Congress may not prohibit the importation of “such Persons as any of the States now existing shall think proper to admit” before 1808. It counts “three fifths of all other Persons” for representation and taxes and requires that a person “held to Service or Labour” who escapes be “delivered up” on claim. The executive and the final draft. The delegates considered electing the executive by the people, by state legislatures, by governors, and by Congress. The result, the National Archives says, was the Electoral College, “a master stroke of compromise.” Mason predicted that the House would choose the president 19 times out of 20. On the question of a single executive, the Yawp notes that James Wilson’s proposal on June 1 was contentious because it conjured up images of an elected monarchy. On August 31 Mason said he “would sooner chop off his right hand than put it to the Constitution as it now stands.” He wanted a bill of rights and a second convention, and the motion was voted down. A Committee of Style and Arrangement, with Gouverneur Morris as its chief architect, produced the final text, which went before the convention on September 12. Signing (September 15 to 17). On September 15 Randolph, Mason, and Gerry proposed that state conventions make amendments to be considered by a second general convention. They were soundly rebuffed, and every state delegation voted aye. On September 17 James Wilson read a speech by Franklin. “I confess that there are several parts of this constitution which I do not at present approve,” Franklin wrote, but he agreed to it “because I expect no better, and because I am not sure, that it is not the best.” He urged every member who still had objections to “doubt a little of his own infallibility.” Before the vote, Nathaniel Gorham proposed changing the ratio of representatives from one for every 40,000 people to one for every 30,000. Washington, who as presiding officer had until then kept his views on questions before the House to himself, said that he wished the change to be adopted. Randolph said that he refused to sign because he feared that nine states would fail to ratify the plan. Mason and Gerry also withheld their signatures. The other delegates present signed and the convention adjourned at 4 p.m., then dined at City Tavern. The Constitution was sent to Congress, then sitting in New York, with a cover letter from Washington, and to the states for ratification by special conventions. Nine states had to approve it. The debate that followed was fierce. Federalists, who supported the Constitution, and Anti-Federalists, who feared a distant government of the wealthy, wrote in newspapers across the country. The Anti-Federalist essays signed “Centinel” warned that the states would be “melted down” into a despotism of the “well-born.” Hamilton, Madison, and John Jay answered with the 85 essays of the Federalist Papers. The absence of a bill of rights became a rallying point for opponents, because the convention had voted down Mason’s proposal. Delaware, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Georgia, and Connecticut had ratified by January 9, 1788. Massachusetts followed on February 6 by 187 to 168, after Federalists agreed to recommend amendments, and Rhode Island’s voters rejected the Constitution ten to one in a referendum in March. New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify, and Congress learned of it on July 2, 1788. Virginia and New York ratified within two months, by very close margins. Hamilton thought that most New Yorkers actually opposed it, and the National Archives says only the promise of amendments secured Federalist victory. The convention created a durable framework of government built on compromise between large and small states, between nation and states, and between North and South. The National Archives calls the Constitution “a model of cooperative statesmanship and the art of compromise.” The bargains over slavery also wrote protections for the institution into the Constitution, and the National Archives article quotes a contemporary critic, the minister Samuel Hopkins, who called the document a sellout and fit for the flames. Because the debates were secret, the record that survives depends on Madison’s notes, which remain central to arguments over what the Constitution means. Opponents’ demand for a bill of rights was met in the first amendments added after ratification. In four months the convention replaced a failing confederation with a national government designed to be strong enough to govern but divided enough to restrain itself. Wisdom and good examples are necessary at this time to rescue the political machine from the impending storm. George Washington letter to James Madison on Shays’s Rebellion I think it will astonish our enemies, who are waiting with confidence to hear that our councils are confounded like those of the builders of Babel. title: COVID-19 Pandemic
subtitle: The coronavirus pandemic in the United States, 2020–2023
summary: COVID-19, a disease caused by a new coronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, reached the United States in January 2020. Within weeks schools, offices, and businesses closed. Unemployment reached 14.7 percent, the highest since the Great Depression, and hospitals, above all in New York, ran short of supplies. Vaccines developed at record speed were authorized in December 2020. But new variants kept the virus spreading, and masks and vaccines became politically divisive. By May 2022 more than one million Americans had died. The Miller Center counts more than 1.1 million deaths in all, the worst toll from one disease since the influenza pandemic of 1918.
thumbAlt: Electron microscope image of the SARS-CoV-2 virus that causes COVID-19
aliases: coronavirus COVID SARS-CoV-2 lockdowns Operation Warp Speed CARES Act American Rescue Plan Delta variant Omicron variant
themeText: Public health Economy and finance Everyday life The presidency
text: Nationwide and worldwide First U.S. case Confirmed January 20, 2020, in Washington State Pandemic declared By the World Health Organization, March 11, 2020 National emergency March 13, 2020; CARES Act signed March 27, 2020 First vaccine authorization December 11, 2020 (Pfizer-BioNTech) U.S. deaths About 378,000 in 2020 alone; more than one million by May 2022 Global emergency ended May 5, 2023 (World Health Organization) In late 2019 a cluster of patients in Wuhan, a city in China’s Hubei Province, fell ill with an unusual pneumonia that did not respond to standard treatment. The first cases seemed connected to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market. Chinese health officials identified a new coronavirus as the cause, and scientists in China and Australia published its genetic sequence in January 2020. The American Yawp notes that other coronaviruses had been identified and contained in earlier years. This one spread before many people showed symptoms, and it was especially dangerous for older people and those with chronic illness. On January 23, 2020, China placed Wuhan, a city of 11 million people, under lockdown, but the virus had already escaped through travel. At the end of January the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern. Early American testing was slow. Some of the first CDC test kits produced “untrustworthy results,” and the FDA later allowed other laboratories to develop their own tests to address shortages. Soon the CDC was finding cases that could not be traced to travel, a sign that the virus was spreading in American communities. The first wave (spring 2020). The CDC confirmed the first American case on January 20, 2020, in Washington State. The CDC reported the first American death in Washington, and the Miller Center dates it to February. On March 11 the World Health Organization declared a pandemic, and on March 13 the Trump administration declared a national emergency. States began shutting down. On March 15 New York City closed its public schools, the largest school system in the country with 1.1 million students. Americans stayed home, schools moved online, and in-person work was largely left to “essential workers.” On March 27 President Donald Trump signed the CARES Act, which the Miller Center values at $2.2 trillion, with payments of $1,200 per adult, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable small-business loans. Hospitals ran short of gowns, masks, and even body bags, especially in New York. States, the Yawp writes, were left to compete with one another for protective equipment. By May unemployment had reached 14.7 percent, with 20.5 million people out of work, and on May 28 the recorded death toll passed 100,000. Masks, waves, and protests. In the spring of 2020 the CDC recommended that people wear masks outside the home. With medical masks scarce, many made their own, but mask-wearing became politicized. Hourly workers without paid sick leave often had to choose between a paycheck and their health. A wave hit the South in the summer of 2020, and the worst came that winter, when nearly three thousand Americans died every day through January and much of February 2021. The Miller Center notes that by April 2020 more Americans had died than people in any other country, a position the country held until the end of the pandemic. Trump downplayed the risks and contracted the virus himself in October 2020. Vaccines (December 2020 onward). On April 30, 2020, the administration had launched Operation Warp Speed, which funded six vaccine candidates while they were still in trials. Public health experts credited it with speeding the vaccines. In November the Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines proved about 95 percent effective in trials. On December 11 the FDA authorized the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, and Sandra Lindsay, a nurse in New York, became the first American outside the trials to be vaccinated. Health workers and residents of long-term care facilities went first. On March 11, 2021, President Joe Biden signed the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan, and by late spring Americans were being vaccinated by the millions. But many refused, swayed by conspiracy theories on social media or by politics. Variants (2021–2022). In June 2021 the Delta variant, first identified in India, became dominant in the United States and brought a third wave. In late November the World Health Organization named Omicron, first identified in South Africa, a variant of concern. The CDC estimated it was about 1.6 times more transmissible than Delta, and the first American case was found in California on December 1. By December 15, 2021, the toll had passed 800,000, and one in every hundred Americans aged 65 or older had died of the virus. In May 2022 the official death toll crossed one million. In 2020 alone about 3.36 million Americans died of all causes, and the age-adjusted death rate rose 15.9 percent. COVID-19 was listed as a cause or contributing cause in about 378,000 deaths and became the third leading cause of death after heart disease and cancer. The CDC found the highest overall death rates among Black and American Indian or Alaska Native people, and the highest COVID-19 death rates among American Indian or Alaska Native and Hispanic people, as well as among men and the elderly. The pandemic upended work and family life. An estimated 5.1 million women left the workforce when schools and child care closed in 2020. By May 2021, the CDC timeline notes, only 56 percent of American women were working for pay, the lowest share since 1986. Many white-collar workers moved to working from home, while essential workers kept going in. The summer of 2020 also saw nationwide protests over the killing of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer, held in the middle of the lockdowns. On May 5, 2023, the World Health Organization declared that COVID-19 was “an established and ongoing health issue” and no longer a global emergency, noting that 13.3 billion vaccine doses had been given worldwide. The Miller Center calls it the deadliest disease to strike the United States since the influenza pandemic of 1918 and 1919, with more than 1.1 million American lives lost. It also deepened Americans’ divisions over masks, vaccines, and scientific expertise. With more than a million American deaths, COVID-19 was the defining public health crisis of the early twenty-first century and deepened the country’s political divisions. Disruption to everyday life may be severe. title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
subtitle: The October 1962 showdown in which the superpowers came closest to nuclear war
summary: In October 1962 an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba. In the days that followed, President John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev faced each other in the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War, the moment when the two superpowers came closest to nuclear conflict. Kennedy imposed a naval “quarantine” of the island; Khrushchev finally agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba, and a secret promise to pull U.S. missiles out of Turkey.
thumbAlt: U.S. aerial reconnaissance photograph of a Soviet medium-range ballistic missile launch site at San Cristobal, Cuba, November 1, 1962
aliases: Cuban missile crisis October Crisis missile crisis
themeText: The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency War and the military
text: Cuba, Washington, and Moscow Discovery October 14, 1962: a U-2 photographs missile sites under construction in Cuba Quarantine Announced on national television on October 22, 1962 Closest call U.S. forces at DEFCON 2, war involving the Strategic Air Command imminent; a U-2 shot down over Cuba on October 27 The deal Soviet missiles removed; U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba; secretly, U.S. Jupiter missiles withdrawn from Turkey (April 1963) Aftermath A White House–Kremlin “Hotline” and the 1963 treaty limiting nuclear tests The crisis brought the world to the edge of nuclear war and then pushed both superpowers to step back: they set up a direct line of communication and took the first steps toward controlling the nuclear arms race. After the failed CIA-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961, the Kennedy administration planned a covert campaign against Fidel Castro’s government, Operation Mongoose. In July 1962 Khrushchev reached a secret agreement with Castro to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, both to deter another invasion and, as historians at the Miller Center note, to offset the large American lead in nuclear weapons. Along with the missiles came some 42,000 Soviet troops. Construction began in late summer. When American surveillance flights detected a general Soviet arms buildup, Kennedy publicly warned on September 4 against bringing offensive weapons into Cuba. The crisis grew out of the arms race and the Cold War rivalry over Cuba. The Soviets wanted to protect Castro’s government, to compete with China for the loyalty of revolutionaries worldwide, and to neutralize the large American advantage in nuclear weapons. The United States, which itself had nuclear missiles in Turkey aimed at the Soviet Union, declared that it would not permit offensive weapons in Cuba. Secrecy and mutual misunderstanding turned the deployment into a showdown. On October 14 a U-2 took pictures clearly showing sites for medium- and intermediate-range nuclear missiles; the next day the photographs reached the White House. Kennedy gathered his closest advisers in secret meetings. All the Joint Chiefs of Staff urged an air strike followed by an invasion; others favored stern warnings. Kennedy chose a middle course. On October 22 he announced on national television a naval “quarantine” of Cuba, a word chosen because a “blockade” would legally mean a state of war, and warned that any missile launched from Cuba would be treated as a Soviet attack on the United States, “requiring a full retaliatory response upon the Soviet Union.” Khrushchev called the quarantine an “act of aggression,” but on October 24 and 25 some Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line. Meanwhile the missile sites neared readiness, and American forces went to DEFCON 2, meaning war involving the Strategic Air Command was imminent. On October 26 a Soviet agent approached ABC News reporter John Scali with an offer: the missiles would go if the United States promised not to invade. That night came a long, emotional letter from Khrushchev with a similar proposal, urging both sides to “untie that knot.” Hope faded the next day, October 27: a second Soviet message demanded the removal of U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey, and an American U-2 was shot down over Cuba. Kennedy chose to answer the first letter and ignore the second, while his brother, Attorney General Robert Kennedy, told the Soviet ambassador privately that the Turkish missiles would be removed soon, but could not be part of any public deal. On October 28 Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be dismantled and taken home. The naval quarantine stayed in place until the Soviets also agreed to remove their IL-28 bombers; the United States ended it on November 20, 1962. The Jupiter missiles left Turkey in April 1963. The outcome strengthened Kennedy’s standing at home and abroad and helped repair the damage done by the Bay of Pigs. Because the two leaders had struggled throughout the crisis to understand each other’s intentions, a direct telephone link between the White House and the Kremlin, the “Hotline”, was set up. Having looked into the abyss, both superpowers began to reconsider the nuclear arms race. In 1963 the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union agreed to ban nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space, and underwater, an agreement Kennedy considered his greatest accomplishment. The State Department’s historians call the crisis a singular event of the Cold War, shaped as much by miscalculation and miscommunication as by calculation, and played out largely between the White House and the Kremlin themselves. title: D-Day
subtitle: The Allied invasion of Normandy, June 6, 1944
summary: On June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 American, British, Canadian, and other Allied troops landed along fifty miles of the heavily fortified Normandy coast of France, supported by more than 5,000 ships and 13,000 aircraft. Called Operation Overlord and commanded by General Dwight D. Eisenhower, it was the largest amphibious assault in history. More than 9,000 Allied soldiers were killed or wounded that day, but the Allies gained a foothold in western Europe that led to the liberation of France and the defeat of Nazi Germany.
thumbAlt: American soldiers wading ashore from a landing craft on Omaha Beach
aliases: Operation Overlord Normandy landings Omaha Beach Utah Beach
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Normandy, France Date June 6, 1944 Supreme commander General Dwight D. Eisenhower Force Nearly 160,000 troops; more than 5,000 ships and 13,000 aircraft; 23,400 airborne troops dropped overnight Beaches Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword Casualties More than 9,000 Allied soldiers killed or wounded on D-Day Allied planners had considered a cross-Channel assault since France fell in 1940. At the Tehran Conference in November 1943, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin pressed Britain and the United States to invade France to relieve pressure on the Eastern Front; Roosevelt agreed, and Eisenhower was named to command the operation. By May 1944 nearly 2.9 million Allied troops had gathered in southern England. A second front in the west would force Germany to fight on two sides and open a direct route to the German heartland. Before dawn on June 5, Eisenhower decided to proceed. In his Order of the Day he told the troops, “The eyes of the world are upon you.” He also wrote out, on a pad of paper, a press release to be issued if the landings failed, mistakenly dating it “July 5.” Overnight, more than a thousand transport planes dropped 23,400 American, British, and Canadian airborne troops behind the beaches. On June 6 troops came ashore on five beaches code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. By day’s end the Allies held a foothold on the continent. The assault phase, Operation Neptune, continued through the end of June as the Allies landed more troops and supplies. Progress across France was much slower than hoped, but Paris was liberated about two months after the landings. With the Soviet Union advancing from the east, D-Day sealed Germany’s defeat; the war in Europe ended eleven months later. The landings remain the defining image of American and Allied sacrifice in World War II. title: The Dust Bowl
subtitle: Drought, dust storms, and migration on the southern Plains in the 1930s
summary: During the 1930s, years of drought combined with farming practices that had stripped the Great Plains of its protective grass, and high winds lifted the exposed soil into enormous dust storms. The worst-hit area (the western third of Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, most of the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico) became known as the Dust Bowl. Farms failed, hundreds of thousands of people left the region, and the disaster pushed the federal government to promote soil conservation.
location: Southern Great Plains: western Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico
thumbAlt: A wall of dust approaching a town in Texas in 1935
aliases: Black Sunday black blizzards Okies Migrant Mother Soil Conservation Service
themeText: Land and environment Economy and finance Everyday life
text: Southern Great Plains: western Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico Droughts 1930–31, 1934, 1936, and 1939–40 Black Sunday April 14, 1935 Name Coined by Associated Press reporter Robert Geiger in April 1935 Relief By 1937, 21% of rural Plains families received federal emergency relief Outmigration Oklahoma lost 440,000 people, 18.4% of its 1930 population In the 1920s, low crop prices and high machinery costs pushed Plains farmers to plow marginal land, and many abandoned soil conservation practices. Plowing destroyed the native sod that had held the dry soil in place; relatively wet years had masked the danger. Drought covered almost the entire Plains for nearly a decade, in at least four distinct episodes that came too quickly for the land to recover. With the ground cover gone and few windbreaks, high winds churned the dry topsoil into storms that people called “black blizzards” or “dusters.” The disaster struck farmers already ruined by years of falling prices and foreclosures during the Great Depression. Dust storms blotted out the sun, choked people and livestock,. Some carried dirt as far east as Washington, D.C., New England, and ships on the Atlantic. The worst came on Sunday, April 14, 1935, “Black Sunday”, when a towering wall of dust swept across the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, turning afternoon into total darkness. The next day an Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, who had been caught in the storm near Boise City, Oklahoma, wrote of the “dust bowl,” and the name stuck. Crops failed across the region, and many families gave up. Hundreds of thousands headed west, especially to California; the migrants, many of them from Oklahoma, were disparagingly called “Okies.” Some states tried to keep them out, and California officials briefly blockaded the border in 1935–1936. Dorothea Lange’s 1936 photograph Migrant Mother, taken at a farmworkers’ camp in Nipomo, California, and John Steinbeck’s 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath made the migrants’ hardship a national story. Federal drought relief began in 1932, with funds specifically for drought relief released in the fall of 1933. In March 1935 soil scientist Hugh Hammond Bennett, a Roosevelt adviser, testified to Congress on the need for better soil conservation, by one widely told account, as dust from the Plains darkened the sky over Washington, and Congress passed the Soil Conservation Act that year. A 1937 Works Progress Administration bulletin reported that 21 percent of rural Plains families were on federal relief. Near-normal rains returned by 1941, and World War II revived the farm economy. The 1930s drought remains the nation’s “drought of record.” Its lessons (soil conservation, windbreaks, and government drought planning) reduced the damage when severe drought returned to the Plains in the 1950s. The Dust Bowl was one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, a human-made catastrophe as much as a natural one, and it changed how Americans farm and manage land. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sxG6Lwkzi7c The Dust Bowl: Darkness in the Great Depression Geographics 19:21 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pJ9QOcVt1Hc The Dust Bowl and the Depression NBC News Learn 3:42 2026-10-22

title: The Election of 1800
subtitle: The first transfer of power between rival parties
summary: In 1800 the Democratic-Republicans under Thomas Jefferson defeated President John Adams and the Federalists in a campaign so bitter that each side predicted disaster, even war, if the other won. A flaw in the Constitution then produced a tie between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, and the Federalist-controlled House of Representatives had to decide. After thirty-five deadlocked ballots it chose Jefferson. Adams accepted defeat and left office peacefully, the first transfer of power from one party to another in the United States.
location: Nationwide; decided in the House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.
thumbAlt: Campaign banner celebrating Thomas Jefferson
aliases: Revolution of 1800 Jefferson–Burr tie Twelfth Amendment Aaron Burr
themeText: Parties and elections The presidency Constitution and law
text: Nationwide; decided in the House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. Electoral votes Jefferson 73, Burr 73, Adams 65, C. C. Pinckney 64 Decided by The House of Representatives, on the thirty-sixth ballot, February 1801 Result Jefferson president, Burr vice president Jefferson’s name for it “The revolution of 1800” Constitutional fix The Twelfth Amendment, ratified June 15, 1804 By 1800 the country was divided between two parties. Federalists, led by Adams and Alexander Hamilton, favored a strong national government and commerce; Democratic-Republicans, led by Jefferson and James Madison, spoke for states’ rights and farmers. Jefferson had been the informal leader of the opposition since the mid-1790s, and as Adams’s vice president he wrote the Kentucky Resolution of 1798, attacking the Alien and Sedition Acts as unconstitutional. Adams had grown unpopular. Besides the Alien and Sedition Acts, Americans resented a direct tax of 1798, military preparations against France, and the use of federal troops to crush a small tax revolt led by John Fries in Pennsylvania. When Adams proclaimed a national thanksgiving in 1798, the American Yawp notes, rioters forced his family to flee Philadelphia until the day was over. A divided Federalist Party. Many Federalists turned against Adams because he made peace with France instead of fighting a war. A private letter in which Hamilton described Adams’s “great and intrinsic defects in his character” was obtained by Burr and leaked to the press. New York. Jefferson knew he had to carry New York, so Burr, a New Yorker, joined the ticket. When Republicans won the New York legislature in 1799, Jefferson’s chances rose. The original electoral rules. Each elector cast two votes, with no way to mark one for president and one for vice president. If every Republican elector voted for both Republican candidates, the result would be a tie. Neither candidate campaigned in person; the battle was fought in party newspapers. One Federalist paper warned that under Jefferson “murder, robbery, rape, adultery, and incest will be openly taught and practiced,” and others attacked him as an infidel. Republican papers in turn mocked Adams as a fool and a would-be tyrant. When the electoral votes were counted, Jefferson and Burr each had 73, Adams 65 and his running mate Charles C. Pinckney 64. The tie went to the House, where the Federalists held a majority. Through thirty-five ballots no candidate won a majority of the state delegations. Hamilton, who despised Burr as unprincipled, persuaded a few Federalists who had backed Burr to turn in blank ballots instead, and on the thirty-sixth ballot Jefferson was elected. In his inaugural address in March 1801 Jefferson offered an olive branch: “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” Adams had made John Marshall chief justice, and the clash between Jefferson’s administration and Marshall’s court led to Marbury v. Madison in 1803. Hamilton’s role in the House vote enraged Burr, who killed him in a duel several years later. Republicans celebrated a “bloodless revolution.” They saw themselves as rescuing the country from an aristocratic takeover, partly because the Constitution made no provision for political parties. Jefferson later wrote that the “revolution of 1800” was accomplished not “by the sword” but “by the rational and peaceable instrument of reform, the suffrage of the people.” The Twelfth Amendment, passed by Congress in December 1803 and ratified in June 1804, required electors to cast separate ballots for president and vice president, a change, the Yawp notes, designed around the way parties actually worked. The election of 1800 established that an American government could be voted out and would leave. That precedent of peacefully handing power to the opposition became the foundation of American democracy. Thirty-five ballots or thirty-six? Accounts number the House votes differently. The Miller Center says Hamilton acted “after … thirty-five ballots,” while the American Yawp says Jefferson won “on the thirty-sixth ballot.” Both are consistent: thirty-five ballots ended in deadlock, and the thirty-sixth decided the election. The 1796 rehearsal The flaw had already shown itself. In 1796 Adams won the presidency with 71 electoral votes and Jefferson, his rival, came second with 68, so the two leaders of opposing parties became president and vice president together. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. Thomas Jefferson First inaugural address, March 4, 1801 By the rational and peaceable instrument of reform, the suffrage of the people. title: The End of the Cold War
subtitle: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991
summary: Between 1989 and 1991, the communist regimes of Eastern Europe collapsed one after another, the Berlin Wall fell, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), and his decision not to use force to prop up allied regimes made peaceful change possible. Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H. W. Bush combined pressure with negotiation. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin, leaving the United States the world’s only superpower.
location: Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union
thumbAlt: East and West Germans at the Brandenburg Gate in 1989
aliases: fall of the Berlin Wall collapse of the Soviet Union Gorbachev perestroika glasnost
themeText: The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union INF Treaty 1987: Reagan and Gorbachev agree to reduce nuclear arsenals Poland Solidarity wins elections, June 4, 1989 Berlin Wall Opened November 9, 1989 Failed coup August 1991, against Gorbachev Soviet Union ends December 25, 1991 By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating, and a costly war in Afghanistan drained its resources. Reagan built up American forces and denounced the Soviet Union, while backing anticommunist movements worldwide. Gorbachev, who came to power in 1985, believed the Soviet system needed reform and sought to end the ruinous arms race. He met Reagan at Geneva in 1985 and Reykjavik in 1986, and the two signed the Intermediate Nuclear Forces Treaty in 1987. Gorbachev also abandoned the policy of using Soviet troops to support communist governments in Eastern Europe. Historians emphasize that the most significant causes of the collapse lay within the Soviet empire itself. In Poland, round-table talks with the banned union Solidarity led to elections on June 4, 1989, which Solidarity won overwhelmingly; by August the country had Eastern Europe’s first non-communist prime minister. Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany followed. On November 9, 1989, jubilant crowds brought down the Berlin Wall. Gorbachev accepted German reunification, and a reunited Germany joined NATO. Inside the Soviet Union, reforms unraveled the system. A failed hard-line coup in August 1991 fatally weakened Gorbachev; republics declared independence, and in December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus formed the Commonwealth of Independent States. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union, and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time, replaced by the Russian tricolor. The Bush administration focused on stability and security in Russia and the other former Soviet states. The end of the Cold War left the United States as the sole superpower and seemed to many to signal the global triumph of democracy and capitalism. It reshaped American defense priorities, alliances, and politics for the decades that followed. The peaceful end of the Cold War closed a four-decade conflict that had shaped American life and lifted the threat of superpower nuclear war. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I79TpDe3t2g The Cold War - OverSimplified (Part 1) OverSimplified 16:03 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L-K19rVDxoM George HW Bush and the End of the Cold War: Crash Course US History #44 CrashCourse 13:53 2026-10-22

title: The Erie Canal
subtitle: The 363-mile waterway that linked the Great Lakes to the Atlantic, 1817–1825
summary: Built between 1817 and 1825, the Erie Canal ran 363 miles across upstate New York from Albany on the Hudson River to Buffalo on Lake Erie. At the time it was the longest artificial waterway and the greatest public works project in North America. Dug largely by hand and climbing hills through 83 locks, it cut shipping costs by 90 percent and opened the interior of the continent to settlers and trade. It made New York City the nation’s leading port and financial center and launched a national canal-building boom. It also sped the dispossession of the Haudenosaunee nations whose homelands it crossed.
thumbAlt: 1839 engraving of the Erie Canal at Lockport, New York, after a picture by W. H. Bartlett
aliases: Erie Canal DeWitt Clinton Wedding of the Waters Mother of Cities Lockport Flight Transportation revolution
themeText: Economy and finance Science and technology Territorial expansion Cities and urban life Immigration
text: Albany to Buffalo, New York Built 1817 (begun at Rome, New York) to 1825 Size 363 miles; 4 feet deep and 40 feet wide; 83 locks and 18 aqueducts; a 571-foot rise from Albany to Buffalo Cost $7,143,789, repaid within ten years Speed and savings Albany to Buffalo in 5 days instead of 2 weeks by stagecoach; shipping costs cut by 90 percent Champion DeWitt Clinton Today Still in use; a National Historic Landmark and, since 2000, a National Heritage Corridor After the War of 1812 Americans looked to strengthen the nation through “internal improvements,” government spending on roads and canals; President Madison called for national roads and canals in his seventh annual message. Overland hauling by ox-drawn wagon was slow and costly. In New York, canals and locks on the Mohawk River, built by a private company, already let freight boats travel west from Schenectady. DeWitt Clinton, a former state legislator, U.S. senator and mayor of New York City, became the canal’s “most persistent and effective champion.” He served on the commission that made the first surveys for a canal across the state and led the political fight to build it. Markets in the West. Farmers, loggers, miners and manufacturers in the Great Lakes region needed a cheap route to eastern markets. State enterprise. New York State built and paid for the canal itself, at a cost of $7,143,789, which it recovered within ten years. Clinton’s vision. Clinton predicted that the canal would make New York America’s leading state. Construction began at Rome, New York, in 1817. Because few engineers or contractors had ever built a canal, the project became “the nation’s first practical school of civil engineering.” Some laborers were Irish immigrants, but most were American-born. For eight years they worked through heat, mud and freezing cold, felling trees and digging mostly with hand tools and animal power, for 80 cents to a dollar a day. They invented machines to pull stumps, developed a hydraulic cement that hardened underwater, and blasted rock with hand drills and black powder. The hardest work was the Lockport Flight, a staircase of five locks blasted through the solid rock of the Niagara Escarpment, raising and lowering boats 49 feet. The canal crossed rivers on 18 aqueducts and climbed 571 feet through 83 locks. In the fall of 1825 Governor Clinton rode the first boat to travel its full length, the Seneca Chief, from Buffalo to New York Harbor for a “Wedding of the Waters” ceremony. Packet boats carried passengers from Albany to Buffalo in five days, less than half the stagecoach time, and freight costs fell by 90 percent compared with ox-drawn wagons. Midwestern produce flowed east to Albany and down the Hudson to New York City, while manufactured goods and settlers flowed west. The canal gave rise to so many towns that it was called the “Mother of Cities”; the populations of Syracuse, Rochester and Buffalo quadrupled between 1830 and 1850. The canal’s success “launched a canal-building boom,” the American Yawp writes; by 1840 Ohio had two all-water links from Lake Erie to the Ohio River. The Erie captured most of the Great Lakes trade, “securing New York City’s position as the nation’s largest and most economically important city.” It carried more westbound immigrants than any other canal across the Appalachians, and ideas traveled along it too: abolitionism, women’s suffrage, utopian experiments and new religious movements all flourished on its corridor. Enlarged three times, the canal system has operated continuously since 1825, longer than any other constructed transportation system in North America; its old towpath is now a 365-mile bike path. The Erie Canal was the centerpiece of the transportation revolution that tied the young nation together. By connecting the Midwest to the Atlantic, it made New York the “Empire State” and showed what public investment and engineering could achieve, at a heavy cost to the Native nations along its route. The canal and the Haudenosaunee The canal ran through the homelands of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy and the Mohican Nation. The Erie Canalway’s own history states that the canal boom “dramatically accelerated the dispossession and disruption” of Native life, during years when state and federal policy promoted “Indian removal” from New York. The irony did not stop at the boat’s name, Seneca Chief. In 1811 Clinton had predicted that “before the passing away of the present generation, not a single Iroquois will be seen in this state.” He was wrong: more members of the Six Nations live in New York today than at the end of the Revolution. How long was it? The Erie Canalway gives the original canal’s length as 363 miles, while the American Yawp describes a “350-mile-long human-made waterway.” Later life The canal was enlarged in the mid-1800s to 7 feet deep with 110-foot locks, reached its peak tonnage in 1880 and ended tolls in 1882. Between 1905 and 1918 the Barge Canal replaced it, with locks for boats up to 300 feet long. The later opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway let ships sail from the Great Lakes straight to the Atlantic, and commercial traffic declined. Before the passing away of the present generation, not a single Iroquois will be seen in this state. title: The First Africans in Virginia
subtitle: 1619: Enslaved Angolans arrive at Point Comfort
summary: In late August 1619, the English privateer White Lion arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia, and traded about twenty Africans for food; the ship Treasurer soon brought a few more. They had been captured in west central Africa, most likely from the kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola, and taken from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico. They were the first documented Africans in English Virginia, and their arrival is often taken as the beginning of the history of slavery in what became the United States.
thumbAlt: Howard Pyle’s 1901 illustration imagining the arrival of Africans at Jamestown in 1619
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Colonial encounters
text: Point Comfort (present-day Hampton), Virginia Arrived August 1619, at Point Comfort, Virginia Ships The privateers White Lion and Treasurer Origin Probably Kimbundu-speaking people from Ndongo, in present-day Angola Status Contested, but historical evidence suggests they were often treated in ways that resemble enslavement By 1619, the Portuguese had been capturing and enslaving people in west central Africa, including from the kingdom of Ndongo, whose people raised crops and animals and mostly followed local religions. Virginia’s tobacco economy, launched in 1612, created a hunger for labor that English indentured servants only partly filled. In 1619 a Portuguese slave ship sailed from west central Africa for New Spain (Mexico) carrying captives from Ndongo. Two English privateers, the White Lion and the Treasurer, attacked it and took some of the captives. Many had probably had contact with Catholic missionaries, since Portuguese law required enslaved Africans to be baptized before reaching America. The White Lion reached Point Comfort in late August 1619, and about twenty Africans were sold in exchange for food. A few days later the Treasurer arrived and sold two or three more. Most were distributed to the households of colonial leaders. Census records from the 1620s and 1630s list Africans living at Jamestown and on plantations such as Flowerdew Hundred, many identified only by first names, among them a woman named Angelo purchased by William Peirce. The legal status of these first Africans is debated. Virginia had not yet written laws defining slavery, and some Africans, such as Anthony and Mary Johnson, gained their freedom and bought land. But the National Park Service notes that the evidence suggests they were often treated in a manner closely resembling enslavement. More captives followed: in 1628 a shipload of about 100 Angolans was sold in Virginia. Over the following decades, Virginia’s laws hardened lifelong, inherited slavery based on race, and enslaved Africans replaced indentured servants as the colony’s main labor force. The year 1619 has become a symbol of slavery’s deep roots in English America, a system that ended only with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. The arrival of the first Africans at Point Comfort marks the beginning of the African American experience in English North America and of the system of racial slavery that shaped the country’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years.

title: The Great Depression
subtitle: The deepest economic collapse in American history, 1929–1941
summary: The Great Depression was the longest and deepest economic downturn in the history of the United States and the modern industrial economy. Beginning in 1929, it brought a stock market crash, thousands of bank failures, collapsing farm prices, and unemployment that reached about a quarter of the workforce. The Federal Reserve’s own historians now say its mistakes made the slump far worse. Herbert Hoover’s reliance on voluntary action gave way to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, which transformed the federal government, but full recovery came only with World War II.
thumbAlt: Dorothea Lange’s photograph Migrant Mother
aliases: Hoovervilles Bonus Army bank runs Mexican repatriation Dust Bowl Black Tuesday Smoot-Hawley Tariff
themeText: Economy and finance Labor and work Everyday life Land and environment Latino history
text: Nationwide and worldwide Began August 1929, when the expansion of the 1920s ended; the stock market crashed that October Bottom March 1933, when the banking system collapsed and Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday Unemployment 24.9 percent (12,830,000 people) in 1933; Black unemployment as high as 50 percent Bank failures About 1,350 in 1930 and more than 2,200 in 1931; some 5,000 between 1929 and 1933 Money supply Fell by nearly 30 percent from the fall of 1930 to the winter of 1933 Stock market The Dow fell 89 percent from its 1929 peak by July 1932 and did not recover until 1954 The 1920s looked like an age of prosperity. Automobiles, telephones, and radios spread across the country, and ordinary men and women bought stocks, often on margin: they put down about 10 percent of the price and borrowed the rest. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose sixfold, from 63 in August 1921 to 381 in September 1929. Just after the peak, the economist Irving Fisher declared that stock prices had reached “what looks like a permanently high plateau.” Beneath the boom lay serious weaknesses. The gains were unequal: per capita income rose 10 percent for all Americans during the decade, but 75 percent for the wealthiest. By 1929, the Miller Center notes, 5 percent of Americans held nearly a third of the nation’s money and property, while more than 80 percent had no savings at all. Industrial wages stagnated while profits poured into the stock market, and the market for cars and appliances was nearing saturation. Even in good years, unemployment hovered around 7 percent. Farmers had been in trouble since 1920–1921, when prices for cotton, grain, and other crops collapsed; by the late 1920s farm incomes had shrunk to a third of the national average, and many farmers could not repay loans taken out in better times. Abroad, the international gold standard, rebuilt after World War I, made the world’s economies rigid and closely linked, so that a shock in one country spread quickly to the others. Historians and economists still debate the Depression’s causes, and most see several working together. The Miller Center lists structural weaknesses in agriculture and industry, a fragile international economy, and a speculative, unstable financial sector, all of which created a badly unequal distribution of wealth: “a consumer economy in which few consumed.” Monetary policy turned a downturn into a catastrophe. In 1928 and 1929 the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to curb stock speculation, and because of the gold standard its tight money pushed other nations into recession too. Then, when banks began to fail, the Fed did not act as a lender of last resort. Some of its leaders even believed that weak banks should be allowed to fail. Hoover’s Treasury secretary, Andrew Mellon, who sat on the Federal Reserve Board, held this “liquidationist” view. From the fall of 1930 through the winter of 1933, the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent, and prices fell with it. That deflation raised the real burden of debts and drove banks, firms, and families into bankruptcy. In 2002, Ben Bernanke, then a Federal Reserve governor, admitted publicly that the Fed’s mistakes had contributed to the “worst economic disaster in American history.” Trade policy made things worse. In June 1930 Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, which raised rates on farm and factory imports to historic levels. Other countries retaliated, and between 1929 and 1932 world trade fell from $36 billion to $12 billion; American exports fell by 78 percent. Some Democrats later claimed that the tariff had caused the Depression, a charge the Miller Center calls politically motivated, since the slump was already well under way. Most economists agree, however, that it deepened the crisis. The crash. On Thursday, October 24, 1929, stock prices suddenly plunged. Leading bankers met at the offices of J. P. Morgan and ostentatiously bought shares to halt the slide, but the panic resumed the next week. On Black Monday, October 28, the Dow fell nearly 13 percent, and on Black Tuesday, October 29, nearly 12 percent more. By mid-November the market had lost almost half its value. Shares of U.S. Steel fell from $262 to $22. Only about 2.5 percent of Americans had brokerage accounts, and the crash alone did not cause the Depression. But it frightened consumers, who stopped buying cars and other goods on credit, and companies like Ford cut production and laid off workers. The market kept sliding until July 1932, when the Dow closed at 41.22, 89 percent below its peak. It did not regain its 1929 level until November 1954. The bank panics. By the fall of 1930 the recession had lasted fifteen months, about as long as earlier downturns, and recovery seemed near. Then, in November 1930, the collapse of Caldwell and Company, the South’s largest financial holding company, set off a chain of failures among the banks that kept their reserves with it, and panic spread from town to town. On December 11 the Bank of United States, the fourth-largest bank in New York City, closed. More waves of panic followed in 1931 and 1932. About 1,350 banks failed in 1930 and more than 2,200 in 1931; between 1929 and 1933, some 5,000 collapsed, taking depositors’ savings with them. The Federal Reserve’s response varied by district. The Atlanta Fed rushed cash to troubled banks, and its region recovered sooner; the St. Louis Fed refused to help banks outside the system, and hundreds of them failed. Hard times. By 1933, 24.9 percent of the workforce, 12,830,000 people, were unemployed, and many who still had jobs worked only part time. Workers who kept their jobs saw their wages fall by 42.5 percent between 1929 and 1933. One in four farms went into foreclosure. Families exhausted their savings, borrowed from relatives, ran up credit at the corner store, and finally turned to charities, which were themselves running dry: by mid-1932 a quarter of New York’s private charities had closed, and relief agencies in Atlanta could give needy families only $1.30 a week. The homeless built shantytowns of packing crates and scrap metal, mockingly called “Hoovervilles,” and young people whose families could no longer feed them rode the rails in search of work. Employers were quicker to fire married women, on the assumption that they did not need to work. Black workers were generally the last hired and the first fired. In 1932, when national unemployment was about 25 percent, Black unemployment reached as high as 50 percent. The Dust Bowl. On the Great Plains, drought began in 1932 and lasted until at least 1936. Decades of plowing had stripped away the grass that held the soil, and winds whipped the exposed topsoil into dust storms that darkened the sky as far east as Washington, D.C., and the Atlantic. Ruined farmers from Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Arkansas headed west to California; Oklahoma alone lost 440,000 people, 18.4 percent of its 1930 population. California, Florida, and Colorado set up “border blockades” in the winter of 1935–1936 to turn poor migrants away. Dorothea Lange’s 1936 photograph Migrant Mother, taken at a camp for farmworkers in Nipomo, California, became the era’s most famous image. Deportation. Fearing competition for scarce jobs, the Hoover administration tightened immigration rules in September 1930, and between 1930 and 1932 some 54,000 people were deported. Mexican immigrants and Mexican Americans were hit hardest. In Los Angeles, officials staged deportation raids and pressured Mexicans and Mexican Americans on relief to leave “voluntarily” for Mexico. From 1930 to 1940 the Mexican-born population of Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Texas fell from 616,998 to 377,433. Hoover’s response. Hoover was not idle, but he believed that voluntary cooperation, not federal relief, was the answer. “Any lack of confidence in the economic future and the basic strength of business in the United States is simply foolish,” he said in November 1929. He won pledges from business leaders not to cut wages, urged states and cities to expand public works, and created committees to coordinate private charity. “We cannot legislate ourselves out of a world economic depression,” he told Congress in 1931. As the crisis deepened he took steps that were radical for him: the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) lent money to banks, railroads, and other businesses, and the Emergency Relief and Construction Act provided $2 billion for public works and $300 million for relief programs run by the states. Critics such as Congressman Fiorello La Guardia called the RFC a “millionaire’s dole.” The Bonus Army. In the summer of 1932, more than fifteen thousand unemployed World War I veterans and their families camped in Washington to demand early payment of a bonus that was not due until 1945. “While there were billions for bankers,” they complained, “there was nothing for the poor.” After the Senate voted the bonus down, most went home, but thousands stayed. Troops under General Douglas MacArthur drove the remaining veterans out with tear gas, bayonets, and tanks and burned their camp at Anacostia Flats. Accounts of the attack differ. The American Yawp writes that Hoover ordered the veterans out and that two marchers and a baby died. The Miller Center says that Hoover ordered a peaceful removal, that War Secretary Patrick Hurley and MacArthur exceeded their orders, and that one veteran was killed. Either way, the images helped seal Hoover’s defeat. In November 1932 voters turned Hoover out in a landslide and elected Franklin D. Roosevelt, who had promised “a new deal for the American people.” By his inauguration on March 4, 1933, the banking system had collapsed, and the Federal Reserve dates the bottom of the Depression to that month. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Roosevelt told the nation. He declared a national bank holiday, and in his first hundred days Congress passed a wave of laws that created the agencies of the New Deal. New banking laws created federal deposit insurance and reformed the financial system, and the United States left the gold standard in 1933. Recovery began in 1933 but was slow and incomplete. After the Federal Reserve doubled banks’ reserve requirements in 1936 and federal fiscal policy tightened, the economy fell in May 1937 into a sharp “recession within the Depression” that lasted until June 1938. Industrial production fell 32 percent, and unemployment rose again to 20 percent. Only when war orders and defense spending poured in did the economy return to full employment. Output grew by 49 percent from 1938 to 1942, and the Depression ended in 1941. The Great Depression changed the relationship between Americans and their government. Before it, Washington played a small role in economic life; afterward, Americans expected the federal government to protect bank deposits, regulate the stock market, provide old-age pensions and unemployment insurance, and act to prevent mass unemployment. The reforms of the 1930s, and the lessons drawn from the Fed’s failures, turned the Federal Reserve into a modern central bank. In 2002 Bernanke, speaking at a conference honoring Milton Friedman, whose research with Anna Schwartz had laid much of the blame on the Fed, promised “we won’t do it again.” The Depression also reshaped American foreign policy. It pushed the United States further into isolation during the 1930s, as Japan, Italy, and Germany began their aggressions. In the long run, the State Department’s historians conclude, the lesson that turning inward had made the crisis worse helped lead the United States to take a leading role in the world economy after World War II. The Roosevelt Library calls it a test of “the fabric of American life” that caused Americans “to doubt their abilities and their values.” The Great Depression was the worst economic disaster in American history. It discredited the belief that the economy would right itself without government help and gave rise to the New Deal and the modern federal government. Any lack of confidence in the economic future and the basic strength of business in the United States is simply foolish. Herbert Hoover November 1929, weeks after the crash The Negro was born in depression. It didn’t mean too much to him. The Great American Depression … only became official when it hit the white man. A Black pensioner interviewed by the oral historian Studs Terkel My salary could keep us going, but—I am to have a baby. A woman from Humboldt County, California writing to Eleanor Roosevelt in 1934 to ask for a job for her husband, out of work for nearly two years So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.
