title: The Great Recession
subtitle: The financial crisis and deep recession of 2007–2009
summary: The Great Recession began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, the longest recession since World War II. It grew out of a housing bubble fueled by risky “subprime” mortgages that were bundled into securities and sold throughout the financial system. When homeowners began to default, major financial firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers collapsed. Home prices fell about 30 percent, stocks fell 57 percent, and unemployment peaked at 10 percent. The federal government and the Federal Reserve intervened on a massive scale to stabilize the financial system.
thumbAlt: Lehman Brothers headquarters in New York City on September 15, 2008, the month the firm filed for bankruptcy
aliases: financial crisis of 2008 subprime mortgage crisis bank bailout Lehman Brothers TARP
themeText: Economy and finance The presidency
text: Nationwide and worldwide Dates December 2007 – June 2009 Output Real GDP fell 4.3 percent, the largest postwar decline Unemployment From 5 percent (December 2007) to a peak of 10 percent (October 2009) Housing Home prices fell about 30 percent from mid-2006 to mid-2009 Stocks S&P 500 fell 57 percent from October 2007 to March 2009 From the 1990s into the 2000s, home prices climbed, and housing-related sectors accounted for roughly 40 percent of net private job creation between 2001 and 2005. Lenders offered high-risk “subprime” mortgages and repackaged them into securities, expanding credit and bidding up prices. Decades of financial deregulation, including the repeal in the 1990s of parts of the Depression-era Glass-Steagall Act and the exemption of credit-default swaps from regulation, had loosened restraints on risky practices. The housing boom peaked in 2006. As prices fell and homeowners defaulted, losses spread through the heavily leveraged financial system, because mortgages had been bundled and resold so often that it was hard to tell who owned what. Major firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers disappeared almost overnight. President George W. Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, and the government poured billions into propping up banks. The Federal Reserve cut its key interest rate from 5.25 percent in September 2007 to nearly zero by December 2008 and began buying mortgage-backed securities and other debt to support the housing market and the financial system. President Barack Obama continued the bank rescue and won an $800 billion economic stimulus, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, in 2009. Millions lost jobs and homes. Resentment of bank bailouts fueled both the conservative Tea Party movement and the left-leaning Occupy Wall Street protests. In 2010 Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act to prevent future meltdowns. Recovery was slow: as of 2013 unemployment was still above 7 percent. The crisis magnified rising inequality and deepened distrust of financial and political elites, shaping American politics for years afterward. The Great Recession was the longest recession since World War II, with the largest drop in output of the postwar era, and a defining event for a generation of Americans. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GPOv72Awo68 How it Happened - The 2008 Financial Crisis: Crash Course Economics #12 CrashCourse 11:24 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZ25uZtey34 Before the Great Recession, “The Warning” (full documentary) FRONTLINE PBS | Official 54:35 2026-10-22

title: The Great Society
subtitle: Lyndon Johnson’s program to end poverty and racial injustice, 1964–1968
summary: The Great Society was President Lyndon B. Johnson’s sweeping program of domestic reform. Announced in a May 1964 speech calling for “an end to poverty and racial injustice,” it produced the most ambitious burst of legislation since the New Deal: the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, food stamps, the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, and an immigration law that abolished the national-origins quotas of 1924. Much of it remains in place today.
thumbAlt: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Medicare bill with Harry Truman beside him
aliases: War on Poverty Medicare Medicaid Head Start Economic Opportunity Act Hart-Celler Act Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965
themeText: The presidency Economy and finance Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Immigration Public health
text: Washington, D.C., and nationwide Announced May 1964, commencement speech at the University of Michigan War on Poverty Economic Opportunity Act of 1964; about $3 billion; Community Action Programs; Head Start Health Medicare and Medicaid Education Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, more than $1 billion Immigration Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (Hart-Celler) abolished the 1924 quota system In an age of postwar affluence, poverty persisted in cities and rural areas, and Jim Crow still ruled the South. After John F. Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963, Johnson asked Congress to honor Kennedy’s memory by passing his tax cut and civil rights bill, and then set out his own, larger agenda. He won election in his own right by a landslide in 1964. Johnson, shaped by the New Deal and by his own family’s poverty in the Texas Hill Country, believed government could abolish poverty and racial injustice in an age of affluence. Speaking at the University of Michigan in May 1964, he challenged Americans to “enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization.” The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 launched the War on Poverty. Its most controversial program, Community Action, sought “maximum feasible participation” by the poor themselves in running antipoverty efforts. Congress went on to create Medicare and Medicaid to provide medical care for the elderly and the poor, the first federal food stamp program, and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, the first major federal investment in public schools. It established the National Endowment for the Arts and the National Endowment for the Humanities. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 effectively ended legal Jim Crow, and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 opened the country to immigrants from around the world, reshaping its population. The War on Poverty and Community Action provoked conservative resistance and helped fuel the rise of Republicans in the South and West. The escalating Vietnam War soon overshadowed Johnson’s domestic agenda, and by 1968 his presidency was consumed by the war. Later presidents and Congresses left intact most of the Great Society: Medicare and Medicaid, food stamps, federal arts funding, and Head Start. Historians continue to debate its record: its programs kept many Americans out of poverty and secured rights for minorities, while reaction against it contributed to a conservative political counterrevolution. The Great Society expanded the federal government’s responsibility for health, education, and poverty more than any reform program since the New Deal. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTV9a88IO1k Lyndon Johnson's GREAT SOCIETY [APUSH Review Unit 8 Topic 9] Period 8 (1945-1980) Heimler's History 4:08 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pD3Vn44F7as What Were LBJ's "Great Society" Programs? | History HISTORY 3:51 2026-10-22

title: The Haymarket Affair
subtitle: A bomb at a Chicago labor rally, May 4, 1886
summary: On May 4, 1886, about 1,500 workers rallied near Chicago’s Haymarket Square to protest police violence against strikers the day before, during a nationwide campaign for the eight-hour day. As police moved to disperse the crowd, someone threw a bomb; police and possibly others opened fire. Seven police officers and at least one civilian died. Eight anarchists were convicted of murder on little evidence linking them to the bomb; four were hanged. The affair set off a wave of anti-labor and anti-immigrant fear.
thumbAlt: Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket bombing
themeText: Labor and work Reform and protest Immigration
text: Haymarket Square, Chicago, Illinois Date May 4, 1886 Deaths Seven police officers and at least one civilian; at least 60 wounded Trial Eight men convicted August 20, 1886; seven sentenced to death Executions Four hanged November 11, 1887; one died by suicide; three later pardoned (1893) In the 1880s strikes spread as workers protested long hours and low wages, and unions launched a national campaign for the eight-hour day, centered on May 1, 1886. Chicago, a fast-growing industrial and immigrant city, was a center of both the labor movement and radical anarchist politics. On May 3, police fired on strikers at the McCormick Harvesting Machine Company, leaving one man dead and many injured. Labor activists called a protest rally for the next evening. On May 4 at 7:30 p.m., around 1,500 people gathered on Desplaines Street near Haymarket Square. Chicago’s mayor, Carter Harrison, attended as an observer and confirmed the meeting was peaceful. As the rally wound down and the mayor left, police arrived to disperse the remaining crowd. Someone threw a bomb. Chaos followed as police, and possibly some in the crowd, opened fire. Seven police officers and at least one civilian died, and at least sixty were wounded. The bomb thrower was never identified. Eight men, the “Chicago Eight,” known for their anarchist politics and pro-labor activism, were charged with murder, though some had not even attended the rally and little evidence connected them to the bomb. On August 20, 1886, a jury found them guilty, and Judge Joseph E. Gary sentenced seven to death. Two sentences were commuted to life imprisonment; Louis Lingg killed himself in his cell; and on November 11, 1887, Adolph Fischer, George Engel, Albert Parsons, and August Spies were hanged. In 1893 Illinois Governor John P. Altgeld pardoned the three surviving defendants. The affair set off a wave of xenophobia and anti-labor sentiment in Chicago and across the country, damaging the Knights of Labor and the eight-hour movement as many Americans associated labor activism with violence and foreign radicals. To many workers at home and abroad, the executed men became martyrs. Haymarket became a symbol of the bitter conflict between labor and capital in the Gilded Age, and of how fear of radicalism could override due process. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6okibrpyeUs Haymarket Strike NBC News Learn 3:40 2026-10-22

title: Independence Day
subtitle: The nation’s birthday, celebrated since 1776 and a federal holiday since 1870
summary: Independence Day marks July 4, 1776, when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, two days after voting for independence. John Adams expected July 2 to become “the great anniversary Festival,” celebrated “with Pomp and Parade… Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other.” Americans adopted his program but chose the Fourth. The day became the stage for national celebration and for protest, from William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass to later reformers, and in 1870 it became one of the first federal holidays.
location: Nationwide; the Declaration was adopted in Philadelphia
thumbAlt: John Lewis Krimmel’s painting of a crowded Fourth of July celebration in Philadelphia’s Centre Square, around 1812
aliases: Fourth of July July 4th July Fourth Independence Day Lee Resolution
themeText: National symbols and holidays Political thought Everyday life
text: Nationwide; the Declaration was adopted in Philadelphia The vote July 2, 1776: the Lee Resolution for independence passed, twelve colonies in favor and New York not voting The date July 4, 1776: Congress adopted the final text of the Declaration The signing The engrossed parchment was signed beginning August 2, 1776 Federal holiday Since June 28, 1870, with New Year’s Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving A famous coincidence John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary On June 7, 1776, in the Pennsylvania State House, Richard Henry Lee of Virginia moved “That these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.” While Congress delayed the vote, it named a Committee of Five, John Adams, Roger Sherman, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston, and Thomas Jefferson, to draft a declaration explaining the decision to the world. The others, Jefferson later recalled, “unanimously pressed on myself alone to undertake the draught.” The holiday grew directly from the vote. Writing to Abigail on July 3, Adams predicted that the day of independence “will be celebrated, by succeeding Generations, as the great anniversary Festival,” to be “commemorated, as the Day of Deliverance by solemn Acts of Devotion to God Almighty” and “solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations.” On July 2, 1776, Congress adopted the Lee Resolution, twelve colonies in favor and New York not voting, and immediately began revising Jefferson’s draft. The revisions continued through July 3 and into the late morning of July 4, when the Declaration was adopted. That day John Dunlap, the official printer to Congress, began printing copies, which carried only the names of John Hancock and Charles Thomson; the names of the other signers were kept secret for a time for fear of British reprisals. The handwritten parchment copy was prepared later, and its signing began on August 2, 1776, with Hancock’s bold signature. Americans took up Adams’s program, but they celebrated July 4, the day of the Declaration, rather than July 2. A day for protest. Because the Declaration proclaimed that all men are created equal, reformers used its anniversary to hold the nation to that promise. On the Fourth of July, 1829, William Lloyd Garrison gave an address on slavery at Boston’s Park Street Church. On July 5, 1852, the day after the holiday, Frederick Douglass asked the Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society of Rochester, New York: “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” Yet Douglass also argued that, read as it ought to be read, the Constitution was “a glorious liberty document.” A federal holiday. On June 28, 1870, Congress made New Year’s Day, Independence Day, Christmas Day, and any day of thanksgiving named by the president holidays for federal employees in the District of Columbia, the first federal holidays. The anniversary became the centerpiece of American civic life. On July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary, both John Adams and Thomas Jefferson died. Near noon, close to the time Jefferson died, Adams woke and said, “Thomas Jefferson survives.” They were his last words. For the Centennial in 1876 the original Declaration went back to Philadelphia; on the Fourth it was read to a crowd on Independence Square and the “faded and crumbling manuscript” was “greeted with cheer after cheer.” The original Declaration has been kept at the National Archives since 1952 and was first displayed there on Independence Day in 1953. For the Bicentennial in 1976 the Archives began its annual July 4 celebration, and President Gerald Ford called the Declaration “the Polaris of our political order—the fixed star of freedom.” In 2026 the Declaration turned 250. The Fourth of July is the nation’s chief civic holiday, a celebration not of a battle or a ruler but of a document and its ideas. Because the Declaration promised that all men are created equal, the day has also given every generation of reformers a stage on which to ask whether the nation is living up to its creed. It ought to be solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other from this Time forward forever more. John Adams letter to Abigail Adams, July 3, 1776 What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim. title: Indian Removal
subtitle: The forced expulsion of Native nations from the East, 1830–1850
summary: Indian removal was the federal policy of forcing Native nations east of the Mississippi River to give up their homelands and move to “Indian Territory” in what is now Oklahoma. President Andrew Jackson made it a central goal, and Congress passed the Indian Removal Act on May 28, 1830. Through coerced treaties, bribery, and the army, the government relocated about 100,000 people between 1830 and 1850, among them the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek, and Seminole nations. The best-known removal, the Cherokee Trail of Tears of 1838–1839, killed thousands. Removal opened millions of acres of rich land east of the Mississippi to white settlers.
location: The Southeast and Old Northwest to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma)
thumbAlt: Map of the forced removal routes of the Five Tribes
aliases: Indian Removal Act Trail of Tears Treaty of New Echota Five Civilized Tribes Indian Territory
themeText: Indigenous history Territorial expansion Slavery and emancipation
text: The Southeast and Old Northwest to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) Indian Removal Act Signed by Andrew Jackson, May 28, 1830 Nations removed Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek, Seminole, and others from the Southeast and Old Northwest People moved About 100,000 between 1830 and 1850 (National Park Service) Treaty of New Echota Signed December 1835 by a small Cherokee faction; ratified by the Senate by one vote, May 23, 1836 Trail of Tears May 1838 to March 1839; deaths estimated from about a thousand on the march to 4,000 or more Resistance Second Seminole War, 1835–1842 From the earliest years of the republic, white settlers pressed onto Native land in the backcountry of the South. Presidents Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe suggested that southeastern nations trade their lands for territory west of the Mississippi, but they did not force the issue. The first great transfer came through war. In 1814 Andrew Jackson defeated the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend and imposed a treaty that took more than twenty million acres, about half of present-day Alabama and a fifth of Georgia. Over the next decade Jackson helped negotiate nine of the eleven major treaties that pushed Native nations off their land. Between 1816 and 1840, the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole nations signed more than forty treaties ceding territory. Many of these nations adopted features of white American society in the hope of keeping what remained. The Cherokee had turned to farming, created a written language through Sequoyah’s syllabary, published a newspaper, and adopted a written constitution. Some Cherokee, like some of their white neighbors, held enslaved people. None of this protected them. State and federal governments kept pressing them to sign away more land. Settlers wanted the land, and the states wanted Native nations gone. When gold was found on Cherokee land in 1830, Georgia held lotteries to hand Cherokee land and gold rights to white settlers, and it passed laws forbidding Cherokees to conduct tribal business, testify in court against whites, or mine gold. Jackson, who had made his name fighting Native nations, held that the federal government had no right to protect the Cherokees against Georgia. He urged Congress to pass a removal law, and on May 28, 1830, he signed the Indian Removal Act. It authorized the president to exchange land west of the Mississippi for the homelands of nations that agreed to leave, to pay for their move, and to guarantee them their new land “forever.” It was the only major law passed at Jackson’s request in his eight years as president. In December 1830 he told Congress that “the benevolent policy of the Government, steadily pursued for nearly thirty years,” was “approaching to a happy consummation.” “What good man,” he asked, “would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms?” With the act in place, the State Department’s historians write, Jackson and his followers were free to “persuade, bribe, and threaten” nations into signing removal treaties. The Choctaws and Chickasaws submitted, and the Creeks agreed under duress. An estimated 3,500 Creeks died in Alabama and on the journey west, some of them transported in chains. In the north, a short campaign in 1832 crushed resistance by Black Hawk’s band of Sauk and Fox. In Florida the Seminoles, joined by free Black people and people who had escaped slavery, fought the Second Seminole War from 1835 to 1842. An American commander called it “a negro, not an Indian War.” By the end of Jackson’s presidency almost seventy removal treaties had moved nearly 50,000 eastern Native people west. The National Park Service counts about 100,000 people removed between 1830 and 1850. The Cherokee fought in the courts. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), Chief Justice John Marshall called the tribes “domestic dependent nations” but ruled that the Court lacked jurisdiction. The next year, in Worcester v. Georgia, the Court held that Georgia’s laws did not apply within Cherokee territory. Jackson refused to enforce the ruling. According to a much-repeated story, he said that Marshall “has made his decision; let him enforce it now if he can.” The National Park Service reports the words as something he “reportedly said.” In December 1835 federal agents met a minority faction at New Echota, Georgia. Only 300 to 500 Cherokees attended, and none were elected officials of the nation. Twenty men signed a treaty giving up all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and new land in Indian Territory. More than 15,000 Cherokees protested, but on May 23, 1836, the Senate ratified it by a single vote. (The State Department’s summary says Congress ratified the treaty in 1835. The National Park Service gives the Senate’s vote of May 1836.) Most Cherokees, including Principal Chief John Ross, did not believe they would really be forced out. In May 1838, under Jackson’s successor Martin Van Buren, federal troops and state militia began rounding up more than 16,000 Cherokees in Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina, and Georgia. Families were separated, the elderly and sick forced out at gunpoint, and white looters ransacked homes as their owners were led away. Three groups sent west by water that summer suffered badly in drought. Ross then won permission from General Winfield Scott to lead the rest of the removal himself. Detachments of about a thousand people each set out on the 800-mile overland route that autumn. The National Park Service counts twelve such overland groups on one page and fourteen detachments in all on another. Heavy rains, mud, ice on the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, and short rations made the winter crossing deadly. “People feel bad when they leave Old Nation,” one survivor remembered. “Womens cry and make sad wails. Children cry and many men cry.” The last survivors reached Indian Territory in March 1839. No one knows how many died. The sources give different figures: The missionary doctor Elizur Butler, who traveled with the Cherokees, estimated more than 4,000, nearly a fifth of the nation. The National Archives says about 4,000 of 16,000. The State Department’s historians give 3,000 to 4,000 of 15,000 to 16,000. Another National Park Service page counts more than a thousand deaths on the march, with perhaps several thousand more from its consequences. The American Yawp says that of 16,000 who set out, only 10,000 completed the journey. By the 1840s, apart from a few Seminoles still resisting in Florida, no Native nation remained in the American South between the Atlantic and the Mississippi. The removed nations rebuilt in Indian Territory. In August 1839 the Cherokee elected John Ross principal chief of the reunited nation, with its capital at Tahlequah, which remains the Cherokee Nation’s headquarters today. About a thousand Cherokees who escaped the roundup in the mountains became the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians in North Carolina. The Cherokee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw built their own school systems in the West. The State Department’s historians conclude that through “coerced treaties and the contravention of treaties and judicial determination,” the government cleared the way for westward expansion. Indian removal stripped the southeastern nations of their homelands and defied the Supreme Court to do it, and the Trail of Tears became the most painful symbol of the policy. What good man would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms? Andrew Jackson annual message to Congress, December 6, 1830 Long time we travel on way to new land. People feel bad when they leave Old Nation. Womens cry and make sad wails. Children cry and many men cry. A survivor of the Trail of Tears as recorded by the National Park Service One each day. Then all are gone. title: The Founding of Jamestown
subtitle: The first permanent English settlement in North America, 1607
summary: In May 1607, 104 English men and boys sent by the Virginia Company, a private company of investors, chose a marshy riverside site on the James River for a settlement they named for King James I. Jamestown nearly failed from disease, hunger, and conflict with the Powhatan peoples whose lands it occupied, and in the winter of 1609 to 1610 most of the settlers died. The colony was saved by gifts of food from Chief Powhatan, by new settlers and supplies, and, from 1612, by John Rolfe’s tobacco. In 1619 it held the first representative assembly in English North America, and within weeks the first documented Africans arrived. Its growth onto Powhatan land led to two major Powhatan attacks, in 1622 and 1644.
thumbAlt: Replicas of the ships that carried the Jamestown colonists
aliases: Virginia Company Powhatan Pocahontas Starving Time John Smith John Rolfe James Fort Opechancanough House of Burgesses General Assembly 1619
themeText: Colonial encounters Indigenous history Economy and finance Slavery and emancipation
text: Jamestown Island, Virginia Founded May 13 or 14, 1607 (sources differ), by 104 English men and boys Sponsor The Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company chartered by James I in 1606 Starving Time Winter 1609–1610; 80 to 90 percent of settlers died (William Strachey, via the National Park Service), over 75 percent (Historic Jamestowne) Cash crop Tobacco, from John Rolfe’s experiments beginning in 1612 1619 First General Assembly (July 30); first documented Africans arrive (late August); about 90 women sent to marry settlers Powhatan wars Attacks of March 1622 and April 1644; each killed 350 to 400 colonists, according to the National Park Service The Chesapeake region was home to the Powhatan, whose chief Wahunsenacawh, called Powhatan by the English, inherited six communities and by the early 1600s ruled more than thirty Algonquian-speaking groups and some fifteen thousand people, who paid him tribute. The Powhatan’s own name for the region was Tsenacommacah. Historic Jamestowne gives its size as 8,000 square miles in one place and 10,000 in another. England’s first colonies in America had failed, including the “Lost Colony” at Roanoke. In April 1606 King James I granted a charter to the Virginia Company of London, a group of investors, to settle “that part of America commonly called Virginia” and any lands “not now actually possessed by any Christian Prince or People.” The charter said that the colonies would spread the Christian religion among people “in Darkness and miserable Ignorance,” and promised the colonists and their children “all Liberties, Franchises, and Immunities” of Englishmen. The Company’s instructions told the colonists to build a secure settlement, find gold, and look for a water route to the Pacific. They were also told to “have Great Care not to Offend the naturals,” meaning Native Americans. The settlers left London in December 1606 on three ships, the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery. The National Park Service dates the departure to December 6, and Historic Jamestowne’s biography of John Smith says the fleet sailed December 20. They reached the Chesapeake in April 1607. The Company had ordered that its council members’ names be kept in a sealed box. When it was opened, Edward Maria Wingfield was named president, and John Smith, who had been imprisoned on the voyage on a charge of mutiny, was released and made a member of the council. The colonists picked a site on the James River for reasons the Company had laid down. It was surrounded by water on three sides and far inland, which made it easy to defend against the Spanish. The water was deep enough to moor ships at the shore, and the site was not occupied by Native people. Its drawbacks showed up later: the settlers drank salty or slimy river water, and by 1609 a drought made food scarce, which the National Park Service links to the collapse of relations with the Powhatan. The National Park Service dates the choice of site to May 13, while Historic Jamestowne says the settlers landed on May 14. The fort. Within days of landing the colonists were attacked by Powhatan warriors, and Historic Jamestowne’s timeline records an attack by about two hundred, in which at least one settler was killed and eleven were wounded. By June 15 they had built a triangular fort with a bulwark at each corner for artillery. Captain Newport sailed for England on June 22, and soon the settlers began to die of disease, hunger, and war. Archaeology has recovered the site of the original fort, which many had thought lost to the river. Jamestown Rediscovery has dug there since 1994. Smith and Powhatan. Chief Powhatan sent gifts of food, and, in the National Park Service’s words, without the Powhatan’s help in the early years the settlement “would most likely have failed.” John Smith, a veteran soldier, was good at trading for corn with glass beads, copper, and iron tools. Captured by Powhatan’s men in December 1607, he later said that Pocahontas saved his life. Historic Jamestowne notes that historians doubt it, and its timeline says most historians now believe it was a mock execution, if it took place at all. As council president from September 1608 Smith enforced the rule that “he that will not worke, shall not eate,” and he strengthened the fort. Relations with the Powhatan went up and down. Newport brought Powhatan a crown, and Powhatan insisted that he was a king too and would not kneel. When Smith left after a gunpowder explosion in October 1609, he never returned to Virginia. The Starving Time (1609–1610). By late 1609 relations had soured because the English were demanding too much food in a drought. The Powhatan besieged the fort. Historic Jamestowne reports that about 300 settlers crowded in and that only 60 were still alive the next spring. Settlers who were afraid to leave the fort ate animals, shoe leather, and sometimes the bodies of the dead. Historic Jamestowne’s timeline cites the remains of a 14-year-old girl, nicknamed “Jane,” as evidence of survival cannibalism. The sources give different death rates: 80 to 90 percent according to William Strachey, quoted by the National Park Service, and more than 75 percent according to Historic Jamestowne. In May 1610 the survivors of the shipwrecked Sea Venture, who had spent ten months in Bermuda, finally reached Jamestown. Sir Thomas Gates found it in ruins and decided to abandon it. Less than a day after sailing, the colonists met a fleet bringing the new governor, Lord De La Warr, and returned. Tobacco and war. Sir Thomas Gates imposed martial law, and the English raided Powhatan towns. Historic Jamestowne’s timeline records that George Percy led an attack on the Paspahegh town, burning houses and cutting down cornfields, and that the Paspahegh queen and her children were kidnapped and later executed. John Rolfe, who had survived the Sea Venture wreck, experimented with a sweeter strain of tobacco in 1612. The colonists had tried silkmaking, glassmaking, lumber, sassafras, and soap ashes without profit. The sources disagree on where he got the seed: Ralph Hamor said it came from somewhere in the Caribbean, possibly Trinidad, and Historic Jamestowne’s timeline says probably Bermuda. In 1613 Captain Samuel Argall kidnapped Pocahontas, Powhatan’s favored daughter, and held her for ransom. She learned English, converted to Christianity, and took the name Rebecca. In April 1614 she married Rolfe, ending the First Anglo-Powhatan War. Tobacco exports rose from 20,000 pounds in 1617 to a million and a half pounds a dozen years later. Before the assembly met, the Virginia Company issued new instructions known as the “Great Charter,” ending martial law, authorizing an assembly, and setting up the headright system: fifty acres for anyone who paid his own passage, and fifty more for each person he brought. The Historic Jamestowne timeline says that system “lays the economic foundation” for legal slavery. On July 30, 1619, Governor George Yeardley opened the first General Assembly in the choir of the church at Jamestown. It had the governor, four councilors, and twenty-two burgesses elected by the free white men of each settlement. Its first law set a minimum price for tobacco. Historic Jamestowne calls it the first representative governing body to meet in the Americas, and the National Park Service the beginning of representative government in what is now the United States. In late August 1619 the White Lion, an English privateer, arrived at Point Comfort with “20. and odd Negroes,” as John Rolfe put it, who had been taken from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico. They were from Angola, and they had been captured in wars between Portugal and the Kongo and Ndongo kingdoms. A second privateer, the Treasurer, may have sold seven to nine more, among them a woman called Angela. The Africans were sold into bondage although Virginia had no laws on slavery. It is contested whether they were considered indentured servants or enslaved people, but the National Park Service writes that the evidence points to treatment close to enslavement. The Company also sent about ninety women that year to marry settlers. Tobacco gave the colonists a reason to take more Powhatan land. In March 1622 Opechancanough, who had become the more powerful leader after Powhatan’s death in 1618 and was tired of English encroachment, planned a coordinated attack. A Powhatan boy living with the English warned Jamestown, which was spared, but 350 to 400 of the 1,200 settlers were killed according to the National Park Service. Historic Jamestowne says 347, about a quarter of the total, in one place and a third of the colonists in another. Ten years of war followed, until a shaky peace in 1632. In 1624 the king took away the bankrupt Company’s charter, and Virginia became a royal colony. In April 1644 Opechancanough attacked again and killed another 350 to 400 settlers of some 8,000. After he was captured and shot by a guard in 1646, the Powhatan chiefdom was reduced to tributary status and its new leader signed treaties making the Powhatan subjects of the English. Jamestown set patterns that shaped the South and the nation. It showed that a private company could found a colony. It produced a plantation economy built on tobacco and a representative assembly open to the free white men of property. It also meant dispossession of Native peoples and a growing system of slavery. In 1676 Bacon’s Rebellion, in which about a thousand settlers followed Nathaniel Bacon against the Native peoples they blamed for frontier raids and against Governor Berkeley, burned much of the town. Afterwards a new treaty set up reservation lands and required yearly tribute of fish and game. Jamestown remained the capital until the statehouse burned in 1698 and the government moved to Williamsburg in 1699. The place itself nearly vanished. By 1893, when the Association for the Preservation of Virginia Antiquities (now Preservation Virginia) received part of the island, river erosion had led many to think that the 1607 fort lay under water. The National Park Service acquired the rest in 1934. Archaeologists have since uncovered the fort, thousands of Native artifacts, and, in 2010, the church where Pocahontas and Rolfe were married. Historic Jamestowne notes that the traditional story painted the settlers as ill-suited to the task, but twenty years of archaeology suggest that many of the artisans and laborers did all they could to build a working colony. Jamestown was where English America began, and where the contradictions of American history first took shape together: self-government alongside slavery and the dispossession of Native peoples. title: Japanese American Incarceration
subtitle: The forced removal and imprisonment of Japanese Americans during World War II
summary: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the United States government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps for most of World War II. Nearly 70,000 of them were American citizens. None was charged with a crime, and none could appeal. The removal rested on Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v. United States (1944). In 1988 Congress acknowledged that the incarceration was a “grave injustice” caused by “racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership.” It apologized and paid $20,000 to each survivor.
location: West Coast exclusion zones; ten War Relocation Centers in California, Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas
thumbAlt: Rows of barracks at the Manzanar War Relocation Center
aliases: Japanese American internment internment camps War Relocation Authority Civil Liberties Act of 1988 redress Executive Order 9066
themeText: Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship War and the military Constitution and law Immigration
text: West Coast exclusion zones; ten War Relocation Centers in California, Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas Executive Order 9066 Signed February 19, 1942, about ten weeks after Pearl Harbor People removed About 122,000 (National Archives); other sources give 110,000 to 120,000 Citizens Nearly 70,000, about two-thirds of those removed Camps Ten War Relocation Centers, after temporary “assembly centers” Supreme Court Korematsu v. United States, December 18, 1944, upheld the removal 6 to 3 Exclusion lifted January 2, 1945 Redress Civil Liberties Act, signed August 10, 1988: apology and $20,000 per survivor; 82,219 people received payments Between 1861 and 1940 about 275,000 Japanese immigrants came to Hawaii and the mainland United States, most of them between 1898 and 1924, when new quotas ended Asian immigration. On the West Coast they farmed marginal land, fished, and ran small businesses. In 1940 Japanese Americans controlled less than 4 percent of California’s farmland but produced more than 10 percent of the value of its farm output. They faced discrimination at every turn. Real estate agents kept them in ethnic enclaves, a 1913 California law barred immigrants who could not become citizens from owning land, and in 1922 the Supreme Court ruled in Ozawa v. United States that Japanese immigrants could be denied citizenship. The immigrant generation, the Issei, therefore remained aliens, while their American-born children, the Nisei, were citizens by birth. Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, set off fears for national security, especially on the West Coast. The National Archives notes that these fears combined with economic competition, distrust of cultural separateness, and long-standing anti-Asian racism. Lobbyists from Western states, many of them representing competing farm interests or nativist groups, pressed Congress and the president to remove all people of Japanese descent, Issei and Nisei alike. Justice Department officials raised constitutional and ethical objections, so the army carried out the plan instead. German and Italian nationals were also interned, more than ten thousand of them, but individually and after reviews. People of Japanese descent were removed as a group. On February 19, 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. It authorized the secretary of war and military commanders to “prescribe military areas … from which any or all persons may be excluded.” It named no ethnic group. Lieutenant General John L. DeWitt of the Western Defense Command then imposed curfews on Japanese Americans only. On March 21 Congress made violating the military orders a crime punishable by up to a year in prison. DeWitt first asked Japanese Americans to leave the coastal zones voluntarily. Only about 7 percent complied, and officials in inland states refused to accept Japanese Americans except under guard. On March 29, 1942, he ordered the forced removal of the remaining West Coast residents of Japanese ancestry on 48 hours’ notice. The speed of the removal forced many families to sell homes, farms, and businesses in a hurry. Over the next six months about 122,000 men, women, and children were moved first to temporary “assembly centers” and then to ten fenced and guarded “relocation centers” in remote parts of six Western states and Arkansas: Manzanar and Tule Lake in California, Poston and Gila River in Arizona, Topaz in Utah, Minidoka in Idaho, Heart Mountain in Wyoming, Granada in Colorado, and Jerome and Rohwer in Arkansas. The federal courts’ educational page counts some 26 sites in all. A civilian agency, the War Relocation Authority (WRA), created on March 18, 1942, ran the camps. Its first director, Milton Eisenhower, had hoped for voluntary resettlement, but when Western governors refused to accept Japanese Americans except under guard, he reluctantly planned a network of permanent camps. Dillon Myer replaced him in June 1942. In early 1943 the government gave every adult in the camps a “loyalty questionnaire.” Question 27 asked men whether they would serve in combat wherever ordered, and question 28 asked everyone to swear allegiance to the United States and renounce any allegiance to Japan’s emperor. Many resented being asked to renounce an allegiance they had never held, and Issei, barred from American citizenship, feared being left stateless. Those judged “disloyal” were segregated at Tule Lake, where guards beat inmates and a strike in November 1943 was distorted by West Coast newspapers into a “riot.” Some Japanese Americans fought the orders in court. Fred Korematsu, a young shipyard welder from the Oakland area, refused to report, changed his name and appearance, and was arrested on May 30, 1942. “I was an American citizen,” he later said, “and I had as many rights as anyone else.” On December 18, 1944, the Supreme Court upheld his conviction 6 to 3. Justice Hugo Black wrote that racial restrictions were “immediately suspect” but that “pressing public necessity” could justify them. Korematsu, he said, was excluded “because we are at war with the Japanese Empire.” Justice Frank Murphy called the order the “legalization of racism.” Justice Robert Jackson likened the principle of military necessity the Court had accepted to “a loaded weapon.” The same day the Court decided a companion case, the Endo case, in the prisoner’s favor, but it sidestepped the constitutional question. The day before, the War Department had announced that the exclusion would end on January 2, 1945. Others served. More than 30,000 Japanese Americans fought for the United States in segregated units, while their families remained behind barbed wire. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, formed on March 23, 1943, with the 100th Infantry Battalion from Hawaii, became the most decorated unit in American military history for its size and length of service. It suffered about 800 killed or missing, and its men won more than 4,000 Purple Hearts and 29 Distinguished Service Crosses. In France in 1944 the 442nd rescued the “Lost Battalion” of Texas soldiers at a cost of casualties several times the number of men saved. “You fought the enemy abroad and prejudice at home and you won,” President Harry Truman told the unit in July 1946. The WRA closed every camp except Tule Lake by the end of 1945, pushing inmates to resettle. Most had lost their homes and property. A congressional commission later estimated their property losses at $1.3 billion and lost income at $2.7 billion, in 1983 dollars. The Japanese American Evacuation Claims Act of 1948 paid only token amounts, because it required documents that few families still had. Encouraged by the civil rights movement, Japanese American activists began calling for redress in 1970. In 1980 Congress created the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians, which heard more than 750 witnesses in twenty cities. Its 1983 report, Personal Justice Denied, gave factual and moral support for reparations. Meanwhile documents uncovered by the legal historian Peter Irons showed that officials had suppressed FBI and Federal Communications Commission reports refuting claims of Japanese American espionage. On November 10, 1983, Judge Marilyn Hall Patel overturned Korematsu’s conviction. His case, she wrote, “stands as a caution that in times of distress the shield of military necessity and national security must not be used to protect governmental actions from close scrutiny and accountability.” President Ronald Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act on August 10, 1988, and the first redress checks, each with a signed presidential apology, were presented in October 1990. In all, 82,219 people received payments. The incarceration showed how quickly fear and racism could override constitutional rights in wartime, and the decades-long fight for redress showed how a democracy can admit a wrong. I was an American citizen, and I had as many rights as anyone else. Fred Korematsu on his decision to challenge the exclusion order I dissent, therefore, from this legalization of racism. Justice Frank Murphy dissent, Korematsu v. United States, 1944 You fought the enemy abroad and prejudice at home and you won. President Harry S. Truman to the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, July 15, 1946 It stands as a caution that in times of distress the shield of military necessity and national security must not be used to protect governmental actions from close scrutiny and accountability. title: Juneteenth
subtitle: June 19, 1865: freedom announced in Texas, now a national holiday
summary: On June 19, 1865, two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation, Union general Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3 in Galveston, informing the people of Texas that all enslaved people were free. The day became known as Juneteenth, a blend of “June” and “nineteenth.” Celebrated by African American communities in Texas since 1866 and later in other states, it is the oldest known celebration of the end of slavery in the United States, and became a national holiday in 2021.
thumbAlt: The handwritten text of General Order No. 3, issued at Galveston, Texas, on June 19, 1865
aliases: Freedom Day Emancipation Day General Order No. 3
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history National symbols and holidays
text: Galveston, Texas Order General Order No. 3, issued by Maj. Gen. Gordon Granger Place Galveston, Texas; Granger’s troops had arrived the day before Other names Freedom Day, Emancipation Day First celebrated In African American communities in Texas, from 1866 National holiday Signed into law on June 17, 2021 General Order No. 3 came two and a half years after President Abraham Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation. The National Archives describes it as the federal government’s final execution and fulfillment of the Proclamation’s terms: the people it addressed were the last group of Americans to be informed that all formerly enslaved persons were free. Maj. Gen. Gordon Granger commanded the Union army’s District of Texas. His troops arrived in Galveston on June 18, 1865, and the next day he issued the order. General Order No. 3 begins: “The people of Texas are informed that, in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free.” It declared an absolute equality of personal and property rights between former masters and the formerly enslaved, and turned their relationship into that of employer and hired labor. But it also advised the freedpeople to stay quietly at their present homes and work for wages, and warned that they would not be allowed to gather at military posts or be “supported in idleness.” The order made freedom official across Texas. Its closing lines, the National Archives notes, used racist language that foreshadowed how long the fight for equal rights would continue. African American communities in Texas began celebrating the day in 1866, and the celebration later spread to other states. Nearly all states and the District of Columbia came to recognize Juneteenth, and on June 17, 2021, President Joe Biden signed legislation making it a national holiday. The original handwritten order survives at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. Juneteenth marks the moment emancipation reached the last enslaved Americans in the Confederacy, and, as the nation’s oldest celebration of the end of slavery, it links the history of freedom to how Americans remember it today. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lq8TNKZVEWs What is Juneteenth, and why is it important? - Karlos K. title: The Lewis and Clark Expedition
subtitle: The Corps of Discovery crosses the continent, 1804–1806
summary: At Thomas Jefferson’s direction, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led the Corps of Discovery, a small party made up mostly of U.S. Army enlisted men, up the Missouri River from near St. Louis in May 1804. They crossed the Rocky Mountains, reached the Pacific coast in November 1805 and returned to St. Louis on September 23, 1806, after a journey the National Archives puts at 8,000 miles. They mapped the West, recorded its plants and animals, and met more than fifty Native nations. Their survival depended on Native hosts and guides, among them Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, and on the labor of York, a man enslaved by Clark.
location: From St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Rockies, to the Pacific coast and back
thumbAlt: Painting of Lewis and Clark’s party on the Columbia River
aliases: Corps of Discovery Meriwether Lewis William Clark York Fort Mandan Fort Clatsop Ocian in view
themeText: Territorial expansion Indigenous history Science and technology
text: From St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Rockies, to the Pacific coast and back Funding $2,500, requested in Jefferson’s confidential message to Congress, January 18, 1803 Departed May 14, 1804, from near St. Louis Party About 31 explorers, mostly U.S. Army enlisted men, plus Sacagawea and her son Reached the coast November 1805, at the Columbia River estuary Returned About noon, September 23, 1806, to St. Louis Distance About 8,000 miles round trip Even before the Louisiana Purchase, Jefferson believed the United States should stretch across the continent. In a secret message of January 18, 1803, while the territory still belonged to France, he asked Congress for $2,500 to explore the West to the Pacific. The National Archives notes that the modest request, explained “principally in terms of promoting commerce,” concealed his larger expansionist goals. In the same message Jefferson described Native nations as increasingly unwilling to sell their land, and proposed ways to bring them to give up hunting and cede territory. Jefferson chose Lewis, his former private secretary, to lead the expedition, and Lewis chose his friend and former commanding officer, William Clark, to share the command. Their orders were to explore the Missouri to its source, find the most direct water route to the Pacific, report on the geography, plants, animals and climate of the West, and establish relations with the Native nations they met while impressing them with American power. Jefferson helped plan the supplies: arms, food, medicines, scientific instruments and gifts for Native leaders. The expedition ran out of whiskey, tobacco and salt, but never of rifles, powder, ink or paper. The Corps started up the Missouri from near St. Louis on May 14, 1804. After five months it built Fort Mandan near the Mandan villages, 1,600 miles upriver in present-day North Dakota, and wintered there. There the captains hired the French-Canadian trader Toussaint Charbonneau and his young Shoshone wife, Sacagawea, as interpreters. In April 1805 the Corps left Fort Mandan and followed the Missouri into country no American had mapped. Along the Lemhi River in present-day Idaho, Sacagawea’s people provided horses and a guide for the crossing of the Continental Divide. After some 600 miles by water down the Clearwater, Snake and Columbia rivers, Clark wrote on November 7, 1805, “Ocian in view! O! the joy,” though he was actually looking at the Columbia’s estuary; the Pacific itself was still a couple of weeks away. The party wintered at Fort Clatsop, named for the local Clatsop people, from December 1805 to March 1806. On the way home the Corps split up to explore more country. Sacagawea guided Clark’s party over Bozeman Pass into the Yellowstone valley, and on July 25, 1806, Clark carved his name on the rock he called “Pompy’s Tower,” after Sacagawea’s son. Lewis’s group had the expedition’s only violent encounter, a fight with a small party of Blackfeet (Pikuni). The Corps reunited, left Sacagawea’s family at the Mandan villages, and reached St. Louis at about noon on September 23, 1806, where, Sergeant John Ordway wrote, “the people gathred on the Shore and Huzzared three cheers.” The expedition did not find an all-water route to the Pacific. But it gave the U.S. government “its first glimpse of the vast lands that lay west of the Mississippi River.” Its maps and specimens went to the American Philosophical Society in Philadelphia. Clark became Indian agent at St. Louis, governor of the Missouri Territory and superintendent of Indian affairs; Lewis became governor of the Louisiana Territory but struggled in the post and died of gunshot wounds in 1809, commonly believed to have been suicide. York, after all his service, was denied both his payment and his freedom. Lewis and Clark became national heroes and their journey a symbol of American exploration. The National Park Service also calls it “a watershed moment that set forth untold loss” to the very tribes who helped the expedition survive. The Corps traded with, learned from and depended on more than fifty Native nations, whose food, knowledge and skills were “essential to the expedition’s survival.” Today the 4,900-mile Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail tells the story from many perspectives, including those of “a president and an enslaved man, women and men, French-speaking boatmen and American Indians.” The Lewis and Clark Expedition carried American claims across the continent and gave the government its first detailed knowledge of the West. It succeeded because of Native hosts and guides, a young Shoshone mother and an enslaved man, and it opened the way for the settlement that would take most of the West’s Native land. Where and when did it begin? The start of the expedition can be dated in several ways. Jefferson’s secret request to Congress came in January 1803, while the Park Service’s Fort Clatsop page says he “announced plans” for the expedition in June 1803. The National Historic Trail commemorates a Corps that “departed Pittsburgh” in 1803; the voyage up the Missouri began from near St. Louis on May 14, 1804. York York was a frontiersman and hunter, enslaved by Clark, and likely the first African American to cross the continent. The Park Service calls him “an American explorer who made important contributions” to the expedition; after it returned, he “was denied his payment and his freedom.” Ocian in view! O! the joy. title: Lexington and Concord
subtitle: April 19, 1775: the first fighting of the American Revolution and “the shot heard ’round the world”
summary: Before dawn on April 19, 1775, about 700 British soldiers marched from Boston to seize military supplies that Massachusetts patriots had stockpiled at Concord. Warned by Paul Revere, William Dawes, Samuel Prescott, and church bells across the countryside, militia turned out. On Lexington Green a shot was fired, no one knows by whom, and British volleys killed eight militiamen. At Concord’s North Bridge the militia fired back, and on the long road back to Boston thousands of them harried the retreating regulars. The day’s fighting, by the Park Service’s count involving some 1,700 British regulars and over 4,000 colonial militia, began the Revolutionary War.
thumbAlt: Amos Doolittle’s 1775 engraving of British regulars firing on the militia on Lexington Green
aliases: Paul Revere’s ride Midnight ride Minute Men Minutemen North Bridge shot heard round the world Battle Road Lexington Green
themeText: War and the military Political thought
text: Lexington, Lincoln, and Concord, Massachusetts Date April 19, 1775 British goal Seize and destroy colonial arms and supplies at Concord, 18 miles from Boston (Park Service) Initial British force About 700 grenadiers and light infantry under Lt. Col. Francis Smith Whole day Some 1,700 British regulars and over 4,000 colonial militia, over 16 miles of road Lexington Seven militiamen killed and one mortally wounded Aftermath About 20,000 militia besieged the British in Boston In 1774, after the Boston Tea Party, British warships closed Boston Harbor, and General Thomas Gage, now royal governor, dismissed the elected Massachusetts legislature under the Massachusetts Government Act. Patriots answered by forming a Provincial Congress, an “essentially illegal body” that took control of the militia and began stockpiling arms, ammunition, and supplies, aiming to raise and equip 15,000 men. Militia companies trained, and some towns organized “minute men” who could turn out quickly. Isolated in Boston, Gage followed advice from London and decided to strike at the supplies before the colonists were ready. Gage ordered Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith to march “with the utmost expedition and secrecy to Concord,” where he was to “seize and destroy all artillery, Ammunition, Provisions, Tents, Small Arms, and all Military Stores whatever,” while taking care that the soldiers did not plunder. The orders said nothing about arresting political leaders, though patriots feared that too: John Hancock and Samuel Adams were staying in Lexington. Patriot intelligence learned of the plan almost at once. The alarm. On the night of April 18, Dr. Joseph Warren sent Paul Revere and William Dawes to warn Hancock, Adams, and the countryside. Dawes took the land route over Boston Neck, while Revere was rowed past a British warship to Charlestown. Two lanterns in the North Church steeple, a signal Revere had arranged, told patriots the troops were crossing by water. After warning Hancock and Adams, Revere, Dawes, and Samuel Prescott rode on toward Concord. A British patrol captured Revere; Dawes fled; Prescott jumped a fence and reached Concord around 1:30 a.m. Ferrying the regulars across the Charles took nearly three hours, and by the time they marched at about 2 a.m., bells and gunfire were spreading the alarm. Lexington. About 5 a.m. the British vanguard reached Lexington Green, where Captain John Parker’s militia company of just over seventy men stood. Parker ordered his men to disperse. A shot rang out, “historians still debate who fired it,” and the British fired volleys that killed seven militiamen and mortally wounded another. Each side blamed the other. The Provincial Congress rushed its account to London, describing British troops who “unprovoked, shed the blood” of Lexington men, while Gage reported that the militia, “about 200 armed Men,” had fired first. The American Battlefield Trust concludes that “we still don’t know the truth.” Concord. The British reached Concord about 8 a.m. and sent about 220 men to hold the North Bridge and search a farm for arms. Seeing smoke rise from the town, close to 400 militia on the high ground assumed the regulars were burning it and advanced. When the British fired, killing Captain Isaac Davis and another Acton man, Major John Buttrick shouted “For God’s sake, fire!” The militia’s volley killed three British soldiers and wounded nine. It became known as “the shot heard round the world.” In town, the widow Mary Moulton persuaded soldiers to put out a fire that threatened the Town House. The Battle Road. As Smith’s column turned back, militia from the surrounding towns attacked it from behind trees, walls, and buildings for the next twelve miles, and Parker’s Lexington men took revenge from cover. Reinforcements met the column near Lexington, but the running fight continued until the troops reached the protection of British ships around Boston. Militiamen poured in from across New England and besieged the British in Boston. The Yawp and the Battlefield Trust both put the force at about twenty thousand. In June the militia fortified Breed’s Hill, and in the misnamed Battle of Bunker Hill the British took the hill only at a heavy cost. When the Second Continental Congress met in May 1775, war had already begun. April 19 turned a political struggle into a war. That summer the Continental Congress adopted the New England militia as the Continental Army under George Washington, and eight years of fighting followed. The Park Service notes that the day has been remembered by later generations as the “shot heard ’round the world,” and that Minute Man National Historical Park is both a battlefield and a graveyard where many soldiers killed that day remain. The fighting at Lexington and Concord was the first armed conflict of the American Revolution. The colonists’ alarm network, local militias, and determination to defend their towns showed that Britain faced not a few agitators but an armed population, and the contest over who fired first showed how quickly both sides fought for public opinion as well. You will march with the Corps of Grenadiers and Light Infantry put under your command, with the utmost expedition and secrecy to Concord, where you will seize and destroy all artillery, Ammunition, Provisions, Tents, Small Arms, and all Military Stores whatever. General Thomas Gage orders to Lt. Col. Francis Smith, April 1775 You'll have noise enough before long! The Regulars are coming! Paul Revere to Sergeant William Munroe at Lexington, as recalled in later accounts The troops of Britain, unprovoked, shed the blood of sundry of the loyal American subjects of the British King in the field of Lexington. title: The Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
subtitle: Ford’s Theatre, April 14, 1865
summary: On the evening of April 14, 1865, five days after Lee’s surrender at Appomattox, President Abraham Lincoln was shot in the head by the actor John Wilkes Booth while watching a play at Ford’s Theatre in Washington. He died the next morning, the first American president to be assassinated. Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, had plotted with others to kill several leaders of the government. Lincoln’s death turned the celebration of victory into national mourning and placed Andrew Johnson in charge of Reconstruction.
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of Lincoln’s assassination at Ford’s Theatre
themeText: The presidency War and the military
text: Ford’s Theatre, Washington, D.C. Date April 14, 1865; Lincoln died the morning of April 15 Assassin John Wilkes Booth, actor and Confederate sympathizer Other targets Secretary of State William H. Seward, Vice President Andrew Johnson, General Ulysses S. Grant Aftermath Booth was found and killed ten days later; four co-conspirators were hanged On April 3, 1865, Lincoln walked through Richmond, the fallen Confederate capital, cheered by crowds of African Americans. On April 9 Lee surrendered at Appomattox. On April 11, Lincoln publicly endorsed voting rights for some Black men. John Wilkes Booth, a member of a well-known acting family and an ardent Confederate sympathizer, had spent much of the war plotting to kidnap Lincoln as a bargaining chip for the Confederacy. When he heard Lincoln endorse Black suffrage on April 11, he conspired with accomplices to kill Lincoln, Secretary of State William Seward, Vice President Andrew Johnson, and General Grant. On April 14, Lincoln and his wife, Mary Todd Lincoln, attended a performance of the comedy Our American Cousin at Ford’s Theatre. Booth entered the presidential box and shot Lincoln point-blank in the back of the head, then leapt to the stage shouting “Sic semper tyrannis!” and escaped. Lincoln died early the next morning. After a frantic search, Booth was found hiding in a barn in rural Virginia ten days later and was killed. Four of his co-conspirators were convicted and hanged. After seven days of official mourning, Lincoln’s funeral train carried his body 1,700 miles to Springfield, Illinois, as crowds gathered in towns and cities along the way. Lincoln’s death made him a national martyr and removed the leader best positioned to guide Reconstruction. His successor, Andrew Johnson, whom Booth’s plot had also targeted, pursued a lenient policy toward the defeated South that sparked a bitter conflict with Congress. Ford’s Theatre is preserved today as part of Ford’s Theatre National Historic Site. The first assassination of an American president cut short Lincoln’s leadership at the moment of victory and profoundly shaped how the nation approached Reconstruction. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hVLM0BSqx5o What Booth Said After He Killed Lincoln Smithsonian Channel 3:15 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ozI11aFfNQ The Assassination of Abraham Lincoln Explained Mr. Beat 13:05 2026-10-22

title: The Little Rock Nine
subtitle: The desegregation of Central High School, 1957
summary: In September 1957, nine Black students tried to enroll at all-white Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, under a court-ordered desegregation plan. Governor Orval Faubus sent the Arkansas National Guard to keep them out, and a white mob gathered outside. After weeks of standoff, President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent troops of the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to escort and protect the students, a dramatic use of federal power to enforce Brown v. Board of Education.
thumbAlt: Members of the Little Rock Nine with New York mayor Robert F. Wagner
aliases: Central High crisis Orval Faubus 101st Airborne
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Constitution and law The presidency
text: Little Rock, Arkansas The Nine Minnijean Brown, Terrence Roberts, Elizabeth Eckford, Ernest Green, Thelma Mothershed, Melba Pattillo, Gloria Ray, Jefferson Thomas, and Carlotta Walls Organizer Daisy Bates, president of the Arkansas NAACP Federal troops 101st Airborne Division, sent by President Eisenhower, September 1957 First Black graduate Ernest Green, May 1958 Honor NAACP Spingarn Medal, 1958 Three years after the Supreme Court ruled in Brown that segregated schools were unconstitutional, Daisy Bates, president of the Arkansas NAACP, recruited nine students to enroll at Central High. Governor Orval Faubus used state power to block the students and defy the federal courts. On September 4, 1957, the first day of school, a white mob gathered in front of Central High, and Faubus deployed the Arkansas National Guard to bar the Black students. NAACP lawyers, including Thurgood Marshall, won a federal injunction against the governor. On September 23 the students entered through a side entrance with police escorts but were rushed home as the mob grew. Martin Luther King Jr. urged Eisenhower to take “a strong forthright stand.” Aware that Little Rock was becoming an international embarrassment, Eisenhower reluctantly sent the 101st Airborne; soldiers and federalized National Guardsmen protected the students for the rest of the school year. In May 1958 Ernest Green became Central High’s first Black graduate; King attended the ceremony. That fall Faubus closed all of Little Rock’s public high schools rather than continue desegregation, but the courts soon ordered the schools reopened and desegregation resumed. Little Rock showed that the federal government would use force to uphold the Constitution against state defiance, and it made the nine students symbols of courage. Central High School is now a National Historic Site, and still an operating public high school. The Little Rock crisis was a defining test of Brown and of the federal government’s willingness to enforce it. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fPVOO5sugMY Nine from Little Rock, 1964 - Restored US National Archives 18:31 2026-10-22

title: The Louisiana Purchase
subtitle: The United States doubles in size, 1803
summary: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million. The land stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains, covered 828,000 square miles, and doubled the size of the country. President Thomas Jefferson had only wanted to buy New Orleans and the Floridas, but Napoleon, who had just lost an army to yellow fever and revolt in Haiti and expected war with Britain, offered the whole territory. The purchase secured the Mississippi for American farmers and opened the way west. It also raised questions that would trouble the country for decades: whether the Constitution allowed it, whether slavery would spread into the new land, and what would become of the many Native nations who lived there.
location: The Mississippi River valley to the Rocky Mountains
thumbAlt: Map of the Louisiana Purchase within the present-day United States
aliases: Louisiana Territory Napoleon Robert Livingston James Monroe Three Flags Day Treaty of Cession Pinckney Treaty
themeText: Territorial expansion Foreign policy and diplomacy Constitution and law Indigenous history Slavery and emancipation
text: The Mississippi River valley to the Rocky Mountains Signed April 30, 1803, in Paris Price $15 million: 60 million francs ($11.25 million) plus 20 million francs ($3.75 million) to cover American claims against France Size 828,000 square miles, about 530 million acres; all or part of fifteen present-day states Negotiators Robert Livingston and James Monroe for the United States; François Barbé-Marbois for France Original instructions To buy New Orleans and the Floridas for up to $10 million Senate vote Ratified October 20, 1803, by 24 to 7 As settlers crossed the Appalachians, the Mississippi River became the main route by which western farmers shipped their produce, and New Orleans was the port where goods were loaded onto ocean-going ships. Spain had owned Louisiana since 1762. The Pinckney Treaty of 1795 gave Americans the right to navigate the river and to move their goods at New Orleans, and with a weak Spain in charge, the Americans expected to expand west without trouble. Then Napoleon Bonaparte revived French plans for an empire in the Americas. France got Louisiana back from Spain by a secret treaty in 1800 and took possession in 1802. Napoleon meant to recapture the sugar colony of Saint-Domingue, today Haiti, from the enslaved people in revolt there, and to use Louisiana as the granary of his empire. In 1802, before the French arrived, Spanish officials closed the Mississippi to American shipping. Westerners were alarmed to see the stronger power of France at New Orleans. Jefferson wrote that “there is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans.” He prepared for conflict in the Mississippi Valley and sent James Monroe to join Robert Livingston, the minister in Paris, to buy New Orleans and West Florida for as much as $10 million. If that failed, they were to seek a military alliance with Britain. Then France's plans collapsed. Yellow fever and the fighting of enslaved rebels destroyed the French army in Haiti, and the Yawp says it was this defeat that took away Napoleon’s ability to control the island. War with Britain also loomed again, and the Miller Center says Napoleon needed money to fight it. Napoleon gave up his American project. The French offered a surprised Monroe and Livingston not only New Orleans but the entire territory for $15 million. This was far beyond their instructions, but they agreed. The National Archives notes that the territory was larger than Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Portugal combined, and that Napoleon threatened to withdraw the offer if the Americans delayed. The agreement had three parts: the Treaty of Cession, signed on April 30, 1803, and two conventions. The first set the price of 60 million francs ($11,250,000), paid in U.S. bonds at 6 percent interest, and the second provided 20 million francs ($3,750,000) to pay American citizens’ claims against France. France's negotiator was the treasury minister François Barbé-Marbois, and Napoleon and his foreign minister Talleyrand signed the financial agreement. Livingston said after signing: “We have lived long but this is the noblest work of our whole lives… The United States take rank this day among the first powers of the world.” Jefferson faced a dilemma. He was known as a strict reader of the Constitution, and it said nothing about buying territory. The sources describe how he resolved it in different ways. The State Department says Jefferson decided to ignore the “legalistic interpretation” and to forgo an amendment, which helped create the principle of implied powers. The National Archives says the desire to expand across the continent “trumped his ideological beliefs.” The Yawp reports that he asked his cabinet and believed he should be able to “throw himself on the justice of his country” when he served the interests of the people. Another account says he argued that his power to make treaties was sufficient. In his annual message of October 17, 1803, Jefferson explained the benefits for security and trade. The Senate ratified the treaty on October 20 by 24 votes to 7. The West was elated at the news. On November 30, 1803, Spain formally returned Louisiana to France, which held it for twenty days. On December 20, at the Cabildo in New Orleans, France transferred the territory to the United States, and the Americans took possession ten days later. Jefferson appointed William C. C. Claiborne and General James Wilkinson to receive it. Claiborne promised the people of Louisiana that they could rely on “the security of your liberty, your property, and the religion of your choice.” Because winter travel up the Mississippi was hard, Upper Louisiana, centered on St. Louis, remained in Spanish hands until March 1804. On March 9 the Spanish flag came down and the French flag went up, and the next morning the American flag replaced it, a ceremony remembered as Three Flags Day. The treaty promised that the people of the ceded territory would be “incorporated in the Union of the United States” and would enjoy “all these rights, advantages and immunities of citizens of the United States,” and in the meantime be protected in their liberty, property, and religion. It also committed the United States to carry out the treaties Spain had made with Native tribes until new ones were agreed by mutual consent. The expedition of Meriwether Lewis and William Clark soon set out to explore the territory and reach the Pacific. The National Archives calls Louisiana the first major cession in a long series of expansions across the nineteenth century. Within fifty years the borders of the contiguous United States were set with the Gadsden Purchase. Each expansion deepened the sectional split over slavery. When Missouri, carved from the Louisiana Purchase, asked for statehood in 1819 with more than ten thousand enslaved people, the Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted it as a slave state and Maine as a free state and prohibited slavery north of the 36°30’ line in the rest of the Purchase. The Haitian Revolution that helped make the sale possible had also inspired free and enslaved Black Americans and terrified white Americans. The purchase also ignored the people who already lived on the land. The National Archives writes that thousands of American Indians across dozens of tribes lived there, and that as Americans moved west, conflict followed, until Native people were forcibly moved onto reservations and lost vast areas of their lands. The treaty itself mentions Native peoples only in a pledge to carry out Spain’s existing treaties with them until new ones were agreed. The price per acre is usually quoted as about four cents. Dividing $15 million by the State Department’s 530 million acres gives less than three cents (our own arithmetic), so the figure is only an approximation. Jefferson’s decision, the State Department says, contributed to the principle of the federal government’s implied powers. The Louisiana Purchase made the United States a continental power and secured the Mississippi, but it also planted the conflicts over slavery and Native land that would define the next half-century. There is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans. Thomas Jefferson on the danger of French control We have lived long but this is the noblest work of our whole lives… The United States take rank this day among the first powers of the world. Robert R. Livingston after signing the treaty The inhabitants of the ceded territory shall be incorporated in the Union of the United States.
