title: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom
subtitle: The 1963 march where King delivered “I Have a Dream”
summary: On August 28, 1963, a crowd that the King Institute puts at more than 200,000 and the National Archives at more than 250,000 gathered in Washington, D.C., for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Conceived by the labor leader A. Philip Randolph and organized by Bayard Rustin in less than two months, it united the major civil rights organizations, labor unions, and churches. They demanded a strong civil rights law, voting rights, school desegregation, jobs, and fair employment. It closed at the Lincoln Memorial with Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech. The march helped build pressure for the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, whose provisions reflected its demands.
thumbAlt: Martin Luther King Jr. among the crowd at the March on Washington
aliases: I Have a Dream 1963 March on Washington Big Six Bayard Rustin A. Philip Randolph
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Labor and work Reform and protest
text: Lincoln Memorial, Washington, D.C. Date August 28, 1963 Crowd More than 200,000 (King Institute) or 250,000 (National Archives) Leaders The “Big Six”: Randolph, Roy Wilkins (NAACP), Whitney Young (National Urban League), King (SCLC), James Farmer (CORE), John Lewis (SNCC) Organizer Bayard Rustin, deputy director, headquartered in Harlem Route Rally at the Washington Monument, march along the National Mall, program at the Lincoln Memorial Afterward Leaders met President Kennedy and Vice President Johnson at the White House The idea had a long history. In 1941 A. Philip Randolph, head of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened to bring 100,000 Black marchers to Washington to protest their exclusion from defense jobs. President Franklin Roosevelt responded with Executive Order 8802, which created the Fair Employment Practices Commission, and Randolph called off the march. Civil rights supporters gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the Prayer Pilgrimage for Freedom in May 1957 and for a Youth March for Integrated Schools in October 1958. By 1963, the centennial of the Emancipation Proclamation, Black Americans still faced high unemployment, low wages, disfranchisement, and segregation. Randolph began planning in 1962. The King Institute dates his first permit letter to May 24, 1962, while the National Archives says he first proposed the march in late 1962 and got little response. In May 1963, at the height of the Birmingham campaign, King joined Randolph, James Farmer of CORE, and Charles McDew of SNCC in calling for a march, declaring, “Let the black laboring masses speak!” The next month President Kennedy asked the nation for civil rights legislation. The march’s official goals, as listed by the King Institute and the American Yawp, were a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregation in public accommodations, protection of the right to vote, desegregation of all public schools in 1963, a federal works program to train and place unemployed workers, a federal fair employment law, and a higher minimum wage. Its full name, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, reflected the economic demands at its heart, which came from Randolph’s labor background. Success depended on cooperation among the “Big Six”: Randolph, Roy Wilkins of the NAACP, Whitney Young of the National Urban League, King of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, James Farmer of the Congress of Racial Equality, and John Lewis of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. The National Archives notes that these leaders competed for funding and press coverage. Bayard Rustin, Randolph’s trusted associate, whom Randolph called “Mr. March-on-Washington,” was appointed deputy director despite the concerns of many civil rights leaders. Working from headquarters in Harlem with a small office in Washington and a core staff of 200 volunteers, Rustin put the event together in less than two months. Sponsors grew to include the NAACP, the National Urban League, the National Council of the Churches of Christ, the National Catholic Conference for Interracial Justice, and the United Auto Workers. The day began with a rally at the Washington Monument featuring celebrities and musicians. Marchers then walked the mile-long National Mall to the Lincoln Memorial for a three-hour program. Performers and speakers included Marian Anderson, Odetta, Joan Baez, Bob Dylan, Daisy Bates, Ossie Davis and Ruby Dee, Rabbi Joachim Prinz, Walter Reuther of the UAW, Roy Wilkins, Whitney Young, and John Lewis. Lewis’s prepared speech caused a crisis. It called Kennedy’s civil rights bill “too little and too late” and threatened to “march through the South, through the heart of Dixie, the way Sherman did.” Reuther, Justice Department official Burke Marshall, and Archbishop Patrick O’Boyle of Washington objected. In a caucus with King, Randolph, and SNCC’s James Forman, Lewis agreed to cut those passages, though he believed the final version was “still a strong speech, very strong.” King spoke near the end. Drawing on themes he had used in speeches for years, including an address to 150,000 people in Detroit two months earlier, he used a metaphor suggested by his adviser Clarence Jones for the unfulfilled promise of constitutional rights: “America has defaulted on this promissory note insofar as her citizens of color are concerned.” He had finished the text only at 3:30 that morning. Partway through, he set the manuscript aside and turned to a refrain he had used before: “I have a dream.” He later recalled, “I just turned aside from the manuscript altogether. I didn’t come back to it.” He closed by imagining the day when all of God’s children could sing, “Free at last! Free at last! Thank God Almighty, we are free at last!” The New York Times columnist James Reston wrote that King “touched all the themes of the day, only better than anybody else.” That afternoon the march leaders met President Kennedy and Vice President Lyndon Johnson at the White House to discuss the need for bipartisan support of civil rights legislation. Not everyone was moved. Malcolm X, who attended, mocked it as “the Farce on Washington,” the Nation of Islam condemned it, and the AFL-CIO’s executive board stayed neutral, though many member unions marched. The National Archives calls the march the largest demonstration for human rights in American history and “a rare display of unity” among civil rights organizations. The American Yawp writes that King’s speech raised the movement’s profile “to new heights and put unprecedented pressure on politicians to pass meaningful civil rights legislation.” After Kennedy’s death, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, whose provisions, the King Institute notes, reflected the march’s demands. “I Have a Dream” became one of the best-known speeches in American history. The March on Washington joined the moral appeal of the civil rights movement to its economic demands. It showed the nation the movement’s size, discipline, and breadth, and it gave King’s dream of racial equality its most lasting expression. America has defaulted on this promissory note insofar as her citizens of color are concerned. Martin Luther King Jr. “I Have a Dream,” August 28, 1963 Free at last! Free at last! Thank God Almighty, we are free at last! Martin Luther King Jr. closing of “I Have a Dream,” quoting a spiritual Dr. King touched all the themes of the day, only better than anybody else. title: The Marshall Plan
subtitle: The European Recovery Program, 1948–1952
summary: The Marshall Plan was a massive American program to rebuild the war-ravaged economies of Western Europe after World War II. Proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in a June 1947 speech at Harvard, it provided more than $12 billion between 1948 and 1952. American leaders saw it as both a humanitarian effort and a way to stop the spread of communism by restoring prosperity. The Soviet Union refused to take part and kept its Eastern European satellites out, deepening the division of Europe.
thumbAlt: Poster promoting the Marshall Plan
aliases: European Recovery Program Economic Cooperation Act
themeText: The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy Economy and finance
text: Western Europe Proposed June 5, 1947, commencement speech at Harvard University Law Economic Cooperation Act, March 1948 Aid More than $12 billion to Western Europe Soviet response Refused to participate and barred Eastern European countries; offered its own “Molotov Plan” Recognition George Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize Two years after the war, much of Europe remained in ruins. The brutal winter of 1946–1947 halted coal production, closed factories, and brought famine close; communist parties in France and Italy won nearly a third of the seats in their parliaments. American officials feared that hunger and unemployment would make Western Europe vulnerable to communism. Coming just months after the Truman Doctrine, Marshall’s proposal argued that the United States should help restore “normal economic health to the world, without which there can be no political stability and no assured peace.” He insisted the plan was directed “not against any country” but against hunger, poverty, and chaos. Congress, spurred by fear of communist expansion and Europe’s deteriorating economy, approved the Economic Cooperation Act in March 1948. American aid poured into Western Europe for reconstruction while trade barriers were loosened. Participation by the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was initially possible, but Stalin, suspicious of American economic domination and unwilling to open Soviet society to Westerners, refused. He saw the plan as a “Trojan Horse” and tightened his control over Eastern Europe; Poland, for instance, was rewarded with a Soviet trade agreement for boycotting the plan. The plan therefore went only to Western Europe. The Marshall Plan fueled a resurgence of European industry and investment and created markets for American goods. Moscow viewed the revival of Western Europe, especially West Germany, with suspicion, and the plan contributed to the hardening division between East and West. Economic historians debate how much the Marshall Plan itself caused Europe’s recovery, but it is widely recognized as a great humanitarian effort. It established foreign aid as a permanent tool of American foreign policy and laid groundwork for European economic integration and the NATO alliance. The Marshall Plan was one of the most ambitious and successful foreign policy initiatives in American history, binding Western Europe to the United States at the start of the Cold War. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMXjsVLOznc What Was the Marshall Plan? | History HISTORY 3:16 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hyYdBtJZEw The Marshall Plan: Rebuilding Europe In the Shadow of Communism Megaprojects 16:49 2026-10-22

title: McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare
subtitle: Anticommunist investigations and accusations, late 1940s–1954
summary: In the early Cold War, fear of communist subversion swept the United States. Congressional committees, the FBI, loyalty boards, and private employers investigated thousands of Americans; many lost their jobs or were blacklisted for past political associations. The era takes its name from Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin, who from 1950 made sensational, unsupported charges that communists had infiltrated the government, until televised hearings in 1954 exposed his tactics and the Senate condemned him.
location: Washington, D.C., Hollywood, universities, unions, and communities nationwide
thumbAlt: Joseph Welch and Senator Joseph McCarthy at the Army-McCarthy hearings
aliases: Red Scare HUAC Hollywood Ten blacklist Army-McCarthy hearings Rosenbergs
themeText: The Cold War Civil rights and citizenship Parties and elections
text: Washington, D.C., Hollywood, universities, unions, and communities nationwide Loyalty program Truman’s Executive Order 9835, March 1947 Wheeling speech February 9, 1950: McCarthy claimed a list of 205 communists in the State Department Hollywood HUAC hearings from 1947; the “Hollywood Ten” and an industry blacklist Army-McCarthy hearings 1954, watched by some 20 million people Senate condemnation December 2, 1954, by a vote of 67–22 A small Communist Party had existed in the United States since the aftermath of the 1917 Russian Revolution; even at its peak it had only about 80,000 members. Real Soviet espionage occurred: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted of passing atomic secrets and executed in 1953, and former State Department official Alger Hiss, accused of spying, was convicted of perjury after a second trial. Combined with the Soviet atomic bomb, the communist victory in China, and the Korean War, these cases fed fears of a vast conspiracy. In March 1947, facing anticommunist pressure, President Truman created loyalty reviews for federal employees. The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) investigated Hollywood beginning in 1947; between 1949 and 1954, congressional committees conducted more than one hundred investigations into subversion. The Internal Security Act of 1950 required “communist organizations” to register with the government. On February 9, 1950, in Wheeling, West Virginia, McCarthy declared he had a list of 205 State Department employees who were members of the Communist Party. He had no such list; the number changed to 57, then 81. A Senate committee called his charges “a fraud and a hoax,” but McCarthy’s accusations made him famous, and he attacked the Truman administration as “soft on communism.” The Red Scare reached far beyond McCarthy. HUAC asked witnesses, “Are you now, or have you ever been, a member of the Communist Party?” and pressed them to name others; hundreds of film artists were blacklisted. Thirty-one University of California professors were dismissed in 1950 for refusing to sign a loyalty oath. The singer and activist Paul Robeson had his passport revoked. In 1954 McCarthy took on the U.S. Army. Twenty million people watched the televised Army-McCarthy hearings, in which Army counsel Joseph Welch rebuked him: “Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?” On December 2, 1954, the Senate voted 67–22 to condemn McCarthy. He died in 1957, and by the late 1950s the worst of the Red Scare was over. The Red Scare cost many Americans their jobs and reputations and pressed the country toward conformity. Playwright Arthur Miller compared it to the Salem witch trials in The Crucible (1953). As early as June 1950, the editor Freda Kirchwey described “McCarthyism” as the means by which “a handful of men, disguised as hunters of subversion, cynically subvert the instruments of justice” for political gain. McCarthyism showed how fear of an external enemy could be turned against Americans’ own civil liberties. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N35IugBYH04 What is McCarthyism? title: The Missouri Compromise
subtitle: The 1820 bargain that drew a line across the West between slavery and freedom
summary: When Missouri asked to join the Union as a slave state in 1819, it set off the first great national crisis over slavery. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the balance between them in the Senate, and banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′. The line held for thirty-four years. But the crisis, as the American Yawp puts it, “made the sectional nature of American politics impossible to ignore,” and the aging Thomas Jefferson heard in it “a fire bell in the night.”
thumbAlt: Map of free and slave territory under the Missouri Compromise
aliases: Missouri Crisis Tallmadge Amendment 36°30′ line Compromise of 1820 Fire bell in the night Henry Clay
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Territorial expansion Constitution and law
text: Washington, D.C. Crisis began February 1819, with the Tallmadge Amendment Compromise Conference committee report of March 1, 1820 Admitted Missouri as a slave state; Maine (separated from Massachusetts) as a free state The line No slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of 36°30′, except Missouri Promoters Senator Jesse Thomas of Illinois and Henry Clay of Kentucky Ended Repealed by the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854); ruled unconstitutional in Dred Scott (1857) Since 1789 Virginia had wielded more influence in the federal government than any other state; four of the first five presidents were Virginians. As the northern states gradually ended slavery while the southern states came to depend on it even more, northerners grew wary of a southern voting bloc united by the defense of slavery. The Louisiana Purchase had added an immense territory with no settled rule on slavery. Missouri, a territory carved out of the Purchase, applied for statehood in 1819. It already held more than ten thousand enslaved people and was poised to join the southern bloc in Congress. The Tallmadge Amendment. In February 1819 Representative James Tallmadge of New York proposed admitting Missouri only if no more enslaved people were brought in and the children of those already there were freed at twenty-five. Tallmadge argued that slavery mocked the Declaration of Independence. A sectional vote. Nearly all northern congressmen, who had a majority in the House, voted for the amendment and it passed; the Senate quickly defeated it. Morals and power. Opponents of slavery in Missouri, the Yawp notes, acted from moral conviction but also wanted to keep a sectional balance of power. When Congress reconvened, Senator Jesse Thomas of Illinois proposed a bargain, and Henry Clay of Kentucky helped push it through, earning the nickname “the Great Compromiser.” Maine, long part of Massachusetts, was seeking statehood, so the two admissions were paired: Missouri as a slave state, Maine as a free state. Slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30′, Missouri’s southern border, while the land to the south, organized as Arkansas Territory, stayed open to slavery. A conference committee reported the compromise on March 1, 1820. A second dispute broke out when Missouri submitted a constitution that barred free Black people from living in the state. Northern congressmen said this violated the Constitution’s guarantee that citizens of each state enjoy the rights of citizens in all states. Congress resolved it by requiring Missouri to promise that no law would be passed under that clause in violation of those rights, and Missouri’s legislature agreed. The crisis ended peacefully, but it split the Democratic-Republican Party along sectional lines. Many Americans were alarmed at how readily politicians spoke of disunion and even civil war. Jefferson warned that “a geographical line, coinciding with a marked principle, moral and political,” would never be erased, and that every new irritation “will mark it deeper and deeper.” For a generation the 36°30′ line kept an uneasy peace. Congress repealed it in the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and in 1857 the Supreme Court’s Dred Scott decision declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional. The question it had postponed, whether slavery would spread west, would, as the Yawp says, “cause worse trouble in years ahead,” leading to the Civil War. The Missouri Compromise was the first great sectional bargain over slavery. It preserved the Union for a time by dividing the West between slavery and freedom, but it also made slavery’s expansion the central question of national politics. Jefferson’s letter In April 1820 Jefferson wrote to John Holmes, thanking him for a letter to his constituents on the Missouri question. He called the Missouri question “the knell of the Union” and said it was “hushed indeed for the moment. but this is a reprieve only, not a final sentence.” On slavery itself he wrote, “we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go. justice is in one scale, and self-preservation in the other.” In the same letter he argued that spreading slavery over a wider area would make it easier to end. What exactly did Tallmadge propose? Sources describe the amendment slightly differently. The American Yawp says it would have freed children born to enslaved people in Missouri at age twenty-five; a Vanderbilt University course summary says it provided for “the gradual emancipation of those already there.” Both agree it would have barred bringing more enslaved people into the state. This momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror. I considered it at once as the knell of the Union. title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
subtitle: The thirteen-month protest that launched the modern civil rights movement
summary: The Montgomery bus boycott began on December 5, 1955, four days after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. For 381 days Montgomery’s Black residents walked, shared rides, and organized carpools rather than ride segregated city buses. The protest was planned by the Women’s Political Council and E. D. Nixon and led by the Montgomery Improvement Association. Its president was a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr. It survived bombings, mass indictments, and court injunctions, and it ended in victory after the Supreme Court affirmed, in Browder v. Gayle, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott made King a national figure and showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat Jim Crow.
thumbAlt: Rosa Parks being fingerprinted after her arrest during the Montgomery bus boycott
aliases: Montgomery Improvement Association Browder v. Gayle Women’s Political Council Holt Street Baptist Church
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Reform and protest
text: Montgomery, Alabama Spark Arrest of Rosa Parks, December 1, 1955 Began December 5, 1955; about 90 percent of Black riders stayed off the buses on the first day Leadership Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA), president Martin Luther King Jr. Carpool About 300 cars Court victory Browder v. Gayle: district court June 1956; affirmed by the Supreme Court November 13, 1956 Ended December 20, 1956, after 381 days; buses integrated the next day Montgomery’s buses were rigidly segregated. The front ten seats were reserved for white passengers, and Black riders were expected to give up seats behind them when the bus filled with white passengers. Black passengers often had to pay at the front and then re-enter by the rear door. Drivers claimed the discretion to move the line between Black and white sections. Jo Ann Robinson, an English professor at Alabama State College, was ordered off a nearly empty bus in 1949 for sitting in the fifth row. The Women’s Political Council (WPC), an organization of Black professional women founded in 1946, made bus segregation a priority after Robinson became its president in 1950. In March 1954 the council asked Mayor W. A. Gayle to end the practice of making Black riders stand over empty seats and to have buses stop at every corner in Black neighborhoods, as they did in white ones. In a May 21 letter Robinson warned that “twenty-five or more local organizations” had talked of a city-wide boycott. Earlier arrests, of fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin and eighteen-year-old Mary Louise Smith in 1955, did not mobilize the community. The American Yawp notes that in 1953 a Black member of the Women’s Army Corps, Sarah Keys, had already challenged segregated interstate buses. On the evening of December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a forty-two-year-old seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store who was active in the local NAACP, was sitting in the first row behind the white section. When the bus filled, driver James Blake ordered her row to stand. Three passengers moved; Parks did not, and she was arrested. E. D. Nixon, a Pullman porter, union leader, and former head of the local NAACP, saw her as the ideal plaintiff: “She’s morally clean, she’s reliable, nobody had nothing on her, she had the courage of her convictions.” With the white attorney Clifford Durr and his wife Virginia, he bailed her out of jail. That night Robinson, two students, and a colleague, John Cannon, mimeographed about 52,500 leaflets calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on Monday, December 5. On December 2 ministers and community leaders met at King’s Dexter Avenue Baptist Church and agreed to support the one-day boycott, which also received unexpected publicity in weekend newspapers and on radio and television. On December 5 about 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black citizens stayed off the buses. That afternoon, at Mt. Zion AME Church, leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association to continue the protest and elected King, new to the city, as president. Nixon became treasurer. Parks later observed that King had not been in Montgomery long enough “to make any strong friends or enemies.” That evening several thousand people packed Holt Street Baptist Church and voted to continue. “If we are wrong,” King told them, “the Supreme Court of this nation is wrong. If we are wrong, the Constitution of the United States is wrong. If we are wrong, God Almighty is wrong.” The MIA’s first demands were moderate: courteous treatment, first-come, first-served seating with Black riders filling from the rear and white riders from the front, and Black drivers on mostly Black routes. When the city refused and began penalizing Black taxi drivers for helping the boycotters, the MIA built a carpool of about 300 cars, modeled on a 1953 bus boycott in Baton Rouge. Weekly mass meetings with sermons and music kept the community together, and money came from collection plates and from supporters in the North, including the fundraising group In Friendship founded by Bayard Rustin, Ella Baker, and Stanley Levison. Resistance was fierce. In early 1956 the homes of King and Nixon were bombed. King calmed the crowd outside his house: “Be calm as I and my family are. … If anything happens to me, there will be others to take my place.” (The American Yawp places the bombings of King’s and Nixon’s homes, along with four Black churches, a year into the boycott.) Police harassed Robinson, and the governor eventually ordered state police to guard boycott leaders’ homes. In February 1956 the city indicted dozens of boycott leaders under a 1921 Alabama law against conspiracies to interfere with lawful business. The King Institute’s boycott article says more than 80 were indicted and its MIA article says 89. King alone was tried, and in March he was convicted and ordered to pay $500 or serve 386 days in jail. Women sustained the movement. Robinson edited the MIA newsletter and Johnnie Carr and others ran committees. Mary Fair Burks of the WPC credited “the nameless cooks and maids who walked endless miles for a year to bring about the breach in the walls of segregation.” Rustin and Glenn Smiley advised King on Gandhian nonviolence. “Christ showed us the way,” King said, “and Gandhi in India showed it could work.” On February 1, 1956, lawyers Fred Gray and Charles Langford filed Browder v. Gayle in federal court on behalf of Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith. Parks was not included, so that the court would decide only the constitutionality of bus segregation. In June 1956 a three-judge district court ruled 2 to 1, citing Brown v. Board of Education, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The King Institute dates the ruling to June 5 and the National Archives to June 4. On November 13, 1956, while King sat in court defending the carpools against an injunction, he learned that the Supreme Court had affirmed the ruling. The MIA kept walking until the order arrived. On December 20, 1956, the community voted to end the boycott, and the next morning King, Ralph Abernathy, E. D. Nixon, and Glenn Smiley rode an integrated bus. “We came to see that, in the long run, it is more honorable to walk in dignity than ride in humiliation,” King said. The boycott’s combination of mass nonviolent protest and Christian ethics became the model for challenging segregation across the South. In January 1957 the MIA became one of the founding organizations of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, which King and other ministers created to coordinate civil rights efforts across the South. The American Yawp writes that the boycott not only crushed segregation on Montgomery’s buses but energized the entire civil rights movement. Parks became known as the “Mother of the Civil Rights Movement.” Robinson later called the boycott “the most beautiful memory that all of us who participated will carry to our final resting place.” Montgomery proved that ordinary people acting together could defeat Jim Crow, and it introduced Martin Luther King Jr. to the nation. If we are wrong, the Supreme Court of this nation is wrong. If we are wrong, the Constitution of the United States is wrong. If we are wrong, God Almighty is wrong. title: The New Deal
subtitle: Franklin D. Roosevelt’s programs of relief, recovery, and reform, 1933–1939
summary: The New Deal was President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s response to the Great Depression: a burst of federal programs to stabilize the banks, put the unemployed to work, raise farm prices, protect workers’ right to organize, and create a safety net for the elderly and the jobless. It did not end the Depression, and it left racial and gender inequalities largely in place. But it transformed the role of the federal government and the presidency, and it built a Democratic coalition that dominated politics for a generation.
thumbAlt: Collage of New Deal programs and posters
aliases: Hundred Days First New Deal Second New Deal alphabet agencies CCC WPA NRA AAA TVA FDIC court-packing fireside chats
themeText: Economy and finance The presidency Labor and work Reform and protest Parties and elections Civil rights and citizenship
text: Washington, D.C., and nationwide The phrase From FDR’s 1932 acceptance speech: “I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people” First Hundred Days (March–June 1933) Emergency Banking Act, CCC, FERA, TVA, AAA, National Industrial Recovery Act, Securities Act, Glass-Steagall Act (FDIC) Second New Deal (1935) Works Progress Administration, Wagner Act, Social Security Act Last major measure Fair Labor Standards Act (1938): the modern minimum wage, starting at 25 cents an hour Setbacks Supreme Court rulings against the NRA (1935) and AAA (1936), the failed court-packing plan (1937), the 1937 recession Unemployment About 25 percent in 1933; still above 19 percent in 1939 By the time Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the economy had collapsed. More than twelve million Americans were out of work, a quarter of the workforce, and a new wave of bank failures had hit in February. Two of every five banks open in 1929 had closed. Herbert Hoover had relied on voluntary action and loans to business, and voters had rejected him in a landslide. Roosevelt, the Democratic governor of New York, had been born to a wealthy Hudson Valley family, served as assistant secretary of the navy in World War I, and been paralyzed by polio in 1921. As governor he had told the legislature that relief was owed “not as a matter of charity, but as a matter of social duty,” and his Temporary Emergency Relief Administration came to support a tenth of the state’s families. Accepting the Democratic nomination on July 1, 1932, he declared, “I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.” Newspaper editors seized on the phrase. Hoover warned that such a program meant “the total abandonment of every principle upon which this government and the American system is founded.” The New Deal had no single blueprint. Roosevelt believed in American capitalism but thought it had to be reformed to survive, and he was a pragmatist: he would try something, and if it failed, try something else. Even the New Deal economist Alvin Hansen admitted in 1940, “I really do not know what the basic principle of the New Deal is.” Its programs rested on different, sometimes contradictory, theories of the Depression’s causes. Some blamed overproduction, some cutthroat competition, some a lack of purchasing power; John Maynard Keynes’s theory of deficit spending was not even published until 1936. Roosevelt surrounded himself with a “Brain Trust” of academic advisers and appointees such as Harry Hopkins and Frances Perkins, the first woman to serve in a cabinet. He often gave overlapping tasks to aides who disagreed with one another. The Hundred Days. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Roosevelt said in his inaugural address. Two days later he declared a national bank holiday, and Congress passed his Emergency Banking Act almost sight unseen. Federal officials would inspect every bank, reopen the sound ones, and close the rest. On March 12 he explained the plan in the first of his radio “fireside chats,” and in the following weeks Americans returned nearly $1 billion to the banks. Between March and June 1933, Congress passed a flood of laws. The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) put 300,000 young men to work in 1,200 camps planting trees, building bridges, and cleaning beaches. The Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA) sent cash to state relief agencies. The Securities Act required honest information about stocks, and the Glass-Steagall Act created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and separated commercial from investment banking. Roosevelt also took the country off the gold standard. Planning for recovery. The heart of the early New Deal was two experiments in economic planning. The Agricultural Adjustment Act (May 1933) paid farmers to cut production in order to raise prices; more than three million farmers joined, and farm income rose by more than half between 1932 and 1935. But in the South, landowners often kept the payments, evicted their tenants and sharecroppers, and bought machinery instead, pushing the poorest farmworkers off the land. The National Industrial Recovery Act (June 1933) suspended the antitrust laws so that businesses could write more than 500 “codes of fair competition” fixing prices, wages, and production. Section 7a promised workers the right to bargain collectively, and cooperating businesses displayed the National Recovery Administration’s Blue Eagle. The codes, the National Archives concludes, “did little to help recovery, and by raising prices, they actually made the economic situation worse.” The same law created the Public Works Administration, which spent more than $3 billion on projects such as the Triborough Bridge in New York. The Tennessee Valley. On May 18, 1933, Roosevelt signed the act creating the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), a federal corporation charged with building dams to control floods, improve navigation, and generate cheap electricity in one of the poorest regions in the country. It was the first time a federal agency was directed to develop the resources of an entire region. Its dams brought electric lights, appliances, jobs, and industry to the valley, but they also displaced thousands of families, sometimes whole towns. The Rural Electrification Administration later brought electricity to millions of farm homes. Critics and the courts. Many Americans thought the New Deal did too little. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana won a mass following for his Share Our Wealth plan to redistribute the fortunes of the rich; more than 27,000 Share Our Wealth clubs sprang up before he was assassinated in 1935. Dr. Francis Townsend campaigned for old-age pensions, and the radio priest Charles Coughlin attacked Roosevelt in broadcasts that, the American Yawp notes, were vitriolic and anti-Semitic. From the right, conservative businessmen and dissident Democrats formed the American Liberty League in 1934 to denounce the New Deal as an un-American attack on free enterprise. The Supreme Court struck hardest. On May 27, 1935, in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, it unanimously ruled the National Industrial Recovery Act unconstitutional, and in 1936 it struck down the AAA. The Second New Deal. Roosevelt answered by moving left. In 1935 Congress created the Works Progress Administration (WPA) with a nearly $5 billion appropriation. By 1937 it employed three million people building schools, hospitals, airports, and more than half a million miles of roads, and it hired artists, writers, and musicians as well. The National Labor Relations Act of July 5, 1935, known as the Wagner Act after its sponsor, Senator Robert Wagner of New York, guaranteed workers “the right to self-organization” and created the National Labor Relations Board to enforce it. Union membership surged: in 1937 sit-down strikers in Flint, Michigan, won recognition for the United Auto Workers from General Motors. On August 14, 1935, Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act, which created old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid to dependent children and the blind. (The National Archives’ own page gives both August 14 and August 15 as the date of signing.) Roosevelt insisted that the pensions be paid from workers’ and employers’ contributions rather than general taxes. “No dole,” he said. “Mustn’t have a dole.” The second term. In 1936 Roosevelt won reelection in a landslide, losing only Maine and Vermont, and in his second inaugural vowed to help the third of the nation that was ill-housed, ill-clad, and ill-nourished. In February 1937, fearing the Court would strike down Social Security, he proposed adding a new justice for every sitting justice over a certain age, up to six in all. The American Yawp gives the age as seventy and the Miller Center as seventy-five. Critics called it “court-packing,” and the plan failed in Congress. But that spring the Court began upholding New Deal laws, including the Wagner Act in NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937), and it has not struck down a major New Deal law since. That same year, believing the economy had recovered, Roosevelt cut federal spending, and the economy plunged into the “Roosevelt recession.” In April 1938 he reversed course and asked Congress for a $5 billion relief and public works program. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a national minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and limited working hours. The New Deal stopped the collapse and brought partial recovery. The banking panic ended, farm incomes rose, and the WPA, CCC, and other agencies gave work to millions. But unemployment stayed high. Still above 19 percent in 1939, it remained in double digits in 1940, and stock prices had not recovered from the crash. Only the vast spending of World War II brought full employment. Politically, the tide turned. The court-packing fight and the 1937 recession helped a conservative coalition of Southern Democrats and Republicans gain ground in the 1938 elections. Roosevelt tried to purge conservative Democrats in that year’s primaries; of the ten he targeted, only one lost. By 1939 he struggled to pass new reforms, and the coming war in Europe increasingly drew his attention. Congress did pass the Reorganization Act of 1939, which created the Executive Office of the President. The New Deal changed what Americans expected from Washington. Before World War I the federal government had been, in the American Yawp’s phrase, a “government out of sight”; after the New Deal, Americans came to see it as an ally in finding work, earning a decent wage, getting a fair price for crops, or organizing a union. Social Security became the centerpiece of the American welfare state, and the floor under wages and ceiling on hours set by the Fair Labor Standards Act continue to this day. Roosevelt also reshaped the presidency: his fireside chats created a direct bond with the public, and the president became chief legislator as well as chief executive. Voter turnout jumped in 1932 and 1936, and most of the new voters stayed loyal to a Democratic coalition of liberals, urban workers, farm workers, and white Southerners well into the 1960s. The New Deal’s benefits were unequally shared. To keep the votes of Southern Democrats, Roosevelt refused to back a federal anti-lynching law or the abolition of the poll tax (“I just can’t take that risk,” he told the NAACP’s secretary), and he accepted the exclusion of farm workers and domestic servants from Social Security pensions, a decision that left out many Black and Mexican American workers. NRA codes kept lower wages for Black workers, and AAA payments helped push Black tenants and sharecroppers off the land. Many programs assumed that men were breadwinners and steered women into means-tested relief, although Roosevelt appointed Frances Perkins and the African American adviser Mary McLeod Bethune to prominent posts, and Eleanor Roosevelt became a major voice for economic and racial justice. Historians still debate when the New Deal ended. Some point to the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938; others see its spirit in wartime controls, the G.I. Bill, and a “New Deal order” that lasted until Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. The New Deal did not end the Great Depression, but it made the federal government responsible for the economic security of ordinary Americans. It created institutions, from Social Security to the FDIC, that still shape American life. I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people. Franklin D. Roosevelt accepting the Democratic presidential nomination, July 1, 1932 So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance. Franklin D. Roosevelt first inaugural address, March 4, 1933 How many men ever went to a barbecue and would let one man take off the table what’s intended for nine-tenths of the people to eat? Huey Long promoting his Share Our Wealth plan This law represents a cornerstone in a structure which is being built but is by no means complete. Franklin D. title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
subtitle: Japan’s surprise attack that brought the United States into World War II
summary: On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours the fleet was devastated and more than 3,500 Americans were killed or wounded, about 2,400 of them killed. The next day President Franklin D. Roosevelt called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy,” and Congress declared war on Japan. The attack ended American isolationism and brought the United States into World War II.
thumbAlt: The battleship USS Arizona burning after the Japanese attack
aliases: Day of Infamy USS Arizona
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii Date Morning of December 7, 1941 Casualties More than 3,500 Americans killed or wounded; about 2,400 killed USS Arizona 1,177 crew members killed; the sunken ship is the resting place of more than 900 Declaration of war December 8, 1941; one dissenting vote, Rep. Jeannette Rankin of Montana Memorial USS Arizona Memorial, dedicated 1962 Through the late 1930s Japan waged a brutal war in China. The United States aided China and gradually cut off the oil, steel, and other materials Japan’s military depended on, while demanding that Japan withdraw from China. Japan joined the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy in September 1940 and moved into French Indochina. After the United States imposed a full embargo and froze Japanese assets, negotiations stalled. Facing severe shortages, unwilling to leave China, and convinced that American officials opposed further talks, Japan’s leaders decided to strike first. Their planners hoped to destroy enough battleships and aircraft carriers to cripple American naval power while Japan seized resource-rich territories in Southeast Asia. U.S. leaders, still hoping for a settlement and doubting Japan could attack American territory, were caught by surprise. Japanese aircraft struck the fleet at anchor. The battleship USS Arizona was sunk with the loss of 1,177 crew members; more than 900 of them remain entombed in the ship. Japan also attacked Hong Kong, the Philippines, and other American and European holdings across the Pacific. Late that afternoon, Roosevelt dictated his request for a declaration of war, revising the first line from “a date which will live in world history” to “a date which will live in infamy.” He delivered it to a joint session of Congress at 12:30 p.m. on December 8. The Senate voted unanimously for war; in the House, only Jeannette Rankin of Montana voted no. Roosevelt signed the declaration that afternoon. Germany and Italy, Japan’s allies, declared war on the United States on December 11, and within a week the United States was at war with all the Axis powers. The attack united Americans behind a massive mobilization. It also fed fear and suspicion of Japanese Americans that led, ten weeks later, to Executive Order 9066 and their mass incarceration. Pearl Harbor became a lasting symbol of national vulnerability and of the dangers of surprise attack, invoked again after the September 11 attacks in 2001. The USS Arizona Memorial, completed in 1961 and dedicated in 1962, honors all the military personnel killed in the attack. The attack on Pearl Harbor turned two regional wars into a true world war and committed the United States to global leadership. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u1EZ55_F7xk Why Japan Attacked Pearl Harbor? title: The Peopling of the Americas
subtitle: How and when the first people arrived, a question science is still answering
summary: People have lived in the Americas for well over twenty thousand years. For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed the first arrivals came roughly 13,000 years ago, walking from Asia across a land bridge exposed by low Ice Age seas. Newer evidence, above all human footprints preserved at White Sands, New Mexico, and dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, has pushed that date much earlier. How and when people first came remains one of the liveliest questions in archaeology.
location: Beringia, the Pacific coast, and the interior of North America
thumbAlt: Map of possible routes of the first peopling of the Americas through Beringia
themeText: Indigenous history
text: Beringia, the Pacific coast, and the interior of North America Earliest firm evidence in the U.S. Human footprints at White Sands National Park, dated to roughly 22,860 and 21,130 years ago Older estimate About 13,500–16,000 years ago, based on stone-tool sites Main routes proposed Overland through Beringia; along the Pacific coast by boat Indigenous perspectives Many Native nations hold that their people have always lived in their homelands During the last Ice Age, so much water was locked in glaciers that sea levels fell dramatically, exposing a broad land mass, Beringia, between Siberia and Alaska. The National Park Service’s Bering Land Bridge National Preserve protects a remnant of this landscape, across which people followed herds of large animals, many now extinct, into North America. People moved for the same reasons as later migrants: to find food and survive. Over generations, small groups of hunters and gatherers spread into a continent of enormous ecological variety, adapting to tundra, forests, plains, deserts, and coasts. For decades, the leading model held that people entered the interior around 13,000 years ago, once an ice-free corridor opened between the great glaciers, and that a distinctive stone-tool tradition called Clovis represented the first Americans. Discoveries at many sites have challenged that view, and the most dramatic evidence comes from White Sands National Park in New Mexico. There, at the edge of an ancient lake, researchers found fossilized human footprints, many apparently made by children and teenagers, in layers of sediment dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago. The National Park Service notes that humans had previously been thought to arrive closer to 13,500–16,000 years ago. Those dates mean people were in North America at the height of the last glacial period, when the interior route would have been blocked by ice. That has strengthened the case that some early migrants traveled along the Pacific coast, perhaps by boat, though the exact routes and timing are still debated. Over thousands of years, the descendants of these first peoples populated both continents. They developed hundreds of languages and distinct cultures, domesticated plants such as maize, squash, and beans, and built societies ranging from small bands to cities. By the time Europeans arrived in 1492, the Americas had been home to human societies for tens of thousands of years. Recognizing that depth of time corrects the old notion of the continent as an empty “New World.” Many Native nations, whose oral traditions describe their origins in their own homelands, view migration theories as only one way of understanding their past. The story of American history begins not in 1492 or 1607 but more than twenty thousand years ago, with the people whose descendants built the societies Europeans later encountered. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEG5MmsXIho HOT Topic: The Latest Genetic and Archaeological Evidence for the Peopling of the Americas Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History 59:25 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jaizoayO9yU Peopling the Americas Khan Academy 9:17 2026-10-23

title: Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag
subtitle: The Pilgrims’ settlement and the alliance that kept it alive, 1620–1621
summary: In December 1620, English colonists from the Mayflower, many of them religious Separatists later called Pilgrims, settled at Plymouth, in the homeland of the Wampanoag people. Half of them died that first winter. In March 1621, the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, whose people had been devastated by diseases brought by earlier English visitors and who faced pressure from the rival Narragansett, made an alliance with the newcomers. That treaty kept the colony alive, and Massasoit honored it for the rest of his life.
location: Plymouth, Massachusetts, in the homeland of the Wampanoag
thumbAlt: Engraving of Plymouth governor John Carver meeting the Wampanoag leader Massasoit
aliases: Pilgrims Massasoit Squanto Thanksgiving
themeText: Colonial encounters Indigenous history Religion
text: Plymouth, Massachusetts, in the homeland of the Wampanoag Arrived November 1620 at Cape Cod; settled at Plymouth in December First winter 50 of the 102 passengers died of disease or exposure Treaty March 22, 1621, between Massasoit (Ousamequin) and Governor John Carver Interpreter Squanto (Tisquantum), a Patuxet man who had been kidnapped and taken to England The land around Plymouth was Wampanoag territory, led by Massasoit Ousamequin, “Massasoit” means Great Sachem. Before 1620, English traders and fishermen had visited the coast. They spread epidemic disease that caused widespread death among the Wampanoag; a plague had devastated Wampanoag society in the years just before the colonists arrived. A weakened Wampanoag nation faced the Narragansett, who sought to take over its land. The colonists, who had signed the Mayflower Compact before landing, arrived too late in the year to plant. Living in temporary shelters and aboard ship, they died in large numbers: by the spring of 1621, 50 of the 102 people who had come on the Mayflower were dead. After a series of encounters, Massasoit and a party of his men approached the English on March 22, 1621. With help from Squanto, a Patuxet man who had been taken as a slave by an Englishman and had lived in England, the two sides negotiated. Massasoit agreed that neither he nor his people would harm the colonists, that offenders would be handed over for punishment, and that each side would aid the other if attacked, “if any did unjustly war against him, we would aid him; if any did war against us, he should aid us.” Massasoit saw in the English a potential ally that could help him secure his people’s independence from the Narragansett. The cooperation that followed brought the colonists a good planting season and harvest, the origin, by some accounts, of the Thanksgiving story. The alliance gave the colony security and access to Native knowledge of planting, and it gave the Wampanoag an ally against the Narragansett. Plymouth survived and grew slowly. Massasoit lived about forty years after the treaty. As English settlement expanded and pressure on Wampanoag land grew, relations broke down. After Massasoit’s death, his son Wamsutta died mysteriously, and his younger son Metacom, known to the English as Philip, became sachem; the conflicts that followed led to King Philip’s War in 1675–76. The Thanksgiving story later Americans told about Plymouth emphasized harmony; the fuller history includes epidemic, alliance, and eventually war and dispossession. Plymouth is a founding myth of the United States, but its real history is one of mutual dependence: the colony survived because of an alliance with a Native nation already reeling from European diseases. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEJF3b6izsQ Pilgrims at Plymouth NBC News Learn 3:19 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x9ISjCyrAho The Plymouth Colony Explained: US History Review Hip Hughes (HipHughes) 23:28 2026-10-23

title: Prohibition
subtitle: The national ban on alcohol, 1920–1933
summary: Prohibition was the nationwide ban on making, selling, and transporting alcoholic beverages, imposed by the Eighteenth Amendment and in force from January 1920 until its repeal by the Twenty-first Amendment in December 1933. The culmination of a century-long temperance crusade, it cut drinking but proved extremely hard to enforce. Bootlegging, speakeasies, and organized crime flourished, and in 1933 the Twenty-first Amendment repealed it.
thumbAlt: Prohibition agents destroying barrels of alcohol
aliases: Eighteenth Amendment Twenty-first Amendment Volstead Act speakeasies temperance movement
themeText: Reform and protest Constitution and law Everyday life Cities and urban life Women's history
text: Nationwide Eighteenth Amendment Passed by Congress December 18, 1917; ratified January 16, 1919 Took effect One year after ratification, in January 1920 Enforcement law The National Prohibition Act, known as the Volstead Act Repeal Twenty-first Amendment, passed February 20, 1933; ratified December 5, 1933 Ratification of repeal By state conventions, not legislatures Americans had campaigned against drinking for nearly a century. The American Temperance Society was founded in 1826; the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union in 1874; and the Anti-Saloon League in 1893, which became a powerful political force. Reformers blamed alcohol for domestic abuse, poverty, crime, and disease. Women were central to the movement, seeing alcohol as a destroyer of families, and many Progressives embraced prohibition as part of their effort to improve society through government. Reformers also associated alcohol with cities and immigrants. Between 1905 and 1917, many states passed laws banning the manufacture and sale of alcohol. Temperance advocates then pushed for a national ban. Congress approved the Eighteenth Amendment in December 1917, during World War I, and enough states ratified it in just thirteen months. The amendment banned “the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors” for beverage purposes, beginning one year after ratification. Congress passed the Volstead Act to enforce it. According to the National Archives, consumption did fall: alcohol use dropped by about 30 percent, arrests for drunkenness declined, and illegal liquor became expensive. But enforcement proved extremely difficult. Bootlegging became rampant; by 1925 New York City alone had somewhere between 30,000 and 100,000 speakeasies. Neither federal nor local authorities would commit the resources needed, Maryland never passed a state enforcement law, and organized crime grew rich supplying illegal alcohol. Speakeasies also became part of the decade’s new nightlife, where young women and men mixed in ways that defied older social rules. By the early 1930s, with the country in the Great Depression, support for Prohibition had collapsed. Congress passed the Twenty-first Amendment in February 1933, sending it to state ratifying conventions instead of legislatures, and it was ratified on December 5, 1933. The amendment returned control of alcohol to the states, some of which remained dry. Herbert Hoover called Prohibition an experiment “noble in motive and far reaching in purpose.” Its failure is often cited in debates over whether government can, or should, legislate personal behavior, including comparisons to the modern war on drugs. Prohibition was the high-water mark of the temperance movement and one of the most ambitious social reforms in American history, written into the Constitution and then written out of it. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AAGIi62-sAU Prohibition - OverSimplified OverSimplified 33:43 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y4BDnlUQ3CA What happened when the United States banned alcohol - Rod Phillips TED-Ed 5:12 2026-10-23

title: The Pueblo Revolt
subtitle: Pueblo nations unite to drive Spanish colonizers out of New Mexico, 1680
summary: In August 1680, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, who lived in dozens of independent towns and spoke several languages, rose together against eight decades of Spanish rule. Planned by a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo known as Popé or Po’pay, the revolt killed hundreds of settlers and missionaries, burned the missions, and forced the Spanish out of Santa Fe. They stayed away for twelve years, and the Penn Museum calls it arguably the most successful Indigenous uprising against a European colonial power in the New World. When the Spanish returned in 1692, they did not restore everything they had lost: the forced labor and aggressive suppression of Pueblo religion did not come back.
location: Santa Fe and the Pueblos of the upper Rio Grande, New Mexico
thumbAlt: Loren Mozley’s 1936 mural of the Pueblo Revolt
aliases: Popé Po'Pay Po’pay Pueblo Rebellion Otermín Diego de Vargas First American Revolution
themeText: Indigenous history Colonial encounters Religion Reform and protest
text: Santa Fe and the Pueblos of the upper Rio Grande, New Mexico Began August 10, 1680, earlier than planned after the Spanish learned of the plot Leader Po’pay (Popé), a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh) Dead About 400 settlers and 21 Franciscan friars (Penn Museum, EBSCO); Pueblo losses unknown Spanish absent Twelve years; Diego de Vargas entered Santa Fe on September 13, 1692 Pueblo population Down from as many as 60,000 in 1600 to about 17,000 by 1680 Spanish conquistadors first reached the Pueblo country in 1540 under Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, looking for gold. In 1598 Juan de Oñate led about four hundred settlers, soldiers, and missionaries from Mexico into New Mexico. The riches never appeared, but the Spanish crown kept paying for the colony because of its Franciscan missions. Spanish Santa Fe was founded in 1607 and made the capital in 1610, according to the Library of Congress. The American Yawp dates the founding to 1610. Few Spaniards ever came. By 1680 only about three thousand colonists lived in the province. The colony rested on Native labor. Under the encomienda, Pueblo families handed over part of their crops every year. Under the repartimiento, they were forced to work in Spanish households for nothing. Violence was part of the system. In 1599 Oñate’s soldiers attacked Acoma Pueblo, where twelve Spanish soldiers had been killed. The sources describe the punishment differently: the Library of Congress says over 600 Acoma people were captured and many mutilated, and the American Yawp says nearly half of the roughly 1,500 inhabitants were killed and that Oñate ordered one foot cut off every surviving male over fifteen. Another account says he sentenced males over twelve to twenty years of servitude and men over twenty-five to lose a foot, a punishment that was not carried out, or not fully. Oñate was removed from office and recalled for his cruelty. The Pueblos were not one people. EBSCO notes that three language families were spoken in the Rio Grande region alone, and that the villages were autonomous and “rarely acted in unison.” Franciscans, according to EBSCO, “recognized no belief system except their own” and saved their harshest punishments for those who kept the old religion. In 1655, it says, Father Salvador de Guerra had a man at Oraibi whipped, doused with turpentine, and burned to death, and missing Mass could bring a flogging. The attack on Pueblo religion was, in EBSCO’s words, “the single greatest cause of the Pueblo Revolt.” The Pueblos believed that harmony with the community and the natural world depended on ceremonies of the kachina spirits in their kivas, and it seemed no coincidence that things went wrong when the priests stopped them. Spanish priests also sexually abused Pueblo women. Physical suffering made things worse. Droughts, famine, Apache raids, and European diseases cut the Pueblo population from about 50,000 or 60,000 around 1600 to about 17,000 by the 1670s. Measles alone killed 3,000 in 1640, and between 1667 and 1672 people were reduced to boiling leather for food. Some Pueblos were shipped south as slaves to the silver mines of Mexico. The spark came in 1675. Spanish authorities arrested forty-seven Pueblo religious leaders for “sorcery.” The sources disagree on their fate: one says four were sentenced to death and the rest whipped and imprisoned, another that three were hanged and one killed himself. The Pueblos forced the release of the prisoners, and one of them, Popé of San Juan Pueblo, began to organize a coordinated uprising. The Architect of the Capitol adds that Po’pay was among those flogged. Planning. In hiding at Taos Pueblo, Popé built a coalition across languages. He recruited Luis Tupatú, a Tiwa speaker and leader at Picuris, Antonio Malacate, a Keresan spokesman from the southern pueblos, and Francisco El Ollita, a Tewa war leader from San Ildefonso, among others. Pedro Naranjo, a San Felipe man who was captured and questioned by the Spanish in 1681, testified that Popé had a cord of knotted maguey fiber passed from pueblo to pueblo. Each town that agreed untied one knot, and the remaining knots counted the days until the rising. Swift young runners carried the cord, on pain of death if they betrayed the secret. The Architect of the Capitol says the legend speaks of deerskin strips, and the sources give different days for the planned start: August 11, August 12, or August 13. Naranjo said the Spanish governor imprisoned two accomplices two days before the date, and the Library of Congress says the Spanish learned of the plot on August 9. The rising. Popé moved the date forward, and on August 10, 1680, the Pueblos attacked. The people of Tesuque killed Father Juan Pío early that morning, and the revolt spread across the country. They burned churches and killed priests, settlers, women, and children. The Penn Museum counts 401 settlers and 21 friars dead, and EBSCO counts 400 settlers and 21 of the 33 priests. A lieutenant governor, Alonso García, gathered the survivors in the south and led them toward El Paso on August 14. On August 15 five hundred Pueblos besieged Governor Antonio de Otermín in Santa Fe and demanded that he free any Native slaves and leave. Otermín attacked, but as more than two thousand warriors gathered and his water supply was cut, he abandoned the capital. The Library of Congress dates the end of the siege to September 21, while EBSCO says Otermín left with more than a thousand settlers on August 21 and reached El Paso on September 29. For twelve years New Mexico was free of Spanish rule. The Pueblos set about undoing Christianity. According to Naranjo’s testimony, Popé ordered the images of Christ and the saints, the crosses, and the temples destroyed and the bells broken. People washed themselves in the root amole to remove their baptismal names, kivas were rebuilt, and the masked kachina dances resumed. Anyone who still kept faith with the priests and the Spaniards was punished, and some were killed. A new kachina entered the Pueblo pantheon, known among the Hopi as Yo-we, the “Priest-killer.” Naranjo’s testimony, the editor notes, is “filtered through Spanish eyes,” and it calls the Pueblo gods devils, so it has to be read with care. EBSCO adds that Popé “had become something of a tyrant himself.” The unity did not last. Drought, disease, and Apache raids continued, and the coalition unraveled. Popé died in 1692. Meanwhile the Spanish launched punitive expeditions from the south, including raids on Santa Ana in 1687 and Zia in 1689, though they could not retake the province. In 1692 a new governor, Diego de Vargas, marched north from El Paso, surrounded Santa Fe with his army and two cannons, and entered it on September 13 after negotiations. Many historians have called this a “bloodless reconquest.” The Penn Museum calls that inaccurate: Vargas offered pardon to the pueblos if they became vassals of the crown, but many Pueblo lives were lost in later campaigns. In 1694 as many as two thousand people from seven Tewa villages held the mesa-top refuge at Tunyo for nine months against Vargas. Revolts in 1694 and 1696 were crushed. But the friars who came back with Vargas could not bring back the forced labor and the harsh suppression of Native religion, and in the 1700s Spaniards and Pueblos began to live together more peacefully. In 1820 the Pueblos were granted equal citizenship in the province. The revolt also changed the Southwest well beyond the Pueblos. EBSCO reports that Spanish sheep reached the Navajo and became the core of a herding way of life, and that horses, now freed by the hundreds, were widely traded. Within a century they had spread to the Plains nations. Pueblo people today see the revolt as a key reason they survived as distinct peoples. Others who had settled with Otermín at El Paso lost much of their language, arts, and customs. The tricentennial in 1980 was marked by events across the country celebrating the “First American Revolution.” In 1997 New Mexico chose Po’pay as its second statue in the National Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol. He is the first person in the collection to have been born on what became American soil, and no image or description of him is known. The Pueblo Revolt shows that Native peoples did not simply endure colonization. They organized across linguistic and political lines to resist it, and for twelve years they won. The God of the Spaniards was worth nothing and theirs was very strong, the Spaniard’s God being rotten wood. title: Puerto Rico Under the United States
subtitle: From Spanish colony to U.S. territory and commonwealth, 1898–1952
summary: Puerto Rico, long a Spanish colony, passed to the United States in 1898 at the end of the Spanish-American War. After two years of military rule, the Foraker Act of 1900 set up a civil government but gave Puerto Ricans no U.S. citizenship. Island leaders such as Luis Muñoz Rivera pressed Congress for years, and the Jones-Shafroth Act of March 2, 1917, made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. In 1952 Puerto Rico became a self-governing commonwealth. Its people are citizens, yet the island is represented in Congress only by a non-voting resident commissioner, and the nature of that relationship is still debated today.
thumbAlt: Members of Puerto Rico’s first autonomous cabinet under Spain, including Luis Muñoz Rivera, as published in 1898
aliases: Puerto Rico Porto Rico Jones Act Jones-Shafroth Act Foraker Act Commonwealth of Puerto Rico Estado Libre Asociado
themeText: Territorial expansion Latino history Foreign policy and diplomacy Constitution and law
text: Puerto Rico Became American Ceded by Spain in the Treaty of Paris, December 10, 1898 Foraker Act (1900) Ended military rule; a “temporary civil government,” but no U.S. citizenship Jones-Shafroth Act March 2, 1917: collective U.S. citizenship, a two-house legislature, and a non-voting resident commissioner in Congress World War I Some 20,000 Puerto Rican men were drafted and served Commonwealth 1952: more self-government; citizenship unchanged Puerto Rico is one of the territories the United States acquired as it became an overseas empire in 1898. Its unresolved status, citizens without full representation, raises lasting questions about democracy, empire, and what it means to be part of the United States. Juan Ponce de León, the Spanish conqueror of Puerto Rico, went on to land in Florida in 1513. Centuries later, island leaders such as Luis Muñoz Rivera and Tulio Larrínaga were fighting for Puerto Rico’s sovereignty while it still belonged to Spain. In 1898 the United States went to war with Spain, which had been fighting Cuban revolutionaries for three years, and in the Treaty of Paris, signed on December 10, 1898, Spain ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States. Victory over Spain left the United States with island colonies and no settled plan for governing them. Many Americans wanted the strategic and commercial advantages of overseas territory; anti-imperialists warned that ruling peoples without their consent betrayed the nation’s founding ideals. Over the following decades Congress would debate more than a hundred bills dealing with citizenship for the island. At first the island was ruled by the U.S. military and a presidentially appointed governor. The Foraker Act of 1900 ended military rule and provided a “temporary civil government for Porto Rico,” as Congress then spelled it, but it did not make Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. Muñoz Rivera and others kept pressing Congress. President Theodore Roosevelt endorsed citizenship during a visit to the island in 1906, and as resident commissioner in Washington, Muñoz Rivera told Congress in 1916: “Give us now the field of experiment which we ask of you.” He died that November, a few months before Congress acted. On March 2, 1917, the Jones-Shafroth Act became law. It collectively naturalized the people of Puerto Rico as U.S. citizens and created a new government: an elected two-house legislature with a 19-member Senate and a 39-member House, a governor and executive council appointed by the president, a Supreme Court and a U.S. District Court, a non-voting resident commissioner in Congress, and protections for individual civil rights. Two months later Congress passed the Selective Service Act, and some 20,000 Puerto Rican men were drafted to serve in World War I. Citizenship did not bring full self-rule: the governor and other top officials were still appointed in Washington. Over the following decades Congress kept adjusting the islanders’ status: according to scholars of the Puerto Rico Citizenship Archives Project, it enacted at least ten laws conferring different kinds of nationality and citizenship, and since 1940 people born in Puerto Rico have been U.S. citizens by birth. In 1952 Puerto Rico became a commonwealth (Estado Libre Asociado) with its own constitution and more autonomy, though the citizenship rights granted in 1917 did not change. Many Americans still do not understand the island’s status: in a 2017 poll only 54 percent of mainland residents knew that people born in Puerto Rico are U.S. citizens. Academics and politicians continue to argue over whether Puerto Ricans’ citizenship leaves them with a second-class, territorial status. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8EOxtY3M6Co Why Puerto Rico is not a US state Vox 3:55 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mk6JrUYLyWw Why didn't Puerto Rico become a US State? title: The Pullman Strike
subtitle: A national railroad boycott crushed by federal troops, 1894
summary: In May 1894, during a severe depression, workers at George Pullman’s sleeping-car factory near Chicago struck after he cut wages by a quarter while keeping rents in his company town unchanged. The American Railway Union, led by Eugene V. Debs, launched a national boycott of trains carrying Pullman cars, halting rail traffic across much of the country. A federal court injunction and thousands of federal troops broke the strike, Debs went to jail, and the union was destroyed.
location: Pullman, Illinois (Chicago), and rail lines nationwide
thumbAlt: Strikers outside the Arcade Building in Pullman, Illinois
aliases: Eugene Debs American Railway Union
themeText: Labor and work Economy and finance Reform and protest
text: Pullman, Illinois (Chicago), and rail lines nationwide Strike began May 11, 1894 Union American Railway Union (ARU), open to all white railroad workers; led by Eugene V. Debs Federal response An injunction under the Sherman Anti-Trust Act; thousands of U.S. Marshals and Army troops Outcome Boycott collapsed in mid-July; Debs and others indicted for contempt George Pullman built a planned company town on Chicago’s South Side for workers who manufactured his luxurious railroad sleeping cars. Pullman owned the houses and stores. When the depression of 1893 hit, he cut wages by about a quarter but kept rents and utility charges the same. Pullman workers formed a grievance committee but got nowhere. Many had joined the new American Railway Union, formed in June 1893, which accepted railroad workers of every craft. Although ARU leaders advised against it, a strike broke out at the Pullman works on May 11, 1894. When the company refused to negotiate, the ARU voted to boycott Pullman cars: its members would not handle any train carrying them. The boycott crippled rail traffic nationwide. The General Managers’ Association, representing 24 railroads, hired strikebreakers and worked to turn public opinion against the strikers. Because the boycott disrupted the U.S. mail, the federal government intervened: a court issued an injunction, citing the Sherman Anti-Trust Act of 1890, a law meant to fight monopolies. Over the objection of Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld, President Grover Cleveland sent thousands of U.S. Marshals and Army troops. Mob violence increased in Chicago, and clashes between soldiers and crowds at rail yards left dozens dead. The boycott collapsed in mid-July, and the ARU was defeated. Debs and other leaders were indicted for contempt for defying the injunction. In late July, President Cleveland appointed a commission to investigate, and George Pullman was widely criticized for refusing to arbitrate with his workers; destitution was widespread in his town. The strike demonstrated how injunctions and federal power could be turned against organized labor. Pullman’s former company town became Pullman National Historical Park in 2015, the first National Park Service unit in Chicago, which also includes a museum named for A. Philip Randolph that explores African American labor history. The Pullman strike was one of the largest labor actions in American history, and its defeat showed the lengths government would go to protect the railroads in the Gilded Age. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fIzpvrwk160 The Pullman Strike of 1894 Explained: US History Review Hip Hughes (HipHughes) 10:17 2026-10-23

title: Reconstruction
subtitle: The struggle to rebuild the Union and define freedom after the Civil War
summary: Reconstruction was the era in which the United States tried to reunite the nation after the Civil War and decide what freedom would mean for four million formerly enslaved people. Congress wrote the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments into the Constitution, abolishing slavery, making Black Americans citizens, and forbidding racial discrimination in voting. Black Southerners built schools and churches, searched for lost family members, voted, and held office, as many as 2,000 of them. Terrorist violence, economic depression, and Northern retreat brought Reconstruction to an end by 1877, opening the way to Jim Crow.
location: The former Confederate states and the nation
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of the first Black members of Congress, including Senator Hiram Revels
aliases: Radical Reconstruction Congressional Reconstruction Presidential Reconstruction Black Codes Redeemers Reconstruction Acts Ku Klux Klan
