text: The former Confederate states and the nation Traditional dates 1865–1877; the National Park Service uses a broader span from 1861 to the 1890s Constitutional amendments 13th (ratified 1865), 14th (1868), 15th (1870) New voters About 400,000 formerly enslaved men voted for the first time in the presidential election of 1868 Black officeholders As many as 2,000, including 16 members of Congress First Black senator Hiram R. Revels of Mississippi, sworn in on February 25, 1870 Ended With the disputed election of 1876 and the withdrawal of the last federal troops from Southern statehouses in 1877 When the Civil War ended in 1865, much of the South lay in ruins. “We had passably good roads,” one South Carolinian told a Northern reporter, “and the next week they were all gone… miles and miles of iron have actually disappeared.” The great questions of the peace were just as unsettled. Would the defeated states return as equals or be governed as conquered territory? Who would rebuild their governments? And what rights did freedom give to formerly enslaved people? In a sense, Reconstruction had begun during the war itself. In November 1861 Union forces won the Battle of Port Royal Sound and took control of the coast of South Carolina around Beaufort. The planters fled, leaving behind more than ten thousand enslaved people, and the Lincoln administration launched the “Port Royal Experiment” to help them become self-sufficient. On St. Helena Island, one of the country’s first schools for freed people opened; at nearby Camp Saxton, where some of the first African Americans joined the U.S. Army, elaborate ceremonies were held on New Year’s Day 1863 to announce and celebrate the Emancipation Proclamation. President Abraham Lincoln began planning for reunion in late 1863. Under his “ten percent” plan, once a tenth of a state’s voters had sworn an oath of loyalty, loyal Unionists could form a new state government; such governments arose in Louisiana, Tennessee, and Arkansas. The Emancipation Proclamation freed people only in areas still in rebellion, leaving more than seven hundred thousand people in bondage in Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri and in Union-held parts of the South. To end slavery everywhere, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment on January 31, 1865, and the states ratified it on December 6 of that year. The amendment abolished slavery “except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted.” In March 1865 Congress also created the Freedmen’s Bureau within the War Department to manage abandoned lands and help formerly enslaved people toward self-sufficiency. Lincoln did not live to carry out his plans. After his assassination in April 1865, Vice President Andrew Johnson became president. A Tennessee Democrat who had been the only Southern senator to keep his seat when his state seceded, Johnson was devoted to the Union but held deeply racist views, and he had no intention of forcing Southern states to grant Black Americans equal rights. Taking advantage of the eight months when Congress was in recess, he rushed through his own program. He handed out thousands of pardons, restored former Confederates’ property, and appointed provisional governors for the Southern states. Those states had only to cancel their ordinances of secession, repudiate their Confederate debts, and ratify the Thirteenth Amendment; on everything else they could do as they pleased. Only planters with more than $20,000 in property had to apply to Johnson personally for a pardon. The new Southern governments quickly passed laws known as Black Codes, beginning in South Carolina and Mississippi. The codes allowed African Americans to own property, marry, and make contracts, but barred them from juries and militias, refused to accept their testimony against white people, apprenticed Black orphans to their former enslavers, and established harsh vagrancy laws. Mississippi required every freedman to carry papers proving he had work; a man without them could be arrested and fined, and if he could not pay, the sheriff could hire him out to anyone willing to pay the tax. One scholar has called such systems “slavery by another name,” and the Miller Center describes the Black Codes as having “essentially maintained slavery under another name.” The codes, together with mob violence against Black Southerners, turned Northern opinion against Johnson. When the president declared the Southern states restored, congressional Republicans refused to seat their representatives. Some Republicans, like Congressman Thaddeus Stevens, believed in racial equality, but most, the American Yawp argues, were moved chiefly by party interest: giving the vote to hundreds of thousands of Black men was the only way to protect Republican power in the South. In 1866 Congress took control. It extended the Freedmen’s Bureau and passed the Civil Rights Act, which for the first time defined all persons born in the United States, except Native Americans, as citizens and protected their “fundamental rights”; both laws passed over Johnson’s vetoes. To ensure that the Civil Rights Act was constitutional, Congress approved the Fourteenth Amendment on June 13, 1866. Its first section declared that “All persons born or naturalized in the United States” were citizens and forbade any state to deny any person “life, liberty, or property, without due process of law” or “the equal protection of the laws.” Its main author, Congressman John A. Bingham of Ohio, intended it to make the Bill of Rights binding on the states as well. Johnson opposed it and took his case to the voters in a speaking tour during the 1866 elections, attacking his opponents in abusive language; one observer estimated that he lost a million Northern votes. Republicans won a veto-proof majority. The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 dissolved the governments of ten Southern states and divided them into five military districts, whose commanders reported to General Ulysses S. Grant. To return to the Union, a state had to write a new constitution giving Black men the vote and ratify the Fourteenth Amendment. When Johnson fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act, the House impeached him by a vote of 126 to 47 in February 1868; the Senate fell one vote short of convicting him. The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified on July 9, 1868. That November, some 400,000 formerly enslaved men voted for the first time, and Grant, campaigning under the slogan “Let us have peace,” defeated the Democrat Horatio Seymour by 214 electoral votes to 80. The Fifteenth Amendment, which forbade any state to deny the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude,” passed Congress in February 1869 and was ratified on February 3, 1870. The result was the first moment of mass democratic participation for African Americans. In 1860 only five Northern states had allowed Black men to vote on equal terms with white men; within a few years the South was governed by Republican-led states with Black men in power for the first time in American history. Hundreds of Black delegates helped write the new state constitutions, which established public schools in a region where they had barely existed; by the end of Reconstruction every Southern state had one. Historians estimate that as many as 2,000 Black men held office, from local levee commissioner to U.S. senator. The American Yawp textbook puts the number at “more than two thousand.” At the local level they served as tax assessors, voter registrars, justices of the peace, school superintendents, sheriffs, and jurors, which gave Black citizens access to a fair hearing in court, public jobs, and public schools. Republican clubs, Union League chapters, and Black churches organized the voters, and Black women, who could neither vote nor hold office, debated the issues, mobilized voters, and accompanied men to the polls as a show of solidarity. Almost 800 Black men served in state legislatures, and for a time they made up a majority of the South Carolina House of Representatives. P. B. S. Pinchback served as governor of Louisiana for thirty-four days, the only Black governor of any state until 1989. On January 20, 1870, the Mississippi legislature elected Hiram R. Revels, a North Carolina-born preacher, to the U.S. Senate. Democrats argued that he had not been a citizen for the nine years the Constitution requires, but on February 25 the Republican majority voted to seat him, and he became the first Black member of Congress. On December 12, 1870, Joseph H. Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House, and within five years fourteen more Black members followed them to Capitol Hill. The abolitionist Wendell Phillips hailed Revels as “the fifteenth amendment in flesh and blood.” Freedom was also lived far from the capitals. Above all, freedpeople wanted land. In January 1865 General William T. Sherman’s Special Field Order No. 15 set aside coastal land in Georgia and South Carolina for them, but Sherman lacked the authority to give it away, and in 1866 land that former Confederates had abandoned was returned to them. The Freedmen’s Bureau, led by General Oliver O. Howard, issued rations and clothing, ran hospitals, supervised labor contracts, helped found schools, legalized marriages made in slavery, and provided transportation for people trying to reunite with their families. Freedpeople placed newspaper advertisements searching for relatives sold away, and kept placing them until the turn of the twentieth century. Many dropped the names their enslavers had given them and took new ones, like Freeman or Lincoln. Schools filled with students from three to eighty years old, and churches became the center of Black community life; by the 1930s, nearly 40 percent of 663 Black churches surveyed traced their roots to the years after emancipation. Reconstruction also opened, and then split, the movement for women’s rights. “Now in the reconstruction,” Elizabeth Cady Stanton declared in May 1866, “is the opportunity, perhaps for the century, to base our government on the broad principle of equal rights for all.” That year women’s rights advocates and abolitionists formed the American Equal Rights Association. But the Fourteenth Amendment wrote the word “male” into the Constitution for the first time, and the Fifteenth did not forbid discrimination by sex. Frederick Douglass insisted that the ballot was a “question of life and death” for Southern Black men, and the movement broke in two. Stanton and Susan B. Anthony formed the National Woman Suffrage Association, while supporters of the Fifteenth Amendment founded the American Woman Suffrage Association. White Southern resistance was fierce and often violent. In 1865 the investigator Carl Schurz found nearly unanimous agreement among white Southerners that “You cannot make the negro work, without physical compulsion.” White mobs attacked Black residents and Republicans in Memphis and New Orleans in 1866, and later in Laurens, South Carolina (1870), Colfax, Louisiana (1873), Yazoo City, Mississippi (1875), and Hamburg, South Carolina (1876). The Ku Klux Klan, organized in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1866, had spread to nearly every former Confederate state by 1868, alongside similar groups such as the Knights of the White Camellia and the White Line. Of the Black delegates to the 1868 state constitutional conventions, one in ten had suffered physical abuse. In Panola County, Mississippi, twenty-four Klan-style murders took place between August 1870 and December 1872. Congress answered with the Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871, which made it a federal crime to deprive African Americans of their civil rights and allowed the use of troops against the Klan, and for a time federal courts and troops worked to put an end to the Klan and similar groups. But the violence continued. In Vicksburg, Mississippi, in 1874, when the Black sheriff Peter Crosby refused white demands that he resign, white men opened fire on the Black citizens who had gathered in protest, killing twenty-nine. Northern commitment faded. After the banking house of Jay Cooke and Company failed in September 1873, the country sank into a six-year depression, and economic questions pushed Reconstruction off the national agenda. Democrats won the House of Representatives in 1874. In the South, white Democrats calling themselves Redeemers promised rule by white men; by 1871 they had already taken back Tennessee, Virginia, and Georgia. In 1875 Mississippi Democrats carried out the “Mississippi Plan,” a campaign of violence to drive Black voters from the polls; the state’s Republican governor begged for federal help, and national Republicans ignored him. The presidential election of 1876 ended the experiment. The Democrat Samuel J. Tilden won the popular vote by about 250,000 and stood one electoral vote short of victory, while both parties claimed Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina, where violence and intimidation had kept Black voters away from the polls. Republican-controlled returning boards in those states then threw out enough Democratic ballots to give Hayes the lead. Congress created a fifteen-member Electoral Commission, which voted eight to seven along party lines to award every disputed state to the Republican Rutherford B. Hayes. The count was completed in the early hours of March 2, 1877, and Hayes won by 185 electoral votes to 184. Historians still debate what was promised behind the scenes. The traditional account, followed by the American Yawp, describes a Compromise of 1877 in which Democrats accepted Hayes in exchange for the withdrawal of federal troops and economic favors for the South; the Miller Center’s historians consider negotiations a virtual certainty but doubt that any deal went beyond what Hayes had already promised in his letter of acceptance. Either way, in April 1877 the last troops were ordered away from the Southern statehouses, and white Democrats returned to power across the South. With federal support withdrawn, the number of Black officeholders declined significantly. Only six new Black members of Congress were elected after 1874, and when George Henry White of North Carolina left the House in 1901, no African American would sit in Congress again until 1928. In the 1890s Southern states wrote literacy tests, “grandfather clauses,” and other devices into their laws to strip Black men of the vote, and in 1896 the Supreme Court approved “separate but equal” segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson. For generations, the defeated side told the story. White Democrats portrayed Reconstruction as a disastrous interlude of corrupt “Negro rule,” and that partisan view shaped textbooks, scholarship, and films such as The Birth of a Nation (1915). Its message, that African Americans were unfit to hold office, was “demonstrably false but dangerously pervasive.” It grew alongside the “Lost Cause” version of the Civil War, which claimed that the Confederacy had fought for constitutional principles rather than slavery. Historians today see Reconstruction as a moment of revolutionary possibility followed by violent backlash. Its economic promises went largely unmet: lacking land, many Black farmers turned to sharecropping, which often trapped families in debt, and under the convict-lease system, which lasted until World War II, arbitrary arrests under vagrancy laws often led to decades of forced, unpaid labor. But its constitutional achievements endured. Black and white citizens kept arguing, in petitions, courts, and dissenting opinions, for the promise of the Fourteenth Amendment, and those arguments became the basis for change in the twentieth century. The Fifteenth Amendment found new force in the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Birthright citizenship, equal protection of the laws, and the right to vote regardless of race all date from these years. Reconstruction rewrote the Constitution to make Black Americans citizens and voters, and its defeat showed how fragile those rights were without the will to enforce them. We were promised Homesteads by the government. . . . The man who tied me to a tree and gave me 39 lashes and who stripped and flogged my mother and my sister . . . that man I cannot well forgive. Freedpeople of Edisto Island, South Carolina replying to Freedmen’s Bureau commissioner Oliver O. Howard, who had come to tell them that the land they farmed would be returned to its former owners It was a whole race trying to go to school. Few were too young, and none too old, to make the attempt to learn. Booker T. Washington recalling the years after emancipation They do not care so much about Congress admitting negroes to their halls . . . but they do not want the negroes over them at home. Henry McNeal Turner a Black member of the Georgia legislature, on white Southerners’ opposition to Black officeholders I am only a poor woman whose husband has been murdered for his devotion to his country. . . . The Rebels imprisoned my Husband. Pardoned Rebels murdered him. Sallie Adkins writing to President Grant after Klansmen killed her husband, the Georgia state senator Joseph Adkins, in May 1869 This is a white man’s government… We regard the Reconstruction Acts (so called) of Congress as usurpations, and unconstitutional, revolutionary, and void. title: The Roanoke Colony
subtitle: England’s “Lost Colony,” 1587
summary: Sponsored by Sir Walter Raleigh, England’s first attempts at a colony in North America centered on Roanoke Island in present-day North Carolina between 1584 and 1590. The last group, 118 men, women, and children led by John White, arrived in 1587. When White returned with supplies three years later, the settlers were gone, leaving the word “CROATOAN” carved into a post. What became of them has never been solved.
thumbAlt: Artist’s reconstruction of the fort at Roanoke Island
themeText: Colonial encounters Indigenous history
text: Roanoke Island, North Carolina Sponsor Sir Walter Raleigh 1587 colonists 118 men, women, and children under Governor John White Virginia Dare White’s granddaughter, born in 1587, the first English child born in the Americas White’s return August 1590, three years after he left Clue “CROATOAN” carved on a post, the name of an island and of a Native people allied with the English In the 1580s England was a latecomer to American colonization, eager to challenge Spain and to find wealth and a base for privateering. Raleigh sponsored a reconnaissance voyage in 1584 and a military colony in 1585–86, which quarreled with the local Algonquian peoples and abandoned the island. The 1587 expedition was meant to be different: a settlement of families, intending to establish itself on the Chesapeake Bay. Instead the colonists were left at Roanoke. The 118 colonists began their journey in April 1587 under John White, intending to settle on the Chesapeake Bay but left instead at Roanoke. Relations with neighboring peoples were tense: at one point the colonists mistakenly attacked friendly Croatoan people, an assault stopped only by Manteo, a Croatoan man working with the English. That August brought the birth of Virginia Dare, White’s granddaughter. Facing the threat of attack, a lack of reliable food, and the coming winter, the colonists persuaded White to sail to England for supplies. White could not return until August 1590. He found the settlement abandoned and the word “CROATOAN” carved on a post. Assuming the colonists had moved to Croatoan, a nearby island home to Native allies, Raleigh and White made several attempts to find them but never did. England abandoned its efforts at Roanoke. It would be seventeen years before the next English colony, at Jamestown in 1607. Theories about the colonists’ fate (that they were killed, died of hunger, or joined nearby Native communities) have circulated for four centuries, and none has been proven. The “Lost Colony” became an enduring American legend. More importantly, Roanoke’s failure taught English promoters lessons about supply, investment, and relations with Native peoples that shaped the Virginia Company’s venture at Jamestown. Roanoke was England’s first serious attempt at settlement in America, and its failure showed how fragile, and how dependent on Native peoples, early colonies were. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kFMnMEYwqIM What Happened to the Lost Colony at Roanoke? | National Geographic National Geographic 3:55 2026-10-23

title: The Salem Witch Trials
subtitle: The 1692 witch hunt in Puritan Massachusetts that sent twenty people to their deaths
summary: In 1692 a panic over witchcraft swept Salem Village and neighboring towns in Puritan Massachusetts. It began when two girls in the household of the village minister fell into fits and three women were arrested for bewitching them; within months hundreds of people had been accused. A special court, relying on “spectral evidence” (testimony that an accused person’s spirit had tormented the victims), sentenced people to death. Nineteen people were hanged and one man was pressed to death with stones before the governor shut the court down. The trials became America’s most famous warning against mass hysteria and false accusation.
location: Salem Village (now Danvers), Salem Town, Andover, and nearby towns, Massachusetts
thumbAlt: T. H. Matteson’s 1855 painting of the 1692 witchcraft trial of George Jacobs in Salem, with an accuser pointing at the old man
aliases: Salem witchcraft trials Salem witch hunt witch trials Court of Oyer and Terminer
themeText: Religion Crime and law enforcement Women's history Everyday life Colonial encounters
text: Salem Village (now Danvers), Salem Town, Andover, and nearby towns, Massachusetts First accused Tituba, Sarah Good, and Sarah Osborne, warrants issued February 29, 1692 First executed Bridget Bishop, hanged June 10, 1692 Death toll Nineteen hanged (fourteen women, five men), Giles Corey pressed to death, and five others died in prison The court A special Court of Oyer and Terminer, set up May 27 and closed October 29, 1692 Last name cleared Elizabeth Johnson Jr., exonerated by the Massachusetts legislature in 2022 Salem showed how fear, local feuds, and unsound legal procedure could combine to destroy innocent lives. It has become the American byword for a “witch hunt” and a lasting argument for due process. Late-seventeenth-century Massachusetts was an anxious place. King Philip’s War of 1675–1676 had devastated New England, tensions with Native peoples endured, and the colony was in political turmoil. Salem Village (now Danvers), a rural community about five miles north of Salem Town, was divided by bitter quarrels among leading families such as the Putnams and the Nurses. Its minister was the Reverend Samuel Parris. Historians point to many causes: local rivalries and family feuds, political turmoil, the enduring trauma of war, and a faulty legal process in which confessing, and accusing others, became the surest way for the accused to save their own lives. Some scholars have even suggested low-level environmental contamination. The court gave spectral evidence an unprecedented status, turning neighbors’ fears and grudges into convictions. In early 1692 Parris’s daughter Betty and her twelve-year-old cousin Abigail Williams began to suffer strange fits, which were diagnosed as witchcraft. On February 29 warrants were issued for three women: Sarah Good, a poor and disreputable woman; Sarah Osborne; and Tituba, a Native American or African woman enslaved in the Parris household. Tituba confessed, setting a fatal pattern: the accused who confessed and named others were spared, while those who insisted on their innocence were condemned. Accusations spread to respected church members such as Martha Corey and Rebecca Nurse, and to Andover, Ipswich, and other towns. On May 27 Governor William Phips created a special Court of Oyer and Terminer. Its first defendant, Bridget Bishop, was convicted largely on spectral evidence and hanged on June 10. When a jury found Rebecca Nurse not guilty, the judges told it to reconsider, and she was hanged on July 19. The minister George Burroughs declared his innocence on the gallows ladder and recited the Lord’s Prayer, which Increase Mather believed no witch could do perfectly, moving spectators to tears, but he was hanged anyway. Giles Corey refused to submit to a trial and was slowly crushed under heavy stones in September. In all, between June 10 and September 22 the court in Salem sent twenty people to their deaths. As doubts about spectral evidence mounted among ministers, Phips closed the court on October 29. As the scale of the injustice sank in, Phips threw out the death sentence of twenty-two-year-old Elizabeth Johnson Jr., convicted in 1693. Some of the jailed could not leave until their prison fees were paid. Tituba remained in jail for thirteen months after Parris refused to pay hers. In 1697 Samuel Sewall, one of the judges, issued a public confession of his wrongdoing. Over the following centuries dozens of the accused were officially cleared, though some names were overlooked. The last, Elizabeth Johnson Jr., was formally exonerated in 2022 after an eighth-grade civics class in North Andover took up her case. Salem itself, where a memorial now marks an execution site, has become a center of remembrance and tourism, with reenactments of the trials. The trials remain a warning about scapegoating, the danger of convicting people on evidence that cannot be tested, and how quickly a community can turn on its own members. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NVd8kuufBhM What really happened during the Salem Witch Trials - Brian A. title: Selma to Montgomery Marches
subtitle: “Bloody Sunday” and the march for voting rights, 1965
summary: In early 1965, local activists, SNCC, and Martin Luther King Jr.’s SCLC campaigned for voting rights in Selma, Alabama, where only 2 percent of Black residents were registered. On March 7, remembered as “Bloody Sunday,” state troopers and local lawmen attacked peaceful marchers with clubs and tear gas at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Televised images shocked the nation. Two weeks later, under federal protection, thousands marched the 54 miles to Montgomery. The campaign led directly to the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
thumbAlt: Marchers on the Selma to Montgomery march
aliases: Bloody Sunday Edmund Pettus Bridge
themeText: Voting rights Civil rights and citizenship African American history
text: Selma to Montgomery, Alabama (54 miles) Bloody Sunday March 7, 1965, Edmund Pettus Bridge Leaders that day Hosea Williams (SCLC) and John Lewis (SNCC) Full march March 21–25, 1965; 54 miles; about 25,000 people at the end Deaths Jimmie Lee Jackson, Rev. James Reeb, Viola Liuzzo Result Voting Rights Act signed August 6, 1965 On January 2, 1965, King and SCLC joined SNCC, the Dallas County Voters League, and other local activists in a voting rights campaign in Selma. SCLC chose Selma partly because they expected the brutality of Sheriff Jim Clark to attract national attention and press Congress for a voting rights law. On February 18, during a night march in nearby Marion, a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson, a 26-year-old church deacon, as he tried to protect his mother; he died eight days later. Activists resolved to march from Selma to the state capitol in Montgomery. On Sunday, March 7, marchers crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge and met a wall of state troopers and lawmen, who ordered them to disperse and then attacked, cheered on by white onlookers. John Lewis was severely beaten. Television coverage of “Bloody Sunday” triggered national outrage. King called on clergy nationwide to join a second march. Facing a pending federal court order, on March 9 he led more than 2,000 marchers to the bridge, stopped to pray, and turned back. That night white men attacked James Reeb, a white Unitarian minister from Massachusetts; he died two days later. On March 15 President Johnson addressed Congress, declaring, “Their cause must be our cause too.” Federal judge Frank M. Johnson then approved the march, and on March 21 it set out, protected by federalized National Guardsmen and FBI agents. By the time it reached the capitol on March 25, the crowd had swelled to 25,000. King told them the goal was “a society at peace with itself.” That night Klansmen shot and killed Viola Liuzzo, a Michigan volunteer. Johnson sent a voting rights bill to Congress on March 17, and he signed the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965, recalling “the outrage of Selma.” King summarized the movement’s legislative arc: “Montgomery led to the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and 1960; Birmingham inspired the Civil Rights Act of 1964; and Selma produced the voting rights legislation of 1965.” The Edmund Pettus Bridge remains a symbol of the struggle for the vote. Selma turned the right to vote into a national cause and produced one of the most consequential laws in American history. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q1_KtW-9tIg March from Selma to Montgomery | American Freedom Stories | Biography | History HISTORY 4:12 2026-10-23

title: The Seneca Falls Convention
subtitle: The first women’s rights convention, July 1848
summary: On July 19 and 20, 1848, about three hundred women and men met at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, for the first women’s rights convention in the United States. Organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, it adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It proclaimed that “all men and women are created equal” and listed the wrongs done to women, beginning with the denial of the vote. One hundred people signed it, 68 women and 32 men. Frederick Douglass was among those who attended. The demand for the vote was the most controversial of its resolutions, and it launched the movement that won the Nineteenth Amendment seventy-two years later.
location: Wesleyan Chapel, Seneca Falls, New York
thumbAlt: The Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, where the 1848 convention met, now part of Women’s Rights National Historical Park

text: Wesleyan Chapel, Seneca Falls, New York Dates July 19–20, 1848 Place Wesleyan Chapel, Seneca Falls, New York Organizers Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, with local reformers Attendance About 300 women and men Declaration of Sentiments Drafted by Stanton with the M’Clintock family; signed by 68 women and 32 men Most controversial demand The right to vote Women in the 1840s could not vote, and married women had few property rights. The Declaration of Sentiments complained that the law made a married woman “civilly dead.” Many of the first women’s rights advocates came to the cause through the fight against slavery. Angelina and Sarah Grimké, Lucretia Mott, Sojourner Truth, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Susan B. Anthony all began as abolitionists. When the Grimké sisters were attacked for speaking in public against slavery, they concluded that they would have to fight for women’s rights in order to fight for the rights of the enslaved. Lucretia Mott was a Philadelphia Quaker, raised in a faith that stressed the equality of all people under God, and a founder of the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society in 1833. In 1840 she was a delegate to the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London. The organizers refused to seat the women delegates. Elizabeth Cady Stanton, on her honeymoon with the abolitionist Henry Stanton, who was also a delegate, met Mott at a tea party in London. Angry at the women’s exclusion, the two promised each other to hold a women’s rights convention when they returned home. Eight years passed. In 1848 the vow became a reality, when Stanton and Mott organized a convention at Seneca Falls, in upstate New York. Stanton, working with the M’Clintock family, drafted the document that the meeting would consider. She deliberately modeled it on the Declaration of Independence to make plain the connection between women’s liberty and the language of the nation’s founding. About three hundred people came to the Wesleyan Chapel on July 19 and 20, 1848, including Mott and Frederick Douglass, the formerly enslaved abolitionist and editor. The Declaration of Sentiments began: “When, in the course of human events, it becomes necessary for one portion of the family of man to assume among the people of the earth a position different from that which they have hitherto occupied…” Then it changed the most famous line in American history: “We hold these truths to be self-evident; that all men and women are created equal.” In place of the Declaration of Independence’s charges against King George, it listed charges against men: “The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her.” The first was that man “has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.” Others were that married women were bound to promise obedience, that divorce and custody laws ignored women’s happiness, that single women who owned property were taxed without representation, that women were shut out of profitable work, the professions, and colleges, and that men had claimed the right “to assign for her a sphere of action, when that belongs to her conscience and her God.” The sources count these grievances differently. The American Yawp counts fifteen grievances and eleven resolutions, while the National Women’s History Museum describes eighteen grievances. The resolutions demanded property rights, access to the professions, and, most controversially, the vote. On the morning of July 20, sixty-eight women signed the Declaration under the words “Firmly relying upon the final triumph of the Right and the True, we do this day affix our signatures to this declaration.” Thirty-two men also signed. The signers expected trouble: “we anticipate no small amount of misconception, misrepresentation, and ridicule; but we shall use every instrumentality within our power to effect our object.” Seneca Falls was the first of many such meetings, held almost entirely in the Northern states. Douglass went on to support women’s suffrage actively. That same year Stanton circulated petitions in support of New York’s Married Women’s Property Act, which let married women keep their own property. The movement grew slowly, however. Few states reformed married women’s property laws before the Civil War, and none was ready to give women the vote. Stanton soon found a partner in Susan B. Anthony, whom she met in 1851, and together they led the movement for half a century. The Declaration of Sentiments set out the agenda of the American women’s rights movement for decades, and the demand for the vote, the most radical part of it, launched the long fight for suffrage. Mott later recalled that she had grown up “so thoroughly imbued with women’s rights that it was the most important question” of her life. Women won a constitutional guarantee of the vote only with the Nineteenth Amendment, ratified on August 18, 1920. Few of the movement’s early supporters lived to see it. The convention’s site is preserved today as Women’s Rights National Historical Park. The Seneca Falls Convention turned scattered complaints into an organized demand for women’s equality and gave the movement its founding document. We hold these truths to be self-evident; that all men and women are created equal. title: September 11 Attacks
subtitle: The al-Qaeda terrorist attacks of 2001
summary: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes. Two were flown into the towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed, and one into the Pentagon outside Washington. The fourth, United Flight 93, crashed in a Pennsylvania field after its passengers and crew fought back. Nearly 3,000 people were killed, more than at Pearl Harbor. The attacks led to the war in Afghanistan, a global “war on terror,” and the Iraq War, and to new security powers at home.
location: New York City; Arlington, Virginia; near Shanksville, Pennsylvania
thumbAlt: Smoke rising from the World Trade Center behind the Statue of Liberty
aliases: 9/11 World Trade Center Pentagon Flight 93 al-Qaeda Osama bin Laden 9/11 Commission War on Terror Patriot Act
themeText: Terrorism and security Foreign policy and diplomacy War and the military The presidency
text: New York City; Arlington, Virginia; near Shanksville, Pennsylvania Hijackers Nineteen al-Qaeda operatives, armed with small knives, box cutters, and Mace or pepper spray World Trade Center North Tower hit 8:46 a.m., South Tower 9:03 a.m.; the South Tower fell at 9:59, the North Tower at 10:28 Pentagon Struck at 9:37 a.m. Flight 93 Crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:03 a.m. after the passengers’ revolt Deaths More than 2,600 at the World Trade Center, 125 at the Pentagon, 256 on the four planes (9/11 Commission) Planner Khalid Sheikh Mohammed’s “planes operation,” approved by Osama bin Laden in late 1998 or early 1999 Al-Qaeda grew out of the war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s. Young Muslims from around the world went to Afghanistan to join the fight, among them Osama bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi, and afterwards he and others formed al-Qaeda to wage holy war elsewhere. The United States had armed and financed the Afghan resistance against the Soviets. Bin Laden attacked the United States for keeping troops in Saudi Arabia, home of Islam’s holiest sites, and for its policies in the Middle East. In February 1998 he and four others issued a “fatwa” declaring it the duty of every Muslim to kill Americans, military or civilian, anywhere in the world. After the Taliban took power in Afghanistan in 1996, al-Qaeda based itself there, and by 2001, the American Yawp writes, it was active in more than sixty countries. The 9/11 Commission traced a decade of warnings: the 1993 truck bomb at the World Trade Center, which killed six, and al-Qaeda’s bombings of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania in August 1998, which killed 224 people, including 12 Americans. In October 2000 an al-Qaeda team blew a hole in the destroyer USS Cole in Yemen, killing 17 sailors. The Clinton administration fired cruise missiles at al-Qaeda camps in Afghanistan and Sudan and pressed the Taliban to expel bin Laden, but neither step dislodged him. By late 1998 or early 1999 bin Laden had approved a plan brought to him by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the “planes operation.” Mohammed said his original idea had called for ten planes to attack both coasts. Training began in the fall of 1999. Four recruits came from a cell of Islamist extremists in Hamburg, Germany, and one of them, Mohamed Atta, became the tactical commander in the United States. Two operatives arrived in Los Angeles in January 2000 after U.S. intelligence briefly tracked them in Asia and then lost them. By the summer of 2000 the future pilots had begun flight training in the United States. In the spring and summer of 2001 American intelligence received a stream of warnings that al-Qaeda planned “something very, very, very big.” CIA Director George Tenet told the Commission that “the system was blinking red.” An August 2001 briefing reminded President George W. Bush that bin Laden was determined to strike in the United States, but the specific threat reports pointed overseas, and domestic agencies were not mobilized. Zacarias Moussaoui was arrested in Minnesota on August 16 after he aroused suspicion at a flight school, and in late August officials realized that the two operatives spotted in Asia were in the country. The Commission concluded that the attacks “were a shock, but they should not have come as a surprise.” The hijackers chose nonstop coast-to-coast flights that were lightly booked, full of fuel, and scheduled to leave at about the same time. In groups of four or five, armed only with small knives, box cutters, and Mace or pepper spray, they seized the planes. At 8:46 a.m. American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center. At 9:03 United Airlines Flight 175 hit the South Tower. Up to 50,000 people worked in the towers each day. At 9:37 American Airlines Flight 77 struck the western face of the Pentagon. At 9:45 the Federal Aviation Administration ordered every aircraft in the sky to land, the first such order in American history, and an estimated 4,500 planes landed safely. The South Tower collapsed at 9:59, and the North Tower at 10:28. United Flight 93, bound from Newark to San Francisco, had left more than 25 minutes late because of heavy traffic. It carried 33 passengers, 7 crew members, and 4 hijackers. At 9:28, near Cleveland, the hijackers stormed the cockpit and turned the plane toward Washington. Passengers and crew, forced to the back, made 37 phone calls and learned of the other attacks. They voted to fight back, and at 9:57 they began their assault on the cockpit. The hijacker at the controls rolled and pitched the plane, and the hijackers chose to crash it rather than lose control. It hit an open field near Shanksville at 10:03, about 20 minutes’ flying time from Washington. Everyone on board died. The sources describe its target in slightly different terms. The 9/11 Commission says it was aimed at the Capitol or the White House, and the National Park Service says the Capitol was most likely, noting that at least one victim’s relative was told it was the White House. More than 2,600 people died at the World Trade Center, 125 at the Pentagon, and 256 on the four planes. The 9/11 Memorial lists the names of nearly 3,000 victims, together with those of the 1993 bombing, on bronze panels around two pools set in the footprints of the Twin Towers. U.S. intelligence quickly identified al-Qaeda, which the Taliban was sheltering in Afghanistan. On September 18 Bush signed a joint resolution of Congress authorizing force against those responsible. Two days later he told Congress: “Our war on terror begins with al Qaida, but it does not end there. It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.” Every nation, he said, had to decide: “Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.” On October 7 American air strikes began against the Taliban and al-Qaeda. With American special forces, the anti-Taliban Northern Alliance took Kabul on November 13, and bin Laden and his followers escaped into the mountains along the Pakistani border. In October 2001 Bush signed the USA PATRIOT Act to expand domestic surveillance and crack down on terrorist financing, and Congress created a new Department of Homeland Security. The attacks transformed American foreign policy. The Bush Doctrine claimed the right to strike preemptively at any regime or terrorist group that threatened the United States. It led to long wars in Afghanistan, the longest in American history, and in Iraq. The journalist Dexter Filkins called it a “forever war.” The Miller Center notes that the response greatly expanded presidential power in matters of national security. The war on terror also raised hard questions at home. The administration held accused terrorists at Guantánamo Bay without the right to challenge their detention in court, and classified them as unlawful enemy combatants outside the protections of the Geneva Conventions. It also approved interrogation methods including waterboarding, which many critics called torture. Some cases reached the Supreme Court, and critics argued that the country was abandoning principles such as the rule of law. A team of Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden at his hideout near Abbottabad, Pakistan, on May 2, 2011. The bipartisan 9/11 Commission, five Republicans and five Democrats, issued its unanimous report in 2004. It found that the nation “was unprepared” and that the government had failed in imagination, policy, capabilities, and management. The Flight 93 National Memorial and the 9/11 Memorial & Museum now mark the crash site and Ground Zero. September 11 was the defining event of the early twenty-first century for the United States. It transformed its foreign policy, its sense of security, and the balance between liberty and security at home. At 8:46 on the morning of September 11, 2001, the United States became a nation transformed. The 9/11 Commission Report 2004 The 9/11 attacks were a shock, but they should not have come as a surprise. The 9/11 Commission Report 2004 Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists. title: Shays’ Rebellion
subtitle: An armed uprising of indebted farmers that shook the new nation
summary: In 1786 and 1787 thousands of farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them Revolutionary War veterans, rose against heavy state taxes and debt collection that threatened to cost them their farms. Led in part by Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain, they closed courts and in January 1787 tried to seize the federal arsenal at Springfield, where militia drove them off. The national government under the Articles of Confederation could do nothing to help. The uprising alarmed leaders across the country and helped bring about the Constitutional Convention.
thumbAlt: Illustration of Shays’s forces fleeing troops at Springfield
aliases: Shays’s Rebellion Shaysites Daniel Shays Springfield arsenal Regulators
themeText: Economy and finance Reform and protest Constitution and law
text: Western Massachusetts Leader Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain, among others Grievances Heavy state taxes to pay war debt, scarce money, foreclosures Courts closed From August 1786 Springfield About 1,500 men tried to take the arsenal in late January 1787; four were killed Militia commander General Benjamin Lincoln Aftermath Leaders sentenced to death but most, including Shays, were pardoned After the Revolution, the economy was weak and money was scarce. Massachusetts set out to pay its war debt quickly through heavy taxes and fees, and creditors pressed farmers who had little cash. Under the Articles of Confederation the national government had no power to tax, so the burden of the war debt fell on the states. The American Yawp explains that this was part of why Massachusetts sided with the wealthy holders of its war bonds over poor western farmers. Some veterans who had never been paid for their service saw their property seized. The farmers asked the state government to protect them from their creditors, but it refused to consider debt relief. Many of them saw their protest as a continuation of the “Spirit of 1776,” and they turned to tactics the patriots had used against Britain: blocking courthouses so judges could not issue foreclosure orders. In August 1786 armed protesters, the “Shaysites,” began seizing county courts to stop debt cases. Governor James Bowdoin called them rebels who wanted to rule by mob violence, and he raised thousands of militiamen under the former Revolutionary general Benjamin Lincoln, who said Massachusetts must prevent “a state of anarchy, confusion and slavery.” The militia was paid for by private Boston businessmen, because the national government had no money to act. In late January 1787 Shays led about 1,500 men toward the federal arsenal at Springfield. The militia met them, four protesters were killed, and the rest scattered. The sources describe the end differently: the National Constitution Center says the group dispersed, while the Yawp says Lincoln’s militia arrested more than a thousand Shaysites and reopened the courts. Shays and other leaders were indicted for treason, and several were sentenced to death, but eventually Shays and most of his followers were pardoned. The National Park Service writes that the rebellion “ended in loss of life and near disaster for the new Commonwealth.” Across the country it set off an intense debate. Thomas Jefferson thought “a little rebellion now and then” helped keep a country free. George Washington was shaken. He wrote to Henry Knox that if anyone had told him three years earlier that he would see “such a formidable rebellion against the laws & constitutions of our own making,” he would have thought him “a bedlamite.” For nationalists such as James Madison, the rebellion was proof that the country needed a stronger central government. “Liberty,” Madison warned, “may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as the abuses of power.” Delegates from five states had already met at Annapolis in September 1786 and called for a convention of all the states the next May. The uprising helped persuade leaders to act, and it changed Washington’s mind about attending. In the summer of 1787 delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia, where they would write a new Constitution giving the national government the power to tax that it had lacked. A local revolt over debt became a national turning point. It exposed the weakness of the Articles of Confederation and convinced key leaders that the union needed a government strong enough to keep order, while raising a question that never went away: when is protest the spirit of 1776, and when is it rebellion? If three years ago any person had told me that at this day, I should see such a formidable rebellion against the laws & constitutions of our own making as now appears I should have thought him a bedlamite. title: The Siege of Yorktown
subtitle: The 1781 American and French victory that effectively won the Revolutionary War
summary: In the fall of 1781, an American army under George Washington and a French army under the Comte de Rochambeau trapped the British general Charles Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, while a French fleet under the Comte de Grasse kept the Royal Navy from rescuing him. After a three-week siege, including a night assault on two British redoubts led in part by Alexander Hamilton, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. It was the last major land battle of the Revolution. Britain’s will to fight collapsed, and the war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
thumbAlt: Auguste Couder’s 1836 painting of Washington and Rochambeau giving their last orders before the attack at Yorktown
aliases: Yorktown Cornwallis surrender Battle of the Capes Rochambeau de Grasse Redoubt 10 Articles of Capitulation
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Yorktown, Virginia Siege September 28 – October 19, 1781 Commanders Washington and Rochambeau (allies); Cornwallis (British) Naval battle Battle of the Capes, September 5, 1781: the French fleet turned back the Royal Navy British army About 9,000 men (American Battlefield Trust) Redoubts 9 and 10 Taken by French and American troops, October 14, 1781 Surrender October 19, 1781 War formally ended Treaty of Paris, signed September 3, 1783 By 1781 both sides were exhausted after six years of war. Britain held only a few coastal areas, was also fighting France and Spain, and faced growing opposition to the war at home. The Americans, deep in debt and short of food, needed a decisive victory. French help had become essential. After the American victory at Saratoga, France signed a treaty with the United States in 1778, and in July 1780 Rochambeau’s expeditionary force of 450 officers and 5,300 men landed in Rhode Island. Meanwhile Britain shifted its attention to the South, where it expected more loyalist support. Its armies took major cities but lacked the men to hold the countryside, and the fighting between patriots and loyalists became, in the American Yawp’s words, “truly a civil war.” In 1780 and early 1781 Cornwallis led his army through the Carolinas, suffering defeats at Kings Mountain and Cowpens and a costly victory at Guilford Courthouse in March 1781. Convinced that the southern colonies could not be held “until Virginia was reduced,” he marched into Virginia, a decision his commander, Sir Henry Clinton in New York, never approved. The young Marquis de Lafayette, with a much smaller American force, shadowed him all summer, avoiding a pitched battle. Under orders from Clinton to take a defensive post at Williamsburg or Yorktown and send part of his army to New York, Cornwallis fortified Yorktown, on the York River, to refit and wait for supplies and reinforcements by sea. Washington and Rochambeau had to choose between attacking New York City and moving south. When de Grasse promised his fleet for operations in the Chesapeake, they chose Virginia. Some 8,000 French and American troops left New York, while fewer than 4,000 stayed behind to guard the Hudson; the Park Service handbook dates the start of the march to August 19, 1781. The Yawp says Washington marched south “in October,” but by then the siege had already begun. The Battlefield Trust calls it “the largest troop movement of the American Revolution.” The Battle of the Capes. On September 5, while the allied armies were still marching, the French fleet met a British fleet at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay and drove it off, leaving Cornwallis cut off by sea. The siege lines. The allies arrived near Yorktown on September 28. Guided by French engineers, soldiers dug parallel trenches toward the British works, where Washington and Rochambeau planned to join and lead about 12,000 more militia, French, and Continental troops. The bombardment. On October 9 the allied guns opened fire, with Washington touching off the first American cannon. For nearly a week the shelling was ceaseless. On October 11 the allies began a second line of trenches 400 yards closer. Redoubts 9 and 10. Two British strongpoints blocked the new line. On the moonless night of October 14, French troops stormed Redoubt 9 while Alexander Hamilton led 400 light infantry against Redoubt 10 with bayonets fixed and muskets unloaded, taking it with only 34 American casualties. Surrender. A British counterattack on October 15 failed. On October 17 a drummer beat a parley and an officer waved a white handkerchief. On October 19 the British and their Hessian allies marched out between lines of American and French troops, their flags cased. Washington refused them the honors of war, as British commanders had refused them to Americans at Charleston earlier in the war. The Articles of Capitulation were drawn up at the Moore House outside town. When news reached London on November 25, Prime Minister Lord North reportedly exclaimed, “Oh God. It is all over.” On March 5, 1782, Parliament authorized the government to make peace, and North resigned fifteen days later. The Yawp writes that the capture of another army “left the British without a new strategy and without public support to continue the war.” Peace talks took place in France, and the war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris on September 3, 1783. Yorktown secured American independence and showed how much the Revolution depended on France: a French fleet sealed the trap, and French soldiers and engineers fought beside the Americans. It became a central scene in the nation’s founding story, and the U.S. government commissioned John Trumbull to paint the surrender. One legend holds that the British band played “The World Turned Upside Down” at the surrender. The Battlefield Trust traces the story to an account published in 1828 and notes that historians doubt it: no widely known tune by that name existed then, and the surrender terms called for the British to march out to “a British or German march.” The siege of Yorktown was the decisive engagement of the American Revolution. It ended Britain’s attempt to defeat the rebellion by force and led directly to the peace that recognized the United States as an independent nation. I was most firmly persuaded, that, until Virginia was reduced, we could not hold the more southern provinces, and that after its reduction, they would fall without much difficulty. title: The Space Race
subtitle: From Sputnik to the moon: the Cold War contest for supremacy in space, 1957–1969
summary: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the world’s first artificial satellite, a beach-ball-sized sphere that circled Earth every ninety-eight minutes. Americans were shocked: if the Soviets could put a satellite in orbit, they could surely send nuclear missiles across the ocean. The Cold War rivalry moved into space. The United States answered with its own satellite, created NASA, and, after the Soviets put the first human in orbit in 1961, President John F. Kennedy pledged to land an American on the moon by the end of the decade, a goal reached with Apollo 11 in July 1969.
thumbAlt: William Pickering, James Van Allen, and Wernher von Braun hold up a model of Explorer 1, America’s first satellite, in 1958
aliases: space race Sputnik NASA Explorer 1 Yuri Gagarin John Glenn Alan Shepard Mercury Apollo
themeText: The Cold War Science and technology Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: United States and Soviet Union Sputnik 1 October 4, 1957: 58 cm across, 83.6 kg, a 98-minute orbit First U.S. satellite Explorer 1, January 31, 1958, which discovered the Van Allen radiation belts NASA Created by the National Aeronautics and Space Act, signed by Eisenhower on July 29, 1958 First humans in space Yuri Gagarin (USSR), April 12, 1961; Alan Shepard (first American), May 5, 1961 The pledge Kennedy to Congress, May 25, 1961: a man on the moon by the end of the decade Finish line Apollo 11 landed on the moon on July 20, 1969 The space race turned science and engineering into instruments of Cold War competition, created NASA, and poured billions of dollars into research. Its triumph, the moon landing, restored American confidence after years of Soviet firsts. The International Geophysical Year, a worldwide scientific project for 1957–1958, called for artificial satellites to map the Earth. In 1955 the White House announced that the United States would launch one, and the Navy’s Vanguard project was chosen. Space was also a military frontier: rockets that could reach orbit could carry nuclear warheads, and both superpowers saw dominance in space as proof of their system’s superiority. The contest grew out of the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their competing ideologies. Each side wanted to prove its technological and military strength to the world, and the Soviet Union, with powerful rockets developed under the engineer Sergei Korolev, struck first. Sputnik caught the American public off guard. A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog, Laika, into orbit; she died soon after launch. The first American attempt, a Vanguard rocket, exploded on its launch pad in December 1957. The Army team under Wernher von Braun then launched Explorer 1 on January 31, 1958; its small instruments discovered the radiation belts around Earth named for the scientist James Van Allen. In July 1958 Eisenhower signed the act creating NASA, which opened for business on October 1. The Soviets kept scoring firsts. On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, orbiting Earth in a flight of an hour and forty-eight minutes. Alan Shepard followed on May 5 with a fifteen-minute suborbital flight, and on May 25 Kennedy told Congress that the nation should commit itself to landing a man on the moon before the decade was out. John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth in February 1962. The race had costs: in January 1967 a fire in the Apollo 1 command module killed astronauts Gus Grissom, Edward White, and Roger Chaffee. In December 1968 Apollo 8 became the first crewed mission to orbit the moon, and on July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of Apollo 11 landed on its surface. Sputnik set off a political furor in the United States. Eisenhower refused panicked demands for huge increases in military spending, confident that American defenses remained strong, but the Defense Department approved funding for a second satellite project, and Eisenhower called for a civilian space agency, which became NASA. Kennedy later placed NASA’s Manned Spacecraft Center in Texas, the home state of his vice president, Lyndon Johnson, who had headed the Senate subcommittee that funded the space program. More than a billion people watched the moon landing, and it gave Americans renewed confidence that their system had prevailed in the most visible arena of the Cold War, though tensions on Earth did not ease. The race left a lasting institution in NASA and a tradition of scientific satellites that began with Explorer 1. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xvaEvCNZymo The Space Race (1955-1975) Simple History 4:26 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FxpC-8f--xo Who won the space race? - Jeff Steers TED-Ed 4:47 2026-10-23

title: The Stamp Act Crisis
subtitle: The first great colonial protest against taxation by Parliament
summary: In March 1765 Parliament passed the Stamp Act, which required newspapers, legal documents, diplomas, and even playing cards in the colonies to be printed on stamped paper showing a tax had been paid. It was the first direct tax Parliament had ever laid on the colonists. Colonists answered with resolutions, a congress of nine colonies, boycotts of British goods, and crowd violence, until no one would serve as a stamp distributor. Parliament repealed the act early in 1766 but declared its power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The crisis gave colonists the argument, “no taxation without representation,” and the methods of resistance that would carry them toward independence.
thumbAlt: Bostonians reading news of the Stamp Act
aliases: Stamp Act Stamp Act Congress Virginia Resolves Declaratory Act Sons of Liberty no taxation without representation virtual representation
themeText: Political thought Economy and finance Reform and protest
text: British North American colonies; London Passed March 1765 Taxed Newspapers, pamphlets, diplomas, legal documents, playing cards, and more Virginia Resolves May 30, 1765 Stamp Act Congress October 1765, New York City; delegates from nine colonies Stamp distributors All twelve had resigned by November 16, 1765 Repealed February 1766 (American Yawp); often dated March 1766 Declaratory Act 1766: Parliament may bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever” Britain won the Seven Years’ War but the war doubled the national debt to 13.5 times Britain’s annual revenue, and it now faced the cost of securing and defending a much larger empire. King George III, crowned in 1760, brought into government men who, the American Yawp writes, held “an authoritarian vision of empire in which colonies would be subordinate.” The Proclamation of 1763 forbade settlement west of the Appalachians. In 1764 the Sugar Act tightened enforcement of duties on molasses and sent smugglers to vice-admiralty courts without juries, and the Currency Act barred colonies from printing paper money during a postwar recession. Some colonists began to fear “a pattern of increased taxation and restricted liberties.” Until 1765 the colonies had paid only “external” taxes, such as customs duties that regulated trade. The Stamp Act was different: it created a new, direct, “internal” tax to raise revenue. The Maryland lawyer Daniel Dulany drew the line clearly, admitting Parliament’s right to regulate trade but denying its right to impose an internal tax “without their consent for the single purpose of revenue.” The act also touched far more people than the Sugar Act had, from printers and lawyers to college graduates and sailors who played cards, which helped make resistance broad and popular. Colonists insisted that as Englishmen they could be taxed only by their own elected representatives. British officials answered that they were “virtually represented” in Parliament, like English districts that elected no members; one colonial pamphleteer called that a “monstrous idea.” The Yawp describes three kinds of resistance, roughly divided by class. Legislatures. On May 30, 1765, Virginia’s House of Burgesses passed the Virginia Resolves, claiming for colonists all the liberties of the people of Great Britain. Newspapers printed them with extra, more radical resolutions that the Burgesses had not passed, and these helped push other assemblies further. In October 1765 delegates from nine colonies met in New York City as the Stamp Act Congress. Its declaration professed loyalty to the king but held that “no taxes be imposed on them, but with their own consent, given personally, or by their representatives.” Merchants. Merchants in the port cities signed nonimportation agreements; in New York “upwards of two hundred principal merchants” refused to buy British goods. By January 1766 London merchants were telling Parliament they faced ruin. Crowds. In Boston, crowds burned the stamp distributor Andrew Oliver in effigy and tore down a building he owned. He resigned the next day, and a week later a crowd wrecked much of the home of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson. Notices in New York warned that the first man to use stamped paper should “take care of his House, Person, & Effects.” By November 16 all twelve stamp distributors had resigned, so the act could not be enforced. Groups calling themselves the Sons of Liberty formed in most colonies. Under this pressure Parliament repealed the Stamp Act. The Yawp dates the repeal to February 1766, while the Declaratory Act passed with it is dated March 18, 1766, so the repeal is often given as March. To save face, Parliament passed the Declaratory Act at the same time, asserting its “full power and authority to make laws and statutes … to bind the colonies and people of America … in all cases whatsoever.” Colonists, busy celebrating, paid it little attention; New Yorkers even raised a lead statue of King George III. The Yawp suggests that colonists may never have felt prouder to be part of the British Empire than in 1766. Britain still needed revenue, and in 1767 the Townshend Acts imposed new duties on goods such as glass, paint, and tea. Colonists resisted again, this time more widely: women organized spinning clubs and signed boycott lists, and Committees of Correspondence linked the colonies. The Stamp Act crisis had given colonists a shared principle, that only their own representatives could tax them, and a set of tools, from intercolonial congresses to boycotts and street protest, that they would use against the Townshend duties, the Tea Act, and the Coercive Acts. The Stamp Act crisis was the moment colonists first acted together against Parliament and spelled out the principle, no taxation without representation, that would lead them to independence. Parliament’s answer, that it could bind them “in all cases whatsoever,” defined the conflict that followed. A right to impose an internal tax on the colonies, without their consent for the single purpose of revenue, is denied, a right to regulate their trade without their consent is, admitted. title: Stock Market Crash of 1929
subtitle: The collapse that ended the Roaring Twenties boom
summary: In October 1929 the great stock market boom of the 1920s collapsed. After panic selling on “Black Thursday,” October 24, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 13 percent on Black Monday, October 28, and nearly 12 percent more on Black Tuesday, October 29. The slide continued until 1932, when stocks had lost 89 percent of their peak value. The crash did not by itself cause the Great Depression, but it frightened investors and consumers and exposed deep weaknesses in the economy.
location: New York Stock Exchange, New York City
thumbAlt: Crowd gathered outside the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929
aliases: Black Tuesday Black Monday Black Thursday Wall Street Crash
themeText: Economy and finance
text: New York Stock Exchange, New York City Peak Dow closed at 381.17 on September 3, 1929 Black Monday October 28, 1929: down nearly 13% Black Tuesday October 29, 1929: down nearly 12% Bottom 41.22 on July 8, 1932, 89% below the peak Recovery The Dow did not regain its 1929 high until November 23, 1954 The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose sixfold, from 63 in August 1921 to 381 in September 1929. New brokerage houses, investment trusts, and margin accounts let ordinary people buy stocks with borrowed money, typically putting down 10 percent of the price and borrowing the rest. Even so, only about 2.5 percent of Americans had brokerage accounts. In mid-October 1929 the economist Irving Fisher declared that stock prices had reached “what looks like a permanently high plateau.” Federal Reserve officials believed speculation was diverting credit from productive uses. The Board urged reserve banks to deny credit to member banks that lent to speculators, and in August 1929 it allowed the New York Fed to raise its discount rate to 6 percent. Lending to brokers continued anyway. Meanwhile the economy had already begun contracting in the summer of 1929. Prices peaked on September 3, 1929. As they fell in October, leading bankers met at the offices of J. P. Morgan, pooled funds, and publicly bought blocks of shares at high prices to restore confidence. The market steadied briefly, but on Black Monday and Black Tuesday frightened investors dumped their holdings. Shares of U.S. Steel eventually fell from $262 to $22, and General Motors from $73 to $8. The crash wiped out savings and confidence. Fearful consumers stopped buying big-ticket items on credit, such as automobiles; firms like Ford cut production and laid off workers, and the downturn deepened. According to the Federal Reserve’s historians, the crash’s direct impact faded within months, and by the fall of 1930 recovery seemed possible, until waves of bank failures turned a sharp recession into the longest and deepest depression in the nation’s history. Economists drew lessons from 1929: that central banks should be cautious about trying to deflate stock market bubbles, and that the damage from a crash can be contained if the financial system is protected. The crash led to new securities regulation in the New Deal, and it remains the reference point for every later market panic. The Crash of 1929 became the symbolic beginning of the Great Depression and a lasting warning about speculation and borrowed money. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GCQfMWAikyU The Great Depression: Crash Course US History #33 CrashCourse 14:27 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D2iuUzkKu9k The 1929 Stock Market Crash - Black Thursday - Extra History Extra History 9:15 2026-10-23

title: Thanksgiving Day
subtitle: How a New England harvest custom became a fixed national holiday, from Washington to Roosevelt
summary: Thanksgiving was built step by step. In 1621 the Plymouth colonists and about ninety Wampanoag men shared a three-day harvest celebration, which nineteenth-century writers came to call the “First Thanksgiving.” In 1789 the first Federal Congress asked George Washington to proclaim a national day of thanks, and he chose Thursday, November 26. After decades of varying dates, the editor Sarah Josepha Hale persuaded Abraham Lincoln to proclaim the last Thursday of November in 1863. When Franklin D. Roosevelt moved it a week earlier in 1939, the country briefly kept two Thanksgivings, until Congress fixed the fourth Thursday of November by law in 1941.
thumbAlt: George Washington’s printed Thanksgiving Day proclamation of October 3, 1789
aliases: Thanksgiving First Thanksgiving Sarah Josepha Hale Franksgiving
themeText: National symbols and holidays The presidency Everyday life
text: Plymouth harvest feast Autumn 1621, about 53 colonists and some 90 Wampanoag men, over three days First under the Constitution Thursday, November 26, 1789, proclaimed by George Washington Campaigner Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey’s Lady’s Book Made annual Lincoln’s proclamation of October 3, 1863: the last Thursday of November The 1939 change Roosevelt moved it a week earlier; 32 states followed, 16 refused Fixed by law Fourth Thursday of November, signed December 26, 1941 Plymouth, 1621. The only eyewitness account of the harvest celebration at Plymouth is a letter by the colonist Edward Winslow, printed in 1622 in the pamphlet now known as Mourt’s Relation. Winslow wrote that after the harvest the governor sent four men out fowling, and that “many of the Indians” came, among them the Wampanoag leader Massasoit “with some 90 men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted”; the Wampanoag killed five deer and gave them to the colonists. About half of the 102 Mayflower passengers were still alive, so the English were outnumbered roughly two to one. Winslow never called the event a thanksgiving. In 1841 the antiquarian Alexander Young printed the passage with a footnote calling it “the first Thanksgiving,” because it resembled the New England holiday of his own day. A national day, 1789. On September 28, 1789, just before a recess, the first Federal Congress asked the president to recommend a day of thanksgiving. A few days later Washington proclaimed Thursday, November 26, 1789, a “Day of Publick Thanksgivin,” the first under the new Constitution. Later presidents issued their own proclamations, but the dates, and even the months, varied. Sarah Josepha Hale’s campaign. Born in New Hampshire in 1788, Hale became editor of Godey’s Lady’s Book, one of the most widely read magazines in the country, and used it to promote New England’s Thanksgiving customs, from roast turkey to pumpkin pie. She petitioned governors and presidents to adopt a single national day, and in one editorial she reported that the last Thursday of November had been kept in twenty-four of the twenty-nine states that held a Thanksgiving at all. Union in wartime. Hale argued that a fixed national festival would bind the states together, and she pressed the point during the Civil War. On September 28, 1863, she wrote to Lincoln asking for a proclamation making Thanksgiving “a National and fixed Union Festival.” The Depression calendar. In 1939 the last Thursday fell on November 30. Worried that a short Christmas shopping season would slow the recovery from the Great Depression, Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving to the second-to-last Thursday. Lincoln acted within days. His proclamation of October 3, 1863, written by Secretary of State William H. Seward, invited Americans at home, at sea and abroad to observe the last Thursday of November “as a day of thanksgiving and praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the heavens,” and to remember the widows, orphans and mourners of the war. From then on presidents proclaimed the holiday every year. Roosevelt’s change in 1939 split the country. Thirty-two states followed him and sixteen kept the last Thursday, so for two years the nation celebrated two Thanksgivings a week apart. On October 6, 1941, the House passed a joint resolution making the last Thursday the legal holiday. The Senate changed it to the fourth Thursday, to allow for Novembers with five Thursdays, and the House agreed. Roosevelt signed the resolution on December 26, 1941, making the fourth Thursday of November the federal Thanksgiving holiday. The holiday’s path, from a colonial harvest feast to a congressional request, to a magazine campaign, to a presidential proclamation and finally a federal law, shows a national tradition built by government as well as by custom. Its story has also changed. The Pilgrim Hall Museum stresses that Indigenous people outnumbered the colonists at the 1621 gathering, and that Wampanoag women and children, unmentioned in the English sources, may also have been there. Thanksgiving is one of the most widely shared American holidays. Its history shows how a regional custom became a symbol of national union, promoted by a magazine editor in the middle of a civil war and fixed in the calendar during the Depression. Counting the people of 1621 Sources count the colonists slightly differently. The Pilgrim Hall Museum lists 53 Mayflower survivors: 22 men, 4 married women, 5 adolescent girls, 9 adolescent boys and 13 young children, noting that some ages are uncertain. Plimoth Patuxet Museums count the same 53 as 24 men, five women, and 24 children and teenagers. Both agree that about 90 Wampanoag men came with Massasoit, and Pilgrim Hall notes that the figure may undercount the Indigenous guests, since Winslow says “many of the Indians” came besides Massasoit’s party. How long did Hale campaign? In her 1863 letter Hale told Lincoln she had promoted the idea in the Lady’s Book “for the last fifteen years.” Plimoth Patuxet Museums date her campaign to the 1830s. Her magazine editorials on a national day survive from at least 1848. Many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some 90 men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted.
