title: The Trail of Tears
subtitle: The forced removal of the Cherokee Nation, 1838–1839
summary: In 1838 federal troops and state militia forced about 16,000 Cherokee people from their homes in the Southeast into stockades, then sent them west to Indian Territory. Traveling by water and over land through the fall and winter of 1838–39, they suffered from disease, exposure, and hunger. About 4,000 died. The Trail of Tears has become the most widely known symbol of Indian removal.
location: From the Cherokee homeland in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to Indian Territory (Oklahoma)
thumbAlt: Map of the forced removal routes of the Five Tribes
aliases: Cherokee removal Treaty of New Echota John Ross
themeText: Indigenous history Territorial expansion
text: From the Cherokee homeland in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to Indian Territory (Oklahoma) Legal basis The Treaty of New Echota (1835), signed by a small minority and ratified by the Senate by one vote in 1836 People removed About 16,000 Cherokee Deaths About 4,000 Distance As many as 1,000 miles; most overland parties walked about 800 miles Cherokee leader Principal Chief John Ross, who opposed the treaty The Cherokee had lived for centuries in the southern Appalachians. Under pressure from settlers, they ceded more than 90 percent of their lands between 1721 and 1819. They adapted in ways many Americans demanded: farming, trading, building a written legal system and constitution, and, through Sequoyah’s syllabary, achieving widespread literacy. None of this protected them. When gold was found on Cherokee land in 1830, the same year as the Indian Removal Act, Georgia held lotteries giving Cherokee land and gold rights to whites and passed laws stripping the Cherokee of the right to govern themselves or testify in court against whites. The Cherokee fought removal through the courts and won: in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court held that Georgia’s laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation. But President Jackson refused to enforce the decision. Most Cherokee, led by Principal Chief John Ross, opposed removal; a minority concluded that resistance was futile and that a treaty was the only way to survive as a people. In December 1835, U.S. officials met with this minority at New Echota, Georgia. Only 300 to 500 Cherokee were present and none were elected officials, yet twenty signed a treaty ceding all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and new land in the West. More than 15,000 Cherokee protested. The Senate ratified the treaty on May 23, 1836, by a single vote. Most Cherokee refused to believe they would be forced out. In May 1838, General Winfield Scott, with 3,000 troops and authority to raise more, began rounding them up into stockades. Despite orders to treat them humanely, families were separated, the old and sick forced out at gunpoint, and homes looted as their owners were led away. Three groups left that summer, mostly by water, but low rivers, drought, and disease brought several deaths a day. The Cherokee asked to delay removal until fall and to conduct it themselves; the request was granted, but they had to wait in crowded internment camps. By November, twelve groups of about 1,000 each were moving overland, roughly 800 miles. Autumn rains turned roads to mud, food was scarce, and two-thirds of the travelers were trapped between the ice-bound Ohio and Mississippi Rivers in January. One survivor remembered losing his father, then his mother, then his five brothers and sisters: “One each day. Then all are gone.” Approximately 4,000 of 16,000 Cherokee died in the stockades or on the way. In Indian Territory, the survivors rebuilt their nation and government, but the bitter division between the treaty signers and the majority who had opposed removal lasted for years. The Trail of Tears stands for the human cost of a national policy that sacrificed treaty promises and a Supreme Court ruling to the demand for land. The routes are commemorated today as the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, administered by the National Park Service. The Trail of Tears is remembered as one of the clearest moral failures in American history, the forced expulsion of a nation that had done everything asked of it, carried out by the government sworn to protect its treaty rights. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7LSkfmCj8Jg Trail of Tears National Historic Trail NationalTrailsNPS 26:27 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VyF8SOSP2YM From the Trail of Tears to Wounded Knee: Ep 11 of Crash Course Native American History CrashCourse 11:07 2026-10-23

title: The Transcontinental Railroad
subtitle: Rails across the continent, 1863–1869
summary: The first transcontinental railroad joined the eastern rail network to the Pacific coast on May 10, 1869, shortening a journey of several months to about one week. It was built by two companies under the Pacific Railway Act of 1862. The Union Pacific built west from Omaha and the Central Pacific built east from Sacramento, both paid with federal bonds and land. Irish, German, and Italian immigrants laid track on the Union Pacific, and some 10,000 Chinese workers did much of the hardest work on the Central Pacific, for lower pay and with their deaths left uncounted. The rails crossed the homelands of at least fifteen Native nations and opened the Plains to settlers, hide hunters, and soldiers.
location: Omaha, Nebraska, to Sacramento, California; joined at Promontory Summit, Utah
thumbAlt: Crews celebrating the completion of the transcontinental railroad at Promontory Summit
aliases: Pacific Railroad Union Pacific Central Pacific Golden Spike Promontory Summit Pacific Railway Act Chinese railroad workers
themeText: Science and technology Economy and finance Immigration Asian American history Indigenous history Territorial expansion
text: Omaha, Nebraska, to Sacramento, California; joined at Promontory Summit, Utah Authorized Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862 Companies Union Pacific (building west from Omaha) and Central Pacific (building east from Sacramento) Workforce More than 8,000 Irish, German, and Italian immigrants on the Union Pacific; over 10,000 Chinese laborers on the Central Pacific (National Archives) Completed 12:47 p.m., Monday, May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory Federal land granted Eventually 174 million acres for four transcontinental lines (National Archives) Record day 10 miles and 56 feet of track laid on April 28, 1869 Congress argued through the nineteenth century about whether the federal government should pay for “internal improvements” such as canals and railroads, and a railroad across the continent had long been a dream. In the 1850s it commissioned surveys of the possible routes. Private companies refused to take on the job without federal help, and fights over where the line should run stalled the project. The American Yawp notes that government aid to railroads had been part of the Republican Party platform since 1856. On July 1, 1862, Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act. It provided government bonds and large grants of land for rights of way to build a railroad and telegraph line from the Missouri River to the Pacific, and it secured the line’s use for the government. The act authorized two companies, the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific. The American Yawp says the bonds ranged from $16,000 to $48,000 per mile of track. Railroad companies received more than 175 million acres of public land between 1850 and 1871, more than the area of Texas. The National Archives counts 174 million acres for the four transcontinental lines eventually authorized. Because subsidies were paid by the mile, the two companies kept grading past each other for about 250 miles between Echo, Utah, and Wells, Nevada, until Congress forced them to agree on a meeting point. The Central Pacific. The company was chartered in 1862 to build the western section. Its first two years went slowly, held up by long supply lines and a shortage of workers, who often quit when news of a gold strike arrived. Its manager Charles Crocker turned to Chinese workers in 1864, against the doubts of some managers who feared that white workers would refuse to work with them. After small first crews proved themselves, the company recruited thousands more, many directly from Guangdong province in southern China. By July 1865 the Chinese workforce was nearly 4,000, and in February 1867 about 8,000 Chinese were working on tunnels and 3,000 laying track, roughly ninety percent of the workforce, according to the Stanford project. Historians estimate that at any one time 10,000 to 15,000 Chinese were working on the line. The National Archives and the National Park Service both put the total at over 10,000. Their jobs ranged from grading and laying track to blasting, tunneling, cooking, carpentry, and masonry. Almost all of it was done by hand. The Sierra Nevada was the hardest part. Chinese crews cut Bloomer Cut near Auburn, hacked a three-mile ledge into the slope at Cape Horn, and in 1865 began fifteen tunnels, the longest of them the Summit Tunnel through solid granite. They worked through two of the harshest winters on record, with forty-four storms between November 1866 and May 1867. Avalanches swept away camps, and one killed twenty workers. The company built 37 miles of snow sheds in 1868 and 1869. Historians disagree about the story that workers were lowered over cliffs in baskets to set explosives at Cape Horn. Some say it began in a 1927 publicity article. The Stanford project says recent research has found earlier accounts of workers using baskets and ropes in the Sierra. The Union Pacific. From 1863 the Union Pacific built west from Omaha with more than 8,000 Irish, German, and Italian immigrants, according to the Archives. The National Park Service says between 8,000 and 10,000 of the workers were Irish. They were often segregated, housed in cramped railroad cars, and paid less than native-born workers. Historians have found evidence that African American workers also helped build the line, although few records of them survive. Both companies, the Archives notes, faced severe weather, punishing terrain, and conflict with American Indians whose ancestral lands the tracks crossed. The race to Promontory. On April 28, 1869, the bet of $10,000 between Crocker and Thomas Durant of the Union Pacific produced a record. Eight Irish rail handlers and a large crew of Chinese workers laid 10 miles and 56 feet of track in a single day. The sources differ on the Chinese crew size. The National Park Service says no fewer than 400 Chinese laborers worked behind the eight track layers, while the Stanford project says about 5,000 workers, mostly Chinese, took part. The railroad recorded the names of the eight Irish workers. None of the Chinese workers' names was recorded. The last spike. On May 10, 1869, the two lines met at Promontory Summit. The National Park Service says eight Chinese men moved the final rail into position. A polished laurel tie and four ceremonial spikes were presented, among them a gold spike cast by the San Francisco contractor David Hewes. Leland Stanford swung at the final spike and hit the tie, and Durant, nursing a hangover, barely swung at all. A regular rail worker drove the last iron spike, and the telegrapher sent a single word: “D-O-N-E.” It was 12:47 p.m. Estimates of the crowd range from 300 to 1,500 in one account from the park and from 800 to 3,000 in another. The journey across the country shrank from months to about a week. From May to December 1869 Promontory was the meeting point of the two lines, a rowdy town of gambling and saloons, until the junction moved to Ogden in 1870. Many Chinese workers stayed with the railroad or took jobs on other lines. They helped build and maintain at least 70 others, and some also built the Canadian transcontinental line. Others went back to China, or took up farm work, mining, logging, levee building, and city jobs in Chinatowns. President Grant, a strong supporter of the transcontinental railroads, oversaw the completion in the first year of his presidency. No other business drew such huge capital or such lavish government subsidies. The business historian Alfred Chandler called the railroads the “first modern business enterprise.” By 1900 the country had 190,000 miles of track, up from 9,000 in 1850. Railroads made ranching and the cattle drives possible and then ended them. They made Chicago the great hub of the Midwest. By 1880 about 400,000 men, nearly 2.5 percent of the workforce, worked in the industry. A congressional critic of the subsidies said in the 1870s that “if there be profit, the corporations may take it; if there be loss, the Government must bear it.” The railroads defined much of the Gilded Age, including its fortunes, its corruption, and its labor conflict. For Native nations the cost was heavy. The railroad crossed the homelands of at least fifteen of them, and in some cases construction went ahead before any formal agreement was in place. The line brought settlers and development, which limited access to hunting grounds, water, and wildlife. Federal policy encouraged widespread bison hunting, and the American Yawp says the bison fell from more than ten million at midcentury to only a few hundred by the early 1880s. Chinese workers' history was largely written out of the story. Twentieth-century accounts often left them out or played down their role. The Central Pacific kept no record of the deaths. Estimates run from 50 to over 1,000, and the National Park Service says over a thousand. A newspaper reported that the Chinese Six Companies organized a search for the remains of 300 along the line to send them home to China for burial. On June 24, 1867, about 3,000 Chinese workers between Cisco and Truckee struck for higher pay, a ten-hour day, and shorter tunnel shifts. The Park Service calls it the largest organized labor strike in the United States up to then. After about a week the company cut off their food and Crocker confronted them with a sheriff and a posse of deputized white men, and the strike ended. The company appears to have quietly raised pay for skilled workers afterward. Chinese workers were paid less than white workers, and had to pay for their own food. The Park Service puts the gap at about 30 percent, and the Stanford project says they were paid less than half as much per month. Within a decade nativist violence and discriminatory laws followed, the Page Act of 1875 and the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which was made permanent in 1902 and repealed only in 1943. See also the Chinese Exclusion Act. The transcontinental railroad tied the nation together economically and made the settlement of the West possible. It was built by immigrant labor and enormous federal subsidies, and at great cost to the Native nations whose lands it crossed. A large majority of the white laboring class on the Pacific Coast find most profitable and congenial employment in mining and agricultural pursuits, than in railroad work. The greater portion of the laborers employed by us are Chinese Leland Stanford report to Congress, 1865 If there be profit, the corporations may take it; if there be loss, the Government must bear it. a congressional opponent of railroad subsidies 1870s May God continue the unity of our Country as this Railroad unites the two great Oceans of the world. title: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
subtitle: A disaster that changed American workplace safety, March 25, 1911
summary: Near closing time on Saturday, March 25, 1911, fire swept the Triangle Waist Company, a blouse factory on the top floors of the Asch Building in Manhattan. It killed 146 of its roughly 500 workers, most of them young Italian and Jewish immigrant women, some only fourteen. On the ninth floor workers found the stairway doors locked or blocked, the fire escape gave way, and the fire department’s ladders could not reach them. Dozens jumped to their deaths in front of crowds on the street. The owners were acquitted of manslaughter. But public anger led New York to create a Factory Investigating Commission, whose work rewrote the state’s labor laws and shaped the career of a future Secretary of Labor, Frances Perkins.
location: Asch Building, Greenwich Village, New York City
thumbAlt: Smoke pouring from the building during the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire
aliases: Triangle Waist Company Asch Building Triangle fire Factory Investigating Commission Max Blanck Isaac Harris Rose Schneiderman
themeText: Labor and work Immigration Women's history Reform and protest Cities and urban life
text: Asch Building, Greenwich Village, New York City Date Saturday, March 25, 1911, near closing time Place Eighth to tenth floors of the ten-story Asch Building, Washington Place and Greene Street Deaths 146 of about 500 employees; 71 injured (American Yawp) Workers Mostly young Italian and Eastern European Jewish immigrant women Trial Owners Max Blanck and Isaac Harris acquitted of manslaughter, December 27, 1911 Settlement $75 per life lost, March 11, 1914 Reform New York Factory Investigating Commission, created June 30, 1911 The Triangle Waist Company, a maker of women’s shirtwaists, filled the top three floors of the ten-story Asch Building near Washington Square. Cornell’s Kheel Center describes it as a typical sweated factory, marked by low wages, very long hours, and unsanitary and dangerous conditions. Its owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, subcontracted much of the work to middlemen who hired the hands and paid whatever rates they chose. The owners said they never knew what the workers were paid, or even exactly how many people worked for them on a given day. Most of the workers were recent Italian and Jewish immigrants who had come with their families to find a better life. For people still learning a new language, complaining could mean losing a job they badly needed. Some had joined the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union, but Triangle remained a non-union shop. In 1909 an incident at the factory set off a walkout of its 400 employees. The Women’s Trade Union League, an organization of middle-class reformers, helped the strikers picket against hired thugs and the police. At a mass meeting at Cooper Union, thousands of garment workers answered the young Clara Lemlich’s call for a general strike. The strikers demanded union recognition, higher wages, and better safety conditions. The American Yawp writes that the owners decided a workable fire escape and unlocked doors were too expensive, and they called in the police to break the strike. A 1910 agreement after a cloakmakers’ strike set up a grievance system in the garment trade, but many shops, Cornell notes, stayed in the hands of owners who ignored workers’ rights and safety. Fire inspection and fire precautions in New York were badly inadequate. On the day of the fire, waste bins full of cloth scraps from the day’s work fed the flames and let them spread fast. The owners had often locked exit doors in the past, saying that workers stole materials. At quitting time workers normally left through one exit on the Greene Street side, where every handbag was inspected. The building’s single fire escape led nowhere safe, and the elevator shaft had only one car. Firefighting equipment could not reach a fire so high up. The Labor Department’s history says the ladders reached only the seventh floor. Near closing time on March 25, 1911, fire broke out in one of the crowded, littered workrooms. Workers on the eighth and tenth floors escaped. Those on the ninth floor were trapped. They crowded against exits that were locked, doors blocked by machinery, and an elevator with a single car. Survivors said they could not open the ninth-floor doors to the Washington Place stairs, their only escape once the Greene Street stairs were engulfed. The sources describe the doors differently. Cornell’s Kheel Center says workers and many others believed the doors had been deliberately locked. The Labor Department calls the exits illegally locked. The American Yawp states that the doors had been chained shut to keep workers from taking breaks, and that the managers who held the keys saved themselves. Whether the owners knew the doors were locked became the question at their trial. The fire escape bent under the weight of the workers trying to use it, and the Yawp says it collapsed. Firefighters’ ladders were several stories too short, and the water from their hoses could not reach the top floors. Women crowded at the windows and, as the flames closed in, began to jump. Life nets held by firemen tore under the falling bodies. A United Press reporter wrote that he learned “a new sound, a more horrible sound than description can picture. It was the thud of a speeding, living body on a stone sidewalk.” About forty people died in the fall and more than a hundred inside the building. By the end, 146 were dead and 71 injured. The reporter Bill Shepherd, remembering the strike of the year before, wrote: “These dead bodies were the answer.” The city spent the following weeks identifying the dead and sorting their belongings. The ILGWU proposed an official day of mourning, and New Yorkers gathered in churches, synagogues, and the streets. On April 5, 1911, more than 100,000 people marched up Fifth Avenue in a funeral procession while another 400,000 watched. The reformer Martha Bruere watched it pass her window for six hours and wrote that “it is dawning on these thousands on thousands that such things do not have to be!” The labor organizer Rose Schneiderman, herself a former Triangle worker, said: “This is not the first time girls have been burned alive in this city… the life of men and women is so cheap and property is so sacred!” ILGWU Local 25 and the Women’s Trade Union League, the Workmen’s Circle, the Jewish Daily Forward, and the United Hebrew Trades formed a Joint Relief Committee. It paid pensions, cared for injured workers and children, and sent money to victims’ families in Russia and Italy. Working with the American Red Cross, it handed out about $30,000. Blanck and Harris insisted their building was fireproof and had just been approved by the Department of Buildings. On April 11, a grand jury indicted them on seven counts of second-degree manslaughter under section 80 of the Labor Code, which forbade locking doors during working hours. Worker after worker testified that the Washington Place door would not open. But the defense attorney Max Steuer raised enough doubt about whether the owners knew it was locked, and on December 27, 1911, the jury acquitted them. The Yawp writes that the jury took less than two hours. Grieving families cried out, “Where is justice?” Twenty-three civil suits followed. In March 1914 the owners settled them for $75 per life lost. Blanck kept running his business the same way. In 1913 he was charged with locking a door of his factory during working hours, and he was fined twenty dollars. The deeper response came from Albany. A mass meeting at the Metropolitan Opera House, held days before the funeral march, created a Committee on Safety that lobbied the state for an investigation. The state senate majority leader Robert F. Wagner and Alfred E. Smith took up the cause, and a law of June 30, 1911, created the Factory Investigating Commission, with Wagner as chairman and Smith as vice-chairman. Samuel Gompers of the American Federation of Labor served on it. The commission could subpoena witnesses, and it looked into fire hazards, sanitation, occupational disease, and factory inspection. In 1911 and 1912 it held 59 public hearings, heard 472 witnesses, and inspected 3,385 workplaces, from bakeries to chemical plants. Between 1912 and 1914, 13 of the 17 bills it sent to the legislature became law. Together they made a new and much stricter factory code, covering fire safety, ventilation, sanitation, machine guards, and elevators. By the end, 20 laws in all came out of its work. New York also adopted workmen’s compensation. When business groups pushed “ripper” bills to weaken the new code, the commission’s supporters rallied, and the governor vetoed all but one of the bills that passed. Frances Perkins, a young social reformer, testified before the commission and led its members on factory visits. She said the commission turned the Triangle flames into “a torch that lighted up the industrial scene” and later called its work a “turning point” in American attitudes toward social responsibility. Perkins went on to serve as Secretary of Labor and carried its lessons into national policy. Wagner later served in the U.S. Senate. The Triangle fire is still remembered as a symbol of the extremes of industrialism, and its victims as martyrs of the labor movement. The Triangle fire made the dangers of industrial work a public scandal. It convinced many Americans that government had to regulate the workplace, and it produced the most thorough investigation of working conditions that any state had yet attempted. This is not the first time girls have been burned alive in this city… the life of men and women is so cheap and property is so sacred! Rose Schneiderman after the fire, 1911 I looked upon the heap of dead bodies and I remembered these girls were shirtwaist makers. Bill Shepherd, reporter after the fire A torch that lighted up the industrial scene. title: Tulsa Race Massacre
subtitle: The destruction of Tulsa’s Greenwood District, 1921
summary: Over about eighteen hours on May 31 and June 1, 1921, white mobs attacked and burned the Greenwood District, the center of Black life in Tulsa, Oklahoma. More than a thousand homes and businesses were destroyed, and credible estimates of the dead range from fifty to three hundred. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History calls it the single worst incident of racial violence in American history. No white person was ever imprisoned, and the massacre was long treated as an unspoken subject.
thumbAlt: Ruins of Tulsa’s Greenwood District after the 1921 massacre
aliases: Tulsa Race Riot Greenwood Black Wall Street
themeText: African American history Civil rights and citizenship Cities and urban life
text: Greenwood District, Tulsa, Oklahoma Dates May 31 – June 1, 1921 Deaths Credible estimates range from 50 to 300 Destruction More than 1,000 homes and businesses Prosecutions No whites were ever sent to prison State commission Formed in 1997; recommended reparations to survivors By 1921 Tulsa was a booming city of more than 100,000 people. Most of its roughly 10,000 Black residents lived in Greenwood, a thriving neighborhood with two newspapers, several churches, a library branch, and scores of Black-owned businesses. It was also a time of intense racial tension, marked by the rapid growth of the second Ku Klux Klan and by Black Americans’ determined resistance to lynching. Tulsa itself had seen a white mob lynch a white teenager taken from the county jail in August 1920 while police did little to stop it. On May 30, 1921, an encounter in a downtown elevator between Dick Rowland, a young Black shoe shiner, and Sarah Page, a white elevator operator, set events in motion; the most common explanation is that he stepped on her foot and she screamed. The next day the Tulsa Tribune reported that Rowland, who had been arrested, had attempted to assault Page, and eyewitnesses recalled an editorial calling for a lynching. By evening hundreds of whites had gathered at the county courthouse demanding Rowland. Armed Black men, many of them World War I veterans, twice went to the courthouse to help protect him and were turned away by the sheriff. As the second group was leaving, a white man tried to disarm a Black veteran, a shot was fired, and fighting broke out. Through the night, armed whites shot into Black neighborhoods and set fires along the edge of Greenwood’s business district. Police deputized members of the mob, while local National Guard units spent the night guarding a white neighborhood against a counterattack that never came. At dawn on June 1, thousands of armed whites invaded Greenwood, looting and burning homes and businesses. Black Tulsans fought to defend their community but were outnumbered and outgunned. By the time additional National Guard troops arrived that morning, most of Greenwood had been burned. The city was placed under martial law, and thousands of Black Tulsans were held under armed guard. Most of Tulsa’s Black population was left homeless, and thousands spent the following winter in tents. Rowland was exonerated, yet an all-white grand jury blamed Black Tulsans for the violence. Despite white efforts to force the community to relocate, residents began rebuilding Greenwood within days. For decades the massacre was rarely discussed, especially in Tulsa. In 1997 Oklahoma formed a state commission to investigate; its report recommended reparations to the remaining survivors. Researchers have found evidence supporting long-held accounts that victims were buried in unmarked graves. The Tulsa massacre showed how white violence could destroy Black prosperity, and the long silence that followed it shows how communities and nations choose what to remember.

title: Valley Forge
subtitle: The Continental Army’s winter encampment of 1777–78
summary: From December 19, 1777, to June 19, 1778, George Washington’s Continental Army camped at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, about twenty miles from British-occupied Philadelphia. More than 12,000 soldiers, together with about 400 women and children, built a city of log huts there. Shortages of food and clothing and outbreaks of disease killed about 2,000 people, though no battle was fought. Over the same months the Prussian officer Baron von Steuben drilled the troops into a disciplined army. The National Park Service treats Valley Forge as both a real event and a national myth, and the two are worth telling apart.
thumbAlt: William Trego’s 1883 painting The March to Valley Forge, showing soldiers marching in snow past Washington
aliases: Valley Forge encampment Winter at Valley Forge Baron von Steuben Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben Blue Book Joseph Plumb Martin
themeText: War and the military
text: Valley Forge, Pennsylvania Dates December 19, 1777 – June 19, 1778 Place About 20 miles from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Army More than 12,000 soldiers, plus about 400 women and children (NPS) Deaths Nearly 2,000 (NPS) or more than 2,000 (Battlefield Trust), mostly from disease Trainer Baron Friedrich von Steuben, arrived February 1778 Next battle Monmouth, New Jersey, June 1778 The year 1777 had gone badly for Washington’s own army. While the northern army won at Saratoga, Washington lost at Brandywine, Paoli and Germantown, and the British took Philadelphia, the American capital. For the winter he chose Valley Forge, a naturally defensible plateau a day’s march from the city. From there the army could keep watch on the British and protect the countryside, and bad roads and weather made major battles unlikely until spring. The loss of Philadelphia. Washington wanted to stay close to the British in the city. A defensible site. The plateau offered water and firewood and could be fortified. The need to rebuild. The army, still largely a collection of state militias, needed rest, supplies and training. The army marched in on December 19 and set to work. Officers organized the men into squads to build log huts on a 14-by-16-foot model, laid out in parallel lines; one officer wrote that from a distance the camp “had the appearance of a little city.” The soldiers also dug trenches, raised five earthen forts and bridged the Schuylkill River. The encampment held free and enslaved African Americans, Indigenous people, European immigrants, and speakers of several languages. Conditions were hard. Freezing, thawing, snow and rain alternated, and food, clothing and shoes ran short. The worst food crisis came in February, when the men went without meat for days. Private Joseph Plumb Martin wrote that they were “in a truly forlorn condition,—no clothing, no provisions, and as disheartened as need be.” Influenza, typhus, typhoid and smallpox spread through the crowded camp. Washington pressed Congress to reform the supply system and sent foraging parties under Nathanael Greene into the countryside. In February 1778 Baron von Steuben arrived and was made temporary inspector general. He wrote a standard drill, in French because he spoke no English, formed a model company to demonstrate it, and trained the men himself. The Marquis de Lafayette also shared the camp’s hardships. In May news came that France had allied with the United States. The British left Philadelphia for New York, and on June 19, 1778, Washington’s army marched out in pursuit. Later that month the army fought the British at Monmouth in New Jersey. The National Park Service writes that “the ordered ranks, martial appearance, revived spirit, and fighting skill” of the soldiers there showed how much had changed. Von Steuben turned his methods into the Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States, the “Blue Book,” approved by Congress in March 1779 and used by the army until 1814. The Park Service calls the reforms in supply, drill, hygiene and organization “the foundation of the modern United States Army.” Valley Forge also became a symbol. The NPS argues that the myth of a starving army saved by its patriotism “reveals something about our character,” but warns that it “often obscures the actual history.” No battle was fought at Valley Forge, yet it is one of the most famous places of the Revolution. Washington held the army together through a hard winter, and the army that left in June was better trained, better organized and allied with France. History and myth Sources disagree about how to picture the winter. The American Battlefield Trust describes “infamously miserable conditions” and low morale after the loss of Philadelphia, and repeats the image of soldiers “leaving bloodied footprints in the snow.” The National Park Service pushes back. It says the soldiers marching in were “not downtrodden — just exhausted and ill-supplied,” that the winter was “neither the coldest nor the snowiest” of the war, and that the picture of men in rags leaving bloody footprints is “not necessarily accurate.” It calls the experience “suffering as usual” for an army that always lacked supplies. The numbers Even the figures vary. The Park Service gives the men unfit for duty for lack of clothing at their worst, in early March, as 2,898; the Battlefield Trust says as many as 3,000. For deaths, the Park Service says nearly 2,000 and the Battlefield Trust more than 2,000. The same Park Service page counts the huts as “2,000-odd” in one paragraph and 1,500 in another. Von Steuben on the drill field Von Steuben came with a letter of introduction and a Russian wolfhound. Unable to speak English, he relied on an aide to swear at the soldiers for him: “My dear Duponceau, come and swear for me in English, these fellows won’t do what I bid them.” In about two months the army had mastered the basic drills. A dreary kind of place and uncomfortably provided. George Washington Describing the site of the encampment In a truly forlorn condition,—no clothing, no provisions, and as disheartened as need be. title: The Watergate Scandal
subtitle: The abuses of power that forced President Nixon to resign, 1972–1974
summary: On June 17, 1972, police arrested five men inside the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex as they tried to install bugging equipment. One worked for President Richard Nixon’s reelection committee. Nixon then joined a cover-up, which reporters, a Senate committee, special prosecutors, and the Supreme Court gradually exposed. His secret White House tapes proved he had obstructed justice. Facing impeachment, he resigned on August 9, 1974, the first and only president to do so, and a month later his successor pardoned him.
thumbAlt: Richard Nixon waving from the steps of a helicopter as he leaves the White House after resigning
aliases: Saturday Night Massacre smoking gun tape CREEP Woodward and Bernstein Nixon resignation Plumbers Ervin committee Ford pardon
themeText: The presidency Constitution and law Parties and elections
text: Washington, D.C. Break-in June 17, 1972; a security guard found taped doors and called police shortly before 2 a.m. Cover-up June 23, 1972: Nixon agreed to have the CIA tell the FBI to stop its inquiry (the “smoking gun” tape) Senate hearings Televised from May 17, 1973, under Senator Sam Ervin Saturday Night Massacre October 1973: Nixon fired special prosecutor Archibald Cox; Attorney General Richardson and his deputy resigned Supreme Court United States v. Nixon, July 24, 1974, 8–0 Resignation Announced at 9:01 p.m. on August 8; effective at noon on August 9, 1974 Pardon Gerald Ford’s Proclamation 4311, September 8, 1974 Nixon, elected in 1968, often felt that enemies were plotting against him. The Miller Center’s Watergate exhibit says he came to believe that Jews, intellectuals, and Ivy Leaguers, along with the press, were conspiring to destroy him. It describes his thinking as an “imitation of the enemy”: he persuaded himself that he was acting in self-defense and could therefore use any means. In 1971 the Pentagon Papers, a secret government history of the Vietnam War, leaked to the press. The Nixon administration tried unsuccessfully to stop the New York Times and the Washington Post from publishing them. Nixon feared the leak was part of a conspiracy and set up a secret White House investigations unit, the Special Investigations Unit, nicknamed “the Plumbers.” The Miller Center historian Ken Hughes writes that it was created without congressional authorization and carried out an illegal break-in without a warrant. Two of its members, the former CIA officer E. Howard Hunt and the former FBI agent G. Gordon Liddy, burglarized the office of the psychiatrist of Daniel Ellsberg, the man who leaked the papers. Nixon was also recorded ordering a break-in at the Brookings Institution to get files on Vietnam: “Get in and get those files. Blow the safe and get it.” The break-in never took place. Nixon had also set up a secret White House taping system. The first recordings were made on February 16, 1971, and on that day Nixon told his aides that the tapes were for his private file. The break-in itself began as a routine security call. Frank Wills, a 24-year-old guard at the Watergate Office Building, found doors taped open shortly after midnight and called the police just before 2 a.m. on June 17, 1972. The police arrested five men inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters. They found the men trying to install sophisticated bugging equipment. One of them, James McCord, was a former CIA employee working as a security aide for the Committee to Re-elect the President (known as CREEP). Liddy had overseen the burglary from a nearby hotel room, and the FBI quickly linked the burglars to Hunt. The sources are careful about who knew what. Yawp states that there is no direct evidence that Nixon ordered the break-in, and the Miller Center says it remains uncertain whether he knew of the plan in advance. What he did next is clear from the tapes. On June 20 he told his aide Charles Colson that “it’s going to be forgotten.” On June 23, the same day his chief of staff H. R. Haldeman proposed it, Nixon agreed to have the CIA tell the FBI to “stay the hell out of this,” falsely claiming that the investigation would expose a CIA operation. (One Miller Center essay prints the date of this tape as July 23, 1972. Its other pages, and the order of events they describe, give June 23, six days after the break-in.) Hughes writes that Nixon launched the cover-up to hide other crimes, including the Plumbers’ earlier break-in. This led to the axiom that the cover-up can be worse than the crime. The cover-up (1972). Administration officials paid hush money to the burglars and White House aides. On August 1, 1972, the Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein reported that a $25,000 check made out to the Nixon campaign had been deposited in a burglar’s bank account. Their informant, the FBI’s associate director Mark Felt, was known only as “Deep Throat”; his identity became public years later. The Post kept tying the burglars to the White House, but Nixon beat George McGovern in a landslide in November. The cover-up unravels (1973). In January 1973 seven men went to trial before Judge John Sirica: the five burglars along with Hunt and Liddy. All pleaded guilty or were convicted. On March 23, Sirica read in court a letter from McCord saying that defendants had been pressured to plead guilty and keep quiet and that perjury had been committed at the trial. Two days earlier White House counsel John Dean had warned Nixon of “a cancer, within, close to the presidency.” Dean soon decided to turn state’s evidence, and on April 30 Nixon announced the resignations of Dean, Haldeman, John Ehrlichman, and Attorney General Richard Kleindienst, while presenting himself as innocent. The Senate had created a select committee under Sam Ervin of North Carolina on February 7, and its televised hearings began on May 17. Attorney General Elliot Richardson appointed Archibald Cox as special prosecutor the next day. Public television broadcast the hearings gavel to gavel and rebroadcast them each evening. Dean told the committee about the cover-up. On July 16, the White House aide Alexander Butterfield disclosed that Nixon had a voice-activated taping system in the Oval Office. The fight over the tapes. Cox and the Senate committee asked for the tapes, and Nixon refused. He said the confidentiality of presidential conversations was at stake. In late October he fired Cox. Richardson and his deputy William Ruckelshaus resigned rather than carry out the order, which was called the “Saturday Night Massacre.” The public outcry forced Nixon to reverse course and turn the tapes over to Judge Sirica. A new special prosecutor, Leon Jaworski, subpoenaed 64 more, including the June 23 tape. In March 1974 a grand jury indicted Haldeman, Ehrlichman, Colson, John Mitchell, and three other Nixon aides. In April the White House instead released more than 1,250 pages of edited transcripts, which raised more questions than they answered. Among the recordings was an 18-minute portion that had been mysteriously erased. The end (1974). On July 24, 1974, the Supreme Court ruled 8–0 in United States v. Nixon that Nixon had to turn over the tapes. Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote that the president had no “absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances.” Three days later the House Judiciary Committee passed the first of three articles of impeachment, for obstruction of justice. The Miller Center says that with the release of the tapes “the bottom fell out” of Nixon’s support. Senator Barry Goldwater told him that at most eighteen senators would vote against conviction, too few to save him. On the evening of August 8, 1974, Nixon announced his resignation in a televised address from the Oval Office at 9:01 p.m. He said he no longer had a strong enough political base in Congress and added: “I have never been a quitter. To leave office before my term is completed is abhorrent to every instinct in my body.” He conceded that “if some of my judgments were wrong, and some were wrong, they were made in what I believed at the time to be the best interest of the Nation.” Secretary of State Henry Kissinger initialed his letter of resignation at 11:35 a.m. the next day. Vice President Gerald Ford took the oath and, in his inaugural remarks, declared, “Our long national nightmare is over.” The House never voted on impeachment. On September 8 Ford signed Proclamation 4311, giving Nixon “a full, free, and absolute pardon” for all offenses against the United States from January 20, 1969, through August 9, 1974. He said that “theirs is an American tragedy in which we all have played a part” and that he must “firmly shut and seal this book.” The pardon at once divided the country. A Gallup poll found 62 percent opposed and 31 percent in favor, and Ford’s approval rating fell from 71 to 50 percent. Ford pardoned only the man who gave the orders. Mitchell, Haldeman, and Ehrlichman were all convicted and sent to prison, and Hunt served 33 months. The White House tapes, the Miller Center writes, ended Nixon’s presidency by proving his involvement in the cover-up. They also fueled a generation’s skepticism about political leaders. The American Yawp adds that Watergate did more to unravel public trust than any other scandal of the period, and it helped Democrats win big gains in the 1974 midterm elections. Ford’s pardon damaged his own chances in 1976, which Jimmy Carter won on an image of honesty set against Nixon’s. The Miller Center cautions that many things worked against Ford, including unemployment of 7.8 percent and a strong primary challenge from Ronald Reagan. Opinion on the pardon changed over time. Gallup found Americans evenly split in 1982 (46 percent to 46 percent) and in favor by 54 to 39 percent in 1986. In 2001 Senator Edward Kennedy, who had opposed it, gave Ford the Profiles in Courage Award for making it possible to begin “the process of healing.” Some historians still disagree. Rick Perlstein argues that the pardon treated the presidency as “too big to fail” and set off “a cascade of élite wrongdoing.” Nixon spent his later years rehabilitating his reputation through the 1977 Frost interviews, his memoirs, and commentary on foreign policy. His arms control agreements and opening to China helped end the Cold War, but Watergate remains the most memorable part of his career. He died in 1994. At his funeral President Bill Clinton asked that Nixon be judged on “his entire life and career.” Watergate showed how far a president could go in abusing power and covering it up. It also showed that the press, Congress, and the courts could hold him to account, and that the law applied even to the president. I have never been a quitter. To leave office before my term is completed is abhorrent to every instinct in my body. Richard Nixon resignation address, August 8, 1974 Our long national nightmare is over. Gerald Ford inaugural remarks, August 1974 Theirs is an American tragedy in which we all have played a part. It could go on and on and on, or someone must write the end to it. title: Woodstock
subtitle: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation
summary: In August 1969 nearly half a million young people gathered on Yasgur’s farm near Bethel, New York, for a music festival billed as “An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music.” Rain, mud, and shortages turned the weekend into an improvised city, and, for many, a demonstration of the counterculture’s ideals of peace and cooperation. Coming weeks after the Moon landing and amid conflict over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics, Woodstock became shorthand for the youth culture of the 1960s.
thumbAlt: Festival-goers with a blanket tent in the crowd at Woodstock, 1969
aliases: Woodstock Music Festival Woodstock festival
themeText: Arts and popular culture Reform and protest
text: Bethel, New York When Three days in August 1969 Where Yasgur’s farm, Bethel, New York Crowd Nearly half a million people Billed as “An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music” In the 1960s protests across the country formed the backdrop for an American counterculture. Rebellion against the supposedly hidebound conservatism of the 1950s spread among the young, and the counterculture (with its music, its experiments with psychedelic drugs, and its search for personal fulfillment) increasingly reached the mainstream through popular culture and even advertising. The festival took place weeks after Americans first walked on the Moon, against the backdrop of a nation divided over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics. PBS describes a sense of an America in transition, a handoff between generations with very different values and ideals. Over three days, a crowd of nearly half a million (rain-soaked, often hungry, many of them on drugs) turned a few acres of farmland into a swarming, impromptu city. PBS’s American Experience calls what happened “nothing less than a miracle of teamwork,” a demonstration of the “peace and love” the festival had promised. To many participants and observers the weekend seemed to validate the counterculture’s promise. The festival quickly became a legend in its own right. The American Yawp calls 1969’s Woodstock concert “shorthand for the new youth culture and its mixture of politics, protest, and personal fulfillment.” The hippies’ rise was exaggerated and short-lived, and the Vietnam War and Richard Nixon shattered much of its idealism, but the counterculture’s liberated social norms and its embrace of personal fulfillment still shape much of American culture. Woodstock is remembered as the high point of the 1960s counterculture, a symbol of a generation that challenged the values of its parents. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YV1QKaNMQRI What Was the Original Woodstock Really Like Weird History 12:09 2026-10-23

title: The Wounded Knee Massacre
subtitle: The U.S. Army kills hundreds of Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, December 1890
summary: On December 29, 1890, soldiers of the U.S. 7th Cavalry surrounded a band of Lakota led by Spotted Elk (Big Foot) at Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge Reservation and attempted to disarm them. A shot was fired, and the soldiers opened fire with heavy weapons, killing between 150 and 300 Lakota men, women, and children. About two dozen soldiers also died, many probably from their own side’s fire. Wounded Knee marked the end of sustained armed Native resistance on the Plains.
location: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota
thumbAlt: The aftermath of the Wounded Knee massacre
aliases: Ghost Dance Big Foot Spotted Elk
themeText: Indigenous history War and the military Religion
text: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota Date December 29, 1890 Lakota dead Estimates range from about 150 to 300, many of them women and children Army dead About 25 Context Federal alarm over the Ghost Dance; the killing of Sitting Bull on December 15 By 1890 the Lakota had lost the Black Hills, their bison-based economy had collapsed, and they lived on shrinking reservations under government agents. A Paiute prophet, Wovoka, taught that if Native people lived justly and performed the Ghost Dance, their ancestors would return, the whites would vanish, and the buffalo would again roam the Plains. Members of many nations, including the Lakota, adopted the Ghost Dance. White settlers and federal officials feared the Ghost Dance meant an armed uprising, and troops were sent to the Lakota reservations. On December 15, 1890, Lakota police trying to arrest Sitting Bull at Standing Rock killed him. Fearing more violence, Spotted Elk led his band toward the Pine Ridge Agency to seek refuge. The 7th Cavalry intercepted them and escorted them to Wounded Knee Creek. On the morning of December 29, cavalrymen entered the camp to disarm the band. Tensions flared and a shot was fired, it is unclear by whom. The soldiers then fired their heavy weaponry indiscriminately into the camp. When the shooting stopped, between 150 and 300 Lakota were dead, nearly half of them women and children by one estimate. About two dozen soldiers were killed, by concealed Lakota weapons or by friendly fire. The dead were buried in a mass grave. The killings ended the Ghost Dance as a mass movement and effectively ended armed Native resistance on the Plains. Wounded Knee became a symbol of the destruction of Native nations by the United States. In 1973, activists of the American Indian Movement occupied the town of Wounded Knee for 71 days, drawing on the site’s meaning to protest treaty violations and conditions on the reservation. The massacre at Wounded Knee is remembered as the violent end of the Plains wars and as one of the gravest atrocities committed by U.S. forces against Native people. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VyF8SOSP2YM From the Trail of Tears to Wounded Knee: Ep 11 of Crash Course Native American History CrashCourse 11:07 2026-10-23

title: The Wright Brothers’ First Flight
subtitle: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, December 17, 1903: the first powered, controlled airplane flights
summary: On the morning of December 17, 1903, on the windswept dunes of North Carolina’s Outer Banks, the Wright brothers’ engine-powered Wright Flyer stayed aloft for twelve seconds, the first powered, controlled flight of a heavier-than-air machine carrying a person. That day Wilbur and Orville made four flights; the longest lasted 59 seconds. Two bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, with no formal engineering training, they succeeded because they treated flight as a scientific problem to be solved step by step.
location: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
thumbAlt: John T. Daniels’s photograph of the Wright Flyer’s first flight on December 17, 1903, with Wilbur Wright running alongside the wingtip
aliases: Wright brothers Wilbur Wright Orville Wright Kitty Hawk Wright Flyer first flight
themeText: Science and technology Everyday life
text: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina First flight Morning of December 17, 1903: twelve seconds aloft Longest flight that day 59 seconds, the fourth of four flights Engine A four-cylinder, 12-horsepower gasoline engine Witnesses Four men from the nearby Kill Devil Hills Lifesaving Station; one, John T. Daniels, took the first photographs of the flights Memorial Wright Brothers National Memorial, Kill Devil Hills; Congress set aside the site in 1927 The first flights opened the age of aviation, which within a few decades transformed war, travel, and commerce. The Wrights’ methodical, experimental approach became a model of American ingenuity. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. Tinkering with bicycles had given them a feel for all things mechanical, and when seasonal slumps hurt their sales they turned to a much bigger problem: building a flying machine. They spent years studying the principles of flight and building gliders and other prototypes. Other inventors had flown unpiloted models, Samuel P. Langley had catapulted one from a houseboat on the Potomac in 1896, but no one had carried a person into the air under power and control. The Wrights needed a place with strong, steady winds to give lift and soft sand for safe landings. After searching the East Coast, they chose the remote dunes near Kitty Hawk, on North Carolina’s Outer Banks. They first came in September 1900 to test gliders, returned in 1901 and 1902, and in 1903 brought a machine powered by a lightweight engine. After months of setbacks, the brothers were ready on December 17, 1903. Men from the Kill Devil Hills Lifesaving Station, about a mile away, had been helping them, ferrying visitors and moving equipment; four of the crewmen came to watch. That morning the Wright Flyer rose under its own power and flew for twelve seconds. One of the lifesavers, John T. Daniels, who had volunteered to work the camera, captured the first images of the Wrights’ success. Three more flights followed that day; the fourth and longest lasted 59 seconds. The Wrights went home to Dayton and kept testing, building more powerful models in the following years. Their achievement (study and scientific experiment, not luck, as the National Park Service stresses) solved the basic problems of powered, controlled flight. Wilbur died of typhoid fever in 1912; Orville died of a heart attack in 1948. In 1927 Congress set aside the site near Kill Devil Hill, and a tall white granite monument now stands on the hill “in commemoration of the conquest of the air”; the site is today the Wright Brothers National Memorial. The National Park Service calls their story the embodiment of “the American ideal of hard work overcoming all obstacles.” Sixty-six years after the twelve-second flight, Americans landed on the moon. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yjccw9o1Pwk The story of the Wright Brothers CBS Sunday Morning 7:40 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K499hKMabMM The Wright Brothers: First in Flight and Family Biographics 22:35 2026-10-23

title: Congress
subtitle: The legislative branch: the Senate and the House of Representatives
summary: Article I of the Constitution vests “All legislative Powers” in a Congress made up of a Senate and a House of Representatives. The House, elected every two years, gives each state seats according to its population; the Senate gives every state two members, whatever its size. This design, the Great Compromise of 1787, saved the Constitutional Convention from collapse. Congress makes the laws, controls taxing and spending, declares war, confirms the president’s nominees, and can impeach and remove officials. As the branch closest to the people, it has been the stage for many of the great debates of American history.
thumbAlt: The west front of the United States Capitol
aliases: U.S. Congress House of Representatives Senate Great Compromise Speaker of the House Power of the purse Seventeenth Amendment
themeText: Constitution and law Parties and elections Voting rights
text: U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C. Constitutional basis Article I House Members “chosen every second Year by the People,” seats by population; 65 seats in the First Congress Senate Two senators per state, six-year terms; tries impeachments, approves treaties and appointments Power of the purse All revenue bills must start in the House Election of senators By state legislatures until the Seventeenth Amendment, ratified April 8, 1913 First Congress 1789–1791 The Revolution was partly a quarrel about representation. Colonists who were used to their own elected assemblies rejected the British idea that they were “virtually represented” in Parliament, and rallied behind the cry “No taxation without representation!” Under the Articles of Confederation each state sent two to seven delegates to Congress but had only one vote. At the Constitutional Convention in 1787 the large and small states fought over representation for weeks, and the dispute nearly ended hopes of a national government. Benjamin Franklin compared the solution to a carpenter’s: when the planks of a table do not fit, “the artist takes a little from both, and makes a good joint.” The “good joint” was the Great Compromise: a House apportioned by population and a Senate with two seats for every state. A census every ten years would adjust the House seats. The convention also adopted the Three-Fifths Compromise, counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person, which gave the slave states extra seats. The Constitution set a ceiling of one representative for every thirty thousand people. The first House, which met in 1789, had 65 members. Senators were chosen by state legislatures; House members have always been elected directly by the people. Article I, Section 8 gives Congress power “To lay and collect Taxes,” to borrow money, to regulate commerce, “To declare War,” to raise armies and a navy, and “To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper” for carrying out its powers. Every bill must pass both houses and go to the president, and Congress can override a veto by two-thirds of each house. The purse. “All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House,” the chamber the people elect directly, and no money can be spent without an appropriation by law. The House Ways and Means Committee has set tariffs and taxes since the earliest Congresses; an Appropriations Committee was created in 1865. War. The framers would not let the president take the country to war alone. Madison and Elbridge Gerry changed the draft from Congress’s power to “make” war to the power to “declare” war, leaving the president room to repel a sudden attack. Impeachment and appointments. The House has “the sole Power of Impeachment” and the Senate tries impeachments; the Senate also approves treaties and confirms or rejects the president’s nominees. Parties and the Speaker. The House chose Frederick Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania as its first Speaker, partly so his state would have a high office alongside Washington’s Virginia, Adams’s Massachusetts and Jay’s New York. Henry Clay, elected Speaker in 1811 in his first House term, made the office nationally important. Political parties, which many founders had hoped to avoid, quickly organized Congress: by the 1790s the House divided into pro- and anti-administration blocs and then into Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. After the Civil War strong Speakers such as Thomas Reed and Joseph Cannon controlled the House, until a revolt in 1910 cut back the Speaker’s powers. Amending the system. After the Civil War, Congress led Reconstruction and proposed the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. The Fourteenth, ratified in 1868, ordered the census to count every person in full, ending the three-fifths rule. By the late 1800s, deadlocked state legislatures left Senate seats empty for months or years, and reformers attacked the Senate as a “millionaires’ club.” Congress proposed the Seventeenth Amendment, providing for the direct election of senators, in 1912, and it was ratified in 1913. The modern era. In the twentieth century Congress enacted the New Deal, the Civil Rights Act and the Great Society. After Vietnam it passed the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which, the American Yawp writes, “dramatically reduced the president’s ability to wage war without congressional consent.” Congress is the first branch of government in the Constitution and the institution through which Americans’ elected representatives make law, control spending and hold presidents to account. Its structure still reflects the bargains of 1787 between large states and small, and between free states and slave states. Why a declaration of war belongs to Congress In 1848, during the war with Mexico, a first-term congressman named Abraham Lincoln explained the framers’ thinking. “Kings had always been involving and impoverishing their people in wars,” he wrote, and the convention “resolved to so frame the Constitution that no one man should hold the power of bringing this oppression upon us.” The three-fifths rule The House historians call the Three-Fifths Compromise “notorious” and the Constitution’s “original sin.” Madison defended it in Federalist No. 54, admitting that the reasoning seemed “a little strained in some points.” The Fourteenth Amendment of 1868 ordered the census to count every person in full. A note on the first House The House historians write that in the First Congress each member “represented 30,000 citizens.” The Constitution itself sets thirty thousand as a ceiling, not a fixed size: the number of representatives “shall not exceed one for every thirty Thousand.” When a broad table is to be made, and the edges of planks do not fit the artist takes a little from both, and makes a good joint. Benjamin Franklin Constitutional Convention, 1787, on representation The approval of the House is the very breath in the nostrils of the Speaker. title: The Continental Congress
subtitle: The colonies’ revolutionary assembly, and the first national government
summary: The Continental Congress began as a meeting of colonial delegates coordinating protest against British policy and became, almost by accident, the government of a new nation. The First Continental Congress, which met in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774, issued a declaration of colonial rights and organized a boycott of British trade through the Continental Association. The Second Continental Congress, which met in May 1775 after fighting had begun, created the Continental Army under George Washington, voted for independence on July 2, 1776, adopted the Declaration of Independence, won French support, and wrote the Articles of Confederation.
location: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and other towns during the war
thumbAlt: Engraving of the First Continental Congress in session
aliases: First Continental Congress Second Continental Congress Continental Association Olive Branch Petition Lee Resolution Congress of the Confederation
themeText: Political thought War and the military Constitution and law
text: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and other towns during the war First meeting September 5, 1774, in Philadelphia; every colony but Georgia sent delegates Continental Association October 20, 1774: boycott of British imports, exports, and the slave trade Second Congress Met from May 1775 in the Pennsylvania State House Independence Lee Resolution passed 12–0 on July 2, 1776 (New York abstaining) France Treaty of Amity and Commerce, February 6, 1778 Succeeded by The Congress of the Confederation, March 1, 1781 After the Boston Tea Party, Parliament’s Coercive Acts of 1774 closed Boston’s port and put Massachusetts under royal control. Instead of isolating Massachusetts, they led Committees of Correspondence across the colonies to agree to send delegates to a Continental Congress “to coordinate an intercolonial response.” The First Continental Congress convened on September 5, 1774, with delegates from every colony but Georgia. Over six weeks it issued a declaration of rights that repeated arguments colonists had made since 1765: that they kept all the rights of Britons, including being taxed only by their own representatives and trial by jury. Its first great act was the Continental Association of October 20, 1774, a continental agreement not to import, consume, or export British goods and to “wholly discontinue the slave trade.” It recommended that every county, city, and town choose a committee to watch for violators and publish their names so they would be “universally condemned as the enemies of American liberty.” The American Yawp calls it “perhaps the most radical document of the period,” because it gave ordinary colonists unprecedented local political power. In wartime the Second Congress acted as a national government. It adopted the Massachusetts militia as a Continental Army, named George Washington commander in chief, and sent diplomats abroad, but without the power to tax it struggled to pay for the war. It met in the Assembly Room of the Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall, though British forces occupied Philadelphia in 1777. War and reconciliation. When the Second Continental Congress met in May 1775, war had already begun at Lexington and Concord. Radical delegates such as John Adams, Samuel Adams, and Richard Henry Lee wanted to support the Massachusetts militia, while moderates from the Middle Colonies feared that would mean war. The compromise was to create a Continental Army under Washington, explain the decision in a Declaration of the Causes and Necessity of Taking Up Arms, and at the same time send the king the Olive Branch Petition. The Declaration of Causes proclaimed: “Our cause is just. Our union is perfect.” King George III answered with a proclamation for suppressing rebellion. Independence. In May 1776 Congress urged the colonies to form new governments. On June 7 Richard Henry Lee moved that “these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, Free and Independent States.” On July 2 the resolution passed 12–0, with New York abstaining, and Congress then approved Jefferson’s Declaration of Independence. War government. In June 1776 Congress also appointed a committee to plan a confederation; it adopted the Articles of Confederation in November 1777. Benjamin Franklin, sent to Paris, won a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with France after the American victory at Saratoga, signed on February 6, 1778; the Yawp writes that it “effectively turned a colonial rebellion into a global war.” Into the Confederation. When Maryland ratified the Articles on March 1, 1781, the Continental Congress became the Congress of the Confederation, which governed until the Constitution took effect in 1789. The Continental Congress turned thirteen separate colonies into a single political community that could declare independence, raise an army, make foreign alliances, and win a war. Its weaknesses, especially its dependence on the states for money, also taught the lessons that shaped the Constitution. Our cause is just. Our union is perfect. title: The Freedmen’s Bureau
subtitle: The federal agency that aided formerly enslaved people, 1865–1872
summary: Officially the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, the Freedmen’s Bureau was created by Congress in March 1865 to help formerly enslaved people make the transition to freedom. Led by General Oliver O. Howard, it issued food and clothing, ran hospitals, supervised labor contracts, helped found schools, legalized marriages made in slavery, and helped families reunite. Underfunded and opposed by President Andrew Johnson and white Southerners, it did most of its work between 1865 and 1868 and closed in 1872.
location: Headquarters in Washington, D.C.; offices throughout the South
thumbAlt: Alfred Waud’s drawing “The Freedmen’s Bureau”
themeText: African American history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Everyday life
text: Headquarters in Washington, D.C.; offices throughout the South Created March 3, 1865, in the War Department Commissioner Maj. Gen. Oliver Otis Howard Main activity June 1865 – December 1868 Abolished 1872 Records National Archives Record Group 105, a key source for African American genealogy During the war, Union commanders and Treasury officials handled the needs of refugees and freedpeople and the management of abandoned and confiscated land. Congress consolidated those duties on March 3, 1865, creating the Bureau in the War Department. In May, President Andrew Johnson appointed Maj. Gen. Oliver Otis Howard as commissioner, with assistant commissioners in each Southern state. The Bureau’s mission was to provide relief and help freedpeople become self-sufficient. It issued rations and clothing, operated hospitals and refugee camps, supervised labor contracts between planters and freedpeople, handled complaints and apprenticeship disputes, assisted benevolent societies in founding schools, helped legalize marriages entered into during slavery, and provided transportation to people trying to reunite with family or relocate. Later it also helped Black veterans obtain back pay and bounties. Congress passed a new Freedmen’s Bureau bill in 1866 in the face of President Johnson’s opposition; Johnson had allowed Southern states to pass black codes that essentially maintained slavery under another name. Most of the Bureau’s work ended by December 1868, and it was abolished in 1872. Its records (letters, labor contracts, marriage registers, and school reports) are now among the richest sources on the lives of African Americans in the first years of freedom. The Freedmen’s Bureau was the federal government’s first large social welfare agency, and its schools helped launch Black education in the South, even as its limited power showed how little the nation was prepared to invest in freedom. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NGPAnLDzQYY Reconstruction: Crash Course Black American History #19 CrashCourse 13:58 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wkMy0PsUZIw Freedmen: The Civil War in Four Minutes American Battlefield Trust 4:55 2026-10-22

title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
subtitle: The League of the Iroquois, a union of nations governed by the Great Law of Peace
summary: The Haudenosaunee, “People of the Longhouse,” are a confederacy of Native nations whose homelands lie mostly in present-day New York. According to their tradition, a prophet called the Peacemaker, helped by Aionwatha (Hiawatha), persuaded five warring nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, to join a Great League of Peace; the Tuscarora joined later. Each nation runs its own affairs, while a Grand Council of fifty chiefs, chosen and held to account by Clan Mothers, decides matters that concern them all. Long a major power between the French and British empires, the Confederacy was split by the American Revolution but still exists today.
location: Present-day New York State and neighboring regions; today also Ontario and Quebec
thumbAlt: Six Nations chiefs at Brantford explaining their wampum belts in 1871
aliases: Iroquois Confederacy Six Nations Five Nations League of the Iroquois Great Law of Peace Grand Council Peacemaker Hiawatha
themeText: Indigenous history Political thought
text: Present-day New York State and neighboring regions; today also Ontario and Quebec Original nations Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca Sixth nation Tuscarora, who joined after the founding; they speak in Grand Council through the Cayuga Grand Council Fifty chiefs; meets on Onondaga territory, where the Onondaga are the Fire Keepers Chiefs Chosen, and if necessary removed, by Clan Mothers Name “Iroquois” was the French term; “League of Five Nations” the English one In the Revolution Cayuga, Mohawk, Onondaga, and Seneca mostly sided with Britain; many Oneida and Tuscarora with the Americans The Confederacy’s own account says it “has been in place since time immemorial,” and its exact founding date is unknown. In that account, the Peacemaker was sent by the Creator to spread the good mind. Traveling from community to community with Aionwatha, he persuaded the chiefs of each nation to join the Great League of Peace. He asked the Clan Mothers to present their chiefs and placed deer antlers on their heads as a sign of authority: nine Mohawk, nine Oneida, fourteen Onondaga, ten Cayuga, and eight Seneca. At Onondaga he planted the Great Tree of Peace, under which the council would meet; its Great White Roots stretched in four directions so that other nations could follow them to the peace. Beneath it the nations buried their weapons, and he bound five arrows together to show their united strength. He then took a string of wampum for each law of the Great Peace and explained its meaning. Each nation keeps its own council and handles its internal affairs, while the Grand Council deals with issues that affect the whole Confederacy. Within the metaphorical longhouse, the Mohawk, Seneca, and Onondaga sit as Elder Brothers and the Oneida and Cayuga as Younger Brothers. The Onondaga, the Fire Keepers, open the council. A question is debated first by the Mohawk and Seneca, then “thrown across the fire” to the Oneida and Cayuga, and returned for confirmation; if the two sides disagree, the Onondaga decide, and they may object only if a plan conflicts with the Great Law. Chiefs are men chosen by the Clan Mothers, whose titles pass down through the female line. A chief holds office for life as long as he follows the Great Law, but if he acts selfishly his Clan Mother warns him and may “remove his antlers,” taking away his authority. The Confederacy’s site counts forty-nine Clan Mothers across the five original nations. A core value, the Seventh Generation, asks leaders to weigh how decisions will affect descendants not yet born. Between empires. The Confederacy was a powerful league in western and upstate New York, and the National Archives writes that its influence in colonial America rested on “its unity and neutrality.” The Revolution. When the Revolution began, the Six Nations called the conflict “a family affair” and told American agents in 1775 that they would “take no part in the Quarrel.” Neutrality did not last. The Cayuga, Mohawk, Onondaga, and Seneca sided with the British, while many Oneida and Tuscarora supported the Americans, turning the Revolution, as the National Archives puts it, into “a civil war among the Six Nations.” Native peoples on every side suffered heavy losses of land during and after the war. After the Revolution. Haudenosaunee leaders remained important in the struggles over land that followed; the American Yawp names the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant and the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake among the figures of Native resistance and revival in the decades after independence. Today. The Confederacy continues to meet and to assert its sovereignty. It says it still enjoys the support of the Six Nations as their representative government, even though an elective system was established in 1924. It also describes itself as one of the oldest participatory democracies in the world, and writes that its constitution “is believed to be a model for the American Constitution.” How much the Great Law influenced the American framers is a claim made by the Confederacy and others; this entry reports it rather than treating it as settled. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is a living system of Native self-government that long predates the United States. Its diplomacy, wars, and divisions shaped the colonial and revolutionary history of the Northeast, and its ideas about balanced councils, accountable leaders, and duty to future generations still inform Haudenosaunee life today. Their hearts shall be full of peace and good will and their minds filled with a yearning for the welfare of the people of the Confederacy.
