title: Political Parties
subtitle: How Americans organized to win elections, from Federalists and Republicans to today’s two-party system
summary: Political parties appear nowhere in the Constitution, and many founders hoped to avoid them. George Washington warned against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party.” Yet parties formed within a few years and have organized American politics ever since. Hamilton’s Federalists and Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans gave way to Andrew Jackson’s Democrats and their Whig opponents. In the 1850s the antislavery Republican Party was born, and since then Democrats and Republicans have dominated a two-party system, even as their coalitions and ideas have changed dramatically.
thumbAlt: Chart of the evolution of American political parties
aliases: Two-party system Federalists Democratic-Republicans Whigs Democratic Party Republican Party First party system Second party system New Deal coalition
themeText: Parties and elections The presidency
text: In the Constitution? No; the founders made no provision for parties First parties Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans, 1790s First modern party Jackson’s Democrats, organized by Martin Van Buren, 1830s Whigs Formally organized against Jackson in 1834 Republican Party Formed in 1854 from the movement against the Kansas-Nebraska Act Great realignment The New Deal coalition of the 1930s, broken apart from the 1960s The founders distrusted parties. In Federalist No. 10 James Madison defined a faction as citizens “united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens,” and argued that a large republic would control “the mischiefs of faction.” In his Farewell Address of 1796 Washington warned Americans “in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally.” But divisions appeared inside Washington’s own administration. Alexander Hamilton wanted a strong national government that promoted commerce and industry; Thomas Jefferson wanted to restrict federal power and preserve an agricultural economy. From these quarrels grew the Federalists and the Republicans, or Democratic-Republicans. By the mid-1790s Jefferson was the informal leader of the nation’s first opposition party. The House historians record that the First and Second Congresses divided into pro- and anti-administration members, and that by the Fourth Congress the labels were Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. Parties have no formal powers under the Constitution, but they do much of the work of democracy: they nominate candidates, organize voters, run campaigns and organize Congress. They also adapted the constitutional machinery. The Twelfth Amendment, passed after the election of 1800, was designed, the American Yawp notes, “to accommodate the way political parties worked.” The first transfer of power. Jefferson’s victory in the election of 1800 brought the first peaceful transfer of power between parties. Republicans called it a “bloodless revolution,” partly because the Constitution “made no provision for political parties” and they thought they had rescued the country from an aristocratic takeover. During the War of 1812, New England Federalists met at the Hartford Convention in 1814 to curb the power of the Democratic-Republicans and even contemplated secession, a stance that, the Yawp notes, “posed the possibility of disaster” for the young country. Democrats and Whigs. Andrew Jackson’s supporters began calling themselves Democrats. Under Martin Van Buren they built “the first modern party in the United States,” with a centralized leadership and a consistent program at every level of government. Jackson’s enemies, mocking him as “King Andrew the First,” took the name Whigs from the patriots of the Revolution and formally organized in 1834; they held their first national convention in 1839 and won the presidency in 1840 with William Henry Harrison. The Republican Party. Slavery broke the Whigs apart. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 set off protests across the North, and the antislavery movements that began that year “coalesced with the formation of a new political party,” which its organizers named the Republican Party, after the founders. It nominated John C. Frémont for president in 1856 and elected Abraham Lincoln in 1860. Realignments. Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal built a Democratic coalition, in the Yawp’s words “the uneasy alliance of national liberals, urban laborers, farm workers, and southern whites.” The civil rights laws of the 1960s, passed under Democratic leadership, pushed white southerners toward the Republican Party, and inflation and slow wage growth eroded the coalition’s working-class base. Ronald Reagan won the presidency in 1980 with 51 percent of the popular vote. Parties are the machinery of American democracy: they turn public opinion into governing coalitions. Their realignments mark the great turning points in American political history, from 1800 to the Civil War, the New Deal and beyond. Party names that changed sides American party names can confuse readers. Jefferson’s party called itself Republican, and historians often call it Democratic-Republican; it is the ancestor of today’s Democratic Party, not the Republican Party. The modern Republican Party, founded in 1854, chose its name to recall the founders. The parties’ regional bases also shifted. Southern whites were a pillar of the Democratic New Deal coalition, but the civil rights laws of the 1960s, passed under Democratic leadership, pushed them toward the Republicans. Third parties The two-party system has always had challengers. In the 1850s the anti-immigrant Know-Nothing, or American, Party made impressive gains in 1854 and 1855 before the antislavery cause overtook it. Earlier, the Anti-Masons were among the groups that fed into the Whig coalition. Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. George Washington Farewell Address, 1796 There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects. title: The Presidency
subtitle: The executive branch, from Washington’s precedents to the modern office
summary: Article II of the Constitution vests “the executive Power” in a president elected for four years, who commands the armed forces and must “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” The framers argued for months over how to choose such an officer and how much power to give him. George Washington shaped the office by his example: he created the cabinet and stepped down after two terms. Crises later expanded it, above all under Abraham Lincoln and Franklin D. Roosevelt, until it became the most powerful position in American government, still checked by Congress, the courts and the voters.
thumbAlt: The north and south sides of the White House
aliases: President of the United States Executive branch Commander in chief Cabinet Twenty-second Amendment Electoral College
themeText: The presidency Constitution and law
text: The White House, Washington, D.C. Constitutional basis Article II Term Four years; limited to two elected terms by the Twenty-second Amendment, ratified February 27, 1951 Chosen by The Electoral College; the House decides if no one has a majority Powers Commander in chief; treaties with two-thirds of the Senate; appointments with Senate consent; the veto Removal Impeachment by the House and conviction by the Senate for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors” First president George Washington, inaugurated April 30, 1789 Under the Articles of Confederation there was no national executive at all. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 the delegates struggled to design one. They considered choosing the president by Congress, by the people, by the state governors, by electors, and even by lottery. Late in the convention they settled on electors chosen in each state, a compromise that, according to the House historians, “preserved states’ rights, increased the independence of the executive branch, and avoided popular election.” Defending the plan in Federalist No. 70, Alexander Hamilton argued that “Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government,” and that its ingredients were “first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.” The Miller Center adds that the delegates could create such an office partly because everyone expected Washington to fill it: Americans “knew they could trust him to wield immense power because he had already done so once.” Article II makes the president “Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy” and gives the power, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,” to make treaties, “provided two thirds of the Senators present concur,” and to appoint ambassadors, judges and other officers. The president may veto bills, which Congress can override by a two-thirds vote of each house, and can be removed through impeachment by the House and conviction by the Senate. The president is supported by the vice president and the cabinet, whose members require Senate approval. Washington’s precedents. “I walk on untrodden ground,” Washington wrote. “There is scarcely any part of my conduct which may not hereafter be drawn into precedent.” He set those precedents deliberately. Every president since has worked with a cabinet, and every one until Franklin Roosevelt followed his example of retiring after two terms. The first contested elections. The original rules had electors cast two undifferentiated votes. In 1796 this made the rivals John Adams and Thomas Jefferson president and vice president; in 1800 Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr tied, and the House needed six days and 36 ballots to choose Jefferson. The crisis led to the Twelfth Amendment. Lincoln’s war powers. The Miller Center calls Lincoln “the most activist President in history.” After Fort Sumter he called out the militias, expanded the army and navy, spent $2 million without an appropriation from Congress, blockaded Southern ports, suspended habeas corpus in several places, and issued the Emancipation Proclamation. Roosevelt’s modern presidency. Franklin D. Roosevelt served from March 1933 to April 1945, the longest tenure in American history. Through radio fireside chats he built a direct bond with the public; he became chief legislator as well as chief executive, and the Executive Reorganization bill of 1939 gave the White House a permanent professional staff. The Twenty-second Amendment, passed by Congress in 1947 and ratified in 1951, then limited presidents to two elected terms. Backlash and limits. After the Vietnam War, Congress passed the War Powers Resolution of 1973. During Watergate, Richard Nixon cited executive privilege to withhold his tape recordings; the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment in July 1974, and Nixon resigned before the full House could vote, the only president ever to do so. The presidency has become the center of American government and politics, embodying the nation at home and abroad. Its history is a long tension between Hamilton’s “energy in the executive” and the founders’ fear of a king. Customs as well as laws The Miller Center stresses how much of the presidency rests on custom rather than law. Washington retired on purpose, it writes, because he “recognized the structural importance of leaving office willingly”: Americans needed to learn how to elect, transfer power to and inaugurate a new president, and that had to start with his example. The two-term tradition he began lasted nearly 150 years before Roosevelt broke it and the Twenty-second Amendment wrote it into the Constitution. Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government. Alexander Hamilton (as Publius) The Federalist No. 70, 1788 I walk on untrodden ground. There is scarcely any part of my conduct which may not hereafter be drawn into precedent. title: The Supreme Court
subtitle: The nation’s highest court and interpreter of the Constitution
summary: The Supreme Court is “the highest tribunal in the Nation for all cases and controversies arising under the Constitution or the laws of the United States.” The Constitution created it but said little about how it should work, so Congress and the justices themselves built the federal judiciary over time. It began as a weak body whose first justices complained of its “limited stature.” Beginning with Chief Justice John Marshall, it became a co-equal branch that can strike down laws as unconstitutional, and its rulings have shaped every era of American history, for better and for worse.
location: Washington, D.C. (first met in New York City)
thumbAlt: The U.S. Supreme Court Building at dusk
aliases: U.S. Supreme Court SCOTUS Judicial review Judiciary Act of 1789 Chief Justice Court-packing plan
themeText: Constitution and law Civil rights and citizenship
text: Washington, D.C. (first met in New York City) Created by Article III of the Constitution; organized by the Judiciary Act of 1789 First session February 1–2, 1790, in the Exchange Building, New York City Size Six justices originally; changed six times before settling at nine in 1869 Tenure Justices serve “during good Behaviour,” in practice for life Key power Judicial review, asserted in Marbury v. Madison (1803) Chief Justices Only 17 since 1790 Article III of the Constitution vests “the judicial Power of the United States” in “one supreme Court” and in such lower courts as Congress creates, and provides that judges hold office during good behavior. Beyond that, the Supreme Court’s own history notes, the Constitution “elaborated neither the exact powers and prerogatives of the Supreme Court nor the organization of the Judicial Branch as a whole.” Establishing a federal judiciary was a high priority. The first bill introduced in the Senate became the Judiciary Act of 1789, which divided the country into thirteen judicial districts and three circuits and created a Supreme Court of a Chief Justice and five associate justices. The Court first assembled in New York City on February 1, 1790, but Chief Justice John Jay had to postpone the meeting a day because some justices could not get there in time. For most of its first century the justices also had to “ride circuit,” holding court twice a year in each district, a burden they complained about along with the Court’s low prestige. Jay resigned in 1795 to become governor of New York and refused to return as chief justice in 1800. The Court hears a few cases directly, such as disputes between states, and many more on appeal on questions of federal law. Its most important power, judicial review, the authority to declare laws unconstitutional, is not written in the Constitution. In Marbury v. Madison (1803) Marshall ruled that the Court could decide whether an act of Congress violated the Constitution; after 1810 the Court extended judicial review to state laws. The Court’s power has limits. Justices are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate; Congress fixes the number of associate justices, currently eight, by statute; and constitutional amendments can override the Court’s interpretations. To protect its independence, judges serve during good behavior and their salaries cannot be reduced while in office. The Marshall Court. Shortly before leaving office, President John Adams made John Marshall of Virginia the fourth chief justice. Marshall served for more than thirty-four years, and his leadership, the Court’s own history says, “was central to the development of its prominent role in American government.” Besides Marbury, his Court upheld broad federal power in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). Not everyone accepted the Court’s authority: Jefferson complained that judicial review “would make the Judiciary a despotic branch,” and Andrew Jackson declared in 1832 that “the opinion of the judges has no more authority over Congress than the opinion of Congress has over the judges.” Slavery and segregation. In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), which the National Archives calls “one of the most notorious decisions ever issued,” the Court held that enslaved people were not citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. After Reconstruction the Court struck down the Civil Rights Act of 1875 in 1883, and in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) it upheld a Louisiana law requiring “equal but separate” railway cars. The New Deal. In the 1930s the Court struck down much of Franklin Roosevelt’s program. In 1937 Roosevelt proposed adding a new justice for every sitting justice over seventy. The “court-packing scheme” failed in Congress, but, the American Yawp writes, “the chastened Court thereafter upheld social security and other pieces of New Deal legislation.” Civil rights. On May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren delivered the unanimous ruling in Brown v. Board of Education, holding that state-sanctioned school segregation violated the Fourteenth Amendment and overturning Plessy’s “separate but equal” rule. The Supreme Court is where Americans have brought their deepest disputes about rights and power, from slavery and segregation to the limits of government, and its interpretations of the Constitution have shaped every era of American history. Continuity and change The number of justices changed six times before settling at nine in 1869. Since 1790 there have been only seventeen chief justices and 104 associate justices, who have served an average of sixteen years. On average a new justice joins the Court almost every two years. George Washington appointed the six original justices and four more; Franklin Roosevelt came close to that record with eight appointments and the elevation of Harlan Fiske Stone to chief justice. Equal Justice Under Law The words “Equal Justice Under Law” are carved above the main entrance of the Supreme Court Building. The Court describes them as expressing its “ultimate responsibility.” Equal Justice Under Law. Inscription Above the entrance to the Supreme Court Building The opinion of the judges has no more authority over Congress than the opinion of Congress has over the judges. title: United Nations
subtitle: The international organization founded in 1945 to keep the peace
summary: The United Nations was founded in 1945 by the victorious Allies of World War II to prevent future wars through collective security and international cooperation. Unlike the League of Nations after World War I, it had strong American backing: the Senate approved the UN Charter 89 to 2. The United States is one of five permanent members of the Security Council, each holding a veto. The UN has been a central, and often contested, arena of American foreign policy ever since.
thumbAlt: The United Nations General Assembly hall
aliases: UN UN Charter Security Council General Assembly Universal Declaration of Human Rights
themeText: Foreign policy and diplomacy War and the military The Cold War The presidency
text: Charter completed in San Francisco, 1945 Founded October 24, 1945, after 29 nations ratified the Charter Charter conference San Francisco, April–June 1945, 50 nations U.S. Senate vote 89–2, July 28, 1945 Security Council Five permanent members with vetoes (the U.S., Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and France) plus elected members Human rights Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted December 10, 1948 On January 1, 1942, 26 nations at war with the Axis signed the Declaration of the United Nations in Washington, endorsing the Atlantic Charter and pledging not to make a separate peace. Planning continued at Allied conferences: at Tehran in 1943, Roosevelt proposed an organization in which the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and China would enforce peace as “four policemen.” At Dumbarton Oaks in Washington in 1944, the four powers drafted a charter, and at Yalta in 1945 Roosevelt and Stalin settled the Security Council voting rules. Determined to avoid Woodrow Wilson’s failure with the League of Nations, the Roosevelt administration cultivated bipartisan support; in 1943 the Republican Party endorsed participation, and both houses of Congress overwhelmingly agreed. The Charter created a General Assembly of all member states; a Security Council with five permanent members, each holding a veto, and elected non-permanent members; an Economic and Social Council; an International Court of Justice; a Trusteeship Council to oversee certain colonial territories; and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General. The organization was built on the principle of collective security. Representatives of 50 nations completed the Charter in San Francisco in the spring of 1945, and the UN came into existence on October 24. Eleanor Roosevelt, appointed to the U.S. delegation by President Truman, chaired the Human Rights Commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948. In 1950 the UN called on member states to give South Korea military assistance against the North Korean invasion, and a U.S.-led UN force fought the Korean War. The Soviet Union’s permanent seat and veto made the UN an arena of Cold War rivalry. The United Nations embodied the American commitment, after two world wars, to lead a rules-based international order rather than retreat from the world. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FnQESSTouNU The United Nations Is Created | Flashback | History HISTORY 3:48 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WF6g23ydyuU Why Does the United Nations Exist? title: Abolitionism
subtitle: The movement to end slavery in the United States
summary: Abolitionism was the movement to end slavery in the United States. Early antislavery reformers, many of them Quakers, worked for gradual emancipation and an end to the slave trade. In the 1830s a new generation, led by Black activists and white evangelicals such as William Lloyd Garrison, demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation and equal rights for Black Americans. A small and often hated minority, abolitionists used newspapers, lectures, petitions, and the Underground Railroad to make slavery the central moral question of American politics. Their cause triumphed only through the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment.
thumbAlt: Frontispiece of the abolitionist book A Tribute for the Negro
aliases: abolitionists The Liberator William Lloyd Garrison Underground Railroad American Anti-Slavery Society immediatism moral suasion Liberty Party gag rule
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Reform and protest African American history Religion Women's history
text: Early organizations Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery; Benjamin Franklin, its president, petitioned the First Congress in 1790 Turn to immediatism 1831: William Lloyd Garrison’s The Liberator demands immediate emancipation National society American Anti-Slavery Society, founded 1833; about 2,000 chapters and nearly 200,000 members by 1840 Key figures Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth, David Walker, Angelina and Sarah Grimké, Lucretia Mott, Wendell Phillips Achieved Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress January 1865 and ratified that December Early antislavery reformers sought gradual emancipation and an end to the slave trade. Many white reformers also supported “colonization,” the plan to send free Black Americans to Africa. Most Black Americans rejected colonization, insisting that America, not Africa, was their only homeland. From the 1830s the movement’s radical wing, following the lead of Black activists, demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation, political and social equality, and citizenship for Black Americans. The American Anti-Slavery Society rested its cause “upon the Declaration of our Independence, and upon the truths of Divine Revelation,” tying abolition to both national and Christian redemption. Petitions and early societies. Quakers questioned slavery as early as the late seventeenth century and worked with British reformers against the slave trade. In February 1790, Benjamin Franklin, as president of the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery, signed a petition asking the First Congress to “devise means for removing the Inconsistency from the Character of the American People.” Congress tabled it, citing the Constitution’s protection of the slave trade until 1808. After the Revolution most Northern states adopted gradual emancipation laws. Immediatism. The Second Great Awakening convinced many evangelical Protestants that slavery was the most God-defying of sins. Black writers led the way. In his 1829 Appeal to the Colored Citizens of the World, David Walker exposed the hypocrisy of American claims to freedom and Christianity, attacked colonization, and warned that God’s justice would bring violence on the slaveholding nation. Walker and James Forten convinced William Lloyd Garrison, who had supported colonization and gradual abolition, that colonization was racist. In 1831 Garrison launched The Liberator in Boston, declaring in its opening editorial: “I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD.” He published it every week for thirty-five years. In 1833 reformers from ten states founded the American Anti-Slavery Society, which had about 2,000 chapters and nearly 200,000 members by 1840. Its strategy was “moral suasion”: convincing enslavers through appeals to conscience to free the people they held. Words and images. Using new steam presses, abolitionists flooded the free states with pamphlets and newspapers and spoke from lecture platforms across the North. In 1835 they mailed antislavery literature to Southern enslavers, and in 1836 they sent thousands of petitions to Congress. Slave narratives exposed the cruelty of bondage. Frederick Douglass’s 1845 Narrative was reprinted in nine editions and translated into several languages, and his tour of Britain won support across the Atlantic. Women in the movement. In the 1830s women formed antislavery societies in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, raised funds, and used their right to petition. The Grimké sisters, Angelina and Sarah, daughters of a South Carolina slaveholding family, lectured to mixed audiences of men and women. When they were attacked for speaking in public, they began to argue for women’s rights as well. When the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London refused in 1840 to seat women delegates, Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton resolved to fight for women’s rights, a resolve that led to the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848. Politics. In 1839 abolitionists split. Garrison and his followers held that the Constitution was a proslavery document and refused to join party politics. Others, arguing that the Constitution could be used against slavery, founded the Liberty Party under James G. Birney. Douglass, once Garrison’s ally, broke with him in 1851 and supported political action. Their work helped prepare the ground for the antislavery Republican Party of the 1850s. Resistance and escape. In the 1840s and 1850s abolitionists increasingly helped freedom seekers escape through networks known as the Underground Railroad, to the North, Canada, Mexico, and beyond, a form of civil disobedience by people of all races. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, armed crowds in Northern cities tried to rescue people seized under the law. A few, like John Brown, turned to violence; his raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859 convinced many Americans that slavery was pushing the nation to the brink. Abolitionists were a small minority, detested by most white Americans in the North as well as the South. Critics attacked them as fanatics who would tear the Union apart, and many were outraged that women spoke in public and that Black and white activists worked together. Northern mobs smashed abolitionist printing presses and killed the antislavery editor Elijah Lovejoy. In 1838 a mob burned the newly built Pennsylvania Hall, where the Anti-Slavery Convention of American Women was meeting. Southern states, blaming abolitionists for Nat Turner’s rebellion of 1831, purged antislavery voices from the region. In Congress, Whigs and Democrats joined in 1836 to pass the “gag rule,” which blocked all discussion of antislavery petitions in the House. Even within the movement, conflict was bitter. In 1840, when Abby Kelley was elected to the American Anti-Slavery Society’s business committee, opponents of women’s leadership left to form a rival society. Abolitionists made slavery impossible to ignore. Their example of Black and white men and women working together offered, the American Yawp writes, “a powerful, if imperfect, model of interracial coexistence.” Although immediatists remained a minority, they prepared the ground for the antislavery Republican Party, and it is hard to imagine Abraham Lincoln’s election in 1860 without them, both as allies and as radicals against whom he could appear moderate. The movement trained a generation of women activists and gave birth to the women’s rights movement. During the Civil War, the Women’s Loyal National League, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, gathered one of the largest petition drives in American history for an amendment abolishing slavery; Senator Charles Sumner presented its first 100,000 signatures in February 1864. Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment in January 1865, and it was ratified in December. Garrison published the last issue of The Liberator on December 29, 1865. Abolitionists disagreed about tactics, whether moral persuasion, politics, or force; about whether the Constitution was proslavery; and about women’s place in the movement. Many white abolitionists also shared the racial prejudices of their time. Even Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin, which did so much for the cause, reinforced racist stereotypes. Most important, the end of slavery did not bring the equality many abolitionists had demanded. Garrison himself kept campaigning; in 1873 he declared, “I am still for immediate, unconditional, everlasting emancipation from oppression of everyone on the face of the earth.” That struggle continued through Reconstruction and long after. Abolitionists turned slavery from an accepted institution into the great moral issue of American politics. Their agitation helped bring about the political crisis of the 1850s, and the Civil War that followed ended slavery. I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD. William Lloyd Garrison opening editorial of The Liberator, 1831 I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. title: Red Power and the American Indian Movement
subtitle: Native activism for sovereignty and self-determination, 1960s–1970s
summary: Inspired by the civil rights movement, young Native Americans in the 1960s and 1970s launched an intertribal movement known as Red Power to protest discrimination and assert tribal sovereignty. Activists held “fish-ins” to defend treaty fishing rights, occupied Alcatraz Island for nineteen months in 1969–1971, and, led by the American Indian Movement (AIM), occupied the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for months in 1973. The movement helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes and win a policy of Indian self-determination.
location: Nationwide, including Alcatraz Island, Washington, D.C., the Pacific Northwest, and Wounded Knee, South Dakota
thumbAlt: Flag of Indians of All Tribes, the group that occupied Alcatraz
aliases: Red Power AIM Indians of All Tribes fish-ins Wounded Knee occupation
themeText: Indigenous history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest
text: Nationwide, including Alcatraz Island, Washington, D.C., the Pacific Northwest, and Wounded Knee, South Dakota National Indian Youth Council Founded 1961 by Native university students Fish-ins 1964, Pacific Northwest Alcatraz Occupied November 20, 1969 – June 11, 1971, by Indians of All Tribes Wounded Knee Occupied by hundreds of activists for several months in 1973 Policy change Termination ended; self-determination became federal policy Activists demanded respect for treaty rights, tribal sovereignty and self-determination, return of land, and an end to discrimination and to federal efforts to dissolve tribes. In 1961 Native university students founded the National Indian Youth Council, whose militant rhetoric and direct action began the Red Power movement. In 1964 it held “fish-ins” in the Pacific Northwest, casting nets in defiance of state laws to defend tribal fishing rights. On November 20, 1969, Indians of All Tribes, led at first by Mohawk student Richard Oakes, began occupying Alcatraz, demanding the island for an Indian university and cultural center. Activists also occupied Bureau of Indian Affairs offices in Washington. In 1973 the American Indian Movement and hundreds of others occupied Wounded Knee, site of the 1890 massacre. Federal authorities rejected the occupiers’ demands. At Alcatraz the government cut off electricity and water and eventually removed the last occupiers on June 10–11, 1971. According to the National Park Service, the Alcatraz occupation helped bring about the end of the federal termination policy and its replacement with a policy of Indian self-determination. During the occupation, President Nixon returned Blue Lake and 48,000 acres to Taos Pueblo, and the occupation of BIA offices led to more Native Americans being hired in the agency. Poverty, land claims, and conflicts over sovereignty and natural resources on reservations continued long after the 1970s. Red Power made Native Americans’ demands for sovereignty visible to the nation and reshaped federal Indian policy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1O2LWteKuRc The Native Civil Rights Movement: Ep 15 of Crash Course Native American History CrashCourse 10:55 2026-10-22

title: Anti-Federalists
subtitle: The opponents of the Constitution whose objections produced the Bill of Rights
summary: The Anti-Federalists were the Americans who opposed ratifying the Constitution in 1787 and 1788. They feared that the new national government would swallow the states and threaten liberty, and they rallied above all around its lack of a bill of rights. Leaders included George Mason and Patrick Henry of Virginia, and essayists such as “Brutus” in New York. They lost the fight over ratification, but their pressure led several states to ratify only with proposed amendments, and those proposals became the Bill of Rights in 1791.
thumbAlt: 1788 newspaper cartoon showing the states as pillars, raised one by one as they ratified the Constitution
aliases: Antifederalists Brutus Patrick Henry George Mason Ratification debate Massachusetts Compromise
themeText: Constitution and law Political thought
text: Active 1787–1788, during the ratification debate Leaders George Mason, Patrick Henry; essayists such as “Brutus” Main demand A bill of rights, and limits on national power Closest votes Virginia 89–79; New York by three votes; Rhode Island by two Lasting result The Bill of Rights, ratified December 15, 1791 Fate of the name “Essentially meaningless” by 1793 (American Yawp) Anti-Federalists did not agree on everything, but most shared a few aims. They wanted power kept close to the people in the states, and they distrusted a strong central government far away. Most of all, they wanted a written guarantee of individual rights. The Philadelphia convention had voted down George Mason’s proposal for a national bill of rights, and the American Yawp writes that this omission “became a rallying point for opponents of the document.” Opponents argued their case in pamphlets and newspapers, in the same public debate that produced the Federalist Papers. Mason, one of three delegates present on the convention’s last day who refused to sign the Constitution, wrote a pamphlet that the National Archives says persuaded many Americans to oppose it. In New York a writer calling himself “Brutus” published essays beginning on October 18, 1787. In the state ratifying conventions Anti-Federalists either voted no or demanded amendments as the price of approval. The Federalists, led by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, answered in the Federalist Papers. They argued that a bill of rights was “not only redundant but dangerous,” in the Yawp’s summary, because listing some rights might seem to limit others; the government, they said, could only use the powers the Constitution gave it. At the Virginia convention in June 1788 Madison, Edmund Randolph and John Marshall faced Patrick Henry and George Mason. Amendments attached to ratification. In Massachusetts, where the Anti-Federalists at first probably had the upper hand, the convention narrowly ratified the Constitution in early 1788 but proposed amendments for the first Congress to consider. Other states followed this pattern. The National Archives calls this the Massachusetts Compromise and says it “paved the way for the passage of the Bill of Rights.” The Bill of Rights. Madison, once the most vocal opponent of a bill of rights, introduced amendments in the First Congress on June 8, 1789. Ten of them were ratified by December 15, 1791. The Yawp notes that he had won election to the House only by promising his Virginia voters such a list. The Anti-Federalists’ deeper fear, that the national government would keep growing at the states’ expense, was not settled by the Bill of Rights. Brutus warned that the “necessary and proper” clause gave Congress a power so broad that it might be used “entirely to abolish the state legislatures.” Arguments about the reach of that clause and about the balance between the states and the nation continued long after the Anti-Federalists themselves had disappeared as a group. The Anti-Federalists lost the ratification fight but shaped the result. Their insistence on written protections for liberty gave the Constitution its Bill of Rights, and their warnings about centralized power began a debate over federalism that has never ended. Brutus No. 1 The first Brutus essay, dated October 18, 1787, asked whether the thirteen states should be reduced to “one great republic.” Its author argued that the proposed government, though not “a perfect and entire consolidation” of the states, came so close that “it must, if executed, certainly and infallibly terminate in it.” The author signed only with the pen name Brutus. The close votes After nearly a month of debate Virginia, the most populous state, ratified 89 to 79. Congress announced on July 2, 1788, that enough states had ratified for the Constitution to take effect, but New York ratified by just three votes, and Rhode Island by two, a full year after Washington took office. Accepting defeat Once Washington was elected, his authority helped settle the matter. By 1793, the Yawp writes, “the term Anti-Federalist would be essentially meaningless,” though many former opponents went on to join the Democratic-Republicans who challenged Hamilton’s policies. Although the government reported by the convention does not go to a perfect and entire consolidation, yet it approaches so near to it, that it must, if executed, certainly and infallibly terminate in it. title: The Civil Rights Movement
subtitle: The mass struggle against segregation and disfranchisement, 1950s–1960s
summary: The civil rights movement was a mass campaign by Black Americans and their allies to end legal segregation and win the right to vote in the South. Building on decades of NAACP lawsuits, it won the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision in 1954 and then turned to nonviolent direct action: the Montgomery bus boycott, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the Birmingham campaign, the March on Washington, Freedom Summer, and the Selma marches. Its victories, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, dismantled Jim Crow in law and transformed American democracy.
thumbAlt: Civil rights demonstrators at a segregated public beach in Fort Lauderdale
aliases: sit-ins Freedom Rides Freedom Summer SNCC SCLC CORE NAACP Black Power nonviolence Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party Birmingham campaign
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Voting rights Reform and protest Constitution and law
text: Landmark ruling Brown v. Board of Education, May 17, 1954, decided 9–0 Key organizations NAACP (1909), CORE (1942), SCLC (1957), SNCC (1960), and local groups such as Montgomery’s Women’s Political Council Largest protest More than 200,000 people at the March on Washington, August 28, 1963 Key laws Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Senate vote 73–27); Voting Rights Act of 1965 Leaders Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, Ella Baker, John Lewis, Diane Nash, Fannie Lou Hamer, Bayard Rustin, Thurgood Marshall, and many local organizers Method Litigation, nonviolent direct action, boycotts, and voter registration The movement set out to destroy Jim Crow, the system of laws and customs that segregated Black Southerners in schools, buses, restaurants, parks, and jobs and kept most of them from voting. After World War II, the “Double V” campaign for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home, and the postwar boom, raised expectations that persistent segregation then disappointed. The demands of the 1963 March on Washington summed up the movement’s program: a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregated public accommodations, “protection of the right to vote,” “desegregation of all public schools,” a federal jobs program, and a law “barring discrimination in all employment.” King described the ultimate end as “the creation of the beloved community,” “a society at peace with itself, a society that can live with its conscience”; by the end of his life he argued that full citizenship also required economic security. In the courts. Beginning in the early 1930s, NAACP lawyers including Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall chose cases on education, voting, and juries to wear away the legal foundations of segregation, first arguing that Southern states failed to provide even “equal” facilities and then, by the late 1940s, that separation itself was unconstitutional. Brown v. Board of Education combined five cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, Washington, D.C., and Kansas. In Clarendon County, South Carolina, the district spent $179 on each white student in 1950 and $43 on each Black student. On May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren announced a unanimous decision that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” But the Court’s 1955 order to desegregate “with all deliberate speed” was so vague that it left the work in the hands of segregation’s defenders. Montgomery. On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a member of the NAACP, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council, who had pressed the city about bus segregation since 1954, called a one-day boycott and printed tens of thousands of leaflets overnight. On December 5, 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black citizens stayed off the buses, and that day the new Montgomery Improvement Association chose a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., as its president. For thirteen months, Black residents walked or rode in a carpool of about 300 cars, while city officials indicted more than eighty leaders and segregationists bombed King’s and E. D. Nixon’s homes. The protest ended in victory on December 20, 1956, after the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation. Women such as Robinson, Johnnie Carr, and the “nameless cooks and maids who walked endless miles” sustained the boycott, and its success led King and other ministers to found the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) in 1957. Students take the lead. On February 1, 1960, four Black students from North Carolina A&T sat down at the whites-only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro and refused to leave. By the end of the month sit-ins had spread to more than thirty places in seven states, and by the end of April more than 50,000 students had taken part. In Nashville, James Lawson trained students such as John Lewis, Diane Nash, and Marion Barry in Gandhian nonviolence. That April, SCLC’s Ella Baker called the student leaders to a conference at Shaw University, where they founded the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). Baker urged them to stay independent and to build “group-centered leaders” rather than follow a single charismatic figure. In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) sent interracial Freedom Riders south to test a Supreme Court ruling against segregated bus terminals. At Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of their buses, and riders were beaten in Birmingham and Montgomery. When CORE halted the rides, Nash and the Nashville students insisted on continuing: “We can’t let them stop us with violence. If we do, the movement is dead.” Students from across the country then crowded into the jails of Jackson, Mississippi, and on November 1, 1961, a federal ban on segregation in interstate bus travel took effect. Birmingham and Washington. In April 1963 SCLC joined Fred Shuttlesworth’s local movement in Birmingham with sit-ins, marches, and a boycott of downtown stores. Arrested on Good Friday, King wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in reply to eight white clergymen who had called the protests “unwise and untimely”: “For years now, I have heard the word ‘Wait!’ … This ‘Wait’ has almost always meant ‘Never.’” In May, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren marched, and the city’s public safety commissioner, Eugene “Bull” Connor, turned fire hoses and police dogs on them. The images caused international outrage and forced a settlement that removed “Whites Only” signs and began the desegregation of lunch counters. President John F. Kennedy went on national television in June to call for a civil rights bill. On August 28, 1963, more than 200,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, organized by A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin, where King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech. Mississippi and Selma. In Mississippi, where violence made mass street protests nearly impossible, SNCC’s Bob Moses built a grassroots voter registration campaign. In the summer of 1964 about 1,000 volunteers, most of them white Northern college students, joined Freedom Summer. About 17,000 Black Mississippians tried to register that summer, but registrars accepted only 1,600 applications, and 41 Freedom Schools taught more than 3,000 young people. The movement’s Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party challenged the state’s all-white delegation at the Democratic National Convention, where Fannie Lou Hamer, a former sharecropper who had been fired for trying to register and savagely beaten in a Mississippi jail, testified on national television. In Selma, Alabama, where only two percent of Black residents were on the voting rolls, SNCC and SCLC launched a voting rights campaign in January 1965. On March 7, “Bloody Sunday,” state troopers clubbed and tear-gassed marchers led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Two weeks later, under federal protection, marchers walked the fifty-four miles to Montgomery, their numbers swelling to 25,000 by the final day. White Southerners fought the movement with defiance, mass arrests, economic reprisals, and terror. In August 1955, fourteen-year-old Emmett Till of Chicago was abducted and murdered in Mississippi for supposedly whistling at a white woman; an all-white jury acquitted his killers, who months later described the crime in Look magazine. His mother’s insistence on an open-casket funeral made his death national news. Desegregation met fierce resistance: in 1957 soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division had to escort nine Black students into Little Rock’s Central High School, and in 1962 two people died in rioting when James Meredith enrolled at the University of Mississippi. Alabama governor George Wallace promised “segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever” in 1963 and stood in the door of the University of Alabama to block its integration. The violence was relentless. The night after the Birmingham agreement, bombs exploded near King’s motel and at his brother’s home; on September 15, 1963, Ku Klux Klan members bombed Birmingham’s Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, killing four young girls. The civil rights leader Medgar Evers was assassinated at his home in June 1963. In June 1964 three civil rights workers, James Chaney, a Black Mississippian, and two white Northerners, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman, were murdered near Philadelphia, Mississippi, by Klan members and local law officers. In 1965 a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson during a march in Marion, Alabama; local white men attacked and fatally injured the Unitarian minister James Reeb in Selma; and Klansmen shot Viola Liuzzo, a volunteer from Michigan, after the march to Montgomery. The federal government was often a reluctant ally. The Kennedy administration intervened only after mobs had attacked the Freedom Riders, and President Lyndon B. Johnson, fearing the loss of white Southern votes, backed a compromise at the 1964 convention that offered the Mississippi Freedom Democrats just two at-large seats. “We didn’t come all this way for no two seats,” Hamer replied. The FBI later made SNCC a target of its COINTELPRO program against Black militancy. The movement destroyed legal segregation. The Civil Rights Act of 1964, which Kennedy proposed and Johnson pushed through after Kennedy’s assassination, outlawed segregation in hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other public places and banned discrimination in employment. Southern senators tried to talk it to death in a filibuster before the Senate passed it 73 to 27, and Johnson signed it on July 2, 1964. The Voting Rights Act, which Johnson introduced after Selma with the words “we shall overcome,” outlawed literacy tests, sent federal examiners to register voters, and required states with a history of discrimination to clear changes to their voting rules with Washington. Johnson signed it on August 6, 1965. By the end of 1965 a quarter of a million new Black voters had been registered, one-third of them by federal examiners. Enforcement of Brown came slowly but dramatically: in 1968, about 80 percent of Black schoolchildren in the South still attended schools that were 90 to 100 percent nonwhite, but by 1972 only 25 percent did, and Southern schools became by many measures the most integrated in the nation. The movement also changed how Americans protested. Its tactics, from the boycott and the sit-in to the mass march, and its moral language, rooted in Black churches, helped inspire new movements of Native Americans, Chicanos, and women in the 1960s. In King’s own summary, “Montgomery led to the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and 1960; Birmingham inspired the Civil Rights Act of 1964; and Selma produced the voting rights legislation of 1965.” The laws of 1964 and 1965 attacked segregation by law, but not the poverty, housing discrimination, and police brutality that shaped Black life in Northern cities as well as Southern ones. Federal housing policy had itself helped create segregated neighborhoods: from the 1930s, maps “redlined” Black neighborhoods as risky, and the Federal Housing Administration and the Veterans Administration refused to back mortgages there. Days after the Voting Rights Act was signed, rioting broke out in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, and riots followed in other cities every summer, most destructively in Newark and Detroit in 1967. The movement itself divided. After the 1964 convention, many SNCC activists lost faith in interracial cooperation and nonviolence. In June 1966 Stokely Carmichael, SNCC’s new chairman, began calling for “Black Power,” and SNCC and CORE soon excluded white members. Malcolm X, a Nation of Islam minister who was killed in 1965, had offered a more militant alternative to King’s approach. King, meanwhile, turned to poverty in the North and to opposition to the Vietnam War, and was planning a Poor People’s Campaign for jobs and income when he was assassinated on April 4, 1968. The Supreme Court in 2013 struck down a key provision of the Voting Rights Act requiring federal oversight of voting rules in nine states. The civil rights movement ended legal segregation in the United States, brought about the greatest change in federal protection of voting since Reconstruction, and showed how ordinary people using nonviolent mass action could change the law of a nation. We came to see that, in the long run, it is more honorable to walk in dignity than ride in humiliation. Martin Luther King Jr. on the Montgomery bus boycott, 1956 We can’t let them stop us with violence. If we do, the movement is dead. Diane Nash urging CORE’s James Farmer to let the Freedom Rides continue after the attacks in Alabama, May 1961 For years now, I have heard the word ‘Wait!’ … This ‘Wait’ has almost always meant ‘Never.’ Martin Luther King Jr. Letter from Birmingham Jail, April 1963 If the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America. Fannie Lou Hamer testifying before the credentials committee of the Democratic National Convention, August 1964 The movement made Martin rather than Martin making the movement. title: The Environmental Movement
subtitle: From Silent Spring to Earth Day and the EPA
summary: In the 1960s, growing alarm about pollution, pesticides, and the destruction of open space produced a mass environmental movement. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) warned of the dangers of pesticides to wildlife and people. The first Earth Day, April 22, 1970, was, in the words of the American Yawp, the largest demonstration in history. A burst of lawmaking followed: the National Environmental Policy Act, the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970, and new laws to protect air, water, and endangered species.
thumbAlt: The whole Earth photographed from space by the Apollo 17 crew
aliases: Silent Spring Earth Day EPA Clean Air Act National Environmental Policy Act
themeText: Land and environment Reform and protest Public health
text: Silent Spring Rachel Carson, 1962 Earth Day April 22, 1970 NEPA National Environmental Policy Act, signed 1970; required environmental impact statements EPA Created 1970; first administrator William Ruckelshaus confirmed December 2, 1970 Other laws Clean Air Act amendments (1970), and laws protecting water and endangered species Environmentalists sought clean air and water, controls on pesticides and toxic chemicals, protection of wilderness and wildlife, and government accountability for the environmental effects of its projects. The movement grew from Americans’ postwar enjoyment of the outdoors and from science-based warnings like Carson’s. Dramatic events, such as the Cuyahoga River near Cleveland bursting into flames, drew attention. Activists organized mass demonstrations such as Earth Day and lobbied for legislation at every level of government. Chemical companies attacked Silent Spring, suggesting it was the product of an emotional woman rather than a scientist. Industries resisted the cost of regulation; President Nixon, while creating the EPA, impounded billions of dollars Congress had authorized for the Clean Air Act and subjected environmental rules to cost-benefit analysis. President Nixon signed the National Environmental Policy Act in 1970, requiring environmental impact statements for federal projects, and created the Environmental Protection Agency. Amendments to the Clean Air Act required reductions in automobile emissions. Laws protecting water, endangered species, and natural areas followed. Debates over the economic costs of regulation, already visible in the Nixon years, have kept environmental policy contested. The environmental movement made protecting nature and public health a permanent responsibility of the federal government. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dMm0dXApxko The Environmental Protection Movement in the U.S. [APUSH Review] Heimler's History 7:01 2026-10-22

title: The Farm Workers Movement
subtitle: The Delano grape strike, the boycott, and the United Farm Workers
summary: In the 1960s, Mexican American and Filipino farm workers in California organized to win union recognition, decent wages, and safe conditions. Their Delano grape strike, begun in 1965, and a nationwide consumer boycott of table grapes led by Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, and Larry Itliong won the first major union contracts in California agriculture by 1970. The United Farm Workers became both a union and a civil rights movement.
location: California’s Central Valley and boycott centers nationwide
thumbAlt: Farm workers on strike in Delano, California, October 1965
aliases: United Farm Workers UFW Delano grape strike La Huelga grape boycott
themeText: Labor and work Latino history Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship
text: California’s Central Valley and boycott centers nationwide Founded National Farm Workers Association, 1962 (Chavez and Huerta); Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee (largely Filipino; leaders included Larry Itliong) Delano strike Began September 8, 1965 March to Sacramento March 17 – Easter 1966, nearly 340 miles Merger United Farm Workers Organizing Committee, AFL-CIO, August 22, 1966 Landmark law California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, 1975 Farm workers sought union recognition, higher wages (grape pickers averaged about 90 cents an hour in 1965), an end to child labor and dangerous conditions, protection from pesticides, and fair treatment. Chavez envisioned the union as both a labor organization and a civil rights movement for Chicano and Filipino workers. On September 8, 1965, Filipino workers of the AWOC, organized by Larry Itliong, struck nine farms near Delano. The NFWA voted to join on September 16. Strikers used roving pickets to persuade strikebreakers to leave the fields. Chavez called for a consumer boycott of non-union grapes, and volunteers organized boycott centers in cities across the country. In 1966 strikers marched nearly 340 miles to Sacramento; on Easter they announced that Schenley had signed a contract. Chavez fasted to draw attention to the cause. Growers used strikebreakers, and police sometimes harassed strikers. The Teamsters union offered growers a more conservative alternative, and the farm workers had to win union elections against them. By 1970 grape growers had signed contracts, and the UFW claimed 50,000 members, with a union hiring hall that ended favoritism by labor contractors, a health clinic and health plan, and higher wages. In 1975 California passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first U.S. law recognizing farm workers’ right to collective bargaining. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 excluded agricultural workers, leaving farm workers without the federal protections most other workers had. The farm workers’ struggle joined labor organizing to the civil rights movement and made Chicano and Filipino workers visible in national politics. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NmvbNp5GYdk The Art of Protest: The United Farm Workers and the Delano Grape Strike | BRIdge from the Past Bill of Rights Institute 10:58 2026-10-22

title: The First Great Awakening
subtitle: A wave of evangelical revivals across the colonies, 1730s–1770s
summary: The First Great Awakening was a surge of evangelical Protestant revival that swept the American colonies from the 1730s to the 1770s, part of a movement also stirring Britain and Germany. Fiery preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and the traveling English evangelist George Whitefield urged listeners to experience a heartfelt conversion. The revivals split churches, challenged the authority of established clergy, and gave many colonists, including women and African Americans, new religious voices.
thumbAlt: Illustration of a religious camp meeting
aliases: Jonathan Edwards George Whitefield New Lights
themeText: Religion Everyday life
text: Throughout British North America Began 1730s, among Presbyterians in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, led by the Tennent family Famous preachers Gilbert Tennent, Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield Best-known sermon Jonathan Edwards, “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” Divisions “New Lights” (supporters) vs. “Old Lights” (opponents) Revivalists sought to awaken what they saw as spiritually complacent congregations. They taught that sinners were totally dependent on God’s grace for salvation and that true religion was felt in the heart, not merely reasoned in the head, a reaction against the rationalism of the Enlightenment. Preachers delivered emotionally charged, often extemporaneous sermons. The Tennents founded a seminary, the “Log College,” to train ministers in this style; its successor institution became Princeton University. George Whitefield, an ordained Anglican, made several trips across the Atlantic after 1739 and preached in every colony, often outdoors to crowds too large for any church, so famous that he was perhaps the only public figure whose name nearly all colonists knew. Itinerant preachers carried the revival from the Middle Colonies to New England and, by the 1740s and 1750s, to the South. Conservative and moderate clergy criticized the revivals’ emotionalism and the disorder that followed them. They especially objected to itinerants who criticized local ministers, and to white women and African Americans who stepped beyond their subordinate status to exhort religious gatherings. Congregations and whole denominations split. Baptists and, later, Methodists grew rapidly; by the eve of the Revolution, evangelical converts made up about a tenth of Southern churchgoers. The revivals encouraged ordinary people to judge religious authority for themselves, and dissenting churches lobbied to end the official, tax-supported status of the Congregational church in New England and the Anglican church in the South. Historians debate how far the Awakening prepared the ground for the Revolution. Its challenge to established authority and its intercolonial reach suggest connections, but the links are indirect. Its most lasting legacy may be the evangelical style (revivals, conversion, voluntary churches) that became central to American religion. The Great Awakening was the first movement to touch nearly every colony, and it left American Protestantism more diverse, more democratic in style, and deeply divided over religious authority. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5vKGU3aEGss The Seven Years War and the Great Awakening: Crash Course US History #5 CrashCourse 10:39 2026-10-22

title: The Great Migration
subtitle: Millions of Black Southerners move North and West, 1910s–1970s
summary: The Great Migration was one of the largest movements of people in American history. From the 1910s to the 1970s about six million Black Southerners left the South for cities in the North, Midwest, and West. They fled racial violence and the oppression of Jim Crow and went looking for jobs, schooling, and freedom. The two world wars opened industrial jobs to them. The migrants transformed American cities, politics, and culture, from Chicago and Detroit to Harlem and Oakland. But in the North and West they also met mob violence, housing discrimination, and segregated neighborhoods that shaped inequality for generations.
thumbAlt: Map of Black urban population changes during the Great Migration
aliases: Second Great Migration Red Summer Harlem Renaissance New Negro
themeText: African American history Cities and urban life Labor and work Civil rights and citizenship Everyday life
text: Total About 6 million people, roughly 1910s to 1970s (National Archives) First phase About 2 million from World War I to World War II, mainly to New York, Chicago, Detroit, and Pittsburgh 1940s About 1.5 million, the largest decade of the migration (American Yawp) Second phase About 3 million in the two decades after World War II, including to Oakland, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Portland, and Seattle Pushes Jim Crow, racial violence, disenfranchisement, rural poverty Migrants sought what the South denied them. The National Archives describes their goals as escaping racial violence, pursuing economic and educational opportunity, and gaining freedom from the oppression of Jim Crow. The American Yawp writes that thousands of Black Southerners traveled north “to escape the traps of southern poverty.” In the 1940s, the Yawp adds, the 1.5 million who left the South were indirectly protesting racism and violence by leaving. The first wave. When the United States entered World War I in 1917, men went to Europe and left industrial jobs empty. Immigration from Europe had fallen, and people of color from elsewhere in the world were barred by law, so Northern industry turned to Black Southerners for its labor. From World War I to World War II about two million Black Southerners moved to cities such as New York, Chicago, Detroit, and Pittsburgh. A city within a city. New York’s Black population grew 257 percent, from 91,709 in 1910 to 327,706 in 1930, while its white population grew only 20 percent. By 1930 Harlem had grown to 164,000 people, mostly African Americans, and nearly half of the 98,620 Black immigrants from abroad lived there as well. The second wave. World War II expanded defense industries and brought more jobs. Between 1940 and 1950 about 1.5 million Black Southerners left, the largest number in any decade of the migration. Many now went west, to Oakland, Los Angeles, and San Francisco, and to Portland and Seattle. Within twenty years of the war, about three million more had moved. The National Archives’ two figures, two million and three million, add up to less than its six-million total for the whole migration, a reminder that these numbers are estimates. The migrants found jobs but not equality. White Northerners and returning veterans fought to take back jobs and neighborhoods from new Black arrivals. In the “Red Summer” of 1919, white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods in at least twenty-five cities, including Chicago and Washington, D.C. Black residents defended themselves, often with force. The National Archives traces that violence to white anger at the changing makeup of their communities. In 1943 riots broke out in Mobile, Beaumont, and Harlem, and the bloodiest, in Detroit, killed twenty-five Black and nine white Americans. After World War II, migrants met restrictive covenants and redlining. Banks marked Black neighborhoods with a red line on maps and limited loans there. The Federal Housing Administration and the Veterans Administration refused to back mortgages in those areas, and new suburbs such as Levittown sold only to white buyers. The National Archives calls these practices a foundation of the racial wealth gap that still exists. The migration built powerful Black urban communities. In Harlem, which James Weldon Johnson called “the Culture Capital,” a generation energized by race pride, wartime service, and city life produced the Harlem Renaissance and the “New Negro” movement. Harlem writers published some twenty-six novels and ten volumes of poetry between 1922 and 1935. Marcus Garvey’s movement, the Yawp notes, built a large following and inspired later Black nationalism. During World War II the NAACP grew tenfold, from 50,000 to 500,000 members. The war, the Yawp writes, ignited in African Americans an urgency for equality that they carried into the years of the civil rights movement. Migrants escaped legal segregation in the South but met segregation in housing and jobs in the North and West. The National Archives notes that this laid a foundation for the racial disparities in wealth that persist in the United States. The Great Migration remade the map of Black America and the culture and politics of American cities. It showed millions of people choosing to leave a system of oppression, and it carried both the hopes and the conflicts of the South into the rest of the nation. The Culture Capital. James Weldon Johnson describing Harlem in the 1920s We are achieving something like a spiritual emancipation. title: The Harlem Renaissance
subtitle: A flowering of Black literature, art, and music in 1920s New York
summary: In the 1920s Harlem, in upper Manhattan, became what James Weldon Johnson called “the Culture Capital”. Writers such as Langston Hughes, Claude McKay, Jessie Redmon Fauset, and Zora Neale Hurston, along with artists, actors, and jazz musicians, produced a burst of creative work that came to be called the Harlem Renaissance or the New Negro Movement. Its leading figure Alain Locke declared that a new generation was achieving “something like a spiritual emancipation.”
thumbAlt: Portrait of the poet Langston Hughes, photographed by Carl Van Vechten in 1936

themeText: African American history Arts and popular culture Cities and urban life
text: Harlem, New York City Also called The New Negro Movement Key book Alain Locke’s anthology The New Negro (1925) Output About 26 novels and 10 volumes of poetry, 1922–1935 Writers Langston Hughes, Claude McKay, Jessie Redmon Fauset, Zora Neale Hurston Music Jazz, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong Black Americans entered the 1920s weighed down by Jim Crow segregation, lynching, and the racial violence of 1919’s “Red Summer.” Harlem Renaissance writers and artists sought to define Black life on their own terms. Alain Locke, one of its leading figures, proclaimed in 1925 that the generation of subservience was over and that African Americans were “achieving something like a spiritual emancipation.” The movement worked through culture: novels, poetry, short stories, theater, painting, and music. Locke’s anthology The New Negro (1925) gathered writing by men and women, young and old, Black and white, a book, as The American Yawp puts it, of African Americans rather than only about them. The Renaissance grew up against Jim Crow and racial violence. Even its successes were shaped by segregation: white audiences traveled to Harlem’s Cotton Club and Smalls to hear “real jazz,” but the surrounding Black community was usually excluded from those venues. The New York Times ridiculed jazz as “savage.” Between 1922 and 1935, Harlem Renaissance writers published some twenty-six novels, ten volumes of poetry, and countless short stories; women such as Jessie Redmon Fauset and Zora Neale Hurston wrote nearly a third of the novels. The movement also flourished in theater, art, and music, as jazz rocketed in popularity and musicians like Louis Armstrong developed their art in New York. As the Renaissance faded, The American Yawp stresses that it was one chapter in a much longer history of Black cultural and intellectual achievement. How far art alone could change a segregated society remained an open question, and other leaders, such as Marcus Garvey and his Harlem-based Universal Negro Improvement Association, offered very different answers. The Harlem Renaissance made Black writers, artists, and musicians central to American culture and gave later civil rights generations a powerful tradition of self-expression. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vKaegbtcE00 Arts and Letters of the Harlem Renaissance: Crash Course Black American History #26 CrashCourse 12:37 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8kZ0gZMCx9U The Harlem Renaissance - An Explosion of Art - US History - Extra History Extra History 9:13 2026-10-22

title: The Labor Movement
subtitle: Workers organize for wages, hours, and a voice on the job
summary: As industrial capitalism remade the United States after the Civil War, millions of wage workers, many of them immigrants, organized to win higher pay, shorter hours, safer conditions, and a say over their work. For half a century their biggest strikes were crushed. The Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the eight-hour campaign that ended at Haymarket, the Homestead strike, and the Pullman boycott were all broken by police, militias, private guards, court injunctions, or federal troops. Workers built new organizations anyway: the Knights of Labor, the American Federation of Labor, the Industrial Workers of the World, and garment unions built by young immigrant women. Only in 1935 did the Wagner Act guarantee most private-sector workers the right to organize and bargain collectively. Union membership then surged.
