themeText: Labor and work Economy and finance Reform and protest Immigration
text: Great Railroad Strike 1877; nearly 100 killed as militias and federal troops broke it Knights of Labor More than 700,000 members by 1886; open to skilled and unskilled workers, including women Eight-hour strike May 1, 1886; 300,000 to 500,000 workers American Federation of Labor Alliance of craft unions pursuing “pure and simple trade unionism” Strikes and lockouts More than 20,000 in the last two decades of the nineteenth century Turning point National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act), signed July 5, 1935 Industrial workers toiled long hours for little pay. A typical industrial laborer, the American Yawp notes, worked sixty hours a week, could expect to be out of work one month a year, and might still earn less than a poverty-line income. Wives and children were pushed into paid work to make up the difference. Mechanization threw skilled workers into unskilled jobs, and as companies grew larger, individual workers felt smaller and more powerless. Unions sought higher wages, shorter hours, safer workplaces, and recognition. The eight-hour day was the demand that most united American workers. Some organizations wanted much more. The Knights of Labor imagined a cooperative society that rewarded labor rather than capital. Socialists such as Eugene Debs called for “the overthrow of the capitalist system and the emancipation of the working class from wage slavery.” Others, like the American Federation of Labor, focused on practical gains. Working women also asked for dignity. The garment unionist Rose Schneiderman said in 1912: “The worker must have bread, but she must have roses, too.” The Great Upheaval of 1877. In 1877, in the stagnant economy that followed the collapse of the railroad bubble in 1873, rail lines slashed wages. Workers struck from Baltimore to St. Louis and shut down rail traffic across the country. Militias fired into crowds in Baltimore, Pittsburgh, and Reading, and in St. Louis a general strike demanded the eight-hour day and an end to child labor. Federal troops finally broke the strike after six weeks. Nearly 100 people died. Its failure convinced workers they needed lasting unions. The Knights of Labor. The Knights tried to unite skilled and unskilled workers and welcomed women. They barred only lawyers, bankers, and liquor dealers. By 1886 they had more than 700,000 members. That spring nearly 200,000 workers struck Jay Gould’s southwestern railroads, but Pinkertons, strikebreakers, and state militias broke the strike. The eight-hour day. On May 1, 1886, between 300,000 and 500,000 workers struck nationwide for the eight-hour day. After Chicago police broke up a strike at the McCormick reaper works, killing one man according to the Illinois library and several according to the Yawp, radicals called a protest meeting at Haymarket Square on May 4. As police moved to break it up, someone threw a bomb. Seven police officers died, along with at least one civilian, according to the University of Illinois library. The American Yawp writes that police fire killed four people in the crowd. Eight anarchists were tried on little evidence linking them to the bomb. The Yawp says they were found guilty of conspiracy, while the Illinois library says they were charged with murder. Four were hanged. Many Americans came to link unions with radicalism, and the Knights and the eight-hour movement collapsed. Craft unions. The American Federation of Labor, an alliance of unions of skilled workers, rejected the Knights’ broad vision. It pursued “pure and simple trade unionism”: higher wages, fewer hours, and safer conditions, won if possible without strikes. Industrial unions and boycotts. Eugene Debs’s American Railway Union, formed in 1893, enrolled every kind of railroad worker and grew to 150,000 members. In 1894 it refused to handle Pullman cars anywhere in the country in support of striking Pullman factory workers, and national rail traffic ground to a halt. Radical unionism and politics. In 1905 William D. “Big Bill” Haywood and other radicals founded the Industrial Workers of the World, the “Wobblies,” which welcomed all workers regardless of race or gender. In 1912 it led textile strikers in Lawrence, Massachusetts. Debs ran for president as a Socialist and won almost a million votes, about 6 percent, in 1912. Women’s strikes. In 1909 thousands of New York garment workers answered the young Clara Lemlich’s call for a general strike, with help from the Women’s Trade Union League. A cloakmakers’ strike in 1910 won a grievance system for the industry. After the Triangle fire of 1911, unions and reformers pushed New York to pass a new code of factory safety laws. The New Deal. In 1933 and 1934 a great wave of strikes, including citywide general strikes and factory takeovers, swept the country. The Wagner Act of 1935 protected workers’ “right to self-organization” and created the National Labor Relations Board. That year John L. Lewis of the United Mine Workers broke with the AFL to found the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO), which organized whole industries. In 1937 auto workers held a sit-down strike in General Motors’ plant in Flint, Michigan, until GM recognized the United Automobile Workers. Employers had money, the law, and often the government on their side. Gould used strikebreakers and the Pinkerton Detective Agency, a private security firm, to break the 1886 rail strike. At Carnegie’s Homestead steel works in 1892, Henry Clay Frick sent hundreds of Pinkertons against striking steelworkers. The workers fought them off, but the governor sent the state militia, broke the strike, and reopened the mill. The union was all but destroyed. During the 1877 strike the head of the Pennsylvania Railroad, Thomas Scott, suggested that unhappy workers be given “a rifle diet for a few days.” The courts became a powerful weapon. In the Pullman strike, federal lawyers won an injunction against the boycott under the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, a law meant to combat monopolies. Going over the head of Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld, who sympathized with the workers, President Grover Cleveland sent thousands of soldiers and marshals. Dozens of people were killed, and Debs was jailed for contempt. Jail convinced Debs that political and judicial leaders were tools of capital. Socialists and other radicals faced government repression and censorship, especially during and after World War I. Even in the 1930s, employers spied on, fired, and blacklisted union members, and Southern mill owners brought in thousands of strikebreakers during the textile strike of 1934. Labor’s long pressure won gains even before the 1930s. Progressive reformers embraced many socialist policies, the American Yawp notes. After the Triangle fire, New York passed more than twenty new factory safety and health laws. The Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914 protected labor’s right to bargain collectively, picket, and boycott. The great breakthrough came with the New Deal. The Supreme Court upheld the Wagner Act in 1937, and it brought a dramatic surge in union membership. By the end of the 1930s more than 800,000 women belonged to unions, three times as many as in 1929. In 1938 the Fair Labor Standards Act created the modern minimum wage. Union members came to see Roosevelt as their protector. One union leader called him an “agent of God.” The labor movement was often divided by race, sex, and skill. The American Railway Union admitted only white railroad workers. The AFL organized mainly skilled craftsmen, and in 1935 the new CIO broke with the craft-oriented federation. In the South, the Colored Farmers’ Alliance, which once had as many as 250,000 members, declined rapidly after 1891, when white violence crushed the cotton pickers’ strikes it sponsored. The Wagner Act itself did not cover farm workers, railroads, airlines, or government employees. Congress later rewrote its provisions in the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 and the Landrum-Griffin Act of 1959. The balance of power between workers and employers, and the government’s role in protecting the right to organize, remained central questions in American politics. The labor movement turned the problems of industrial work into public questions. Its defeats in the Gilded Age and its victory in the New Deal shaped the rights that American workers have today. The worker must have bread, but she must have roses, too. Rose Schneiderman speech, 1912 I believe a rich plunderer like Pullman is a greater felon than a poor thief. Eugene V. Debs speech, May 16, 1894 The right to self-organization, to form, join, or assist labor organizations, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing. title: Populism and the People’s Party
subtitle: The farmers’ revolt of the 1890s
summary: Populism was a mass political movement of farmers in the South and West who believed that railroads, banks, and the two major parties served “the moneyed power” at the expense of ordinary producers. Organized first through the Farmers’ Alliance, they formed the People’s Party, which won congressional seats in 1890 and issued the sweeping Omaha Platform in 1892. In 1896 the Populists endorsed the Democrat William Jennings Bryan and soon faded, but many of their proposals later became law.
thumbAlt: Judge magazine cartoon of William Jennings Bryan in 1896
aliases: People's Party Omaha Platform free silver Farmers' Alliance
themeText: Parties and elections Economy and finance Reform and protest Labor and work
text: First breakthrough 1890 midterms: nine congressional seats and state and local victories Omaha Platform Adopted July 4, 1892, at the party’s first national convention Key demands Unlimited coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads and telegraphs, direct election of senators 1896 Endorsed Democrat William Jennings Bryan Populists believed national policies favored industry, banks, and the Northeast over farmers, who faced falling crop prices, debt, and high railroad rates. They sought to expand the money supply, especially through the free coinage of silver, to ease debts; to regulate or nationalize railroads and telegraphs; to institute a graduated income tax; and to make government more directly answerable to voters. Farmers organized through cooperative Farmers’ Alliances and then turned to independent politics. Meeting in Omaha on the 116th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1892, the People’s Party declared that the nation had been “brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin” and that both major parties had permitted “grievous wrongs” against “a plundered people.” Republicans were attacked by the Populists for serving the “moneyed” power of the Northeast, and Southern Democrats were put on notice as small farmers broke away. Both major parties, business interests, and much of the press in turn portrayed the Populists as dangerous radicals. Though their presidential bids failed, the Populists set the stage for William Jennings Bryan’s Democratic campaign of 1896. Several of their demands were later written into the Constitution: a federal income tax (Sixteenth Amendment, 1913) and the direct election of senators (Seventeenth Amendment, 1913). Historians debate Populism’s character: a democratic movement of producers against concentrated power, or one that also carried nativist and racial prejudices. The word “populism” is still used to describe movements that claim to speak for ordinary people against elites. The Populist revolt was the largest third-party challenge of the Gilded Age, and it put the regulation of corporations and the expansion of democracy on the national agenda. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8G_OS1O5Bd4 The Populist Movement Explained Mr. Beat 7:29 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V6ueX6hqzNk Populism and the Populist Movement in America for Dummies Hip Hughes (HipHughes) 10:01 2026-10-23

title: Progressivism
subtitle: Reformers confront the problems of industrial America, c. 1890s–1920
summary: Progressivism was not one movement but many. In the decades around 1900, reformers of every kind set out to fix the problems of industrial America: monopolies, corrupt political machines, dangerous workplaces, child labor, and city slums. Journalists exposed abuses, settlement workers moved into poor neighborhoods, ministers preached a social gospel, and women’s clubs, unions, and suffragists organized. Under Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, and Woodrow Wilson, the federal government took on new powers to regulate business. Four constitutional amendments followed between 1913 and 1920. Progressivism also had a darker side. In the South, white reformers presented disfranchisement and segregation as progressive measures, and many reformers shared the racial and anti-immigrant prejudices of their time.
thumbAlt: Jacob Riis’s photograph of Bandits’ Roost, an alley on Mulberry Street in New York
aliases: Progressive Era muckrakers Square Deal New Freedom New Nationalism Jane Addams Hull House social gospel trust busting Bull Moose Party
themeText: Reform and protest Political thought Labor and work Cities and urban life Women's history
text: Era About the 1890s to 1920 Key figures Jane Addams, Florence Kelley, Theodore Roosevelt, Woodrow Wilson, Ida B. Wells, W. E. B. Du Bois Muckrakers Journalists, so named by Theodore Roosevelt, who exposed corruption and abuses Antitrust laws Sherman Act (1890), Hepburn Act (1906), Clayton Act and Federal Trade Commission (1914) Constitutional reforms 16th (income tax) and 17th (direct election of senators) Amendments, 1913; 18th (Prohibition), 1919; 19th (woman suffrage), 1920 Other landmark laws Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts (1906), Federal Reserve Act (1913), Keating-Owen Child Labor Act (1916) Americans in these years had many different ideas about how the country should develop and whose interests needed the most protection. Reformers wanted to clean up politics, and Black Americans kept up their long fight for civil rights. Women demanded the vote and a more equal place in society, and workers demanded higher wages, safer workplaces, and union recognition. What united them, the American Yawp writes, was that reform became “the word of the age.” They hoped to bring order to chaos, efficiency to inefficiency, and justice to injustice. Many reformers believed that concentrated wealth threatened democracy itself. In The Promise of American Life, one of the defining books of the era, Herbert Croly argued that “the millionaire and the trust have appropriated too many of the economic opportunities formerly enjoyed by the people.” Some reformers pursued moral goals as well, above all temperance and then the full prohibition of alcohol, which many blamed for poverty, crime, and domestic abuse. Exposure. Journalists whom Theodore Roosevelt called “muckrakers” exposed business practices, poverty, and corruption in magazines such as McClure’s. Jacob Riis’s How the Other Half Lives (1890) used photographs to show the city’s slums and led to housing reform. Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle (1906), meant to build support for socialism, instead shocked readers about how their food was made and led to the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act that same year. In 1908 the National Child Labor Committee hired Lewis Hine to photograph working children across the country. The social gospel. Protestant ministers such as Walter Rauschenbusch, who served a church in New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, urged Christians to seek the salvation of society and not only of individual souls. Charles Sheldon’s best-selling novel In His Steps (1896) asked readers: “What Would Jesus Do?” Settlement houses. Jane Addams founded Hull House in Chicago in 1889 with Ellen Gates Starr, after visiting Toynbee Hall in London. It ran a nursery, a kindergarten, classes, and clubs for its immigrant neighbors. Florence Kelley, who lived there from 1891 to 1899, pushed Addams toward reform. Hull House surveyed its neighborhood, exposed local sweatshops, and lobbied for laws limiting the hours of women and children. Organizing. The General Federation of Women’s Clubs (1890) and the National Association of Colored Women (1896) gave women national networks. The Woman’s Christian Temperance Union, under Frances Willard, adopted a “do everything” policy that took in prison reform, the eight-hour day, and child labor laws. The Women’s Trade Union League, founded in 1903, joined working-class and wealthier women. Black activists founded the Niagara Movement and then the NAACP, whose magazine The Crisis was edited by W. E. B. Du Bois from 1909 to 1934. Regulating business. Roosevelt’s administration broke up the Northern Securities railroad trust in 1904, and the Hepburn Act of 1906 let the Interstate Commerce Commission set railroad rates. Roosevelt’s “Square Deal” called for reform of the workplace and government regulation of industry, and he set aside nearly 200 million acres for national forests, reserves, and wildlife refuges. Taft more than doubled the number of antitrust breakups of Roosevelt’s seven years in office. Wilson’s New Freedom called for lower tariffs, banking reform, and laws to restore competition. He signed the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 and the Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914, and Congress created the Federal Trade Commission to enforce it. Changing the Constitution. Progressives also changed the Constitution itself. The Sixteenth Amendment, ratified in February 1913, allowed a federal income tax. The Seventeenth, ratified in April 1913, let voters elect senators directly, replacing a system in which state legislatures had chosen them and reformers had called the Senate a “millionaires’ club.” The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in January 1919, prohibited the manufacture and sale of alcoholic drinks. The Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote in 1920. Business leaders and their allies resisted regulation, and the courts were often on their side. The courts seized on the vague language of the Sherman Act and used it to limit the power of labor unions. Congress passed the Keating-Owen Act in 1916 to ban the interstate sale of goods made by children, but the Court struck it down in Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918). It struck down a second child labor law in 1922. A Child Labor Amendment stalled in the 1920s amid charges that it was a communist plot. Conservatives in Congress proposed the income tax amendment in 1909 in the hope of killing the idea, believing three-fourths of the states would never ratify it. To their surprise, the states did. Progressives also disagreed among themselves. Roosevelt wanted to regulate big corporations, while Taft preferred to break them up in court. In 1912 Roosevelt ran against Taft on a Progressive, or “Bull Moose,” ticket and lost to Wilson, who had promised to restore competition through small business. Conservationists such as Gifford Pinchot, who wanted resources used efficiently, clashed with preservationists such as John Muir over whether to dam the Hetch Hetchy Valley in Yosemite. Congress approved the dam in 1913. Progressives made government responsible for regulating the economy and protecting public welfare to an extent never seen before. Federal antitrust law, railroad regulation, food and drug inspection, the Federal Reserve, and the income tax all date from these years. At the state and city level, reformers won laws on working hours, workplace safety, sanitation, and public health. After the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist fire, New York’s Factory Investigating Commission produced more than twenty new safety and health laws. The direct election of senators and woman suffrage enlarged American democracy. Frances Perkins, who worked with that commission, later applied its lessons nationally as Secretary of Labor under the New Deal. Progressivism did little for Black Americans and in the South worked against them. White Southern Democrats described disfranchisement and segregation as reforms that would “purify” the ballot box and prevent racial conflict, and progressive Democrats and former Populists were their strongest supporters. Between 1890 and 1908 every Southern state adopted poll taxes, literacy tests, and other devices to stop Black citizens from voting. In 1900 Alabama had 121,159 literate Black men of voting age, but only 3,742 were registered. In Washington, Wilson’s administration expanded segregation in federal offices and the civil service. Even in Congress, an early version of the Seventeenth Amendment carried a “race rider” meant to block federal protection of Black voters. A substitute amendment dropped it. Many reformers also looked down on the people they meant to help. Temperance crusaders blamed cities, immigrants, and Catholics for drink. Game laws in Pennsylvania fell hardest on poor Italian immigrants. Many white suffragists argued that white women’s votes would offset Black votes, and most social gospel ministers ignored women and racial minorities. Black leaders such as Booker T. Washington, Ida B. Wells, and Du Bois fought back by their own different strategies. Progressivism remade American government for the industrial age. It established that the state should act to correct the excesses of the market. It also showed how reform could serve exclusion as well as democracy. The great corporations which we have grown to speak of rather loosely as trusts are the creatures of the State, and the State not only has the right to control them, but it is in duty bound to control them wherever the need of such control is shown. title: Second-Wave Feminism
subtitle: The women’s liberation movement of the 1960s and 1970s
summary: In the 1960s and 1970s a new wave of feminism challenged discrimination against women at work, in law, in education, and in family life. Many of its activists had worked in the civil rights and labor movements and found that male leaders there were not interested in gender inequality. Galvanized by Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963), they founded the National Organization for Women, formed consciousness-raising groups, and fought for equal pay, reproductive rights, and an Equal Rights Amendment. They won major legal changes, including the use of Title VII against job discrimination and Roe v. Wade in 1973. But a conservative countermovement led by Phyllis Schlafly stopped the ERA three states short of ratification.
thumbAlt: President Kennedy signing the Equal Pay Act with members of the American Association of University Women
aliases: women’s liberation The Feminine Mystique NOW National Organization for Women Equal Rights Amendment ERA consciousness-raising Phyllis Schlafly STOP ERA Ms. magazine
themeText: Women's history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Labor and work
text: Commission on the Status of Women Chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt; report released 1963 The Feminine Mystique Betty Friedan, 1963 NOW Founded 1966; Friedan its first president Women’s Strike for Equality August 26, 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of woman suffrage ERA Sent to the states March 22, 1972; ratified by 35 of the 38 states needed; expired June 30, 1982 Roe v. Wade 1973, decided 7 to 2; overruled in 2022 Feminists sought equal treatment in jobs and pay, an end to sex discrimination in law, access to contraception and abortion, child care, and equality in marriage. NOW’s founding statement, written by Friedan, pledged “to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now, exercising all the privileges and responsibilities thereof in truly equal partnership with men.” The movement’s central constitutional goal was the Equal Rights Amendment, first proposed in Congress in 1923, which declared: “Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of sex.” Working through government. In the early 1960s an older generation of women worked through official institutions. President John F. Kennedy’s Commission on the Status of Women, chaired by former first lady Eleanor Roosevelt, issued its report in 1963 as an “invitation to action.” It documented discrimination in law, in labor, and in government and called for changes in employment, taxes, and labor law. The sources date the commission differently: the American Yawp says it was established in 1961, while the National Women’s History Museum says Roosevelt took the chair in 1960. The Yawp notes that the report mostly addressed the concerns of middle-class and elite white working women. Roosevelt also worked on the Equal Pay Act, passed in 1963. Thanks partly to Black feminists such as Pauli Murray, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 included a ban on sex discrimination in employment in Title VII. “If sex is not included,” Murray told members of Congress, “the civil rights bill would be including only half of the Negroes.” Naming the problem. Friedan, a former labor journalist and a suburban mother, surveyed her Smith College classmates and interviewed women across the country for five years. In The Feminine Mystique she named “the problem that has no name,” the dissatisfaction of many middle-class housewives, and argued that it was a social problem and not a personal failing. Organizing. In 1966 Friedan, Pauli Murray, and Aileen Hernandez founded the National Organization for Women, with Friedan as its first president, according to the National Women’s History Museum. The Yawp lists Shirley Chisholm among its founders, while the museum’s biography of Chisholm says she was a member. NOW’s first campaign pressed the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce Title VII, and it ended sex-segregated help-wanted ads. Women sued to enter jobs reserved for men, and protests pushed the EEOC to issue stronger protections between 1968 and 1971. Friedan also helped found the National Association for the Repeal of Abortion Laws in 1969. In 1971 she joined Gloria Steinem, Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, and Fannie Lou Hamer in founding the National Women’s Political Caucus. The personal is political. Younger women formed consciousness-raising groups that met in homes and women’s centers to talk about discrimination, pregnancy, relationships, and self-image. They argued that individual experiences reflected society-wide sexism, summed up in the slogan “the personal is political.” Poor women and women of color. Mostly African American mothers on welfare organized the National Welfare Rights Organization in 1966. Leaders such as Johnnie Tillmon won larger grants and fair hearings before benefits were cut off. Shirley Chisholm, a member of NOW, became the first African American woman in Congress, elected in 1968, and in 1972 the first woman and first African American to seek a major party’s presidential nomination. Protest and the press. On August 26, 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of woman suffrage, NOW’s Women’s Strike for Equality brought women into the streets to demand equal employment, political equality, abortion rights, free child care, and equality in marriage. Steinem helped found Ms. magazine, which first appeared in 1971 and became a regular magazine in 1972. The movement faced opposition from women as well as men. Phyllis Schlafly, a conservative activist, founded the Eagle Forum in 1972 and led the campaign called STOP ERA, for “Stop Taking Our Privileges.” She argued that the amendment would take away women’s exemption from the military draft, the “dependent wife” benefits of Social Security for widows, and the preference that mothers received in custody cases. Her coalition, the museum estimates, numbered only about 20,000 people, but it was tightly focused, and it lobbied legislators with gifts of homemade bread. With the support of evangelical Christians and other religious conservatives, Schlafly spoke for “the millions of happily married women who believe in the laws which protect the family and require the husband to support his wife and children.” In 1980 the religious leader Jerry Falwell urged Americans to stand against the Equal Rights Amendment and the feminist movement. The movement also divided from within. Women of color challenged white feminists’ racism, and younger radical feminists criticized Friedan for speaking mainly for white, middle-class, educated women and for cooperating with men. Feminists won enforcement of Title VII and stronger EEOC protections, and women moved slowly but steadily into jobs once held by men, into politics, and into corporate management. In Roe v. Wade (1973) the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that the “right of privacy … is broad enough to encompass a woman’s decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy.” The ERA passed Congress and went to the states on March 22, 1972. Hawaii ratified it the same day, and thirty states ratified it within a year. President Jimmy Carter supported it, proclaimed Women’s Equality Day in 1978, and signed the extension of the ratification deadline from March 1979 to June 30, 1982. The ERA stalled. Indiana became the thirty-fifth state to ratify in 1977, but no more followed, and the amendment expired in 1982, three states short of the thirty-eight it needed. The Yawp writes that the defeat showed the limits of a movement that could not fully represent half the country’s population, divided as it was by class, race, culture, and religion. Abortion became one of the most divisive issues in American politics, and in 2022, in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Supreme Court overruled Roe. Second-wave feminism transformed women’s legal status and opportunities and changed American expectations about work, family, and equality, while also provoking a lasting conservative reaction. title: The Underground Railroad
subtitle: Escape from slavery, and the networks that helped freedom seekers reach liberty
summary: The Underground Railroad was not a railroad and not underground. The National Park Service defines it as “the efforts of enslaved African Americans to gain their freedom by escaping bondage,” and the help others gave them. Those helpers included free and enslaved Black people, white abolitionists, American Indians and others. Freedom seekers fled to the North, Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida, Indian territory, the West, the Caribbean and Europe, sometimes guided by “conductors” such as Harriet Tubman. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made helping them more dangerous, the networks grew more organized, and the Underground Railroad became, in the Park Service’s words, a “widespread form of civil disobedience.”
thumbAlt: Charles T. Webber’s 1893 painting The Underground Railroad, showing freedom seekers arriving by wagon at a farmhouse in winter
aliases: Freedom seekers Network to Freedom Conductors Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 William Still Harriet Tubman
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Reform and protest Civil rights and citizenship
text: What it was Escape from slavery through flight, and help with that escape, from slavery’s beginning to the end of the Civil War Destinations The free states, Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida, Indian territory, the West, the Caribbean and Europe Famous conductor Harriet Tubman, who led about 70 people to freedom in the 1850s Philadelphia The Black abolitionist William Still helped freedom seekers and recorded their stories 1850 law Federal commissioners were paid $10 for ruling a captive enslaved, $5 for ruling a captive free Preferred term “Freedom seeker,” not “fugitive” or “runaway” The goal was freedom. Enslaved people sought to escape bondage and reach places beyond the reach of recapture. Those who helped them, sometimes on the spur of the moment and sometimes as part of organized networks, aimed to get them there safely in defiance of the law. The Park Service stresses that “there is no Underground Railroad without freedom seekers,” who are at the center of the story. Escape began at home. The Underground Railroad “started at the place of enslavement.” Freedom seekers followed rivers, canals, bays, the Atlantic coast, ferries, roads and trails, and many escapes began near ports, free territory or international borders. Ingenuity. They used “disguises, forgeries and other strategies” to slip past slave catchers who watched the expected routes for advertised rewards. Conductors and stations. A conductor escorted or directed freedom seekers between “stations,” or safe houses; a conductor did not need to belong to any organized network. The sea. The maritime industry spread information and offered jobs and passage; ties to whaling even made the Pacific coast a destination. War. During the Civil War many freedom seekers escaped to the lines of the Union army. Slavery was legal, and so was hunting those who fled it. Enslavers advertised rewards, and slave catchers watched the routes. A fugitive slave clause in the Constitution and a federal law of 1793 already provided for the return of escapees, and in Prigg v. Pennsylvania (1842) the Supreme Court ruled that the federal law overrode a Pennsylvania law against carrying Black people out of the state to enslave them. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, part of the Compromise of 1850, was far harsher. It created federal commissioners who decided cases without a jury trial, barred Northern authorities from interfering with captures, and required citizens to help in arrests when called upon. Commissioners were paid $10 if they ruled a captive enslaved and only $5 if they ruled the person free, which, the American Yawp writes, “fostered corruption and the enslavement of free Black northerners.” Many reached freedom. Harriet Tubman escaped from Maryland to Philadelphia, learned about the networks from William Still in Philadelphia, and returned again and again; between 1850 and 1860 she brought about 70 people, including her parents, to freedom. “I never ran my train off the track and I never lost a passenger,” she said. William Still, the Yawp notes, “frequently risked his life” helping freedom seekers and preserved their letters and stories. After 1850 many fled all the way to Canada. The Underground Railroad also changed Northern opinion. The Yawp writes that no part of the Compromise of 1850 “proved more troubling to antislavery Americans than the Fugitive Slave Act,” and Northern resistance to it helped bring on the sectional crisis. Historians and the National Park Service now debate even the words used to tell the story. Terms such as “fugitive,” “runaway” and “escapee,” the Park Service writes, were “constructs of slave-holding society and patronizing abolitionists” that take away individual agency, so it prefers “freedom seeker.” But it also notes that “there is not universal consensus”: some historians keep “fugitive” to stress that people who freed themselves were breaking the law. Research continues, and new routes are still being discovered. The Park Service calls the Underground Railroad “one of the earliest grass roots movements in the United States in which people united across racial, gender, religious, and class lines in hopes of promoting social change.” At its center were the freedom seekers themselves. How many trips did Tubman make? Even a single source can count differently. The National Women’s History Museum says Tubman made eleven trips from Maryland to St. Catharines, Ontario, between 1850 and 1860, “19 in total” over the years, and that she brought about 70 people to freedom; the same biography later speaks of “the hundreds of enslaved that she freed over the course of her lifetime.” The museum also credits her with helping coordinate the 1863 Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed about 750 people. I never ran my train off the track and I never lost a passenger. title: The Woman Suffrage Movement
subtitle: Seventy-two years of struggle for women’s right to vote, 1848–1920
summary: The woman suffrage movement was the long campaign to win American women the right to vote. It began at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848 and ended in victory with the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. Over seventy-two years, generations of women and some men lectured, petitioned, marched, lobbied, went to court, picketed the White House, and went to jail. The movement split over the Fifteenth Amendment, reunited in 1890, won state victories first in the West, and finally gained a federal amendment during World War I. Many of its white leaders sidelined Black women. Ida B. Wells and others fought for a movement that included them, and many women of color could not vote for decades after 1920.
thumbAlt: Illustration of suffrage activism in New York City
aliases: suffragists National Woman’s Party Alice Paul NAWSA Silent Sentinels Carrie Chapman Catt
themeText: Women's history Voting rights Reform and protest Civil rights and citizenship
text: Began Seneca Falls Convention, July 19–20, 1848 Split 1869: National Woman Suffrage Association (Stanton and Anthony) and American Woman Suffrage Association (Stone) Reunited 1890 as the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) First amendment introduced 1878 (National Archives) Militant wing Alice Paul’s Congressional Union (1913) and National Woman’s Party; White House pickets from January 1917 Victory Nineteenth Amendment passed June 4, 1919; ratified August 18, 1920 The movement’s central goal was the vote. Its founding document, the Declaration of Sentiments of 1848, listed first among women’s grievances that man “has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.” Early leaders also sought property rights, divorce and custody rights, education, and equal pay, and they saw the vote as the means to win the rest. Some suffragists argued that women’s votes were needed to clean up politics and combat social evils. Lecturing and petitioning. From the 1850s Susan B. Anthony traveled the country giving speeches, circulating petitions, and organizing local societies, often with speeches written by Elizabeth Cady Stanton. Testing the Constitution. After the Civil War some suffragists argued in the “New Departure” that the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, by making citizenship national, already gave women the vote. Roughly seven hundred women registered to vote between 1868 and 1872. Anthony voted in the 1872 presidential election and was arrested, tried, and fined $100. State campaigns. The movement won first in the West. By 1911 six western states had amended their constitutions to give women the vote, according to the American Yawp. The National Archives counts nine western states by 1912. Carrie Chapman Catt helped win suffrage in Colorado in 1893. Coalitions. Women’s clubs, the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union, the Women’s Trade Union League, and Black women’s organizations such as the National Association of Colored Women all joined the cause. Ida B. Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago in 1913 to organize Black women voters. Militancy. Alice Paul, who had learned picketing and hunger strikes in the British suffrage movement, organized a march of about eight thousand women in Washington on March 3, 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration. Crowds attacked the marchers while police did little. She founded the Congressional Union to lobby Congress for a federal amendment and then the National Woman’s Party. Beginning in January 1917, more than a thousand “Silent Sentinels” picketed the White House for eighteen months, holding signs such as “Mr. President, how long must women wait for liberty?” Police arrested Paul and dozens of others. At the Occoquan Workhouse, where Paul led a hunger strike and was force-fed, jailers beat the prisoners in what became known as the Night of Terror. Lobbying. NAWSA, which Catt first led as Anthony’s successor in 1900, combined state campaigns with pressure on Congress for an amendment. Suffragists faced ridicule, hostility, and violence. The signers at Seneca Falls expected “no small amount of misconception, misrepresentation, and ridicule.” At the 1913 parade, spectators tripped and assaulted marchers, and some police told them that “there would be nothing like this happen if you would stay at home.” Nearly 300 women were hurt. The National Archives notes that opponents heckled, jailed, and sometimes physically abused suffragists. Wilson at first said it was not yet time for a constitutional amendment. By 1916 almost all the major suffrage organizations stood behind a federal amendment. New York adopted woman suffrage in 1917, and in January 1918 Wilson announced his support. The House approved the amendment in January 1918, according to the National Women’s History Museum. The National Archives dates the House vote that sent it to the states to May 21, 1919, and the Senate followed two weeks later. On August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the thirty-sixth state to ratify, and on August 26 Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the Nineteenth Amendment: “The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.” Few of the movement’s early supporters lived to see it. Victory was incomplete. The split of 1869 had already exposed racism in the movement. Stanton and Anthony opposed the Fifteenth Amendment because it enfranchised Black men but not women, and Anthony, the National Women’s History Museum writes, “adopted the racist positions used by many other white women at that time.” As NAWSA grew it distanced itself from Black women’s voting rights, and the American Yawp notes that some suffragists argued that white women’s votes were needed to maintain white supremacy. At the 1913 parade, organizers told Black women to march at the back. Wells refused and joined the march from the sidelines. After 1920, discriminatory state laws kept many African American and other women of color from voting for decades. In 1921 Alice Paul and Crystal Eastman drafted an Equal Rights Amendment. It was ratified by 35 states in the 1970s but fell three states short by the 1982 deadline. The suffrage movement showed how a disenfranchised group could change the Constitution through decades of organized pressure. It also revealed the racial divisions that ran through American reform. He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise. Declaration of Sentiments Seneca Falls, 1848 Mr. President, how long must women wait for liberty? Banner of the Silent Sentinels White House pickets, 1917 This world taught woman nothing skillful and then said her work was valueless. It permitted her no opinions and said she did not know how to think. title: Abigail Adams
subtitle: Political partner, letter writer, and early voice for women’s rights
summary: Abigail Adams was the wife of the second president, John Adams, the mother of the sixth, John Quincy Adams, and one of the sharpest political minds of the Revolutionary generation. Through a lifetime of letters she advised her husband, reported on the war around Boston, and ran the family farm and finances alone for years at a time. In March 1776 she urged him to “Remember the Ladies” in the new nation’s laws, warning that women would “not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.” She also wrote against slavery and argued for women’s education. As First Lady she was so influential that critics called her “Mrs. President.”
thumbAlt: Portrait of Abigail Adams
aliases: Remember the Ladies Portia Mrs. President Abigail Smith
themeText: Women's history Political thought Everyday life
text: Abigail Smith Adams Weymouth, Massachusetts Quincy, Massachusetts Correspondent and political adviser to John Adams Manager of the Adams farm and finances First Lady (1797–1801) Mother of President John Quincy Adams Born November 1744, Weymouth, Massachusetts (the Park Service gives November 11; the National Women’s History Museum, November 22) Married John Adams, October 25, 1764 Children Abigail (Nabby), John Quincy, Susanna (died in infancy), Charles, Thomas Boylston Best-known letter “Remember the Ladies,” March 31 – April 5, 1776 First Lady 1797–1801; first to live in the President’s House in Washington, November 1800 Died October 28, 1818, of typhoid fever, Quincy, Massachusetts Abigail Smith was born in Weymouth, Massachusetts, in November 1744, the second child of Elizabeth Quincy Smith and the Reverend William Smith, pastor of the town’s North Parish Congregational Church. The Park Service and the National Women’s History Museum give different days for her birth, November 11 and November 22. New England schools usually admitted only boys, so she was taught at home and educated herself in her father’s library, regretting all her life that formal education had been closed to her. Her grandfather Colonel John Quincy, once speaker of the Massachusetts House, gave her a sense of public duty. She married John Adams, a young lawyer from Braintree, on October 25, 1764, with her father presiding. They lived in the farmhouse John had inherited in Braintree, and their children were Abigail (“Nabby”), John Quincy, Susanna, who died in infancy, Charles, and Thomas Boylston. In Boston their circle included Samuel Adams, John Hancock, James Otis, and Joseph Warren. When John agreed to defend the British soldiers accused in the Boston Massacre of 1770, a decision that angered many patriots, she supported him. Running the farm and the family. When John left for the First Continental Congress in 1774, Abigail stayed in Braintree to run the farm and teach their children, a role the National Women’s History Museum calls “deputy husband.” Married women then had few property rights, yet she began to call the family property her own, made profitable investments in war bonds, ran a small business importing European goods, and bought land her husband had not approved. The American Yawp describes her managing planting and harvest in the middle of severe labor shortages and inflation. Witness to the war. Her letters reported British and American movements around Boston. On June 17, 1775, she took her son John Quincy to the top of Penn’s Hill to watch the Battle of Bunker Hill. Abroad and in the capital. John Adams went to France in 1778 and stayed in Europe for most of the next decade. Abigail joined him and spent four years in France and England while he served as minister to Great Britain; the Park Service dates her stay from 1784 to 1788, while the National Women’s History Museum writes 1783 to 1788. During his vice presidency and presidency she moved between Braintree and the successive capitals of New York, Philadelphia, and Washington. In November 1800 she and John became the first residents of the Executive Mansion, today’s White House. “Remember the Ladies.” In a long letter written between March 31 and April 5, 1776, between news of Boston and an epidemic among her neighbors’ children, Abigail wrote: “I long to hear that you have declared an independency -- and by the way in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could.” She used the patriots’ own argument against them: women, too, would refuse to obey laws “in which we have no voice, or Representation.” John replied that he could only laugh at her “extraordinary Code of Laws,” joking that “We know better than to repeal our Masculine systems.” Slavery. In the same letter she doubted that “the passion for Liberty cannot be Eaquelly Strong in the Breasts of those who have been accustomed to deprive their fellow Creatures of theirs.” Elsewhere she wished “that there was not a slave in the province.” Women’s education. She was among the first advocates of equal education for women and of women’s property rights. “If we mean to have Heroes, Statesmen and Philosophers,” she wrote, “we should have learned women.” Like many of her generation she embraced what historians call Republican Motherhood, the belief that mothers shaped the virtue of future citizens. As First Lady, Abigail was widely believed to steer her husband’s decisions, and opponents mocked her as “Mrs. President.” The Park Service notes that she actually disagreed with his policy of neutrality toward France, but the belief that she set his policies weakened him politically. She supported the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, which aimed to restrict foreign influence and to weaken the opposition press, because she felt the press was undermining her husband; the acts proved very unpopular and contributed to his defeat in 1800. After the 1800 election the Adamses retired to Quincy, where Abigail advised her son John Quincy as he rose to be a senator, minister to Russia, and secretary of state. She died of typhoid fever on October 28, 1818. John wrote, “I wish I could lay down beside her and die too.” Her grandson Charles Francis Adams published her letters in 1848. The Park Service quotes President Harry Truman as saying she “would have been a better President than her husband.” Abigail Adams’s letters are among the richest records of the Revolutionary era, and they show how a woman with no formal role shaped events through intelligence, management, and argument. Her “Remember the Ladies” letter is one of the earliest and best-known American appeals for women’s rights. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If perticuliar care and attention is not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation. title: Abraham Lincoln
subtitle: Sixteenth president, who preserved the Union and ended slavery
summary: Abraham Lincoln rose from a one-room log cabin on the Kentucky frontier to become the sixteenth president of the United States. Elected in 1860 as the first Republican president, he led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and pushed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery through Congress. He was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth in April 1865, days after the war’s end. Historians and the public alike rank him as the nation’s greatest president.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Abraham Lincoln
aliases: Lincoln Honest Abe Great Emancipator Lincoln-Douglas debates Gettysburg Address House Divided
themeText: The presidency Slavery and emancipation War and the military Parties and elections Constitution and law
text: Abraham Lincoln Hardin County, Kentucky Washington, D.C. Illinois lawyer and legislator U.S. representative (1847–1849) Sixteenth president (1861–1865) First Republican president Born February 12, 1809, in a one-room log cabin in Hardin County, Kentucky Party Whig, then Republican from 1856; the first Republican president Lincoln–Douglas debates Seven debates in the 1858 Illinois Senate race, which he lost but which made him a national figure Elections 1860 (180 electoral votes of 303) and 1864 (55 percent of the popular vote) Great speeches House Divided (1858), Gettysburg Address (1863), Second Inaugural (1865) Death Shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865; died the next morning Lincoln saved the Union and destroyed slavery, and he did both by appealing to the nation’s founding ideals, above all the Declaration’s promise that all men are created equal. His wartime presidency also transformed the office, setting precedents for presidential power in a national emergency that historians still debate. Abraham Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809, in a one-room log cabin with a dirt floor in Hardin County, Kentucky. His father, Thomas, a farmer and carpenter who could barely sign his name, moved the family to the Indiana frontier when Abraham was seven. His mother, Nancy Hanks, died when he was nine; his stepmother, Sarah Bush Johnston, encouraged his education and took his side in his frequent arguments with his father. Abraham grew up with farm chores and little schooling, reading by firelight. At nineteen he built a flatboat and took a load of produce down the Mississippi to New Orleans, then dutifully, if resentfully, handed his earnings to his father. In 1831, at twenty-two, he struck out on his own in the village of New Salem, Illinois. Six feet four inches tall and strong enough to win a wrestling match against the town bully, he clerked in a store, served as postmaster, worked as a surveyor, and split rails, and his wit and his ability to read and write made him a popular figure. He volunteered in the Black Hawk War of 1832, and his company elected him captain, an honor he later said meant more to him than his nomination for president; he saw no fighting. He lost his first race for the state legislature that year, though he won 277 of the 300 votes cast in New Salem, and then won four terms from 1834 to 1840 as a Whig who favored roads, canals, and a state bank. He taught himself law, received his license in 1837, and moved to Springfield, where he became one of the most successful lawyers in Illinois. As a young legislator Lincoln was one of only six members, out of eighty-three, who voted against a 1837 resolution condemning abolitionists. Elected to Congress in 1846, he challenged President James Polk’s claim that Mexico had started the Mexican-American War on American soil, an unpopular stand at home, and served only a single term. After several years practicing law, he returned to politics in 1854, and in 1856 he joined the new Republican Party, which was dedicated to repealing the Kansas-Nebraska Act and stopping the spread of slavery into the West. In 1858 the Republicans nominated Lincoln for the Senate against Stephen A. Douglas, the Democratic “Little Giant.” He opened with his “House Divided” speech: “A house divided against itself cannot stand,” he warned; the nation could not remain permanently half slave and half free. In seven debates across Illinois, followed by reporters from around the country, Lincoln insisted that slavery was a moral wrong that violated the Declaration of Independence and must not spread, while Douglas defended letting each territory decide. The state legislature, which then chose senators, returned Douglas by 54 votes to 46, but the contest made Lincoln a national leader of his party. At the Republican convention in Chicago in May 1860, Lincoln trailed the favorite, Senator William H. Seward of New York, on the first ballot but won on the third. The Democrats split, with Northern Democrats nominating Douglas and Southern Democrats John C. Breckinridge, and a new Constitutional Union Party nominated John Bell. Lincoln, who was not on the ballot in any Southern state, carried all but one free state and won 180 electoral votes, a clear majority, against 72 for Breckinridge, 39 for Bell, and 12 for Douglas. Before he took office, seven states of the Lower South seceded and formed the Confederate States of America. In his inaugural address of March 4, 1861, Lincoln promised not to interfere with slavery where it existed but vowed to hold federal property, and pleaded, “We must not be enemies.” When he sent unarmed ships to resupply Fort Sumter, Jefferson Davis ordered the fort attacked; it surrendered after thirty-three hours, and the war began. As commander in chief, Lincoln adopted General Winfield Scott’s Anaconda strategy of blockade and encirclement and kept the four slaveholding border states in the Union. He replaced general after general, frustrated by commanders like George McClellan and George Meade who let Lee’s army escape after victories at Antietam and Gettysburg, until he found in Ulysses S. Grant a general who would press the enemy relentlessly. His administration also built the modern American state: it financed the war with greenbacks, the first federal income tax, national banks, and $2.6 billion in loans, and it passed the Homestead Act and the Morrill Act creating land-grant colleges. Lincoln moved step by step toward emancipation. At first he insisted that his purpose was to save the Union, not to free the slaves, and he proposed compensated, gradual emancipation in the border states, which they refused. But thousands of enslaved people were escaping to Union lines, Black Northerners and Radical Republicans demanded action, and emancipation would make it hard for Britain or France to recognize the Confederacy. On July 22, 1862, he told his cabinet he would issue an emancipation proclamation as a war measure, and after the Union victory at Antietam he announced it; on January 1, 1863, he declared all enslaved people in the rebellious areas “forever free” and opened the army to Black men. By the war’s end more than 180,000 Black soldiers had served. At Gettysburg in November 1863 he redefined the war in a few short paragraphs as a struggle for “a new birth of freedom.” Reelected in 1864 with 55 percent of the vote, helped by Sherman’s capture of Atlanta and the votes of Union soldiers, he used every power of his office to push the Thirteenth Amendment through the House, which passed it on January 31, 1865. Lincoln hated slavery, which he believed mocked the Declaration of Independence and threatened the survival of the Union. Yet he was also a careful politician who compromised on the issue for most of his career. He identified with antislavery forces that opposed slavery’s expansion rather than with abolitionists who demanded its immediate end, and he believed the Constitution gave the federal government no power to touch slavery where it already existed. He was a believer in “free labor”: every man, Black or white, had the right to the fruits of his own work. He held that the Union was permanent and secession legally void, and that the right of revolution existed only against real oppression, which the South could not claim. Lincoln’s views on race reflected many of the prejudices of his time. In the 1858 debates, under attack from Douglas, he said that he opposed giving Black Americans the right to vote, serve on juries, or hold office, and for years he supported the voluntary colonization of freed people abroad, even funding failed projects in Central America and Haiti. Only near the end of his life, on April 11, 1865, did he publicly endorse voting rights for some Black men. His use of power was also hotly contested. He called up troops, spent money without congressional approval, and suspended the writ of habeas corpus; between fifteen and twenty thousand civilians, mostly in the border states, were arrested on suspicion of disloyalty. The antiwar Democrat Clement Vallandigham was convicted by a military court for his speeches, and after the war the Supreme Court ruled that military trials of civilians where civilian courts were open were unconstitutional. Lincoln defended his actions as emergency measures, asking whether it made sense “to lose the nation and yet preserve the Constitution.” On April 3, 1865, Lincoln walked through the streets of Richmond, the fallen Confederate capital, cheered by crowds of freed people. Six days later Lee surrendered at Appomattox. On the evening of April 14, while Lincoln watched the comedy Our American Cousin at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, the actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot him in the back of the head; Lincoln died the next morning. Booth, who had decided to kill the president after hearing him endorse Black suffrage, was cornered in a Virginia barn, where he either shot himself or was killed, and four of his co-conspirators were hanged. Lincoln’s funeral train carried his body some 1,700 miles back to Springfield, as crowds gathered along the route to mourn him. Within days of his death, Americans began to see Lincoln as a martyr and the “Great Emancipator.” Historians, too, have ranked him first among the presidents: in a 1982 survey of forty-nine historians and political scientists he led in every category. His greatest achievements, in their judgment, were the preservation of the Union, the vindication of democracy, and the death of slavery. His home in Springfield is preserved today as the Lincoln Home National Historic Site. A house divided against itself cannot stand. title: Alexander Hamilton
subtitle: First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system
summary: Alexander Hamilton was born in the British West Indies, came to the mainland colonies as a teenager, and became one of the most influential of the nation’s founders. He served as George Washington’s aide during the Revolution, helped call the Constitutional Convention, and wrote most of the Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution. As the first secretary of the Treasury, from 1789 to 1795, he paid the Revolutionary War debts in full, had the federal government take over the states’ debts, and created the First Bank of the United States. His program and his preference for Britain divided the government and helped create the first political parties. He was killed in a duel with Vice President Aaron Burr in 1804.

aliases: Federalist Party Report on Public Credit assumption First Bank of the United States Hamilton-Burr duel Publius
themeText: Economy and finance Constitution and law Parties and elections Immigration
text: Alexander Hamilton Charlestown, Nevis, British West Indies New York City Aide-de-camp to George Washington (1777–1781) Member of the Continental Congress Delegate to the Constitutional Convention (1787) Principal author of the Federalist Papers First secretary of the Treasury (1789–1795) Lawyer in New York City Born January 11, 1757 (or perhaps 1755), Charlestown, Nevis, British West Indies Revolution Artillery captain in 1776; aide-de-camp to Washington, March 1777 to February 1781 Constitution Helped call the Constitutional Convention; wrote most of the 85 Federalist essays Treasury First secretary of the Treasury, 1789–1795: debt funding, assumption of state debts, the Bank, excise taxes Family Married Elizabeth Schuyler during the Revolution; built The Grange in upper Manhattan, completed in 1802 Death Mortally wounded by Aaron Burr in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, July 11, 1804; died July 12 Hamilton designed the financial foundations of the federal government. He established the public credit of the United States, created its first national bank, and argued for a broad reading of the Constitution’s powers, a view the Supreme Court later echoed. His vision of a commercial, industrial nation tied to a strong central government, set against Jefferson’s agrarian republic, defined one of the most lasting debates in American politics. Alexander Hamilton was born in Charlestown on the Caribbean island of Nevis, in the British West Indies. The Historical Society of the New York Courts gives his birth date as January 11, 1757, “or perhaps 1755,” and the year is still disputed. His early education came from his mother and a local clergyman. As a poor orphan he worked as a clerk for a shipping company that was partly involved in the slave trade, and the National Park Service notes that he saw the cruel treatment of enslaved people on the island’s sugar plantations at first hand. Local mentors raised money to send him north. In 1772 he attended an academy in Elizabethtown, New Jersey, and then studied at King’s College, now Columbia University, in New York. When the Revolution began, Hamilton joined the Continental Army in New York in 1776 as a captain of artillery. On March 1, 1777, Washington made him an aide-de-camp, and he served on the general’s staff until February 16, 1781. During the war he married Elizabeth Schuyler, the daughter of a wealthy and influential New York family whose estates were worked by enslaved people. The Park Service notes that Hamilton had to reconcile his disapproval of slavery with his ties to the Schuylers and to Washington. After the war New York relaxed its rules for veterans who had broken off their legal studies to fight, and in July 1782 Hamilton was admitted to the bar. He opened a law office on Wall Street once the British left New York City and became one of the state’s leading lawyers. He served in the Continental Congress in 1782, 1783, and 1788. Making the Constitution. Hamilton believed the Articles of Confederation left the nation dangerously weak. In 1786 he and James Madison wrote the report of the Annapolis Convention that called on the states to send delegates to Philadelphia to revise the Articles. At the Constitutional Convention, on June 18, 1787, he offered his own plan, calling the British government “the best in the world” and proposing an executive and senators who would serve for life during good behavior. The convention did not adopt it. To win ratification in New York, he enlisted John Jay and James Madison to write a series of newspaper essays, published under the name “Publius” and now known as the Federalist Papers. Hamilton wrote most of the 85 essays, and he then helped bring New York to ratify. In the first essay he wrote that Americans would decide “whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force.” The Treasury. In 1789 Washington appointed Hamilton the first secretary of the Treasury, and he built the department. He faced a chaotic treasury and heavy war debts. “The debt of the United States,” he wrote, “was the price of liberty,” and he insisted it be repaid in full. His plan had three parts. First, the federal government would assume the states’ remaining war debts, about $25 million. Second, the government would redeem Revolutionary bonds at face value, paying whoever held them. Since many veterans had sold their bonds cheaply, this meant speculators would profit, and Madison and Jefferson objected. Third, a national bank would hold federal funds and provide credit. Southerners who had already paid their own debts resisted assumption. Hamilton won it by agreeing, in a bargain struck at a dinner at Jefferson’s house, to support placing the permanent capital on the Potomac River. By the end of 1794, 98 percent of the country’s domestic debt had been converted into new federal bonds. To pay the interest he created a revenue system based on customs duties and excise taxes, including a 1791 tax on whiskey. Hamilton believed that tying the fortunes of wealthy creditors to the government would give them a stake in its success, and that a funded debt would circulate like money, as “an engine of business.” The Bank and the Constitution. Jefferson and Madison argued that the Constitution gave Congress no power to charter a bank. Hamilton answered with an opinion of some 13,000 words, arguing that every power granted to a government includes “a right to employ all the means requisite and fairly applicable” to carry it out. Washington signed the bill on February 25, 1791, creating the First Bank of the United States, which served as the Treasury’s financial agent and issued paper currency. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Marshall unanimously upheld a later national bank, taking a similarly broad view of the powers of Congress. He also proposed a national mint, though it was placed under the State Department in 1792. Hamilton wanted a strong, energetic national government. He believed that self-interest was the “most powerful incentive of human actions” and that a wise government should harness citizens’ desire for property to serve the public good. He saw America’s future as a commercial and industrial society, in contrast to Jefferson’s nation of small farmers. The American Yawp argues that his vision proved the more enduring. He did not think government should equalize property, and he wrote that it must be “a Repository of the Rights of the wealthy.” In foreign policy he favored close commercial ties with Britain. He disapproved of slavery. In the 1780s he helped found the New York Manumission Society, which campaigned for abolition and in 1794 established the African Free School, which educated enslaved and free Black students. Hamilton’s opponents saw his program as a scheme to enrich speculators and northern financiers. Jefferson became convinced that Hamilton secretly favored monarchy and aristocracy, and the two men fought constantly inside Washington’s cabinet. Hamilton sometimes went around the secretary of state. Encyclopedia Virginia says he privately assured the British minister that the administration would not stand firm on Jefferson’s demands. Washington usually sided with Hamilton, and the quarrel helped produce the first party system, with Hamilton’s Federalists against Jefferson and Madison’s Republicans. The whiskey tax fell hardest on western farmers, and when armed farmers in western Pennsylvania attacked tax collectors in July 1794, Hamilton rode west with the militia army and oversaw the arrest and trial of rebels. Most were released or pardoned. Hamilton resigned in 1795, partly because his $3,500 salary could not support his family, but he remained Washington’s adviser and helped draft the 1796 Farewell Address. His feud with John Adams, the leader of his own party, damaged the Federalists. The Miller Center’s Jefferson essay states that in 1796 he influenced South Carolina’s electors to withhold votes from Adams. Its Adams essay is more cautious, saying that many believed he sought to do so. In October 1800 he published a pamphlet arguing that Adams should not be reelected. When Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied in the electoral vote that year, Hamilton urged the House to choose Jefferson, whom he disliked, over Burr, whom he considered an unprincipled opportunist. In 1801 Hamilton commissioned The Grange, a Federal-style country house on a 32-acre estate in upper Manhattan, named for his father’s ancestral home in Scotland. It was completed in 1802. In 1804, while arguing a libel case in Albany, he remarked at a dinner that Burr was a dangerous man who should not be trusted with power. The remark was reported in letters printed in the Albany Register, and the long bitterness between the two men came to a head. On July 11, 1804, they met in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey. Burr mortally wounded Hamilton, who died in New York City the next day. Burr was indicted for murder, and his political career was over. Elizabeth Hamilton continued to use The Grange for thirty years after his death, and the house is now preserved as Hamilton Grange National Memorial. Hamilton’s institutions outlived him. The Treasury Department he designed, the public credit he established, and the doctrine of implied powers became lasting parts of the federal government. So did the argument he started with Jefferson over how strong the national government should be. The debt of the United States ... was the price of liberty.
