title: Henry Ford
subtitle: Automaker who put America on wheels with the Model T, the moving assembly line, and the Five Dollar Day
summary: Henry Ford did not invent the automobile or the assembly line, but more than anyone else he turned the car from a rich man’s novelty into a machine for the multitude. His Model T of 1908 was cheap, rugged, and easy to fix; his moving assembly line of 1913 cut its assembly time dramatically; and his Five Dollar Day of 1914 doubled workers’ pay so that they could buy the cars they built. Ford became a folk hero, and also one of the most notorious antisemites in American history, whose newspaper spread conspiracy theories that the Nazis admired.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Henry Ford, about 1919
aliases: Ford Model T assembly line Five Dollar Day Ford Motor Company
themeText: Economy and finance Science and technology Labor and work Everyday life
text: Henry Ford Dearborn, Michigan Engineer, Edison Electric Illuminating Company Founder of Ford Motor Company (1903) Owner of *The Dearborn Independent* Ford Motor Company Founded June 16, 1903, after two failed car companies Model T Introduced October 1, 1908; about 15 million sold before production ended in 1927 Assembly line 1913: chassis assembly time cut from 12.5 hours to 1.5 Five Dollar Day January 1914: double the going factory wage, for an eight-hour day “The International Jew” Antisemitic series in his Dearborn Independent, 1920–1922 Ford’s methods of mass production and mass consumption (standardized products, assembly lines, and high wages that let workers buy what they made) became a model for twentieth-century industry. His career also shows how fame and wealth could amplify hatred: his antisemitic publications circulated worldwide for decades. Henry Ford was born on July 30, 1863, on a farm in what is now Dearborn, Michigan. As a boy he showed a gift for machinery, a talent for leadership, and a preference for learning by trial and error. At sixteen he left the farm to find work in Detroit. In 1888 he married Clara Bryant, and in 1891 they moved to Detroit, where he became an engineer for the Edison Electric Illuminating Company, the only steady job he ever held. In his spare time he built his first car, the Quadricycle, in 1896: four bicycle-style wheels, a tiller instead of a steering wheel, and two forward speeds with no reverse. He sold it for $200 and used the money to build another. Ford’s first two car companies failed. In 1901 his racing car beat the era’s top driver, and on June 16, 1903, a new group of investors founded the Ford Motor Company; its first Model A sold on July 23, and by October the company had turned a profit. Ford wanted “a motorcar for the great multitude,” and on October 1, 1908, he introduced the Model T: simple, durable, built of light, strong vanadium steel for rough roads, and easy to operate and repair. To keep up with demand, Ford adapted methods from other industries and in 1913 introduced the moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant, eventually cutting the time to assemble a Model T chassis from 12.5 hours to 1.5. Workers hated the endless, repetitive labor, and turnover soared. Ford’s answer, in January 1914, was his boldest move: the Five Dollar Day, double the existing factory wage, for a shorter eight-hour day. The day after it was announced, some 10,000 people lined up outside his employment office. The policy stabilized his workforce and let his workers buy the cars they built. By 1925 his factories turned out a Model T every ten seconds, and some 15 million were sold before production ended in 1927. In 1917 he began building the River Rouge complex, which became the largest integrated factory in the world, with its own steel mills, glass factory, and power plant. Ford idealized small-town, rural life even as his factories transformed industrial America, and he blamed immigrants for the problems he associated with cities. He was a pacifist: in 1915 he chartered a “Peace Ship” to Europe in a failed attempt to end World War I, and he opposed American entry into World War II. He was also fiercely anti-union and held out against the United Auto Workers until 1941. Ford used his fame to spread antisemitism. After the failure of his Peace Ship, which the press mocked as a “Ship of Fools,” he blamed Jews for the war. In 1918 he bought a weekly newspaper, The Dearborn Independent, and from May 1920 it ran a series called “The International Jew,” drawing on the forged Protocols of the Elders of Zion to claim a Jewish conspiracy to control the world. Ford dealers were required to distribute the paper, and it was reissued as books translated into more than a dozen languages. After a libel suit by a Jewish lawyer, Aaron Sapiro, ended in a mistrial in 1927, Ford signed a public apology and closed the paper, but the books kept circulating. Adolf Hitler praised him in Mein Kampf, and in 1938 the Nazi government awarded him the Grand Cross of the German Eagle. His long resistance to unions also brought years of conflict with his workers. In 1919, after battles with his stockholders, Ford bought them out so that his family controlled the company. After his son Edsel died in 1943, the elderly Ford returned as president until his grandson Henry Ford II took over in 1945. Ford died in 1947. His Model T and assembly line made the automobile part of everyday American life; his museum and Greenfield Village in Dearborn preserve his collections. His antisemitic writings, however, are still in circulation today. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tQAFS1d-0hY Henry Ford: The Boy Who Hated Horses - US History - Part 1 - Extra History Extra History 11:41 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RhP-HdZJkIY Henry Ford: The Complicated Captain of Industry Biographics 23:07 2026-10-22

title: Ida B. Wells
subtitle: Journalist who exposed lynching and fought for civil rights and suffrage
summary: Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Mississippi in 1862 and became the leading crusader against lynching in American history. After a Memphis mob lynched three Black grocers, one of them her close friend, in 1892, she investigated lynchings across the South. In Southern Horrors and A Red Record she exposed the charge of rape used to justify them as a myth. A white mob destroyed her newspaper, and she carried her campaign to the North and to Britain. In Chicago she helped found Black women’s clubs, helped organize the NAACP, and fought for women’s suffrage. In 2020 she was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Ida B. Wells
aliases: Ida B. Wells-Barnett Iola Princess of the Press Southern Horrors A Red Record Alpha Suffrage Club
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Women's history Voting rights Reform and protest
text: Ida Bell Wells-Barnett Holly Springs, Mississippi Chicago, Illinois Teacher Journalist and newspaper owner (“Iola”) Anti-lynching crusader Suffragist and founder of the Alpha Suffrage Club Co-founder of Black women’s organizations and an organizer of the NAACP Born July 16, 1862, Holly Springs, Mississippi, enslaved Train protest Forcibly removed from a first-class car in May 1884; won in a lower court, lost on appeal to the Tennessee Supreme Court Newspaper Co-owner and editor of the Memphis Free Speech, destroyed by a mob in 1892 Writings Southern Horrors (1892), The Reason Why (1893), A Red Record (1895) Suffrage Founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago, January 30, 1913 Died March 1931, Chicago (sources give March 15 and March 25) Honors Pulitzer Prize special citation, 2020 Wells used investigative journalism, statistics, and the reports of white newspapers themselves to expose lynching and the excuses made for it. She linked the fight against racial violence to the fight for women’s votes, and her career shows how Black women shaped both the civil rights and suffrage movements. Ida Bell Wells was born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on July 16, 1862, the oldest daughter of James and Elizabeth (Lizzie) Wells. She and her parents were freed at the end of the Civil War. During Reconstruction her parents were active in the Republican Party, and her father helped found Rust College, a historically Black college, where she studied. In the fall of 1878 yellow fever killed both of her parents and one of her siblings. At sixteen she became the main support of her six surviving brothers and sisters, persuading a school official that she was eighteen so she could get a job as a teacher. In 1882 she moved with her sisters to Memphis, Tennessee, to live with an aunt, and she taught in the city’s segregated schools. In May 1884, riding the train with a first-class ticket, she was ordered out of the ladies’ car. She refused, bit a crew member, and was dragged off the train while white passengers, she later wrote, “stood on the seats so that they could get a good view and continued applauding the conductor.” She sued the railroad and won $500 in a lower court, but the Tennessee Supreme Court reversed the decision. (The National Park Service places the ride between Memphis and Nashville, while the National Women’s History Museum describes it as her commute to a school in Shelby County, on May 4, 1884.) The case launched her career as a writer. Under the pen name “Iola” she wrote for Black newspapers on race and politics, earning the nicknames “Princess of the Press” and “The Brilliant Iola.” In 1889 she became a partner and editor of the Memphis Free Speech and Headlight. In 1891 she was fired from her teaching job after criticizing conditions in the city’s Black schools, and she turned to journalism full time. The Memphis lynching. In 1892 a white mob lynched Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell, and a third man (the National Park Service names him Will Stewart, the National Women’s History Museum Henry Steward). They owned the People’s Grocery, which had drawn customers from a white-owned store. After a clash with white men, they were jailed, and a mob took them from their cells and killed them. Moss was Wells’s close friend. She investigated, wrote articles condemning the killings, and at the risk of her own life began traveling the South to document other lynchings. “The old thread-bare lie.” On May 21, 1892, Free Speech published an editorial listing eight recent lynchings and declaring, “Nobody in this section of the country believes the old thread-bare lie that Negro men rape white women.” White newspapers called for violence against the writer, and a mob destroyed the paper’s office and press. Wells was away, in New York according to the National Park Service or visiting Oklahoma according to the National Women’s History Museum, and with her life threatened she stayed in the North. From the North she published a long report in T. Thomas Fortune’s New York Age and then the pamphlet Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases (1892). Quoting the white press’s own reports, she described how lynch mobs formed and exploded the excuses offered for them, above all the claim that Black men were raping white women, which the American Yawp calls the myth of the Black rapist. “A Winchester rifle should have a place of honor in every black home,” she wrote, “and it should be used for that protection which the law refuses to give.” A Red Record. In 1893 Wells moved to Chicago, where she and Frederick Douglass protested the exclusion of Black Americans from the World’s Columbian Exposition with the pamphlet The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World’s Columbian Exposition. She lectured in Britain in 1893 and 1894, inspiring the formation of the London Anti-Lynching Committee. In 1895 she published A Red Record, a statistical history of lynchings for 1892–1894. “The first demand,” she explained, “is for facts and figures.” Later, she and her allies hired a white private detective to investigate the lynching of Sam Hose in Georgia and published his report as Lynch Law in Georgia. In 1898 she took the anti-lynching campaign to President William McKinley. Clubs, the NAACP, and the vote. In 1895 she married the Chicago lawyer and editor Ferdinand L. Barnett, with whom she had four children. She kept her own name alongside his, which few women then did. She helped found the National Association of Colored Women and other Black women’s organizations, and in 1909 the Negro Fellowship League in Chicago, which offered housing, job help, education, and legal advice to working-class Black residents. In 1909 she presented “Lynching, Our National Crime” to the conference that led to the NAACP. On January 30, 1913, she founded the Alpha Suffrage Club, which organized Black women in Chicago to elect candidates who would serve their community. Its work helped win the Illinois Equal Suffrage Act that June. At the 1913 women’s suffrage parade in Washington, organizers told Black women to march at the back to avoid offending white Southerners. Wells refused, waited on the sidelines, and joined the march when the Chicago contingent of white women passed. Wells believed that exposing the facts was the most powerful weapon against injustice, and that Black Americans had the right to defend themselves when the law would not. She held that the fight for women’s rights must include Black women. She respected Susan B. Anthony’s pioneering work but criticized her for not putting Black women’s concerns first in order to keep white women’s support. She was wary of reform organizations she found too cautious. The Library of Congress notes her skepticism of the early NAACP’s white leadership and moderate stance. Wells’s outspokenness put her at odds with allies as well as enemies. After her 1892 editorial, a white Memphis newspaper called its unknown writer a “black scoundrel” and warned that “we have had enough of it.” The sources describe her role in the NAACP differently. The NAACP lists her among the signers of the 1909 call that founded it, and the National Park Service considers her a founder. The National Women’s History Museum notes that she was left off the list of the “Founding Forty” chosen at the conference. The Library of Congress says she helped organize the association but, skeptical of its white leadership and moderate stance, became inactive after 1912. In 1915 she joined William Monroe Trotter’s delegation protesting segregation to President Woodrow Wilson. In 1918 she protested to Wilson against an army order telling Black soldiers to stay out of public places where they were resented. Her letter on behalf of the Negro Fellowship League called it as vicious and undemocratic an order as any issued in the armies fighting Germany and urged Wilson to “protect American soldiers in Democracy at home before sending them abroad in Democracy’s War.” Wells ran unsuccessfully to be a delegate to the 1918 Republican National Convention and for the Illinois State Senate in 1930. She died of kidney disease in Chicago in March 1931. The National Women’s History Museum gives the date as March 15, the National Park Service as March 25. Her autobiography, Crusade for Justice, was published in 1970, and only then, the Museum notes, did her achievements begin to be fully recognized. Her Chicago home became a National Historic Landmark in 1974. In 2020 the Pulitzer Prize board gave her a special citation “for her outstanding and courageous reporting on the horrific and vicious violence against African Americans during the era of lynching.” Nobody in this section of the country believes the old thread-bare lie that Negro men rape white women. title: Jackie Robinson
subtitle: The ballplayer who broke baseball’s color barrier in 1947, and a civil rights advocate
summary: On April 15, 1947, Jackie Robinson took the field for the Brooklyn Dodgers and became the first African American player in the twentieth century in the American or National League. Chosen by Dodgers executive Branch Rickey, he endured hostile crowds, opposed teammates, and threats while starring on the field: Rookie of the Year in 1947, Most Valuable Player in 1949, and six pennants in ten seasons. After retiring he became an outspoken advocate for civil rights.
thumbAlt: Jackie Robinson in the uniform of the Kansas City Monarchs
aliases: Jack Roosevelt Robinson
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Arts and popular culture
text: Jack Roosevelt Robinson Cairo, Georgia Stamford, Connecticut Kansas City Monarchs, Negro Leagues (1945) Brooklyn Dodgers (1947–1956) Civil rights advocate Major league debut April 15, 1947, Brooklyn Dodgers Honors Rookie of the Year (1947); National League MVP (1949); Hall of Fame (1962) Career .313 batting average, 1,563 hits, 200 stolen bases Dodgers success Six pennants in his ten seasons and the 1955 World Series title Remembered Every major league team celebrates Jackie Robinson Day on April 15 Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born on January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia, the youngest of five children of sharecroppers Jerry and Mallie Robinson. His father left the family when Jackie was an infant, and in 1920 his mother moved the children by train to Pasadena, California, where she worked as a domestic. The Robinsons bought a house in a mostly white neighborhood; neighbors petitioned to get rid of them and harassed the family for years. Athletic talent ran in the family, his older brother Mack finished second to Jesse Owens in the 200 at the 1936 Olympics, then could find work only as a city janitor. At UCLA Robinson became the school’s first four-sport letterman, in baseball, basketball, football, and track, and won the NCAA long-jump title; there he met Rachel Isum, whom he married in 1946. Money troubles forced him to leave college in 1941. Drafted in 1942, he became an Army officer. In July 1944, at Camp Hood, Texas, he refused a bus driver’s order to move to the back of an Army bus, the War Department had already banned segregation on military buses. He was court-martialed, acquitted of all charges, and honorably discharged. In 1945 he played shortstop for the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro Leagues. Brooklyn Dodgers president Branch Rickey chose Robinson to break baseball’s unwritten color line: for his talent, but also because he was college-educated, had competed with and against white athletes, and could stand the spotlight. In their now-legendary meeting, Rickey extracted a promise that Robinson would hold his temper and not fight back. The signing was announced on October 23, 1945. In 1946, with the Montreal Royals, the Dodgers’ top farm club, Robinson led the International League with a .349 average and carried the Royals to the pennant; more than a million fans came to watch them. On April 15, 1947, he started at first base for Brooklyn. He hit .297, led the league in stolen bases, helped the Dodgers win the pennant, and won the first Rookie of the Year award. Two years later he was the National League’s Most Valuable Player, leading the league with a .342 average and 37 steals. His real weapon was the base paths: taking huge leads, faking steals, and rattling pitchers into mistakes, he stole home 19 times in his career, including a famous steal in Game 1 of the 1955 World Series, the year Brooklyn won its first championship. The Dodgers won six pennants in his ten seasons. After the 1956 season the club traded him to the rival New York Giants; Robinson, who had already decided to quit, announced his retirement in Look magazine instead. After baseball he became a vice president of the Chock Full o’Nuts coffee company, chaired Freedom National Bank, which lent to Black customers ignored by established banks, wrote a newspaper column, and campaigned for civil rights. In 1962 he was elected to the Hall of Fame on the first ballot, its first African American member. “A life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives,” Robinson said. He kept his promise to Rickey through his early seasons, but he was by nature proud and aggressive, and in later years he spoke out sharply against discrimination in baseball and beyond. He supported Martin Luther King Jr. and the NAACP and wrote to Presidents Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson about civil rights. In 1960 he endorsed Richard Nixon over John F. Kennedy, saying Kennedy had not made it “his business to know colored people”, a choice he reportedly came to regret. His wife, Rachel, later stressed his role as “an informal civil rights leader.” Robinson’s arrival was fiercely resisted. Before the 1947 season some Dodgers circulated a petition against playing with him, which Rickey and manager Leo Durocher shut down. Pitchers threw at his head, a Cardinals star appeared to try to injure him with his spikes, he received death threats, and the Philadelphia Phillies, led by manager Ben Chapman, taunted him so viciously that Robinson later said it brought him “nearer to cracking up than I had ever been.” The abuse backfired: public anger at Chapman ran so high that he had to ask Robinson to pose for a photograph with him. His last years in Brooklyn were unhappy: he disliked owner Walter O’Malley, who had forced Rickey out, and as he grew more outspoken the club hoped he would quietly step aside. Robinson suffered from diabetes in his later years and died of a heart attack on October 24, 1972, at fifty-three. Thousands lined the streets of Harlem and Brooklyn for his funeral procession. In 1987 the Rookie of the Year award was renamed for him, and on April 15, 1997, the fiftieth anniversary of his debut, his number 42 was retired by every major league team. Martin Luther King Jr. said, “Jackie Robinson made my success possible. Without him, I would never have been able to do what I did.” Robinson integrated the national pastime in 1947, showing millions of Americans what equal opportunity could look like, and then used his fame to press for civil rights. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-VE0-ynbg4A Jackie Robinson: The First African American to Play in the MLB | Mini Bio | BIO Biography 4:16 2026-10-22

title: James Madison
subtitle: Architect of the Constitution and fourth president
summary: James Madison, a Virginia planter and enslaver, did more than anyone to design the Constitution of the United States. His exertions earned him the title “Father of the Constitution,” though he insisted the document was the work of “many heads & many hands.” He drafted the Virginia Plan that framed the Convention’s debates, wrote twenty-nine of the Federalist Papers, and steered the Bill of Rights through the first Congress. With Thomas Jefferson he founded the Republican Party, which opposed Hamilton’s Federalists. As Jefferson’s secretary of state and then as president from 1809 to 1817, he led the country through the troubled years before and during the War of 1812.
thumbAlt: Portrait of James Madison
aliases: Father of the Constitution Virginia Plan Publius Helvidius Mr. Madison’s War Virginia Resolutions
themeText: Constitution and law Political thought The presidency Parties and elections Slavery and emancipation War and the military
text: James Madison Jr. Port Conway, Virginia Montpelier, Virginia Member of the Continental Congress Delegate to the Constitutional Convention Co-author of the Federalist Papers U.S. representative who drafted the Bill of Rights Secretary of state (1801–1809) Fourth president (1809–1817) Rector of the University of Virginia Born March 16, 1751, at Belle Grove plantation, Port Conway, King George County, Virginia Education College of New Jersey (Princeton), 1769–1771 Constitution Author of the Virginia Plan (1787); wrote 29 Federalist essays; proposed the amendments that became the Bill of Rights Party Co-founder, with Jefferson, of the Republican (Democratic-Republican) Party Presidency 1809–1817; elected 1808 (122 electoral votes to 47) and 1812 (128 to 89) War of 1812 Signed the declaration of war June 18, 1812; British troops burned Washington in August 1814 Died June 28, 1836, at Montpelier Madison’s ideas about large republics, factions, and checks and balances, set out in the Federalist Papers, remain central to American constitutional thought. The Miller Center calls him the most relevant constitutional philosopher in American history. His notes of the Constitutional Convention are its most important record. James Madison was born on March 16, 1751, at Belle Grove, his mother’s family plantation at Port Conway in King George County, Virginia. He was the eldest of twelve children of James Madison Sr. and Nelly Conway Madison. He grew up on the family estate in Orange County that came to be called Montpelier, a plantation worked by a large enslaved population. After schooling from his mother, at a school run by the Reverend Donald Robertson, and from a tutor, he went in 1769 to the College of New Jersey, now Princeton, rather than the College of William and Mary. He finished four years of study in three, getting by on “the minimum of sleep & maximum of study.” Under the college’s president, John Witherspoon, he absorbed the philosophy of the Scottish Enlightenment and read Hume, Adam Smith, and Montesquieu. He graduated in 1771 and stayed on to study Hebrew, perhaps thinking of the ministry. Back in Virginia, often in poor health and without direction, Madison found his cause in the Revolution and in religious liberty. In December 1774 he joined the Orange County Committee of Safety, and in 1776 he was elected to the Virginia Convention, which wrote the new state’s constitution. Disturbed by the persecution of Baptists, Presbyterians, and other dissenters by authorities tied to the established Anglican Church, he amended George Mason’s Virginia Declaration of Rights so that it guaranteed not mere toleration but the “full and free exercise” of religion. He lost reelection in 1777 because he refused to treat voters to whiskey, which he considered buying votes. In 1780, at twenty-nine, Madison became the youngest member of the Continental Congress, where he took copious notes and tried without success to give Congress its own revenue through a 5 percent tax on imports. In the Virginia House of Delegates he opposed Patrick Henry’s bill to tax citizens to support Christian teachers. His anonymous “Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments” (1785) argued that religion “must be left to the conviction and conscience of every man.” The bill was defeated, and in January 1786 Madison won passage of Jefferson’s Virginia Statute for Establishing Religious Freedom. The Constitution. Madison studied the failures of earlier confederacies and concluded that the United States needed a strong national republic. His Virginia Plan, adopted in May 1787 as the Convention’s agenda, proposed three branches of government and a two-house legislature based on population. He won on representation by population in the House and on separate executive and judicial branches, but he lost on equal representation in the Senate and on a congressional veto over state laws, and for a time he doubted the new government could succeed. Throughout the Convention he kept detailed notes of the debates. The Federalist. At Alexander Hamilton’s invitation, Madison wrote twenty-nine of the essays signed “Publius” between November 1787 and March 1788. In Federalist No. 10 he argued, against the common view that only small republics could last, that a large republic would contain so many factions that no single majority could easily oppress the rest: “Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests.” In Federalist No. 51 he explained the logic of checks and balances: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. … If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” In Federalist No. 54 he defended counting enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation and taxation. At the Virginia ratifying convention of June 1788 he answered Patrick Henry, and to meet George Mason’s objection that the Constitution lacked a bill of rights, he promised to make one the first business of the new Congress. The Bill of Rights. Elected to the House of Representatives, Madison became, in the Miller Center’s words, a sort of prime minister to President Washington. In June 1789 he proposed nineteen amendments. Congress reduced them to twelve, and the states ratified ten, which took effect as the Bill of Rights on December 15, 1791. Madison had wanted the changes woven into the text of the Constitution itself, but they were added as separate amendments. Party leader and secretary of state. Madison soon broke with Hamilton over the national debt, the Bank, and relations with Britain. In 1790 he and Jefferson helped broker the deal that traded Southern support for federal assumption of state debts for a capital on the Potomac. By 1792 he described the country as divided into “republican” and “anti-republican” parties, and he and Jefferson led the Republicans. He married Dolley Payne Todd, a widow, in 1794, and she became a political partner who did much to define the role of first lady. Against the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 he wrote the Virginia Resolutions, which defended freedom of the press and asserted that states might “interpose” against unconstitutional laws. As Jefferson’s secretary of state from 1801 to 1809 he oversaw the Louisiana Purchase and persuaded Jefferson to adopt the Embargo of 1807, which proved unpopular and ineffective. Madison believed that liberty was best protected not by small, homogeneous republics but by a large federal republic whose many interests would check one another, and by a government whose separate branches would restrain each other. He was a lifelong champion of religious freedom. He favored congressional over presidential power and wanted the presidency to keep a republican simplicity. Over time his views on federal power shifted. He opposed Hamilton’s national bank in 1791 but accepted a second national bank after the War of 1812. Mr. Madison’s War. As president, Madison faced British and French attacks on American shipping, British impressment of American sailors, and a Native confederacy in the Ohio Valley led by Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa. He won election in 1808 with 122 electoral votes to 47, and on June 18, 1812, he signed a declaration of war against Britain. He was reelected that fall over DeWitt Clinton, 128 electoral votes to 89, despite Federalist opposition to “Mr. Madison’s War.” His invasions of Canada failed in 1812 and did little better in 1813, though Oliver Hazard Perry won control of Lake Erie. In August 1814 British troops routed American militia at Bladensburg, occupied Washington, and burned the White House and the Capitol. Dolley Madison and the enslaved valet Paul Jennings were among those who saved Gilbert Stuart’s portrait of Washington. The defense of Fort McHenry at Baltimore inspired Francis Scott Key’s poem that became the national anthem. New England Federalists met at the Hartford Convention. The Miller Center says they considered secession, while Encyclopedia Virginia says only that the meeting prompted rumors of it. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814, cost the United States no territory and no concessions to British demands, and Andrew Jackson’s victory at New Orleans helped Americans remember the war as a triumph. Historians still debate whether Madison was a panicky wartime leader or, as some recent scholars argue, a resolute one. He had also been criticized in 1812 for spending $50,000 of public money on the papers of a British spy, John Henry, which failed to prove the Federalist plot he suspected. Slavery. Madison enslaved more than one hundred people. He called slavery an evil and supported gradual, compensated emancipation tied to resettling freed people outside the country, and in 1833 he became president of the American Colonization Society. But he did not free the people he held, he doubted that Black and white Americans could live together in freedom, and in 1834 he sold sixteen enslaved people to a relative in Louisiana to pay debts. The Miller Center calls him “an anti-slavery enslaver” whose complicity was less visible than Jefferson’s but more tangled than Washington’s, since Washington freed the people he enslaved in his will. After the war Madison, once an opponent, signed a charter for a Second Bank of the United States and accepted protective tariffs. On his last day in office he vetoed an internal improvements bill because no constitutional amendment authorized such spending. He retired to Montpelier in 1817. He advised on farming, served as rector of the University of Virginia from 1826 to 1834, and organized his notes on the Constitutional Convention, which he hoped would support Dolley after his death. In his last years he denied that his Virginia Resolutions justified South Carolina’s nullification doctrine. He died at Montpelier on June 28, 1836. His enslaved servant Paul Jennings later wrote that “he ceased breathing as quietly as the snuff of a candle goes out.” His final message urged that the “Union of the States be cherished and perpetuated.” Facing debts, Dolley later sold Montpelier and the enslaved community that lived there. Scholars usually rate Madison higher as a constitution-maker and legislator than as president. Some have asked whether George Washington, whose presence gave the Convention its legitimacy, deserves the title “Father of the Constitution” as much as Madison. The Miller Center suggests that Madison might as fairly be called a father of the nation itself, for persuading thirteen states to become one. Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens. title: Joe Biden
subtitle: Forty-sixth president, after thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as vice president
summary: Joe Biden, a working-class Catholic from Scranton who overcame a severe childhood stutter, was elected to the Senate at twenty-nine, weeks before a car crash killed his wife and baby daughter. He served thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as Barack Obama’s vice president, then defeated Donald Trump in 2020 to become, at seventy-eight, the oldest president inaugurated up to that time. He led the country through the end of the Covid-19 pandemic and signed major laws on economic relief, infrastructure, semiconductors, and clean energy, but faced high inflation, a chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan, and doubts about his age, and he withdrew from the 2024 race.
thumbAlt: Official portrait of President Joe Biden, 2021
aliases: Biden Joseph R. Biden Amtrak Joe 46th president
themeText: The presidency Parties and elections Foreign policy and diplomacy Economy and finance Public health
text: Joseph Robinette Biden Jr. Scranton, Pennsylvania U.S. Senator from Delaware (1973–2009) Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee Vice president under Barack Obama (2009–2017) Forty-sixth president (2021–2025) Presidency January 20, 2021 – January 20, 2025; Democrat 2020 election 306 electoral votes to Trump’s 232; about 81 million popular votes, 7 million more than Trump Major laws American Rescue Plan (2021), Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021), CHIPS and Science Act and Inflation Reduction Act (2022), Respect for Marriage Act (2022) Supreme Court Appointed Ketanji Brown Jackson, the first Black woman on the Court (2022) Nickname “Amtrak Joe,” for decades of daily train commutes between Wilmington and Washington Biden’s long career spanned the Senate of the 1970s to the polarized politics of the 2020s. His presidency combined major new federal investments with an effort to rebuild alliances after the Trump years; its record on the pandemic, inflation, immigration, and foreign wars remains a subject of debate. Joseph Robinette Biden Jr. was born on November 20, 1942, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, the oldest child of a working-class Irish Catholic family. When his father’s business fortunes collapsed after World War II, Joe Sr. took whatever work he could find; in 1953 he found a job selling cars and moved the family to Delaware. Young Joe had a severe stutter. Classmates at his Catholic high school mocked him as “Dash”, “I talked like Morse code,” he later wrote, and he practiced in front of a mirror, memorizing Yeats and Emerson, until he largely overcame it. As a boy of about ten he accepted a $5 dare to climb a smoldering 200-foot heap of coal-mine waste. A star halfback in high school, he went to the University of Delaware and Syracuse University law school, briefly worked for a corporate law firm, and then became a public defender in Wilmington. In 1972, at twenty-nine, he challenged a popular two-term Republican senator, J. Caleb Boggs, and won by fewer than 3,000 votes. On December 18, before he took office, a tractor trailer struck his wife Neilia’s car while she was Christmas shopping, killing her and their infant daughter, Naomi, and badly injuring their sons, Beau and Hunter. Biden considered giving up the seat; persuaded by fellow senators, he was sworn in at the hospital chapel beside his sons, and for years commuted home to Wilmington every day by train. In 1977 he married Jill Jacobs. In the Senate Biden became a leading figure on the Judiciary and Foreign Relations Committees and chaired the confirmation hearings of five Supreme Court justices, including the bitterly contested nominations of Robert Bork and Clarence Thomas. After failed presidential runs in 1988 and 2008, he became Barack Obama’s running mate in 2008 and a close partner as vice president. Grieving the death of his son Beau from cancer in 2015, he did not run in 2016, but he entered the 2020 race against Trump, declaring, “We are in the battle for the soul of this nation.” With Senator Kamala Harris as his running mate (the first woman, first Black, and first South Asian American vice president) he won in 2020. Biden took office on January 20, 2021, two weeks after the attack on the Capitol, amid a pandemic that eventually killed more than 1.1 million Americans. He signed the American Rescue Plan, which sent relief payments and expanded the child tax credit, and pushed vaccine distribution. With Republican votes he passed the $1.2 trillion Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act; in August 2022 he signed the CHIPS and Science Act for semiconductor research and manufacturing and the Inflation Reduction Act, which lowered prescription drug prices and invested in domestic energy production, especially clean energy. He also signed laws making Juneteenth a national holiday and finally outlawing lynching (the Emmett Till Antilynching Act), and he rejoined the Paris climate agreement and the World Health Organization on taking office. Biden presented himself as a believer in bipartisan deal-making, the institutions of the Senate, and American alliances, and his political identity rested on his working-class roots and personal resilience. He rejected Trump’s “America First” approach in favor of rebuilding ties with allies and bodies such as NATO, and he supported abortion rights, calling the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade a “tragic error.” The withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021, carrying out the agreement Trump had made with the Taliban, turned chaotic: the Afghan government collapsed, the Taliban took Kabul, and a suicide bomber killed thirteen American service members at the airport. His approval ratings fell and never recovered. Inflation reached 7 percent in his first year; Republicans blamed his spending, including the infrastructure law’s price tag, and although inflation fell below 3 percent by 2024, many Americans felt worse off. Encounters at the southern border nearly doubled to more than two million a year. Critics also faulted his reliance on officials from the Obama years, and the Supreme Court struck down his broadest student-debt relief plan. Questions about his age grew, and after a disastrous debate performance against Trump in 2024 he withdrew from the race. Biden endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris, who became the Democratic nominee but lost the 2024 election to Trump. He left office on January 20, 2025, as the economy, by most major indicators, had recovered from the pandemic faster than those of comparable nations, though many voters did not feel it in their household budgets. Historians are only beginning to assess his single term, which fell between Trump’s two. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jPUpwGvsbzE Biden's long and painful path to Democratic presidential nomination PBS NewsHour 17:52 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gr2Ak01iSi8 Joe Biden - The United States' 47th Vice President | Mini Bio| Biography Biography 3:15 2026-10-22

title: John Adams
subtitle: Revolutionary leader, diplomat, and second president, who kept the young nation out of war with France
summary: John Adams was a blunt, brilliant Massachusetts lawyer who became one of the leading voices for American independence, a diplomat who helped negotiate the peace with Britain, the nation’s first vice president, and its second president. In the Continental Congress he nominated George Washington to command the army, led the faction pushing for independence, and served on the committee that prepared the Declaration. As president he faced an undeclared naval war with Revolutionary France; he built up the navy and signed the Alien and Sedition Acts, but he refused to let the conflict become a full war and made peace instead. Split from his own Federalist Party, he lost the election of 1800 to Thomas Jefferson. He died on July 4, 1826, the same day as Jefferson.
thumbAlt: Portrait of John Adams by Gilbert Stuart
aliases: Adams Atlas of Independence Thoughts on Government Quasi-War XYZ Affair Alien and Sedition Acts
themeText: The presidency Foreign policy and diplomacy Parties and elections Political thought Constitution and law
text: John Adams Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts Quincy, Massachusetts Lawyer Delegate to the Continental Congress (1774–1777) Diplomat in Europe (1778–1788) First U.S. minister to Great Britain (1785) First vice president (1789–1797) Second president (1797–1801) Presidency March 4, 1797 – March 4, 1801; Federalist Boston Massacre trial Defended the British soldiers in 1770; none was sent to jail In Congress Nominated Washington to command the Continental Army; served on about ninety committees and chaired twenty Diplomacy Helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris (1783); first U.S. minister to Britain (1785) Elections Won 1796 by 71 electoral votes to 68; finished third in 1800 Died July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration Adams was born on October 30, 1735, into a comfortable but not wealthy farming family in Braintree, Massachusetts, about fifteen miles south of Boston. His father, a deacon, farmed and made shoes and hoped his son would become a minister. Adams entered Harvard at fifteen and graduated in 1755, then taught school in Worcester while studying law. He began practicing in Boston in 1758; he had one client his first year, but by 1770 he may have had the largest caseload of any lawyer in the city. In 1764 he married Abigail Smith, the daughter of a Weymouth minister, beginning one of the great partnerships in American history. The Boston Massacre trial. In 1770 Adams agreed to defend the British soldiers charged after the Boston Massacre, a decision that angered many patriots. Through his defense, none of the accused was sent to jail. Revolutionary leader. Adams was at first reluctant to join the protests against the Stamp Act, fearing for his law practice and distrusting radicals such as his cousin Samuel Adams, but he gradually became an open foe of British policy. He went to the First Continental Congress in 1774 and the Second in 1775. In June 1775 he nominated George Washington to command the new Continental Army, and he became the leader of the faction pushing for independence. He served on more committees than any other member, about ninety, chairing twenty, and headed the Board of War. In June 1776 he was named to the committee that prepared the Declaration of Independence. On July 3 he wrote Abigail that the day of independence would be celebrated “with Pomp and Parade… from one End of this Continent to the other.” Political thinker. In Thoughts on Government (1776) Adams argued that the executive, legislative, and judicial powers must be separated to prevent tyranny. In his Defence of the Constitutions (1787) he warned against both unchecked democracy and an aristocracy that could become an oligarchy, and he called for a strong executive. Some contemporaries wrongly believed his later essays favored a hereditary monarchy. During a brief visit home in 1779 he helped draft the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780. Diplomat. From 1778 Adams served in France and the Netherlands, where he won a needed loan, and with Franklin, John Jay, and Henry Laurens he negotiated the Treaty of Paris that ended the war. In 1785 he became the first U.S. minister to Britain. He came home in 1788 after ten years abroad. Vice president. Adams was elected vice president in 1789 and again in 1792, an office he found “devoid of power.” In 1796 he defeated Jefferson by 71 electoral votes to 68, and under the rules then in force Jefferson became his vice president. Adams distrusted both concentrated power and unchecked majorities. The Miller Center describes him as one of the “natural aristocrats” who believed leaders should be chosen for “superior reason and virtue,” and who thought the executive should stand above party politics. He favored property requirements for voting, believing that “the rich, the well-born, and the able” should lead. His views on the place of women drew a famous challenge from Abigail. When she urged him in 1776 to “Remember the Ladies,” he replied that “We know better than to repeal our Masculine systems.” The Quasi-War. France, angered by Jay’s Treaty with Britain, began seizing American ships. When French officials demanded bribes from Adams’s envoys in what became known as the XYZ Affair, Congress built up the navy, created the Navy Department, and cancelled the treaties of alliance and commerce signed with France during the Revolution, and an undeclared naval war followed. Many Federalists hoped for full war. The Alien and Sedition Acts. In 1798 the Federalist Congress passed four laws, which Adams signed. Three targeted immigrants, most of whom voted Democratic-Republican: they lengthened the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years and gave the president power to detain or deport aliens. The Sedition Act punished “subversive speech” with fines and prison. There were fifteen indictments and ten convictions under it. Jefferson and Madison secretly drafted the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions declaring the acts void. The Miller Center notes that Adams neither openly advocated the acts nor personally enforced them. Fries’s Rebellion. New taxes to pay for the military buildup led farmers in Pennsylvania to resist tax collectors. Their leaders were sentenced to death for treason, but Adams pardoned them, ignoring Hamilton’s call for a strong show of force. Adams sent a new peace mission to France in 1799 over the objections of much of his party, and he fired two cabinet members who opposed his policy. The peace he sought split the Federalists. Alexander Hamilton published a pamphlet calling Adams unfit to be president, and in 1800 Adams finished third behind Jefferson and Aaron Burr. The Miller Center adds that the three-fifths clause helped the South, and that without it Adams might have won. He made a number of last-minute “midnight appointments” of Federalist judges, which led to Marbury v. Madison. In retirement at Peacefield, his farm in Quincy, Adams wrote constantly. In 1812 friends brought him and Jefferson back into correspondence, and the two exchanged hundreds of letters. Both died on July 4, 1826. Near noon, close to the time Jefferson died, Adams woke and said, “Thomas Jefferson survives.” He died that evening. Born in October 1735, he was ninety, though the Miller Center gives his age as ninety-one. His son John Quincy Adams had been elected president in 1824. Historians have found his presidency hard to judge. His aloofness and independence isolated him politically, but most agree he was right not to expand the naval war with France into a full war that might have broken the young union. John Adams helped lead the colonies to independence, secured the peace that recognized it, and as president kept the new nation out of a war it might not have survived, at the cost of his own reelection. His peaceful handover of power to a political rival in 1801 set an important precedent. It ought to be solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other from this Time forward forever more. title: John Brown
subtitle: Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry
summary: John Brown was a white abolitionist who believed slavery was a sin that only violence could end. After killing pro-slavery settlers in “Bleeding Kansas,” he led twenty-one men in an attack on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, in October 1859, hoping to spark an uprising of enslaved people. The raid collapsed within thirty-six hours; Brown was captured, tried for treason, and hanged. Hailed as a martyr in the North and denounced as a terrorist in the South, he deepened the division that led to the Civil War.
thumbAlt: Daguerreotype of John Brown with his hand raised
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Reform and protest War and the military
text: John Brown Torrington, Connecticut Charles Town, Virginia (now West Virginia) Abolitionist Tanner, farmer, and wool merchant Antislavery fighter in Kansas Leader of the raid on Harpers Ferry Born May 9, 1800, Torrington, Connecticut Raid October 16–18, 1859, with 21 followers Captured by U.S. Marines commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee Executed December 2, 1859, in Charles Town, Virginia Brown was born on May 9, 1800, in Torrington, Connecticut, and grew up in Hudson, Ohio. As a boy he saw an enslaved boy he had befriended savagely beaten, a sight that, with his conviction that slavery was a sin against God, shaped the rest of his life. He set out to study for the ministry, but eye trouble and lack of money forced him home to his father’s trade of tanning leather. He married twice and fathered twenty children, only eleven of whom survived to adulthood. For decades Brown failed at one business after another (tanner, farmer, surveyor, land speculator, wool merchant) while helping fugitives where he could: his Pennsylvania tannery had a secret room to hide people escaping slavery. In 1849 he moved his family to North Elba, in the Adirondacks of New York, to live among Black farmers settled on land given by the abolitionist Gerrit Smith, a community Brown called “Timbukto,” and taught his neighbors how to clear land and build cabins. When the Kansas-Nebraska Act turned Kansas into a battleground over slavery, Brown followed members of his family there to “strike a blow for freedom.” In retaliation for pro-slavery violence, he and his followers murdered several pro-slavery settlers, the most controversial act of his life before Harpers Ferry. Convinced that a strike at the heart of slavery would do more than fighting on the plains, he moved east and planned a bigger blow, recruiting men including Black radicals from Oberlin, Ohio, and Canada; he asked Frederick Douglass to join, but Douglass refused. On the night of October 16, 1859, Brown and twenty-one followers seized the U.S. armory and rifle factory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia. He meant it as a “trumpet blast” that would launch a guerrilla campaign in the mountains and make “property in slaves insecure.” No uprising came; white townspeople rose against the raiders far faster than Brown expected. Ten of his men, including his own sons, were killed, and on October 18 U.S. Marines under Army Colonel Robert E. Lee captured Brown. Virginia tried him for treason against the state, conspiring with slaves to rebel, and murder; he was convicted and hanged at Charles Town on December 2, 1859. Brown’s abolitionism was religious and absolute: slavery was a sin against God. He came to believe that only force could destroy it, and he lived among Black farmers at North Elba and recruited Black allies for his raid. On the day of his execution he wrote: “I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood.” Few figures in American history are judged so differently. To many in the North, his execution made him a martyr; to white Southerners, the raid proved that abolitionists meant to incite slave insurrection and murder. Even Republicans tried to distance themselves from him, presenting their party as moderate. Historians still debate whether his violence, especially the killings in Kansas, should be understood as terrorism, as justified resistance to a violent system, or as both. Brown’s raid and execution hardened sectional attitudes on the eve of the 1860 election, and his prophecy that slavery would end only in blood was fulfilled within two years. In death he became an icon: decades later, the painter Thomas Hovenden portrayed him as a saint, stooping to kiss a Black baby on his way to the gallows. John Brown’s raid convinced many Southerners that the North would not leave slavery alone, and many Northerners that slavery could not be ended peacefully, pushing the nation closer to civil war. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6JaSMJ9l-bY The Life and Times of John Brown Mr. Beat 15:44 2026-10-22

title: John F. Kennedy
subtitle: Thirty-fifth president: the youngest ever elected, assassinated in Dallas in 1963
summary: John F. Kennedy was the youngest person ever elected president and the first Roman Catholic to hold the office. A rich Bostonian who became a war hero in the Pacific, he beat Richard Nixon in 1960 in one of the closest elections in American history, helped by a series of televised debates. In less than three years he faced the Bay of Pigs fiasco, the building of the Berlin Wall, and the Cuban Missile Crisis, launched the race to the moon, and sent a civil rights bill to Congress. His assassination in Dallas on November 22, 1963, became one of the great national traumas.
thumbAlt: Official White House portrait photograph of President John F. Kennedy, July 1963
aliases: JFK Jack Kennedy Kennedy
themeText: The presidency The Cold War Civil rights and citizenship Foreign policy and diplomacy Science and technology
text: John Fitzgerald Kennedy Brookline, Massachusetts Dallas, Texas U.S. Navy officer in World War II U.S. Representative from Massachusetts (1947–1953) U.S. Senator from Massachusetts (1953–1960) Thirty-fifth president (1961–1963) Presidency January 20, 1961 – November 22, 1963; Democrat Election of 1960 Beat Richard Nixon by fewer than 120,000 votes out of 68.8 million; 303 electoral votes to 219 Firsts Youngest person elected president; first Roman Catholic president; first president born in the twentieth century Wartime heroism After a Japanese destroyer rammed his boat, PT 109, in 1943, he towed a burned crewman to safety by a strap held in his teeth Book Profiles in Courage won the Pulitzer Prize for biography in 1957 Assassinated November 22, 1963, in Dallas; the Warren Commission found that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone Kennedy's presidency brought the Cold War to its most dangerous moment and then to a first step back from it, the 1963 test ban treaty. His youth, eloquence, and command of television changed American politics, and his murder left a lasting sense of what might have been. John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on May 29, 1917, in Brookline, Massachusetts, into a rich, politically connected family of Irish Catholics; his maternal grandfather had been mayor of Boston, and his father, Joseph P. Kennedy, had made a fortune in the stock market and entertainment and pulled his money out just before the crash of 1929. Jack and his eight siblings grew up with private schools, sailboats, servants, and summer homes, but he was sick so often that he spent much of his childhood recovering. In 1938 President Franklin Roosevelt made his father ambassador to Britain. Jack’s Harvard senior essay on Britain’s unreadiness for war was published as Why England Slept and became a bestseller. Poor health at first kept him out of the Navy; after his father intervened he was admitted and given command of a small torpedo boat in the South Pacific. In August 1943, with the crew asleep and no watch posted, a Japanese destroyer rammed PT 109. Towing a badly burned crewman by a life-jacket strap clenched in his teeth, Kennedy led the ten survivors on a three-mile swim to a tiny island and eventually summoned help. He won a Navy and Marine Corps Medal and a Purple Heart. When his older brother Joseph Jr., the son his father had groomed for the presidency, was killed on a bombing mission in Europe, the family’s ambitions fell on Jack. In 1946, at twenty-nine, he won a seat in Congress from a working-class Boston district; in 1952 he took a Senate seat from Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. That year he met Jacqueline Bouvier at a dinner party and, as he put it, “leaned across the asparagus and asked her for a date”; they married in 1953. Behind his image of youthful vigor he suffered from Addison’s disease, malaria, and constant back pain, relying on painkillers and steroids. Recovering from back surgery, he wrote Profiles in Courage, about senators who took unpopular moral stands, with help from his aide Theodore Sorensen; it won the 1957 Pulitzer Prize for biography. In 1960 Kennedy won the Democratic nomination by beating Hubert Humphrey in the primaries, above all in heavily Protestant West Virginia, where he had to prove a wealthy Catholic could win. He met religious doubts head-on, answering questions from Protestant ministers in Houston, and challenged Vice President Richard Nixon to a series of televised debates, the first extensive use of television in a presidential campaign. Seventy million people watched the first one, in which a pale, perspiring Nixon looked uneasy beside a tanned, relaxed Kennedy. Kennedy won the popular vote by fewer than 120,000 out of a record 68.8 million ballots. At his inauguration he declared that “the torch has been passed to a new generation of Americans.” Abroad, his first months went badly. In April 1961 some 1,500 CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs and were quickly overwhelmed, and the administration’s denial of involvement collapsed. That August the Soviets and East Germans built a wall separating East and West Berlin. In October 1962, when spy planes found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, Kennedy chose a naval “quarantine” over an air strike or invasion, and the Cuban Missile Crisis ended with the missiles withdrawn. In 1963 he signed a treaty with Britain and the Soviet Union banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space, and underwater, the achievement he considered his greatest. He created the Peace Corps, whose first volunteers went to teach in Ghana in 1961, and vowed to land Americans on the moon by the end of the decade, a goal reached with Apollo 11 in 1969. He also deepened the commitment in Vietnam, where 16,000 American military advisers were serving by late 1963. At home, a Congress dominated by conservative Southern Democrats blocked much of his “New Frontier,” though he won a higher minimum wage and aid for Appalachia. In 1962 he sent federal marshals and troops to enforce James Meredith’s admission to the University of Mississippi. After Alabama’s governor tried to block the integration of his state university and the civil rights leader Medgar Evers was murdered in June 1963, Kennedy went on television and sent Congress the bill that became the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Kennedy ran as a Cold War liberal who promised to “get the country moving again” and to lead the nation toward a “New Frontier.” He believed in energetic presidential leadership guided by experts, and his advisers thought they could “fine tune” the economy. He was a determined anticommunist who warned of a “missile gap” with the Soviet Union, yet after the missile crisis he worked to lower Cold War tensions, a goal he set out in a June 1963 speech at American University. Critics charged that Kennedy moved too slowly on civil rights: he concentrated on enforcing existing laws and delayed new legislation to protect the rest of his program, and to please Southern senators he appointed federal judges in the South who resisted desegregation. The Bay of Pigs was a self-inflicted humiliation, and his administration had no realistic plan to end the deepening war in Vietnam. His victory in 1960 drew charges of vote irregularities in Illinois and Texas, and his campaign’s money overwhelmed rivals. The image of vigor hid serious illnesses from the public, and later historians examined his questionable personal morals and the seamier side of his family’s dealings. On November 22, 1963, while riding in a motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Kennedy was shot twice and died soon after at Parkland Memorial Hospital. Police arrested Lee Harvey Oswald, a former Marine who had defected to the Soviet Union and returned; two days later Oswald himself was shot dead by a nightclub owner, Jack Ruby. The Warren Commission concluded that Oswald acted alone, but in 1979 a House committee suspected that Kennedy was “probably assassinated as a result of a conspiracy,” and conspiracy theories have never faded. An estimated one million people lined the streets of Washington for his funeral. Kennedy’s presidency was, in a biographer’s phrase, “an unfinished life,” and assessments remain mixed, but he made television central to American politics and still fascinates Americans as a charismatic leader in a time of danger. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kFeiM_Mxsv8 Assassination of John F. title: John Marshall
subtitle: The chief justice who made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch of government
summary: John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice of the United States, presiding over the Supreme Court from 1801 until his death in 1835. A Revolutionary War officer and Virginia lawyer, he took over a weak tribunal whose first justices had complained of its “limited stature,” and his leadership, the Court’s own history says, was “central to the development of its prominent role in American government.” In Marbury v. Madison he established the Court’s power to strike down unconstitutional laws. In McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden he gave the federal government broad power. More than any other judge, he defined what the Constitution would mean in practice.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Chief Justice John Marshall
aliases: Chief Justice Marshall The Great Chief Justice Marshall Court Gibbons v. Ogden Worcester v. Georgia XYZ Affair
themeText: Constitution and law
text: John Marshall Virginia; Washington, D.C. Continental Army officer Virginia lawyer and legislator U.S. representative (1799–1800) Secretary of state (1800–1801) Chief Justice of the United States (1801–1835) Born September 24, 1755, Virginia Appointed By John Adams; nominated January 20, 1801, confirmed January 27, 1801 Served February 4, 1801, to July 6, 1835, over thirty-four years Landmark opinions Marbury v. Madison (1803), McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), Worcester v. Georgia (1832) Before the Court Envoy to France in the XYZ Affair; congressman; Secretary of State Died July 6, 1835, Philadelphia Marshall was born on September 24, 1755, in Virginia and grew up on his father’s estate, Oak Hill. At a local academy he befriended a future president, James Monroe. When the Revolution came he served as a lieutenant in the Culpeper County Minutemen and then as an officer in the Continental Army’s Eleventh Virginia Regiment, rising to captain. In 1780 he studied at the College of William and Mary, then practiced law in Fauquier County and, from 1783, in Richmond, where he spent most of his adult life. He served several terms in the Virginia legislature, and in 1788 he was a delegate to the Virginia convention that ratified the Constitution. The XYZ Affair. In 1797 President John Adams sent Marshall, Elbridge Gerry and Charles Cotesworth Pinckney to France to stop French seizures of American ships. Agents of Foreign Minister Talleyrand, later identified only as X, Y and Z, demanded a loan and a bribe before talks could begin. The affair led to the undeclared Quasi-War with France, and Marshall came home praised nationally for refusing to give way. To the Court. After a term in Congress, Marshall became Adams’s secretary of state in 1800. Weeks before leaving office, Adams nominated him chief justice; the Senate confirmed him on January 27, 1801, and he took the oath on February 4. Judicial review. In Marbury v. Madison (1803) he wrote that “a Law repugnant to the Constitution is void,” the first time the Court struck down a law passed by Congress. After 1810 the Court extended judicial review to state laws. National power. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) he upheld Congress’s implied power to charter a national bank and barred states from taxing it: “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) he struck down New York’s steamboat monopoly, ruling that Congress, not the states, regulates interstate commerce. Jeffersonian Republicans saw Marshall as a Federalist using the bench against them. Jefferson complained that judicial review “would make the Judiciary a despotic branch.” Marshall’s ruling for the Cherokee in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), holding that Georgia’s laws did not apply in Cherokee territory, was ignored by Georgia and not enforced by the federal government, and it did not prevent the Cherokee’s forced removal on the Trail of Tears. The case exposed the limits of a court that cannot enforce its own judgments. Marshall died in Philadelphia, where he had gone for medical treatment, on July 6, 1835, at seventy-nine, and was buried in Richmond. He served thirty-four years and five months. The National Archives writes that after Gibbons the federal government “increasingly exercised its authority by legislation and judicial decision over the whole range of the nation’s economic life,” and that the Court’s power to invalidate laws contrary to the Constitution “has never been seriously challenged.” Marshall turned a weak, little-respected court into a co-equal branch of government. His opinions on judicial review, federal power and commerce remain foundations of American constitutional law. Small disagreements in the record Even Marshall’s basic biography varies by source. The Federal Judicial Center gives his birthplace as Prince William County, Virginia, while the American Battlefield Trust says Fauquier County. The Judicial Center dates his service as a Minuteman lieutenant to 1775–1776 and his captaincy to 1777; the Battlefield Trust says he enlisted in 1776 and was a captain “by July of 1778.” The Battlefield Trust also says he completed a law degree at William and Mary, while the Judicial Center lists only his attendance there in 1780. The Liberty Bell story When Marshall died, the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia was rung. A local legend says that this was when the bell cracked; the American Battlefield Trust calls it a myth. title: Louis Armstrong
subtitle: New Orleans trumpeter and singer who made jazz a soloist’s art and a world music
summary: Louis Armstrong grew up poor in New Orleans, learned the cornet in a reform school, and followed his mentor Joe “King” Oliver to Chicago in 1922. His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings of the 1920s put the improvising soloist at the center of jazz and popularized scat singing. Over a career of relentless touring, radio, and film, from “Heebie Jeebies” to “Hello, Dolly!” and “What a Wonderful World,” “Satchmo” became one of the most famous musicians in the world.
thumbAlt: Louis Armstrong holding his trumpet, smiling
aliases: Satchmo Pops Ambassador Satch
themeText: Arts and popular culture African American history Cities and urban life
text: Louis Armstrong New Orleans, Louisiana Corona, Queens, New York Cornetist and trumpeter Singer and bandleader Film performer Unofficial goodwill ambassador abroad Nickname “Satchmo”; abroad, “Ambassador Satch” Breakthrough Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings, 1925–1928 Signature records “Heebie Jeebies” (1926), “Hello, Dolly!” (1964), “What a Wonderful World” (1968) Firsts First African American to host a sponsored national radio broadcast (1937); first jazz musician on the cover of Time (1949) Birth date August 4, 1901, though he often claimed July 4, 1900 Armstrong was born on August 4, 1901, in New Orleans, though for most of his life he claimed July 4, 1900. Raised largely by his mother, Mary “Mayann” Albert, in a poor “back of town” neighborhood so rough it was nicknamed “The Battlefield,” he grew up surrounded by the music that was becoming jazz: blues, ragtime, brass-band marches, and spirituals. Not allowed inside the Funky Butt Hall, he watched the bands through cracks in its walls; delivering coal in the Storyville red-light district, he listened to some of the city’s best musicians. “We were poor and everything like that,” he recalled, “but music was all around you.” He left school after fifth grade to work for the Karnofsky family, who encouraged his music, and he bought his first cornet with his wages. On New Year’s Eve 1912 he was arrested for firing a blank from his stepfather’s pistol and sent to the segregated Colored Waif’s Home for Boys, where teacher Peter Davis taught him to play properly and read music, and he became leader of the Home’s brass band. Released in 1914, he played at night while doing manual labor by day, then on Mississippi riverboats, where he learned to sight-read. The city’s top cornetist, Joe “King” Oliver, became his mentor, and at eighteen Armstrong was hired by trombonist Kid Ory to replace Oliver in Ory’s band. In 1922 Oliver sent for Armstrong to join his Creole Jazz Band in Chicago, where their intricate two-cornet breaks became the talk of the town; they began recording in 1923. Armstrong married the band’s pianist, Lil Hardin, in 1924, and she urged him to strike out on his own. After a year in New York with Fletcher Henderson’s orchestra, he returned to Chicago in 1925 and began recording under his own name. His Hot Five and Hot Seven records (1925–1928), “Cornet Chop Suey,” “Potato Head Blues,” “West End Blues”, are often called the most influential in jazz. Instead of the band playing as one ensemble, Armstrong stepped out front for daring improvised solos, turning jazz into a soloist’s art. He did not invent scat singing, but his 1926 hit “Heebie Jeebies,” his first scat record, made it famous. At the end of the decade he appeared on Broadway in the all-Black revue Hot Chocolates, and from then on he toured almost without stopping, eventually giving more than 300 performances a year for 30 years. In 1937 he became the first African American to host a sponsored national radio broadcast, and in 1949 the first jazz musician on the cover of Time. When big bands faded he formed a small group, the All Stars, in 1947. Abroad he was so popular that he was called “Ambassador Satch,” and the State Department sent him on tours to counter Soviet influence. In 1964 his recording of “Hello, Dolly!” knocked the Beatles off the top of the Billboard chart at the height of Beatlemania, making him the oldest artist with a number-one song. His last hit, “What a Wonderful World,” followed in 1968. By the 1950s Armstrong’s gregarious, old-fashioned stage persona struck some modern jazz musicians and, later, Black Power advocates as out of date, and critics called him an “Uncle Tom.” His appearance as King of Zulu at the 1949 Mardi Gras, in the blackface makeup that was the Krewe of Zulu’s traditional, satirical attire, puzzled many fans who did not understand the custom. Admirers point out that he had broken many racial barriers as a young man and that he spoke out forcefully over Little Rock. The touring took a heavy physical toll. Trumpet playing is brutal on the lips; Armstrong suffered lip damage most of his life, once had to stop performing for a year, and treated his scar tissue himself with salves and a razor blade. He had his first heart attack in 1959. After treatment for heart and kidney problems in 1968, doctors told Armstrong to stop playing, but he kept practicing every day at the modest house in Corona, Queens, that he and his fourth wife, Lucille, had shared since 1943. He returned to the stage in 1970 and died in his sleep on July 6, 1971, a few months after his last engagement. In the years after his death, a new generation led by the New Orleans trumpeter Wynton Marsalis championed his music. His Queens home was designated a National Landmark in 1976 and is now the Louis Armstrong House Museum. He is remembered as a pioneer who ushered in a new era of jazz and a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. Armstrong turned jazz into an art of individual improvisation and carried it around the world, making a music born in Black New Orleans one of America’s best-known cultural exports. Armstrong built his art on reaching the widest possible audience; he toured relentlessly, playing, as the National Park Service puts it, “for anyone who would listen.” The Louis Armstrong House Museum calls him a great civil rights pioneer who broke down numerous barriers as a young man. In 1957, during the crisis over the integration of Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, he spoke out publicly against President Eisenhower’s handling of it. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sIILBeUrYLk Louis Armstrong: Broke Down Barriers for African American Artists | Biography Biography 3:56 2026-10-22

title: Lyndon B. Johnson
subtitle: Thirty-sixth president: the Great Society, civil rights, and Vietnam
summary: Lyndon Baines Johnson, the thirty-sixth president of the United States (1963–1969), was a Texas Hill Country schoolteacher who became one of the most skilled legislators in American history. Thrust into the presidency by John F. Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963, he pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, won a historic landslide, and launched the Great Society: Medicare, Medicaid, federal aid to education, and the War on Poverty. But his escalation of the Vietnam War tore the country apart, and in 1968 he declined to seek another term.

aliases: LBJ
themeText: The presidency Civil rights and citizenship Economy and finance War and the military The Cold War
text: Lyndon Baines Johnson Texas Hill Country U.S. Representative from Texas (1937–1949) U.S. Senator and Senate Majority Leader Vice President (1961–1963) Thirty-sixth president (1963–1969) Born August 27, 1908, in the Texas Hill Country Presidency November 22, 1963 – January 1969; Democrat 1964 election Won 61.1% of the popular vote against Barry Goldwater Domestic legacy Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, Medicare and Medicaid, War on Poverty, immigration reform Vietnam U.S. troops rose to almost 200,000 by the end of 1965 and more than 500,000 within three years Johnson was born on August 27, 1908, in a farmhouse on the Pedernales River, the first of five children; his father, a state legislator, rode up and down the river announcing that his son would be governor of Texas someday. Their house in Johnson City had neither electricity nor indoor plumbing. At twelve Lyndon told classmates he would one day be president. His father, a better politician than farmer, piled up debts and lost the family farm when Lyndon was a teenager; Johnson later said that at fourteen he resolved never to be the victim of a system that let cotton prices crash and ruin families like his own. After high school he drifted (to California for odd jobs, then onto a Texas road crew, where he fell into drinking and fighting) before enrolling at Southwest Texas State Teachers College in 1927. Student-teaching at an impoverished Mexican American school in Cotulla, he pushed long-neglected children to take pride in their achievements. In 1931 he went to Washington as a congressional aide and was electrified by politics. In 1934 he met Claudia Alta Taylor, known as “Lady Bird,” and married her three months later. Appointed Texas director of the New Deal’s National Youth Administration in 1935, Johnson helped young people stay in school and find work. In 1937, at twenty-eight, he won a seat in Congress as a Roosevelt ally and brought electricity to the Hill Country of his youth, the achievement he called his proudest. He lost a 1941 Senate race in which both sides were accused of fraud, then won a Senate seat in 1948 by just 87 votes in a primary marred by suspicious tallies, earning the mocking nickname “Landslide Lyndon.” In the Senate he found his true calling: majority leader from 1955, he made the post one of the most powerful in government and passed the Civil Rights Act of 1957, the first in almost a century. As Kennedy’s running mate in 1960, he helped carry the South. On November 22, 1963, riding two cars behind Kennedy in Dallas, he became president and was sworn in aboard Air Force One that afternoon. He won passage of Kennedy’s civil rights bill and tax cut and declared a War on Poverty. After defeating Barry Goldwater in a 1964 landslide, he won Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, the Voting Rights Act, and a 1965 immigration law that abolished national-origin quotas: along with programs for urban renewal, environmental protection, consumer safety, and the arts and humanities. Johnson believed the federal government could and should end poverty and racial injustice. A child of the New Deal who had seen his own family ruined by forces beyond its control, he saw government as an engine of opportunity, and in May 1964 he called for a Great Society that would end “poverty and racial injustice.” As vice president he had publicly backed Kennedy’s decision to send military advisers to South Vietnam to resist a communist insurgency. Johnson escalated the war in Vietnam without finding a strategy for victory, withdrawal, or peace with honor; American casualties mounted and the antiwar movement grew. By 1968 his approval rating had fallen below 30 percent. His road to power had been shadowed by the disputed 1948 primary. Critics on the right saw the Great Society as government overreach, and the reaction against it helped fuel a conservative countermovement. Johnson left office in January 1969 demoralized and discredited, and died at his Texas ranch on January 22, 1973, a few hundred feet from where he was born. His civil rights and social welfare programs kept many Americans out of poverty and secured the rights of citizenship for minorities. But Vietnam, where more than 58,000 Americans and millions of Southeast Asians died, clouded his legacy, and historians continue to debate how to weigh the two. Johnson enacted the most sweeping domestic reforms since the New Deal, while his Vietnam policy tore the country apart. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zm_HodLdQe0 Lyndon B.
