title: Sacagawea
subtitle: The Lemhi Shoshone woman who traveled with Lewis and Clark to the Pacific and back
summary: Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman who, at sixteen or seventeen and carrying her newborn son, traveled with the Lewis and Clark Expedition to the Pacific and back. She was the only woman in the Corps of Discovery. She is often remembered as its guide, but the journals show something different and arguably more important. Her presence told the tribes they met that the party was not a war party, and when the explorers reached her homeland in the Rockies, she helped them find the Shoshone and the horses they needed to cross the mountains. Little else about her is certain, from the spelling of her name to the date of her death.
location: Lemhi River valley (present-day Idaho); Knife River villages (present-day North Dakota)
thumbAlt: Alice Cooper’s statue of Sacagawea at the 1905 Lewis and Clark Exposition in Portland, Oregon
aliases: Sacajawea Sakakawea Bird Woman Jean Baptiste Charbonneau Pomp Toussaint Charbonneau
themeText: Indigenous history Women's history Territorial expansion
text: Sacagawea Lemhi River valley (present-day Idaho); Knife River villages (present-day North Dakota) Member of the Corps of Discovery (1805–1806) Interpreter and intermediary People Lemhi Shoshone, from present-day Idaho Born About 1788 Captured At about eleven or twelve, by a Hidatsa raiding party With the Corps Left Fort Mandan on April 7, 1805, with her two-month-old son Role Interpreter with her husband, Toussaint Charbonneau; the only woman in the expedition Died Probably December 1812 at Fort Manuel Lisa; some oral histories say 1884 Sacagawea was born around 1788 among the Lemhi Shoshone in the mountains of present-day Idaho. When she was eleven or twelve, a Hidatsa raiding party captured her and carried her east to the Knife River villages in present-day North Dakota, where she lived at the Awatixa village. There Toussaint Charbonneau, a French-Canadian fur trader living among the Hidatsa, claimed her as one of his wives. In the winter of 1804–05 Meriwether Lewis and William Clark built Fort Mandan near the villages. They hired Charbonneau as an interpreter, and Sacagawea came too, valued for her experience with the peoples, languages and land farther west. On February 11, 1805, she gave birth to a son, Jean Baptiste Charbonneau. Lewis recorded that “one of the wives of Charbono was delivered of a fine boy”; Clark later nicknamed the boy “Pomp.” On the river. Sacagawea, Charbonneau and the baby left Fort Mandan with the Corps on April 7, 1805. She dug roots and found other food, and showed the men how to make leather clothing and moccasins. On May 14, 1805, when a gust of wind nearly overturned the boat Charbonneau was steering, she calmly rescued instruments, books, medicines and other supplies from the water. A token of peace. Her presence dispelled the idea that the party was a war party. Clark wrote that she “reconciles all the Indians, as to our friendly intentions. A woman with a party of men is a token of peace.” Finding the Shoshone. Everything depended on trading for horses to carry the supplies over the mountains. Recognizing landmarks from her childhood, Sacagawea assured the captains that her people were near. On August 15, 1805, the expedition met the Shoshone. According to the National Women’s History Museum, she discovered while interpreting that the chief, Cameahwait, was her brother, and the Shoshone provided horses and guides. The return. After wintering at Fort Clatsop on the Pacific coast, she traveled with Clark’s party in 1806 and recommended a route through the mountains now known as Bozeman Pass. Popular legend made Sacagawea the guide who led Lewis and Clark across the continent. The National Park Service says the journals “offer little evidence of this” and that historians believe she joined because her husband was hired as an interpreter. The National Women’s History Museum also calls her a guide, but says her guiding was limited to the Idaho and Montana region where she grew up. The Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation’s Sacagawea Project has published its own account, Our Eagle Woman, Sacagawea: They Got It Wrong, challenging the standard story. Sacagawea and her family left the Corps when it returned to the Hidatsa villages in August 1806. When Jean Baptiste was about five, she and Charbonneau took him to St. Louis to be educated under Clark’s care. Records from Fort Manuel Lisa, a fur-trading post in present-day South Dakota, indicate that she died there of a fever in December 1812, not yet thirty; some Native oral histories say she lived on in Shoshone country in Wyoming until 1884. Sacagawea is one of the most commemorated women in American history and a reminder that the expedition depended on Native people. Her real story, a captive teenager and young mother whose presence and knowledge helped the Corps survive, is both more modest and more remarkable than the legend of the guide who led the way west. Sacagawea, Sacajawea or Sakakawea? Her name appears in eight different spellings in the Lewis and Clark journals, all with a hard “g.” Lewis wrote on May 20, 1805, that the party named a river “Sah-ca-gah-we-ah or bird woman’s River, after [our] interpreter the Snake woman.” The spelling “Sacajawea” first appeared in Nicholas Biddle’s 1814 edition of the journals, for no known reason; some Shoshone people hold that it is a Shoshone name meaning “boat launcher.” North Dakota uses “Sakakawea,” built from Hidatsa words for “bird” and “woman.” What the sources disagree on Even her capture is told differently. The National Park Service places it about four years before 1804 and says she was taken to the villages near present-day Bismarck; the Knife River site says the raid “likely” happened and that she lived at the Awatixa village. Her death is the largest question: Fort Manuel Lisa’s records point to 1812, but oral tradition points to 1884. A woman with a party of men is a token of peace. title: Sitting Bull
subtitle: Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation
summary: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka) was a Hunkpapa Lakota war chief and holy man who led the Lakota who refused to accept life on a reservation. He rejected the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and kept his people hunting buffalo on the open plains. In June 1876 his vision of soldiers “falling into camp” came before the Lakota and Cheyenne victory over George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn. Pursued by the army, he led his followers into Canada and surrendered in 1881. He toured briefly with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West and lived at Standing Rock. In December 1890, amid fears of the Ghost Dance, he was killed by Lakota reservation police sent to arrest him.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Sitting Bull
aliases: Tatanka-Iyotanka Tatanka Iyotake non-treaty Lakota Greasy Grass Battle of the Little Bighorn
themeText: Indigenous history Religion War and the military
text: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka) Near the Grand and Missouri Rivers, present-day South Dakota Standing Rock Reservation Hunkpapa Lakota war leader Leader of the Strong Heart warrior society Spiritual leader Leader of the non-treaty Lakota Performer in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West (1885) Born Between 1831 and 1837, near the confluence of the Grand and Missouri Rivers, present-day South Dakota Nation Hunkpapa band of the Lakota Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) Refused to take part; became leader of the non-treaty Lakota Little Bighorn June 25–26, 1876; his village was attacked by Custer’s 7th Cavalry, which lost five companies under Custer Exile Led followers to Canada in 1877; surrendered at Fort Buford, July 20, 1881 Died December 15, 1890, killed during an arrest at his cabin on the Standing Rock Reservation Sitting Bull became the best-known symbol of Native resistance to American conquest of the Great Plains. His refusal to sign away Lakota land or way of life, and the victory at the Little Bighorn associated with his name, made him famous among white Americans as well as his own people. Sitting Bull was born into a prominent Hunkpapa Lakota family sometime between 1831 and 1837, near where the Grand River meets the Missouri in present-day South Dakota. His father and two of his uncles were chiefs. He killed his first buffalo at ten and counted his first coup, an honor earned in immediate proximity to the enemy, at fourteen. After that he took his father’s name, Tatanka-Iyotanka, Sitting Bull. The National Park Service writes that he already showed the four cardinal Lakota virtues of bravery, fortitude, generosity, and wisdom. He joined the Kit Fox society and the elite Midnight Strong Heart society of warriors, became one of its two Sash Wearers, and then its leader. Sitting Bull was also a holy man. Through the Sun Dance and vision quests he sought guidance from Wakan-Tanka, and many Lakota believed his visions came true. In the 1850s, as the Lakota argued over how to deal with the expanding United States, he spoke for those who wanted to avoid trade and diplomacy with whites altogether. “I have seen nothing that the white man has,” he said, “which is as good as our right to roam and live on the open plains as we choose.” He stayed away from white settlements and forts almost entirely until the 1880s. The non-treaty Lakota. In 1866 the Lakota leader Red Cloud waged a successful war against forts along the Bozeman Trail, and in 1868 he and other leaders signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie. The treaty created the Great Sioux Reservation in the western half of present-day South Dakota, including the Black Hills, which are sacred to the Lakota. Sitting Bull refused to take part and held that those who signed spoke only for themselves. The Lakota split between those who followed Red Cloud and Spotted Tail onto the reservation and the “non-treaty” bands who followed Sitting Bull and kept living as before. (The treaty’s list of signatures, as transcribed by the National Archives, includes a mark for a “Sitting Bull,” while the National Park Service states that Sitting Bull refused to join the negotiations.) The road to war. In 1874 an army expedition under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer found gold in the Black Hills, and miners poured onto the reservation in violation of the treaty. The Lakota refused to sell the Black Hills. The government then ordered all Lakota onto the reservation by January 31, 1876, or be treated as “hostiles.” Sitting Bull ignored the deadline and sent word to the reservation Lakota that while they lived on scant rations, his people were feasting on buffalo. In mid-June 1876, at a Sun Dance, he gave fifty pieces of flesh from each arm and went without water for two days and nights. He then saw a vision of soldiers falling upside down into the Lakota camp, “like grasshoppers.” A voice told him, “I give these to you because they have no ears,” which the Lakota understood as a promise of victory. The Little Bighorn. On June 25, 1876, Custer’s 7th Cavalry attacked the great camp of Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho along the Little Bighorn River, which the Lakota called the Greasy Grass. The National Park Service estimates the village at about 7,000 people on its Sitting Bull page and about 8,000 on its battle page, with 1,500 to 1,800 warriors. Sitting Bull, past fighting age, did not fight himself but sent his nephews White Bull and One Bull into battle with his own protective medicine. The warriors drove Major Marcus Reno’s battalion back across the river and destroyed the five companies under Custer’s direct command. The Park Service estimates about 80 Lakota and Cheyenne deaths, and the American Yawp says Custer and 268 of his men were killed. The victory made Sitting Bull internationally famous as the “architect of Custer’s defeat,” whether or not that was accurate. Sitting Bull believed the Lakota should keep their freedom to hunt and live on the open plains, and that no treaty signed by others could bind those who did not consent to it. His authority rested as much on spiritual power as on military skill. He sought visions through the Sun Dance and vision quest, and his followers saw his prophecies fulfilled. After the Little Bighorn, Americans demanded revenge, and the army under Generals George Crook and Nelson Miles pursued the non-treaty bands for a year and a half. The Black Hills were taken by the government without compensation in 1877. The National Archives notes that ownership of the Black Hills is still the subject of a legal dispute between the United States and the Sioux. In the fall of 1877 Sitting Bull led his followers into Canada, which the Lakota called the land of the White Grandmother. Buffalo were scarce there, and sickness and harsh winters wore his people down. One by one his followers drifted back to the reservations, and on July 20, 1881, he surrendered at Fort Buford in Dakota Territory. By then the buffalo herds had been destroyed: the American Yawp says the bison population fell from over ten million at midcentury to only a few hundred by the early 1880s. On the Standing Rock Reservation, Indian agents refused to recognize chiefs. Many Lakota, including Sitting Bull’s protégé Gall, took up farming. In 1885 Sitting Bull was allowed to tour with Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show, where he was the star attraction and became Cody’s friend, but after one season the Standing Rock agent, James McLaughlin, refused to let him go again. The two men clashed for years. In 1890 the Ghost Dance, a religious movement begun by the prophet Wovoka, spread to the Lakota. It promised that if Native people lived justly and danced, their ancestors would return, the buffalo would come back, and whites would vanish from the West. Agents and the army feared an uprising. McLaughlin believed Sitting Bull was involved, and at six in the morning on December 15, 1890, more than forty Lakota Indian police broke into his cabin to take him in for questioning. As they led him outside, a crowd gathered and shouting turned to gunfire. Sitting Bull was killed by a shot to the chest. Two weeks later the 7th Cavalry, Custer’s old regiment, surrounded Spotted Elk’s (Big Foot’s) band at Wounded Knee Creek and, after a shot was fired, massacred them. The American Yawp estimates that between 150 and 300 Lakota men, women, and children were killed. HISTORY puts the toll at almost 150, nearly half of them women and children, and notes that some historians put it twice as high. The American Yawp calls Wounded Knee the end of sustained armed Native resistance on the Plains. Sitting Bull is remembered as a defender of Lakota land and freedom who refused to give up his people’s way of life. The Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument now presents the battle as a clash between the buffalo-and-horse culture of the northern Plains and the industrial culture of the United States. I have seen nothing that the white man has which is as good as our right to roam and live on the open plains as we choose. Sitting Bull on relations with the United States I give these to you because they have no ears. A voice in Sitting Bull’s vision Sun Dance, June 1876, as recounted by the Lakota I did not think anyone would come and attack us so strong as we were. title: Sojourner Truth
subtitle: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York
summary: Sojourner Truth was born into slavery in New York as Isabella Baumfree, freed herself in 1826, and became one of the most powerful speakers of the nineteenth century against slavery and for women’s rights. She was the first Black woman to win a lawsuit against a white man, for the return of her son, sold illegally into Alabama. Never formally educated, she dictated a celebrated autobiography and moved audiences with speeches such as the one at Akron in 1851 later known as “Ain’t I a Woman?” In 2009 she became the first Black woman honored with a bust in the U.S. Capitol.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Sojourner Truth
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Women's history Reform and protest Religion
text: Sojourner Truth (born Isabella Bomfree) Ulster County, New York Battle Creek, Michigan Abolitionist and women’s rights lecturer Preacher Recruiter for Black Union troops Freedmen’s relief worker Born About 1797, enslaved in Ulster County, New York; she spoke only Dutch as a child Freedom Escaped with her infant daughter in 1826 Legal victory Sued to recover her son Peter, illegally sold to Alabama, and won New name Took the name Sojourner Truth in 1843 Isabella Baumfree was born about 1797 in Ulster County, New York, one of perhaps ten to twelve children of enslaved parents, James and Elizabeth; all her siblings were sold away. Her first language was the Dutch of her enslavers. At nine she was sold away from her parents, together with a flock of sheep, for $100; she was sold twice more, and from 1810 was held by John Dumont of West Park, New York. There she endured harassment from Dumont’s wife and rape by Dumont. In 1815 she fell in love with Robert, an enslaved man from a neighboring farm, whose owner beat him to death for meeting her. She had five children (James, who died young; Diana, born of the rape; and Peter, Elizabeth, and Sophia, with an older enslaved man named Thomas) and later recalled struggling to feed her own babies because she was made to nurse her enslaver’s white children. New York’s gradual emancipation law promised freedom on July 4, 1827, to those born before 1799. Dumont promised to free her before that date, then reneged. So in 1826 she walked away with her infant daughter Sophia, leaving her older children behind, and found refuge with Isaac and Maria Van Wagenen in New Paltz, who paid Dumont $20 for her labor until emancipation day. When Dumont illegally sold her five-year-old son Peter to an enslaver in Alabama, she took the case to court and, after a long fight, won his return in 1828: becoming, the National Women’s History Museum notes, the first Black woman to sue a white man and win. A religious awakening followed. She moved to New York City and worked as a housekeeper, and in 1843, feeling called by God to “testify the hope that was in her,” took the name Sojourner Truth and set out to preach across the countryside. At the Northampton Association, a utopian abolitionist community in Massachusetts, she met William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass. In 1850 Garrison published The Narrative of Sojourner Truth, which she had dictated to Olive Gilbert; she paid for her house in part by selling photographs of herself captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She spoke at the first National Women’s Rights Convention in Worcester in 1850 and, in May 1851, at the Ohio Women’s Rights Convention in Akron. During the Civil War she recruited Black men for the Union Army, her grandson served in the 54th Massachusetts, and in 1864 she worked for the National Freedmen’s Relief Association in Washington, met President Lincoln, and rode the city’s streetcars to challenge their segregation. After the war she lobbied for federal land grants for freed people and met President Grant. A devout Christian who first learned Bible stories by ear, Truth tied her abolitionism to her faith and to a demand for equality that included women, and Black women in particular. Her speeches exposed how ideals of womanhood excluded Black women and the double burden of race and sex they bore. She also campaigned for prison reform and against capital punishment, and she supported women’s right to vote; in 1872 she went to the polls in Battle Creek and was turned away. Truth’s most famous words are also the hardest to pin down. She spoke without notes at Akron, and the first full account, published within a month, does not contain the phrase “Ain’t I a Woman?” That version appeared twelve years later, written by the suffragist Frances Dana Gage, who put a stereotyped Southern dialect into the mouth of a woman who had grown up speaking Dutch in New York. Gage’s version, reprinted for decades, is the one most people know. Earlier, while working in New York City, Truth had been falsely accused of poisoning and robbing an employer and was acquitted. Truth spent her last decades in Battle Creek, Michigan, where she died on November 26, 1883, at about eighty-six. She is remembered in murals and statues, in the name of NASA’s 1997 Mars rover Sojourner, and, since 2009, in a bust in the U.S. Capitol, the first honoring a Black woman there. Her life story, from the auction block to the lecture platform, made her a lasting symbol of the joined struggles for racial and gender equality. Sojourner Truth made the case, from her own experience, that the struggles against slavery and for women’s rights were one struggle, and that neither could succeed while ignoring Black women. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0sn8CUyvG2k The electrifying speeches of Sojourner Truth - Daina Ramey Berry TED-Ed 4:39 2026-10-23

title: Susan B. Anthony
subtitle: Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement
summary: Susan B. Anthony was the best-known organizer of the nineteenth-century woman suffrage movement. For more than fifty years, often in partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton, she traveled the country giving speeches, circulating petitions, and building organizations. Raised a Quaker, she began as a temperance and antislavery reformer. After the Civil War she opposed the Fifteenth Amendment because it enfranchised Black men but not women, and she co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1872 she was arrested and convicted for voting. She died in 1906. The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, was widely called the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.”

aliases: Susan B. Anthony Amendment The Revolution National Woman Suffrage Association Failure is impossible History of Woman Suffrage
themeText: Women's history Voting rights Reform and protest Labor and work
text: Susan Brownell Anthony Adams, Massachusetts Rochester, New York Teacher Temperance and antislavery reformer; American Anti-Slavery Society agent Co-founder of the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869) Publisher of *The Revolution* President of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (1892–1900) Born February 15, 1820, Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children Partnership Met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851; they worked together for the rest of their lives The Revolution Published from 1868; motto “Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less” Arrest Voted in the 1872 presidential election; arrested November 18, 1872; convicted and fined $100 in June 1873 Organizations National Woman Suffrage Association (1869); president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, 1892–1900 Died March 13, 1906, Rochester, New York; buried in Mount Hope Cemetery Anthony turned woman suffrage into a national, organized movement and kept it focused on a federal constitutional amendment. Her record also includes the racist arguments she adopted after the Civil War, which divided the movement and alienated former allies such as Frederick Douglass. Susan Brownell Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children of Daniel and Lucy Anthony. Her father, a Quaker, built a cotton mill, where Susan worked for a time with one of her sisters. Even as a girl she wondered why he would not make a woman an overseer. He also tried to avoid buying cotton grown by enslaved people. Shortly after she turned thirteen Anthony joined the Society of Friends, whose belief in “the equality of all people before God” guided her life. In 1837 she went to a Friends’ seminary near Philadelphia, but the next year the financial panic bankrupted her father and she had to leave school. Anthony became a teacher. In Canajoharie, New York, in 1848, according to the National Park Service and the National Women’s History Museum, she learned that male teachers earned $10 a month while women earned $2.50. (The Susan B. Anthony Museum dates the start of her Canajoharie post to 1846, at a yearly salary of $110.) In 1845 the family moved to a farm near Rochester, New York, where antislavery Quakers met almost every Sunday, sometimes joined by Frederick Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison. Anthony’s parents and a sister attended the Rochester woman’s rights convention of August 1848. She herself first joined the temperance movement. In 1852, told at a temperance convention that women should “listen and learn,” she turned toward women’s rights. Partnership with Stanton. In 1851, on a street corner in Seneca Falls, Amelia Bloomer introduced Anthony to Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls convention. Their partnership lasted the rest of their lives. Stanton, raising seven children, often stayed home and wrote speeches, and Anthony, who never married, delivered them across the country. The National Park Service credits a speech by Lucy Stone at the 1852 Syracuse convention with persuading Anthony to commit herself to women’s rights. From 1853 she campaigned for married women’s property rights in New York, collecting signatures, lobbying the legislature, and speaking alone in town after town. Antislavery. By 1856 Anthony was an agent of the American Anti-Slavery Society, arranging meetings and distributing pamphlets. In 1861 her campaign across New York under the slogan “No Union with Slaveholders. No Compromise” met hostile crowds. In Syracuse a mob burned her in effigy and dragged it through the streets, and she later called the period “The Winter of Mobs.” In 1863 she, Stanton, and Lucy Stone formed the Women’s Loyal National League to press for a constitutional amendment abolishing slavery, which came with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. The Revolution and the split. In 1868 Anthony and Stanton began publishing The Revolution, under the motto “Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less.” Anthony also organized Working Women’s Associations for women in the printing and garment trades. When Congress proposed the Fifteenth Amendment, which barred denying the vote on account of race but not sex, the old coalition broke apart. Anthony and Stanton opposed the amendment, while Lucy Stone, Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, and Frederick Douglass supported it. In 1869 Anthony called the first woman suffrage convention ever held in Washington, D.C., and she and Stanton founded the National Woman Suffrage Association to work for a federal amendment. Stone and Harper formed the rival American Woman Suffrage Association. Voting in 1872. Anthony urged women to claim the vote under the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. In November 1872 she and her sisters registered and voted in Rochester for Ulysses S. Grant and two congressmen. On November 18 a U.S. marshal arrested her at home. At her trial in June 1873 at the Ontario County Courthouse in Canandaigua, the judge directed the jury to find her guilty and fined her $100. She refused to pay, and because he did not jail her, she could not appeal to the Supreme Court. The case nonetheless made national headlines. (The sources differ on who voted with her. The National Park Service says her three sisters, while the National Women’s History Museum adds a Quaker friend and eleven other women who registered.) Leading a national movement. With Stanton and Matilda Joslyn Gage, Anthony compiled the History of Woman Suffrage, beginning in 1881. In 1890 the two rival associations merged as the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Stanton was its first president, but Anthony was effectively its leader and became president in 1892. She helped create the International Council of Women and organize the World’s Congress of Representative Women at the 1893 Chicago world’s fair. In 1900 she handed the presidency to Carrie Chapman Catt, “my ideal leader.” The same year she pledged the value of her life insurance so that the University of Rochester would admit women. Anthony’s Quaker faith taught the equality of all people before God, and she argued that the Constitution’s promise of liberty belonged to “we, the whole people … women as well as men.” She believed the vote was the key to every other right for women, and in 1854 she wrote that woman suffrage was “this great central question, which underlies all others.” The Revolution also argued for equal pay and the eight-hour day, and she called for the education of women and Black Americans. Anthony’s opposition to the Fifteenth Amendment led her into racist arguments. The National Women’s History Museum writes that although she had worked for the abolition of slavery, she “adopted the racist positions used by many other white women at that time,” and the National Park Service describes Douglass as hurt by her and Stanton’s “insulting arguments” against African Americans. The quarrel turned ugly at a public meeting of the American Equal Rights Association in New York in 1869. The History of Woman Suffrage she helped write focuses on white suffragists and leaves out suffragists of color. Ida B. Wells, who respected Anthony’s pioneering work, criticized her for not putting Black women’s concerns first in order to keep the support of white women. In 1905 Anthony met President Theodore Roosevelt to urge him to submit a suffrage amendment to Congress. At her eighty-sixth birthday celebration in February 1906 she declared that, with so many women devoting their lives to the cause, “failure is impossible.” She died at her Rochester home on March 13, 1906, of heart failure and pneumonia, and was buried in Mount Hope Cemetery. The National Archives dates the first introduction in Congress of the amendment that became the Nineteenth to 1878. The National Women’s History Museum dates the first proposed federal women’s suffrage amendment to March 1869. Congress passed it in June 1919, and it was ratified on August 18, 1920. It was widely known as the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.” She was the first non-fictional woman depicted on U.S. currency, on the dollar coin issued from 1979 to 1981 and again in 1999. Her house in Rochester, where she was arrested, is a National Historic Landmark and museum. It was we, the people; not we, the white male citizens; nor yet we, the male citizens; but we, the whole people, who formed the Union. Susan B. Anthony speech after her arrest for voting, 1873 Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less. Motto of The Revolution Anthony and Stanton’s newspaper, 1868 There have been others also just as true and devoted to the cause, … but with such women consecrating their lives, failure is impossible! title: Tecumseh
subtitle: Shawnee leader who tried to unite Native nations against American expansion
summary: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who, with his brother Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet,” tried to build an alliance of Native nations from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico to stop American expansion. He traveled from Canada to Georgia calling for unity, resistance and “the restoration of sacred power,” and he refused to concede any more land. After American troops destroyed his headquarters at Prophetstown in 1811, his confederacy fought alongside Britain in the War of 1812. His death at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813, broke the confederacy apart.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Tecumseh
aliases: Tekoomsē Blazing Comet Tenskwatawa The Prophet Prophetstown Tecumseh’s Confederacy Battle of Tippecanoe Battle of the Thames
themeText: Indigenous history War and the military Territorial expansion
text: Tecumseh (Tekoomsē) Shawnee war leader and diplomat Organizer of a pan-Native confederacy British ally in the War of 1812 Born 1769, in a Kispoko Shawnee village in the Scioto River valley, Ohio country Name Tekoomsē, linked to a great comet visible in 1769 Brother Tenskwatawa, a religious leader known as “the Prophet” Headquarters Prophetstown, in present-day Indiana Southern journey Reached the Creek town of Tukabatchee, September 19, 1811 Died October 5, 1813, at the Battle of the Thames, in Upper Canada Tecumseh was born in 1769 while his parents, Pukeshinwau of the Kispoko Shawnee Panther Clan and Methoataaskee of the Piqua Shawnee Turtle Clan, were staying in a village in the Scioto River valley of present-day Ohio. His parents came from Shawnee communities living among the Creeks on the Tallapoosa River in present-day Alabama, and he always said that valley was his home. His name, Tekoomsē, was given while a great comet crossed the sky; the Shawnee called comets “sky panthers.” In 1774, when Tecumseh was six, his father was killed at the Battle of Kanawha near Point Pleasant in present-day West Virginia. His oldest brother, Cheeseekau, trained him as a warrior, and his sister Tecumapease taught him the customs and spirituality of his people. He grew up amid constant war with settlers pushing into the Ohio Valley. He fought in the Native confederacy that destroyed an American army on the Wabash in 1791, saw Cheeseekau killed, and was at the defeat at Fallen Timbers in August 1794. He refused to sign the Treaty of Greenville of 1795, which gave up most of present-day Ohio. The Prophet’s revival. Tenskwatawa preached that the Master of Life had charged the brothers with returning Native peoples to “the one true path” and ridding their communities of the corrupting influence of American trade and culture. The brothers founded towns at Greenville and then Prophetstown, in present-day Indiana, in defiance of the Greenville treaty. A confederacy. Tecumseh turned the revival into a political and military alliance. He offered Native peoples, the American Yawp writes, “a distinctly Native American identity” under a common spirituality. When the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne required Indiana tribes to sell three million acres, he organized a confederation to resist. The southern journey. On September 19, 1811, Tecumseh, Tenskwatawa and their cousin Seekaboo arrived at the Creek town of Tukabatchee to call for unity and the reclaiming of Native land. A great comet visible that year, later called Tecumseh’s Comet, was taken as a sign. The Creek prophet Hillis Hadjo, who traveled with him, carried his ideas to the Red Stick Creeks. The British alliance. While Tecumseh was in the South, Governor William Henry Harrison marched about 1,000 men against Prophetstown. Tenskwatawa attacked them on November 7, 1811, against Tecumseh’s warnings, and lost; Harrison burned the town. Tecumseh returned three months later to find it in ruins and allied his remaining forces with Britain, where they played an important part in British successes around the Great Lakes. Not all Native leaders followed Tecumseh, and his movement deepened divisions. The Yawp notes that the brothers used their message to strengthen their own authority over rival leaders, and that Tenskwatawa denounced opponents and those who sought accommodation with the Americans as witches. Among the Creeks, some warriors who fought with him were later killed on the orders of the Creek National Council for their raids. Much of what is known about Tecumseh comes from American and British sources, and accounts of his death differ: an 1846 Currier lithograph shows Colonel Richard M. Johnson shooting him, while the Encyclopedia of Alabama records that his body was carried from the field and buried in secret. At the Thames, British General Henry Procter retreated and fled, leaving Tecumseh and his warriors to make a last stand in a swamp. When he fell, his fighters scattered and his confederacy, “built up of numerous Native American tribes, collapsed.” His opponent Harrison later rode the fame of Tippecanoe to the presidency as the Whig candidate of 1840. Tecumseh led the last great attempt to unite the Native nations east of the Mississippi against American expansion. With his death, the American Battlefield Trust writes, “many tribes who followed his leadership peeled away,” and organized resistance in the Old Northwest ended. A long tradition of resistance The Yawp places Tecumseh’s confederacy at the end of a long line of Native movements: the Delaware prophet Neolin and the Ottawa leader Pontiac in the 1760s, and the “Western Confederacy” that defeated two American armies in the early 1790s before losing at Fallen Timbers. Tecumseh’s experience in that war, the Yawp suggests, “probably influenced his later efforts to generate solidarity.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cH-T2aY4DPY Tecumseh and the Native American Resistance Kings and Generals 58:03 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aTVCPWqaybU The OTHER United States of America | The Life & Times of Tecumseh History Abridged 13:02 2026-10-29

title: Theodore Roosevelt
subtitle: Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”
summary: Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901, at forty-two, after the assassination of William McKinley. He was the youngest person ever to hold the office. Historians often call him the first modern president, because he made the White House, rather than Congress or the parties, the center of American politics. His “Square Deal” used federal power to regulate big business, protect consumers, and conserve the nation’s forests and wild lands. Abroad he built up the Navy, secured the Panama Canal, and declared the United States the “policeman” of the Western Hemisphere. In 1912 he ran again as the candidate of his own Progressive Party.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Theodore Roosevelt
aliases: TR Teddy Roosevelt Square Deal Rough Riders Bull Moose big stick Roosevelt Corollary bully pulpit
themeText: The presidency Reform and protest Land and environment Foreign policy and diplomacy War and the military
text: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. New York City Oyster Bay, New York New York assemblyman (1882–1884) U.S. Civil Service commissioner President of the New York City Police Board Assistant secretary of the Navy (1897–1898) Rough Rider in the Spanish-American War Governor of New York Vice president (1901) Twenty-sixth president (1901–1909) Progressive (“Bull Moose”) Party candidate (1912) Born October 27, 1858, New York City Presidency 1901–1909; Republican; took office after McKinley’s assassination and was elected in his own right in 1904 Domestic program The Square Deal: the Northern Securities suit, the Hepburn Act, the Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts (1906) Conservation 150 national forests, 51 bird reserves, 5 national parks, and 18 national monuments Foreign policy “Speak softly and carry a big stick”; Panama Canal; Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine Nobel Peace Prize For mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War (1905); the first U.S. president to win it Died January 6, 1919, Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay, New York Roosevelt changed what Americans expected of a president. He argued that the president could use any power the Constitution did not specifically deny him, and he lent the prestige of the White House to the progressive causes of regulation, consumer protection, and conservation. He also led the United States toward an active, often interventionist role in the world. Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York City on October 27, 1858, the second of four children of Theodore Roosevelt Sr., a wealthy businessman and philanthropist, and Martha “Mittie” Roosevelt, who had grown up on a Georgia plantation. A sickly child with asthma, “Teedie” resolved as a teenager to “make his body” through gymnastics and weight-lifting, and he remained a lifelong champion of exercise and what he called the “strenuous life.” He was taught at home, traveled with his family in Europe and the Middle East, and entered Harvard College in 1876, where he studied natural history and took up boxing and wrestling. In October 1880 he married Alice Hathaway Lee. He enrolled at Columbia Law School but left after a year for politics, and from 1882 to 1884 he served in the New York Assembly. That same year he published his first book, The Naval War of 1812. On February 12, 1884, Alice gave birth to a daughter. Two days later Roosevelt’s mother died of typhoid fever and his wife died of kidney disease, within hours of each other and in the same house. Leaving the baby with his sister, he went to the Dakota Badlands, where he had first come to hunt in 1883. He bought two ranches, herded cattle, and served as a frontier sheriff, and what he saw there of vanishing bison and overgrazed land shaped his later interest in conservation. In 1886 he returned east, ran unsuccessfully for mayor of New York City, and married his childhood sweetheart, Edith Kermit Carow. They settled at Sagamore Hill in Oyster Bay, New York, and had five children, Theodore, Kermit, Ethel, Archibald, and Quentin, besides Alice. Roosevelt kept writing, producing biographies and the four-volume The Winning of the West. He was appointed to the U.S. Civil Service Commission by the Republican Benjamin Harrison and reappointed by the Democrat Grover Cleveland, and he clashed constantly with politicians who wanted jobs handed out as party rewards. In 1895 he became president of the New York City Police Board, where he fought corruption. In 1897 President McKinley made him assistant secretary of the navy, a post that the American Yawp connects to his support for McKinley in 1896. A believer in sea power, influenced by the naval theorist Alfred Thayer Mahan, he put the Navy on alert after the battleship Maine exploded in Havana Harbor in 1898 and told Commodore George Dewey to prepare for war with Spain. When war came, Roosevelt resigned and became commander of the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry, the “Rough Riders,” a mix of Ivy League gentlemen, cowboys, sheriffs, prospectors, police officers, and Native Americans. In Cuba he led them in a charge on foot up San Juan Hill (in fact Kettle Hill) outside Santiago. “I would rather have led that charge and earned my colonelcy than served three terms in the United States Senate,” he wrote. He came home a hero and was elected governor of New York in 1898 by a few thousand votes. In office he refused to give the top patronage jobs to party regulars and backed a tax on utility companies, angering the state Republican boss Thomas Platt. Platt and the national party leader Mark Hanna decided to “kick him upstairs” to the vice presidency in 1900. Roosevelt campaigned tirelessly for McKinley, traveling more than 21,000 miles. When McKinley was shot in September 1901, “that damned cowboy,” as Hanna called him, became president. The Square Deal. Roosevelt believed government had the right to regulate big business for the public good, though he did not want to abolish it. In 1902 his Justice Department sued the Northern Securities Company, a giant railroad combination organized by J. P. Morgan and other financiers, under the Sherman Antitrust Act. In 1904 the Supreme Court ordered it broken up. When an anthracite coal strike threatened the nation’s winter heating in 1902, he called the mine owners and labor representatives to the White House. When the owners refused to negotiate, he threatened to have troops seize and run the mines, and both sides agreed to arbitration. He called the result a “square deal,” and the phrase became the name of his domestic program. The Elkins Act of 1903 banned railroad rebates, and the Hepburn Act of 1906, passed after he took his case directly to the public on a speaking tour, let the Interstate Commerce Commission regulate railroad rates. After reading Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle, he pushed for the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906. Conservation. Roosevelt was, in the Miller Center’s words, the nation’s first conservationist president. He wanted the country to move from exploiting its natural resources to managing them carefully. With Gifford Pinchot he built up the Forest Service. He signed the Newlands Reclamation Act of 1902 for western irrigation and the Antiquities Act of 1906, which let presidents declare national monuments without Congress. He created 150 national forests, 51 bird reserves, five national parks including Mesa Verde, and eighteen national monuments, among them Devil’s Tower and the Grand Canyon, which he protected as a monument when Congress resisted making it a park. The sources give different totals for the land he protected. The Miller Center’s overview says nearly 200 million acres, its domestic-affairs essay says the national forests grew from 42 million to 172 million acres, and the National Park Service says about 230 million acres of public land. The bully pulpit. Roosevelt was the first president to use the press systematically to appeal to the public over the heads of Congress and party bosses. He used the office as a “bully pulpit” to shape public opinion. He also named the investigative reporters of the day “muckrakers,” in a 1906 speech. In 1904 he won the presidency in his own right, defeating Alton Parker 336 electoral votes to 140. He was the first president who had inherited the office to win election to it. He then promised not to seek another term. A world power. Roosevelt’s maxim was “speak softly and carry a big stick.” He made the Navy one of the largest in the world and in 1907 sent sixteen battleships, the “Great White Fleet,” on a fourteen-month voyage around the globe. When Colombia balked at an American canal across Panama, then part of Colombia, the United States backed a Panamanian revolution with money and a naval blockade. The 1903 Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty gave it perpetual control of the canal zone. The canal opened in 1914. In 1906 Roosevelt visited the works, the first president to leave the country while in office. As the Russo-Japanese War dragged on, he brought the two sides to peace talks at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in 1905, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize for it, the first American president to do so. He also helped settle a crisis between France and Germany over Morocco at Algeciras in 1906. Roosevelt believed that the president could use any power not specifically denied him by the Constitution or the laws. He was a reformer but not a radical. He saw big business as a natural stage of economic development and often argued that reform was needed to head off socialism. He distinguished between “good” and “bad” trusts and preferred to regulate corporations rather than break them up. His 1912 program, which he called the “New Nationalism,” cast the federal government as a “trustee” for the people, supervising the economy in the public interest. Abroad he believed that American power and values would benefit the world. He also spoke of a “manly duty” to police the Caribbean and spread what he called the benefits of Anglo-Saxon civilization. Roosevelt’s record on race was, in the Miller Center’s words, “a mixed bag.” He invited Booker T. Washington to dine at the White House in October 1901 and refused to apologize when the Southern press attacked him, but he did little to stop Southern states from taking the vote away from Black citizens, and he believed Black Americans as a race were inferior to whites. In 1906, after a shooting in Brownsville, Texas, was blamed on Black soldiers despite conflicting accounts and no physical evidence, he ordered the dishonorable discharge of three companies, 160 men, without a trial. His foreign policy also drew criticism. In December 1904 he announced what became the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine. Where Monroe had warned Europe out of the Americas, Roosevelt claimed for the United States the right to intervene in Latin American countries guilty of “chronic wrongdoing.” The policy, the Miller Center notes, created much resentment in Latin America. The sources describe his first use of it in the Dominican Republic differently. The Miller Center says an American collector took over its customs houses, while the American Yawp says Roosevelt sent the Marines to occupy the country in 1905 and imposed financial supervision. Historians have also questioned his reputation as a “trust buster.” The Yawp calls it “wildly exaggerated” and notes that his successor, William Howard Taft, brought more than twice as many breakups in four years as Roosevelt did in seven. Roosevelt chose Taft as his successor in 1908 but soon fell out with him over conservation and appointments. In 1912 he won a series of Republican primaries that put him ahead in the race for delegates, but Taft’s supporters controlled the convention and renominated the president. Roosevelt and his followers formed the Progressive Party. Saying he felt “as strong as a Bull Moose,” he campaigned for a minimum wage for women, an eight-hour day, social insurance, and the direct election of senators. Near the end of the campaign he was shot and insisted on finishing his speech, the bullet slowed by the thick manuscript in his coat. He finished second with 27.4 percent of the vote, ahead of Taft but behind the Democrat Woodrow Wilson. His new party became one of the most significant third parties in American history. After the 1912 defeat Roosevelt explored the River of Doubt in the Brazilian Amazon with his son Kermit and came back weakened by malaria and infection. When World War I began, he argued loudly for military preparedness and attacked Wilson’s neutrality. After the United States entered the war, the War Department turned down his offer to raise a volunteer division. All four of his sons served, and the death of the youngest, Quentin, a pilot shot down over Germany, devastated him. Roosevelt died in his sleep at Sagamore Hill on January 6, 1919. The Miller Center sees Roosevelt’s 1912 platform as a forerunner of nearly every later liberal program, from his cousin Franklin’s New Deal to Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. He was the first president to give his domestic program a name, a practice later presidents followed. A national park in the North Dakota Badlands, where his interest in conservation began, bears his name. I would rather have led that charge and earned my colonelcy than served three terms in the United States Senate. Theodore Roosevelt on the charge at San Juan (Kettle) Hill, 1898 Chronic wrongdoing, or an impotence which results in a general loosening of the ties of civilized society, may in America, as elsewhere, ultimately require intervention by some civilized nation. Theodore Roosevelt annual message to Congress, December 6, 1904 (the Roosevelt Corollary) Leave it as it is. You cannot improve on it. The ages have been at work on it, and man can only mar it. Theodore Roosevelt on the Grand Canyon We stand at Armageddon, and we battle for the Lord. title: Thomas Edison
subtitle: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory
summary: Thomas Edison, a boy with only a few months of schooling who sold newspapers on a Michigan railroad, became one of the most celebrated inventors in American history. At his Menlo Park, New Jersey, laboratory, the first industrial research lab, he invented the phonograph in 1877 and developed a practical electric light and the whole system needed to power it; in 1882 his Pearl Street station began lighting lower Manhattan. Later, at West Orange, he helped create the recording and motion picture industries. To his countrymen he became a living symbol of American ingenuity.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Thomas Edison, seated, around 1922
aliases: Edison Menlo Park
themeText: Science and technology Economy and finance Everyday life Arts and popular culture
text: Thomas Alva Edison Milan, Ohio West Orange, New Jersey Telegrapher Inventor Industrialist Head of the Naval Consulting Board (World War I) Phonograph 1877: the first machine that could record and play back sound Electric light A carbonized-thread filament burned for 13½ hours; Menlo Park was lit up in December 1879 Power station Pearl Street, lower Manhattan, opened in September 1882, “the electric age had begun” Laboratories Menlo Park (1876), the first of its kind; West Orange (1887), where up to 10,000 people worked during World War I Honors A special Congressional medal in 1928 Edison did not just invent devices; he built complete systems (power plants, wiring, records, film studios) that turned inventions into industries, and his research laboratory became the model for modern corporate science. Electric light, recorded sound, and movies reshaped everyday American life. Thomas Alva Edison was born on February 11, 1847, in Milan, Ohio, the seventh and last child of Samuel and Nancy Edison; when he was seven the family moved to Port Huron, Michigan. He attended school for only a few months. His mother taught him reading, writing, and arithmetic, and he taught himself the rest from books. At thirteen he went to work selling newspapers and candy on the railroad between Port Huron and Detroit, reading scientific books in his spare time and learning to operate a telegraph. By sixteen he was a full-time telegrapher, drifting from city to city in a booming industry. In Boston in 1868 he began to turn from telegrapher to inventor. His first patent, an electric vote recorder for legislatures, was a commercial failure, and he resolved to invent only things the public would want. In New York his improved stock ticker earned him $40,000: enough to open his first laboratory and factory in Newark, New Jersey, in 1871. There he improved the telegraph and married Mary Stilwell. In 1876 Edison moved to the village of Menlo Park, New Jersey, and built a laboratory equipped to work on any invention, the first research and development lab anywhere, sometimes called his greatest invention. His first great success there was the tinfoil phonograph of 1877, the first machine that could record and reproduce sound. It made him world famous; he demonstrated it at the White House for President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1878. So great was his fame that when a New York paper ran a fake April Fool’s interview describing an Edison machine that made food out of air, water, and dirt, readers wrote asking when it would be on sale. Next he took on electric light. The idea was not new, but no one had made it practical for the home. After a year and a half, a lamp with a filament of carbonized sewing thread burned for thirteen and a half hours, and in December 1879 Edison lit up the Menlo Park complex. He then built everything else an electric system needed, and in September 1882 his Pearl Street power station began supplying a square mile of lower Manhattan. His electric companies later merged into what became General Electric. In 1887 he opened a much larger laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, where he could run ten or twenty projects at once. There he turned the phonograph into a home product, creating the recording industry, and developed a device to do “for the eye what the phonograph does for the ear”: motion pictures, first shown in 1891 and filmed from 1893 in a studio called the Black Maria. After ten years of work he produced an alkaline storage battery that became his most profitable product. Edison believed in self-improvement, practical results, and relentless work. After his first patent failed, he insisted on inventing only what people would buy, and he approached each problem by developing the whole system it needed. He favored military preparedness before World War I and headed the Navy’s board of civilian inventors. Edison’s greatest failure was a decade-long attempt in the 1890s to mine iron ore in New Jersey with new methods; he sold all his General Electric stock to pay for it and lost everything he put in. He never controlled the company that bore his name, bankers such as J. P. Morgan financed the electric industry, and in 1892 “Edison” was dropped from General Electric’s name. In motion pictures, many others soon improved on his early work, and by 1918 competition drove him out of the business. His achievements also depended on staffs of skilled assistants and on capital from investment bankers. In later life Edison became a cultural icon, a real-life Horatio Alger hero. Congress voted him a special medal in 1928, and in 1929, for the fiftieth anniversary of the electric light, Henry Ford gave a banquet in his honor at Greenfield Village, where Ford had restored the Menlo Park laboratory; President Herbert Hoover attended. At Ford’s and Harvey Firestone’s request, Edison spent his last years testing thousands of plants as an American source of rubber, settling on goldenrod. He died at his home, Glenmont, in West Orange on October 18, 1931. His laboratory and home are now Thomas Edison National Historical Park. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8k6zyXAXW5o Thomas Edison: His Kaleidoscope Mind Biographics 21:07 2026-10-23

title: Thomas Jefferson
subtitle: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president
summary: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, served as the first secretary of state and the third president, doubled the size of the nation with the Louisiana Purchase, and founded the University of Virginia. He was the leading voice of a republic of independent farmers, limited government, and religious freedom. He was also a lifelong slaveholder who owned more than 600 people over his lifetime, freed only a handful, and most likely fathered six children with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household. As Encyclopedia Virginia puts it, each generation has claimed him “on both sides of almost every important question.”
thumbAlt: Portrait of Thomas Jefferson by Rembrandt Peale
aliases: Jefferson Monticello Notes on the State of Virginia Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom Jeffersonian Republicans Kentucky Resolutions
themeText: The presidency Political thought Slavery and emancipation Territorial expansion Parties and elections
text: Thomas Jefferson Shadwell, Virginia Monticello, Virginia Principal author of the Declaration of Independence Governor of Virginia (1779–1781) Minister to France (1785–1789) First U.S. secretary of state Vice president (1797–1801) Third president (1801–1809) Founder of the University of Virginia Born April 13, 1743 (April 2, Old Style), at Shadwell, Virginia Party Republican (Democratic-Republican), which he founded with James Madison in the 1790s Elections Lost to John Adams in 1796 (71–68); tied with Aaron Burr in 1800 (73 each) and won in the House on the 36th ballot; reelected easily in 1804 Louisiana Purchase 1803: 828,000 square miles for $15 million, about four cents an acre Enslaved people More than 600 over his lifetime, of whom he freed only a handful Self-chosen epitaph Author of the Declaration of Independence and of the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and father of the University of Virginia; he left out the presidency Death July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration, the same day as John Adams Jefferson wrote the creed of the American nation, that “all men are created equal,” and later Americans have used it against the very inequalities he lived with. As president he cut the federal government, doubled the nation’s territory, and built the first opposition party to win power peacefully. As a slaveholder and a theorist of Black inferiority, he embodies the contradiction between liberty and slavery at the heart of the early republic. Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743 (April 2 by the Old Style calendar), at Shadwell, on the Rivanna River in what became Albemarle County, Virginia. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a surveyor and planter who helped make the famous Fry-Jefferson map of Virginia; his mother, Jane Randolph, came from one of the colony’s most powerful families. When his father died in 1757, the fourteen-year-old inherited more than 5,000 acres and about twenty enslaved people. At the College of William and Mary he studied mathematics and science with the Scottish professor William Small and law with George Wythe. He learned Latin, Greek, French, Italian, and Spanish and became perhaps the best-read lawyer in Virginia. In 1769 he began building Monticello, his house on a hilltop overlooking Shadwell. He would remodel it for four decades, and his enslaved craftsmen built much of its fine furniture. On January 1, 1772, he married Martha Wayles Skelton, a young widow. When her father, John Wayles, died in 1773, Jefferson inherited more than 11,000 acres, 135 enslaved people, including the Hemings family, and a large debt. Of their six children only two daughters, Martha and Mary, reached adulthood. Martha Jefferson died in 1782 after a difficult childbirth, on September 6 according to Encyclopedia Virginia (the Miller Center gives November 6), and Jefferson reportedly promised her never to remarry. Revolutionary. A member of the House of Burgesses from 1769, Jefferson won fame in 1774 with A Summary View of the Rights of British America, which argued that Parliament had no authority over the colonies at all. In the Second Continental Congress he was named to the committee to draft a declaration of independence. The other members deferred to him; John Adams admired his writing, and Franklin said he would never write anything for others to edit. Jefferson’s draft, revised by Congress, which struck out his attack on the king for the slave trade, was adopted on July 4, 1776. His authorship did not become widely known until the 1790s. Virginia reformer. Back in Virginia, Jefferson led a revision of the state’s laws. His bills abolished entail and primogeniture, which had kept great estates intact, and his plan for public schools failed. His Statute for Religious Freedom, carried through the legislature by James Madison, passed on January 16, 1786, and separated church and state in Virginia. Wartime governor. Elected governor in 1779, Jefferson had little power under the state constitution, and his term was a series of disasters. In January 1781, partly because Jefferson was slow to call out the militia, Benedict Arnold’s British force occupied Richmond. That June British cavalry raided Charlottesville and Jefferson barely escaped capture at Monticello. Critics accused him of cowardice, charges Encyclopedia Virginia calls “almost certainly unfounded,” but the legislature ordered an inquiry, which later thanked him. Writer and diplomat. In Notes on the State of Virginia, written after his governorship and published in 1785–1787, Jefferson praised farmers as “the chosen people of God,” defended American nature against European claims of inferiority, and denounced slavery as an evil. In the same book he wrote that Black people were “inferior to the whites in the endowments both of body and mind.” (The Miller Center calls Notes his only book; Encyclopedia Virginia calls that description inaccurate.) In Congress in 1784 he drafted a plan for governing the western territories that would admit them as equal states and ban slavery there after 1800. Congress dropped the slavery ban by one vote, but kept the principle of admitting new states as equals. From 1785 to 1789 he served as minister to France, where he became Europe’s leading interpreter of America, designed the Virginia State Capitol on a Roman temple, and urged Madison to add a bill of rights to the new Constitution. Secretary of state and party leader. As Washington’s first secretary of state (1790–1793), Jefferson clashed with Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton. He helped broker the compromise that traded federal assumption of state debts for a capital on the Potomac, but he came to believe that Hamilton was a secret monarchist. With Madison he organized the Republican Party, which favored states’ rights, a strict reading of the Constitution, and sympathy for revolutionary France. After finishing second to Adams in 1796 and becoming vice president, he secretly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, which claimed a state’s right to nullify the Alien and Sedition Acts. President. In 1800 Jefferson and his running mate, Aaron Burr, tied with 73 electoral votes each, and the Federalist House elected Jefferson only on the thirty-sixth ballot, on February 17, 1801. It was a peaceful transfer of power from one party to another. In his inaugural address he declared, “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” He walked to his inauguration, dressed simply, and sent his messages to Congress in writing. His administration cut the army and navy, repealed internal taxes, pardoned the last prisoners under the Sedition Act, and reduced the national debt from $80 million to $57 million, even after paying for Louisiana. He never vetoed a bill. In 1803 Napoleon offered to sell all of Louisiana. Jefferson’s envoys agreed to pay $15 million for 828,000 square miles, doubling the size of the nation. Jefferson had doubts that the Constitution allowed the purchase, but he set them aside. He sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the new lands, and their expedition crossed to the Pacific and back between 1804 and 1806. He also sent the navy against Tripoli in the Barbary War rather than pay higher tribute. Reelected easily in 1804, he struggled in his second term as Britain and France seized American ships. After a British warship fired on the USS Chesapeake in 1807, Jefferson chose economic pressure over war: the Embargo Act of December 1807 banned American foreign trade. It failed. Exports fell from $108 million to $22 million, smuggling flourished, and Congress replaced it as Jefferson left office. Following Washington’s example, he refused a third term. Jefferson believed in a republic of independent landowning farmers, a “wise and frugal Government, which shall restrain men from injuring one another” but otherwise leave them free. He favored strict limits on federal power, freedom of religion, public education, and the spread of property. A deist, he believed in a creator who governed the world through natural laws, and he opposed any official religion. On slavery he wrote eloquently against the institution while holding hundreds of people in bondage. He believed that Black and white Americans could not live together as equals in freedom and that emancipation had to be combined with deportation. In 1820 he called the Missouri crisis “a fire bell in the night” and wrote of slavery, “we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go.” Jefferson’s slaveholding is the central controversy of his reputation. Over his lifetime he owned more than 600 people, mostly through inheritance and natural increase. He sold people to raise money, sold others out of state as punishment, sanctioned whippings, and pursued those who escaped. Beginning in Paris, by the Miller Center’s account, or in the late 1780s or early 1790s, by Encyclopedia Virginia’s, he had a long sexual relationship with Sally Hemings, the enslaved half-sister of his late wife, who had come to Paris at fourteen as a companion to his daughter. In 2000 the Thomas Jefferson Foundation concluded, based on documents, the oral histories of Monticello’s Black families, and DNA studies, that Jefferson “most likely was the father of all six of Sally Hemings’s children.” He freed or allowed to leave all four who survived. Federalists exposed the relationship as a national scandal during his presidency; Jefferson kept a public silence. His presidency had its critics too. Federalists called the Louisiana Purchase unconstitutional. He led attempts to remove Federalist judges by impeachment, succeeding against John Pickering but failing against Samuel Chase. He pressed treason charges against Aaron Burr, who was acquitted in 1807, and his embargo devastated the economy. His Kentucky Resolutions were later invoked in the nullification crisis of the 1830s and by opponents of civil rights enforcement in the 1960s. In retirement at Monticello, Jefferson sold his library of roughly 6,700 volumes to Congress for $23,950 in 1815 to replace the books burned by the British. It became the core of the modern Library of Congress. His last great project was the University of Virginia, chartered in 1819 and opened in 1825. He designed its buildings, chose its faculty and books, and left out a chapel. In 1812 he and John Adams reconciled and began one of the great correspondences in American letters. Jefferson lived beyond his means all his life, and debts left his estate insolvent. At his death he owed $107,273.63, and in 1827 more than 100 enslaved people were sold at auction to pay his creditors. He died at Monticello on July 4, 1826, fifty years to the day after the Declaration was adopted, a few hours before John Adams. He chose his own epitaph, naming only the Declaration, the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and the University of Virginia. “If Jefferson was wrong, America is wrong,” the biographer James Parton wrote in 1874. “If America is right, Jefferson was right.” We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. Thomas Jefferson first inaugural address, March 4, 1801 Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, if ever he had a chosen people, whose breasts he has made his peculiar deposit for substantial and genuine virtue. Thomas Jefferson Notes on the State of Virginia We have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go. Justice is in one scale, and self-preservation in the other. Thomas Jefferson on slavery, during the Missouri crisis, 1820 This momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror. title: Thurgood Marshall
subtitle: Civil rights lawyer and first Black justice of the Supreme Court
summary: Thurgood Marshall was the lawyer who led the legal campaign against segregation and, in 1967, became the first African American justice of the Supreme Court. As chief counsel of the NAACP and director of its Legal Defense and Educational Fund, he won nearly thirty Supreme Court cases, above all Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which struck down school segregation. He then served as a federal appeals judge and as solicitor general before joining the Court, where until 1991 he was a forceful liberal voice for individual and civil rights.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Justice Thurgood Marshall
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Constitution and law
text: Thurgood Marshall Baltimore, Maryland Chief counsel, NAACP (from 1938) Director, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund (from 1940) Judge, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (1961) Solicitor General (1965–1967) Associate Justice of the Supreme Court (1967–1991) Born July 2, 1908, Baltimore Education Lincoln University (B.A. 1930); Howard University Law School (J.D. 1933) Major cases argued Smith v. Allwright (1944), Morgan v. Virginia (1946), Sweatt v. Painter (1950), Brown v. Board of Education (1954) Supreme Court 1967–1991; first African American justice Died January 24, 1993 Marshall was born on July 2, 1908, in Baltimore, the son of a kindergarten teacher and a railroad dining-car waiter. On his days off, his father took the boys to watch trials and then made them argue legal questions at home, challenging every point. Baltimore was segregated, Marshall attended an all-Black grade school and once could not find a restroom he was allowed to use, and as punishment for misbehaving in high school he was sent to read the Constitution, which he came to know backwards and forwards. At Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, a classmate of Langston Hughes, he was suspended for hazing, then found his calling in the debate club and helped desegregate a local movie theater. Rejected by the University of Maryland’s law school because of his race, he went to Howard University; his mother sold her wedding ring to help pay the tuition. There the assistant dean, Charles Hamilton Houston, was training a generation of civil rights lawyers to use the law itself against discrimination. Marshall graduated first in his class in 1933, turned down a scholarship to Harvard, and opened a practice in Baltimore, turning away no one who could not pay. One of Marshall’s first victories forced the University of Maryland’s law school, the school that had rejected him, to admit a Black student. He joined the NAACP’s national staff, succeeded Houston as its chief counsel in 1938, and from 1940 directed the new NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. He traveled through the South investigating lynchings and the denial of voting rights and fair trials, often at personal risk. In the Supreme Court he won Smith v. Allwright (1944), which opened Texas primaries to Black voters; Morgan v. Virginia (1946), which banned segregation on interstate buses; and Sweatt v. Painter (1950), which required the University of Texas Law School to admit a Black applicant. Then he attacked segregation itself. In 1949 he met Black parents in Clarendon County, South Carolina, whose case, Briggs v. Elliott, became part of Brown. Using social science evidence that segregation harmed Black children, he argued in 1952 and 1953 that separate could never be equal; on May 17, 1954, the Court agreed unanimously. “Equal,” he once said, “means getting the same thing, at the same time and in the same place.” In 1957 his team won the injunction that opened Little Rock’s Central High School to nine Black students. President Kennedy appointed him to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit in 1961; none of his opinions there was reversed by the Supreme Court. In 1965 Lyndon Johnson made him solicitor general, the government’s chief lawyer before the Court, and in 1967 nominated him to the Supreme Court itself. Marshall saw the Constitution as a living document and the courts as the surest road to equality. He respected Martin Luther King Jr. as “a great speaker” and conceded that the protests “reached people’s consciousness,” but he distrusted civil disobedience: “If you want to write a book,” he recalled telling King, who often cited Thoreau, “you go to jail and write it.” On the Court he championed individual rights and civil rights and sought to limit criminal punishment; with Justice William Brennan he argued that the death penalty was unconstitutional in all circumstances. Marshall’s preference for lawsuits over street protest put him at odds with King and younger activists over tactics. As the Court shifted toward conservatism, he found himself increasingly in dissent and frustrated as his influence waned, dissenting, for example, when the Court reversed course on the death penalty in Gregg v. Georgia. Marshall retired in 1991 and was succeeded by Clarence Thomas. He died of heart failure in Bethesda, Maryland, on January 24, 1993. The strategy he and Houston built, case by case, until segregation itself could be challenged, laid the constitutional foundation on which the civil rights movement stood. His career ran from a segregated Baltimore schoolroom to the Supreme Court bench. Thurgood Marshall led the legal assault that dismantled segregation and became a pioneering figure on the nation’s highest court.
