title: Ulysses S. Grant
subtitle: Union general who won the Civil War and eighteenth president
summary: Ulysses S. Grant was the Union general who won the Civil War and the eighteenth president of the United States (1869–1877). A quiet tanner’s son who failed at farming and business before the war, he rose in four years to command all Union armies, took Vicksburg, wore down Robert E. Lee’s army, and accepted its surrender at Appomattox. As president he fought for the Fifteenth Amendment and sent troops against the Ku Klux Klan, but scandals among his appointees long dominated his reputation, which historians are now reassessing.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Ulysses S. Grant
themeText: War and the military The presidency Civil rights and citizenship
text: Hiram Ulysses Grant Point Pleasant, Ohio Mexican-American War officer Commanding general of the Union armies Eighteenth president (1869–1877) Author of *Personal Memoirs* Education U.S. Military Academy at West Point Civil War victories Forts Henry and Donelson, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, and the final campaign against Lee Presidency 1869–1877 Memoirs Written while dying of throat cancer, completed just before his death in 1885 Hiram Ulysses Grant was born on April 27, 1822, in Point Pleasant, Ohio, the eldest of six children of a tanner. He hated the stinking tannery and swore he would never work in one as an adult. Quiet and small, he was mocked by other children as “Useless,” but he was famous locally for handling unruly horses. His father secured him an appointment to West Point, where a clerical error made him “Ulysses S. Grant” for life. He graduated twenty-first in a class of thirty-nine; though the finest horseman at the academy, he was assigned to the infantry. In the Mexican-American War he served as his regiment’s quartermaster, learning the logistics of war, and was twice cited for bravery, yet he mourned the waste of war. After the war he married Julia Dent, his West Point roommate’s sister; three of his wedding attendants, including James Longstreet, would later fight against him. Posted to the Pacific Coast far from his family, he grew depressed, by some accounts drinking heavily, and resigned from the army in 1854. Over the next several years he failed at farming a plot he called “Hardscrabble” and at a string of other jobs; one Christmas he pawned his watch for $22 to buy his family presents. He freed the one man he was given as a slave rather than sell him. By 1860 he was clerking in his family’s leather shop in Galena, Illinois. When the Civil War began, the Union needed trained officers. Grant turned an unruly Illinois regiment into a disciplined unit and was soon a brigadier general. In February 1862 he captured Forts Henry and Donelson in Tennessee. Donelson, where he took the surrender of an entire Confederate force, was the Union’s first real victory and made him famous overnight as “Unconditional Surrender” Grant. He survived blame for the costly surprise at Shiloh, then in 1863 marched his army down the west bank of the Mississippi, crossed below Vicksburg, cut loose from his supply lines, and won five battles before besieging the city. On July 4, 1863, Vicksburg surrendered with more than 27,000 men, giving the Union control of the Mississippi. “Grant is my man,” Lincoln declared, “and I am his.” In 1864 Lincoln made him lieutenant general and commander of all Union armies. Grant coordinated simultaneous campaigns, Sherman’s march through Georgia, Sheridan’s in the Shenandoah, while he himself fought Lee across Virginia at the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, and Cold Harbor and then besieged Petersburg. On April 9, 1865, at Appomattox Court House, he accepted Lee’s surrender on generous terms: the Confederates could go home if they laid down their arms. Elected president in 1868 under the slogan “Let us have peace,” Grant lobbied hard for the Fifteenth Amendment, guaranteeing the vote regardless of race, and sent the army to protect Black Southerners from the Ku Klux Klan. He presided over the completion of the first transcontinental railroad in 1869, attempted reforms in Native American policy and the civil service, and improved relations with Britain. He was re-elected in a landslide in 1872. Grant disliked politics but shared the Republican creed that had won the war: the Union was perpetual, slavery was dead, and the freedpeople were entitled to the rights of citizens. He sought reconciliation with the white South without abandoning Black Americans. His sense of war was unromantic; he mourned the dead, and from his first fight he took the lesson that the enemy “had as much reason to fear my forces as I had his.” Grant’s relentless fighting in 1864 produced such enormous casualties that Democratic newspapers called him “the Butcher.” As president he chose his cabinet without consulting party leaders and was loyal out of all proportion to friends and associates; some appointees proved incompetent or corrupt. He was never personally implicated in the scandals, but he failed to cut loose those who were, and his reputation suffered. During his second term a depression that spread from Europe brought high unemployment, and many Americans blamed him for the country’s economic troubles. After leaving office Grant lost his fortune in a financial swindle and learned he was dying of throat cancer. To provide for his family, he wrote his Personal Memoirs, working on his porch wrapped in blankets and in terrible pain, and finished them days before his death in 1885. The book was a great success and secured his family’s finances. Long ranked near the bottom of presidential lists because of the scandals, Grant has risen sharply in recent rankings as historians give weight to his defense of African American rights. Grant won the war that ended slavery and, as president, tried, more than most Northern leaders of his time, to secure the rights of the people it had freed. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dkEv515UQ4A Ulysses S. title: Walt Disney
subtitle: Creator of Mickey Mouse, the animated feature film, and Disneyland
summary: Walt Disney grew up on a Missouri farm and in Kansas City, went bankrupt with his first cartoon studio, and moved to Hollywood with almost nothing. With his brother Roy and the animator Ub Iwerks he created Mickey Mouse, who became a star in Steamboat Willie (1928), a cartoon with synchronized music that became the most successful sound cartoon of its day. His studio made Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length animated feature, and later used television to build a new kind of entertainment empire, crowned by Disneyland in 1955. He won more Academy Awards than anyone in history.
thumbAlt: Walt Disney on the Place de la Concorde in Paris in 1935
aliases: Disney Walter Elias Disney Uncle Walt
themeText: Arts and popular culture Science and technology Everyday life Economy and finance
text: Walter Elias Disney Chicago, Illinois Animator and cartoon producer Co-founder of the Walt Disney Studio Film and television producer Creator of Disneyland (1955) Mickey Mouse Debuted in Steamboat Willie (1928); Disney himself was Mickey’s voice First animated feature Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) Disneyland Opened in 1955 with financial backing from ABC; Main Street, U.S.A. was modeled on Marceline, Missouri Record Holds the record for most Academy Awards won Honors Presidential Medal of Freedom from Lyndon Johnson Disney turned animated cartoons into feature-length art and an industry, and pioneered the merging of film, television, merchandise, and theme parks that defines modern entertainment. His sentimental vision of small-town America shaped how generations of Americans imagined childhood and their own past. Walter Elias Disney was born on December 5, 1901, in Chicago, the son of Elias and Flora Disney; his brother Roy would later run the business side of his company. In 1906 the family moved to a farm near Marceline, Missouri, where Walt began to draw animals. “More things of importance happened to me in Marceline than have happened since,” he wrote in 1938. When the farm failed in 1911, the family moved to Kansas City, and nine-year-old Walt got up at 3:30 every morning, seven days a week, to deliver newspapers before school; on Saturdays he took classes at the Kansas City Art Institute. In 1918, after lying about his age with his mother’s help, he joined the Red Cross Ambulance Corps and spent nine months in France driving ambulances and supply trucks. Back in Kansas City he met the artist Ub Iwerks and learned animation making one-minute advertisements to run before films. In 1922 he started his own studio, Laugh-O-Gram Films, and made Alice’s Wonderland, about a real girl entering a cartoon world. He had good ideas but was not a good businessman: his unpaid staff left, and in July 1923 he declared bankruptcy and left for Hollywood. With $500 borrowed from an uncle, Walt and Roy started the Disney Brothers Studio and sold a series of Alice Comedies. In 1927 they had a hit with Oswald the Lucky Rabbit, until their New York distributor hired away most of the animators and claimed that Universal owned the character. Determined to own his creations from then on, Disney worked with Roy and his one loyal animator, Iwerks, on a new character. Iwerks drew Mickey Mouse, Disney gave him his voice, and Steamboat Willie, with synchronized music, made him famous in 1928. Through the Depression the studio kept experimenting. Disney bought exclusive rights to the new three-color Technicolor process, won his first Academy Award in 1932 for Flowers and Trees, and in 1937 released Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first full-length animated feature. Pinocchio, Fantasia, Dumbo, and Bambi followed in the early 1940s, and during World War II the studio turned to training and patriotic films. In the 1950s Disney moved into live-action movies and television; his Disneyland show’s Davy Crockett episodes set boys everywhere wearing coonskin caps, and The Mickey Mouse Club began on ABC in 1955. That same year, with ABC’s financial backing, he opened Disneyland, a park where visitors could step into his films instead of just watching them. Its Main Street, U.S.A. was modeled on the downtown of Marceline. Disney built his empire on what he considered good, old-fashioned fun and a sentimental picture of small-town America. He had a profound sense of what the public wanted and tapped the moods of each era, the hardships of the Depression, the patriotism of the 1940s, the anticommunism of the 1950s. He insisted on owning everything he created, and he believed great work took a team: “You can dream, create, design, and build the most wonderful place in the world,” he said, “but it requires people to make that dream a reality.” In 1941 his animators went on strike for fair wages and job security; the strike ended that fall, but Disney felt personally betrayed. In 1947 he testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee in its investigation of communist influence in Hollywood, hearings that led to a blacklist barring hundreds of film artists from work. In the 1960s Disney’s “Imagineers” developed new technology such as audio-animatronics, and he began buying land for a second park in central Florida, which opened as Walt Disney World in 1971, after his death. He helped found the California Institute of the Arts, received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Lyndon Johnson, and died of lung cancer on December 15, 1966. His studio’s hits of the 1960s included One Hundred and One Dalmatians, Mary Poppins, and The Jungle Book. He still holds the record for most Academy Awards won. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bAtMP73ok78 Walt Disney: Entrepreneur & Producer | Mini Bio | BIO Biography 4:27 2026-10-23

title: W. E. B. Du Bois
subtitle: Scholar, editor, and co-founder of the NAACP
summary: W. E. B. Du Bois was the foremost Black intellectual of the early twentieth century and one of its most uncompromising voices for civil rights. The first African American to earn a PhD at Harvard, he pioneered the sociological study of Black life and wrote The Souls of Black Folk (1903), which challenged Booker T. Washington’s accommodation to segregation. He founded the Niagara Movement in 1905, helped found the NAACP in 1909, and for nearly a quarter century edited its magazine, The Crisis. He was also a leader of the Pan-African movement. He died in Ghana on the eve of the 1963 March on Washington.
thumbAlt: Photograph of W. E. B. Du Bois
aliases: The Souls of Black Folk double consciousness the color line Talented Tenth Niagara Movement The Crisis
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Political thought
text: William Edward Burghardt Du Bois Great Barrington, Massachusetts Accra, Ghana Sociologist and historian Professor at Wilberforce and Atlanta University Co-founder of the Niagara Movement (1905) and the NAACP (1909) Editor of *The Crisis* (1910–1934) Pan-Africanist Born February 23, 1868, Great Barrington, Massachusetts (one source gives 1869) Education Fisk University; Harvard, where in 1895 he became the first Black American to earn a PhD; graduate study in Germany Major books The Philadelphia Negro (1899), The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Darkwater (1920), Black Reconstruction in America (1935) Organizations Niagara Movement (1905); NAACP (1909), its only Black officer at first The Crisis Founding editor, November 1910 to July 1934 Died August 27, 1963, Accra, Ghana Du Bois insisted that Black Americans demand full civil and political equality without compromise, and he used scholarship, journalism, and organizing to press that demand. His idea of “double consciousness” and his warning that “the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line” remain among the most quoted ideas in American thought. William Edward Burghardt Du Bois was born in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, in 1868, three years after the end of the Civil War. The American Yawp and the Library of Congress give 1868. The Academy of American Poets heads its biography “1868–1963” but gives his birth date in the text as February 23, 1869. He was raised mainly by his mother. His early years were spent in a small farmhouse near the Housatonic River on land his mother’s family had held for more than 150 years. He graduated at the top of his high school class, and as a teenager he reported on the town’s politics as a correspondent for a Philadelphia newspaper. Du Bois went south to Fisk University in Nashville. His years in the South in the 1880s shaped his life’s work, the study of what was then called the “Negro problem,” the system of racial and economic discrimination that he predicted would be the problem of the twentieth century. He then studied at Harvard, did graduate work in Germany, and in 1895 became the first Black American to earn a PhD at Harvard. He taught at Wilberforce University in Ohio and at Atlanta University in Georgia, and his early studies of the Atlantic slave trade and of Black life in Philadelphia, published as The Philadelphia Negro, helped establish sociology as an academic discipline. The Souls of Black Folk. In 1903 Du Bois published The Souls of Black Folk, a collection of essays that combined history, sociology, and literature. It opened with a prophecy: “The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line.” It described the “double-consciousness” of Black Americans, “this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others,” and the feeling of being “an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings.” In the chapter “Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,” Du Bois criticized Washington’s accommodationism, which, he said later, had “implicitly abandoned all political and social rights.” Du Bois argued instead that a “Talented Tenth” of educated Black leaders should guide the race and press for civil rights immediately and without compromise. The Niagara Movement and the NAACP. In July 1905 Du Bois and William Monroe Trotter gathered twenty-nine Black leaders at Niagara Falls, on the Canadian side because hotels on the American side barred Black guests. Their platform demanded free speech, a free press, manhood suffrage, and the abolition of all distinctions based on race. Washington’s allies, the “Tuskegee Machine,” worked to undermine the movement. In 1909 Du Bois joined white and Black reformers, including veterans of Niagara, in founding the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. In 1910 he left academia to become its director of publicity and research, at first its only Black officer. The Crisis. In November 1910 the NAACP launched The Crisis, with Du Bois as editor. For its largely Black readers he personified the NAACP. The magazine carried news, editorials, fiction, poetry, art, and reports on the achievements of people of color around the world. In the 1920s, with a circulation of more than 100,000, it became the premier outlet for writers of the Harlem Renaissance. In 1919 he went to France to report on the Paris Peace Conference, investigate the treatment of Black soldiers, and organize a Pan-African Congress. He also wrote novels, poetry, and a historical pageant, The Star of Ethiopia, seen by nearly 30,000 people. Books such as The Souls of Black Folk, The Philadelphia Negro, and Black Reconstruction in America (1935) helped transform the study of African American history. Du Bois believed that Black Americans should demand full equality at once, refusing the compromises Washington accepted. In the Yawp’s words, he urged them “to concede to nothing.” He trusted in the power of social science to expose and defeat white supremacy, and he saw American racism as part of a worldwide color line linked to colonialism. His thinking changed over time. An early socialist, he joined the Communist Party in 1961 and moved to Ghana at the invitation of President Kwame Nkrumah. Du Bois’s rivalry with Booker T. Washington defined Black politics for a generation. Yet he had congratulated Washington on his 1895 Atlanta speech, and he later admitted, “I admired much about him.” Four years after attacking Washington in print, the two men spoke from the same lectern at Philadelphia Divinity School. In the 1920s he and other NAACP leaders traded accusations with the Black nationalist Marcus Garvey, and he criticized Harlem Renaissance writers whose portraits of the “Negro underworld” he feared would harm the civil rights cause. In January 1934 Du Bois published an editorial in The Crisis proposing voluntary segregation as an economic strategy for Black workers and farmers. The NAACP board, led by Walter White, rejected the idea and insisted on the primacy of integration. Amid that conflict, White’s personal rivalry with Du Bois, and the magazine’s financial troubles, Du Bois resigned as editor and from the board in July 1934. He later returned to the NAACP as director of special research, and in 1947 he submitted to the United Nations An Appeal to the World, linking racism in the United States to colonialism abroad. In his last years Du Bois moved to Ghana, where he died on August 27, 1963, on the eve of the March on Washington. The Housatonic Heritage organization calls him the father of both the modern civil rights movement and Pan-Africanism. His boyhood homesite in Great Barrington, purchased in 1967 and dedicated as a memorial in 1969, became a National Historic Landmark in 1979. Washington, he once joked, “died in 1915. A lot of people think I died at the same time.” He lived nearly half a century longer. The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line. W. E. B. Du Bois The Souls of Black Folk, 1903 It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity. W. E. B. Du Bois “Of Our Spiritual Strivings,” The Souls of Black Folk, 1903 One ever feels his twoness,—an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body. title: Woodrow Wilson
subtitle: Twenty-eighth president: progressive reformer, wartime leader, and segregationist
summary: Woodrow Wilson, the twenty-eighth president of the United States (1913–1921), was a political scientist who rose within three years from president of Princeton University to the White House. His “New Freedom” reforms created the Federal Reserve and expanded federal regulation of business; he led the nation into World War I and proposed, in his Fourteen Points, a League of Nations to keep the peace. The Senate rejected his treaty, and a stroke left him incapacitated. His vision shaped American internationalism, but he also extended segregation in the federal government and suppressed wartime dissent.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Woodrow Wilson
themeText: The presidency War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy Reform and protest Civil rights and citizenship
text: Thomas Woodrow Wilson Staunton, Virginia President of Princeton University Governor of New Jersey Twenty-eighth president (1913–1921) Architect of the League of Nations Presidency 1913–1921; Democrat Domestic program The New Freedom: tariff reduction, the Federal Reserve Act (1913), regulation of corporations Foreign policy Neutrality, then war against Germany (1917); the Fourteen Points (1918) Stroke Incapacitated by a stroke in October 1919 for the last seventeen months of his term Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on December 28, 1856, in Staunton, Virginia, the son of a Presbyterian minister, and grew up in Augusta, Georgia, and Columbia, South Carolina. His earliest memories were of the Civil War: Union soldiers marching into Augusta and his mother nursing wounded Confederates. His father, a leader of the Southern Presbyterian church, taught him to see secession as justified and God as the guide of human destiny. Weak eyesight and possible dyslexia delayed his reading, and with few schools in the war-torn South, his father educated him at home. “The only place in the world where nothing has to be explained to me,” he said later, “is the South.” After a year at Davidson College he entered the College of New Jersey (later Princeton), graduating in 1879. He tried law in Atlanta, found it boring, and earned a PhD in history and political science at Johns Hopkins in 1886. His dissertation, Congressional Government, became a classic: it criticized the weak post–Civil War presidency and admired the British system, in which a prime minister leads both government and Parliament, an early sign of the strong executive he would become. In his last year of graduate school he married Ellen Louise Axson, an artist who encouraged his commitment to reform until her death in 1914. Wilson taught at Bryn Mawr, Wesleyan, and Princeton, publishing books including a five-volume history of the United States. In 1902 he became Princeton’s first president who was not a clergyman and began remaking it into a modern university, introducing small-group “preceptorials.” In 1910 New Jersey’s Democratic bosses, expecting a naive professor, made him their candidate for governor; he promised to be “an unconstitutional governor,” won decisively, and turned on the machine: passing direct primaries, a corrupt-practices act limiting campaign spending, a utility commission, and workers’ compensation. In 1912 Republicans split between President Taft and Theodore Roosevelt, and Wilson won the presidency with just under 42 percent of the vote. His New Freedom lowered tariffs and brought new controls on big business and support for unions; its crowning achievement, the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, created the framework that still regulates the nation’s banks, credit, and money supply. Re-elected narrowly in 1916 on the slogan “He Kept Us Out of War,” he asked Congress for war in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and tried to draw Mexico into an alliance against the United States. The government took over the railroads, launched huge shipbuilding programs, and paid for the war with a new income tax and Liberty Bonds. On January 8, 1918, Wilson laid out his Fourteen Points for a just peace: an end to secret alliances and trade barriers, reduced armaments, independence for subject peoples, and a League of Nations. He became the first president to travel to Europe while in office, and at the Paris Peace Conference he attached the League’s Covenant to the Treaty of Versailles. A Presbyterian who believed God was guiding his course, Wilson brought a preacher’s moral certainty to politics. He wanted a strong president who would lead Congress and the public, as a prime minister does; he wanted government to restore economic competition against abusive corporations; and he believed the United States had a duty to help build a new world order of democracy, self-determination, and collective security. Wilson’s democratic ideals had sharp limits. His administration expanded racial segregation in federal offices and the civil service and ignored protests from Black and white opponents, even as violence against African Americans seeking equality reached new heights. His “moral diplomacy” was often high-handed: he intervened militarily in Latin America more often than any predecessor. During the war his administration sponsored the Espionage and Sedition Acts, which outlawed criticism of the government and the war; violators were imprisoned or fined, and even mainstream publications were censored or banned. The Treaty of Versailles departed far from the Fourteen Points. Campaigning for it across the country in September 1919, Wilson collapsed from exhaustion and days later suffered a massive stroke; for the last seventeen months of his term he was largely incapacitated, seeing almost no one but his doctors and his second wife, Edith Bolling Galt Wilson, who became a kind of surrogate president. Refusing to compromise with the Senate, he told his supporters to vote against the amended treaty, and it was defeated twice. The United States never joined the League, but twenty-five years later the United Nations made its home in New York. Most historians rank Wilson among the five most important presidents, while his record on race and civil liberties draws growing criticism. Wilson expanded the federal government’s role in the economy and defined a vision of American internationalism, while his own policies showed the racial limits of Progressive-era democracy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbdhxLVlrhI Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points | History HISTORY 4:49 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2YZQZzJMbSs Woodrow Wilson: The Worst Great President? title: Alcatraz Island
subtitle: San Francisco Bay island: a prison, then the site of the 1969–1971 Indian occupation
summary: Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay is best known as a former prison, but it is also a landmark of Native American activism. From November 1969 to June 1971, a group calling itself Indians of All Tribes occupied the island, demanding it for an Indian university and cultural center. Their nineteen-month occupation drew national attention to Native rights and helped change federal Indian policy. The island is now part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.
location: San Francisco Bay, California (Golden Gate National Recreation Area)
thumbAlt: Alcatraz Island seen from the east
themeText: Indigenous history Civil rights and citizenship
text: West San Francisco Bay, California (Golden Gate National Recreation Area) First claim March 9, 1964: five Sicangu Lakota landed for four hours, citing the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty Occupation November 20, 1969 – June 11, 1971 Occupiers Indians of All Tribes; about 100 at first, including 80 UCLA students Leader Richard Oakes (Akwesasne Mohawk) Today Golden Gate National Recreation Area, National Park Service Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay. It served for many years as a prison holding both military prisoners and civilians. Today the National Park Service interprets both the prison and the Native occupation. Before the prison. Ohlone people lived around San Francisco Bay for thousands of years; oral history suggests Alcatraz was used to isolate tribal members who had broken laws, to gather bird eggs and sea life, and as a hiding place for Indians escaping the Spanish missions. Prison. Once Alcatraz became a prison, Native Americans were among those held there, in 1895, nineteen Hopi men were imprisoned on the island. The occupations. On March 9, 1964, five Sicangu Lakota led by Belva Cottier and Richard McKenzie claimed the island for four hours, citing the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty. On November 9, 1969, Richard Oakes and other Native students and Bay Area Indians claimed it symbolically, and on November 20 a full occupation began. The occupiers elected a council, and everyone had a job, from security and sanitation to day care and a school. Over time, leadership fractured, non-Native residents moved in, the government cut off power and water, and a fire destroyed historic buildings. On June 10–11, 1971, federal marshals removed the last fifteen occupiers. Though the occupiers did not win the island, the Park Service concludes that the occupation helped end the federal termination policy and gave birth to a lasting political movement for Indian self-determination. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW7cG0apZwU Drain Alcatraz: The World's Most Notorious Prison (Full Episode) | Drain the Oceans SPECIAL National Geographic 47:22 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLXj3Mm-C-k What It Was Like To Be An Inmate At Alcatraz Weird History 13:03 2026-10-22

title: Angel Island Immigration Station
subtitle: The West Coast station built to enforce exclusion, 1910–1940
summary: The immigration station on Angel Island in San Francisco Bay opened in 1910 and, in the words of the foundation that preserves it, “was designed to detain, rather than welcome, newcomers.” Under the Chinese Exclusion Act and later laws, Chinese and other Asian immigrants faced medical inspections, long detentions, and grueling interrogations to prove their right to enter. Some waited weeks, others years. Detainees carved poems into the barracks walls, and their rediscovery in 1970 led to the station’s preservation as a National Historic Landmark and museum.
thumbAlt: The detention barracks at the Angel Island Immigration Station
aliases: Angel Island paper sons paper daughters Board of Special Inquiry Angel Island poetry
themeText: Immigration Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship
text: West San Francisco Bay, California Opened January 21, 1910 Closed October 1940, after a fire in August Operated by U.S. Bureau of Immigration (predecessor of today’s USCIS) Arrivals About 550,000 through the port of San Francisco, 1910–1940; over 300,000 detained Origins Above all China, but people from more than 80 countries Poems 154 Chinese poems and inscriptions recorded and translated Today National Historic Landmark (1997); museum opened 2022 The station stands on Angel Island, in San Francisco Bay. The Bureau of Immigration chose the site for its isolation, believing it would keep detainees from escaping or communicating with friends and relatives in San Francisco. Visitors today can see the restored barracks, where Chinese detainees carved poems into the wooden walls, and the Angel Island Immigration Museum, opened in 2022 in the former hospital building. Exclusion. Immigrants from Guangdong Province in southern China began arriving in California in the mid-nineteenth century, driven by famine, rebellion, and economic collapse. Welcomed at first as laborers during the Gold Rush and railroad boom, they became scapegoats when the economy faltered in the 1870s. In 1882 Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act. The National Archives calls it “the first significant law restricting immigration into the United States”; it imposed a ten-year ban on Chinese laborers and barred courts from granting citizenship to Chinese immigrants. The ban was extended by the Geary Act in 1892 and made permanent in 1902. Paper sons and daughters. The law still allowed a few classes to enter: merchants, teachers, students, diplomats, clergy, and the children of those already here. After the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed the city’s birth and immigration records, Chinese residents could claim citizenship and report children born in China. Some sold these places to young people who wanted to come, often at about $100 per year of the buyer’s age. Each “paper child” memorized a detailed history of a family and village they might never have seen. The station. Ships from Asia took three weeks or more to cross the Pacific. On arrival passengers were separated by race, gender, and class. European and first-class travelers were usually processed on board, while Asian and Pacific Islander immigrants, especially those in steerage, were ferried to the island for medical inspections and interrogations. Before a Board of Special Inquiry, Chinese applicants answered long lists of questions about their supposed families, neighbors, and the layout of their villages, and any difference between their answers and a witness’s could mean deportation. The station’s foundation counts over 300,000 people detained there out of more than 550,000 who arrived at San Francisco between 1910 and 1940. They came from more than 80 countries, among them India, Japan, Russia, the Philippines, and Mexico; in the late 1930s they also included several hundred Jewish refugees fleeing persecution in Europe. The poems. Most of the poets were Cantonese-speaking men from villages of the Pearl River Delta, often with little formal schooling, writing in traditional Chinese forms about disappointment, daily hardship, and anger at their confinement. Most poems are unsigned and undated, probably out of fear of punishment, and none identified so far appear to have been written by women. Closing and rediscovery. In August 1940 a fire destroyed the administration building and many records, and the station closed that October. During World War II the site briefly held Japanese internees and prisoners of war. Congress repealed the exclusion acts in 1943, when China was a wartime ally, though a quota of 105 Chinese immigrants a year remained. In 1970 the state park ranger Alexander Weiss found hundreds of poems carved into the walls of the abandoned barracks. Chinese American activists organized to save the site, the state funded restoration in 1976, and it became a National Historic Landmark in 1997. In 2011 and 2012 both houses of Congress passed resolutions condemning the Chinese Exclusion Act. Angel Island shows the exclusionary side of American immigration history. Its foundation contrasts it with Ellis Island: on the West Coast, entry “was mediated through racial exclusion, restrictive legislation, and the US government’s attempt to control Pacific migration.” The poems on its walls preserve the voices of people the law tried to keep out. The coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended. title: Cahokia
subtitle: The largest city in North America north of Mexico before 1492
summary: Around a thousand years ago, Cahokia, near the Mississippi River in present-day Illinois, was the greatest city north of Mexico. Estimates of its population at its height range from about 10,000 to 30,000, comparable to many cities of the time in Europe and the ancient Near East, and its builders raised more than a hundred earthen mounds around great plazas. Cahokia was the leading center of the Mississippian culture, which spread across the Mississippi Valley and the Southeast.
location: Collinsville, Illinois, east of St. Louis
thumbAlt: Earthen mounds at Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site
aliases: Cahokia Mounds Mississippian culture Monks Mound
themeText: Indigenous history Cities and urban life
text: Midwest Collinsville, Illinois, east of St. Louis Peak About 1050–1150 Population Estimates vary: the National Park Service gives 10,000–20,000 for Cahokia proper (40,000–50,000 including nearby centers); the National Library of Medicine’s Native Voices gives 20,000–30,000 Extent The original complex of mounds, homes, and farms covered more than 4,000 acres Status today Illinois state historic site, National Historic Landmark, and UNESCO World Heritage Site (1982) Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site lies a few miles east of the Mississippi River and St. Louis. It preserves the remains of a planned city: neighborhoods of houses, large plazas, public buildings, and more than one hundred earthen mounds, the largest of which is known as Monks Mound. The site is administered by the state of Illinois and is a National Historic Landmark and World Heritage Site. Cahokia was the pre-eminent cultural, religious, and economic center of the Mississippian culture, which flourished across the Mississippi Valley and the southeastern United States between roughly 1000 and 1350. Like other mound builders, Cahokians cleared fields and planted family farms within the city to supply its people with corn, squash, and sunflowers, and satellite towns spread outward from the center. Building the mounds, by carrying earth, basket by basket, required labor organized on a vast scale. The city declined after its peak and was largely abandoned by about 1350. Why remains a subject of research; archaeologists have proposed environmental, economic, and political explanations. Mississippian societies elsewhere in the Southeast continued long after Cahokia’s decline. Cahokia shows that Native North Americans built urban societies with monumental architecture, long-distance trade, and complex political organization centuries before European contact, a powerful corrective to the myth of an untouched wilderness. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ruWuAas8T7Y Why Was Ancient America's Greatest City Abandoned? title: Little Rock Central High School
subtitle: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site
summary: Little Rock Central High School became the center of a national crisis in September 1957, when nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, tried to enter under a court-approved desegregation plan. Governor Orval Faubus sent the Arkansas National Guard to keep them out, and President Dwight D. Eisenhower answered by sending the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to protect them. The standoff led to Cooper v. Aaron (1958), in which the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that states could not nullify its desegregation decisions. Central High is still an operating public high school and is also a National Historic Site run by the National Park Service.
thumbAlt: Little Rock Central High School
aliases: Little Rock Crisis Little Rock Senior High School Cooper v. Aaron Executive Order 10730 Lost Year
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history
text: South Little Rock, Arkansas Built Construction began 1926, as Little Rock Senior High School Crisis September 1957 to May 1958 Federal troops 101st Airborne Division, then federalized National Guard, for the rest of the school year Court ruling Cooper v. Aaron, decided September 29, 1958 1957–58 enrollment About 1,800 (Park Service) or more than 2,000 (Supreme Court) Today An operating public high school of about 2,500 students and a National Historic Site Central High is an active school in the Little Rock School District, so access to the building is limited to students and staff. National Park Service rangers lead guided tours of the grounds. Construction of the school, first called Little Rock Senior High School, began in 1926 at a cost of $1.5 million. The Park Service visitor center stands across the street on a road named for Daisy Bates, the NAACP leader who guided the nine students. Before the crisis. On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were unconstitutional. Central High was not the first Arkansas school to respond. Schools in Charleston and Fayetteville desegregated in the fall of 1954, Hoxie in 1955, and Bentonville in 1956. The Little Rock School Board adopted a gradual plan, and nine Black students were scheduled to enter Central High in September 1957. They were recruited by Daisy Bates, president of the Arkansas NAACP: Minnijean Brown, Terrence Roberts, Elizabeth Eckford, Ernest Green, Thelma Mothershed, Melba Pattillo, Gloria Ray, Jefferson Thomas, and Carlotta Walls. The governor’s stand. Just before school opened, Governor Orval Faubus sent the Arkansas National Guard to the school and placed it “off limits” to the Black students. The Supreme Court later found that the school authorities had not asked for this and that no crowds or violence had occurred until then. Sources date the Guard’s deployment slightly differently: the Supreme Court gives September 2, the day before the students were due, while the King Institute dates it to September 4, the first day they tried to enter, when a white mob gathered outside. NAACP lawyers, among them Thurgood Marshall, won a federal injunction against the governor. On September 23 the students entered under police protection, but they were removed that morning because officers could not control the crowd. Federal troops. Martin Luther King Jr. telegraphed Eisenhower urging him “to take a strong forthright stand in the Little Rock situation.” On September 24, 1957, Eisenhower signed Executive Order 10730 and spoke to the nation on radio and television. The next day federal troops escorted the nine students into the school. The King Institute writes that Eisenhower acted “reluctantly,” aware that Little Rock was becoming an international embarrassment. Regular Army troops stayed until November 27, 1957, and were replaced by federalized National Guardsmen for the rest of the year. Eight of the nine finished the year; the Supreme Court later quoted a lower court’s finding of “repeated incidents of more or less serious violence directed against the Negro students and their property.” At the end of the school year Ernest Green became the first Black student to graduate from Central High, with King in the audience. Cooper v. Aaron. In 1958 the school board asked to delay desegregation for two and a half years because of “chaos, bedlam and turmoil.” On September 29, 1958, the Supreme Court refused in an opinion signed by all nine justices. It held that the rights declared in Brown “can neither be nullified openly and directly by state legislators or state executive or judicial officers, nor nullified indirectly by them through evasive schemes for segregation,” and that Brown was “the supreme law of the land.” The closed schools. Faubus then closed all four of Little Rock’s public high schools in the fall of 1958 rather than continue desegregation. The King Institute writes that the schools reopened after a December 1959 ruling. The American Yawp notes that Little Rock’s schools “closed rather than allow integration.” Central High became a symbol of the struggle over Brown v. Board of Education. The crisis drew a president into using federal troops to enforce a court order against a state’s governor, and it produced Cooper v. Aaron, one of the strongest statements of the Supreme Court’s authority over the states. This is a great opportunity for you and the federal government to back up the longings and aspirations of millions of peoples of good will and make law and order a reality. Martin Luther King Jr. telegram to President Eisenhower, September 9, 1957 The interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment enunciated by this Court in the Brown case is the supreme law of the land. U.S. Supreme Court Cooper v. title: Chaco Canyon
subtitle: Ceremonial center of the ancestral Pueblo world
summary: In a high, dry canyon in northwestern New Mexico, ancestral Pueblo people built a center unlike anything else in North America. Beginning in the mid-800s they raised planned, multistory stone “great houses” with hundreds of rooms, aligned buildings to the sun, moon, and cardinal directions, and built long, strikingly straight roads. By about 1050 Chaco was the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of the San Juan Basin, linked to more than 150 great houses across the region. Historians still disagree about how many people lived there and why the center declined. Pueblo and Navajo peoples regard it as a sacred place today.
location: San Juan Basin, northwestern New Mexico
thumbAlt: The great kiva plaza at Chetro Ketl in Chaco Canyon
aliases: Pueblo Bonito Chaco Culture Chetro Ketl Una Vida Great North Road Chacoan roads great houses
themeText: Indigenous history Religion
text: Southwest San Juan Basin, northwestern New Mexico Flourished Mid-800s to the 1100s (Park Service); 900–1300 CE in the American Yawp Great houses Pueblo Bonito, Una Vida, Peñasco Blanco, Hungo Pavi, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto, and others Largest Pueblo Bonito, the center of the Chacoan world; Chetro Ketl is second, over 3 acres Roads Up to about 30 feet wide; the Great North Road and the South Road are the best documented Timber About 200,000 wooden beams carried in from distant mountains Descendants Pueblo peoples of the Southwest; Chaco is central to the origins of several Navajo clans Protected as Chaco Culture National Historical Park Chaco Canyon’s long winters, short growing seasons, and scant rainfall make it, in the Park Service’s words, “an unlikely place for a major center of ancestral Puebloan culture to take root and flourish.” Yet its builders used masonry techniques unique for their time. Unlike earlier villages that grew room by room, the great houses were planned from the start, and work on some of them went on for decades or centuries. They were placed in a landscape of sacred mountains, mesas, and shrines that still hold deep meaning for descendant peoples. Visitors can walk through Pueblo Bonito, Chetro Ketl, and Una Vida, the last left nearly untouched by excavation. The great houses. In the middle and late 800s the people of Chaco built Pueblo Bonito, Una Vida, and Peñasco Blanco, then Hungo Pavi, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto, and others. Pueblo Bonito, built in stages between about 850 and 1150, was “the center of the Chacoan world,” a world that eventually reached across parts of present-day New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, and Arizona. The American Yawp notes that it covered more than two acres and rose five stories. Chetro Ketl, the second largest great house, covers more than three acres and includes a great kiva and an elevated plaza twelve feet above the canyon floor. The buildings were often oriented to solar, lunar, and cardinal directions, with lines of sight between them and astronomical markers, water-control features, and earthen mounds around them. Their builders imported an astonishing amount of material, including some 200,000 wooden beams, often whole ponderosa pine trunks, carried from the Chuska Mountains and Mount Taylor. The roads. Chaco’s roads are straight, carefully built, and wide: about 15 feet inside the canyon and about twice that heading toward outlying sites. Where they meet a cliff, stairs are often carved straight up the rock, as at the Jackson Stairway above Chetro Ketl. Most have been found through aerial photography. Archaeologists disagree about their purpose. Some argue they were mainly religious or symbolic, pointing out that a society without pack animals or wheeled vehicles had little practical need for roads thirty feet wide, and that Zuni and Acoma pilgrims still walk sacred trails that sometimes follow old Chacoan segments. Others note that walking on the roads takes less energy, so they would also have helped people carry heavy loads such as roof beams. A regional center. By 1050 Chaco’s great houses were linked by roads to more than 150 great houses across the San Juan Basin. What held this system together is still debated. The Park Service lists several possibilities: a turquoise-trading network that brought macaws, copper bells, and shells from distant lands; a way of sharing food when the climate failed; or a religious “center place” that bound the region together. Pueblo descendants describe Chaco as a gathering place where many peoples and clans came together to share ceremonies, traditions, and knowledge. How many people? Here the sources differ. The American Yawp writes that as many as fifteen thousand people lived in the Chaco Canyon complex. The Park Service suggests instead that the great houses were probably not farming villages with large permanent populations but “public architecture” used from time to time for ceremonies and trade, when people gathered in the canyon. Decline. In the 1100s and 1200s new construction slowed and Chaco’s role as a regional center shifted to Aztec, Mesa Verde, the Chuska Mountains, and other places. The two sources again explain this differently. The Yawp says that ecological problems, including deforestation and overirrigation, “ultimately caused the community to collapse and its people to disperse to smaller settlements.” The Park Service describes a gradual change in which people “shifted away from Chacoan ways, migrated to new areas, reorganized their world.” Their descendants are the Pueblo peoples of the Southwest, many of whom see Chaco as an important stop along their clans’ sacred migration paths. Chaco is evidence of large-scale planning, astronomy, engineering, and regional organization in North America centuries before Europeans arrived. It also shows how historians and archaeologists can read the same ruins differently, and it remains a living sacred place for the Pueblo and Navajo peoples connected to it. The monumental scale of its architecture, the complexity of its community life, the high level of its community social organization, and its far-reaching commerce created a cultural vision unlike any other seen before or since. National Park Service Chaco Culture National Historical Park In a society that had neither pack animals nor wheeled vehicles it is unclear what, if any, practical need could have required roads thirty feet wide. title: Ellis Island
subtitle: The nation’s busiest immigration station, 1892–1924
summary: From 1892 to 1924, Ellis Island in New York Harbor was America’s largest and busiest immigration station. The Park Service counts over 12 million immigrants processed there, usually in three to seven hours. For most it was an “Island of Hope,” the first step to a new life; for the rest it was an “Island of Tears,” where families were separated and people were sent back. The quota laws of the 1920s cut immigration sharply, and the station spent its last decades mainly detaining and deporting people before it closed in 1954. Restored as a museum, it is now part of Statue of Liberty National Monument.
location: New York Harbor, New York and New Jersey
thumbAlt: Ellis Island immigration station in 1902
aliases: Island of Hope Island of Tears Annie Moore Registry Room line inspection Fort Gibson
themeText: Immigration Everyday life Cities and urban life
text: Northeast New York Harbor, New York and New Jersey Opened January 1, 1892; first immigrant processed: Annie Moore of Ireland Main building Opened December 17, 1900, after a fire destroyed the first station in 1897 Immigrants processed Over 12 million, 1892–1924 (another Park Service page: almost 12 million, 1892–1954) Inspection time Typically 3–7 hours Busiest year 1.2 million people examined Closed 1954 Today Part of Statue of Liberty National Monument Ellis Island was once one of three small “Oyster Islands” in New York Harbor; landfill later enlarged it to 27.5 acres. Its main building, a fireproof brick structure by the architects Boring and Tilton, opened in 1900, and a hospital complex with contagious disease wards was built on the added land beside it. Since a 6–3 Supreme Court ruling, New York has held the original 3.3 acres and New Jersey the 24 acres of landfill. Before immigration. In the 1670s the English governor of New York granted the island to the customs collector William Dyre, and it passed through a series of owners and names. Pirates were hanged there, giving it the name “Gibbet Island.” The merchant Samuel Ellis advertised “That pleasant situated island” for sale in 1785 but could not sell it; his heirs still owned it when New York State bought it in 1808 and conveyed it to the United States. Before the War of 1812 the army built Fort Gibson there, which never saw action, and the navy later kept a powder magazine on the island until complaints about the danger led Congress to order it removed. The federal station. The Immigration Act of 1891 moved control of immigration from the states to the federal government and created what became the Bureau of Immigration. Ellis Island’s first station, built of Georgia pine, opened on January 1, 1892, and Annie Moore of Ireland was the first immigrant processed. A fire destroyed it in June 1897; the Park Service dates the fire to June 14 on one page and June 15 on another. No one was killed. The new main building opened on December 17, 1900. Inspection. Doctors of the Public Health Service watched the long lines climbing into the Registry Room for signs of disease or weakness, such as trachoma, tuberculosis, or a poor physique. Anyone suspected was marked in chalk with a letter, such as “H” for heart, and pulled aside for a closer examination. Then an immigrant inspector questioned each person against the ship’s passenger list. He could admit only those “clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to enter,” and had to exclude contract laborers, polygamists, paupers, convicted criminals, anarchists, and anyone “likely to become a public charge.” Doctors only diagnosed and treated; the decision to admit belonged to the inspectors. At the peak, 1.2 million people were examined in a single year. President Theodore Roosevelt launched a campaign against corruption and mistreatment of immigrants at the station. Quotas. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 “ended U.S.’s open door immigration policy,” limiting each nationality to 3 percent of its share of the 1910 census, and stranding thousands of immigrants on the island. The Immigration Act of 1924 cut the limit to 2 percent of the 1890 census, aimed especially at southern and eastern Europeans, and moved inspection to American consulates abroad, so most immigrants no longer needed to pass through Ellis Island. Detention and closing. In the 1930s, for the first time, deportations far outnumbered admissions. During World War II, about 1,000 German, Italian, and Japanese “enemy aliens” and their families were held there, while the Coast Guard trained 60,000 enlisted men and 3,000 officers on the island. After the Internal Security Act of 1950 the number of detainees rose from 400 to 1,200. The last detainees left in 1954 and the island was abandoned. President Lyndon Johnson later made it part of Statue of Liberty National Monument, and after a restoration announced by President Ronald Reagan it reopened to the public as a museum. A different gateway. Ellis Island’s experience was not shared by all immigrants. On the West Coast, the Angel Island Immigration Station, opened in 1910, was “designed to detain, rather than welcome,” and Asian immigrants there faced far harsher treatment. Ellis Island is the best-known symbol of the great wave of European immigration that reshaped American cities around 1900, and of the national debate over who should be allowed in. Its history runs from open entry through the quota laws to wartime and Cold War detention. For the vast majority of immigrants, Ellis Island truly was an “Island of Hope” - the first stop on their way to new opportunities and experiences in America. For the rest, it became the “Island of Tears.” National Park Service Ellis Island history Clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to enter the United States. title: Harpers Ferry
subtitle: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery
summary: Harpers Ferry, a small town where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers cut through the Blue Ridge, packs an unusual amount of American history into a few streets. A federal armory built there in the 1790s became a center of early industry, where John H. Hall made rifles with interchangeable parts. In October 1859 the abolitionist John Brown seized the armory in a failed attempt to start a war against slavery, a raid that pushed the country closer to civil war. In 1862 Confederate troops captured the Union garrison there, the largest surrender of Federal troops in the war. After the war Storer College educated formerly enslaved people, and in 1906 W. E. B. Du Bois and the Niagara Movement met on its campus.
location: Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet
thumbAlt: The armory engine house known as John Brown’s Fort at Harpers Ferry
aliases: Harper’s Ferry John Brown’s raid John Brown’s Fort Storer College Niagara Movement U.S. Armory and Arsenal Hall’s Rifle Works
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Science and technology War and the military
text: South Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet Armory founded Chosen by George Washington under a 1794 law; production began about 1802 Interchangeable parts John H. Hall’s rifle works, 1820–1840 John Brown’s raid October 16–18, 1859 Union surrender September 15, 1862: more than 12,700 Union troops captured Storer College 1865/1867–1955; more than 7,000 students Niagara Movement First meeting in the United States, August 15–19, 1906 Today Harpers Ferry National Historical Park The town stands on steep ground at the point where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet and break through the Blue Ridge. Thomas Jefferson, who stood on a rock above the rivers on October 25, 1783, called the passage “one of the most stupendous scenes in Nature” and wrote that it was “worth a voyage across the Atlantic.” The National Park Service, which preserves much of the town, describes its history as “multi-layered,” and its archeological record goes back millennia. The armory. In 1794 Congress approved a bill “for the erecting and repairing of Arsenals and Magazines.” After Springfield, Massachusetts, was chosen for the first national armory, President George Washington picked Harpers Ferry for the second. The government bought 125 acres between the two rivers in 1796, construction began in 1799, and full-scale production of muskets, rifles, and later pistols began three years later. By 1810 the armory made about 10,000 arms a year. It struggled with weak waterpower and charges of mismanagement, and it was rebuilt between 1845 and 1854. Its workforce grew from 25 men in 1802 to about 400 by 1859. Interchangeable parts. In 1819 the New England gunmaker John H. Hall contracted to make 1,000 of his breechloading rifles at Harpers Ferry. Over the next two decades he built machines to make rifles with interchangeable parts, a “boldly ambitious goal” in an industry based on skilled handwork. In 1822 he reported that he had found “methods for fabricating arms exactly alike, & with economy, by the hands of common workmen.” The Park Service credits him with “laying a solid foundation for America’s developing factory system.” The town was also reached by one of the first successful American railroads. John Brown’s raid. In the summer of 1859 John Brown rented a farm in Maryland about five miles away, where his men hid. They numbered twenty-one at the time of the raid. The American Yawp notes that the group included Black radicals from Oberlin, Ohio, and from Canada. On the night of October 16, the raiders seized the bridges, the armory and arsenal, and Hall’s rifle works, took local enslavers hostage, and freed people they enslaved. The first person mortally wounded was Heyward Shepherd, a free African American railroad worker. Townspeople and militia soon surrounded the raiders, and Brown retreated into the armory’s brick fire-engine house with his remaining men and hostages. On the morning of October 18, U.S. Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee broke in and captured him. Brown was tried for murder, conspiring with enslaved people to rebel, and treason against Virginia, convicted after a five-day trial, and hanged on December 2, 1859. The Yawp writes that his execution “made him a martyr in abolitionist circles and a confirmed traitor in southern crowds.” The Civil War. When Virginia passed its ordinance of secession in April 1861, the U.S. officer guarding the armory set fire to it and retreated, and Confederate forces later carried off its machinery and burned more buildings. By 1862 the armory lay in ruins, and only about 100 of the town’s prewar population of 3,000 remained. In September 1862, as Lee invaded Maryland, Stonewall Jackson surrounded the Union garrison on the heights around the town. On September 15 the Union commanders surrendered. The Park Service counts more than 12,700 Union troops captured, the largest single capture of Federal forces in the war, though another Park Service page describes a garrison of 12,500. Storer College. After the war, the Freewill Baptists of New England, the Freedmen’s Bureau, and the Maine businessman John Storer founded a school for the many formerly enslaved people of the Shenandoah Valley. Park Service pages date its start differently: one says the school began in 1865, another that the Freewill Baptists opened it in 1867. Teachers faced mob violence and stoning, but for twenty-five years Storer was the only school in West Virginia where a Black student could get an education beyond the primary level. It closed in 1955, after the state ended its funding, having taught more than 7,000 students. The Niagara Movement. From August 15 to 19, 1906, W. E. B. Du Bois’s Niagara Movement held its first public meeting in the United States at Storer College. Its members made a barefoot dawn pilgrimage to John Brown’s Fort. The meeting ended with Du Bois’s “Address to the Country.” The movement met yearly in other cities afterward. The Library of Congress says it disbanded in 1910, while the Park Service says it lasted until 1911, when almost all its members became the backbone of the new NAACP. John Brown’s Fort. The engine house where Brown made his last stand had a strange afterlife. It was taken apart and shown in Chicago in 1891, rebuilt on a farm outside town in 1895, moved to the Storer campus in 1909, and returned to Lower Town by the Park Service in 1968, about 150 feet from its original site. Harpers Ferry concentrates several stories of the nineteenth century in one small town: the rise of machine-made manufacturing, the violent struggle over slavery that John Brown’s raid sharpened, the Civil War, and the long fight for Black education and civil rights that carried on at Storer College and the Niagara Movement. This scene is worth a voyage across the Atlantic. John Brown note written on the day of his execution, December 2, 1859 We will not be satisfied to take one jot or tittle less than our full manhood rights. W. E. B. title: Independence Hall
subtitle: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed
summary: Built as the Pennsylvania State House, Independence Hall is where the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776 and where the Constitutional Convention wrote the Constitution in 1787. The National Park Service calls it “the birthplace of America.” After the founding it became a shrine to the Revolution, visited by Lafayette in 1824 and by Abraham Lincoln in 1861, and today it is part of Independence National Historical Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
thumbAlt: Independence Hall in Philadelphia
aliases: Pennsylvania State House Assembly Room Rising Sun chair hall of Independence Independence National Historical Park
themeText: Constitution and law Political thought
text: Northeast Chestnut Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Construction began 1732; main building finished (without tower) in 1748 Original purpose Pennsylvania State House, home to the colony’s three branches of government Designer Master builder Edmund Woolley, under Speaker Andrew Hamilton Events here Washington named commander in chief (1775); Declaration adopted (1776); Articles of Confederation took effect (1781); Constitution written (1787) Name First called “the hall of Independence” for Lafayette’s visit in 1824 Managed by National Park Service, Independence National Historical Park Independence Hall is a red-brick building in the Georgian style, which the Park Service says looks more like a country house than an urban public building. Its plan includes a 105-foot main block joined by covered arcades to two wing buildings, and its tower and steeple were added around 1750. The rotted wooden steeple was removed in 1781, and in 1828 the architect William Strickland built a new one with a clock. Inside, the Assembly Room has been restored with tables for each colony, though no one knows exactly how the delegates were seated. The State House. Speaker Andrew Hamilton oversaw construction, and the master builder Edmund Woolley drew the designs. Work began in 1732. The Pennsylvania Assembly was already meeting there in 1735, and the main building was finished in 1748. It housed all three branches of Pennsylvania’s colonial government. The Second Continental Congress. In May 1775, a month after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, the Pennsylvania legislature lent its Assembly Room to the Second Continental Congress. There the delegates approved George Washington as commander in chief, voted to create the Marine Corps, and drafted the Olive Branch Petition to the king, which went unanswered. On July 2, 1776, they voted for independence, and on July 4 they approved the Declaration of Independence. The Declaration was signed in the same room on August 2. The Articles of Confederation officially took effect there in 1781. The Constitutional Convention. In May 1787 the legislature lent the room again, this time to delegates from twelve states who came to repair the Articles of Confederation. Their debates over the balance between large and small states and over the slave trade were sometimes heated. In four months they wrote a new Constitution, which Washington called “little short of a miracle.” As the delegates signed, Benjamin Franklin looked at the sun carved on the back of Washington’s chair and said he was happy to know that it was “a rising and not a setting sun.” From State House to shrine. Congress met next door in Congress Hall from 1790 to 1800, while Philadelphia was the temporary capital. The state government moved away in 1799, and in 1818 Pennsylvania sold the building to the city. When the Marquis de Lafayette was welcomed in the Assembly Room in 1824, his hosts called it “the hall of Independence”; decades passed before the whole building took that name. The city had removed the room’s original paneling, which angered the public, and in 1831 the architect John Haviland was hired to restore it. A redecoration in 1854–55 made the room a shrine, at a time when the nativist movement was using Revolutionary symbols in its campaign to keep immigrants out of public office. The building was also the scene of fugitive slave hearings. Lincoln. On his way to his inauguration in 1861, President-elect Abraham Lincoln stood in the Assembly Room and said he would rather be “assassinated on the spot” than give up the ideals of the Declaration of Independence. Four years later his body lay there for two days after his assassination, and upwards of 85,000 mourners filed past. Few buildings anywhere have hosted as many founding political acts. Independence Hall is also a record of how Americans remember their founding: it was neglected, stripped, restored, and turned into a shrine, and generations from Lafayette’s hosts to Lincoln to the Park Service have used it to say what the Revolution meant. Independence Hall is the birthplace of America. National Park Service Independence National Historical Park Little short of a miracle. title: Manzanar
subtitle: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
summary: Manzanar was one of ten War Relocation Centers where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II. Built in 1942 on land the Army leased from the city of Los Angeles in California’s Owens Valley, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, it held families forcibly removed from the West Coast under Executive Order 9066. Today it is a National Historic Site that preserves the camp’s story, and the earlier displacement of the valley’s Paiute people and farm settlers.
location: Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395)
thumbAlt: People exercising at Manzanar with mountains behind
aliases: Manzanar War Relocation Center Manzanar National Historic Site Owens Valley
themeText: Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship Indigenous history War and the military
text: West Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395) Name Spanish for “apple orchard” Camp built 1942, on 6,200 acres leased by the Army from Los Angeles Buildings About 800 during the war; all but three were dismantled or moved afterward Pilgrimage Held each year on the last Saturday of April, sponsored by the Manzanar Committee Today Manzanar National Historic Site, National Park Service Manzanar lies on the floor of the Owens Valley, with Mount Williamson rising directly to the west. Most of the camp’s buildings are gone; the site includes a cemetery, historic orchards, and a visitor center. Photographers including Ansel Adams and Dorothea Lange documented life there during the war. Earlier displacements. People used the Owens Valley for almost 10,000 years, and about 1,500 years ago the Owens Valley Paiute established settlements there, practicing a form of irrigated agriculture. After miners and ranchers moved in during the 1860s, the Army forcibly relocated nearly 1,000 Paiute to Fort Tejon in 1863. From 1910 the farm town of Manzanar grew apples, pears, peaches, and other crops. But Los Angeles bought up the valley’s water rights for its aqueduct, completed in 1913; by 1929 the city owned all of Manzanar’s land and water, and within five years the town was abandoned. The camp. In 1942 the Army leased 6,200 acres at Manzanar from Los Angeles to confine Japanese Americans. Some valley residents opposed the camp; others helped build it and worked there. Families lived there in a fenced and guarded camp. Remembrance. After the war nearly all of the camp’s roughly 800 buildings were removed. Former incarcerees and their descendants return each April on a pilgrimage, and the National Park Service has collected more than 715 oral history interviews about the camp and the valley. Manzanar’s layered history of removal (Paiute, settler, and Japanese American) makes it a powerful place to reflect on who has been forced from the land. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XgmY2P-xT_Y THE NATIONAL PARKS | Manzanar: "Never Again" | PBS PBS 14:21 2026-10-22

title: Mesa Verde
subtitle: Cliff dwellings of the Ancestral Pueblo people
summary: Mesa Verde, in southwestern Colorado, has some of the largest and best-preserved cliff dwellings in North America. People lived in the area for about 12,000 years, and Ancestral Pueblo farmers built villages on the mesa tops for centuries. Then, between about 1180 and 1300, they built stone villages tucked into the cliff alcoves, most likely to be near the springs as droughts made water scarce. Within a few decades of the late 1200s they had moved south to join communities in present-day New Mexico and Arizona, where their Pueblo and Hopi descendants live today. In 1906 Mesa Verde became the first national park created to protect cultural heritage.
thumbAlt: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde
aliases: Cliff Palace Balcony House Long House Spruce Tree House Step House Wetherill Mesa cliff dwellers
themeText: Indigenous history Land and environment
text: Southwest Southwestern Colorado Human history About 12,000 years; oldest object a spear point 12,300–10,900 years old Cliff dwellings built About 1180–1300 CE Typical size Most average 8–10 rooms Largest Cliff Palace: about 150 rooms and 23 kivas, home to over 100 people Sites in the park Nearly 5,000 ancestral sites Protected Mesa Verde National Park, June 29, 1906; later a UNESCO World Heritage Site Associated tribes 27 Pueblos, Tribes, and Nations, including Ute, Navajo, and Apache The cliff dwellings sit in alcoves that water and frost carved out of the Cliff House Sandstone. Rain and snow seep down through the porous sandstone until they hit a layer of shale, then flow sideways and emerge from the canyon walls as seeps and springs, the only permanent water on the mesa. The same process loosens blocks of sandstone, which the builders used for their homes. Living rooms can be recognized by their hearths and grinding bins, and narrow rooms served as granaries. The park preserves nearly 5,000 ancestral sites, and rangers lead tours into Cliff Palace, Balcony House, Long House, and other dwellings. Before the cliff dwellings. Human history at Mesa Verde goes back about 12,000 years, to hunters who used spear points to kill mammoths, ground sloths, and giant bison. Between about 500 and 1300 CE, tens of thousands of Ancestral Pueblo people lived across the Four Corners region. Over those centuries they shifted from a mix of farming, hunting, and gathering to a diet in which corn, beans, and squash made up 90 percent of what they ate, supported by dams, terraces, and reservoirs. They traded for ocean shells, macaw feathers, and gemstones, and made the black-on-white pottery for which Mesa Verde is known. At Step House people built pithouses around 700 CE and returned to build a masonry village around 1200, five centuries later. Building in the cliffs. Most cliff dwellings were built between 1180 and 1300. They are among the last structures built in the region, and their residents were among the last to leave. Why build there? The Park Service says most scholars point to water: tree rings show long droughts, reservoirs on the mesa tops were becoming less reliable, and the dwellings were placed near seep springs. People carved small basins into the rock to collect the water. The American Yawp emphasizes defense instead, calling the dwellings “highly defensible.” The villages. Most dwellings were small, averaging eight to ten rooms. Balcony House had 38 rooms and two kivas for over thirty people. Long House had about 150 rooms and 21 kivas around a large plaza, and Spruce Tree House about 130 rooms. Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling in North America, had about 150 rooms and 23 kivas for over 100 people. The Park Service notes that it had one kiva for every three rooms, twice the usual share, and suggests it became a public center because of its size: “they became important because they were big, they weren’t big because they were important.” Sources date its construction slightly differently: the Park Service gives 1190 to 1280, while the Yawp says it was built from 1190 and expanded until 1260. Leaving. People had always moved between communities. In the mid-1200s they began to move south, and over several decades they left Mesa Verde entirely. The Park Service points to “persistent drought, limited resources, and social change,” and adds that for Pueblo people migration is an important cultural activity: people “may have decided it was simply time to move on and continue their people’s journey.” They joined or founded villages along the Rio Grande, the Little Colorado River, and the Hopi Mesas. Ute, Navajo, and Apache peoples also used Mesa Verde as hunting and gathering grounds. Rediscovery and protection. The 1859 San Juan Exploring Expedition was the first to officially use the name Mesa Verde. The photographer William Henry Jackson later took the first photographs of a cliff dwelling in the region. One December day, the local rancher Richard Wetherill and his brother-in-law Charles Mason, guided by the Ute Acowitz, came upon Cliff Palace while looking for lost cattle. The Wetherills went on to enter 182 cliff dwellings and to collect and sell artifacts. Their father wrote to the Smithsonian asking that the area be made a national park, fearing that “the tourists, will destroy them.” The Swedish scientist Gustaf Nordenskiöld excavated and photographed many sites and shipped about 600 objects to Europe. The Colorado Cliff Dwellings Association, led by Virginia McClurg and Lucy Peabody, campaigned for protection. After several failed bills, Congress created Mesa Verde National Park, signed by President Theodore Roosevelt on June 29, 1906. In 2006 the park reburied all Native American human remains found within its boundaries after twelve years of consultation with associated tribes. Mesa Verde shows how Ancestral Pueblo communities adapted to a demanding environment, and its creation as the first national park devoted to cultural heritage began federal efforts to protect the archaeological record of Native America. It remains a sacred place for the 27 Pueblos, Tribes, and Nations connected to it. They became important because they were big, they weren’t big because they were important! National Park Service on Cliff Palace and other large cliff dwellings For Pueblo people, migration is an important cultural activity, and people may have decided it was simply time to move on and continue their people’s journey.
