title: Mount Rushmore
subtitle: Four presidents carved into the Black Hills, on land sacred to the Lakota
summary: Between 1927 and 1941, sculptor Gutzon Borglum and about 400 workers blasted and carved the faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln into a granite mountain in South Dakota’s Black Hills. Meant to represent the nation’s birth, growth, development, and preservation, it draws more than two million visitors a year. But the Black Hills were recognized by treaty as Lakota land and are sacred to many tribes, and the memorial remains a contested symbol.
thumbAlt: The carved faces of Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Lincoln on Mount Rushmore
aliases: Mount Rushmore National Memorial Shrine of Democracy Six Grandfathers
themeText: National symbols and holidays Indigenous history The presidency
text: Midwest Black Hills, South Dakota Carved 1927–1941; completed October 31, 1941 Sculptor Gutzon Borglum; finished by his son Lincoln Borglum The four presidents Washington (birth), Jefferson (growth), Theodore Roosevelt (development), Lincoln (preservation) Lakota name for the mountain Six Grandfathers Workers About 400; no one died during the 14 years of construction The memorial sits on a granite face of the Black Hills, the easternmost extension of the Rocky Mountains, in Pennington County, South Dakota. Borglum chose each president to stand for an idea: Washington the birth of the United States, Jefferson its growth (through the Declaration of Independence and the Louisiana Purchase), Theodore Roosevelt its development, and Lincoln its preservation. The National Park Service calls the memorial a symbol of freedom and hope; others see in it colonialism and racism. The name Black Hills comes from the Lakota Paha Sapa, “hills of black.” By the late 1700s the Lakota controlled the region after defeating the Cheyenne, and religious ceremonies were held there every year. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie recognized the Black Hills as Lakota territory, but the discovery of gold in 1874 drew prospectors and settlers who violated the treaty. The Lakota and Northern Cheyenne fought back in the Great Sioux War of 1876, which included the Battle of the Little Bighorn, but many Lakota were forced onto reservations by the end of the 1800s. In the 1920s South Dakota’s state historian, Doane Robinson, proposed a mountain carving to attract tourists; the first idea was to carve Native Americans and pioneers on granite spires called the Needles. Borglum, fresh from a bitter break with the Confederate memorial at Stone Mountain, Georgia, chose instead a cliff the Lakota called the Six Grandfathers, a choice, the Park Service says, that “completely disregarded” the site’s cultural significance, and the subject became four presidents. Carving began in 1927, with President Calvin Coolidge’s support bringing federal funding. Workers used dynamite to remove about 90 percent of the rock. Borglum died in March 1941, and his son Lincoln oversaw the final work, completed on October 31, 1941. In the 1970s the American Indian Movement held demonstrations at Mount Rushmore, demanding recognition of tribal sovereignty and the restoration of treaty rights. Mount Rushmore is both a celebration of American democracy and a reminder of broken treaties, one of the clearest places to see how a single monument can carry opposite meanings. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bvj2URpgRc8 Mount Rushmore Was Supposed to Look Very Different Smithsonian Channel 3:58 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hX4IvoP1HTk The dark history of Mount Rushmore - Ned Blackhawk and Jeffrey D. title: The National Mall
subtitle: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.
summary: The National Mall is the long open space at the heart of Washington, D.C., running from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River. Its open spaces go back to Pierre L’Enfant’s plan for the capital, commissioned by George Washington, and it was reshaped in the early twentieth century to frame the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial. Lined with monuments and memorials, it has also been the nation’s stage for inaugurations, celebrations, and protests, most famously the 1963 March on Washington, where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech.
location: Washington, D.C., from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River
thumbAlt: Aerial view of the National Mall
aliases: Washington Monument Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool McMillan Plan Senate Park Commission L’Enfant plan America’s Front Yard
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship The presidency Cities and urban life
text: Washington, D.C. Washington, D.C., from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River Origins Pierre L’Enfant’s plan for the Federal City, commissioned by President George Washington (1791) Washington Monument Built 1848–1854 and 1876–1884; 555 feet, 5⅛ inches; dedicated February 21, 1885 Lincoln Memorial Proposed 1902; built 1914–1922; dedicated May 30, 1922 March on Washington August 28, 1963; more than 200,000 people Managed by National Mall and Memorial Parks, National Park Service, more than 1,000 acres The Mall is a long swath of lawn and elm trees with the Capitol at one end, the Washington Monument near the middle, and the Lincoln Memorial and its Reflecting Pool at the western end. The National Park Service unit that cares for it manages more than 1,000 acres, including the Washington Monument; the Jefferson, Lincoln, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, World War I, World War II, Korean War Veterans, Vietnam Veterans, and Martin Luther King Jr. memorials; Constitution Gardens; and Pennsylvania Avenue from the Capitol to the White House. About 2,000 American elms line the Mall, and 3,000 Japanese cherry trees grow around the nearby Tidal Basin. L’Enfant’s plan. The Park Service traces the Mall’s origins to the 1791 plan for the Federal City drawn by Pierre L’Enfant at George Washington’s request. Its open spaces created “an ideal stage” for national remembrance, celebration, and the exercise of First Amendment rights. The plan reserved a prominent place for a monument to Washington where a line running south from the White House crossed one running west from the Capitol. The Washington Monument. In 1833 a private group, the Washington National Monument Society, set out to build a monument “unparalleled in the world.” It chose Robert Mills’s design for a 600-foot obelisk ringed by columns. The cornerstone was laid on July 4, 1848, before a crowd of upwards of 20,000. By 1854 the shaft stood 156 feet high, but a faction aligned with the controversial Know-Nothing Party took over the society, donors fled, and the money ran out. For more than twenty years the stump stood unfinished, “doing more to embarrass the nation than to honor” Washington. Congress took over in 1876, and the Army Corps of Engineers under Thomas Lincoln Casey strengthened the foundation, simplified the design, and finished it at 555 feet. The stone came from different quarries, and the change in color one-third of the way up can still be seen. When the capstone was set on December 6, 1884, it was the tallest building in the world. The McMillan Plan and the Lincoln Memorial. In 1901 Senator James McMillan formed the Senate Park Commission, which included the architects Daniel Burnham and Charles McKim, the landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted Jr., and the sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens. In 1902 it proposed a Lincoln Memorial at the edge of the Potomac as the western end of the Mall, with a bridge to Arlington National Cemetery linking the former Union and Confederate sides. Construction began on February 12, 1914, on filled land that needed 122 concrete piers sunk to bedrock. Henry Bacon modeled the building on the Parthenon and used stone from many states, from Massachusetts granite to Tennessee pink marble, to symbolize the reunited Union. Daniel Chester French’s nineteen-foot statue was carved from 28 blocks of Georgia marble. The memorial was dedicated on May 30, 1922, and the Reflecting Pool was finished soon after. A stage for protest. The Mall has been the setting for presidential inaugurations and for demonstrations. Civil rights activists gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for a Prayer Pilgrimage for Freedom in May 1957 and a Youth March for Integrated Schools in October 1958. On August 28, 1963, more than 200,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, which called for a comprehensive civil rights bill, protection of the right to vote, and fair employment. Speakers and performers included A. Philip Randolph, John Lewis, Daisy Bates, Marian Anderson, Joan Baez, and Bob Dylan. Toward the end, King spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. The American Yawp says his speech put “unprecedented pressure on politicians to pass meaningful civil rights legislation.” The King Institute notes that the march was not universally embraced; Malcolm X called it “the Farce on Washington.” More memorials. Memorials to later presidents, wars, and leaders, among them the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, now stand in the park, and the Park Service writes that the park “continues to evolve as Americans seek new ways to recognize our heritage.” The National Mall is the premier civic and symbolic space of the United States. Its monuments show how Americans have chosen to remember their past, and its lawns have been where citizens come to celebrate, mourn, and demand that the country live up to its founding promises. In this temple, as in the hearts of the people for whom he saved the Union, the memory of Abraham Lincoln is enshrined forever. Royal Cortissoz inscription above the statue in the Lincoln Memorial, dedicated 1922 Everyone who believed in man’s capacity to better himself had a moment of inspiration and confidence in the future of the human race. title: Route 66
subtitle: The “Mother Road” from Chicago to Santa Monica
summary: U.S. Highway 66 was created in 1926 as part of the first national system of numbered highways, to meet the growing demand for automobile travel. Its roughly 2,400 miles linked the main streets of small towns to cities from Chicago to Southern California. It carried families fleeing the Dust Bowl in the 1930s and military convoys in World War II, then fed the postwar boom in road-trip tourism. Decommissioned as a federal highway in 1985, “Route 66” lives on in literature, film, and song as a symbol of mobility, freedom, and the American Dream.
location: Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California
thumbAlt: A Route 66 highway shield sign
aliases: U.S. Highway 66 Mother Road US 66 U.S. numbered highway system Cyrus Avery
themeText: Everyday life Science and technology Arts and popular culture
text: Midwest Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California Created 1926, when the U.S. numbered highway system was adopted on November 11 Length About 2,400 miles Ends Chicago to Santa Monica (Park Service); the 1926 plan describes it as Chicago to Los Angeles Nickname The “Mother Road” Decommissioned 1985, as a federal highway Historic sites More than 250 buildings, bridges, and road sections on the National Register of Historic Places Route 66 did not run straight across the country. The Federal Highway Administration describes it as “a crescent route” from Chicago to the Pacific, which crossed most of the transcontinental highways and was bound to be one of the busiest. Much of the old road survives. More than 250 buildings, bridges, road alignments, and other sites along it are listed on the National Register of Historic Places, among them motels, filling stations, and diners built for travelers. From trails to numbers. In the early twentieth century, long-distance roads were known by names such as the Lincoln Highway or the Dixie Highway, promoted by private trail associations. In 1925 the Secretary of Agriculture appointed a Joint Board of federal and state highway officials to lay out a national system of numbered routes with uniform signs, so that, as the Federal Highway Administration puts it, “people may travel across the continent following the same number.” One of its members was Cyrus Avery of Oklahoma. Why 66? The planners first gave the number 60, a number normally reserved for major east-west routes, to a highway curving from Chicago to Los Angeles through Avery’s state. Kentucky’s governor protested that his state was the only one in the Mississippi Valley without a route ending in zero, and he threatened to ignore the new numbers. At a meeting in Springfield, Missouri, on April 30, 1926, Oklahoma’s chief highway engineer noticed that 66 had not been used, and Avery and his Missouri colleague telegraphed Washington: “We prefer sixty six to sixty two.” Kentucky accepted the compromise, and the national highway system was adopted on November 11, 1926. The Mother Road. The Park Service writes that the highway “facilitated one of the most comprehensive movements of people in the history of the United States,” helping to transform the American West “from a rural frontier to a pace-setting metropolitan region.” In the 1930s it was the road west for many Dust Bowl families. The American Yawp notes that these migrants, “disparagingly called” Okies by their new neighbors, were the most visible people on the move during the Depression. John Steinbeck’s novel The Grapes of Wrath (1939), about one such family, became a hit film a year later and, the Yawp says, helped turn public sympathy toward the migrants. War and tourism. During World War II the highway carried military convoys. After the war it fed the boom in automobile tourism, and the hotels, filling stations, and restaurants that served travelers still line the road. Decommissioning and memory. U.S. 66 was decommissioned as a federal highway in 1985. Yet the Park Service writes that it “continues to live on in the American consciousness as ‘Route 66,’” and it now promotes the road’s surviving landmarks through a travel itinerary of more than 100 historic sites. Route 66 is the classic American road: a record of how the automobile and federal highway planning remade everyday life, of Depression-era migration and wartime mobilization, and a lasting symbol of hope, progress, and the open road. We prefer sixty six to sixty two. Cyrus Avery and B. H. Piepmeier telegram to the Bureau of Public Roads, April 30, 1926 Perhaps more than any other highway, Route 66 has come to symbolize hope, progress, and the spirit of adventure. title: St. Augustine
subtitle: The oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the United States
summary: Spanish forces under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565, beside a Timucua village called Seloy. They came to guard the route of Spain’s treasure fleets and to destroy a nearby French Protestant colony, Fort Caroline, which they did within weeks, killing hundreds of French prisoners at an inlet afterward named Matanzas, “slaughters.” The town survived English raids and sieges behind its stone fort, the Castillo de San Marcos, and passed from Spain to Britain, back to Spain, and in 1821 to the United States.
thumbAlt: Aerial view of the Castillo de San Marcos and the town of St. Augustine, Florida, 1965
aliases: San Agustín Castillo de San Marcos Fort Matanzas Matanzas Inlet Fort Caroline Pedro Menéndez de Avilés Seloy Timucua
themeText: Colonial encounters Religion Latino history
text: Southeast St. Augustine, Florida Founded September 8, 1565, by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés Original site The Timucua village of Seloy Matanzas 111 French prisoners killed in September 1565 and 134 more on October 12 Castillo de San Marcos Begun October 2, 1672 Rulers Spain 1565–1763; Britain 1763–1784; Spain 1784–1821; United States from 1821 Landmarks today Castillo de San Marcos and Fort Matanzas National Monuments St. Augustine stands on the Atlantic coast of northeast Florida, south of the St. Johns River. Its best-known landmark is the Castillo de San Marcos, a Spanish stone fort begun in 1672; a smaller fort guards the Matanzas Inlet to the south, the town’s back door, where the Spanish kept a watchtower as early as 1569. Much of the old town also reflects a later era, when the railroad builder Henry Flagler made it a winter resort in the 1880s. The Timucua. People had lived in Florida for about 12,000 years before Europeans came. The Timucua lived along the St. Johns River in northeast Florida, and the Park Service writes that they were peaceful toward the newcomers: Chief Seloy offered Menéndez his council house as a shelter when the Spanish arrived. The French artist Jacques Le Moyne, who escaped from Fort Caroline, made drawings that are among the best records of Timucua life. France and Spain. The Frenchman René de Laudonnière had already built Fort Caroline for French Huguenots, or Protestants, near present-day Jacksonville. King Philip II of Spain was incensed: the colony sat on land Spain claimed, it could threaten the treasure fleets sailing along the coast, and its settlers were Protestants. In 1565 both sides sent fleets. Menéndez arrived with some 800 people and landed on September 8 at Seloy, naming his settlement for St. Augustine, on whose feast day, August 28, they had first sighted land. The Matanzas killings. The French commander, Jean Ribault, sailed to attack the new Spanish town, but a hurricane wrecked his ships far to the south. Meanwhile Menéndez led a force against Fort Caroline, took it, killed most of the men, and sent the women and children to Havana. Then he found the shipwrecked Frenchmen trapped by an inlet south of St. Augustine. They surrendered; 111 were killed and sixteen spared, among them a few who said they were Catholic and four artisans the town needed. Two weeks later, on October 12, Ribault and another group surrendered, and 134 were killed. The Park Service asks readers to weigh the causes: religious hatred, orders from Spain, or the fear that the colony could not feed so many prisoners through the winter. Raids and sieges. In 1586 the English privateer Sir Francis Drake burned the wooden town. The English founded Charles Town in 1670 and Georgia in 1733, both on land Spain claimed, and the colony came under repeated attack. On October 2, 1672, the governor broke ground for the Castillo de San Marcos, and the town’s soldiers protected it through two major sieges. By the late 1600s enslaved people from the English colonies had learned they could find freedom in Spanish Florida if they became Catholic and pledged to serve the Spanish crown. The Yawp notes that Spanish missions among the Timucua, Guale, and Apalachee were linked to St. Augustine by a royal road, the Camino Real, yet Spain held Florida only “tenuously.” War and slave raids, and above all disease, devastated Florida’s Native peoples. Britain, Spain, and the United States. Under the Treaty of Paris of 1763, Spain gave Florida to Britain to get back Cuba, and the Spanish population of St. Augustine left for Cuba. Britain brought Menorcan indentured workers, whose descendants gave the town much of its Mediterranean character. The 1783 Peace of Paris returned Florida to Spain, and most of the British left. Spain could not hold it for long. American settlers backed by Georgians tried to seize Florida in the Patriot Rebellion of 1811–1812, and in 1821 Spain ceded it to the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty. An American city. Under U.S. rule the Castillo, renamed Fort Marion, was taken by Confederate troops in 1861 and abandoned to Union forces in March 1862. In 1885 Henry Flagler opened his 540-room Ponce de León Hotel, and wealthy families made the city their winter home. Visitors who toured the old forts pressed Congress to save them, and in 1916 it granted $1,025 for repairs, which the Park Service calls the first time the federal government gave money for historic preservation. How long was it Spanish? The Park Service writes that the 1565 killings “initiated Spanish control of Florida for 235 years.” The same Park Service pages also describe a British period from 1763 to 1784, which interrupted Spanish rule. St. Augustine is a reminder that the European colonization of what became the United States began with Spain, in the South, and that the colonial story was shaped by Spanish, French, British, African, and Indigenous peoples as much as by the English. From that time, the inlet was called Matanzas -- meaning “slaughters” in Spanish. Manuel de Cendoya, Governor and Captain General of these provinces . . . with spade in hand . . . began the foundation trenches for the construction of the Castillo. title: Statue of Liberty
subtitle: France’s gift to the United States, and a welcome to generations of immigrants
summary: The Statue of Liberty, officially Liberty Enlightening the World, was a gift from the people of France, designed by sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi with an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel, on a pedestal paid for by Americans. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, in New York Harbor, it was meant to celebrate American independence and French-American friendship. Next to Ellis Island, and later inscribed with Emma Lazarus’s poem “The New Colossus,” it became a symbol of welcome to immigrants.

themeText: Immigration National symbols and holidays Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Northeast Liberty Island, New York Harbor Dedicated October 28, 1886, by President Grover Cleveland Creators Bartholdi (sculptor), Eiffel (framework), Richard Morris Hunt (pedestal) Height 151 feet; about 305 feet including the pedestal Tablet JULY IV MDCCLXXVI, July 4, 1776 National monument Since October 15, 1924; cared for by the National Park Service since 1933 The statue stands on Liberty Island (formerly Bedloe’s Island) in New York Harbor, on a pedestal set within Fort Wood, an 11-point Army fort built in the early 1800s. Lady Liberty holds a torch in her right hand and, in her left, a tablet inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence. Her crown’s spikes evoke rays of light, and a broken shackle and chains, symbols of the end of slavery, lie at her feet, invisible from below. Her copper skin is only 3/32 of an inch thick. In 1865 the French historian and abolitionist Édouard de Laboulaye proposed a monumental gift from the people of France to the people of the United States, to mark the centennial of American independence and to celebrate the recent abolition of slavery. Sculptor Bartholdi took up the idea. France paid for the statue; Americans were to pay for the pedestal. The Franco-Prussian War delayed the work, and when the first engineer died in 1879, Gustave Eiffel designed the internal framework. To raise money, the torch-bearing arm was displayed in Philadelphia in 1876 and in New York’s Madison Square from 1877 to 1882. France formally presented the statue on July 4, 1884. Fundraising for the pedestal lagged until Joseph Pulitzer used his newspaper, the New York World, to appeal to the public, promising to print every donor’s name; about 120,000 people gave more than $100,000. The statue crossed the Atlantic in 214 crates, arriving on June 17, 1885, and was dedicated on October 28, 1886. President Grover Cleveland promised, “We will not forget that Liberty has here made her home.” Emma Lazarus had written “The New Colossus” in 1883 for a fundraising auction; in 1903 a plaque with the poem, “Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free”, was placed in the pedestal. Because the statue stood next to the immigration station at Ellis Island, it became a symbol of welcome, and in 1965 President Lyndon B. Johnson signed a major immigration act at its base. It was restored for its 1986 centennial, when a replica of Bartholdi’s original torch replaced the much-altered original. The Statue of Liberty is perhaps the best-known symbol of the United States, a monument to independence and the end of slavery that came to stand above all for the promise America offered immigrants. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGkqh-iwS28 What "Lady Liberty" and Ellis Island Mean Today | National Geographic National Geographic 4:15 2026-10-23

title: The White House
subtitle: The president’s home and office since 1800
summary: The White House has been the home and workplace of every American president since John and Abigail Adams moved in, in November 1800. Designed by the Irish-born architect James Hoban, it was built between 1792 and 1800 by free workers and by enslaved people hired out by their owners. British troops burned it in 1814, and it was rebuilt by 1817. Long called the “President’s House” or “Executive Mansion,” it got its official name from Theodore Roosevelt in 1901. Today it is a residence, an office, a stage for ceremonies and a museum that welcomes over 500,000 visitors a year.
thumbAlt: The north front of the White House, with its columned portico, seen across the lawn
aliases: President’s House Executive Mansion 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue West Wing James Hoban
themeText: The presidency National symbols and holidays Slavery and emancipation
text: Washington, D.C. 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C. Architect James Hoban, winner of a 1792 design competition Cornerstone October 13, 1792, at a Masonic ceremony First residents John and Abigail Adams, November 1800 Builders Free white workers and over 200 known enslaved people (with the Capitol) Burned By British troops, August 24, 1814; rebuilt by 1817 Official name “White House,” adopted at Theodore Roosevelt’s direction, October 1901 The White House stands on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., on a site chosen by George Washington’s commissioners and the city’s planner, Pierre (Peter) Charles L’Enfant. Its sandstone came from a quarry on Aquia Creek in Stafford County, Virginia, which the federal government bought in 1791. The main house is flanked by the West Wing, with the president’s offices, and the East Wing. The White House Historical Association describes it as at once a family home, the president’s office, “the ceremonial stage upon which our nation welcomes its most important visitors,” and a museum. Building the President’s House. After the Residence Act of 1790 placed the capital on the Potomac, Washington appointed three commissioners to manage construction. In March 1792 they announced a national design competition, and in July they chose Hoban’s design. The cornerstone was laid on October 13, 1792. Enslaved people worked on every stage of construction from 1792 to 1800, as axemen, stone cutters, carpenters, brick makers, sawyers and laborers, alongside free white workers and craftsmen. All three original commissioners were enslavers. On April 13, 1792, they resolved to hire “good labouring negroes by the year,” paying the owners, who collected the wages. Historian Bob Arnebeck has identified over 200 enslaved people who worked on the White House and the Capitol, and there were likely many more. Hoban himself owned enslaved carpenters: a May 1795 payroll lists Peter, Ben, Harry and Daniel, whose wages Hoban signed for. Fire and rebuilding. In 1798 the stone walls received a lime whitewash to protect them from winter freezes. On August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops burned the house. It was rebuilt by 1817, again partly with enslaved labor. Presidents kept changing it: Jefferson added colonnades, James Monroe the South Portico, and Andrew Jackson the North Portico. The modern White House. In 1902 Theodore Roosevelt modernized the house and added the West Wing as the president’s office space; Franklin Roosevelt added the East Wing in 1942. By the time the Trumans moved in in 1945, decades of careless alterations and the lack of foundations under its interior walls had left it “on the verge of literal collapse.” From 1948 to 1952, while the Trumans lived across the street at Blair House, the interior was gutted and rebuilt on a steel frame with 22-foot-deep foundations, at a cost of $5.7 million. Truman had the old cracked beams milled into paneling for the ground-floor rooms. The White House is one of the best-known symbols of the American presidency and of the nation itself. Its history also holds a contradiction that the White House Historical Association now highlights: the home of the leader of a nation founded on liberty was built in part by people held in slavery, a “paradoxical relationship” between slavery and “the ideals of freedom and liberty enshrined in America’s founding documents.” Why “white”? A popular story says the house was painted white to cover the scorch marks of 1814. In fact it was first whitewashed in 1798. The name “White House” appeared now and then in nineteenth-century newspapers, but most people said “President’s House” or “Executive Mansion.” On October 17, 1901, at Roosevelt’s direction, his secretary asked that official papers be headed “White House.” Four dates in the floor A marker in the Entrance Hall floor records four dates: 1792 (the cornerstone), 1817 (the rebuilding after the fire), 1902 (Theodore Roosevelt’s renovation) and 1952 (the end of the Truman reconstruction). The cornerstone itself has never been found, even during the Truman gutting. James Hoban Hoban, born to a modest family in County Kilkenny, Ireland, studied architectural drawing in Dublin before emigrating. In Charleston, South Carolina, he bought at least one enslaved person, a carpenter named Peter, and in 1789 advertised a reward for his return after Peter “absented himself.” The White House Historical Association writes that enslaved workers played a vital role in Hoban’s “rise to prominence and prosperity” in Washington. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MdL47Bi-G2A History of the White House C-SPAN's American History TV 1:47:42 2026-10-29 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gnZPoWMVoSs The Evolution of the White House, EXPLAINED! title: Yellowstone National Park
subtitle: The world’s first national park, set aside in 1872 on top of an active volcano
summary: On March 1, 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law that set aside more than two million acres of the Rocky Mountains, mostly in what is now Wyoming, as “a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.” Yellowstone became the world’s first national park. It sits on one of the world’s largest volcanic calderas and holds more than half of all the geysers on Earth. People had lived in and traveled through the region for more than 11,000 years before it became a park.
thumbAlt: Thomas Moran’s 1872 painting of the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, with the Lower Falls between golden cliffs
aliases: Yellowstone Old Faithful first national park National Park Service Yellowstone National Park Protection Act
themeText: Land and environment National symbols and holidays Indigenous history Territorial expansion
text: West Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho Established March 1, 1872, signed by President Ulysses S. Grant Size About 2.2 million acres (3,472 square miles), larger than Rhode Island and Delaware combined Location 96% in Wyoming, 3% in Montana, 1% in Idaho Geysers More than 500 active, over half the world’s total, among 10,000+ hydrothermal features Volcano A caldera about 45 by 30 miles Visits 4.74 million in 2024 Yellowstone lies in the northwest corner of Wyoming, reaching into Montana and Idaho. About 80 percent of the park is forest, mostly lodgepole pine. Beneath it is an active volcano whose caldera is one of the largest in the world, and its heat powers more than 10,000 hot springs, mud pots, steam vents, and geysers. The park is home to 67 species of mammals, including bison, elk, and grizzly bears; the Lower Falls of the Yellowstone River plunge 308 feet. More than 1,800 archeological sites record the long human presence there. For thousands of years many tribes and bands, among them the Tukudika (“Sheep Eaters”), lived in, hunted in, and traveled through the region. In the years before 1872 the Washburn and Hayden expeditions explored it, and William Henry Jackson’s photographs and Thomas Moran’s paintings captured the imagination of Congress. Members of the expeditions, including Nathaniel Langford, lobbied for a bill modeled on the 1864 law that had given Yosemite Valley to California to protect. Closing so large an area to settlement broke with the government’s usual policy of transferring public land to private owners, but Congress agreed, and Grant signed the act six months after the Hayden Expedition. Because the area lay across three territories, it became a federal park rather than a state one. The early park had little money and no laws to protect it. Langford served as an unpaid superintendent; his successor, Philetus Norris, built the first roads, but he also spread a myth that Native Americans had avoided the area out of fear of the geysers, to reassure tourists during the wars between the United States and Native nations. Poachers, squatters, and vandals ravaged the park until the U.S. Army took charge in 1886. When soldiers caught a poacher killing bison in 1894 and could only expel him, a national outcry pushed Congress to pass a law giving the Army real power to protect the park. Yellowstone’s experience helped lead to the creation of the National Park Service in 1916, and rangers replaced the Army in 1918. After World War II visitors poured in, a million a year by 1948, and the Park Service’s Mission 66 program rebuilt roads and visitor facilities. Yellowstone established a new idea: that some land should belong permanently to the whole public and be protected for its natural wonders rather than sold. That idea grew into the national park system, today more than 80 million acres in all fifty states and several U.S. territories. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCYSEDqPv4o A Brief History of Yellowstone National Park | National Geographic National Geographic 4:22 2026-10-23

title: The American Revolution
subtitle: The war for independence from Britain, 1775–1783, and the revolution in ideas that made a new nation
summary: In little more than a decade after 1763, colonists who had been proud to be British came to see Parliament’s taxes and controls as a threat to their liberty, and in 1776 they declared independence. The war that followed, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 to the Treaty of Paris in September 1783, pitted the new United States, with France as its ally from 1778, against the world’s largest military. The Revolution created a republic founded on the idea that government rests on the consent of the governed, but it left slavery in place and opened Native lands to settlement, contradictions that shaped the nation for generations.
location: The thirteen colonies, the Atlantic, and battlefields from Canada to Georgia
thumbAlt: John Trumbull’s painting of the British surrender at Yorktown
aliases: Revolutionary War War of Independence War for Independence Patriots Loyalists Continental Army Saratoga Valley Forge Treaty of Paris
themeText: War and the military Political thought Foreign policy and diplomacy African American history Indigenous history Women's history
text: The thirteen colonies, the Atlantic, and battlefields from Canada to Georgia Belligerents United States and allies France (from 1778), Spain, and the Dutch Republic vs. Great Britain, Loyalists, German auxiliaries, and allied Native nations Commanders George Washington (Continental Army); Thomas Gage, William Howe, Henry Clinton, Charles Cornwallis (Britain) Key battles Lexington and Concord (1775), Bunker Hill (1775), Trenton (1776), Saratoga (1777), Yorktown (1781) Independence declared Resolution passed July 2, 1776; Declaration approved July 4, 1776 Ended by Treaty of Paris, signed September 3, 1783 Black Americans An estimated 5,000–6,000 fought for independence; about 20,000 joined the British On one side stood the Patriots, colonists who came to support independence, organized first in local committees and provincial congresses and then in the Continental Congress and the Continental Army under George Washington. From 1778 France was their ally, and Spain and the Dutch Republic also went to war with Britain, turning the rebellion into a global conflict. On the other side stood Great Britain, its regular army and navy, tens of thousands of hired German soldiers, usually called Hessians, and the Loyalists, colonists of every rank who remained faithful to the king. Many Americans were neither. A good number of colonists tried to stay neutral. The roughly 250,000 Native Americans in British North America, in more than eighty nations east of the Mississippi, mostly tried at first to stay out of the conflict; when they took sides, they did so to protect their lands and sovereignty. Many, including Shawnee, Creek, Cherokee, and most of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee, sided with Britain, while the Oneida and Tuscarora supported the Americans. Black Americans, free and enslaved, also weighed which side offered freedom: an estimated 5,000 to 6,000 fought for independence, while about 20,000 fought for the British. Seen from 1763, nothing would have seemed less likely than an American revolution. Colonists had just helped Britain win the Seven Years’ War, and most had never been prouder to be British. Over the previous century they had grown used to running their own affairs. Each colony had an elected assembly that taxed residents and paid royal officials, and because land was easier to get than in England, a larger share of colonial men could vote. Many colonists embraced the ideology of republicanism, which warned that power corrupts and that a free people must be virtuous and watchful against conspiracy and tyranny. The ideas of John Locke and the religious revivals of the Great Awakening both encouraged ordinary people to question inherited authority. Victory left Britain in control of North America east of the Mississippi, but it also doubled the national debt and left the empire with expensive new frontiers to defend. King George III’s government set out to bring the colonies under firmer control. The Royal Proclamation of 1763 forbade settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains, hoping to avoid costly wars with Native nations after Pontiac’s War, and colonists who had fought for that land protested. The imperial crisis, 1764–1774. Parliament’s attempts to raise revenue set off a decade of escalating resistance. The Sugar Act of 1764 tightened enforcement of duties on molasses and sent smugglers to courts without juries, and the Currency Act restricted colonial paper money in the middle of a postwar recession. The Stamp Act of 1765, the first direct tax Parliament had ever laid on the colonies, required stamps on newspapers, legal documents, diplomas, and even playing cards. Colonists resisted in three ways: assemblies passed resolutions such as the Virginia Resolves, and nine colonies sent delegates to a Stamp Act Congress; merchants organized boycotts of British goods; and crowds burned effigies and drove every stamp distributor to resign. Parliament repealed the act in 1766 but declared its full power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The Townshend Acts of 1767 placed duties on everyday imports such as lead, glass, paint, and tea and used the money to pay royal officials, freeing governors from the assemblies’ control. Resistance now drew in colonists of every rank. Merchants and consumers signed nonimportation and nonconsumption agreements, committees policed them, and women organized spinning clubs so that families could wear homespun instead of British cloth. Troops sent to Boston in 1768 clashed with townspeople until the Boston Massacre of March 1770. Parliament then repealed every Townshend duty except the one on tea. When the Tea Act of 1773 tried to rescue the East India Company by selling its tea in America, Bostonians dumped 342 chests into the harbor at the Boston Tea Party. Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts of 1774, which closed Boston’s port, took over Massachusetts’s government, and allowed troops to be quartered in colonists’ houses. Rather than isolating Massachusetts, the acts united the colonies. The First Continental Congress met in September 1774 and adopted the Continental Association, a continent-wide boycott enforced by local committees of ordinary colonists. From war to independence, 1775–1776. Fighting began on April 19, 1775, at Lexington and Concord, and some twenty thousand militiamen soon besieged the British in Boston. At Bunker Hill (actually Breed’s Hill) in June, the British took the colonists’ fortifications but suffered twice as many casualties as the Americans. The Second Continental Congress adopted the army besieging Boston and made George Washington its commander, while still sending the king an Olive Branch Petition; George III instead proclaimed the colonies in rebellion. In the opening months of 1776 Thomas Paine’s pamphlet Common Sense attacked monarchy itself and turned independence into a popular cause. On July 2, 1776, Congress voted for Richard Henry Lee’s resolution that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, Free and Independent States,” and on July 4 it approved the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson. The war in the North, 1776–1778. That summer the largest expeditionary force in British history landed at New York, and the Continental Army, badly beaten in Brooklyn and Manhattan, retreated across New Jersey. With morale collapsing and enlistments expiring, Washington crossed the icy Delaware River on Christmas night 1776 and surprised a garrison of 1,500 Hessians at Trenton, then won again at Princeton a week later. In 1777 the British took Philadelphia, but a British army marching south from Canada under General John Burgoyne was surrounded and forced to surrender at Saratoga, New York. The Continental Army suffered through the winter of 1777–1778 at Valley Forge, where more than 2,500 men died of disease and exposure. Washington learned that his untrained army could not win head-on battles against British professionals; as long as he kept it intact, the war would go on, however many cities the British captured. The war in the South and the world, 1778–1783. In 1778 Britain shifted its effort to the South, where it expected more Loyalist support. British campaigns captured major cities from Georgia to Virginia, but Britain lacked the troops to hold the countryside, and bitter fighting between local Patriots and Loyalists made the Southern war a true civil war. In 1781 Washington and the French army marched south and, with a French fleet blocking the coast, trapped General Charles Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, forcing his surrender in 1781. Saratoga (1777) was the decisive turning point. The surrender of an entire British army convinced the French government that the American cause could succeed. France had already been sending secret aid; when news of Saratoga reached Foreign Minister Vergennes in December 1777, he decided for an alliance, and the Treaty of Alliance and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce were signed on February 6, 1778. The war became a global conflict that stretched British forces from Europe to India. Yorktown (October 1781) left Britain with no new strategy and no public support for continuing the war. By then Britain was also fighting France, Spain, and the Netherlands, and the capture of a second army brought the government to the peace table. Peace talks opened in Paris in September 1782. Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay insisted on British recognition of independence and refused a separate peace without France. Two months of hard bargaining produced preliminary articles in which Britain accepted American independence and the new nation’s boundaries and settled questions of fishing rights off Newfoundland, prewar debts, and Loyalist property. The final Treaty of Paris was signed on September 3, 1783. Three months later, on December 23, 1783, Washington resigned his command, a gesture that ensured civilian rule over the new republic. The Revolution’s most immediate result was a wave of constitution writing. In 1776 and 1777 the new states drafted written constitutions based on popular sovereignty, the idea that government’s authority comes from the people; several, following Virginia, included a bill of rights. Pennsylvania’s constitution allowed all free men to vote, and Massachusetts’s 1780 constitution, debated in town meetings, created a government of three branches with checks and balances. The Articles of Confederation, ratified in 1781, joined the states in a weak union whose Congress could not tax or regulate trade. Politics became more democratic and society less deferential, and the end of British trade restrictions opened new markets and manufacturing. The Revolution’s promise of equality also had sharp limits. Women had organized boycotts and run farms and shops during the war, but they gained no political rights; instead they were praised as “republican mothers” responsible for raising virtuous citizens. About sixty thousand Loyalists left the country, many for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec, and states kept seizing Loyalist property despite the peace treaty. For enslaved people, the war was the largest flight from slavery before the Civil War: historians estimate that as many as 80,000 to 100,000 escaped their Patriot enslavers, and 8,000 to 10,000 Black Loyalists left with the British in 1783 to begin new lives across the Atlantic world. Several Northern states passed gradual emancipation laws, but in the South slavery endured, and the Declaration’s words about equality became a challenge the nation would face again and again. For Native nations, American victory brought a rush of settlers into the West and governments hostile to their land claims, and Native peoples would continue to be pushed west throughout the next century. The American Revolution created the United States and launched what historians call the age of democratic revolutions, followed by revolutions in France, Haiti, and South America. Its ideals, above all the Declaration’s claim that “all men are created equal,” became the shared language that later movements, from abolitionists to suffragists and civil rights activists, used to demand that the nation live up to its founding. There is something absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island. title: The Civil War
subtitle: The war for union and against slavery, 1861–1865
summary: The Civil War was fought between the United States and eleven Southern states that seceded after Abraham Lincoln’s election in 1860 to form the Confederate States of America, a nation whose leaders openly identified it with slavery. It began with the Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter in April 1861 and ended with Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House in April 1865. What started as a war to preserve the Union became, through the actions of enslaved people, Congress, and Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation, a war to end slavery. It was the deadliest war in American history: traditional counts put the dead at about 620,000, and more recent estimates at about 750,000.
location: From Virginia and the Mississippi Valley to the border states, the Southwest, and the sea
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of the Battle of Gettysburg
aliases: War Between the States American Civil War Union Confederacy Confederate States of America Anaconda Plan Appomattox Gettysburg Antietam Vicksburg Sherman's March
themeText: War and the military Slavery and emancipation African American history The presidency Constitution and law
text: From Virginia and the Mississippi Valley to the border states, the Southwest, and the sea Union 20 free states and the loyal slaveholding border states; President Abraham Lincoln; population about 18.5 million, plus 3 million in the border states Confederacy 11 states; President Jefferson Davis; 5.5 million free people and 3.5 million enslaved Deaths About 620,000 in the traditional count; about 750,000 in more recent estimates Black soldiers and sailors About 179,000 in the U.S. Army and 19,000 in the Navy Bloodiest battle Gettysburg, July 1–3, 1863: about 51,000 casualties Ended Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House, April 9, 1865 The United States, the Union, included twenty Northern and Western free states, from Maine to California and Oregon, led by President Abraham Lincoln. Four slaveholding border states, Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri, stayed loyal despite deep divisions and bitter guerrilla fighting; Lincoln reportedly said that to lose Kentucky was “nearly the same as to lose the whole game.” The Confederate States of America comprised eleven states, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Tennessee, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia, under President Jefferson Davis, with its capital first at Montgomery, Alabama, and from May 1861 at Richmond, Virginia. The Union had overwhelming material advantages. Its population was about 18.5 million, against 5.5 million free people and 3.5 million enslaved people in the Confederacy; it had more than eleven times as many factory workers, twice as many horses, and far more money in banks and coin. The Confederacy led only in crops such as tobacco and rice, and it counted on its cotton, the raw material of Europe’s textile mills, to win foreign support. Even with close to total conscription, the South could not match the North in numbers, and Southern soldiers were significantly more likely to be killed, wounded, or captured. The war grew out of the long national quarrel over slavery and its expansion into the West, which the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act had each tried to manage. The election of 1860 broke the political system apart. The Democratic Party split, with Southern Democrats nominating their own candidate, and Lincoln, the candidate of the new Republican Party, which opposed the spread of slavery, won the presidency. South Carolina acted almost at once. On December 20, 1860, its convention voted 169 to 0 to dissolve its union with the United States. Six more states of the Lower South followed, and on February 4, 1861, delegates of the seven seceding states met in Montgomery, Alabama, to organize a new nation and chose Jefferson Davis as president. Their own statements left no doubt about the cause. “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world,” Mississippi declared; every rationale for secession could be tied to slavery. In his inaugural address in March 1861 Lincoln declared secession “legally void” and promised to hold federal property in the seceded states, though he did not intend to invade them. The war begins, 1861. Attention fixed on Fort Sumter, a federal fort in Charleston Harbor. On April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries opened fire, and after some thirty hours Major Robert Anderson accepted terms and evacuated the fort. Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to serve three months, and the call for troops pushed Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas into the Confederacy. The Union adopted General-in-Chief Winfield Scott’s Anaconda Plan, which aimed to strangle the Confederacy with a naval blockade of its ports and control of its rivers, above all the Mississippi. Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus, allowing military commanders to arrest secession-minded activists without charge. Any hope of a short war died that summer at the First Battle of Bull Run near Manassas, Virginia, just twenty-five miles from Washington, where Confederate forces routed a Union army that had been pushed to advance on Richmond. A war for union, 1862. In the West, Union victories at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson in February 1862 opened Tennessee to Ulysses S. Grant, and in April the Battle of Shiloh, with almost 24,000 casualties, shocked both sides with its carnage and ended Confederate hopes of blocking the Union advance into Mississippi. Led by Secretary of the Navy Gideon Welles, the Union navy steadily tightened the Anaconda. In the East, General George B. McClellan’s Peninsula Campaign approached Richmond, but Robert E. Lee, newly in command of the Army of Northern Virginia, drove him back. Lee then invaded Maryland, hoping a victory on Union soil might influence the Northern elections and win European recognition for the Confederacy. On September 17, 1862, at Antietam Creek near Sharpsburg, the armies fought a battle that cost about 22,700 casualties in a single day. The battle itself was inconclusive, but Lee withdrew to Virginia. A war for emancipation, 1863. From the first months of the war, enslaved people took freedom into their own hands by escaping to Union lines. At Fort Monroe in Virginia, General Benjamin Butler began accepting people who escaped to his lines, calling them “contraband of war” rather than returning them, and Congress affirmed his policy in the First Confiscation Act. Congress abolished slavery in the District of Columbia in April 1862 and in the territories that summer, and the Second Confiscation Act of July 1862 freed people whose enslavers served the Confederacy. Antietam gave Lincoln the victory he needed: on September 22, 1862, he issued a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, and on January 1, 1863, he declared all persons held as slaves in the rebellious areas “are, and henceforward shall be free.” The proclamation exempted the loyal border states and parts of the Confederacy already under Union control, but it changed the war’s purpose from union alone to freedom. It also opened the army to Black men. The War Department created the U.S. Colored Troops in May 1863; by the end of the war about 179,000 Black men had served in the army, about a tenth of its strength, and 19,000 in the navy. They received less pay than white soldiers, faced murder or enslavement if captured, and mostly served on garrison and labor duty, but they fought in more than four hundred battles and engagements, including Milliken’s Bend, Port Hudson, Fort Wagner, and Nashville, and fifteen Black soldiers received the Medal of Honor. Hard war, 1864–1865. In 1864 Grant, now general-in-chief, ordered simultaneous offensives along the whole Confederate frontier, understanding that the South could not win a war of attrition. His Overland Campaign through the Wilderness and Cold Harbor attacked Lee’s dwindling army again and again, and from June 1864 he besieged Petersburg, the gateway to Richmond. In the West, William Tecumseh Sherman fought his way toward Atlanta, the Confederacy’s great rail and industrial center, and took it on September 2, 1864. Two months later he cut loose from his supply lines and marched 62,000 men across Georgia to the sea, destroying railroads, factories, and stores to break the South’s will to fight; he reached Savannah in time to present it to Lincoln as a Christmas gift. Three moments did the most to change the war’s course. Antietam (September 1862), though tactically inconclusive, ended Lee’s first invasion of the North, gave Lincoln the occasion for the Emancipation Proclamation, and all but ended the danger that Britain or France would recognize the Confederacy. Confederate diplomats had expected the cotton trade to force Europe’s hand, but Britain proclaimed neutrality in May 1861, the other powers followed, and no foreign government ever recognized the Confederacy. Gettysburg and Vicksburg (July 1863) came within a day of each other. At Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, July 1–3, Lee’s second invasion of the North ended in defeat after three days of fighting that cost some 51,000 casualties, the bloodiest battle of the war. On July 4, after a 47-day siege, Confederate General John C. Pemberton surrendered Vicksburg, Mississippi, to Grant. With the fall of Port Hudson five days later, the Union controlled the whole Mississippi, and the Confederacy was split in two. Lincoln had called Vicksburg “the key,” and Jefferson Davis had called it the “nailhead that holds the South’s two halves together.” Atlanta (September 1864) came at a moment when Lincoln himself doubted he would be reelected and his opponent, General McClellan, hoped for the votes of war-weary soldiers. Sherman’s capture of the city, together with overwhelming support from Union troops, gave Lincoln an easy victory in November and ensured that the war would be fought to its end. By the spring of 1865 the Confederacy was collapsing. In March, in desperation, the Confederate Congress authorized the enlistment of Black soldiers, but only a few dozen enlisted before the end. On April 2 Richmond was abandoned as Jefferson Davis and his government fled. A week later, on April 9, 1865, Grant and Lee met in the parlor of a house at Appomattox Court House, Virginia. Grant’s terms were generous: Lee’s men could go home in safety if they pledged to stop fighting and gave up their arms. On April 12 the infantry of the Army of Northern Virginia stacked their weapons, folded their flags, and received parole papers. Other Confederate forces surrendered over the following weeks. Lincoln did not live to see the peace. Less than a week after Lee’s surrender he was killed by an assassin’s bullet. In his second inaugural address, delivered on March 4, 1865, he had asked the nation to finish the war “with malice toward none; with charity for all,” and “to bind up the nation’s wounds.” The war destroyed slavery. The Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress in January 1865 after Lincoln made it part of the Republican platform, was ratified on December 6, 1865, and abolished slavery throughout the United States, except as punishment for crime. Together with the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, it began the vast and contested project of Reconstruction: deciding what freedom and citizenship would mean for some four million formerly enslaved people. The human cost was staggering. About 620,000 soldiers died in the traditional count, roughly two percent of the population, and some historians now estimate about 750,000. More Americans became casualties at Gettysburg alone than in the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812 combined. Disease accounted for more than half of all casualties, falling hardest on men from rural areas who had little immunity, and nearly as many men died in prison camps as were killed in the whole of the Vietnam War. More than two hundred thousand women became widows. The war also transformed the nation’s government and society. To fight it, the federal government introduced a draft, suspended habeas corpus, and expanded its power over the economy and the states. The first Northern draft provoked the New York City Draft Riots in July 1863, in which white rioters killed about 120 people, including at least eleven Black New Yorkers who were lynched; in the Confederacy, food shortages and inflation drove women to lead bread riots in Richmond and other cities. Women North and South ran farms and businesses, served as nurses, and organized sanitary fairs that raised millions of dollars for soldiers. Above all, the Union survived, and with it the principle Lincoln had defended from his inaugural address on: that secession was legally void. The Civil War decided that the United States would remain one nation and that slavery would end. By turning a war for union into a war for freedom, and by enlisting nearly 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors, it began a new definition of American citizenship that Reconstruction and the long civil rights struggle would fight over for the next century. Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world. State of Mississippi declaration of the causes of secession, January 1861 That all persons held as slaves within any State or designated part of a State, the people whereof shall then be in rebellion against the United States, shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free. Abraham Lincoln Emancipation Proclamation, January 1, 1863 Vicksburg is the key! The war can never be brought to a close until that key is in our pocket. title: The Cold War
subtitle: The global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, 1947–1991
summary: The Cold War was a global political and ideological rivalry between the capitalist countries led by the United States and the communist countries led by the Soviet Union. It grew out of the failure of the World War II allies to agree on the postwar world and lasted from the late 1940s until the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. The two superpowers never fought each other directly. Instead they built rival alliances, raced to build nuclear weapons and to reach space, and backed opposing sides in wars from Korea to Vietnam. The closest they came to nuclear war was the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962.

text: Worldwide: Europe, East Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and the arms and space races Strategy U.S. containment of Soviet influence, formulated by George F. Kennan (1946–1947) Alliances NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) Hot wars Korea (1950–1953), Vietnam, and other conflicts Space race Sputnik 1 (1957) and Yuri Gagarin (1961) were Soviet firsts; the U.S. landed on the Moon in 1969 Closest call The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962 End The Soviet Union dissolved; Gorbachev resigned on December 25, 1991 The United States led an alliance of Western democracies and market economies, formalized in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) in 1949. Its original members were the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Italy, Portugal, Norway, Denmark, and Iceland. The Soviet Union led the socialist states of Eastern Europe, which formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955 after West Germany joined NATO: Albania, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and East Germany. The People’s Republic of China, founded in 1949, was at first a Soviet ally and later a rival. As European empires collapsed, both superpowers competed for influence in the newly independent nations of Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America. The Soviet Union and the United States had been allies against Germany, but the alliance rested on necessity. Suspicion ran deep on both sides: the United States had sent troops against the Red Army during the Russian Civil War and did not recognize the Soviet Union for years after its founding in 1922. At Yalta and Potsdam in 1945, the Big Three failed to reach a lasting settlement over Germany and Eastern Europe. Stalin regarded the territory his armies had won from Germany in Eastern Europe as a Soviet sphere of influence, while American leaders feared that communism would spread through a ruined Europe. When Truman told Stalin at Potsdam about a “new weapon of unusual destructive force,” the Soviet leader simply said he hoped the Americans would make “good use” of it. Relations worsened in 1946. Disputes over Soviet troops in northern Iran, Soviet pressure on Turkey over the Straits, and the failure of plans for international control of atomic energy ended hopes for a durable postwar partnership. In February 1946 George Kennan, a U.S. diplomat in Moscow, sent his “Long Telegram” urging that Soviet power be “contained.” In March, Winston Churchill declared in Missouri that an “iron curtain” had descended across Europe. In 1947 Kennan’s anonymous “X” article called for “long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment” of Soviet expansion. That idea became the basic American strategy for the next four decades. The division of Europe (1947–1949). On March 12, 1947, President Harry S. Truman asked Congress for $400 million for Greece and Turkey and pledged to support “free peoples” resisting outside pressure: the Truman Doctrine. The State Department’s historians note that Stalin had in fact deliberately refrained from aiding the Greek communists. In June 1947 Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a program to rebuild Europe, and the Marshall Plan eventually provided over $12 billion (the American Yawp puts the figure at $13 billion from 1948 to 1952). The Soviet Union declined to take part and kept the countries of Eastern Europe out, seeing the plan as an instrument of American economic domination, and offered its own program of aid to the East. In June 1948, after the Western powers introduced a new currency in their zones of Germany, Soviet forces blockaded land access to West Berlin. American and British planes supplied the city by air, at the peak landing one every forty-five seconds, until the blockade ended in May 1949. That year the North Atlantic Treaty created NATO, and Germany was divided into two states. Globalization and the arms race (1949–1962). In August 1949 the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb, years earlier than American officials had expected, and in October the Chinese Communist Party took power in China. A secret 1950 report, NSC-68, called for a massive American military buildup and expanded containment to the whole world: “a defeat of free institutions anywhere is a defeat everywhere.” In June 1950 war broke out in Korea, where more than 30,000 Americans and millions of Koreans died before an armistice in July 1953. Both superpowers built hydrogen bombs, the United States in 1952 and the Soviet Union in 1953, and a strategy of deterrence took hold. J. Robert Oppenheimer compared it to “two scorpions in a bottle.” At home, fear of communism fed the Red Scare of Senator Joseph McCarthy. The space race. The Soviet Union took the lead in space. On October 4, 1957, it launched Sputnik 1, the world’s first artificial satellite. In 1959 its Luna 2 became the first human-made object to reach the Moon, and on April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in orbit. The United States created NASA in 1958, and President John F. Kennedy used the Soviet lead to win funding for a Moon landing. The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). After the failed U.S.-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed with Fidel Castro in July 1962 to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba to deter another invasion. On October 14 an American U-2 spy plane photographed the missile sites. Rejecting advice to bomb and invade, Kennedy ordered a naval “quarantine” of Cuba on October 22. After days of tense messages, and the downing of a U-2 over Cuba, the two leaders made a deal. On October 28 Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be removed; Kennedy promised not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove American Jupiter missiles from Turkey, which was done in April 1963. The crisis led to a direct “Hotline” between Washington and Moscow and to the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963. Détente (1969–1979). By the late 1960s the arms race had become enormously expensive for both nations. The Soviet Union had split with China, and the United States was mired in Vietnam. The superpowers entered a period of relaxed tensions known as détente. They signed the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (1968), the first Strategic Arms Limitation Talks agreements and the Antiballistic Missile Treaty (1972), and the Helsinki Final Act (1975), which recognized Europe’s borders and promoted trade, cultural exchange, and human rights. Détente faded in the late 1970s, and after Soviet troops entered Afghanistan in 1979 arms talks stalled. The last decade (1980–1991). President Ronald Reagan greatly increased military spending in his first term. Yet, the American Yawp notes, he “helped bring the Cold War to an end through negotiation,” a tactic he had once scorned. Arms control talks resumed when Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in the Soviet Union. Gorbachev’s reforms loosened Soviet control over Eastern Europe. The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, communist governments across Eastern Europe gave way, and Gorbachev accepted the reunification of Germany. The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947–1948): committed the United States to containing Soviet influence in Europe. 1949: the end of the Berlin blockade, the founding of NATO, the first Soviet atomic bomb, and the communist victory in China. The Korean War (1950–1953): turned containment into a global military commitment. Sputnik (1957): opened the space race and shocked Americans into investing in science and rockets. The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): the moment the superpowers came closest to nuclear war, followed by the first arms control agreements. The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the end of the Soviet Union (1991). The Cold War ended with the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe in 1989 and the breakup of the Soviet Union. Gorbachev’s introduction of multiparty elections and a Soviet presidency began a democratization that, the State Department’s historians write, “eventually destabilized Communist control.” An unsuccessful coup by hard-line Communists in August 1991 weakened Gorbachev and brought Boris Yeltsin to the forefront of Russian politics. In December 1991 Yeltsin and the leaders of two other Soviet republics formed the Commonwealth of Independent States. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time and replaced by the Russian tricolor. The United States then worked with the new governments to secure the former Soviet nuclear arsenal. The Cold War reshaped American life. Instead of demobilizing after World War II, the United States built a permanent defense establishment, which President Dwight Eisenhower in 1961 called the “military-industrial complex.” Defense spending transformed regions from Southern California to the South. The arms race produced arsenals capable of destroying civilization, and fear of nuclear war became part of everyday culture. The space race created NASA and pushed both nations to remarkable achievements in science and engineering. At home, anticommunism led to loyalty investigations of federal employees, congressional hearings, blacklists, and the career of Senator McCarthy, who claimed without evidence to hold lists of communists in the government. The Senate condemned him in 1954. Abroad, the logic of containment and the “domino theory” drew the United States into interventions across Asia, Latin America, and Africa, most painfully in Vietnam, where more than 500,000 American troops eventually served and nearly 60,000 died. The Soviet Union, for its part, pointed to racial injustice in the United States in its propaganda, an embarrassment for a nation claiming to lead the “Free World.” The superpowers never fought each other directly, but millions died in the wars of the Cold War era, including more than 30,000 Americans in Korea and nearly 60,000 in Vietnam. For more than four decades the Cold War defined world politics. It divided Europe, spread conflict and competition to every continent, and produced the nuclear arms race and the space race. Its peaceful end in 1989–1991 was one of the great surprises of the twentieth century. The main element of any United States policy toward the Soviet Union must be that of a long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies. George F. title: The French and Indian War
subtitle: The North American front of the Seven Years’ War, 1754–1763
summary: The French and Indian War was the North American part of a world war, known elsewhere as the Seven Years’ War, between Britain and France. It began in 1754 when a young George Washington led Virginia militia into the Ohio Valley, a region both empires claimed. France and its Native allies won the early battles, but British victories at Louisbourg, Quebec, and Montreal ended French rule in Canada by 1760. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 gave Britain most of eastern North America. Victory left Britain deep in debt, faced with Pontiac’s War, and determined to tighten control of its colonies, which set off the conflicts that led to the American Revolution.
location: Ohio Valley, New York, Pennsylvania, Canada, and the Great Lakes
thumbAlt: Illustration of George Washington on horseback at the Battle of the Monongahela
aliases: Seven Years’ War Fort Necessity Jumonville Braddock’s defeat Plains of Abraham Treaty of Paris (1763) Proclamation of 1763 Pontiac’s War
themeText: War and the military Colonial encounters Indigenous history Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Ohio Valley, New York, Pennsylvania, Canada, and the Great Lakes Start 1754, in the disputed upper Ohio Valley First clash May 28, 1754: Washington’s militia kill the French commander Joseph Jumonville and several soldiers Fort Necessity July 3–4, 1754: Washington’s only surrender Braddock’s defeat July 9, 1755, at the Monongahela Turning point 1758–1759: Louisbourg falls; Wolfe defeats Montcalm outside Quebec Treaty Treaty of Paris, February 10, 1763 The war pitted Britain and its North American colonists against France, French colonists, and Native allies. The American Yawp stresses that these were not simply European wars: American militiamen fought for Britain against the French and their Native allies, and French victories early in the war “were often the result of alliances with Native Americans.” Native nations fought for their own reasons, above all trade and the defense of their lands, and the Six Nations of the Iroquois met Washington’s first mission in 1753, unimpressed by his tiny force. The name “French and Indian War” reflects the British colonists’ view of their enemies. Of the eighty-seven years between 1688 and 1775, the Yawp counts thirty-seven in which Britain was at war with France and its Native allies, with raids and captive-taking along the border of New England and New France. By the 1750s the two empires were feuding over their boundaries, especially the upper Ohio Valley, which Britain and Virginia land speculators claimed. In late 1753 Virginia’s lieutenant governor, Robert Dinwiddie, sent the young Major Washington with six frontiersmen to demand that the French leave. The French refused. 1754–1757: French victories. In 1754 Washington returned with about 140 men. On May 28 his Virginians and their Native allies attacked a French party, killing several soldiers and their commander, Joseph Jumonville. The sources describe the clash differently: the Yawp writes that Washington’s force “killed a French diplomat,” while Encyclopedia Virginia calls it a skirmish that the French “portrayed as an assassination.” Washington wrote, “I heard Bulletts whistle and believe me there is something charming in the sound.” On July 3–4 the French and their allies forced him to surrender at Fort Necessity, the only time he ever surrendered. In July 1755 General Edward Braddock’s column of about 1,700 regulars and militia was ambushed and routed near Fort Duquesne; Braddock was killed, and Washington, a volunteer aide, had two horses shot from under him. The French burned British outposts such as Fort William Henry in 1757 and repulsed a British attack on Fort Carillon (Ticonderoga) in 1758. 1756: A world war. In Europe the war began in earnest in 1756, when Prussia, Britain’s ally, invaded Saxony. Britain paid subsidies to Prussia and smaller German states, while its navy defeated the French at sea and Robert Clive won at Plassey in India. 1758–1760: British conquest. Control of the sea let Britain send more troops to America. Louisbourg fell in 1758, and in 1759 General James Wolfe defeated General Louis-Joseph de Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec. The British called 1759 their “year of miracles.” With the capture of Montreal in 1760, the war in North America ended. Britain then fought Spain, which entered the war in 1762, and took Cuba and the Philippines. Sea power. British naval victories allowed reinforcements to reach North America and isolated French Canada. Louisbourg (1758) and Quebec (1759). The fall of France’s great Atlantic fortress and of Quebec broke French power in Canada. Colonial unity. At the Albany Congress of 1754 Benjamin Franklin proposed a plan of union to coordinate colonial defenses, and tens of thousands of colonists fought in the war, which the Yawp says “pushed the thirteen American colonies closer together politically and culturally than ever before.” The Treaty of Paris, signed on February 10, 1763, ended French power on the North American mainland. Britain received much of Canada and North America from France, and Spain, to recover Cuba and the Philippines, gave up Florida. The Fort Necessity park notes that the war “ended in 1763 with the removal of French power from North America and India.” Pontiac’s War. The British replaced the French as the power in the Great Lakes and Ohio country, and the commander Jeffrey Amherst ended the French custom of diplomatic gift-giving and restricted sales of guns and ammunition to Native peoples, which many saw as preparation for war. Inspired in part by the prophet Neolin, the Ottawa leader Pontiac besieged Fort Detroit in May 1763 and Native warriors captured other British forts. The war lasted until 1766. The Proclamation of 1763. In October 1763 King George III reserved the lands west of the Appalachian divide for Native nations and forbade colonists “from making any Purchases or Settlements whatever” there. Colonists who had fought for that land protested. The road to revolution. The war doubled Britain’s national debt, and the Yawp writes that victory gave Britain “a larger empire than they could control.” To pay for it and govern it, Parliament turned to new taxes and enforcement, from the Sugar Act to the Stamp Act, provoking the protests that led to independence. The French and Indian War made Britain the dominant power in eastern North America, but the costs of victory and the problems of governing a vast new empire pushed Britain and its colonies into the conflict that became the American Revolution. It also gave George Washington his first military experience, including his only surrender. I can with truth assure you, I heard Bulletts whistle and believe me there is something charming in the sound. George Washington on Braddock’s defeat, 1755, quoted in Encyclopedia Virginia And We do hereby strictly forbid, on Pain of our Displeasure, all our loving Subjects from making any Purchases or Settlements whatever, or taking Possession of any of the Lands above reserved.
