title: Persian Gulf War
subtitle: The U.S.-led coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait, 1990–1991
summary: On August 2, 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein invaded and annexed neighboring Kuwait. President George H. W. Bush organized a broad international coalition, backed by United Nations resolutions, and built up forces in Saudi Arabia (Operation Desert Shield). When Iraq refused to withdraw, the coalition launched an air war in January 1991 (Operation Desert Storm), followed by a ground offensive that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait in four days. The swift victory boosted Bush’s popularity and seemed to many to exorcise the “ghosts of Vietnam.”
thumbAlt: U.S. Air Force jets flying over burning Kuwaiti oil fields during Desert Storm
aliases: Operation Desert Shield Operation Desert Storm Gulf War
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Kuwait, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia Invasion August 2, 1990: some 100,000 Iraqi troops overran Kuwait UN authorization Resolution 678 authorized force if Iraq did not withdraw Air war Began January 1991 Ground war February 24–28, 1991 Outcome Kuwait liberated; Saddam Hussein remained in power A U.S.-led coalition of many nations, acting under UN Security Council resolutions, fought Iraq under Saddam Hussein. Iraq emerged from its 1980–1988 war with Iran deeply in debt, owing some $37 billion to Gulf creditors. Saddam Hussein demanded that Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates forgive Iraq’s loans, accused Kuwait of overproducing oil and stealing from a shared oil field, and revived old territorial claims. Invasion and Desert Shield (August 1990 – January 1991). Iraq overran Kuwait in hours and declared it Iraq’s nineteenth province. The UN Security Council demanded withdrawal and imposed sanctions; Resolution 678 authorized force if Iraq did not leave. Congress granted Bush authority to intervene, and the coalition massed forces in the region. Desert Storm (January–February 1991). After the deadline passed, coalition air forces won control of the skies within a day and struck Iraqi command centers, infrastructure, and troops. Iraq fired missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia, but Israel did not retaliate. Americans watched laser-guided bombs and round-the-clock coverage on cable news. The ground war (February 24–28, 1991). A ground offensive routed Iraqi forces in about a hundred hours. The Iraqi military set fire to Kuwait’s oil fields, many of which burned for months. UN Resolution 678: gave the coalition international legal authority. Air supremacy in the first days of Desert Storm: crippled Iraq’s ability to fight. Kuwait was liberated. Bush and his advisers decided not to march on Baghdad, fearing an occupation and insurgency, and Saddam Hussein stayed in power. The United States maintained sanctions, weapons inspections, and no-fly zones over Iraq for the next decade. Bush’s approval rating reached 89 percent, though a recession helped defeat him in 1992. Continuing conflict with Saddam Hussein set the stage for the Iraq War of 2003. The Gulf War demonstrated American military dominance after the Cold War and began a long U.S. military involvement in the Persian Gulf. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jS-g2JjQSJ4 Desert Storm: The Gulf War 1990-1991 (Documentary) Real Time History 30:29 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UI0XaUDeLaA The Gulf War Explained Mr. Beat 15:40 2026-10-22

title: Iraq War
subtitle: The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, 2003–2011
summary: In March 2003, the United States led an invasion of Iraq to overthrow Saddam Hussein, whom the Bush administration accused of possessing weapons of mass destruction and linked to terrorism. Baghdad fell within weeks, but no weapons of mass destruction were ever found, and a long, bloody insurgency followed. A 2007 troop “surge” reduced violence, and the last U.S. combat forces left in December 2011. The war remains one of the most controversial in American history.
thumbAlt: The toppling of Saddam Hussein’s statue in Baghdad
aliases: Operation Iraqi Freedom weapons of mass destruction Mission Accomplished the surge Abu Ghraib
themeText: War and the military Terrorism and security Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Iraq Congressional authorization October 2002 Invasion Bombing of Baghdad began March 20, 2003; Baghdad fell April 9 WMD None were found Saddam Hussein Captured December 13, 2003; executed December 30, 2006 U.S. withdrawal Last combat forces left December 18, 2011 A U.S.-led coalition fought Saddam Hussein’s regime and then a range of insurgents, including al-Qaeda in Iraq. After the 1991 Gulf War, the United States maintained sanctions, weapons inspections, and no-fly zones over Iraq. In 1998 President Clinton ordered strikes on suspected weapons sites. After 9/11, Bush administration officials championed “regime change,” claiming Iraq had weapons of mass destruction; Bush declared there was “no doubt” of it. Invasion (2003). Congress authorized force in October 2002. Although Iraq began cooperating with UN inspectors, the administration pressed on, and Secretary of State Colin Powell presented allegations of an Iraqi weapons program to the UN in February 2003. Protests broke out worldwide. The first bombs fell on Baghdad on March 20, 2003; the regime collapsed and Baghdad fell on April 9. On May 1, beneath a “Mission Accomplished” banner, Bush announced that major combat operations had ended. Insurgency (2003–2006). No weapons of mass destruction were found. An insurgency grew; revelations of prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib damaged the U.S. cause, and groups such as al-Qaeda in Iraq bombed civilians. Saddam Hussein was captured in December 2003 and executed in 2006. Surge and withdrawal (2007–2011). In 2007, 27,000 additional U.S. troops under General David Petraeus used new counterinsurgency strategies, and with Sunni cooperation pacified many cities. After Iraq’s government approved a U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement in December 2008, U.S. combat forces withdrew from Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009, and the last combat forces left the country on December 18, 2011. The fall of Baghdad (April 2003): a quick conventional victory that gave way to occupation. The failure to find WMD: undermined the war’s justification. The surge (2007): reduced violence and enabled withdrawal. Saddam Hussein’s regime was destroyed, but violence and instability continued after American forces left. The war deepened distrust of government claims, and became a central issue in the 2004 and 2008 elections; Barack Obama’s early opposition to it helped him win the presidency. The Iraq War became a cautionary tale about preventive war, faulty intelligence, and the difficulty of occupation. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9hoe43sI758 2003 Invasion of Iraq (Full Documentary) | Animated History The Armchair Historian 31:42 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWICnxeVLp4 The Iraq War Explained Mr. Beat 29:43 2026-10-22

title: Korean War
subtitle: The first major armed conflict of the Cold War, 1950–1953
summary: On June 25, 1950, communist North Korea invaded South Korea. Under a United Nations mandate, the United States led a multinational force to defend the South. After dramatic swings (a near-collapse, the landing at Inchon, a drive to the Chinese border, and a massive Chinese intervention), the war settled into a bloody stalemate near the 38th parallel. An armistice in July 1953 ended the fighting but left Korea divided. More than 30,000 Americans and millions of Koreans died.
thumbAlt: U.S. Marines climbing a seawall during the Inchon landing
aliases: Forgotten War Inchon 38th parallel MacArthur’s dismissal
themeText: War and the military The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Korean Peninsula Dates June 25, 1950 – July 27, 1953 (armistice) Sides South Korea, the United States, and UN forces vs. North Korea and China, backed by the Soviet Union U.S. commander General Douglas MacArthur, until President Truman dismissed him in April 1951 U.S. deaths More than 30,000 Result Armistice near the 38th parallel; Korea remains divided South Korea (the Republic of Korea), led by Syngman Rhee, fought with the United States and forces from other UN member states. North Korea (the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea), led by Kim Il Sung, was joined in late 1950 by hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops and backed by the Soviet Union. At the end of World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union divided Korea at the 38th parallel to accept the surrender of Japanese forces. The Soviets backed a communist government in the North; the United States backed Rhee in the South. Each government claimed the whole peninsula, and armed clashes were frequent. American troops withdrew from the South in the late 1940s, and U.S. officials did not count Korea as vital to their defense strategy. In the spring of 1950 Stalin reluctantly endorsed Kim Il Sung’s plan to unify Korea by force. Invasion (June–September 1950). North Korea’s surprise attack captured Seoul on June 28 and nearly overran the peninsula. The UN called on members to help South Korea, and President Harry S. Truman committed American forces under General Douglas MacArthur. Inchon and the drive north (September–November 1950). UN troops landed at Inchon, near Seoul, and retook the capital on September 28. They crossed the 38th parallel on October 1 and on October 26 reached the Yalu River, Korea’s border with China. Chinese intervention (November 1950–1951). About 300,000 Chinese troops struck the UN forces and drove them back across the 38th parallel; Seoul fell again in January 1951. The UN forces regrouped, and the war became a stalemate. MacArthur sought authorization to use nuclear weapons against North Korea and China and publicly denounced Truman when refused; Truman dismissed him in April 1951. Stalemate and armistice (1951–1953). Cease-fire talks began in mid-1951 and dragged on for two years amid continued fighting. After Dwight D. Eisenhower’s election and Stalin’s death in March 1953, an armistice was signed on July 27, 1953. The Inchon landing (September 1950): reversed the North Korean invasion. Chinese entry (late 1950): turned a near-victory into a long, bloody stalemate. MacArthur’s dismissal (April 1951): affirmed civilian control of the military and the decision to keep the war limited. The armistice left an uneasy truce near the 38th parallel, crystallizing a division between North and South that persists today. In 1953 the United States signed a mutual security treaty with South Korea. The Korean War globalized the Cold War and spurred a massive American military buildup that began the nuclear arms race in earnest. It made South Korea and Japan key American allies. At home, the stalemated war contributed to Truman’s unpopularity. Because it ended without clear victory so soon after World War II, many Americans came to call it “the forgotten war.” Korea was the first “hot” war of the Cold War, a limited war fought to contain communism without triggering a wider conflict with the Soviet Union or China. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yxaegqvl4aE The Korean War (1950–53) Simple History 4:31 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CoZexC7M4hM The Korean War 1950-53 (4K Documentary) Real Time History 48:06 2026-10-22

title: The Mexican-American War
subtitle: The United States conquers half of Mexico, 1846–1848
summary: Within a year of annexing Texas, the United States went to war with Mexico over a disputed border and President James K. Polk’s ambition to acquire California and the Southwest. American armies occupied New Mexico, California, and northern Mexico, landed at Veracruz, and captured Mexico City in September 1847. In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico gave up more than 525,000 square miles, the National Archives says 55 percent of its territory. Many Americans opposed the war as an aggression, and the victory immediately reopened the question of whether slavery would spread into the new lands, pushing the country toward civil war.
location: Texas, northern Mexico, New Mexico, California, and central Mexico
thumbAlt: Carl Nebel’s print of General Winfield Scott’s entry into Mexico City
aliases: U.S.-Mexican War Mexican War Mr. Polk’s War Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Mexican Cession Wilmot Proviso Nicholas Trist
themeText: War and the military Territorial expansion Latino history Slavery and emancipation Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Texas, northern Mexico, New Mexico, California, and central Mexico Declared May 13, 1846 Commanders Zachary Taylor, Stephen Watts Kearny, Winfield Scott (U.S.); Antonio López de Santa Anna (Mexico) Mexico City taken September 14, 1847 (Miller Center) Treaty Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed February 2, 1848; ratified by the Senate March 10, 1848 Territory ceded More than 525,000 square miles: California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, most of Arizona and Colorado, parts of Oklahoma, Kansas, and Wyoming U.S. deaths More than 13,000, of whom 2,053 died from combat (Miller Center); Mexican casualties nearly 50,000 The United States, under President James K. Polk, fought Mexico, whose government changed hands several times during the war. Mexican civilians and the Native nations of the borderlands, above all the Comanche, who had long raided northern Mexico, were caught up in the war, and the American Yawp sees the war partly as the culmination of that violence. Texas won its independence from Mexico in 1836. Mexico had invited American settlers into Texas in the 1820s, but they largely ignored its ban on slavery and its requirement that newcomers become Catholic. Mexico never recognized the new republic. For nearly a decade the United States hesitated to annex Texas, because Mexico threatened war and Northerners opposed adding a slave state. President John Tyler’s annexation treaty was defeated in the Senate in June 1844, but with the support of President-elect Polk, who had won on a platform of expansion, Congress passed a joint resolution for annexation on March 1, 1845. Texas accepted on July 4 and was admitted as a state on December 29, 1845. The sources date Mexico’s break in diplomatic relations differently: the State Department links it to the annexation treaty of April 1844, while Polk told Congress that relations were suspended in March 1845. Mexico called annexation “an act of aggression, the most unjust which can be found recorded in the annals of modern history.” The two countries also disagreed about Texas’s border. Mexico drew the border at the Nueces River, while Texans claimed the Rio Grande, roughly 150 miles farther west. The American Yawp notes that neither claim was realistic, because the strip between them was actually controlled by Native Americans. Polk wanted more than Texas. By the end of his term he meant for the United States to stretch from coast to coast, in possession of Oregon and California. The road to war (1845–1846). In July 1845 Polk sent General Zachary Taylor’s army into Texas. The State Department says he was ordered into the disputed lands, while the Yawp places his 4,000 men at Corpus Christi, just northeast of the Nueces. In November Polk sent John Slidell to Mexico with an offer to buy the disputed border land along with New Mexico and California. The Mexican government, under pressure from opponents who had seized on the Texas question, refused to receive him, and a military revolt then brought General Paredes to power. The Yawp calls the mission an “empty gesture” to satisfy those who insisted on diplomacy before war. On January 13, 1846, Polk ordered Taylor to the Rio Grande. On April 24 Mexican cavalry attacked a detachment of Taylor’s troops north of the river and killed eleven Americans. Polk told Congress on May 11 that Mexico “has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil.” Congress declared war on May 13. Only a few members, notably John Quincy Adams and John C. Calhoun, voted against it, and Congress called for 50,000 volunteers. Northern Mexico and the West (1846–1847). Taylor won at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma and took Monterrey in September 1846. General Stephen Watts Kearny marched from Fort Leavenworth and occupied Santa Fe on August 18, 1846. Part of his force went on to California, where American settlers under John C. Frémont had already declared an independent “Bear Flag” republic. Polk allowed the exiled General Antonio López de Santa Anna to return to Mexico after he promised to make peace for $30 million. Instead, Santa Anna took command of the Mexican army and became president. He attacked Taylor at Buena Vista on February 22, 1847, and was beaten. The road to Mexico City (1847). General Winfield Scott landed and captured the port of Veracruz in March 1847, then fought his way two hundred miles inland. The Miller Center notes that his army was outnumbered and cut off from its supply bases, and European observers predicted disaster. Scott’s army held Mexico City by September 14, 1847. Scott’s men occupied the capital for more than four months while the two governments negotiated. Peace (1847–1848). Polk sent Nicholas Trist, chief clerk of the State Department, to negotiate. Worried that Trist would not press hard enough and that he had grown close to Scott, a Whig presidential hopeful, Polk recalled him in October 1847. Some expansionist Democrats were now calling for the annexation of “All Mexico.” Trist ignored the recall. “I decided today at noon to attempt to make a treaty; the decision is altogether my own,” he wrote to his wife on December 4. He negotiated with Mexican commissioners Luis Gonzaga Cuevas, Bernardo Couto, and Miguel Atristain, and the treaty was signed on February 2, 1848. The National Archives places the signing at Guadalupe Hidalgo, where the Mexican government had fled, while the State Department says Mexico City. The march to the Rio Grande (January 1846): Polk’s order sent Taylor into the land both nations claimed, which made a clash almost certain. Buena Vista (February 1847): Taylor’s victory over Santa Anna’s much larger army made him a Whig hero and a future president. Scott’s landing at Veracruz (March 1847): the amphibious landing opened the road to the Mexican capital. The fall of Mexico City (September 1847): led the Mexican government to negotiate. Under the treaty, Mexico gave up all claims to Texas, recognized the Rio Grande as the border, and ceded the land that became California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, most of Arizona and Colorado, and parts of Oklahoma, Kansas, and Wyoming. The United States paid $15 million and took over debts the Mexican government owed to American citizens. Mexicans living in the ceded lands could move to Mexico or stay. Those who stayed and did not choose within a year to keep Mexican citizenship would become U.S. citizens. The sources describe the size of Mexico’s loss differently: the National Archives says 55 percent of its territory, the American Yawp roughly half, and the Miller Center over one-third. They also disagree on the Senate vote on March 10, 1848, which the National Archives gives as 34 to 14 and the Miller Center as 38 to 14. According to the Miller Center, half of the no votes came from Democrats who wanted more Mexican land and half from Whigs who wanted none. The Senate struck out Article X, which had guaranteed Mexican land grants. The war was costly. More than 13,000 Americans died, but only 2,053 from combat, and the rest died of disease. Mexico suffered nearly 50,000 casualties. The American Yawp writes that disease killed seven times as many American soldiers as combat; the Miller Center’s figures suggest a ratio closer to five to one. Harsh discipline and clashes with civilians led many volunteers to desert. The war was the first covered by large numbers of reporters, and the divided press fought over the news. At home it was bitterly controversial. Most Whigs opposed it. Abraham Lincoln, a first-term Whig congressman, condemned it as unconstitutional and challenged Polk to show him “the spot” where American blood had been shed. Ralph Waldo Emerson predicted: “We will conquer Mexico, but it will be as the man who swallows the arsenic which will bring him down in turn. Mexico will poison us.” On August 8, 1846, Representative David Wilmot proposed an amendment to a war appropriations bill that would have banned slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico. The House passed it, but the Senate did not vote before adjourning. The House passed it again in February 1847, and the Senate voted it down. The fight over the Wilmot Proviso divided Congress along sectional lines and helped lead to the Compromise of 1850 and the founding of the Republican Party. The new lands drew settlers and fortune seekers. On January 24, 1848, just before the treaty was signed, James W. Marshall found gold at John Sutter’s sawmill at Coloma, setting off the California Gold Rush. Mexicans in the ceded territories, stripped of the land-grant guarantees of Article X, faced competition for land and abuse alongside Native Americans. The war made Zachary Taylor president and trained many of the Civil War’s commanders. With the Gadsden Purchase, which the National Archives dates to 1853 and the Yawp to 1854, it set the southern border of the present-day United States. The Mexican-American War made the United States a continental nation at the cost of half of Mexico. It also made the expansion of slavery the question that would tear the Union apart. Mexico has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil. James K. Polk message to Congress, May 11, 1846 We will conquer Mexico, but it will be as the man who swallows the arsenic which will bring him down in turn. Mexico will poison us. Ralph Waldo Emerson at the start of the war I decided today at noon to attempt to make a treaty; the decision is altogether my own. title: The Spanish-American War
subtitle: A short war that made the United States an overseas empire, 1898
summary: In 1898 the United States went to war with Spain over Cuba, where revolutionaries had been fighting for independence since 1895. In less than four months, U.S. forces destroyed Spanish fleets at Manila Bay and Santiago and defeated Spanish garrisons in Cuba. In the peace treaty, Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States, which also annexed Hawaii during the war. Victory made the United States a colonial power, and led directly to a bloody war against Filipino independence fighters.
location: Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and Guam
thumbAlt: Theodore Roosevelt and the Rough Riders on San Juan Hill in 1898
aliases: Maine Rough Riders Philippine-American War
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy Territorial expansion Latino history Asian American history
text: Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and Guam War declared April 25, 1898 Spark The explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbor, February 15, 1898 Key battles Manila Bay (May 1), San Juan Heights (July 1), Santiago naval battle (July 3) Treaty of Paris December 10, 1898: Cuba independent; Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines ceded to the U.S. Aftermath Philippine-American War, 1899–1902 The United States against Spain. Cuban revolutionaries had already been fighting Spain for three years, and Filipino revolutionaries under Emilio Aguinaldo fought Spain in the Philippines; both expected independence. Since the mid-nineteenth century Cubans had tried to win independence from Spain, and a new revolution began in 1895. Americans followed the conflict closely: the instability hurt U.S. economic interests, and public outrage over brutal Spanish tactics, combined with a long-held interest in ridding the hemisphere of European colonial powers, created widespread sympathy for the Cuban revolutionaries. Toward war (February–April 1898). The battleship USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbor on February 15 under mysterious circumstances. On April 11, President William McKinley asked Congress for authority to end the fighting in Cuba. Congress’s joint resolution of April 20 recognized Cuban independence, demanded Spain’s withdrawal, and renounced any intention to annex Cuba. Spain declared war, and Congress followed on April 25. The Pacific (May 1898). On May 1, Commodore George Dewey’s squadron destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay. Cuba (June–July 1898). U.S. troops landed at Guantánamo Bay and near Santiago. On July 1 they took the San Juan Heights, the war’s most famous battle, in which Theodore Roosevelt’s volunteer “Rough Riders” and Black regular soldiers of the 24th and 25th Infantry fought. On July 3 the U.S. Navy destroyed Spain’s Caribbean squadron as it tried to escape Santiago. Peace (August–December 1898). A cease-fire was signed August 12 and the Treaty of Paris on December 10. Secretary of State John Hay called it “a splendid little war.” Manila Bay (May 1): gave the United States control of the gateway to the Philippines. San Juan Heights and Santiago (July 1–3): destroyed Spain’s ability to hold Cuba. Spain relinquished Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States. During the war the United States also annexed Hawaii, where a “Committee of Safety,” supported by the U.S. minister and Marines from the USS Boston, had overthrown Queen Liliʻuokalani in January 1893. The United States became a Pacific power and dominant in the Caribbean. Annexing the Philippines provoked intense debate at home, where anti-imperialists argued that ruling colonies betrayed American principles, or, for some, that it would bring non-white peoples into the nation. In the Philippines, fighting broke out on February 4, 1899, between U.S. forces and nationalists led by Emilio Aguinaldo who sought independence. The Philippine-American War killed over 4,200 American and over 20,000 Filipino combatants, and as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians died from violence, famine, and disease. Cuba became nominally independent but subject to U.S. intervention under the Platt Amendment (1903). The Spanish-American War marked the moment the United States became an overseas empire, raising questions about democracy, race, and power abroad that would shape the twentieth century. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CaOKfu7ZK7I The Spanish American War: Explained (Short Animated Documentary) History Matters 4:20 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qpVIvNpyM5M The Spanish-American War - Explained in 11 minutes Knowledgia 11:30 2026-10-23

title: The Vietnam War
subtitle: America’s longest war of the Cold War era, 1964–1973
summary: The Vietnam War was a long struggle over the future of Vietnam in which the United States fought to keep a non-communist South Vietnam from being reunited with the communist North. It grew out of Vietnam’s war for independence from France and the American belief that if one country fell to communism, its neighbors would follow. American involvement deepened from advisers in the 1950s to more than 500,000 troops by 1968. Unable to win, the United States withdrew under the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973, and in April 1975 North Vietnamese forces took Saigon and reunified the country. The war killed 58,220 Americans, divided American society, and shook Americans’ trust in their government.
thumbAlt: A U.S. soldier guiding a UH-1 helicopter in to land in Vietnam
aliases: Second Indochina War Gulf of Tonkin Tet Offensive My Lai Vietnamization Paris Peace Accords antiwar movement Kent State Pentagon Papers domino theory
themeText: War and the military The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency Reform and protest
text: Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia Tonkin Gulf Resolution August 7, 1964; passed the House unanimously, with only two senators voting no U.S. troops About 16,000 advisers in 1963; more than 175,000 by November 1965; 536,000 by the end of 1968 U.S. deaths 58,220 in the official casualty file Tet Offensive January 1968 Peace agreement Paris Peace Accords, signed January 27, 1973 End of the war North Vietnamese tanks entered Saigon on April 30, 1975 The United States and South Vietnam (the Republic of Vietnam), with smaller allied contingents, fought North Vietnam (the Democratic Republic of Vietnam) and the Viet Cong, communist guerrillas in the South. North Vietnam was led by Ho Chi Minh and received material support from the Soviet Union and China. The fighting spread into neighboring Laos and Cambodia. The Miller Center suggests seeing the conflict through three lenses: a civil war within the South, a war of reunification waged by the North, and, in Washington’s eyes, a front in the global struggle against communism. Vietnam had been ruled by France since the nineteenth century and was occupied by Japan during World War II. In 1945 the nationalist leader Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam’s independence, quoting the American Declaration of Independence. He had earlier asked the United States for help, and the State Department’s historians note that, despite his communist leanings, he was not at first anti-American. But France fought to restore its colony, and after the communist victory in China in 1949 the United States helped pay for the French war effort with funds, arms, and advisers. President Eisenhower explained American fears with the image of falling dominoes: if one country fell to communism, the rest would follow. On May 7, 1954, after a four-month siege, the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu fell to Ho Chi Minh’s Viet Minh forces. The Geneva Conference that followed divided Vietnam temporarily at the seventeenth parallel and called for elections in 1956 to reunite the country. The communists seemed likely to win, so the U.S.-backed leader of the South, Ngo Dinh Diem, refused to hold the vote, with American support. By 1959 the Viet Cong, aided by the North, had begun a large-scale insurgency in the South. Diem’s government was corrupt and unpopular; in November 1963 his own generals overthrew and killed him with the tacit approval of the Kennedy administration. By then about 16,000 American military advisers were serving in South Vietnam. Escalation (1964–1965). In August 1964 two American destroyers reported attacks by North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin, on August 2 and again on August 4. The first attack happened, but a National Security Agency study released in 2007 concluded that the second never did. The Maddox had been supporting secret South Vietnamese raids on the North, a fact the public did not know. Johnson presented the incidents as unprovoked aggression, and on August 7 Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, authorizing him “to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack.” Only two senators, Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening, voted no. The resolution became the legal basis for the war. On February 13, 1965, Johnson began Operation Rolling Thunder, a bombing campaign against the North, and on March 8 two battalions of Marines, 3,500 men, landed near Da Nang. By November 1965 more than 175,000 American troops were in Vietnam. The ground war (1965–1968). Under General William Westmoreland, American forces fought both the Viet Cong and the regular North Vietnamese Army. Progress was measured not by territory taken but by “body counts.” Johnson chose a “middle way,” rejecting calls to invade the North or threaten nuclear weapons for fear of drawing in China or the Soviet Union, but Hanoi was willing to absorb the bombing and keep fighting indefinitely. Officials kept announcing progress, but reporters in Saigon called the daily military briefings “the Five o’Clock Follies.” Television brought the war into American homes, making it the first “living room war.” By the end of 1968, 536,000 Americans were in Vietnam and more than 30,000 had died. Tet (1968). In January 1968 communist forces attacked more than one hundred American and South Vietnamese sites across South Vietnam, including the American embassy in Saigon. American and South Vietnamese forces threw back the Tet Offensive and inflicted heavy losses on the Viet Cong, but the attacks showed that the enemy could still strike anywhere after years of war. The gap between official optimism and reality, the “credibility gap,” became impossible to ignore. On March 31, 1968, Johnson announced that he would not seek reelection. Vietnamization (1969–1973). President Richard Nixon promised “peace with honor.” He gradually withdrew American troops while building up South Vietnam’s army, a policy called “Vietnamization,” and pursued secret talks in Paris, where Henry Kissinger met North Vietnam’s Le Duc Tho. At the same time he secretly bombed North Vietnamese bases in Cambodia, and in April 1970 he sent American and South Vietnamese forces into Cambodia. After North Vietnam’s Easter Offensive in 1972, Nixon mined the North’s harbors and launched heavy bombing. Kissinger and Le Duc Tho reached an agreement in October, but South Vietnam’s President Nguyen Van Thieu rejected it, and in December Nixon ordered the “Christmas Bombing” of the North. The Paris Peace Accords were signed on January 27, 1973, allowing the United States to withdraw and bring its prisoners of war home. The fall of Saigon (1975). Neither Vietnamese side honored the agreement, and the war went on. Congress was unwilling to send American forces back, and the Watergate scandal weakened Nixon. In March 1975 North Vietnam launched a major offensive, and on April 30 its tanks rolled through the gates of the Presidential Palace in Saigon. Vietnam was united under a communist government. Dien Bien Phu (1954): the French defeat led to the partition of Vietnam and deepening American involvement. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964): gave Johnson a free hand to escalate the war. The Tet Offensive (1968): a military setback for the communists but a political turning point that turned many Americans against the war. Johnson’s withdrawal from the 1968 race: marked the end of escalation. The Paris Peace Accords (1973): ended direct American participation. North Vietnam won. After the American withdrawal in 1973, the war continued until North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on April 30, 1975, and Vietnam was reunited under a communist government. For the world’s greatest military power, the American Yawp observes, it was a stunning failure. The war tore American society apart. As the draft took young men to Vietnam, protesters burned draft cards, occupied buildings, and filled the streets; by 1967 antiwar demonstrations drew hundreds of thousands. Revelations deepened the anger. In 1969 the journalist Seymour Hersh reported that American soldiers had massacred hundreds of civilians at the village of My Lai. When Nixon sent troops into Cambodia in 1970, campus protests erupted. Police and National Guard troops killed six students, four of them at Kent State University in Ohio on May 4 and two at Jackson State in Mississippi. In 1971 the Pentagon Papers, a secret Defense Department history leaked to the press, showed how presidents from Truman to Johnson had misled the public about the war. Many other Americans, however, still regarded the war as just and resented the protesters, and Nixon appealed to this “silent majority.” The war also drained government finances and cut short the promise of Johnson’s Great Society. Congress tried to rein in presidential war-making. It repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in 1971, and in 1973 it passed the War Powers Resolution, which limited the president’s power to wage war without congressional consent. Above all, the war, together with Watergate, left many Americans deeply distrustful of their government and its role in the world. 58,220 U.S. military deaths are recorded in the Defense Department’s casualty file (the American Yawp rounds this to nearly 60,000). The Vietnam War was a defeat for American Cold War policy and a turning point in American history. It divided a generation, undermined faith in government, and made Americans wary of foreign wars for decades. I can’t get out, I can’t finish it with what I have got. So what the hell do I do? title: War in Afghanistan
subtitle: America’s longest war, 2001–2021
summary: After the September 11 attacks, the United States invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda and topple the Taliban government that sheltered it. Kabul fell within weeks, but Osama bin Laden escaped, and the Taliban regrouped. For twenty years American and NATO forces fought an insurgency while trying to build a stable Afghan government. U.S. forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011. When the last American troops withdrew hastily in August 2021, the Taliban immediately retook the country. It was the longest war in American history.
location: Afghanistan and the Pakistan border region
thumbAlt: U.S. soldiers on horseback in Afghanistan in 2001

text: Afghanistan and the Pakistan border region Began October 7, 2001 (Operation Enduring Freedom) Kabul taken November 13, 2001 Surge 2009: 17,000 additional U.S. troops Bin Laden killed May 2011, in a raid in Pakistan Withdrawal August 2021; the Taliban returned to power The United States and NATO allies, with the Afghan Northern Alliance and later the new Afghan government, fought the Taliban and al-Qaeda. During the 1980s the United States armed the Mujahideen resisting the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; Osama bin Laden also fought with them. After the Soviets withdrew in 1989, civil war followed, and the Taliban took power in 1996 and sheltered al-Qaeda. Invasion (2001). On October 7, 2001, U.S. air and missile strikes hit targets across Afghanistan, and Special Forces joined anti-Taliban Northern Alliance fighters. Major cities fell quickly, and Kabul fell on November 13. Bin Laden and al-Qaeda fighters escaped into the mountains along the Pakistani border. Nation-building and insurgency (2002–2008). The mission shifted to building a democratically elected Afghan government. With U.S. attention focused on Iraq, the Taliban reemerged by 2006, as the Afghan government proved corrupt and unable to provide security. Surge and bin Laden (2009–2014). President Obama sent 17,000 more troops in 2009 to “disrupt, dismantle, and defeat” al-Qaeda and the Taliban. In May 2011 Navy SEALs killed bin Laden in Pakistan. The United States and NATO began a phased withdrawal of combat troops. Withdrawal (2021). U.S. money and troops continued to prop up the Afghan government until American forces withdrew in August 2021. The fall of Kabul (November 2001): toppled the Taliban but let al-Qaeda’s leaders escape. The shift to Iraq (2003): drew U.S. resources away as the Taliban regrouped. Bin Laden’s death (2011): fulfilled a central goal and opened the way to drawdown. The Taliban took over the country immediately after U.S. forces left in August 2021, outlasting a twenty-year American occupation. The war’s end, with the Taliban back in power, raised hard questions about the limits of military power and nation-building. Afghanistan, America’s longest war, showed both the reach of U.S. military power and its limits in remaking another society. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2sueJoTVqxw How the US created a disaster in Afghanistan Vox 7:52 2026-10-23

title: The War of 1812
subtitle: The “second war of independence” against Britain, 1812–1815
summary: Caught between Britain and France in the Napoleonic Wars, the United States declared war on Britain on June 18, 1812, the first time it had formally declared war. Americans went to war over British seizures of their ships and sailors, and over western expansion and British support for Native resistance. American invasions of Canada failed, and British troops burned Washington, D.C. The Treaty of Ghent, signed on December 24, 1814, restored the prewar situation. Americans nonetheless remembered the war as a “Second War of Independence,” while for Native nations east of the Mississippi it was a decisive defeat.

aliases: Second War of Independence Mr. Madison’s War Treaty of Ghent Burning of Washington Battle of New Orleans Fort McHenry Old Ironsides Hartford Convention
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy Indigenous history Territorial expansion
text: Declared June 18, 1812, after Madison’s request of June 1 Ended Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814; ratified in February 1815 U.S. Army in 1812 About 6,700 men, against a British army of over 240,000 worldwide U.S. deaths About 15,000 Famous moments Burning of Washington (August 24, 1814); defense of Fort McHenry (September 1814); Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815) Terms Status quo ante bellum, “the way things were before the war” The United States fought Great Britain and its Canadian colonists. Many Native nations, above all the confederacy of the Shawnee leader Tecumseh, fought alongside the British in the hope of defending their lands. In the Southeast a civil war within the Creek Nation became part of the wider conflict. At New Orleans, Andrew Jackson’s army included frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, Free Men of Color, Choctaw warriors and the privateers of Jean Lafitte. Since 1793 Britain and France had been at war, and both tried to choke each other’s trade. In 1806 France banned neutral trade with Britain, and in 1807 Britain banned trade between France, its allies and the Americas. Britain also stopped American ships to search for deserters and “impressed” American sailors into the Royal Navy. Jefferson’s Embargo of 1807 closed American ports to foreign trade and plunged the country into depression without changing British policy. In the West, Americans blamed Britain for arming Native nations resisting settlement, and many who wanted war saw British Canada and Spanish Florida as possible prizes. President James Madison asked Congress for a declaration of war on June 1, 1812, and, pushed by the young “war hawks,” Congress declared it on June 18. Ironically, Britain was already repealing its trade restrictions; the news crossed the Atlantic too slowly to stop the fighting. Failed invasions (1812–1813). The American plan was to seize Canada as a bargaining chip. By the end of 1812 American forces had been routed at Queenston Heights, turned back from Québec, and had surrendered Detroit. In 1813 Oliver Hazard Perry won control of Lake Erie in September, and in October Harrison’s army defeated the British and Tecumseh’s warriors at the Battle of the Thames, where Tecumseh was killed. The war at sea. The small U.S. Navy won early single-ship battles. When the Chesapeake was lost in 1813, its dying captain James Lawrence gave the rallying cry “Don’t give up the ship!”, and the Constitution earned the name “Old Ironsides” when cannonballs seemed to bounce off its hull. The Creek War (1813–1814). A war among the Creeks pitted the Red Sticks, influenced by Tecumseh, against those who sought accommodation. Andrew Jackson defeated the Red Sticks at Horseshoe Bend on March 27, 1814, and in the Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the whole Creek Nation, even his own allies, to cede nearly 23 million acres. Britain strikes back (1814–1815). Napoleon’s first exile in 1814 freed British troops for America. On August 24, 1814, they burned the public buildings of Washington, including the White House. Baltimore held in September: militia stopped the land attack at North Point, and Fort McHenry withstood the British fleet, inspiring Francis Scott Key’s “Star-Spangled Banner.” An American victory on Lake Champlain stopped another invasion from Canada. On January 8, 1815, Jackson’s army crushed a British assault below New Orleans; about 2,000 of 3,000 attacking British soldiers became casualties in less than thirty minutes. Lake Erie and the Thames (1813): secured the Northwest for the United States and destroyed Tecumseh’s confederacy. Horseshoe Bend (1814): broke Red Stick power and forced huge Creek land cessions. Baltimore and Lake Champlain (1814): stopped Britain’s major offensives; by 1814, the State Department’s historians write, “neither side could claim a clear victory.” Under the mediation of the Russian tsar, negotiators met at Ghent in the summer of 1814 and signed a treaty on Christmas Eve. It restored the prewar boundaries, set up a commission for border disputes, and provided for peace with the Native nations. It said nothing about impressment; Britain had already stopped its trade restrictions. The State Department concludes that “the real causes of the war of 1812, were not merely commerce and neutral rights, but also western expansion, relations with American Indians, and territorial control of North America.” Americans emerged with a surge of nationalism and new heroes, above all Andrew Jackson. The war was followed by the “Era of Good Feelings,” and the Federalist Party, which had opposed the war and met at the Hartford Convention in 1814, collapsed. The Battlefield Trust calls Native Americans “the worst losers of the war”: Britain abandoned their hope for a recognized Native nation in the peace talks, and without British arms they lost the ability to defend their lands. Canada gained a proud military heritage, and relations between Britain and the United States generally improved. The War of 1812 confirmed American independence and launched Andrew Jackson’s career, but it was a disaster for the Native nations east of the Mississippi and opened their lands to rapid American expansion. Was New Orleans pointless? The Battle of New Orleans was fought two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent was signed, because the news had not yet crossed the Atlantic. The Battlefield Trust’s overview calls it “a stunning but ultimately pointless victory.” The Trust’s own page on the battle disagrees: the treaty said fighting would stop only when both governments ratified it, so the battle “was, indeed, justified.” Small disagreements in the sources The Battlefield Trust’s overview says Madison ratified the treaty on February 18, 1815, while its New Orleans page says it was ratified by Congress on February 16. The overview describes a 25-hour bombardment of Fort McHenry; the American Yawp says twenty-seven hours. A Yawp caption even dates the burning of Washington to 1813, though its own text gives August 24, 1814. Tell the men to fire faster! Don’t give up the ship! James Lawrence Captain of the USS Chesapeake, June 1, 1813 We should have to fight hereafter not for ‘free Trade and sailors rights,’ not for the Conquest of the Canadas, but for our national existence. title: World War I
subtitle: The United States enters the Great War, 1917–1918
summary: The United States stayed neutral for nearly three years after war broke out in Europe in 1914, though its trade and loans flowed mostly to Britain and France. Germany’s return to unrestricted submarine warfare and its secret offer of an alliance with Mexico led President Woodrow Wilson to ask Congress for war in April 1917, to make the world “safe for democracy.” About two million American soldiers joined the Allied counteroffensives of 1918 that forced Germany to accept an armistice. More than 100,000 Americans died, many of them from influenza. Wilson’s plan for a lasting peace built on his Fourteen Points and a League of Nations failed in the U.S. Senate.

text: Western Front in France and Belgium; the Atlantic; the home front U.S. declaration of war Senate April 4, House April 6, 1917; war on Austria-Hungary December 7, 1917 Draft Selective Service Act, approved by Congress May 18, 1917 Served More than 4.7 million Americans in all branches; about 2 million in the American Expeditionary Forces in France U.S. military deaths Over 100,000, about 53,000 in battle and more from disease (American Yawp) Armistice November 11, 1918 Peace Treaty of Versailles, signed June 1919; defeated in the Senate 49 to 35 in March 1920 The Allies, Britain, France, Russia (until it left the war), Italy, and from 1917 the United States, fought the Central Powers led by Germany and Austria-Hungary. In the American forces, Black soldiers served in segregated units, mostly as laborers. Women served as Army telephone operators, Navy yeomen, Marines, and about 25,000 nurses, and millions more volunteered at home. The war began in the summer of 1914 after a Serbian nationalist assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. Within weeks the alliances of Europe pulled Germany, Russia, France, and Britain into the conflict. President Wilson declared American neutrality at once and asked Americans to be neutral “in fact as well as in name.” But neutrality was hard to keep. By 1914 the United States produced about a third of the world’s manufactured goods, and its trade went overwhelmingly to the Allies. American munitions shipments to Britain and France rose from about $6 million in 1914 to almost $500 million in 1917, and American bankers lent the Allies more than $2 billion. German submarines answered the British blockade by attacking ships. On May 7, 1915, a U-boat sank the British liner Lusitania. The sources count the American dead differently: the National Archives says 128, the Miller Center 120, and the State Department gives 131 for the Lusitania and the Arabic together. After the sinking of the French ship Sussex in March 1916, Wilson threatened to break relations, and Germany promised on May 4 not to attack passenger ships and to let crews abandon merchant ships before an attack. Wilson won reelection in 1916 on the slogan “He kept us out of war.” The road to war (January–April 1917). In January 1917 the German navy persuaded the Kaiser that unrestricted submarine warfare could defeat Britain within five months. Chancellor Bethmann-Hollweg warned that it would bring the United States into the war, and he was overruled. On January 31 Germany announced that its submarines would attack all ships in the war zones from the next day. Wilson broke off diplomatic relations on February 3. On January 19, British intelligence had intercepted a telegram from German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann. In the event of war with the United States, it offered Mexico an alliance and “an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.” Britain gave it to Wilson on February 24, and the American press published it on March 1. The Mexican government declined the offer. On April 2 Wilson asked Congress to declare war, saying “the world must be made safe for democracy.” The Senate voted on April 4 and the House two days later. The State Department notes that historians still debate Wilson’s precise reasons for choosing war. Mobilization (1917–1918). The nation entered the war with a small and unprepared army. Congress passed the Selective Service Act on May 18, 1917. Unlike the Civil War draft, it avoided the unpopular bonuses and substitutes, and it was received without major objection. The government took over the railroads, launched shipbuilding and aircraft programs, introduced daylight saving time, and paid for the war with a new income tax and Liberty Bonds. Wilson created the Committee on Public Information under George Creel to promote the war. The Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 outlawed criticism of the government and the war, critics were imprisoned, and immigrants, unions, and radicals became targets. W. E. B. Du Bois and other Black leaders supported the war in the hope that service would win full citizenship, but the War Department relegated most Black soldiers to segregated labor units. The war at sea and in France (1917–1918). German submarines had sunk more than a thousand ships by the time the United States entered the war. American escorts and a convoy system sharply reduced the losses. After the collapse of the tsarist regime and the Bolshevik seizure of power in November 1917, Russia made a separate peace, and Germany moved hundreds of thousands of troops west. Its five great spring offensives of 1918 all failed by mid-July. From August 8, the American Expeditionary Forces joined British and French counteroffensives that pushed the German lines back across France. Germany’s general Erich Ludendorff called the opening day “the black day of the German army.” The Kaiser abdicated, and Germany’s new government accepted an armistice on November 11, 1918. Unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram (1917): brought the United States into the war. The convoy system (1917): American naval escorts helped defeat the U-boat threat just as American troops began to arrive. The failure of Germany’s 1918 spring offensives and the Allied counteroffensives from August 8: made German defeat inevitable. The Allies won. On January 8, 1918, Wilson had presented his Fourteen Points to Congress, prepared with the help of a group of experts called The Inquiry. Five of the points stated general principles: “open covenants of peace, openly arrived at,” freedom of the seas, free trade, reduced armaments, and a fair adjustment of colonial claims. Eight dealt with specific territories, and the last proposed a “general association of nations” to guarantee the independence of “great and small states alike.” The sources describe his language differently. The National Archives credits the speech with the promise of “self-determination,” while the Miller Center notes that Wilson did not use that phrase in the address itself and only adopted it later. French Prime Minister Clemenceau scoffed that “the good Lord only had ten.” Wilson became the first president to travel abroad in office for the Paris Peace Conference. Most of the Fourteen Points were dropped by Britain, France, and Italy, which wanted to punish Germany and recover what they had lost. But the Covenant of the League of Nations became Part I of the Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919. At home, Senate Republicans led by Henry Cabot Lodge feared the League would commit the United States to Europe’s quarrels and limit its ability to defend its own interests. Wilson took his case to the people on a speaking tour in September 1919 but collapsed and then suffered a massive stroke. In March 1920 the Senate defeated the treaty and Covenant 49 to 35, and the United States never joined the League. By the end of the war more than 4.7 million Americans had served. The United States lost over 100,000 men, about 53,000 in battle and even more from disease, a small number compared with Europe’s losses. France lost almost a million and a half soldiers and Germany even more. An influenza pandemic, which appeared in Haskell County, Kansas, in the spring of 1918 and soon hit nearby Camp Funston, spread through training camps and troopships and killed an estimated fifty million people worldwide. During the war more American soldiers died of influenza than in combat, and almost half a million were hospitalized with it. The war remade the map. The German, Russian, Austro-Hungarian, and Ottoman empires fell, new nations appeared in Europe, and the former Ottoman lands in the Middle East were divided into British and French mandates. At home, the government’s wartime powers over the economy prefigured the national security state of the Second World War. Fear of radicals after the Russian Revolution fed a Red Scare. Wartime labor shortages had drawn Black Southerners north in the Great Migration, and in the “Red Summer” of 1919 white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods in at least twenty-five cities, including Chicago and Washington. Black residents defended their homes, often with force. “We return. We return from fighting. We return fighting,” Du Bois wrote. “Make way for Democracy!” World War I showed the United States to be a world power, but the nation’s rejection of the League of Nations signaled a retreat from the international leadership Wilson had wanted. The State Department notes that most historians believe the League worked much less effectively without the United States. The world must be made safe for democracy. title: World War II
subtitle: The United States in the global war, 1941–1945
summary: World War II was the deadliest and most destructive war in human history: perhaps eighty million people died. The United States entered after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, and fought alongside Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and other Allies against Germany, Italy, and Japan. The Soviet Union bore the heaviest burden of the war against Germany and broke Hitler’s army, while American factories armed the Allies and American forces fought in North Africa, Italy, and France and across the Pacific. The war ended with Germany’s surrender in May 1945 and Japan’s in August, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It left the United States the world’s leading economic and military power.

thumbAlt: Japan’s foreign minister signing the instrument of surrender aboard USS Missouri

themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency Economy and finance Civil rights and citizenship Asian American history Women's history
text: Europe, North Africa, the Pacific and Asia, the Atlantic; the home front U.S. entry December 8, 1941, declaration of war on Japan; within a week the United States was at war with all the Axis powers Allies United States, Britain, Soviet Union, China, and others Americans in uniform Almost 18 million; more than 10 million were drafted U.S. military deaths 407,316 killed and 671,278 wounded (National WWII Museum casualty table) Soviet losses About 24 to 25 million soldiers and civilians Victory in Europe Germany surrendered May 8, 1945 Japan’s surrender Announced August 15; signed September 2, 1945, aboard the USS Missouri The Allies were led by the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and China, the nations Roosevelt called the “Four Policemen.” They fought the Axis powers of Germany, Italy, and Japan, which had linked themselves in the Tripartite Pact of September 1940. Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin, the “Big Three,” coordinated strategy at Tehran in 1943 and Yalta in February 1945; Harry S. Truman, Stalin, and Churchill (replaced partway through by Clement Attlee) met at Potsdam in July 1945. Almost eighteen million Americans served, more than ten million of them draftees. They included about 900,000 African Americans by the National WWII Museum’s count (the American Yawp says more than a million), mostly in segregated units; 33,000 Japanese Americans, many of whose families were incarcerated at home; and more than 350,000 women in the women’s branches and nurse corps. For Japan, the war began a decade before Pearl Harbor. In September 1931 an explosion on a Japanese-owned railway in Manchuria, most likely staged by the Japanese themselves, gave Japan’s army a pretext to seize the region. On July 7, 1937, Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China, and when its army took the Chinese capital, Nanjing, in December, it killed between 250,000 and 300,000 people. In Europe, Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. His Nazi regime crushed democracy, rearmed in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles, and sought Lebensraum, “living space,” in Eastern Europe. Germany annexed Austria in 1938 and, after Britain and France agreed to let it take Czechoslovakia’s Sudetenland, seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war two days later. Germany conquered France in the spring of 1940 and bombed British cities in the Blitz, but the Royal Air Force won the Battle of Britain. Disillusioned by the carnage of World War I, many Americans wanted to stay out. Roosevelt declared that the nation would be neutral in law but could not be “neutral in thought.” In September 1940 he traded more than fifty old destroyers to Britain for leases on bases in Newfoundland and the Caribbean. In 1941 Congress approved Lend-Lease, which let the United States “lend” war supplies to nations fighting the Axis; by the war’s end more than thirty countries had received some $50 billion in aid. On June 22, 1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union in the largest land invasion in history. In the Pacific, the United States had tried to pressure Japan to leave China. It gave credits to China, and after Japan moved into French Indochina in 1941 it imposed a full embargo on exports to Japan and froze Japanese assets. Japan’s leaders regarded the oil embargo as an act of war. On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours more than 3,500 Americans were killed or wounded, about 2,400 of them killed. “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked,” Roosevelt told Congress the next day. The Senate voted for war unanimously, with a single dissenting vote in the House, that of Jeannette Rankin of Montana. Days later Germany declared war on the United States, and the separate wars in Asia and Europe became one world war. The Atlantic and North Africa (1942–1943). German U-boats sank Allied shipping in the Atlantic, but code-breaking, convoys, sonar, and depth charges won the Battle of the Atlantic for the Allies. In November 1942 American troops landed in French Morocco, and with the British advancing from El Alamein they drove Axis forces out of Africa by 1943. Meeting at Casablanca in January 1943, Roosevelt and Churchill agreed to invade Italy next and announced that they would accept nothing less than unconditional surrender. The air war and Italy (1943–1945). American bombers struck German factories, rail yards, and oil fields by day while the British bombed cities at night. Unescorted American bombers suffered terrible losses until long-range fighters could accompany them. Allied bombing killed perhaps 400,000 German civilians. The campaign in Italy, which Churchill had called Europe’s “soft underbelly,” proved slow and bloody in mountainous terrain. Mussolini’s government fell, and a new Italian government made peace. The Eastern Front. The decisive land war in Europe was fought between Germany and the Soviet Union. After Germany’s invasion in June 1941, the Soviets moved their factories east of the Urals and defended Moscow, Leningrad, and Stalingrad. Leningrad endured a long siege by starvation, and at Stalingrad German forces and their allies suffered some 850,000 casualties. “It was the Soviet Union that broke Hitler’s army,” the American Yawp concludes. About 80 percent of all German casualties came on the Eastern Front, and roughly 25 million Soviet soldiers and civilians died in what Russians call the Great Patriotic War; the National WWII Museum estimates 24 million. At Tehran in November 1943, Stalin pressed Roosevelt and Churchill to open a second front in France to relieve the pressure on the Red Army, and Roosevelt agreed. Normandy to the Elbe (1944–1945). On June 6, 1944, American, British, and Canadian troops landed in Normandy in Operation Overlord, the largest amphibious assault in history. The night before, General Dwight D. Eisenhower drafted two statements, one for success and one for failure. Paris was liberated about two months later. Germany’s last offensive in the west, the Battle of the Bulge, failed that winter. Soviet forces reached Germany in January 1945, and the Americans crossed the Rhine in March. In late April American and Soviet troops met at the Elbe River, and Soviet forces took Berlin in early May, days after Hitler’s suicide. Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945. The Pacific (1941–1945). After Pearl Harbor, Japan took the Philippines. American and Filipino prisoners were forced on a march of some eighty miles without food or water, and about ten thousand died on the Bataan Death March. In 1942 the naval battles of the Coral Sea and Midway crippled Japan’s navy, and American forces began “island hopping,” seizing islands that could hold airfields and bypassing others. The fighting was savage. At Iwo Jima, seventeen thousand Japanese defenders inflicted almost thirty thousand casualties on seventy thousand Marines before the island fell; at Okinawa, captured in June 1945 after eighty days, tens of thousands were killed or wounded. American bombers firebombed more than sixty Japanese cities, killing about 100,000 civilians in a single raid on Tokyo in March 1945. Midway (June 1942). The carrier battle, with the earlier fight in the Coral Sea, crippled Japan’s naval operations in the Pacific. Stalingrad (1942–1943). At Stalingrad, where German forces and their allies suffered some 850,000 casualties, the Soviet victory was followed by a Soviet advance west that German counterattacks could not stop. D-Day (June 6, 1944). The Normandy landings opened the second front in Western Europe that Stalin had long demanded. The atomic bomb (August 1945). Fearing that Germany might build an atomic bomb, the United States had launched the secret Manhattan Project. The first test, Trinity, took place in New Mexico in July 1945. American officials estimated that invading Japan could cost half a million American casualties and perhaps millions of Japanese lives, numbers they later cited to justify the decision. Historians still debate the motives behind the decision, and many American officials criticized it. On August 6 a B-29, the Enola Gay, dropped a uranium bomb on Hiroshima, a city of almost 300,000. Some 70,000 people probably died from the blast, heat, and radiation, and the toll passed 100,000 by the end of 1945. On August 9 a plutonium bomb struck Nagasaki, killing about 40,000 people at once and perhaps 70,000 by January 1946 (the American Yawp gives about 80,000). The day after Nagasaki, Emperor Hirohito overruled Japan’s military leaders and offered to surrender. He announced Japan’s surrender on August 15, and on September 2, 1945, Japanese delegates signed the formal surrender aboard the USS Missouri. The Allies won. Germany was disarmed and divided into four occupation zones run by the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union, and the Allies agreed at Potsdam to try German war criminals and remake German society along democratic lines. Poland’s borders were moved westward, and several million Germans were expelled from the territories transferred to Poland and from other countries. At Yalta, Stalin had agreed to enter the war against Japan in return for southern Sakhalin, the Kurile Islands, and rights in Manchuria. As the Allies advanced, they uncovered the full scale of the Holocaust, the systematic murder of some eleven million civilians, including six million Jews. Americans had done little to help Jewish refugees before the war. In 1939 the ship St. Louis, carrying more than nine hundred Jewish refugees, was turned away, and hundreds of its passengers later died in the Holocaust. In 1944 Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau formed the War Refugee Board, which may have saved some 200,000 Jews. On June 26, 1945, fifty nations signed the charter of the United Nations in San Francisco, with a Security Council of five permanent members, each holding a veto. The home front. “Economies win wars no less than militaries,” the American Yawp observes. Government spending during the war doubled all federal spending in American history up to that time, and unemployment, a quarter of the workforce a decade earlier, virtually disappeared. Americans lived with rationing of gasoline, meat, sugar, and coffee, bought war bonds, and paid income taxes that reached a top rate of 94 percent. Millions of women took factory and office jobs. “Rosie the Riveter” became their symbol, and more than 350,000 women served in uniform, though most lost or left their jobs when the men came home. Under the Bracero Program, begun in 1942, Mexican workers came north on contracts to work on farms and railroads. Race and rights. In 1941 A. Philip Randolph threatened a march on Washington until Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802, which banned discrimination in defense industries. About a million African Americans served, mostly in segregated units. The Tuskegee Airmen flew more than 1,500 missions. Black newspapers called for a “Double V,” victory over fascism abroad and racism at home, and NAACP membership grew tenfold, to 500,000. On February 19, 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, under which more than 110,000 people of Japanese descent, 70,000 of them American citizens, were removed from their homes and confined in camps. In 1982 a congressional commission blamed “race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership,” and in 1988 the government apologized and paid reparations. A new world. The war pulled the United States out of the Depression and into an unprecedented boom. The G.I. Bill of 1944 paid for veterans’ education and helped close to four million of them buy homes, though women and Black veterans received far fewer of its benefits. The United States emerged as the world’s strongest economic and military power. But the wartime alliance with the Soviet Union soon broke down, and disputes over Eastern Europe began at Yalta and Potsdam and grew into the Cold War. About 407,000 U.S. military dead and 671,000 wounded (the National WWII Museum’s country table gives 416,800 military deaths); worldwide, estimates range from about 60 million dead (National WWII Museum) to perhaps 80 million (the American Yawp), including about 24 to 25 million in the Soviet Union and about 20 million in China. World War II was the most destructive conflict in history. It defeated fascism and Nazism through the combined efforts of the Allies; the Soviet Union, at a cost of some 24 to 25 million lives, broke the German army, while Britain and the United States fought in the west and the Pacific. It made the United States the world’s leading military and economic power and set the stage for the Cold War, the civil rights movement, and the postwar boom.
